title: The Carriage of Goods by Sea Act, 2025

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of Carriage of Goods by Sea Act, 2025
Objective
The main objectives of the Act are:
•	To replace the outdated Indian Carriage of Goods by Sea Act, 1925 with a modern legal framework.
•	To define the rights, liabilities, responsibilities, and immunities of carriers and cargo owners.
•	To align Indian maritime law with internationally accepted rules governing carriage of goods by sea.
•	To promote ease of doing business and strengthen India's maritime trade.
•	To facilitate efficient, transparent, and legally certain cargo transportation by sea.
Key Provisions
1.	Application of the Act
o	Applies to the carriage of goods by sea from any port in India to another port in India or to a foreign port under contracts covered by bills of lading or similar documents of title.
2.	Carrier's Responsibilities
o	Requires carriers to exercise due diligence to ensure that the ship is seaworthy, properly manned, equipped, and supplied, and that cargo is properly loaded, handled, stowed, carried, cared for, and discharged.
3.	Bills of Lading
o	Prescribes rules governing bills of lading, including their issuance, evidentiary value, and legal effect in contracts for the carriage of goods by sea.
4.	Rights and Liabilities
o	Clearly defines the rights, duties, liabilities, and immunities of carriers, shippers, and consignees, including circumstances in which a carrier may be exempt from liability.
5.	Limitation of Liability
o	Prescribes the circumstances under which a carrier's liability for loss or damage to cargo may be limited, subject to the provisions of the Act and the applicable rules.
6.	No Absolute Warranty
o	Clarifies that there is no implied absolute undertaking by the carrier beyond the obligations imposed under the Act and its Schedule.
7.	Applicable Rules
o	Incorporates a Schedule containing the applicable rules relating to contracts of carriage, responsibilities of carriers, and rights of cargo owners, largely reflecting internationally accepted maritime standards.
8.	Repeal of the 1925 Act
o	Repeals the Indian Carriage of Goods by Sea Act, 1925, while preserving the validity of actions and proceedings taken under the repealed law through appropriate saving provisions.

THE CARRIAGE OF GOODS BY SEA ACT, 2025
ACT NO. 19 OF 2025

[8th August, 2025.]


An Act to provide for the responsibilities, liabilities, rights and immunities attached to carriers with respect to the carriage of goods by sea and for matters connected therewith or related thereto.
WHEREAS the delegates at the International Conference on Maritime Law held at Brussels in October, 1922, agreed unanimously to recommend their respective Governments to adopt as the basis of a Convention a draft Convention for the unification of certain rules relating to bills of lading;
AND WHEREAS at a meeting held at Brussels in October, 1923, the rules contained in the said draft Convention were amended by the Committee appointed by the said Conference;
AND WHEREAS the said rules were amended by the Protocol signed at Brussels on 23rd February, 1968 and by the Protocol signed at Brussels on 21st December, 1979;
AND WHEREAS it is expedient that the said rules as so amended and as set out with modifications in the Schedule thereto should, subject to the provisions of this Act, have the force of law with a view to establishing the responsibilities, liabilities, rights and immunities attaching to carriers under bills of lading.
BE it enacted by Parliament in the Seventy-sixth Year of the Republic of India as follows:---

Precedent & Historical Rationale
●	Repeal and Overhaul of Colonial Maritime Framework: Repeals the century-old Indian Carriage of Goods by Sea Act, 1925 (26 of 1925) to replace outdated maritime transport norms with a modern statutory framework tailored for modern global trade.
●	Alignment with International Rules & Digital Trade: Harmonizes carrier liabilities, shipper duties, and immunities with updated international standards (Hague–Visby and elements of the Hamburg Rules) while introducing explicit legal recognition for electronic bills of lading and paperless shipping documentation.

●	Formulation: Introduced as the Carriage of Goods by Sea Bill, 2024 (Bill No. 112C of 2024) by the Union Minister of Ports, Shipping and Waterways, Shri Sarbananda Sonowal, to modernize trade laws and support India's maritime growth strategy.

●	Enforcement: Enforced on September 10, 2025.

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of Coastal Shipping Act, 2025
The Coastal Shipping Act, 2025 is a landmark piece of maritime legislation enacted in August 2025. It replaces the outdated Part XIV of the colonial-era Merchant Shipping Act, 1958, establishing a modern, dedicated legal framework to govern India's coastal shipping sector. 
Primary Objectives
•	Modernization & Growth: To streamline and update laws governing coastal trade, aiming to increase coastal cargo movement to 230 million metric tonnes by 2030. 
•	Self-Reliance and Maritime Security: To build a robust, citizen-owned and operated coastal fleet supporting the visions of Aatmanirbhar Bharat (Self-Reliant India) and Viksit Bharat (Developed India). 
•	Ease of Doing Business: To ease regulatory compliances, remove redundant barriers, and promote domestic participation in the maritime sector. 
•	Supply Chain Efficiency: To lower domestic logistics costs and integrate coastal shipping seamlessly with inland waterways. 
Key Provisions
1. Simplified Licensing Framework
•	Exemptions for Indian Vessels: Vessels wholly owned by Indian citizens or entities are exempted from licensing requirements, drastically reducing compliance burdens and operational delays. 
•	Regulation of Foreign Vessels: While domestic ships face fewer barriers, strategic regulatory control and mandatory licensing are retained for foreign vessels operating within Indian coastal waters. 
2. Expanded Scope of Coasting Trade
•	Unlike previous laws that narrowly defined coasting trade around cargo and passenger movement, the 2025 Act broadens the definition to include modern commercial activities such as marine exploration, offshore research, and specialized services. 
•	Covers a diverse range of watercraft, including ships, boats, sailing vessels, and mobile offshore drilling units (regardless of whether they are self-propelled). 
3. National Coastal and Inland Shipping Strategic Plan
•	Mandates the Central Government to formulate a comprehensive strategic roadmap (with biennial updates) to guide infrastructure development, route optimization, and operational efficiency across coastal and inland water networks. 
4. National Database of Coastal Shipping
•	Establishes a centralized, real-time national database to ensure data-driven governance, transparency, and accessible insights for potential investors and policymakers. 
5. Strict Enforcement and Penalties
•	Empowers the Director General of Shipping with clear regulatory oversight to issue directives concerning coastal security. 
•	Introduces strict enforcement measures—including the detention of vessels—for severe violations, such as operating without a required license, furnishing false data, or defying official instructions.

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of Bills of Lading Act, 2025
 It simplifies the law while preserving the rights and liabilities of parties involved in the carriage of goods by sea, thereby promoting legal certainty and facilitating international maritime trade.
Key Provisions
1. Transfer of Rights and Liabilities
•	Rights of Suit: The consignee named in the bill of lading and every lawful endorsee acquires all rights of suit under the contract of carriage. 
•	Liabilities: The consignee or lawful endorsee also assumes the same liabilities as if they had originally entered into the contract. 
2. Recognition of Bills of Lading
•	Evidence of Contract: A bill of lading serves as evidence of the contract for the carriage of goods by sea. 
•	Transfer of Goods: It enables the lawful transfer of ownership and possession of goods through endorsement and delivery. 
3. Government Powers
•	Implementation: The Central Government may take necessary measures for the effective implementation of the Act. 
•	Administrative Authority: Empowered to issue directions to ensure the smooth operation of the Act.

THE BILLS OF LADING ACT, 2025
ACT NO. 18 OF 2025

[24th July, 2025.]


An Act to make provisions for the transfer of rights of suit and all liabilities to the consignee named in a bill of lading and every endorsee of a bill of lading, to whom the property in the goods mentioned in the bill of lading shall pass, upon or by reason of a consignment or an endorsement, and for matters connected therewith or related thereto.
WHEREAS by the custom of merchants, a bill of lading of goods being transferable by endorsement, the property in the goods may thereby pass to the endorsee, but nevertheless all rights in respect of the contract contained in the bill of lading continue in the original shipper or owner;
AND WHEREAS it is expedient that such rights should pass with the property;
AND WHEREAS it frequently happens that the goods in respect of which bills of lading purport to be signed have not been laden on board;
AND WHEREAS it is proper that such bills of lading in the hands of a bona fide holder for value should not be questioned by the master or other person signing the same, on the ground of the goods not having been laden as aforesaid.
BE it enacted by Parliament in the Seventy-sixth Year of the Republic of India as follows:---

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of The Mussalman Wakf (Repeal) Act, 2025
Primary Provisions
1.	Repeal: *Act Repealed: The Mussalman Wakf Act, 1923 (Act 42 of 1923)
2.	Implications of Repeal:
*Retrospective Validation: All actions, proceedings, and decisions under the repealed Act are deemed valid and unaffected.
*Continuity of Obligations & Liabilities: Pre-repeal obligations, legal proceedings, and liabilities remain in force as if the repeal had not occurred.
3. Rationale for Repeal
*Obsolescence: The 1923 Act was outdated and insufficient for modern governance of waqf properties in India.
*Uniformity & Governance: Repeal ensures alignment with the Waqf Act, 1995, promoting transparency, accountability, and uniform management of waqf properties across India.
4.  Operational Impact
*Pre-Repeal Cases: Continue under the provisions of the repealed Act as if it were still in force.
*Post-Repeal Governance: The Waqf Act, 1995, becomes the sole governing legislation for waqf properties, streamlining administration and oversight.

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of Merchant Shipping Act, 2025
Act aligns Indian shipping laws with international maritime conventions, strengthens vessel safety, environmental protection, and seafarer welfare, while promoting the development of the Indian shipping industry and ensuring ease of doing business.
Key Provisions
1. Registration and Regulation of Vessels
Mandatory Registration: Indian vessels must be registered in accordance with the provisions of the Act.
Survey and Certification: Vessels are required to undergo periodic surveys, audits, and certification to ensure seaworthiness and compliance with safety standards.
2. Seafarer Welfare and Maritime Education
Seafarers' Rights: Provides for the welfare, training, certification, employment, and working conditions of seafarers.
Maritime Education: Establishes standards for maritime education and training institutions to ensure competent maritime professionals.
3. Safety and Environmental Protection
Safety Measures: Prescribes requirements for vessel safety, security, emergency preparedness, and accident prevention.
Pollution Control: Provides measures for the prevention and containment of pollution from vessels and establishes liability for environmental damage.
4. Maritime Liability and Investigation
Compensation and Liability: Lays down provisions relating to collisions, maritime claims, limitation of liability, and compensation for oil pollution damage.
Marine Casualty Investigation: Establishes procedures for investigating marine accidents, casualties, and wrecks to improve maritime safety.

Precedent & Historical Rationale
●	Overhaul & Modernization of Legacy Maritime Laws: Repeals the sprawling Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 and the colonial-era Coasting Vessels Act, 1838, replacing 561 outdated sections with 325 streamlined clauses across 15 clean parts.
●	Compliance with Global Conventions & Seafarer Welfare: Codifies Indian obligations under key International Maritime Organization (IMO) and ILO conventions—including SOLAS, MARPOL, the Nairobi Wreck Removal Convention, and the Maritime Labour Convention (MLC, 2006). It expands vessel ownership eligibility (permitting OCIs, NRIs, and bareboat charters) and introduces unified "Marine Casualty" investigation protocols.

●	Formulation: Introduced by the Union Minister of Ports, Shipping and Waterways, Shri Sarbananda Sonowal, as the Merchant Shipping Bill, 2024 (Bill No. 183C of 2024) to reduce compliance burdens, digitize ship registration, and support Maritime India Vision 2030.
●	Parliamentary Passage: Introduced in the Lok Sabha on December 10, 2024; passed by the Lok Sabha on August 6, 2025; and passed by the Rajya Sabha on August 11, 2025.
●	Presidential Assent: Received the assent of the President of India on August 18, 2025.
●	Enforcement: Enforced on April 15, 2026.

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of The Inland Vessels Act, 2021
Objective and Scope
•	Purpose: Ensures safe, economical transportation in inland waters, promoting uniformity, safety, and pollution prevention.
•	Extent: Applicable across India, with specific provisions for different vessel types.
Key Provisions
1. Registration
•	Mandatory Registration:
•	Authority: Registering authority of the State where the vessel is kept.
•	Certificate of Registration:
•	Validity: State-specific, but valid across other states without needing a fresh certificate.
•	Transfer of Registry: Possible across states with application to the new state's registering authority, requiring delivery of the old certificate and issuance of a new one.
•	Procedure (Section 19K):
1.	Application to the new state's authority with the certificate.
2.	Entry of particulars in the new register.
3.	Issuance of a fresh certificate.
•	Alterations and Updates (Section 19J): Mandatory reporting within a prescribed period for alterations, with potential for new registration or provisional updates.
•	Change of Owner/Operator Address (Section 19L): Notification required within 30 days to the registering authority, with updates in the certificate.
2. Operational Compliance
•	Prohibition Against Transfer of Ownership (Section 19M):
•	Restriction: Transfer to persons in another State or outside India requires prior State Government approval.
•	Procedure:
•	Joint report by owner and transferee within 30 days.
•	Forwarding certificate for updates.
•	Pilotage and Safety: Emphasized with significant penalties for non-compliance.
3. Offences and Penalties
| Offence | Penalty | | --- | --- | | Unauthorized Transfer of Certificate | As per Act | | Failure to Report Alterations | As per Act | | Pollution/Other Offences | Fines (e.g., ₹50,000 for pollution) and/or Imprisonment |
4. Administrative and Judicial Aspects
•	State and Central Government Roles: In rule-making, oversight, and judicial processes.
•	Judicial Trials: Conducted by or above Magistrate of the First Class.
•	Appeals (Section 19P): Against registration refusal, suspension, or cancellation to the State Government.
5. Additional Provisions
•	Suspension of Certificates (Section 19N): For unfit vessels, with notification to the original authority if different.
•	Cancellation of Registration (Section 19-0): For destroyed or permanently unfit vessels, upon owner's report and return of the certificate.
•	Reciprocity (Section 19Q): For vessels from other countries, under Central Government notification.
Repeal and Savings
•	Repeals Previous Act: With continuity for previous registrations and notifications unless inconsistent.

o	Prior to 2021, inland water transport in India was governed by the century-old Inland Vessels Act, 1917. 2.	Unlocking the Potential of National Waterways:
o	Grounded in national strategic objectives to develop low-cost, eco-friendly logistics, reduce freight costs, and promote seamless trade through India’s extensive river networks and national waterways, the legislation was enacted to create a uniform, transparent, and legally sound national regulatory regime.

•	Parliamentary Passage: Introduced in the Lok Sabha as the Inland Vessels Bill (Bill No. 99 of 2021) on July 22, 2021; passed by the Lok Sabha on July 29, 2021; and subsequently passed by the Rajya Sabha on August 2, 2021. 
•	Presidential Assent: Received formal Presidential Assent on August 11, 2021, entering the statute book as Act No. 24 of 2021. 
•	Enforcement: Brought into active operational force through phased notifications starting in February and June 2022.

meta.dc.description.abstract:
The Recycling of Ships Act, 2019 (Refined with New Context)
Overview
*Purpose: To ensure environmentally sound and safe ship recycling practices in alignment with the Hong Kong International Convention for the Safe and Environmentally Sound Recycling of Ships, 2009. 
*Governance Structure:
•	Central Government: Overall policy and rule-making.
•	National Authority: Oversight, administration, and supervision.
•	Competent Authority: Operational enforcement within designated areas/expertise.
Key Provisions
1. Regulatory and Certification Framework
•	Mandatory Certifications:
•	Ready for Recycling Certificate: For ship owners, post-verification.
•	Certificate on Inventory of Hazardous Materials: For all ships, with periodic updates (Section 8), issued or renewed for up to 5 years, with extensions possible under specific conditions (e.g., voyage completion to a survey port or Administration approval, not exceeding 3 months).
•	Definitions and Compliance: Clear definitions (e.g., Ship Recycling, Hazardous Materials) with strict compliance measures.
2. Ship Recycling and Survey Requirements
•	Survey Types for Compliance (Section 7):
•	Initial, Renewal (every 5 years), Additional (post-modifications), and Final (pre-recycling) Surveys.
•	Ship Recycling Plan: Mandatory, approved by the Competent Authority, emphasizing hazardous material removal.
3. Responsibilities and Obligations
•	Ship Owners:
•	Advance intimation of recycling intent.
•	Clearance of all port dues and residues before recycling.
•	Ship Recyclers:
•	Maintain accredited facility standards.
•	Ensure environmental protection and worker safety (aligned with the Factories Act, 1948).
•	Provide comprehensive worker insurance.
4. Operational, Safety, and Environmental Standards
•	Facility Authorization: With periodic (at least annual) audits for compliance.
•	Emergency Preparedness and Response Plans: As per the Factories Act, 1948, and environmental regulations.
5. Enforcement, Penalties, and Compensation
•	Penalty Framework:
•	Imprisonment (up to 1 year for severe offences).
•	Fines (up to ₹10 lakh).
•	Compensation for Non-Compliance or Damages: To affected parties.
6. Transparency and Reporting
•	Reporting Mechanism:
•	Statement of Completion to the Competent Authority.
•	Regular activity reports to the National Authority.
•	Public Access to Information: On approved facilities and recycling activities.
7. Miscellaneous and Transitional Provisions
•	Exemptions with Conditions: For warships and ships under 500 GT, with specific measures.
•	Rules, Regulations, and Parliamentary Oversight:
•	Central Government empowered to make rules.
•	Mandatory laying of rules before Parliament.
•	Protection for Good Faith Actions and Difficulty Removal Clause for operational challenges.
•	Repeals and Savings: Previous enactments repealed with continuity for existing notifications, rules, certificates, and registrations under this Act.

ACT NO. 49 OF 2019

[13th December, 2019.]

An Act to provide for the regulation of recycling of ships by setting certain standards and laying down the statutory mechanism for enforcement of such standards and for matters connected therewith or incidental thereto.
WHEREAS, the International Maritime Organisation adopted the Hong Kong International Convention for the Safe and Environmentally Sound Recycling of Ships, 2009 which ensures that ships, when being recycled after the end of their operational lives, do not pose any unnecessary risk to the environment and to human health and safety;
AND WHEREAS, the said Convention was developed with inputs from International Maritime Organisation Member States, Non-Governmental Organisations and in co-operation with the International Labour Organisation and the Parties to the Basel Convention on the Control of Transboundary Movements of Hazardous Wastes and their Disposal, 1989;
AND WHEREAS, the Hong Kong Convention lays down the aspects relating to design, construction, operation and preparation of ships so as to facilitate safe and environmentally sound recycling, without compromising the safety and operational efficiency of ships and the establishment of an appropriate enforcement mechanism for recycling of ships;
AND WHEREAS, the said Convention contains the provisions which are not covered in the Shipbreaking Code (Revised), 2013 notified by the Government of India to regulate the recycling of ships in India;
AND WHEREAS, the said Convention lays down the multilateral framework to be followed internationally by countries which become a party to it;
AND WHEREAS, India, being a Member-State of the International Maritime Organisation, had participated in the said Convention and expressed views for the protection of environment and human health and safety during the process of recycling of ships;
AND WHEREAS, it is considered expedient to accede to the aforesaid Convention now and to have an appropriate legislation on issues relating to the recycling of ships.
BE it enacted by Parliament in the Seventieth Year of the Republic of India as follows:--

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of The Dalmia Dadri Cement Limited (Acquisition and Transfer of Undertakings) Act, 1981

Key Provisions:
1.	Acquisition of Undertaking: 
o	Provides for the transfer and vesting of the undertakings of Dalmia Dadri Cement Limited in the Central Government. 
o	The acquisition includes all assets, rights, powers, and interests connected with the cement undertaking. 
2.	Transfer and Vesting of Assets: 
o	All properties, movable and immovable assets, licenses, contracts, records, and other rights of the company relating to the undertaking are transferred to and vested in the Central Government. 
o	Ensures continuity of operations after acquisition. 
3.	Management and Administration: 
o	Empowers the Central Government to manage and administer the acquired undertaking. 
o	Allows the Government to operate the undertaking directly or through a government-controlled entity or authority. 
4.	Transfer of Liabilities: 
o	Specifies the liabilities and obligations that are transferred to the Central Government or the acquiring authority. 
o	Provides for the settlement of claims and responsibilities arising from the undertaking. 
5.	Compensation: 
o	Provides for payment of compensation to the shareholders and other interested persons for the acquisition of the undertaking. 
o	Prescribes the procedure for determining and distributing compensation. 
6.	Protection of Employees: 
o	Provides safeguards for employees of Dalmia Dadri Cement Limited. 
o	Ensures continuity of service and preservation of employment-related benefits under the acquiring authority. 
7.	Contracts and Legal Proceedings: 
o	Provides that existing contracts, agreements, and legal proceedings relating to the undertaking continue and may be enforced by or against the Central Government or the acquiring authority.

Summary of The National Institutes of Food Technology, Entrepreneurship and Management Act, 2021
The National Institutes of Food Technology, Entrepreneurship and Management Act, 2021 (Act No. 19 of 2021) – Brief Summary
The National Institutes of Food Technology, Entrepreneurship and Management Act, 2021 was enacted to declare certain food technology institutes as Institutions of National Importance (INI) and to promote excellence in education, research, innovation, entrepreneurship, and skill development in the food processing sector. The Act came into force on 1 October 2021. 
Objectives
•	To establish world-class institutions for education and research in food technology, entrepreneurship, and management. 
•	To develop skilled professionals for the food processing industry. 
•	To promote innovation, entrepreneurship, and industry collaboration. 
•	To strengthen India's food processing sector through advanced research and technology. 
Key Provisions
•	Declares the following institutes as Institutions of National Importance: 
o	National Institute of Food Technology Entrepreneurship and Management (NIFTEM), Kundli, Haryana. 
o	Indian Institute of Food Processing Technology (IIFPT), Thanjavur, Tamil Nadu (now National Institute of Food Technology, Entrepreneurship and Management–Thanjavur). 
•	Provides for the incorporation of these institutes as autonomous statutory bodies. 
•	Establishes governance through: 
o	Board of Governors, 
o	Senate, 
o	Director, 
o	Finance Committee, 
o	Building and Works Committee, and 
o	A Central Council for coordination among the institutes. 
•	Empowers the institutes to award degrees, diplomas, and other academic distinctions. 
•	Provides for Central Government funding, maintenance of institute funds, accounts, and audits. 
•	Authorizes the Central Government to make rules and the institutes to frame Statutes and Ordinances for administration. 
Significance
•	Enhances the quality of higher education and research in food technology. 
•	Supports the growth of India's food processing industry by producing skilled manpower. 
•	Encourages innovation, startup creation, and entrepreneurship in the agri-food sector. 
•	Strengthens India's competitiveness in food processing and contributes to food security and economic development

title: The Public Examinations (Prevention of Unfair Means) Act, 2024

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of Public Examinations (Prevention of Unfair Means) Act, 2024
 Designed to prevent unfair means in public examinations conducted by various authorities under the Central Government, enhancing transparency, fairness, and credibility. It outlines offenses, punishments, and procedural safeguards to deter individuals, groups, and institutions from engaging in unfair practices for monetary or wrongful gain.
Key Provisions
1.	Definition of Unfair Means (Section 3)
•	Leakage of question papers or answer keys
•	Unauthorized access to or possession of question papers or answer sheets
•	Providing unauthorized solutions during exams
•	Tampering with answer sheets, documents, or computer systems
•	Other specified acts aimed at facilitating unfair means
2.	Offenses
•	Conspiracy for Unfair Means (Section 4)
•	Disruption to Conduct Public Examination (Section 5)
•	Other Offences (Section 6), including non-reporting of offenses by service providers
•	Using Unauthorized Premises for Exams (Section 7)
•	Offences by Service Providers and Others (Section 8)
3.	Punishments (Sections 9, 10, 11)
•	Cognizable, Non-Bailable, Non-Compoundable Offences (Section 9)
•	Imprisonment for 3-5 years & Fine up to ₹10 Lakhs for Individuals (Section 10)
•	Service Providers: Fine up to ₹1 Crore, 4-Year Ban from Exam Responsibilities (Section 10)
•	Organised Crimes: 5-10 Years Imprisonment & Fine of at least ₹1 Crore (Section 11)
4.	Procedural and Administrative Provisions
•	Members of Exam Authority as Public Servants (Section 13)
•	Protection for Actions in Good Faith (Section 14)
•	Power to Make Rules (Section 16) & Laying of Rules (Section 17)
•	Power to Remove Difficulties (Section 18)

Summary of The Marine Aids to Navigation Act, 2021
1. Governance & Key Provisions
•	Authority: Central Government oversees aids to navigation, with powers to designate, inspect, and control.
•	Director General of Aids to Navigation: Appointed for operational oversight.
2. Management of Aids to Navigation
•	General Aids: Vest in the Central Government.
•	Local Aids: Subject to Central Government inspection (Section 14) and potential control (Section 15).
•	Heritage Lighthouses: Specifically designated and protected.
3. Offences & Penalties
•	Obstruction/Damage: Penalties include imprisonment (up to 12 months) and fines (up to ₹5 lakh).
•	Non-Compliance: Fines for evasion of dues (up to 5 times payable amount) and non-compliance with directions (up to ₹1 lakh).
•	Vessel Non-Compliance: Penalties for unsafe navigation, pollution, and lack of safety appliances (fines up to ₹50,000 to ₹1 lakh, and imprisonment in some cases).
4. Financial & Regulatory Provisions
•	Marine Aids to Navigation Dues: Levied for maintenance and development.
•	Rule Making Authority: Central Government empowered to make rules for the Act’s implementation.
5. Enforcement & Jurisdiction
•	Trial & Jurisdiction: Specified courts handle offences, with cognizance only upon complaint by authorised officers.
•	Good Faith Protection: For actions taken under the Act.
Overall Purpose Ensures safe, efficient navigation through comprehensive management of aids to navigation, with clear governance, financial, and penal structures, aligning with international maritime standards.

Summary of National Sports Governance Act, 2025
The Act aims to promote transparency, accountability, ethical governance, athlete welfare, and effective dispute resolution by regulating the functioning of national sports bodies in accordance with international best practices and the Olympic and Paralympic Charters. 
Key Provisions
1. Recognition and Governance of Sports Bodies
•	National Sports Bodies: Provides for the recognition and regulation of National Olympic Committee, National Paralympic Committee, National Sports Federations, and Regional Sports Federations. 
•	Good Governance: Mandates transparency, accountability, democratic functioning, and ethical practices in sports administration. 
2. National Sports Board
•	Regulatory Authority: Establishes the National Sports Board to oversee the functioning and recognition of sports bodies. 
•	Compliance Monitoring: Ensures adherence to governance standards and statutory obligations by recognised sports organisations. 
3. Sports Dispute Resolution
•	National Sports Tribunal: Establishes a specialised tribunal for the speedy adjudication of sports-related disputes and grievances. 
•	Appeal Mechanism: Provides for appeals against decisions of the Tribunal in accordance with the Act and applicable international sports rules. 
4. Athlete Welfare and Ethical Standards
•	Sportsperson Welfare: Promotes the welfare, rights, and representation of sportspersons in sports governance. 
•	Code of Ethics: Requires recognised sports bodies to adopt codes of ethics, fair play, and conflict-of-interest policies. 

5. Government Powers and Compliance
•	Rule-Making Power: Empowers the Central Government to frame rules for implementing the provisions of the Act. 
•	Recognition and Exemptions: The Government may regulate recognition, compliance requirements, and grant exemptions where necessary in the public interest

Summary of the Coal Mines (Special Provisions) Act, 2015
Key Components
Allocation, Management, and Acquisition
Auction Process for Schedule I Mines:
•	Competitive bidding with eligibility norms.
•	Fees structure (not exceeding ₹5 crore). 
Direct Allotment to Government Entities:
•	For public sector undertakings or joint ventures.
•	Private sector participation limited to ≤26% in joint ventures. 
Designated Custodian's Role:
•	Manages unallocated or terminated mines post-auction.
•	Powers include operation, financial control, and manpower direction. 
Acquisition and Development (per The Coal Bearing Areas Act, 1957):
•	Central Government's power to acquire land/rights for coal development.
•	Compensation and procedural safeguards for affected parties.
2. Rights, Obligations, and Compliance
Prior Allottees:
•	Conditional participation in auctions with additional levy.
•	Ineligibility under specific criminal conviction criteria. 
Successful Bidders/Allottees:
•	Comprehensive rights via vesting orders.
•	Mandatory utilization of funds for coal conservation and development. 
Non-Compliance Penalties:
•	Up to 2 years imprisonment or significant fines for obstruction or non-compliance.
•	Extended liability to company officers for corporate offences. 
Mining Lease and Permit Conditions (per Mines and Minerals Act, 1957 Amendments):
•	Specification of coal mines/coal bearing areas, their location, and minimum size.
•	Other conditions for rationalized mining operations.
3. Governance, Oversight, and Judicial Framework
Central Government & Nominated Authority:
•	Oversight of auctions and allotment processes.
•	Management of auction proceeds. 
Dispute Resolution:
•	Exclusive jurisdiction of the Tribunal under the Coal Bearing Areas (Acquisition and Development) Act, 1957.
•	Limited role for civil courts; Supreme Court and High Courts retain jurisdiction. 
Regulatory Compliance (Mines and Minerals Act, 1957):
•	Terms and conditions for auction by competitive bidding.
•	Detailed mine specifications and minimum sizes for operational efficiency.
4. Financial Provisions, Protection, and Development
Financial Management:
•	Net proceeds allocation for coal sector development.
•	Priority payment to secured creditors and prior allottees. 
Protection Clause:
•	Immunity for actions taken in good faith under the Act. 
Development Alignment:
•	With The Coal Bearing Areas (Acquisition and Development) Act, 1957, for coordinated development.
•	Compliance with Mineral Concession Rules for operational standards.

Presidential Assent Date - March 30, 2015

Official Gazette Publication - March 30, 2015 (Extraordinary Gazette Part II, Section 1)

Enforcement Date - Deemed to have come into force on October 21, 2014

Nodal Ministry - Ministry of Coal

Precedent & Statutory Rationale

1. The Supreme Court's Landmark Coal Cancellation Judgment (2014):

o For decades, coal blocks in India had been allocated via administrative screening committees or government routes dating back to 1993. In the landmark judgment Manohar Lal Sharma v. Principal Secretary (2014), the Supreme Court of India declared allocations made via these non-transparent routes arbitrary and illegal, resulting in the cancellation of 204 out of 218 coal blocks.

2. Restoring Legal Certainty and Ensuring Energy Security:

o The mass cancellation threatened nationwide power generation, steel production, cement manufacturing, and critical industrial operations. The legislation was urgently enacted to create a secure, transparent, and competitive statutory framework to reallocate the cancelled coal mines, protect national energy security, and ensure uninterrupted fuel supply.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

• Formulation: Developed and piloted by the Ministry of Coal to establish a permanent legislative architecture following judicial intervention.

• Parliamentary Passage: Initially promulgated as an emergency Executive Ordinance on October 21, 2014 (re-promulgated in January 2015), the provisions were subsequently formalized into a Bill, debated extensively, and passed by both Houses of Parliament in March 2015.

• Presidential Assent: Received formal Presidential Assent on March 30, 2015, entering the statute book as Act No. 11 of 2015.

• Enforcement: Retroactively brought into active operational force from October 21, 2014 to maintain continuity with the preceding ordinances

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of The Surrogacy (Regulation) Act, 2021
Overview
Purpose: Regulate surrogacy, establish regulatory bodies, and oversee the surrogacy process, ensuring ethical practices and protection of all parties involved.
Key Provisions
1.	Types of Surrogacy
•	Altruistic Surrogacy: Permitted, with no monetary compensation beyond approved medical and related expenses.
•	Commercial Surrogacy: Strictly prohibited, with significant penalties for violations.
2.	Eligibility Criteria
•	Intending Couple/Woman:
•	Must be a legally married Indian couple (with the man ≥21 years and the woman ≥18 years) or a single woman ≥25 years.
•	Requires a medical necessity certificate and a court order establishing parentage.
•	Surrogate Mother:
•	Must be ever-married, with at least one child, and aged between 25-35 years.
•	Mandatory voluntary participation with validated medical and psychological fitness.
3.	Regulatory Framework
•	National Assisted Reproductive Technology and Surrogacy Board: Oversees national regulation.
•	State Assisted Reproductive Technology and Surrogacy Boards: Manage state-level regulation.
•	Compulsory Registration of all surrogacy clinics, with strict standards enforcement.
4.	Rights and Protections
•	Surrogate Child: Legally recognized as the biological child of the intending parents, with full inheritance and social rights.
•	Surrogate Mother:
•	Right to withdraw consent prior to embryo implantation.
•	Protected from exploitation and abandonment through legal safeguards.
5.	Penalties for Non-Compliance
•	Commercial Surrogacy Offences: Up to 10 years imprisonment and a ₹10 lakh fine.
•	Other Violations: Varied penalties, including imprisonment and fines, depending on the offence.
6.	Miscellaneous Provisions
•	Abortion: Permitted only under the Medical Termination of Pregnancy Act, 1971, with the surrogate's consent.
•	Record Keeping and Inspections: Clinics must maintain detailed records for 25 years, subject to authorized inspections.
7.	Transitional and Operational Provisions
•	Transitional Provision (Section 53): A 10-month gestation period for existing surrogate mothers to ensure their well-being.
•	Power to Remove Difficulties (Section 54): The Central Government can issue orders to address implementation challenges within two years of the Act's commencement.
•	Appointment of Appropriate Authorities (Section 35): Mandatory within 90 days for Union territories and states to oversee compliance and enforcement.
•	Functions and Powers of Authorities (Sections 36 & 37): Include registration, standard enforcement, complaint investigation, and legal action against violations.

Precedent & Statutory Rationale

1. Limitations of the Colonial 1927 Framework:

o Prior to 2021, the governance of navigational aids in India was anchored in the Lighthouse Act, 1927, enacted when lighthouses functioned primarily as passive visual signals. 2. Global Compliance and Technological Modernization:

o Grounded in international commitments such as the International Convention for the Safety of Life at Sea (SOLAS), 1974 and guidelines by the International Association of Marine Aids to Navigation and Lighthouse Authorities (IALA), the legislation was enacted to update India's maritime infrastructure, promote ease of doing business, and replace obsolete colonial structures with modern standards.

• Formulation: Developed and piloted by the Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways under the Union Government to revamp coastal navigation laws.

• Presidential Assent: Received formal Presidential Assent on July 31, 2021, entering the statute book as Act No. 20 of 2021.

• Enforcement: Brought into active operational force on March 31, 2022

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of the Central Agricultural University Act, 1992
The Central Agricultural University Act, 1992 was enacted to establish and incorporate the Central Agricultural University (CAU) for the North-Eastern Region of India. The Act aims to promote higher education, research, and extension in agriculture and allied sciences to support agricultural development in the region. It was enacted on 26 December 1992 and came into force on 26 January 1993. 
1. Objective
The Act seeks to:
•	Establish a Central Agricultural University for the North-Eastern Region. 
•	Promote education, research, and extension in agriculture and allied sciences. 
•	Develop skilled manpower for agriculture and rural development. 
•	Improve agricultural productivity and technological advancement in the region. 
2. Establishment of the University (Section 3)
•	The Act establishes the Central Agricultural University as a body corporate with perpetual succession and a common seal. 
•	The University has the power to acquire, hold, and dispose of property and to sue or be sued in its own name. 
3. Objects of the University (Section 4)
The University aims to:
•	Provide instruction in agriculture and allied sciences. 
•	Conduct research to improve agricultural practices. 
•	Disseminate agricultural knowledge through extension programmes. 
•	Promote innovation and rural development in the North-Eastern Region. 
4. Powers of the University (Section 5)
The University may:
•	Establish colleges, schools, research centres, and extension institutions. 
•	Confer degrees, diplomas, and other academic distinctions. 
•	Grant scholarships, fellowships, and prizes. 
•	Collaborate with national and international institutions. 
•	Undertake consultancy, training, and research projects. 
5. Jurisdiction (Section 6)
•	The University's jurisdiction extends to the North-Eastern States specified under the Act. 
•	It serves as a regional institution to meet the educational and research needs of the region.

title: The Multimodal Transportation of Goods Act, 1993

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of the Multimodal Transportation of Goods Act, 1993
Overview
 Regulates multimodal transportation of goods from India to outside India under a multimodal transport contract.
Key Definitions
*Multimodal Transportation: Carriage of goods by at least two different modes of transport (e.g., road, rail, sea, air) under a single contract. *Multimodal Transport Operator (MTO): Entity undertaking multimodal transportation for hire. *Multimodal Transport Document (MTD): Evidences the multimodal transport contract (can be negotiable or non-negotiable).
Core Provisions
1.	Registration: - Mandatory for MTOs with specific requirements (e.g., minimum turnover/capital).
•	Cancellation possible for non-compliance or inactivity.
2.	Multimodal Transport Document (MTD):
•	Issuance at consignor’s option.
•	Acts as a document of title.
•	Must contain specified particulars (e.g., goods description, route, freight).
•	Evidentiary Value: Prima facie evidence of the contract and goods.
3.	Liabilities and Responsibilities: - Operator’s Liability: For loss, damage, or delay unless proven otherwise.
•	Limit of Liability: Based on declared goods value or a statutory amount, whichever is higher.
•	Delay Liability: Limited to the freight payable for the delayed consignment.
•	Intentional/Reckless Acts: Nullify liability limits.
4.	Miscellaneous: - Special Provisions for Dangerous Goods.
•	Lien on Goods/Documents for unpaid charges.
•	General Average principles apply.
•	Limitation Period for Actions: 9 months from delivery or due delivery date.
•	Jurisdiction and Arbitration: Specified for disputes.
Actionable Points for Stakeholders
•	Operators:
•	Register and maintain compliance.
•	Clearly understand and communicate liability terms.
•	Accurately issue and manage MTDs.
•	Consignors:
•	Verify MTO registration.
•	Accurately declare goods value and nature.
•	Understand procedures for reporting loss/damage.
•	Authorities:
•	Enforce registration and compliance.
•	Apply the Act in jurisdiction and arbitration cases.

Precedent & Historical Rationale

1. Inadequacy of Traditional Single-Mode Laws:

o Prior to 1993, the transport of goods in international and domestic commerce was governed by fragmented, modal-specific laws (such as the Indian Railways Act, Carriers Act, and Merchant Shipping Act) that failed to address modern containerized transport involving multiple modes (such as ship, rail, road, and air) under a single contract.

2. Global Trade Integration and Unified Liability:

o With the rapid growth of international containerization and global supply chains, India required a comprehensive statutory framework to regulate multimodal transport operators (MTOs), establish a single-document transport system, and provide a uniform legal regime governing carrier liability, loss, damage, and delay.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

• Formulation: Initially promulgated as an Ordinance by the President on October 16, 1992, to immediately meet international trade requirements and register Multimodal Transport Operators.

• Parliamentary Passage: Introduced as a Bill to replace the Ordinance, it was reviewed and passed by both the Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha during the Budget Session of 1993.

• Presidential Assent: Received Presidential Assent on April 2, 1993.

• Enforcement: Enforced on October 16, 1992.

title: The SAARC Convention (Suppression of Terrorism) Act, 1993

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of the SAARC Convention (Suppression of Terrorism) Act, 1993
Overview
Objective: To implement the SAARC Convention on Suppression of Terrorism, signed at Kathmandu on 4th November, 1987, aiming to combat terrorism in the SAARC region.
Key Provisions
1.	Scope and Application: - Applies to the whole of India.
•	Extends to Indian citizens and ships/aircraft registered in India, worldwide.
•	Covers offences committed outside India under specific conditions (Section 6).
2.	Definitions: - Convention: Refers to the SAARC Convention on Suppression of Terrorism.
•	Convention Country: A country where the Convention is in force.
3.	Offences and Penalties: - Hostage-Taking (Section 4): Punishable with imprisonment up to 10 years and a fine.
•	Offences Under Article I of the Convention (listed in The Schedule):
•	Includes murder, manslaughter, assault, kidnapping, hostage-taking, and offences involving firearms, explosives, etc., when used for indiscriminate violence or to intimidate populations.
•	Penalties Not Explicitly Detailed in the provided context for these specific offences, implying reliance on broader Indian penal laws or the Convention's guidelines.
4.	Jurisdiction, Extradition, and Cooperation:
•	Jurisdiction Over Offences Committed Outside India (Section 6): Permits trial in India under specified conditions.
•	Extradition (Section 5): Offences under this Act are not considered political for extradition purposes, facilitating cooperation among SAARC countries.
5.	Prosecution and Protection: - Mandatory Previous Sanction for Prosecution (Section 7): Requires Central Government's prior approval for prosecution.
•	Protection for Actions in Good Faith (Section 8): Immunizes actions taken in good faith under this Act from legal repercussions.
The Schedule
*Incorporates the SAARC Regional Convention on Suppression of Terrorism. *Article I Lists Offences for Extradition Purposes, Including:
•	Offences under specified international conventions.
•	Acts of violence against individuals or groups to intimidate populations or compel governments to act.

Act Number 36 of 1993

Presidential Assent Date April 26, 1993

Nodal Ministry Ministry of Home Affairs

Precedent & Historical Rationale

1. Regional Commitment to Counter Terrorism:

o Recognizing terrorism as a grave transnational threat to regional peace, security, and stability, member states of the South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation (SAARC) signed the SAARC Regional Convention on Suppression of Terrorism in Kathmandu on November 4, 1987.

2. Need for Domestic Legal Implementation:

o Under international law, treaty obligations cannot be directly enforced within India's domestic legal system without enabling municipal legislation. To give full effect to the provisions of the SAARC Convention—specifically regarding extradition, mutual legal assistance, and the exclusion of terrorist offences from being treated as political crimes—a dedicated statutory enactment was necessary.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

• Formulation: Drafted by the Ministry of Home Affairs in consultation with the Ministry of External Affairs to translate India's international treaty commitments under the SAARC framework into enforceable municipal criminal law.

• Parliamentary Passage: Introduced as a Bill, deliberated, and passed by both Houses of Parliament (Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha) during the Budget Session of 1993.

• Presidential Assent: Received Presidential Assent on April 26, 1993.

• Enforcement: Enforced on April 26, 1993.

• Source: Official Records of Parliament, India Code, and Ministry of Home Affairs.

Summary of the Multi-State Co-operative Societies Act, 2002
1. Financial Governance & Protections
•	Provision for Provident Fund: Mandatory for employee benefit, funded by employee and society contributions as per bye-laws, ensuring financial security.
•	Protection of Provident Fund Assets:
•	Exclusion from Society Assets: Separate from the society's business assets.
•	Immunity from Legal Processes: Protected against attachment, court processes, or other authorities.
2. Governance & Compliance
•	Registration & Bye-Laws Alignment: Societies must register with the Central Registrar, adhering to specified bye-laws.
•	Penalties for Non-Compliance:
•	Destruction/Falsification of Documents: Imprisonment (1 month to 1 year) and/or fine (₹5,000 to ₹1 lakh).
•	Unlawful Investments or Losses: Similar penalties apply for violations of section 64 or causing unlawful losses.
•	Personal Gains by Directors/Officers: Penalties include imprisonment and recovery of unlawful gains.
3. Judicial & Procedural Aspects
•	Cognizance of Offences: Only Metropolitan Magistrates or Judicial Magistrates of the first class can try offences under this Act.
•	Prosecution Procedure: Requires a written complaint from a society member or the Central Registrar.
•	Supremacy of Act: Provisions are additional to, not in derogation of, other laws.

ACT NO. 82 OF 1985

Act Number/Year - 82 of 1985

Presidential Assent Date - December 30, 1985

Enforcement Date - October 27, 1986

Nodal Ministry - Ministry of Shipping

Precedent & Historical Rationale

Untapped Potential of Inland Water Transport:

Despite possessing an extensive network of rivers, canals, backwaters, and creeks spanning thousands of kilometers, India’s inland water transport system remained heavily underutilized. Prior to 1985, responsibility for developing and regulating waterways was fragmented across various state and central agencies without a dedicated, centralized expert body to coordinate policy, plan infrastructure, or direct investments for shipping and navigation.

Need for a Specialized Statutory Body:

Recognizing the cost-effectiveness, fuel efficiency, and eco-friendly nature of water transport compared to congested rail and road networks, the Government felt an urgent necessity to create a specialized national apex body. Modelled similarly to authorities governing ports and railways, this institution was conceptualized to exclusively manage, regulate, and develop national waterways and foster private or public-private cooperation in inland shipping.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

Formulation:

Drafted by the Ministry of Shipping to establish the Inland Waterways Authority of India (IWAI) as a statutory body corporate endowed with powers to survey economic feasibility, construct infrastructural facilities (such as terminals, navigational channels, and storage), and advise the Central Government on matters related to inland water transport.

Parliamentary Passage:

Introduced and debated across both Houses of Parliament (Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha) during the winter session of 1985, successfully securing legislative approval.

Presidential Assent:

Received Presidential Assent on December 30, 1985.

Enforcement: Enforced on October 27, 1986.

Nodal Ministry Ministry of Finance

Precedent & Statutory Rationale

1. Fragmentation of Legacy Oversight:

o Prior to 2007, India’s payment and settlement mechanisms—including paper-based clearing, card networks, and early electronic fund transfers—operated without a unified, dedicated statutory framework. Regulation was scattered across various administrative guidelines or general banking laws, leaving systemic vulnerabilities unaddressed.

2. Mitigating Systemic Risk and Providing Legal Clarity:

o With the rapid growth of electronic transactions, automated clearing houses, and high-value financial transfers, the legislature recognized an urgent need for a comprehensive legal architecture. The Act was formulated to grant explicit legal recognition to transaction netting and settlement finality, protect against systemic financial collapse, and safeguard consumer interests.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

• Formulation: Drafted and piloted by the Ministry of Finance in close coordination with the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) to establish an institutional baseline for secure financial commerce.

• Parliamentary Passage: Tabled, debated, and passed by both Houses of Parliament during the winter session of 2007.

• Presidential Assent: Received formal Presidential Assent on December 20, 2007, entering the statute book as Act No. 51 of 2007.

• Enforcement: Enforced on August 12, 2008.

title: The Territorial Waters, Continental Shelf, Exclusive Economic Zone and Other Maritime Zones Act, 1976

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of the Territorial Waters, Continental Shelf, Exclusive Economic Zone and Other Maritime Zones Act, 1976
Objective
The Territorial Waters, Continental Shelf, Exclusive Economic Zone and Other Maritime Zones Act, 1976 was enacted to define India's maritime zones and regulate the exercise of sovereignty, sovereign rights, jurisdiction, and control over its territorial waters, contiguous zone, continental shelf, exclusive economic zone (EEZ), and other maritime areas. The Act provides the legal framework for protecting India's maritime interests, managing marine resources, and safeguarding national security. 
Key Provisions
•	Territorial Waters: Declares India's sovereignty over its territorial waters, extending up to 12 nautical miles from the baseline, along with the airspace above, seabed, and subsoil. 
•	Contiguous Zone: Empowers the Central Government to declare a contiguous zone extending up to 24 nautical miles from the baseline, where India may enforce customs, fiscal, immigration, and sanitary laws. 
•	Continental Shelf: Confers sovereign rights on India over its continental shelf for exploring and exploiting mineral and other natural resources of the seabed and subsoil. 
•	Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ): Provides for the declaration of an Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ) extending up to 200 nautical miles from the baseline, where India has sovereign rights over the exploration, exploitation, conservation, and management of natural resources. 
•	Maritime Boundaries: Empowers the Central Government to determine maritime boundaries with neighbouring coastal States through agreements or other lawful means. 
•	Regulation of Foreign Activities: Authorises the Central Government to regulate scientific research, resource exploitation, installation of offshore structures, and the entry and passage of foreign vessels in designated maritime areas. 
•	Rule-making Power: Empowers the Central Government to make rules and issue notifications for implementing and administering the provisions of the Act.

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of the Diplomatic Relations (Vienna Convention) Act, 1972
Objective
The Diplomatic Relations (Vienna Convention) Act, 1972 was enacted to give effect in India to the Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations, 1961. It provides the legal framework for recognizing the privileges, immunities, and facilities granted to diplomatic missions, diplomatic agents, and their staff, while ensuring compliance with India's international obligations.
Key Provisions
•	Implementation of the Vienna Convention: Gives the force of law in India to the provisions of the Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations, 1961. 
•	Privileges and Immunities: Grants diplomatic agents and members of diplomatic missions privileges and immunities, including immunity from the jurisdiction of Indian courts, subject to the Convention. 
•	Inviolability of Diplomatic Premises: Ensures the inviolability of embassy premises, diplomatic residences, archives, and official documents. 
•	Exemptions and Facilities: Provides exemptions from certain taxes, customs duties, and other obligations as specified under the Convention. 
•	Reciprocity: Empowers the Central Government to restrict or withdraw privileges and immunities of a foreign State's diplomatic mission where that State does not accord corresponding treatment to Indian diplomatic missions. 
•	Rule-making Power: Authorizes the Central Government to make rules and issue notifications for carrying out the provisions of the Act and the Convention.

Legislative History: The Diplomatic Relations (Vienna Convention) Act, 1972

Source: India Code (indiacode.gov.in) and Ministry of External Affairs Official Records

Key Legislative Metadata

Legislative Stage / Attribute Official Details

Short Title The Diplomatic Relations (Vienna Convention) Act, 1972

Act Number / Year Act No. 43 of 1972

Act ID (India Code) 197243

Presidential Assent / Enactment Date August 29, 1972

Official Gazette Publication August 1972

Enforcement Date August 29, 1972

Administrative Nodal Ministry Ministry of External Affairs

Precedent & Statutory Rationale

1. Giving Municipal Effect to International Treaty Obligations:

o While India had previously acceded to or recognized various international diplomatic frameworks, the specific privileges, immunities, and exemptions outlined under the Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations (1961) required explicit legislative incorporation to have the direct force of municipal law within Indian courts and jurisdictions.

o The Act was formulated to fulfill India's sovereign obligations under international law by formally incorporating the provisions of the 1961 Vienna Convention into the domestic legal system, ensuring reciprocity, clarity, and adherence to global diplomatic standards.

2. Core Statutory Provisions and Scope:

o Force of Law: Under Section 2, the provisions of the Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations (adopted on April 14, 1961) as set out in the Schedule to the Act have the explicit force of law in India, overriding any contrary provisions in other domestic laws.

o Reciprocity and Restrictions: Empowers the Central Government to restrict privileges and immunities if it appears that a foreign state party is in breach of its obligations or accords lesser privileges to Indian missions abroad (Section 4).

o Customs and Citizens: Places specific statutory restrictions on customs duty exemptions for imported goods (Section 6) and outlines limitations regarding privileges granted to Indian citizens serving in diplomatic missions (Section 7).

o Inviolability of Premises: Imposes strict boundaries on the entry of public servants or state agents into diplomatic premises without official consent (Section 8).

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

• Formulation: Drafted and piloted by the Ministry of External Affairs to seamlessly align domestic legal processes with international diplomatic norms.

• Parliamentary Passage: Tabled, debated, and passed by both Houses of Parliament, receiving Presidential Assent on August 29, 1972.

• Enforcement: Enforced on August 29, 1972.

title: The Taxation Laws (Extension to Jammu and Kashmir) Act, 1972

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of The Taxation Laws (Extension to Jammu and Kashmir) Act, 1972
Objective
The Taxation Laws (Extension to Jammu and Kashmir) Act, 1972 was enacted to extend certain Central taxation laws to the State of Jammu and Kashmir with effect from 1 July 1972. The Act aimed to ensure the uniform application of specified Central taxes in the State and facilitate the collection of additional revenue. 
Key Provisions
•	Extension of Central Tax Laws: Extends Chapter VII of the Finance (No. 2) Act, 1971 (Foreign Travel Tax), the Tax on Postal Articles Act, 1971, and the Inland Air Travel Tax Act, 1971 to Jammu and Kashmir, along with the rules, notifications, and regulations made under those laws. 
•	Application of Criminal Procedure: Provides that references to the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898 in the extended laws shall, in relation to Jammu and Kashmir, be construed as references to the corresponding law then in force in the State. 
•	Power to Remove Difficulties: Authorizes the Central Government to issue orders to remove difficulties in implementing the extended taxation laws in Jammu and Kashmir, provided such orders are not inconsistent with the Acts and are made within two years of the commencement of the Act. 
•	Commencement: The Act came into force on 1 July 1972.

•	Employers contribute at rates specified (historical rates noted, with potential for updates).

title: The Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of the Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974
Objective
The Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974 was enacted to prevent and control water pollution and to maintain or restore the wholesomeness of water. It provides for the establishment of Central and State Pollution Control Boards to monitor, regulate, and enforce measures for protecting water resources from pollution. 
Key Provisions
•	Central and State Pollution Control Boards: Establishes the Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) and State Pollution Control Boards (SPCBs) to prevent, control, and abate water pollution. 
•	Functions of the Boards: Empowers the Boards to advise Governments, monitor water quality, prescribe standards, conduct research, inspect industries, and promote pollution control measures. 
•	Consent for Discharge: Requires industries and other establishments to obtain the prior consent of the State Pollution Control Board before discharging sewage or trade effluents into streams, wells, sewers, or land. 
•	Prohibition of Water Pollution: Prohibits the discharge of poisonous, noxious, or polluting matter into water bodies beyond prescribed standards. 
•	Inspection and Sampling: Authorises Pollution Control Boards to enter premises, inspect facilities, collect water and effluent samples, and conduct investigations to ensure compliance. 
•	Enforcement and Penalties: Prescribes penalties, including imprisonment and fines, for violations of the Act and empowers authorities to issue directions, including closure of polluting industries or stoppage of utilities in appropriate cases. 
•	Appeals and Rule-making: Provides for appeals against orders of the Pollution Control Boards and empowers the Central and State Governments to make rules for implementing the Act.

Long Title An Act to provide for the prevention and control of water pollution and the maintaining or restoring of wholesomeness of water, for the establishment, with a view to carrying out the purposes aforesaid, of Boards for the prevention and control of water pollution, for the conferring on and assigning to such Boards of powers of and functions relating thereto and for matters connected therewith.

Presidential Assent / Enactment Date March 23, 1974

Administrative Nodal Ministry Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change

Precedent & Statutory Rationale

1. First Comprehensive Federal Environmental Legislation:

o Prior to 1974, India lacked comprehensive national laws dedicated to controlling environmental pollution, relying instead on fragmented municipal bylaws and older nuisance or riparian rights provisions.

o Following international momentum generated by the historic United Nations Conference on the Human Environment held in Stockholm in June 1972 (where India was a participant), and pursuant to resolutions passed by various State legislatures under Article 252(1) of the Constitution, Parliament enacted this landmark legislation to regulate water bodies and industrial effluents.

2. Establishment of Institutional Regulatory Boards:

o The 1974 Act was enacted to create an institutional framework comprising the Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) at the national level and State Pollution Control Boards (SPCBs) at the state level.

o It empowered these regulatory bodies to set and enforce effluent standards, issue consents (licenses) for discharging industrial and municipal sewage into water bodies, inspect pollution sources, establish testing laboratories, and institute penal proceedings against violators polluting water resources.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

• Formulation: Drafted through collaborative federal initiatives and resolutions where participating state legislatures authorized Parliament to legislate on a state-list subject (Water, Entry 17 of List II) for a uniform national standard.

• Parliamentary Passage: Tabled, deliberated, and passed by both Houses of Parliament, receiving Presidential Assent on March 23, 1974.

• Enforcement: Enforced on March 23, 1974.

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of the Interest-tax Act, 1974
Objective
The Interest-tax Act, 1974 was enacted to levy a special tax on the chargeable interest earned by specified credit institutions on loans and advances. The Act aimed to raise Government revenue and regulate the cost of borrowed funds by imposing a tax on interest income. 
Key Provisions
•	Levy of Interest Tax: Imposes a tax on the chargeable interest earned by specified credit institutions on loans and advances. 
•	Assessment and Returns: Requires assessees to file returns of chargeable interest and provides for assessment, reassessment, and recovery of interest-tax by the tax authorities. 
•	Advance Payment of Tax: Mandates payment of interest-tax in advance in prescribed instalments during the financial year. 
•	Interest, Penalties and Prosecution: Prescribes interest for delayed filing or payment, penalties for concealment of chargeable interest, and prosecution for tax evasion and false statements. 
•	Appeals and Revision: Provides for appeals before the Commissioner (Appeals) and the Appellate Tribunal, along with powers of revision and rectification of mistakes. 
•	Application of Income-tax Provisions: Applies several provisions of the Income-tax Act, 1961 to the administration, collection, recovery, and enforcement of interest-tax. 
•	Rule-making Power: Empowers the Central Government and the Central Board of Direct Taxes (CBDT) to make rules for implementing the provisions of the Act and to grant exemptions in specified cases.

Precedent & Historical Rationale

• Rationale & Context: Promulgated during an era of significant economic inflation and monetary instability, the Act was designed to serve dual monetary and fiscal policy objectives.

• The Legislative Problem: Traditional corporate and income taxes did not adequately capture the high yields generated by financial institutions through lending operations, nor did they provide a direct fiscal mechanism to influence commercial bank lending rates or curb excessive credit expansion.

• The Remedy: Parliament enacted the Interest-tax Act, 1974 to impose a special statutory tax on the total amount of interest earned by scheduled banks (and later expanded to other credit institutions) on loans and advances made in India. This served to raise the cost of borrowed funds, cool down speculative credit creation, and supplement public revenues.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

• Formulation: Conceptualized by the Ministry of Finance as a targeted fiscal instrument to regulate financial sector liquidity and widen the direct tax base.

• Parliamentary Passage: Introduced and reviewed during the autumn session of Parliament in September 1974, passing both houses swiftly to address prevailing macroeconomic challenges.

• Presidential Assent: Received assent from the President of India on September 23, 1974.

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of the Oil Industry (Development) act, 1974
Objective
The Oil Industry (Development) Act, 1974 was enacted to promote the planned development of the oil industry in India by establishing an institutional mechanism for providing financial assistance to the sector. The Act also provides for the levy of a cess on crude oil and natural gas to create an Oil Industry Development Fund for supporting exploration, production, refining, research, and other developmental activities. 
Key Provisions
•	Oil Industry Development Board: Establishes the Oil Industry Development Board (OIDB) to promote and assist the development of the oil industry. 
•	Financial Assistance: Empowers the Board to provide loans, grants, and other financial assistance for projects relating to oil exploration, production, refining, processing, transportation, marketing, and research. 
•	Levy of Cess: Provides for the levy and collection of a cess (duty of excise) on crude oil and natural gas to finance the development of the oil industry. 
•	Oil Industry Development Fund: Creates the Oil Industry Development Fund, into which cess proceeds, Government grants, loans, and other receipts are credited and utilised exclusively for the purposes of the Act. 
•	Accounts and Audit: Requires the Board to maintain proper accounts, which are audited by the Comptroller and Auditor General of India (CAG), and to submit annual reports to the Central Government. 
•	Government Control: Empowers the Central Government to issue directions to the Board, require maintenance of records by persons engaged in the oil industry, and supervise the implementation of the Act. 
•	Penalties and Rule-making: Prescribes penalties for non-compliance with the Act and empowers the Central Government to make rules for carrying out its provisions.

Precedent & Historical Rationale

1. Rationale & Context: Set against the backdrop of the global oil shocks of the 1970s, India faced massive strains on its foreign exchange reserves due to surging crude oil import bills. This fund was designed to be continuously financed through a statutory duty of excise levied on domestically produced crude oil and natural gas, providing a steady capital stream for the domestic petroleum sector.

• Formulation: Conceived by the central government to build a robust, self-reliant domestic hydrocarbon ecosystem capable of financing its own capital-intensive exploration and infrastructure projects.

title: The Economic Offences (Inapplicability of Limitation) Act, 1974

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of The Economic Offences (Inapplicability of Limitation) Act, 1974
Objective
The Economic Offences (Inapplicability of Limitation) Act, 1974 was enacted to exclude the application of the limitation period prescribed under Chapter XXXVI of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 to specified economic offences. The Act ensures that prosecutions for serious economic offences are not barred merely because they come to light after prolonged investigation or adjudication. 
Key Provisions
•	Inapplicability of Limitation: Provides that the limitation provisions contained in Chapter XXXVI of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 do not apply to offences specified in the Schedule to the Act. 
•	Scheduled Economic Offences: Covers offences under various economic laws, including the Income-tax Act, Customs Act, Central Excise laws, Foreign Exchange Regulation Act, General Insurance Business (Nationalisation) Act, and other enactments listed in the Schedule. 
•	Connected Offences: Extends the exemption from limitation to any other offence that may be tried together with a scheduled economic offence. 
•	Cognizance by Courts: Empowers courts to take cognizance of the specified offences without being restricted by the statutory period of limitation under the Code of Criminal Procedure. 
•	Commencement: The Act came into force on 1 April 1974 and applies to the territories where the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 is in force.

Precedent & Historical Rationale

1. Rationale & Context: Prior to 1974, the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (CrPC) introduced Chapter XXXVI (Sections 468–473), which established strict statutory periods of limitation for taking cognizance of various offences based on the gravity of punishment.

2. The Legislative Problem: Economic and financial crimes—such as tax evasion, foreign exchange violations, and customs smuggling—are inherently covert, sophisticated, and complex. They rarely come to light immediately and usually require extensive, multi-layered audits, investigations, or departmental adjudications.

3. The Remedy: Parliament recognized that applying standard limitation periods would allow white-collar criminals to evade prosecution merely due to the time consumed by necessary investigations. Consequently, the Economic Offences (Inapplicability of Limitation) Act, 1974 was enacted to explicitly render Chapter XXXVI of the CrPC inapplicable to the specific economic statutes enumerated in its Schedule.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

● Formulation: Conceptualized alongside the transition to the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, to prevent statutory limitation bars from inadvertently shielding major financial and economic wrongdoers from criminal accountability.

● Parliamentary Passage: Tabled, debated, and passed by both Houses of Parliament in March 1974 to ensure timely alignment with the enforcement of the CrPC on April 1, 1974.

● Presidential Assent:Received assent from the President of India on March 27, 1974.

● Enforcement: Enforced on April 1, 1974.

title: The Richardson and Cruddas Limited (Acquisition and Transfer of Undertaking) Act, 1972

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of the Richardson and Cruddas Limited (Acquisition and Transfer of Undertaking) Act, 1972
Objective
The Richardson and Cruddas Limited (Acquisition and Transfer of Undertaking) Act, 1972 was enacted to acquire and transfer the undertaking of Richardson and Cruddas Limited to the Central Government in order to ensure its continued operation in the public interest, protect employment, maintain the production of essential engineering goods, and resolve disputes relating to the company's shareholding. 
Key Provisions
•	Acquisition and Transfer: Provides for the acquisition of the undertaking of Richardson and Cruddas Limited by the Central Government and its transfer to a Government company. 
•	Vesting of Assets and Liabilities: Transfers all assets, rights, liabilities, contracts, and obligations of the undertaking to the Central Government and subsequently to the Government company. 
•	Protection of Employees: Ensures continuity of service and protects the pay, pension, gratuity, and other service benefits of employees. 
•	Compensation: Provides for payment of ₹30 lakh as compensation for the acquisition of the undertaking. 
•	Tribunal for Share Disputes: Establishes a Tribunal to determine genuine shareholders, resolve disputes relating to duplicate or fraudulent share certificates, and facilitate reconstruction of the register of members. 
•	Custodian and Management: Provides for the appointment of a Custodian to manage the affairs of the company and supervise the reconstruction process. 
•	Penalties and Rule-making: Prescribes penalties for violations of the Act and empowers the Central Government to make rules for its implementation.

WHEREAS the Richardson and Cruddas Limited, a company formed and registered under the Indian Companies Act, 1913 (7 of 1913), is engaged in the production of goods needed by the defence establishments, railways, steel plants and power projects;

title: The Petroleum and Minerals Pipelines (Acquisition of Right of User in Land) Act, 1962

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of the Petroleum and Minerals Pipelines (Acquisition of Right of User in Land) Act, 1962 
Objectives of the Act
•	To enable the acquisition of the right of user in land for laying and maintaining pipelines. 
•	To facilitate the efficient transportation of petroleum, petroleum products, and minerals through pipelines. 
•	To avoid the need for outright acquisition of land wherever possible. 
•	To provide for compensation to persons whose rights in the land are affected. 
Key Provisions
•	Acquisition of Right of User: The Central Government may acquire only the right to lay, maintain, inspect, repair, alter, or remove pipelines in land, while ownership of the land remains with the landowner. 
•	Notification and Objections: Before acquiring the right of user, the Government issues a notification identifying the land, and interested persons are given an opportunity to file objections, which are considered by the competent authority. 
•	Declaration of Acquisition: After considering objections, the Government may declare the acquisition of the right of user, which then vests in the Central Government or the authorised entity. 
•	Compensation: The Act provides for payment of compensation to landowners and other interested persons for any loss, damage, or restrictions arising from the acquisition of the right of user and the laying of pipelines. 
•	Restrictions on Land Use: Landowners may continue to cultivate and use the land, but they cannot undertake activities—such as constructing buildings, digging deep excavations, or planting certain trees—that could damage or interfere with the pipeline. 
•	Entry and Maintenance: Authorised persons may enter the land to survey, lay, inspect, maintain, repair, or replace pipelines, subject to the provisions of the Act. 
•	Dispute Resolution: The Act provides mechanisms for determining compensation and resolving disputes relating to compensation through the competent authority and courts. 
•	Rule-making Power: The Central Government is empowered to make rules for carrying out the provisions of the Act.

•	Academic and training programs in sports sciences

•	Statutes:

meta.dc.description.abstract:
The Jammu and Kashmir Reorganisation Act, 2019
1.	Territorial Reorganisation: - Union Territory of Ladakh (without Legislature): Comprising Kargil and Leh districts.
•	Union Territory of Jammu and Kashmir (with Legislature): Comprising the remaining territories.
2.	Governance Structure: - Lieutenant Governor: Common for both UTs until a Presidentially determined period ends.
•	Legislative Assembly for Jammu and Kashmir UT:
•	Composition: 107 seats (provisionally increased to 114 from December 26, 2023, under the Jammu and Kashmir Reorganisation (Amendment) Act, 2023).
•	Reserved Seats: For Scheduled Castes and Tribes, proportionate to their population (ceases when Article 334 of the Constitution's provisions for SC/ST reservation in the House of the People expire).

3.	Constitutional and Legislative Implications: - Constitutional Amendments: Updates to the First and Fourth Schedules regarding Union Territories and Rajya Sabha representation.
•	Representation in Parliament:
•	Rajya Sabha: 4 seats for Jammu and Kashmir UT.
•	Lok Sabha: 5 seats for Jammu and Kashmir UT, 1 seat for Ladakh UT.
•	Application of Article 239A: Similar to Puducherry, for Jammu and Kashmir UT (amended in 2021).
4.	Administrative and Financial Provisions: - Assets, Liabilities, and Revenues: Framework for distribution and management between the UTs.
•	Services and Employees: Continuity and adjustment provisions.
•	Adaptation of Laws: Mechanism for adapting existing laws to the new UTs.
