Summary of the Black Money (Undisclosed Foreign Income and Assets) and Imposition of Tax Act, 2015
Key Provisions
1.	Taxation and Penalties
•	Tax Rate: 30% on undisclosed foreign assets.
•	Penalty: 100% of the tax charged for non-compliance.
2.	Declaration Process
•	Eligibility: Applies to persons with undisclosed foreign assets from income taxable before April 1, 2016.
•	Procedure: Declaration to be made in a prescribed form with verification.
3.	Payment Consequences
•	Deadline: Tax and penalty payment notified by the Central Government.
•	Non-Compliance: Declaration nullified if payment missed.
•	Refund: No refund for tax paid under this Act.

•	Exclusion from Income: Declared assets excluded from total income if paid on time.
•	Assessment Finality: No reopening of assessments or set-offs allowed.
5.	Exemptions and Non-Applicability
•	Persons Under Detention/Criminal Proceedings: Act does not apply.
•	Wealth Tax: Exemption for declared assets under certain conditions.
6.	Offences and Prosecutions
•	Penalties for Non-Filing/Evasion: Rigorous imprisonment and fines.
•	Limitation Period for Penalties: Specified.

title: The Admiralty (Jurisdiction and Settlement of Maritime Claims) Act, 2017

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of the Admiralty (Jurisdiction and Settlement of Maritime Claims) Act, 2017
Primary Objective: To establish admiralty jurisdiction, manage maritime claims, and facilitate their settlement in India, with nuanced applications to naval service and related establishments.
Key Provisions (Aligned with Naval Service Context)
1.	Application to Naval Personnel and Establishments
•	The Act extends to persons subject to naval law, covering those in naval service, including ships, aircraft, vehicles, and armouries, as well as those undergoing training or in uniform.
•	Example: Naval personnel on ships or aircraft, or those called up for training, fall under the Act's jurisdiction for maritime claims.
2.	Jurisdiction Over Naval Vessels and Assets
•	High Courts with admiralty jurisdiction have oversight over claims involving naval vessels, equipment, and related maritime assets, ensuring structured dispute resolution.
3.	Priority and Protection of Maritime Claims in Naval Context
•	The Act prioritizes and safeguards maritime liens and claims related to naval service, protecting the interests of the Indian Navy and its personnel in maritime disputes.
4.	Regulatory Framework for Naval Estate Settlements
•	In cases of deceased or missing naval personnel, the Act's provisions, guide the settlement of estates with maritime assets or liabilities.

Summary of the Durgah Khawaja Saheb Act, 1955

Objectives

•	To provide for the proper administration and management of the Durgah Khawaja Saheb at Ajmer. 
•	To ensure the efficient management and protection of the Durgah's properties, endowments, and funds. 
•	To promote the religious, charitable, and public purposes for which the Durgah was established. 
•	To establish a statutory committee for the administration of the Durgah. 

Key Provisions

•	Establishes the Durgah Committee as the statutory body responsible for the administration and management of the Durgah and its properties. 
•	Prescribes the composition, appointment, powers, functions, and tenure of the members of the Durgah Committee. 
•	Vests the management and control of the Durgah's properties, endowments, income, and funds in the Committee. 
•	Requires the Committee to maintain proper accounts, prepare budgets, and ensure the audit of its finances. 
•	Empowers the Central Government to exercise supervisory powers and issue directions for the proper administration of the Durgah. 
•	Provides for the appointment of officers and employees and regulates matters relating to the management and maintenance of the shrine. 
•	Empowers the Central Government to make rules for carrying out the purposes of the Act.

Precedent & Historical Rationale

1. Replacement of the Durgah Khawaja Saheb Act, 1936: The earlier colonial legislation (Act XXIII of 1936) was found inadequate to address administrative mismanagement, financial irregularities, and disputes over the collection of offerings at the holy shrine of Hazrat Khwaja Moinuddin Chishti at Ajmer.

2. Establishment of Statutory Administration: Enacted following the recommendations of the Judicial Inquiry Committee (Chishti Committee, 1949) to provide for the better administration and management of the Durgah Endowment and properties. The Act established a statutory body—the Durgah Committee—to oversee financial governance, maintenance, pilgrim welfare, and the regulation of hereditary offices (Sajjadanashin and Khadims).

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of the Wealth-tax Act, 1957

Key Provisions:
1.	Charge of Wealth Tax 
o	The Act provided for the levy of wealth tax on the net wealth of individuals, Hindu Undivided Families (HUFs), and companies exceeding the prescribed exemption limit as on the valuation date. 
2.	Net Wealth 
o	Net wealth was calculated by deducting debts owed in relation to taxable assets from the aggregate value of specified assets owned by the assessee. 
3.	Taxable Assets 
o	The Act specified the categories of assets liable to wealth tax, including certain: 
	Residential houses and buildings. 
	Urban land. 
	Motor cars. 
	Jewellery, bullion, and precious metals. 
	Yachts, boats, and aircraft (subject to prescribed exceptions). 
	Cash in excess of the prescribed limits. 
4.	Exemptions 
o	The Act exempted certain assets from wealth tax, including assets used for business or profession and other categories specified under the Act. 
5.	Valuation of Assets 
o	The value of taxable assets was determined according to the valuation rules prescribed under the Act. 
o	The Act also provided for the appointment of valuation officers in appropriate cases. 
6.	Assessment and Returns 
o	Assessees were required to file wealth-tax returns where applicable. 
o	Tax authorities were empowered to assess net wealth, reassess escaped wealth, and recover tax due. 
7.	Penalties and Appeals 
o	The Act prescribed penalties for non-compliance, concealment of wealth, and failure to furnish returns. 
o	It also provided appellate remedies against assessment and other orders.

Precedent & Historical Rationale

1. Kaldor Report on Tax Reform (1956): Prof. Nicholas Kaldor submitted a seminal report recommending an integrated direct tax system combining income tax, capital gains tax, expenditure tax, and wealth tax to reduce wealth concentration and combat tax evasion.

2. Levy of Annual Direct Tax on Net Wealth: Enacted to levy an annual direct tax on the net wealth of Individuals, Hindu Undivided Families (HUFs), and Companies as on the valuation date. meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of the Gift-tax Act, 1958

Key Provisions:
1.	Charge of Gift Tax 
o	The Act provided for the levy of gift tax on gifts made during a financial year. 
o	The tax was payable by the donor (the person making the gift). 
2.	Definition of Gift 
o	A "gift" was defined as the transfer of any existing movable or immovable property voluntarily and without consideration. 
o	Certain transfers made for inadequate consideration were also treated as gifts to the extent of the difference between the value and consideration. 
3.	Taxable Gifts 
o	The Act covered gifts such as: 
	Immovable property. 
	Money and securities. 
	Jewellery and other valuable assets. 
	Other forms of property as specified under the Act. 
4.	Exemptions 
o	Certain gifts were excluded from taxation, including specified gifts to relatives, charitable institutions, and other categories provided under the Act. 
o	The Act prescribed limits and conditions for exemptions. 
5.	Assessment and Returns 
o	Persons liable to pay gift tax were required to furnish gift-tax returns. 
o	Tax authorities were empowered to assess taxable gifts and determine the amount of tax payable. 
6.	Valuation of Gifts 
o	The Act provided methods for determining the value of gifted property. 
o	The value was generally based on the fair market value of the property on the date of the gift. 
7.	Penalties and Appeals 
o	The Act provided penalties for concealment of gifts, failure to furnish returns, and non-compliance with tax provisions. 
o	It also provided appellate remedies against assessment orders.

Summary of The National Dental Commission Act, 2023 
I. Overview
•	Title & Scope: Regulates the dentistry profession across India, ensuring quality education and healthcare, with specific provisions for temporary registrations for practitioners from other states or countries under certain conditions.
•	Commencement: Effective from specified dates, including February 29, 2024, for key sections.
•	Objective: To enhance the quality of dental education, make it affordable, and improve accessibility to high-quality oral healthcare, considering the integration of existing state-level practices.
II. Key Components
•	National Dental Commission (NDC):
•	Role: Overseeing dentistry regulation in India, harmonizing state and national standards.
•	Autonomous Boards:
1.	Dental Assessment and Rating Board: Evaluates dental institutions, considering state-specific accreditation.
2.	Ethics and Dental Registration Board: Manages ethical standards and registrations, including temporary ones for out-of-state practitioners.
3.	Under-Graduate and Post-Graduate Dental Education Board: Regulates dental education, aligning with the Medical Practitioners Act's principles.
•	Dental Advisory Council: Provides policy and regulatory advice, incorporating feedback from state dental councils.
III. Regulatory Framework
•	Qualification Recognition:
•	Domestic & Interstate: Managed by the Under-Graduate and Post-Graduate Dental Education Board, with provisions for state-qualified practitioners.
•	Foreign: Requires passing the National Exit Test (Dental) or Screening Test, with temporary registration options under specific conditions (e.g., principal livelihood for at least two years).
•	Registration Process:
•	National & State Registers: For dentists and dental auxiliaries, with clear pathways for temporary to permanent registration based on practice duration and location.
•	Temporary Registration: Detailed conditions for out-of-state or foreign citizens, including a five-year temporary registration for those practicing as principal livelihood for at least two years prior to application.
IV. Education and Assessments
•	Entrance and Exit Tests:
•	National Eligibility-cum-Entrance Test (Dental): For undergraduate admissions, applicable nationwide.
•	National Exit Test (Dental): For graduation, licensing, and validation of foreign and interstate qualifications.
V. Governance and Oversight
•	Central Government Oversight:
•	Directional Powers: Over NDC and Autonomous Boards, ensuring uniform application across states.
•	Provision for Supersession: Of the NDC under extraordinary circumstances, protecting the integrity of the profession.
•	Legal Protections: For actions taken in good faith, including those related to temporary registrations and interstate practice approvals.
VI. Financial Provisions and Audits
•	Funding Source: Central Government grants, potentially supplemented by state contributions for specific initiatives.
•	Audit Authority: Comptroller and Auditor General of India, ensuring transparency across all financial transactions.

Purpose: - To improve the legal condition of societies established for literature, science, fine arts, diffusion of useful knowledge, political education, or charitable purposes.

1.	Key Provisions Mentioned in the Context: - Registration:
•	Societies can register under the Act (Section 17 for those existing before the Act).
•	Requires filing a memorandum with the Registrar of Joint-stock Companies (amended in some contexts to "Registrar" or specific state/regional authorities).
•	Society Composition and Management:
•	No specific composition rules mentioned in the provided snippets for the 1860 Act itself, but amendments and other acts (e.g., Delhi's) require at least 10 members under certain conditions.
•	Legal Implications:
•	Property vests in the society (Section 5).
•	Suits can be brought by and against the society (Sections 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11 mentioned but details not provided in the snippet for the 1860 Act).
•	Amendments and Extensions:
•	Modifications for application in specific regions (e.g., Arunachal Pradesh, Haryana, Delhi) with changes in terminology (e.g., "Registrar" instead of "Registrar of Joint-stock Companies", "Administrator" or "State Government" instead of "State Government" in some, then back to "State Government" in amendments).
•	Renewal of registration certificates (Arunachal Pradesh Amendment).

meta.dc.legislation.history:
Legislative History:

The Societies Registration Act, 1860

● Act Title - The Societies Registration Act, 1860

● Act Number / Year - 21 of 1860

● Act ID (India Code) - 186021

● Presidential Assent Date - May 21, 1860

● Enforcement Date - May 21, 1860

● Nodal Ministry - Ministry of Corporate Affairs

Precedent & Historical Rationale

● Improving the Legal Status of Non-Profit Associations - Prior to 1860, voluntary, non-profit, literary, and scientific associations lacked a formal corporate personality or uniform legal framework in British India. As a result, such bodies could not easily hold property in a corporate capacity, enter into binding contracts, or sue and be sued as distinct entities. Modeled on the UK Literary and Scientific Institutions Act, 1854, statutory intervention was needed to grant these entities legal recognition.

● Institutional Framework for Educational & Charitable Growth - Formulated to improve the legal condition and promote the formal organization of societies established for the promotion of literature, science, fine arts, diffusion of useful knowledge, political education, or charitable purposes. The Act enabled seven or more persons to form a registered society by subscribing to a Memorandum of Association, creating a structured mechanism for property vesting, internal governance, and democratic dissolution.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

● Formulation - Introduced to provide for the registration, governance, and legal standing of literary, scientific, and charitable societies across British India.

● Parliamentary Passage - Considered and passed by the Legislative Council of India in mid-1860.

● Presidential Assent - Received the assent of the Governor General of India on May 21, 1860.

● Enforcement - Enforced on May 21, 1860.

Sources - Official Records of the Legislative Council of India, India Code, and Ministry of Corporate Affairs.

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of the Indian Treasure Trove Act, 1878

Key Provisions

•	Defines "treasure" as money, coins, gold, silver, bullion, jewellery, or other valuable objects hidden in the soil or otherwise concealed, whose owner is unknown. 
•	Requires any person finding treasure exceeding the prescribed value to report the discovery to the designated Government authority. 
•	Provides for an inquiry to determine the ownership of the treasure and the circumstances of its discovery. 
•	Authorizes the Government to claim the treasure or acquire it upon payment of the prescribed compensation or reward, particularly where it is of public, historical, or archaeological importance. 
•	Prescribes the procedure for the delivery, custody, and disposal of treasure. 
•	Provides penalties for failure to report the discovery of treasure or for making false statements regarding its discovery.

Legislative History:

The Northern Indian Ferries Act, 1878

● Act Title - The Northern India Ferries Act, 1878

● Act Number / Year - 17 of 1878

● Act ID (India Code) - 187817

● Assent Date - November 9, 1878

● Enforcement Date - November 9, 1878

● Nodal Ministry - Ministry of Shipping

Precedent & Historical Rationale

● Fragmentation and Inadequacy of Regional River Ferry Regulations - Prior to 1878, the control and management of public and private ferries across Northern India were governed by fragmented and rudimentary provincial regulations (such as Bengal Regulation XIX of 1816 and various local provincial rules). In the absence of an overarching, unified enactment, local authorities lacked clear statutory powers to declare public ferries, regulate unsafe private boat transport, prevent overcrowding and accidents, and ensure proper maintenance of river approaches across major waterways in Northern India.

● Unified Statutory Control, Safety Standards, and Toll Management - Formulated to regulate ferries in Northern India (originally extending to Uttar Pradesh, Punjab, the Central Provinces, Assam, and parts of Bengal). The Act empowered provincial/state governments to declare public ferries, define river boundaries, regulate private ferries within specified limits to prevent unauthorized competition with public routes, lease toll collection rights through transparent auctions, establish safety and navigation standards for passenger vessels, and impose penal sanctions for safety violations and toll evasion.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

● Formulation & Introduction - Drafted by the Legislative Department of the Council of the Governor-General of India to consolidate and amend the law relating to public ferries across the northern provinces.

● Legislative Council Passage - Considered, debated, and passed by the Imperial Legislative Council (Council of the Governor-General of India) at Simla/Calcutta during its 1878 legislative sittings.

● Governor-General's Assent - Received the assent of the Viceroy and Governor-General of India (Lord Lytton) on November 9, 1878, and was published in the Gazette of India on November 16, 1878.

● Enforcement - Enforced on November 9, 1878

Sources - Proceedings of the Council of the Governor-General of India (1878), The Gazette of India, India Code, and Ministry of Shipping.

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of the Revenue Recovery Act, 1890 

Title and Extent
•	Title: Revenue Recovery Act, 1890 (Act No. 1 of 1890)
•	Extent: Originally extended to the whole of India, except for modifications and exclusions in various regions over time.

Key Definitions
•	District: Includes a presidency-town.
•	Collector: The chief officer in charge of the land-revenue administration of a district (amended in Uttar Pradesh).
•	Defaulter: A person from whom an arrear of land-revenue or a sum recoverable as such is due, including sureties.

Provisions Summary
1.	Recovery Across Districts: - A Collector can send a certificate to another district's Collector to recover arrears.
•	The receiving Collector treats the amount as if it were a local arrear of land-revenue.
2.	Certificate for Recovery: - Specifies the defaulter's details, amount payable, and the account.
•	Conclusive proof of the stated matters unless otherwise provided.
3.	Other Provisions Mentioned: - Protection to Persons Acting Under the Act: No suit lies against persons acting in good faith under the Act.
•	Recovery by Collectors: Can recover sums from other public officers or local authorities.

meta.dc.legislation.history:
Legislative History:

The Revenue Recovery Act, 1890

● Act Title - The Revenue Recovery Act, 1890

● Act Number / Year - 1 of 1890

● Act ID (India Code) - 189001

● Presidential Assent Date - February 14, 1890

● Enforcement Date - February 14, 1890

● Nodal Ministry - Ministry of Finance

Precedent & Historical Rationale

● Territorial Inadequacy in Recovering Inter-District and Inter-Provincial Arrears - Prior to 1890, the statutory machinery for recovering land revenue and other public dues was strictly localized within each district or province. When a revenue defaulter possessed no attachable property within the district where the default occurred, or relocated their assets to another district or province, the local Collector lacked the statutory jurisdiction to enforce recovery outside their own territorial boundaries, necessitating cumbersome and expensive regular civil suits.

● Streamlined Certificate Procedure for Nationwide Revenue Recovery - Formulated to create a uniform, summary procedure for realizing public revenues and statutory sums recoverable as arrears of land revenue throughout British India. The Act enabled the Collector of a district where an arrear accrued to issue a formal revenue recovery certificate to the Collector of any other district where the defaulter held property, authorizing the receiving Collector to attach, sell, and realize the dues under their local revenue recovery laws as if the arrear had accrued within their own jurisdiction.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

● Formulation - Introduced to establish an efficient inter-provincial and inter-district certificate system to eliminate jurisdictional bottlenecks in the recovery of public debts and land revenue arrears.

● Parliamentary Passage - Considered, reviewed by a Select Committee, and passed by the Council of the Governor General of India for making Laws and Regulations in early 1890.

● Presidential Assent - Received the assent of the Governor General of India on February 14, 1890.

● Enforcement - Enforced on February 14, 1890

Sources - Official Records of the Governor General in Council, India Code, and Ministry of Finance.

title: The Indian Tolls (Army and Air Force) Act, 1901

meta.dc.description.abstract:
The Indian Tolls (Army and Air Force) Act, 1901

Objective
•	To facilitate the free and efficient movement of the Army and Air Force in the discharge of official duties.
•	To prevent delays in military operations caused by the payment of tolls.
•	To support national defence by granting statutory exemptions from toll charges.
Key Provisions
•	Exempts members of the Indian Army and the Indian Air Force, when on official duty, from payment of specified tolls.
•	Provides toll exemption for military vehicles, animals, stores, ammunition, and other government property used for defence purposes.
•	Applies to tolls levied on roads, bridges, ferries, and similar public crossings where the Act is in force.
•	Authorizes the Central Government to interpret and administer the provisions relating to such exemptions.
•	Ensures that the exemption is available only for official military purposes and not for private use.

meta.dc.legislation.history:
Legislative History:

The Indian Tolls (Army and Air Force) Act, 1901

● Act Title - The Indian Tolls (Army and Air Force) Act, 1901

● Act Number / Year - 2 of 1901

● Act ID (India Code) - 190102

● Assent Date - February 22, 1901

● Enforcement Date - April 01, 1901

● Nodal Ministry - Ministry of Defence

Precedent & Historical Rationale

● Deficiencies and Inconsistencies of the Tolls (Army) Act, 1888 - Prior to 1901, toll exemptions for armed forces traversing public transit routes were governed by the Tolls (Army) Act, 1888 (Act I of 1888). Experience revealed that the 1888 statute was narrowly drawn, ambiguous regarding the scope of exemptions for modern military baggage trains, irregular corps, and remount animals, and contained drafting loopholes that led to recurring disputes between toll-lessees or local authorities and moving military units.

● Unified Statutory Code for Toll Exemptions and Movement Protection - Formulated to consolidate and amend the law relating to the toll exemptions of military and defense personnel across India. The Act granted absolute statutory exemption from the payment of road, bridge, ferry, and canal tolls to officers, soldiers, reservists, auxiliary forces, their transport animals, carriages, and authorized baggage while on duty or moving under lawful military orders, providing summary penalties against toll-gatherers demanding unlawful charges.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

● Formulation - Drafted by the Military and Legislative Departments of the Government of India to replace the Tolls (Army) Act, 1888 with a comprehensive, dispute-free code safeguarding military troop mobility across provincial and municipal jurisdictions.

● Parliamentary Passage - Introduced as The Indian Tolls (Army) Bill, 1901 in the Council of the Governor General of India for the purpose of making Laws and Regulations, examined by a Select Committee, and passed during the Winter Session of 1901.

● Governor-General's Assent - Received the assent of the Governor-General of India (Lord Curzon) on February 22, 1901.

● Enforcement - Enforced on February 22, 1901

Sources - Official Records of the Council of the Governor General of India, India Code, and Ministry of Defence.

Summary of the Indian Reserve Forces Act, 1888

2.	Service Commitment: - Members are liable for service both within India and beyond its borders.
3.	Governance and Discipline: - The Central Government has the authority to formulate rules for the forces' governance, discipline, and regulation.

Legislative History:

The Indian Reserve Forces Act, 1888

Legislative History: The Indian Reserve Forces Act, 1888

● Act Title - The Indian Reserve Forces Act, 1888

● Act Number / Year - 4 of 1888

● Act ID (India Code) - 188804

● Presidential Assent Date - March 2, 1888

● Enforcement Date - March 26, 1888

● Nodal Ministry - Ministry of Defence

Precedent & Historical Rationale

● Absence of a Statutory Framework for Indian Military Reserves - Prior to 1888, the native army in British India operated almost entirely as a regular standing force without a well-organized, statutory reserve corps. Following geopolitical tensions in Central Asia (such as the Panjdeh Incident of 1885) and the strategic requirement to expand military mobilization capabilities rapidly without maintaining an expensive permanent standing army, a reserve system for Indian soldiers became critically necessary.

● Establishment, Training, and Disciplinary Control of the Indian Reserve Forces - Formulated to provide for the constitution, regulation, and discipline of the Indian Reserve Forces. The Act established two distinct divisions—the Active Reserve and the Garrison Reserve—empowered the Governor-General in Council to frame rules for periodic military training, and brought reservists under the discipline of the Indian Articles of War whenever called out for service or training.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

● Formulation - Introduced by the Military Department of the Government of India to provide a modern legislative basis for creating and mobilizing auxiliary and reserve armed forces across British India.

● Parliamentary Passage - Considered, debated, and passed by the Council of the Governor General of India for making Laws and Regulations in early 1888.

● Presidential Assent - Received the assent of the Governor General of India on March 2, 1888.

● Enforcement - Enforced on March 26, 1888

Sources - Official Records of the Governor General in Council, India Code, and Ministry of Defence.

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary  of Mediation Act, 2023, 

Key Provisions
1.	Scope and Application
•	Governs mediations in India, with specified conditions (Section 2).
•	Excludes disputes listed in the First Schedule (e.g., criminal prosecutions, certain third-party rights, environmental/competition law, tax disputes, and cases involving minors, mental illness, or professional discipline).
2.	Mediation Agreement and Pre-Litigation Mediation
•	Agreement: Must be in writing (Section 4).
•	Pre-Litigation: Mandatory for certain commercial suits unless exempt (Section 12A of the Commercial Courts Act, 2015, as amended).
3.	Mediation Proceedings
•	Conduct and Neutrality: Mediator facilitates settlement impartially (Section 15).
•	Duration: Typically 120 days, extendable by 60 days with consent (Section 18).
•	Confidentiality: Strict confidentiality obligations (Sections 22 & 23).
4.	Mediated Settlement Agreement (MSA)
•	Form and Authentication: Written and authenticated by the mediator (Section 19).
•	Registration and Enforcement: Voluntary registration; enforceable as a court order if registered (Section 20).
5.	Mediator’s Role and Responsibilities
•	Facilitation: Assists in reaching a voluntary settlement (Section 16).
•	Conflicts and Prohibitions: Cannot later act as an arbitrator or witness in the same matter (Section 17).
6.	Costs and Fees
•	Sharing: Equally borne by parties unless otherwise agreed (Section 25).
•	Mediator’s Fee: As prescribed (Section 25 and amendments to other Acts).
7.	Overriding Clause and Amendments
•	Precedence: This Act overrides conflicting provisions in other laws (Section 55).
•	Amendments: Modifies the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996; the Commercial Courts Act, 2015; the Consumer Protection Act, 2019; and others to align with mediation principles.
8.	Mediation Council of India
•	Establishment: Body corporate for promoting and regulating mediation (Section 31).
•	Functions: Includes setting guidelines, accrediting mediators, and maintaining standards (Section 38).
9.	Mediation Service Providers and Institutes
•	Recognition and Roles: Providers accredited by the Mediation Council; responsibilities include facilitating mediation and maintaining mediator panels (Sections 40-42).

Legislative History: 
The Mediation Act, 2023 

Source: Official Record of Parliament, India Code, and Ministry of Law and Justice 

Act Title- The Mediation Act, 2023 
Act Number - Act No. 32 of 2023 
Act ID (India Code) - 202332 
 Presidential Assent date - September 14, 2023.
 Enforcement Date - October 09, 2023 
Nodal Ministry - Ministry of Law and Justice 

Precedent & Historical Rationale

●	First Standalone Mediation Framework: Replaces fragmented provisions scattered across statutes like Section 89 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, establishing India's first comprehensive standalone law to encourage, govern, and enforce civil and commercial mediation.
●	Establishment of MCI & Statutory Enforceability: Creates the Mediation Council of India (MCI) to regulate mediation service providers and institutes, while granting Mediated Settlement Agreements (MSAs) the same legal status and enforceability as a civil court decree.
 
Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment
●	Formulation: Introduced by the Ministry of Law and Justice to promote institutional mediation, reduce judicial pendency across Indian courts, and strengthen India's position as a hub for international and domestic alternative dispute resolution.
●	Parliamentary Passage: Introduced in the Rajya Sabha on December 20, 2021; referred to the Parliamentary Standing Committee on Personnel, Public Grievances, Law and Justice; passed by the Rajya Sabha on August 1, 2023; and passed by the Lok Sabha on August 7, 2023.
●	Presidential Assent: Received the assent of the President of India on September 14, 2023.
●	Enforcement: Enforced on October 09, 2023.

Legislative History:

The Suits Valuation Act, 1887

● Act Title - The Suits Valuation Act, 1887

● Act Number / Year - 7 of 1887

● Act ID (India Code) - 188707

● Presidential Assent Date - February 11, 1887

● Enforcement Date - March 1, 1889

● Nodal Ministry - Ministry of Law and Justice

Precedent & Historical Rationale

● Divergence Between Fiscal Court-Fee Valuation & Pecuniary Jurisdiction - Prior to 1887, the Court-fees Act, 1870 prescribed rules for calculating fiscal court fees payable on plaints, but provided no uniform statutory mechanism to determine the separate valuation of suits for the purpose of deciding the pecuniary jurisdiction of civil courts. Litigants frequently manipulated suit valuations to choose favorable forums (forum shopping) or evade higher-tier judicial scrutiny, creating widespread confusion across provincial civil courts.

● Statutory Rules for Jurisdictional Valuation & Curative Procedural Safeguards - Formulated to prescribe the mode of valuing certain suits for the purpose of determining jurisdiction of courts. The Act empowered Provincial Governments to frame rules for valuing land and real property suits for jurisdictional purposes, linked jurisdictional valuation directly to court-fee computation for specified civil suits (Section 8), and introduced an important curative rule (Section 11) ensuring that appellate courts would not entertain objections to jurisdictional over-valuation or under-valuation unless raised at the earliest opportunity and resulting in a failure of justice.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

● Formulation - Introduced to complement the Court-fees Act, 1870 and Civil Courts Acts by establishing a clear, uniform method for computing pecuniary jurisdiction across British India.

● Parliamentary Passage - Considered, reviewed by a Select Committee, and passed by the Council of the Governor General of India for making Laws and Regulations in early 1887.

● Presidential Assent - Received the assent of the Governor General of India on February 11, 1887.

● Enforcement - Enforced on March 1, 1889

Sources - Official Records of the Governor General in Council, India Code and Ministry of Law and Justice.

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of The National Commission for Allied and Healthcare Professions Act, 2021
I. Governance and Establishment
•	National Commission for Allied and Healthcare Professions:
•	Established by the Central Government to oversee allied and healthcare professions.
•	Composition: Includes a Chairperson, Vice-Chairperson, and members from various backgrounds (government, institutions, and professions).
•	State Allied and Healthcare Councils:
•	Established at the state level with similar compositional structures.
•	Primary Function: Verify educational standards in state-level allied and healthcare institutions.
II. Regulatory and Standardization Framework
•	Key Functions of the Commission:
•	Standard Setting: Defines basic standards for education, professional conduct, and ethics.
•	Registration: Maintains a Central Allied and Healthcare Professionals' Register.
•	Uniform Examinations: Conducts entry and exit exams to ensure competency.
•	State Council Responsibilities:
•	Approve new institutions, courses, and capacity expansions based on predefined factors (financial resources, facilities, standards of education).
III. Practice and Registration
•	Registration Imperative:
•	Mandatory for practice; entitles professionals to official positions and fee collection.
•	Certificate and Renewal:
•	Issued upon registration; renewable with specified fees and procedures.
•	Removal from Register:
•	Grounds include misrepresentation, criminal conviction, and unethical conduct.
IV. Enforcement and Penalties
•	Offences and Penalties:
•	Falsely claiming registration or using titles without registration.
•	Penalties include fines (up to ₹1,000 for certain violations) and potential imprisonment.
•	Good Faith Protection:
•	Actions taken in good faith under the Act are protected from legal repercussions.
V. Administrative and Financial Provisions
•	Funding:
•	Grants, funds, and financial regulations for the Commission and State Councils.
•	Reporting and Audit:
•	Annual reports and audits ensure transparency and accountability.
VI. Establishment of New Institutions and Courses
•	Permission Process:
•	Mandatory permission from State Council (or Commission if no State Council) for new establishments, courses, or expansions.
•	Scheme Submission: Requires detailed plans, fees, and adherence to specified standards.
Key Takeaways
•	Unified Regulation: Aims to standardize and regulate allied and healthcare professions nationally.
•	Protection of Legitimate Practice: Safeguards registered professionals while penalizing unauthorized practice.
•	Quality Assurance: Emphasizes standards in education and practice through regular assessments and inspections.

THE INDIAN ANTARCTIC ACT, 2022
ACT NO. 13 OF 2022

[6th August, 2022.]

An Act to provide for the national measures for protecting the Antarctic environment and dependent and associated ecosystems and to give effect to the Antarctic Treaty, the Convention on the Conservation of Antarctic Marine Living Resources and to the Protocol on Environmental Protection to the Antarctic Treaty and for matters connected therewith or incidental thereto.
WHEREAS, the Antarctic Treaty was signed at Washington D.C. on the 1st day of December, 1959;
AND WHEREAS, the Antarctic Treaty was initially signed by twelve countries and since then forty-two other countries have acceded to the Treaty;
AND WHEREAS, of the total of fifty-four State Parties to the Treaty, twenty-nine countries have the status of Consultative Party with a right to vote in the Antarctic Consultative Meetings and twenty-five countries are Non-Consultative Parties having no right to vote therein;
AND WHEREAS, India signed the Antarctic Treaty on the 19th day of August, 1983 and received the consultative status on the 12th day of September, 1983;
AND WHEREAS, the Convention on the Conservation of Antarctic Marine Living Resources was signed at Canberra on the 20th day of May, 1980, inter alia, for the protection and preservation of the Antarctic environment and, in particular, for the preservation and conservation of marine living resources in Antarctica;
AND WHEREAS, India ratified the said Convention on the 17th day of June, 1985 and is a member of the Commission for Conservation of Antarctic Marine Living Resources under that Convention;
AND WHEREAS, the Protocol on Environmental Protection to the Antarctic Treaty was signed at Madrid on the 4th day of October, 1991, @inter alia, to strengthen the Antarctic Treaty system and for the development of a comprehensive regime for the protection of the Antarctic environment and dependent and associated ecosystems;
AND WHEREAS, India signed the Protocol on Environmental Protection to the Antarctic Treaty on the 14th day of January, 1998;
AND WHEREAS, the Antarctica lies south of 60° South Latitude and which is a natural reserve, devoted to peace and science and should not become the scene or object of any international discord;
AND WHEREAS, it is considered necessary to give effect to the said Treaty, the Convention and the Protocol and to make provisions for the protection of the Antarctic environment and dependent and associated ecosystems and for the regulation of various activities envisaged in Antarctica and for matters connected therewith or incidental thereto.
BE it enacted by Parliament in the Seventy-third Year of the Republic of India as follows:--

Precedent & Statutory Rationale
•	Alignment with International Legal Frameworks:
Gives domestic statutory effect to the Antarctic Treaty (1959), the Convention on the Conservation of Antarctic Marine Living Resources (1980), and the Protocol on Environmental Protection to the Antarctic Treaty (Madrid Protocol, 1991). 
•	Expanded Scope and Prohibitions:
Provides a robust legal framework to protect the Antarctic environment, prohibit mining, illegal activities, and nuclear explosions or disposal of radioactive waste. It applies jurisdiction over Indian citizens, corporate entities registered in India, foreign participants in Indian expeditions, and vessels/aircraft part of an Indian expedition. 
•	Governance and Penal Mechanisms:
Establishes the Committee on Antarctic Governance and Environmental Protection (CAG-EP) chaired by the Secretary of the Ministry of Earth Sciences to issue permits and monitor activities. Introduces strict penal consequences, ranging from heavy fines to imprisonment and life sentences for severe ecological violations like nuclear waste dumping. 

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment
•	Formulation: Drafted and piloted by the Ministry of Earth Sciences to fulfill India's international obligations as a Consultative Party to the Antarctic Treaty and regulate a transparent national program.
•	Parliamentary Passage: Introduced in the Lok Sabha on April 1, 2022; passed by the Lok Sabha on July 22, 2022, and subsequently passed by the Rajya Sabha on August 1, 2022. 
•	Presidential Assent: Received formal Presidential Assent on August 6, 2022, entering the statute book as Act No. 13 of 2022. 
•	Enforcement: Formally brought into operational force across India on August 7, 2023, via Official Gazette notification.

Summary of Fugitive Economic Offenders Act, 2018
The Act empowers Special Courts to declare a person as a Fugitive Economic Offender (FEO) and provides for the attachment and confiscation of their properties to ensure accountability and preserve the rule of law. 
Key Provisions
1. Declaration of Fugitive Economic Offender
•	Eligibility: A person against whom an arrest warrant has been issued for a scheduled economic offence involving ₹100 crore or more and who has left India or refuses to return to face prosecution may be declared a Fugitive Economic Offender. 
•	Application to Special Court: The Director or Deputy Director under the Prevention of Money-laundering Act, 2002 may apply to the Special Court for such a declaration. 
2. Attachment and Confiscation of Property
•	Attachment of Property: The authorities may attach the offender's properties, including proceeds of crime, before the declaration by the Special Court. 
•	Confiscation: Upon declaration as a Fugitive Economic Offender, the Special Court may order confiscation of the offender's properties, whether in India or abroad, subject to the Act. 
3. Proceedings before the Special Court
•	Notice to the Individual: The Special Court issues a notice requiring the alleged offender to appear at the specified place and time. 
•	Declaration: If the individual fails to appear within the prescribed period, the Court may declare the person a Fugitive Economic Offender after considering the evidence. 



4. Disentitlement from Civil Claims
•	Restriction on Civil Proceedings: A declared Fugitive Economic Offender, or a company in which they hold a majority interest, may be barred from pursuing or defending civil claims in Indian courts. 
•	Deterrence: This provision discourages offenders from evading criminal prosecution while continuing to benefit from the Indian legal system.

Precedent & Statutory Rationale

1. Combating High-Profile Financial Flight and Defraudment:

o Prior to 2018, the Indian financial and judicial systems faced severe challenges when prominent individuals accused of major economic scams, loan defaults, and banking frauds fled the country to evade criminal prosecution and trial.

o Traditional mechanisms under the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC) and the Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA) often fell short in swiftly attaching properties and preventing the dissipation of assets situated within or outside India by fugitives avoiding judicial summons.

2. Deterrence, Asset Confiscation, and Rule of Law:

o The Act was formulated to provide for measures to deter fugitive economic offenders from evading the process of law in India by staying outside the jurisdiction of Indian courts, thereby preserving the sanctity of the rule of law.

o It empowers designated Special Courts to declare individuals as "fugitive economic offenders" and order the immediate confiscation of their proceeds of crime and properties, while barring them from defending civil claims in legal proceedings.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

• Formulation: Initially promulgated via the Fugitive Economic Offenders Ordinance, 2018, in April 2018 before being introduced as a comprehensive bill by the Ministry of Finance.

• Parliamentary Passage: Debated and passed by both houses of the Parliament of India, receiving formal presidential assent on July 31, 2018.

• Enforcement: Enforced on April 21, 2018.

The Bilateral Netting of Qualified Financial Contracts Act, 2020 (Refined for Dispute Resolution Context)
Purpose in Dispute Resolution
•	Facilitates efficient dispute resolution in financial markets by ensuring the enforceability of bilateral netting agreements for qualified financial contracts, reducing potential disputes over contract obligations.
Key Components Relevant to Dispute Resolution
1.	Enforceability of Netting Agreements
•	Legally Binding: Ensures netting agreements are enforceable, minimizing disputes over contractual obligations.
•	Prevents Unilateral Backout: Reduces likelihood of one party backing out of agreed-upon netting terms, thus preventing a common source of disputes.
2.	Close-Out Netting in Insolvency/Default Scenarios
•	Clear Process: Defines a clear, enforceable process for close-out netting upon default or insolvency, reducing ambiguity that could lead to disputes.
•	Final and Binding Net Balance: The calculated net balance is final and binding, aiming to conclude disputes efficiently.
3.	Limitations on Administration Practitioner’s Powers
•	Protection of Netting Transactions: Safeguards against the invalidation of legitimate netting transactions, except in cases of fraud or undervaluation, thereby protecting parties from unjust reversal of agreements.
•	Reduces Potential for Disputes Over Asset Management: By limiting the powers of administrators, it reduces conflicts over the management of assets under netting agreements.
4.	Dispute Resolution Implications
•	Override Clause: The Act’s overriding power can preempt conflicting laws that might otherwise complicate dispute resolution.
•	Rule Making and Difficulty Removal: Empowers the Central Government to address emerging disputes or operational challenges through rule-making and difficulty removal provisions.
Implementation Aspects Affecting Dispute Resolution
•	Effective Date: Uniform application from October 1, 2020, ensures consistency in dispute resolution approaches.
•	Enactment: Act No. 30 of 2020 provides a clear legal framework for judges and arbitrators.

Summary of the National Medical Commission Act, 2019
The National Medical Commission Act, 2019
Brief Summary
The National Medical Commission (NMC) Act, 2019 was enacted to reform medical education and the regulation of the medical profession in India. It replaced the Medical Council of India (MCI) with the National Medical Commission (NMC) to improve transparency, accountability, and the quality of medical education and healthcare. The Act seeks to ensure the availability of qualified medical professionals, promote affordable medical education, and maintain high standards of medical practice across the country.
Objective
The main objectives of the Act are:
•	To establish the National Medical Commission as the apex regulatory body for medical education and practice.
•	To improve the quality, accessibility, and affordability of medical education.
•	To ensure transparent and accountable regulation of medical institutions and practitioners.
•	To maintain uniform standards of undergraduate and postgraduate medical education.
•	To promote ethical medical practice and protect the interests of patients.
•	To increase the availability of qualified medical professionals across India.
Key Provisions
1.	Establishment of the National Medical Commission (NMC)
o	The Act establishes the National Medical Commission to regulate medical education, medical institutions, medical professionals, and ethics in India.
2.	Replacement of the Medical Council of India
o	The Medical Council of India (MCI) was dissolved, and its regulatory functions were transferred to the NMC.
3.	Autonomous Boards
o	The NMC functions through four autonomous boards:
	Undergraduate Medical Education Board (UGMEB)
	Postgraduate Medical Education Board (PGMEB)
	Medical Assessment and Rating Board (MARB)
	Ethics and Medical Registration Board (EMRB)
4.	National Exit Test (NExT)
o	The Act provides for a common National Exit Test (NExT), which serves as:
	the final-year MBBS examination,
	the licentiate examination for registration to practice medicine,
	the entrance examination for postgraduate medical courses.
5.	Medical Institution Assessment
o	The Medical Assessment and Rating Board evaluates and assesses medical institutions to ensure compliance with prescribed standards.
6.	Regulation of Medical Colleges
o	The NMC is empowered to regulate the establishment of new medical colleges, increase in seats, and commencement of new courses, subject to the provisions of the Act.
7.	Medical Register
o	The Ethics and Medical Registration Board maintains the National Medical Register containing the details of all licensed medical practitioners.
8.	Fee Regulation
o	The Act empowers the NMC to regulate fees and other charges for up to 50% of seats in private medical institutions and deemed universities, as prescribed by regulations.
9.	Promotion of Ethics
o	The Act lays down mechanisms for maintaining professional ethics, investigating misconduct, and taking disciplinary action against registered medical practitioners.
10.	Community Health Providers
•	The Act enables the Commission to grant limited licences to specified categories of Community Health Providers to deliver primary and preventive healthcare, subject to prescribed qualifications and conditions.
11.	Advisory Role

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of the Code on Wages, 2019
The Code on Wages, 2019 is a landmark reform in India's labour framework. It modernizes, simplifies, and consolidates multiple fragmented laws into a single, comprehensive regulation. 
1. Objectives of the Code
The primary objective of the Code on Wages is to establish uniformity, transparency, and accountability in the payment of wages and bonuses while fostering a progressive economic environment. Key aims include: 
•	Consolidation of Laws: Amalgamating 4 central labor legislations into a single code to eliminate multiplicity of definitions and authorities. 
•	Universal Wage Security: Extending the statutory right to minimum wages and timely payment protections to all employees across both the organized and unorganized sectors. 
•	Ease of Compliance: Simplifying regulatory procedures through technology (e.g., single filings, digital registries) to reduce compliance burdens for establishments. 
•	Removal of Disparities: Eradicating gender discrimination in recruitment and wage payments for work of similar nature. 
2. Laws Subsumed
The Code on Wages replaces the following four central acts: 
1.	The Payment of Wages Act, 1936
2.	The Minimum Wages Act, 1948
3.	The Payment of Bonus Act, 1965
4.	The Equal Remuneration Act, 1976
3. Key Provisions
A. Universal Coverage & Unified Definition of Wages
•	Universal Applicability: Unlike older laws that limited protections to specific wage ceilings or "scheduled employments," the Code covers all employees in both the public and private sectors. 
•	Standardized Wage Structure: Defines wages explicitly to comprise three core components: Basic Pay, Dearness Allowance (DA), and Retaining Allowance. 
o	The 50% Rule: If an employee's excluded components (such as house rent, conveyance, or other special allowances) exceed 50% (or any specified percentage) of their total remuneration, the excess amount is added back into the wage pool. This directly standardizes calculations for social security benefits like Provident Fund (PF) and Gratuity. 
B. National Floor Wage & Minimum Wages
•	Floor Wage: The Central Government is empowered to fix a National Floor Wage based on the living standards of workers. 
•	State Obligations: State governments cannot set minimum wage rates lower than the national floor wage. If a state's existing minimum wage is higher than the floor wage, it cannot be reduced. 
•	Revision Intervals: Minimum wages must be reviewed and revised by the appropriate government at least once every 5 years. 
•	Determinants: Minimum wage structures are fixed based on geographical areas, skill levels (unskilled, semi-skilled, skilled, highly skilled), and the arduousness/difficulty of the work. 
C. Timely Payment of Wages
The Code mandates strict timelines for wage clearance depending on the wage period: 
•	Daily / Shift-end: At the end of the shift or day. 
•	Weekly: Before the weekly holiday. 
•	Fortnightly: Within two days of the end of the fortnight. 
•	Monthly: Before the expiry of the 7th day of the succeeding month. 
•	Resignation / Termination: Wages must be settled within 2 working days of separation. 
•	Modes of Payment: Payments can be made in coins, currency notes, via cheque, or by direct digital credit to the employee’s bank account. 
D. Permissible Deductions
Employer deductions from an employee’s wage are restricted to specific categories (e.g., fines, absence from duty, damage to property, recovery of advances, or accommodation provided by the employer). Total deductions cannot exceed 50% of an employee’s total wages. 
E. Bonus Payments
•	Eligibility: Employees drawing wages below a specific notified monthly threshold and who have worked for at least 30 days in an accounting year are eligible for an annual bonus. 
•	Calculation: The minimum bonus is fixed at 8.33% of wages or ₹100, whichever is higher, scaling up to a maximum cap of 20% of annual wages. 
F. Gender Equality
•	The Code strictly prohibits gender-based discrimination in matters concerning wage payment, hiring, and conditions of employment for work of the same or similar nature (evaluated on parameters of skill, effort, experience, and responsibility). 
G. Enforcement, Penalties, and Dispute Resolution
•	Inspector-cum-Facilitators: Replaces traditional inspectors with "Inspectors-cum-Facilitators" who provide advisory support for compliance alongside enforcement capabilities.
•	Extended Limitation Period: The time limit for employees to file wage-related claims has been expanded to 3 years (up from previous limits ranging between 6 months to 2 years). 
•	Graded Penalties: Penalties are structured based on the gravity of the violation. For minor, first-time infractions not punishable by imprisonment, provisions for compounding (settling) offenses are emphasized over immediate criminal prosecution.

1. Rationalization and Simplification of Complex Labor Laws:

o Prior to 2019, India's labor regulatory framework consisted of over 40 central laws characterized by complex compliance hurdles, overlapping definitions of wages, fragmented enforcement mechanisms, and a lack of universal minimum wage protection across diverse sectors.

o To ease compliance, eliminate administrative red tape, and align labor standards with modern economic realities, the Second National Commission on Labour recommended codifying dozens of central statutes into four broad labor codes.

o The Act was formulated to amend and consolidate the laws relating to wages and bonus and matters connected therewith or incidental thereto.

Summary of the International Financial Services Centres Authority Act, 2019
Overview
*Title: The International Financial Services Centres Authority Act, 2019 *Act No: 50 of 2019 *Purpose: Establishes a unified regulatory authority for International Financial Services Centres (IFSCs) in India, overseeing financial products, services, and institutions within these zones.
Key Provisions
1.	Authority Establishment
•	Name: International Financial Services Centres Authority
•	Structure: Body Corporate with a Chairperson, members from key financial regulators (RBI, SEBI, IRDAI, PFRDA), and Central Government nominees.
2.	Regulatory Scope
•	Jurisdiction: Exclusive regulation of financial products, services, and institutions in IFSCs.
•	Powers:
•	Regulate and develop IFSCs.
•	Exercise powers of RBI, SEBI, IRDAI, and PFRDA within IFSCs as specified.
•	Recommend new financial products/services to the Central Government.
3.	Amendments to Existing Legislation
•	Affected Acts: Multiple, including the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007, and the Pension Fund Regulatory and Development Authority Act, 2013.
•	Amendment Nature: Exempts IFSCs from the regulatory ambit of the amended acts, placing them under the International Financial Services Centres Authority.
4.	Operational and Governance Provisions
•	Reporting: Annual reports to the Central Government, to be laid before Parliament.
•	Rule Making: Empowers the Central Government and the Authority to make rules.
•	Immunity and Protection: For actions taken in good faith under the Act.

meta.dc.legislation.history:
Legislative History:

The International Financial Services Centres Authority Act, 2019

● Act Title - The International Financial Services Centres Authority Act, 2019

● Act Number / Year - 50 of 2019

● Act ID (India Code) - 201950

● Assent Date - December 19, 2019

● Enforcement Date - April 27, 2020

● Nodal Ministry - Ministry of Finance

Precedent & Historical Rationale

● Multiplicity of Regulators and Jurisdictional Bottlenecks in IFSCs - Under Section 18 of the Special Economic Zones Act, 2005, the establishment of India's first International Financial Services Centre (GIFT-IFSC in Gandhinagar) was permitted. However, entities operating within the IFSC were governed separately by four distinct domestic regulators: the Reserve Bank of India (RBI), the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI), the Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India (IRDAI), and the Pension Fund Regulatory and Development Authority (PFRDA), resulting in regulatory overlaps, friction, and compliance delays.

● Unified Statutory Architecture for Global Competitiveness - Formulated to establish a unified financial regulator to develop and regulate financial products, services, and institutions across International Financial Services Centres in India. The Act created the International Financial Services Centres Authority (IFSCA) as a single-window statutory regulator consolidating all regulatory, supervisory, and enforcement powers of the RBI, SEBI, IRDAI, and PFRDA within IFSCs, benchmarking the regime against premier global offshore financial hubs.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

● Formulation & Initial Introduction - Drafted by the Ministry of Finance (Department of Economic Affairs); initially introduced in the Rajya Sabha on February 12, 2019, during the 16th Lok Sabha, but subsequently withdrawn to incorporate stakeholder inputs and re-introduced in the 17th Lok Sabha.

● Parliamentary Passage - Re-introduced as The International Financial Services Centres Authority Bill, 2019 (Bill No. 343 of 2019) by Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman in the Lok Sabha on November 25, 2019, debated and passed by the Lok Sabha on December 11, 2019, and passed by the Rajya Sabha on December 12, 2019.

● President's Assent - Received the assent of the President of India (Ram Nath Kovind) on December 19, 2019, and was published in the Gazette of India on December 20, 2019.

● Enforcement - Enforced on April 27, 2020

Sources - Parliamentary Debates (Lok Sabha & Rajya Sabha), The Gazette of India, India Code, and Ministry of Finance.

meta.dc.description.abstract:
The Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Marriage) Act, 2019
Objective:
Protect the rights of married Muslim women by prohibiting instantaneous and irrevocable divorce (talaq-e-biddat) and ensuring their rights are safeguarded.
Key Provisions:
1.	Prohibition of Instantaneous Talaq:
•	Declares talaq-e-biddat (and similar forms) void and illegal.
2.	Penalties for Violation: - Imprisonment: Up to 3 years for the husband.
•	Fine: As determined by the court.
3.	Rights of the Aggrieved Wife: - Maintenance: Entitled to subsistence allowance for herself and dependent children.
•	Custody of Children: Right to custody of minor children, with the court deciding the arrangement.
4.	Legal Proceedings: - Cognizable Offence: Police can act without a warrant if reported by the wife or her relatives.
•	Compoundable Offence: Can be settled with the wife’s consent and court approval.
•	Conditional Bail: Granted only after considering the wife’s views.
5.	Jurisdictional Extension: - Initially excluded Jammu and Kashmir, later extended to Union Territories of Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh (Notification No. S.O. 3912 (E), 30th October 2019).
6.	Commencement: - Retroactive Effect: Deemed effective from 19th September, 2018.
Impact:
•	Strengthens legal protection for Muslim women against arbitrary divorce.
•	Ensures financial and custodial rights are protected through judicial oversight.

1. Upholding Gender Equality and Constitutional Rights:

o Prior to 2019, despite the historic Supreme Court judgment in Shayara Bano v. Union of India (2017) which declared instantaneous triple talaq (talaq-e-biddat) unconstitutional and void, many married Muslim women continued to face arbitrary and instantaneous divorces without adequate legal recourse or protection.

o The legislative action was necessitated to eliminate discriminatory customary practices, secure gender equality, protect the fundamental rights of married Muslim women, and uphold human dignity under the rule of law.

2. Prohibition and Penal Deterrence:

o The Act was formulated to protect the rights of married Muslim women and to prohibit divorce by pronouncing talaq (in any form of instantaneous or irrevocable divorce) by their husbands.

THE NATIONAL CAPITAL TERRITORY OF DELHI (RECOGNITION OF PROPERTY RIGHTS OF RESIDENTS IN UNAUTHORISED COLONIES) ACT, 2019
ACT NO. 45 OF 2019

[11th December, 2019.]

An Act to provide special provisions for the National Capital Territory of Delhi for recognising the property rights of resident in unauthorised colonies by securing the rights of ownership or transfer or mortgage in favour of the residents of such colonies who are possessing properties on the basis of Power of Attorney, Agreement to Sale, Will, possession letter or any other documents including documents evidencing payment of consideration and for the matters connected therewith or incidental thereto.
WHEREAS there has been phenomenal increase in the population of the National Capital Territory of Delhi in the last few decades owing to migration and other factors but development of planned housing colonies have not kept pace with the requirements of a burgeoning population resulting in the increase of unauthorised colonies;
AND WHEREAS number of unauthorised colonies have been identified in the National Capital Territory of Delhi on the basis of applications made by the Residents Welfare Associations for regularisation in pursuance to notification number S.O. 683(E), dated the 24th March, 2008 of the Delhi Development Authority, published in the Gazette of India, Extraordinary, Part II, Section 3, Sub-section (ii), dated the 24th March, 2008;
AND WHEREAS the properties in these colonies are not being registered by registering authority and thereby the residents do not have any title documents in respect of such properties and the Banks and financial institutions do not extend any credit facilities in respect of said properties;
AND WHEREAS the ownership of the properties in unauthorised colonies have been transferred several times through registered or un-registered or notarised Power of Attorney, Agreement to Sale, Will, possession letter and other documents including documents evidencing payment of consideration and stamp duty on these multiple transactions have neither assessed nor been paid;
AND WHEREAS the stamp duty on the conveyance deed or authorisation slip, as the case may be, is leviable as per minimum rates (circle rates) specified in the notification of the Government of the National Capital Territory of Delhi published vide number F.1(953) Regn. Br./ Div. Com/HQ/2014, dated the 22nd September, 2014 or the sale consideration mentioned in the conveyance deed or authorisation slip, as the case may be, whichever is higher;
AND WHEREAS the Supreme Court in the case of Suraj Lamp & Industries (P) Ltd. Vs. State of Haryana & others vide its judgment dated the 11th October, 2011 had held that sale agreement/general Power of Attorney or Will transactions are not “transfers” or “sales” and that such transactions cannot be treated as completed transfers or conveyances and they can continue to be treated as existing agreement of sale;
AND WHEREAS keeping in view the socio-economic conditions of the residents of these unauthorised colonies and ground realities, it is desirable to recognise and confer rights of ownership or transfer or mortgage to the residents of such colonies on the basis of Power of Attorney, Agreement to Sale, Will, possession letter and other documents including documents evidencing payment of consideration and to facilitate development or re-development that may improve existing infrastructure, civic and social amenities which may lead to better quality of life;
AND WHEREAS it is expedient to have a law to recognise and confer rights of ownership or transfer or mortgage to the residents of unauthorised colonies as one time special measure.
BE it enacted by Parliament in the Seventieth Year of the Republic of India as follows:--

1. Securing Property Rights for Residents of Unauthorized Colonies:

o Prior to 2019, millions of residents living across hundreds of unauthorized colonies in the National Capital Territory of Delhi faced severe legal and financial vulnerability because their properties were held on the basis of intermediate documentation like General Power of Attorney (GPA), Agreements to Sell, Wills, or possession letters rather than registered conveyance deeds.

o This lack of formal title prevented residents from accessing bank credit, transferring property legally, or enjoying secure land tenure, leading to systemic socio-economic distress and urban squalor.

2. Granting Legal Recognition and Ownership Rights:

o The Act was formulated to provide special provisions for the National Capital Territory of Delhi for recognising the property rights of residents in unauthorised colonies by securing the rights of ownership, transfer, or mortgage in favour of such residents.

o It establishes a structured process for conferring ownership or conveyance rights based on payment of nominal considerations and existing transactional documents, bringing millions of urban citizens into the formal property economy.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

• Formulation: Prepared and brought forward by the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs following comprehensive cabinet reviews and spatial policy frameworks formulated to address Delhi's long-standing urban housing challenges.

• Parliamentary Passage: Debated and passed by both houses of the Parliament of India, receiving the formal assent of the President of India on November 12, 2019.

• Enforcement: Enforced on December 11, 2019.

Source: India Code (indiacode.gov.in) and Ministry of Law and Justice Official Records.

THE NATIONAL FORENSIC SCIENCES UNIVERSITY ACT, 2020
ACT NO. 32 OF 2020

28th September, 2020.

An Act to establish and declare an institution to be known as the National Forensic Sciences University as an institution of national importance to facilitate and promote studies and research and to achieve excellence in the field of forensic science in conjunction with applied behavioural science studies, law, criminology and other allied areas and technology and other related fields, and to provide for matters connected therewith or incidental thereto.
BE it enacted by Parliament in the Seventy-first Year of the Republic of India as follows:--
meta.dc.legislation.history:
Legislative History:

The National Forensic Sciences University Act, 2020

● Act Title - The National Forensic Sciences University Act, 2020

● Act Number / Year - 32 of 2020

● Act ID (India Code) - 202032

● Assent Date - September 28, 2020

● Enforcement Date - October 1, 2020

● Nodal Ministry - Ministry of Home Affairs

Precedent & Historical Rationale

● Severe National Shortage of Forensic Capacity and Criminal Justice Delays - India’s criminal justice system suffered from an acute, systemic shortage of trained forensic science experts, behavioral scientists, digital forensic investigators, and forensic pathologists. This deficit caused severe bottlenecks in the investigation of serious crimes, a backlog of evidence awaiting laboratory testing in Central and State Forensic Science Laboratories (FSLs), low conviction rates, and a lack of standardized advanced academic and research institutions dedicated exclusively to forensic and investigative sciences.

● Elevation of the Gujarat Forensic Sciences University and Statutory Central Mandate - In 2008, the Government of Gujarat established the Gujarat Forensic Sciences University (GFSU) at Gandhinagar under a state act. Recognizing the national necessity for an apex, dedicated central institution, the Union Government decided to elevate GFSU and absorb the Lok Nayak Jayaprakash Narayan National Institute of Criminology and Forensic Sciences (LNJN-NICFS, New Delhi) into a single central university of national importance.

● Statutory Incorporation as an Institution of National Importance - Formulated to establish and incorporate the National Forensic Sciences University (NFSU) as an Institution of National Importance. The Act provided for the dissolution of the erstwhile GFSU and the integration of LNJN-NICFS into the new university, mandated it to facilitate and promote studies and research in applied forensic science, cyber security, digital forensics, criminology, and behavioral sciences, and empowered it to affiliate colleges, establish off-campuses across India and abroad, and train police officers, prosecutors, judges, and forensic specialists.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

● Formulation - Drafted by the Ministry of Home Affairs to build modern forensic capabilities for the criminal justice system and support police modernization reforms.

● Parliamentary Passage - Introduced as The National Forensic Sciences University Bill, 2020 (Bill No. 86 of 2020) by Minister of State for Home Affairs G. Kishan Reddy in the Lok Sabha on March 23, 2020, during the Budget Session.

○ Lok Sabha - Debated and passed on September 20, 2020, during the Monsoon Session.

○ Rajya Sabha - Considered and passed on September 22, 2020.

● President's Assent - Received the assent of the President of India (Ram Nath Kovind) on September 28, 2020.

● Enforcement - Enforced on October 1, 2020

Sources - Parliamentary Debates (Lok Sabha & Rajya Sabha), The Gazette of India, India Code, and Ministry of Home Affairs.

THE RASHTRIYA RAKSHA UNIVERSITY ACT, 2020
ACT NO. 31 OF 2020

28th September, 2020.

An Act to establish and declare an institution to be known as the Rashtriya Raksha University as an institution of national importance and to provide for its incorporation and matters connected therewith or incidental thereto.
BE it enacted by Parliament in the Seventy-first Year of the Republic of India as follows:--
meta.dc.legislation.history:
Legislative History:

The Rashtriya Raksha University Act, 2020.

● Act Title - The Rashtriya Raksha University Act, 2020

● Act Number / Year - 31 of 2020

● Act ID (India Code) - 202031

● Assent Date - September 28, 2020

● Enforcement Date - October 1, 2020

● Nodal Ministry - Ministry of Home Affairs

Precedent & Historical Rationale

● Deficiencies in Specialized National Security, Policing, and Strategic Training - India's internal security landscape, policing apparatus, and national defense agencies faced evolving, multi-dimensional threats spanning cross-border terrorism, border management, cyber warfare, coastal security, and organized crime. Traditional police training academies and defense colleges primarily offered in-service tactical or administrative instruction, lacking an apex academic and research institution dedicated to multi-disciplinary education, strategic analysis, research, and skill development in policing and internal security for both civilian students and security forces.

● Elevation of Raksha Shakti University to Central Status - In 2009, the Government of Gujarat established the Raksha Shakti University (RSU) at Gandhinagar under The Raksha Shakti University Act, 2009 (Gujarat Act No. 17 of 2009) as a pioneer state-level security and police university. Recognizing the critical need to scale this model into a premier national institution catering to the entire country's security architecture, the Union Government sought to elevate RSU into a central university of national importance.

● Statutory Incorporation as an Institution of National Importance - Formulated to establish and incorporate the Rashtriya Raksha University (RRU) at Gandhinagar, Gujarat, and declare it to be an Institution of National Importance. The Act dissolved the state-level Raksha Shakti University Society and University, vesting all its properties, assets, and liabilities into the new central university, mandated it to provide specialized education, research, and training in national security, police sciences, military affairs, cybersecurity, and maritime security, and empowered it to establish off-campuses, regional centers, and affiliate institutions across India and globally.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

● Formulation - Drafted by the Ministry of Home Affairs to build a robust cadre of internal security and law enforcement professionals under the police modernization drive.

● Parliamentary Passage - Introduced as The Rashtriya Raksha University Bill, 2020 (Bill No. 85 of 2020) by Minister of State for Home Affairs G. Kishan Reddy in the Lok Sabha on March 23, 2020, during the Budget Session.

○ Lok Sabha - Debated and passed on September 20, 2020, during the Monsoon Session.

○ Rajya Sabha - Considered and passed on September 22, 2020.

● President's Assent - Received the assent of the President of India (Ram Nath Kovind) on September 28, 2020.

● Enforcement - Enforced on October 1, 2020.

Sources - Parliamentary Debates (Lok Sabha & Rajya Sabha), The Gazette of India, India Code, and Ministry of Home Affairs.

THE BILATERAL NETTING OF QUALIFIED FINANCIAL CONTRACTS ACT, 2020
ACT NO. 30 OF 2020

[28th September, 2020.]

An Act to ensure financial stability and promote competitiveness in Indian financial markets by providing enforceability of bilateral netting of qualified financial contracts and for matters connected therewith or incidental thereto.
BE it enacted by Parliament in the Seventy-first Year of the Republic of India as follows:---
meta.dc.legislation.history:
Legislative History:

The Bilateral Netting of Qualified Financial Contracts Act, 2020

Short Title - The Bilateral Netting of Qualified Financial Contracts Act, 2020

Act Number / Year - 30 of 2020

India Code Act ID - 202030

Introduced In - Lok Sabha

Presidential Assent Date - September 28, 2020

Official Gazette Publication - September 28, 2020

Enforcement Date - October 1, 2020

Nodal Ministry - Ministry of Finance

Precedent & Statutory Rationale

1. Gross-Basis Capital Constraints and Systemic Risk:

o Prior to 2020, India lacked a formal statutory framework recognizing bilateral netting for over-the-counter (OTC) derivative and financial transactions. Financial institutions and banks were legally mandated to measure counterparty credit exposure on a gross basis rather than a net basis. This artificially inflated capital requirements, blocked significant amounts of liquidity, and amplified systemic risk during default events.

2. Enhancing Financial Stability and Market Competitiveness:

o Grounded in recommendations from international multilateral organizations (such as the International Swaps and Derivatives Association - ISDA) and domestic financial sector reforms, the legislation was enacted to provide legal certainty, encourage efficient margining, reduce capital burdens on banks, and deepen India's corporate bond and derivatives markets.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

• Formulation: Developed and piloted by the Ministry of Finance (Department of Economic Affairs) to modernize India's financial architecture and align it with global regulatory standards.

• Parliamentary Passage: Introduced as the Bilateral Netting of Qualified Financial Contracts Bill in the Lok Sabha on September 14, 2020; debated and passed by the Lok Sabha on September 20, 2020; and subsequently passed by the Rajya Sabha.

• Presidential Assent: Received formal Presidential Assent from President Ram Nath Kovind on September 28, 2020, entering the statute book as Act No. 30 of 2020.

• Enforcement: Brought into active operational force on October 1, 2020

Source: India Code and Ministry of Finance Official Records.

Summary of The Dam Safety Act, 2021
Overview
*Purpose: Ensures the safe functioning of specified dams through surveillance, inspection, operation, and maintenance to prevent dam failure-related disasters. *Jurisdiction & Commencement: Applicable across India, with commencement on 30th December, 2021.
Key Institutional Mechanisms
1.	National Committee on Dam Safety
•	Evolves dam safety policies.
•	Recommends necessary regulations.
2.	National Dam Safety Authority (Authority)
•	Implements policies and makes regulations.
•	Provides technical assistance to State Dam Safety Organisations.
•	Resolves disputes between State Dam Safety Organisations or with dam owners.
•	Maintains a national database of specified dams.
3.	State Committee on Dam Safety & State Dam Safety Organisation
•	State-level oversight and implementation of dam safety guidelines.
Core Provisions
1.	Dam Safety Units & Inspections
•	Mandatory dam safety units within owner's operation and maintenance setup.
•	Annual pre and post-monsoon inspections, plus inspections after natural/man-made calamities.
2.	Instrumentation & Data Collection
•	Installation of specified instrumentations for performance monitoring.
•	Establishment of hydro-meteorological and seismological stations for data collection.
3.	Comprehensive Dam Safety Evaluation
•	First evaluation within 5 years of Act's commencement, then at intervals specified by regulations.
•	Includes design, construction, operation, and seismic safety reviews.
4.	Emergency Preparedness
•	Emergency Action Plans: Mandatory for all specified dams, updated regularly.
•	Risk Assessment Studies: At intervals specified by regulations, first within 5 years.
5.	Qualifications & Construction/Alteration
•	Prescribed qualifications for individuals in dam safety.
•	Accreditation requirements for agencies involved in dam construction/alteration.
6.	Oversight & Reporting
•	Annual reports by State Dam Safety Organisations and the Authority.
•	Reports laid before Parliament/State Legislatures.
Regulatory & Miscellaneous Provisions
•	Regulatory Framework: Rules by Central/State Governments and Regulations by the Authority.
•	Overriding Effect: Precedence over inconsistent provisions in other laws.
•	Transboundary Considerations: Provisions for dams outside India affecting Indian interests.
Schedules (Summarized from Provided Context)
•	The First Schedule: Outlines 11 functions of the National Committee on Dam Safety, including policy evolution, distress condition relief, and research identification.
•	The Second Schedule: Details 32 functions of the National Dam Safety Authority, encompassing regulation, dispute resolution, database maintenance, and accreditation.
•	The Third Schedule: (Not summarized due to lack of provided content) Functions of State Committee on Dam Safety, including guideline adherence, work review, and mitigation coordination.
Enforcement & Compliance
•	Enforceable Directions: By the Authority for safety and remedial measures.
•	Funding Responsibility: Owners must provide adequate funds for remedial measures.
•	Penalties: (Not detailed in the summary, implies presence in the full Act for non-compliance)
