THE DAM SAFETY ACT, 2021
ACT NO. 41 OF 2021

[13th December, 2021.]

An Act to provide for surveillance, inspection, operation and maintenance of the specified dam for prevention of dam failure related disasters and to provide for institutional mechanism to ensure their safe functioning and for matters connected therewith or incidental thereto.
BE it enacted by Parliament in the Seventy-second Year of the Republic of India as follows:—
meta.dc.legislation.history:
Legislative History: 
The Dam Safety Act, 2021

Sources : India Code (indiacode.nic.in), Ministry of Jal Shakti Official Records

Short Title -  The Dam Safety Act, 2021
Act Number / Year -  Act No. 41 of 2021
Act ID (India Code) - 202141
Presidential Assent / Enactment Date -  December 13, 2021
Official Gazette Publication -  December 30, 2021
Enforcement Date -  December 30, 2021
 Nodal Ministry - Ministry of Jal Shakti
 Nodal Department - Department of Water Resources, River Development and Ganga Rejuvenation

Precedent & Statutory Rationale
1.	Need for a Uniform Standard for Dam Safety:
o	Prior to 2021, the safety of specified dams across India was governed by a patchwork of state-level regulations, institutional frameworks, and guidelines, leading to inconsistencies in surveillance, inspection, operation, and maintenance.
o	With thousands of large dams aging across the country, catastrophic failures posed severe risks to human life, property, and river ecology, necessitating a robust, centralized, and standardized national legal framework.
2.	Establishment of Institutional Mechanisms:
o	The Act provides for the surveillance, inspection, operation, and maintenance of specified dams to prevent dam failure-related disasters.
o	It establishes key institutional bodies at both national and state levels: the National Committee on Dam Safety, the National Dam Safety Organisation, State Dam Safety Organisations, and State Committees on Dam Safety to ensure uniform safety protocols and accountability.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment
•	Formulation: Piloted and drafted by the Ministry of Jal Shakti (Department of Water Resources, River Development and Ganga Rejuvenation) to address nationwide dam safety concerns and fulfill long-standing recommendations of various expert panels.
•	Parliamentary Passage: Tabled, debated, and passed by both Houses of Parliament, receiving Presidential Assent on December 13, 2021.
•	Enforcement: Enforced on December 30, 2021.

THE CRIMINAL PROCEDURE (IDENTIFICATION) ACT, 2022
ACT NO. 11 OF 2022

[18th April, 2022.]

An Act to authorise for taking measurements of convicts and other persons for the purposes of identification and investigation in criminal matters and to preserve records and for matters connected therewith and incidental thereto.
BE it enacted by Parliament in the Seventy-third Year of the Republic of India as follows:--
meta.dc.legislation.history:
Legislative History:
The Criminal Procedure (Identification) Act, 2022

Source: India Code Official Repository (indiacode.nic.in) and Ministry of Home Affairs Official Records 
 
Short Title - The Criminal Procedure (Identification) Act, 2022
Act Number / Year - Act No. 11 of 2022
India Code Act ID - 2022-11
Introduced In - Parliament (Lok Sabha as The Criminal Procedure (Identification) Bill, 2022)
Presidential Assent Date - April 18, 2022
Official Gazette Publication - April 18, 2022 (Extraordinary Gazette Part II, Section 1)
Enforcement Date - August 4, 2022 (vide Gazette Notification No. S.O. 3653(E))
 Nodal Ministry  - Ministry of Home Affairs (Department of Internal Security)
Statutory Predecessor Framework - Repealed and replaced the colonial-era Identification of Prisoners Act, 1920 (Act No. 33 of 1920).

Precedent & Statutory Rationale
•	Modernization and Technological Alignment:
The 1920 colonial law was heavily restricted to collecting baseline fingerprints, foot-print impressions, and photographs. The 2022 Act modernized identification techniques to match global investigative standards by incorporating advanced digital, biometric, and biological metrics. 
•	Expanded Definition of "Measurements":
Broadened the scope of data collection to include finger-impressions, palm-print impressions, foot-print impressions, photographs, iris and retina scans, physical and biological samples along with their analysis, and behavioral attributes including signatures and handwriting. 
•	Broadened Applicability & Centralized Data Repository:
Expanded the framework to authorize data collection not only from convicts but also from persons detained under preventive detention laws and individuals arrested for any punishable offence. Furthermore, it authorized the National Crime Records Bureau (NCRB) to store, process, and preserve these records digitally at a national level for up to 75 years. 

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment
•	Formulation: Drafted and piloted by the Ministry of Home Affairs to upgrade investigative capabilities and address recommendations made by various committees (such as the Malimath Committee on reforms in the criminal justice system).
•	Parliamentary Passage: Introduced in the Lok Sabha on March 28, 2022; debated and passed by the Lok Sabha on April 4, 2022, and subsequently passed by the Rajya Sabha on April 6, 2022. 
•	Presidential Assent: Received formal Presidential Assent on April 18, 2022, entering the statute book as Act No. 11 of 2022. 
•	Enforcement: Formally brought into operational force across India on August 4, 2022, via Official Gazette notification.

Summary of The Farm Laws Repeal Act, 2021
Key Provisions and Impacts
1.	Repealed Legislation: - 1. The Farmers (Empowerment and Protection) Agreement on Price Assurance and Farm Services Act, 2020
•	Impact: Abolishes contractual farming reforms, reverting to pre-2020 arrangements for farmer-producer agreements.
•	The Farmers' Produce Trade and Commerce (Promotion and Facilitation) Act, 2020
•	Impact: Ends the facilitation of interstate and e-commerce trade of agricultural produce outside traditional mandis, potentially reinstating previous regulatory frameworks.
•	The Essential Commodities (Amendment) Act, 2020
•	Impact: Removes the 2020 amendments, which had liberalized the control over essential commodities, possibly tightening regulations on stockholding limits and price controls.
2.	Amendment: - Affected Act: The Essential Commodities Act, 1955
•	Change: Omission of Sub-section (1A) of Section 3
•	Implication: Reverts the regulatory framework for declaring commodities as essential, impacting how the government manages supply and prices of critical goods.
Broader Implications and Considerations
•	Policy Reversal: Undoes the 2020 reforms aimed at market liberalization and contractual farming, reflecting a shift in policy approach to agricultural regulation.
•	Regulatory Reversion: For essential commodities and trade practices, the legal framework may revert to a more controlled pre-2020 state, with potential impacts on market dynamics and consumer prices.
•	Omissions in Provided Context:
•	Detailed Rationale for Repeal: Not specified in the context, implying the need for external information to understand the political, social, or economic motivations.
•	Full Pre-Repeal Legal Framework: Partially outlined, suggesting a need for additional legal context to fully grasp the implications of the repeal on agricultural trade, pricing, and contractual agreements.

Legislative History: 
The Farm Laws Repeal Act, 2021

Source: Official Records of Parliament, India Code, and Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare (Department of Agriculture, Cooperation and Farmers Welfare)

Act Title - The Farm Laws Repeal Act, 2021
Act Number - Act No. 40 of 2021
Act ID (India Code) - 202140
Presidential Assent Date - November 30, 2021
Enforcement Date - November 30, 2021
Nodal Ministry -Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare 

Precedent & Historical Rationale
Farmer Agitations and Nationwide Protests:
•	Following the enactment of the three contentious farm ordinances in mid-2020 and their subsequent passage as acts in September 2020, widespread protests and prolonged agitations erupted, predominantly led by farmer unions primarily stationed around the borders of New Delhi.
•	The legislative measures aimed at deregulating agricultural trade, enabling contract farming, and amending stock limit rules faced severe opposition from agricultural communities concerned about minimum support prices (MSP), market security, and corporate dominance in the agricultural sector.
Legislative Intent and Repeal Mandate:
•	In response to sustained demonstrations and after months of dialogue, the government announced its decision to repeal the contested legislations in the interest of the nation's farmers and national unity.
•	The Act was formulated to formally rescind the Farmers (Empowerment and Protection) Agreement on Price Assurance and Farm Services Act, 2020, the Farmers' Produce Trade and Commerce (Promotion and Facilitation) Act, 2020, and the Essential Commodities (Amendment) Act, 2020, while restoring the original framework of the parent Essential Commodities Act, 1955.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment
•	Formulation: Drafted rapidly by the Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare to execute the executive policy decision to roll back the three farm statutes.
•	Parliamentary Passage: Introduced, debated, and passed by both Houses of Parliament (Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha) during the opening days of the winter session of Parliament in November 2021 without prolonged legislative committee referral.
•	Presidential Assent: Received Presidential Assent on November 30, 2021.
•	Enforcement: Brought into force immediately upon receiving assent on November 30, 2021, marking the formal statutory closure of the 2020 agricultural reform laws.

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of the Nalanda University Act 2010 
Key Provisions
1.	Objects of the University: - Disseminate and advance knowledge, wisdom, and understanding.
•	Promote innovations in teaching-learning, inter-disciplinary studies, and application of knowledge for social advancement and human welfare.
•	Impart liberal and humane education to South Asian nations in science, technology, and other areas.
•	Foster sound civic sense and train students to become useful citizens of democratic societies.
•	Build a South Asian community of learning and harmonise academic standards and accreditation norms across Member States.
2.	Powers and Functions: - Provide instruction in various branches of learning and make provisions for research.
•	Establish special centres, laboratories, and units for research and instruction.
•	Plan and prescribe courses of study; grant and withdraw degrees, diplomas, and certificates.
•	Confer honorary degrees and distinctions.
•	Organise open learning programmes, extramural studies, training, and extension services.
•	Institute academic positions and appoint personnel.
•	Recognise teachers and create administrative posts as necessary.
3.	Governance and Oversight: - Central Government Oversight: The Central Government may review the University's work, conduct inspections, and issue directions. The University must abide by these directions.
•	University's Response Rights: The University has the right to make representations to the Central Government before any inspection or inquiry and to appoint a representative during such processes.
4.	Accessibility and Social Responsibility: - Open to All: The University is open to persons of any sex, caste, creed, race, or class, without religious belief tests.
•	Special Provisions: Allowed for women, persons with disabilities, and weaker sections of society, including Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes, and other backward classes, without consideration of domicile.
5.	Unique Aspects: - South Asian Focus: Emphasis on building a South Asian community of learning.
•	Academic Harmonisation: Aim to harmonise academic standards and accreditation norms across South Asian Member States.
•	Innovative Curriculum: Introduction of semester systems, continuous evaluation, choice-based credit systems, and innovative courses with periodic review provisions.
•	Student Participation: Active participation of students in academic activities, including teacher evaluation.
•	Accreditation and Governance: Mandatory accreditation from national accrediting agencies and implementation of e-governance with effective management information systems.

meta.dc.description.abstract:
summary of the Customs Tariff Act, 1975
Objective
The Customs Tariff Act, 1975 was enacted to consolidate and amend the law relating to customs duties. It provides the legal framework for levying customs duties on imported and exported goods, classifying goods under tariff schedules, and imposing additional, anti-dumping, countervailing, safeguard, and protective duties to protect domestic industry and regulate international trade. 
Key Provisions
•	Tariff Schedules: Prescribes the rates of import and export duties through the First Schedule (import tariff) and Second Schedule (export tariff). 
•	Additional Customs Duty: Provides for the levy of additional duty on imported goods equivalent to the excise duty or other applicable domestic taxes on similar goods produced in India. 
•	Preferential Tariff: Enables the application of preferential or lower rates of customs duty under trade agreements entered into by India. 
•	Protective and Emergency Duties: Empowers the Central Government to impose protective duties, increase import or export duties in emergencies, and modify tariff rates in the public interest. 
•	Anti-Dumping and Countervailing Duties: Authorises the levy of anti-dumping duties on dumped imports and countervailing duties on subsidised imported goods to protect domestic industries from unfair trade practices. 
•	Safeguard Measures: Provides for the imposition of safeguard duties where a surge in imports causes or threatens serious injury to domestic producers. 
•	Rule-making Power: Empowers the Central Government to amend tariff schedules in specified circumstances and make rules for implementing the provisions of the Act.

meta.dc.legislation.history:
Legislative History:

The Customs Tariff Act, 1975

● Act Title - The Customs Tariff Act, 1975

● Act Number / Year - 51 of 1975

● Act ID (India Code) - 197551

● Presidential Assent Date - August 18, 1975

● Enforcement Date - August 2, 1976

● Nodal Ministry - Ministry of Finance

Precedent & Historical Rationale

● Modernization of Tariff Classification Systems - Enacted to consolidate and reform the law relating to customs duties, replacing the outdated Indian Tariff Act, 1934.

● Alignment with International Trade Standards - Formulated to replace old, ambiguous tariff structures with a systematic commodity classification system based on the Brussels Tariff Nomenclature (BTN), which was later updated to align with the internationally recognized Harmonized Commodity Description and Coding System (HSN). This provided a standardized 8-digit tariff code structure for import and export items to minimize litigation and ease international trade.

● Statutory Machinery for Trade Remedies & Duties - Serves as the charging schedule companion to the procedural Customs Act, 1962. It establishes mechanisms for imposing Basic Customs Duty (BCD), Countervailing Duties (CVD) to neutralize local taxes/excise, Integrated Goods and Services Tax (IGST) components post-GST reform, Anti-Dumping Duties, and Safeguard Duties against predatory import practices.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

● Formulation - Introduced by the Ministry of Finance to establish a scientific, standardized framework for assessing import and export rates, promoting domestic manufacturing, and preventing trade distortion.

● Parliamentary Passage - Debated and passed by both Houses of Parliament (Fifth Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha) during the monsoon session in July–August 1975.

● Presidential Assent - Received Presidential Assent on August 18, 1975.

● Enforcement - Enforced on August 2, 1976.

Source - Official Record of Parliament, India Code, and Ministry of Finance.

title: The Unified Waqf Management, Empowerment, Efficiency and Development Act, 1995

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of the Unified Waqf Management, Empowerment, Efficiency and Development Act, 1995 
Key Provisions
•	Survey and Registration of Waqfs: The Act provides for the survey, identification, and registration of waqf properties and the maintenance of records relating to such properties. 
•	Central Waqf Council: It provides for the constitution of the Central Waqf Council to advise the Central Government and State Waqf Boards on matters concerning the administration and development of waqfs. 
•	State Waqf Boards: The Act establishes State Waqf Boards responsible for the general superintendence, administration, and protection of waqfs within their respective States and Union Territories. 
•	Management of Waqf Properties: The Boards are empowered to supervise waqfs, ensure proper maintenance of accounts, safeguard properties, and take measures for their development and effective utilization. 
•	Waqf Tribunals: The Act provides for the establishment of Waqf Tribunals for the adjudication of disputes, questions, and matters relating to waqfs and waqf properties. 
•	Protection of Waqf Properties: The Act contains provisions to prevent encroachment, unauthorized occupation, alienation, or misuse of waqf properties and provides mechanisms for their recovery. 
•	Accounts and Audit: Mutawallis (managers of waqfs) are required to maintain accounts and comply with audit and reporting requirements to ensure transparency and accountability. 
•	Rule-making Power: The Central Government and State Governments are empowered to make rules for carrying out the provisions of the Act, while the Central Waqf Council and State Waqf Boards may frame regulations consistent with the Act.

Legislative History:

The Unified Waqf Management, Empowerment, Efficiency and Development Act, 1995

Act Title The Unified Waqf Management, Empowerment, Efficiency and Development Act, 1995 (Originally enacted as The Waqf Act, 1995; renamed via major legislative amendment)

Act Number 43 of 1995

Act ID (India Code) 199543

Presidential Assent Date November 22, 1995

Enforcement Date January 1, 1996

Nodal Ministry Ministry of Minority Affairs

Precedent & Historical Rationale

1. Evolution from Colonial Laws to the 1995 Statute:

o Prior to 1995, waqf administration was regulated by older statutes like the Mussalman Wakf Act, 1923 and regional acts. The original Waqf Act, 1995 was enacted to provide a centralized, uniform framework for better administration and protection of waqf properties across India through state and central boards.

2. Comprehensive Overhaul for Transparency and Accountability (UMEED Act, 2025):

o Over decades of implementation, structural challenges emerged, including property disputes, survey inefficiencies, complex "waqf by user" definitions, and concerns regarding transparency and representation. To remedy these lacunae, modernize record-keeping, incorporate strict ownership verification, and introduce broad-based representation (including non-Muslim members and Muslim women), Parliament comprehensively amended the statute, officially renaming it the Unified Waqf Management, Empowerment, Efficiency and Development Act, 1995 (UMEED Act).

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

• Formulation: Originally passed as the Waqf Act in late 1995. Decades later, following extensive review—including consultations and recommendations by a Joint Parliamentary Committee (JPC)—the overarching structural amendment framework was introduced and processed by Parliament.

• Parliamentary Passage: The amendment bill modernizing the statute was debated and passed by both the Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha in April 2025.

• Presidential Assent: Received assent on November 22, 1995.

• Enforcement: Enforced on July 1, 1996.

• Source: Official Records of Parliament, India Code, and Ministry of Minority Affairs.

title: The National Commission for Minorities Act, 1992

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of the National Commission for Minorities Act, 1992
Overview The National Commission for Minorities Act, 1992, establishes a commission to safeguard the interests of minority communities in India. While the Act broadly outlines the commission's structure, functions, and powers, the context of "Grants by Central Government" highlights the financial aspect of its operation.
Key Aspects with Emphasis on Grants
1. Establishment & Funding Implication
•	Established By: Central Government (implying central funding).
•	Implication: Establishment and ongoing operations are funded through grants from the Central Government.
2. Composition & Associated Costs
•	Members: Chairperson, Vice-Chairperson, and at least five Members, mostly from minority communities.
•	Cost Implication: Salaries, allowances, and benefits for members are covered by Central Government grants.
3. Functions with Budgetary Considerations
•	Evaluate Development: Requires research funding.
•	Investigate Complaints: May involve operational and travel costs.
•	Studies and Recommendations: Imply need for research grants.
•	All Functions: Funded through allocated grants to ensure operational capacity.
4. Powers & Financial Independence
•	Civil Court Powers: Exercise of these powers may require additional, specially allocated funds.
•	Financial Independence: Not fully autonomous; reliant on Central Government for all financial needs.
5. Miscellaneous with Financial Oversight
•	Term & Conditions: Managed within the budget allocated by the Central Government.
•	Public Servants: Status implies standardized, centrally funded remuneration and benefits.
•	Annual Report & Audit: Financial transparency and accountability to Parliament, ensuring prudent use of grants.

meta.dc.legislation.history:
Legislative History:

The National Commission for Minorities Act, 1992

Short Title The National Commission for Minorities Act, 1992

Act Number / Year 19 of 1992

Act ID (India Code) 199219

Presidential Assent / Enactment Date May 17, 1992

Enforcement Date May 17, 1992

Nodal Ministry Ministry of Minority Affairs

Precedent & Statutory Rationale

• Limitations of Executive Resolutions for Minority Safeguards:

o Prior to 1992, the protection and monitoring of minority rights relied upon a Minorities Commission set up merely through an executive resolution by the Ministry of Home Affairs in January 1978.

o Lacking statutory powers, binding investigative authority, or formal legal recourse, the advisory body struggled to effectively address grievances, evaluate the implementation of constitutional safeguards, or summon records and witnesses.

• Legislative Intervention and Regularization:

o Enacted in the 43rd Year of the Republic of India, the 1992 Act established a permanent, statutory National Commission for Minorities (NCM) equipped with official powers equivalent to a civil court.

o The core objectives include evaluating the progress of the development of minorities under the Union and States, monitoring the working of safeguards provided in the Constitution and in laws enacted by Parliament and State Legislatures, looking into specific complaints regarding deprivation of rights, and making recommendations for effective implementation of safeguards.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

• Formulation: Conceived by the Central Government to fulfill a commitment toward strengthening institutional mechanisms for the protection of religious minorities (notified initially to include Muslims, Christians, Sikhs, Buddhists, and Zoroastrians/Parsis, with Jains added subsequently in 2014).

• Parliamentary Passage: Introduced in Parliament, reviewed by relevant legislative committees, passed by both the Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha, and received formal presidential assent on May 17, 1992.

• Enforcement: Enforced immediately upon receiving presidential assent on May 17, 1993 laying the groundwork for the formal constitution of the statutory commission.

• Source: India Code (indiacode.gov.in), Ministry of Minority Affairs Official Records, and Parliament of India Records.

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of the Cess and Other Taxes on Minerals (Validation) Act, 1992
Overview
*Act Name: Cess and Other Taxes on Minerals (Validation) Act, 1992 *Enactment & Commencement: Enacted on 4th April, 1992, deemed effective from 15th February, 1992 *Jurisdiction: Applicable across the whole of India
Core Provisions
1.	Validation of State Laws: - Scope: Validates specific State laws pertaining to the imposition and collection of cesses and other taxes on minerals.
•	Effectivity: These State laws are retroactively deemed valid as if enacted by Parliament, up to 4th April, 1991.
2.	Legitimization of Past Actions: - Actions & Collections: All actions, rule makings, notifications, and tax/cess collections under the validated laws are confirmed as legally valid.
•	Refund Prohibition: Suits for refunds of collected cesses/taxes are barred, except for amounts paid in excess of the legally due amount.

meta.dc.legislation.history:
Legislative History:

The Cess and Other Taxes on Minerals (Validation) Act, 1992

Legislative Stage / Attribute Official Details

Short Title The Cess and Other Taxes on Minerals (Validation) Act, 1992

Act Number / Year 16 of 1992

Act ID (India Code) 199216

Presidential Assent / Enactment Date April 4, 1992

Enforcement Date February 15, 1992

Nodal Ministry Ministry of Mines

Precedent & Statutory Rationale

• Judicial Invalidations and Financial Liabilities for States:

o Prior to 1992, various state governments enacted independent legislations imposing cesses, royalties, and local taxes on mineral rights and mineral-bearing lands.

o In several landmark judgments (including rulings by the Supreme Court of India), these state laws were struck down on the grounds of legislative incompetence, holding that Parliament—under the Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957—occupied the field relating to mineral development and regulation, leaving states devoid of taxing power in this domain.

o These judicial strikes exposed state treasuries to massive financial liabilities, forcing them to refund thousands of crores of rupees collected over the years.

• Legislative Intervention and Regularization:

o Enacted to overcome the financial crisis faced by state governments and to legally validate the past imposition and collection of cesses and taxes on minerals under specific state laws listed in the schedule (spanning states like Andhra Pradesh, Bihar, Karnataka, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, Orissa, and Tamil Nadu).

o The core objective was to provide parliamentary sanction retrospectively up to April 4, 1991, for those collections, abate court proceedings demanding mass refunds (while keeping open claims for excess payments made by individuals), and protect state revenues.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

• Formulation: Developed by the Central Government via an Ordinance route to urgently stabilize state fiscal systems before replacing it with a formal parliamentary enactment.

• Parliamentary Passage: Passed by both houses of Parliament, receiving formal presidential assent on April 4, 1992.

• Enforcement: Enforced on February 15, 1992.

• Source: India Code and Ministry of Mines Official Records.

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of the Dock Workers (Regulation of Employment) (Inapplicability to Major Ports) Act, 1997
Key Provisions
1.	Purpose: - Exempts major port trusts from the Dock Workers (Regulation of Employment) Act, 1948, particularly for activities outlined in the new context (e.g., loading/unloading, ship maintenance, construction within ports).
•	Addresses transitional matters for affected workers.
2.	Definitions: - Appointed Day: Notification date for a major port's transition.
•	Board: As per the Major Port Trusts Act, 1963.
•	Major Port: Defined in the Indian Ports Act, 1908.
3.	Inapplicability: - The Dock Workers (Regulation of Employment) Act, 1948, ceases to apply to a major port post-notification, following a settlement under the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947.
4.	Transitional Arrangements: - Assets, Liabilities, and Funds: Transferred from the Dock Labour Board to the Board of the major port.
•	Employees: Transferred with conditions not less favourable than before, without entitlement to compensation.
Implications and Contextual Understanding
•	Focus: Primarily on inapplicability and transition for specified port activities, not on introducing new safety, health, and welfare regulations.
•	Safety, Health, and Welfare:
•	Governed by the Dock Workers (Safety, Health and Welfare) Act, 1986, ensuring:
•	Medical supervision
•	Ambulance, first aid, and rescue facilities
•	Safety and health organization
•	Training for dock workers on safety and health rights
•	Investigation of occupational accidents and diseases
•	Submission of accident and health statistics

ACT NO. 31 OF 1997

[18th August, 1997.]

An Act to provide for inapplicability of the Dock Workers (Regulation of Employment) Act, 1948 to dock workers of major port trusts and for matters connected therewith or incidental thereto.

meta.dc.legislation.history:
Legislative History:

The Dock Workers (Regulation of Employment) (Inapplicability to Major Ports) Act, 1997

Short Title The Dock Workers (Regulation of Employment) (Inapplicability to Major Ports) Act, 1997

Act Number / Year 31 of 1997

Act ID (India Code) 199731

Presidential Assent / Enactment Date March 4, 1948

Enforcement Date March 4, 1948

Nodal Ministry Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways

Precedent & Statutory Rationale

• Dual-System Redundancy and Administrative Friction in Major Ports:

o Prior to 1997, major ports operated under a dual-management structure where port operations were managed by Port Trusts under the Major Port Trusts Act, 1963, while dock labor was separately regulated by independent Dock Labour Boards (DLBs) established under the Dock Workers (Regulation of Employment) Act, 1948.

o Over time, this bifurcation resulted in operational rigidities, overstaffing, lack of administrative flexibility, and friction in matching dynamic cargo-handling requirements with available labor pools.

• Legislative Intervention and Regularization:

o Enacted to empower the Central Government to render the 1948 Act inapplicable to any major port, but strictly contingent upon a formal settlement being reached between the Dock Labour Board, the port workmen, and the port management under the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947.

o The core objective was to streamline port administration, merge duplicate institutional structures by transferring all assets, liabilities, and ongoing legal proceedings of the Dock Labour Board directly to the respective Port Trust Board, and safeguard existing employee terms.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

• Formulation: Framed to resolve long-standing structural inefficiencies in major ports and to integrate dock labor management directly into port trust frameworks through negotiated industrial settlements.

• Parliamentary Passage: Passed by both houses of Parliament, receiving formal presidential assent on August 18, 1997.

• Enactment: Received Presidential Assent on March 4, 1948.

• Enforcement: Enforced on March 4, 1948.

• Source: India Code and Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways Official Records.

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949

Key Provisions:
1.	Establishment of the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India (ICAI): 
o	Constitutes the ICAI as a statutory body corporate. 
o	Entrusts the Institute with regulating and developing the profession of Chartered Accountancy in India. 
2.	Registration and Membership: 
o	Prescribes the qualifications and procedure for admission as a member of the ICAI. 
o	Maintains a Register of Members and classifies members as Associates or Fellows, subject to eligibility criteria. 
3.	Council of the ICAI: 
o	Provides for the constitution of the Council, the governing body of the Institute. 
o	Empowers the Council to manage the affairs of the Institute, frame regulations, and oversee professional education, training, and examinations. 
4.	Education, Training, and Examinations: 
o	Authorizes the ICAI to prescribe the syllabus, conduct examinations, and regulate practical training for aspiring Chartered Accountants. 
o	Ensures that members possess the requisite professional knowledge and skills. 
5.	Certificate of Practice: 
o	Requires members intending to practice as Chartered Accountants to obtain a Certificate of Practice from the ICAI. 
o	Regulates the conditions under which members may engage in professional practice. 
6.	Professional Misconduct and Discipline: 
o	Prescribes standards of professional and ethical conduct for members. 
o	Establishes disciplinary mechanisms to inquire into cases of professional or other misconduct and impose appropriate penalties. 
7.	Quality and Professional Standards:

Short Title The Chartered Accountants Act, 1949

Act Number / Year Act No. 38 of 1949

Presidential Assent / Enactment Date May 1, 1949

Enforcement Date July 1, 1949

Nodal Ministry Ministry of Corporate Affairs

Precedent & Statutory Rationale

1. Need for an Autonomous Professional Accounting Body Post-Independence:

o Prior to 1949, the accountancy and auditing profession in British India lacked a unified self-regulatory body, relying instead on restricted certificate holders registered under the Indian Companies Act, 1913, or qualifications granted under various provincial and colonial boards.

o With rapid post-independence industrialization, corporate expansion, and complex tax structures, the government recognized the imperative need to establish an organized, highly disciplined, and autonomous professional body to regulate the accountancy trade and safeguard public and corporate financial integrity.

2. Establishment of the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India (ICAI):

o The 1949 Act was enacted to make provision for the regulation of the profession of chartered accountants and for that purpose to establish the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India (ICAI).

o The core statutory objective was to set rigorous educational standards, conduct professional examinations, maintain a register of qualified members, enforce ethical codes of conduct, and exercise disciplinary control over practitioners of the profession across the country.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

• Formulation: Drafted and piloted by the Ministry of Commerce to professionalize and institutionalize accounting standards in support of national economic development.

• Parliamentary Passage: Tabled, debated, and passed by the Constituent Assembly of India (Legislative), receiving formal assent from the Governor-General on May 1, 1949.

• Enforcement: Enforced on July 1, 1949.

Precedent & Statutory Rationale

1. Obsolescence of Colonial Reserve Frameworks:

o Prior to 1948, citizen military reserves were structured under the Indian Auxiliary Force Act, 1920 and the Indian Territorial Force Act, 1920, both of which carried racial discriminations, restrictive enrollment criteria, and operational limitations unsuited to a sovereign, democratic nation.

o Following independence, national leaders and defense planners recognized the vital need for a dedicated citizen force comprising civilians who could receive military training during their spare time and be mobilized to support the Regular Army in times of national emergency, internal security crises, or national defense.

2. Creation of a Citizen-Soldier Reserve Force:

o The 1948 Act was enacted to constitute and regulate the Territorial Army as a second line of defense for India.

o The core statutory objective was to provide an opportunity for able-bodied citizens from various walks of life to voluntarily train in military skills, relieve the regular army from static duties, assist civil authorities in maintaining law and order or handling natural disasters, and safeguard vital infrastructure during emergencies.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

• Formulation: Drafted and piloted by the Ministry of Defence to replace discriminatory colonial statutes with a modern, national citizen-reserve framework.

• Parliamentary Passage: Tabled, debated, and passed by the Constituent Assembly of India (Legislative), receiving formal Presidential Assent on September 10, 1948..

• Enforcement: Enforced on September 10, 1948.

o Prior to 1948, the employment of dock workers across Indian ports was completely unregulated, heavily exploitative, and characterized by casual hiring methods (such as the "tindal" or "serang" system).

o This fluctuating demand left dock workers vulnerable to chronic underemployment, arbitrary wage cuts, lack of safety, and total economic insecurity during slack periods.

2. Legislative Intervention and Regularization:

o Enacted shortly after independence, the 1948 Act was designed to empower the government to frame comprehensive schemes for the registration of dock workers and employers.

o The core objective was to ensure greater regularity of employment, guarantee minimum pay during periods of insufficient work, and regulate terms of remuneration, hours of work, and working conditions across major and minor ports.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

• Formulation: Drafted and introduced post-independence to protect maritime and port laborers from systemic exploitation and to establish structured administrative machinery like Dock Labour Boards.

• Parliamentary Passage: Processed and enacted by the Dominion Legislature, receiving formal assent on March 4, 1948.

• Enforcement: Brought into force immediately upon enactment on March 4, 1948, paving the way for targeted port-wise employment schemes.

Precedent & Statutory Rationale

1. Need for Independent Overseas Legal and Notarial Competence:

o Following independence and the establishment of India's own diplomatic missions abroad, diplomatic and consular officers required explicit statutory authority under Indian law to perform notarial acts, administer oaths, and take affidavits for use back home.

o Prior mechanisms relied heavily on colonial statutes or lacked a unified domestic framework empowering newly appointed Indian diplomatic representatives to execute binding legal functions in foreign countries.

o The 1948 Act was enacted to empower diplomatic and consular officers to exercise statutory powers equivalent to those of a notary public, ensuring that affidavits, oaths, and official acts performed abroad are fully admissible in Indian courts of law.

o It also established a uniform structure for prescribing, levying, and accounting for official fees collected in respect of services rendered by Indian missions overseas.

• Formulation: Drafted and piloted by the central government to set up standard legal procedures for independent India's expanding foreign service network.

Summary of Presidency-Towns Insolvency Act, 1909:
Key Features 
•	Government Ownership of Buildings: Declares that buildings erected by or on behalf of the Government remain Government property, irrespective of the ownership of the land. 
•	Separation of Ownership: Distinguishes ownership of the building from ownership of the land on which it stands. 
•	Protection of Government Property: Prevents Government buildings from being treated as part of the land merely because they are constructed on privately owned or non-Government land. 
•	Resolution of Ownership Disputes: Provides legal clarity to resolve disputes regarding ownership and possession of Government buildings. 
•	Applicability: Applies to Government buildings constructed on land that does not belong to the Government.
meta.dc.legislation.history:
Legislative History:

The Presidency-Towns Insolvency Act, 1909

● Act Title - The Presidency-Towns Insolvency Act, 1909

● Act Number / Year - 3 of 1909

● Act ID (India Code) - 190903

● Assent Date - March 12, 1909

● Enforcement Date - March 12, 1909

● Nodal Ministry - Ministry of Corporate Affairs

Precedent & Historical Rationale

● Obsolescence of the Indian Insolvency Act, 1848 (Imperial Statute 11 & 12 Vict. c. 21) - Prior to 1909, personal and commercial insolvency proceedings within the Presidency towns of Calcutta, Madras, and Bombay were governed by an antiquated British Imperial statute, the Indian Insolvency Act, 1848. That statutory regime lacked modern investigative mechanisms to uncover fraudulent debtor preferences, provided inadequate statutory protection for bona fide commercial creditors, maintained an inefficient system for the discharge of insolvent debtors, and failed to incorporate the comprehensive procedural and substantive reforms introduced in England under the Bankruptcy Acts of 1883 and 1890.

● Modernized Insolvency Architecture for Presidency High Courts - Formulated to amend the law of insolvency in the Presidency-towns into a comprehensive, modern enactment aligned with contemporary commercial developments and modern bankruptcy jurisprudence. The Act conferred exclusive original insolvency jurisdiction upon the High Courts of Calcutta, Madras, and Bombay, codified specific statutory "acts of insolvency", established the statutory office of the Official Assignee to take custody of and realize debtor estates, standardized rules for the proof and distribution of debts, and instituted strict judicial inquiries before granting orders of discharge.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

● Formulation - Drafted by the Legislative Department of the Government of India under Law Member Sir Henry Erle Richards and Sir Satyendra Prasanna Sinha, in close consultation with Presidency High Courts, mercantile associations, and Chambers of Commerce, complementing the Provincial Insolvency Act, 1907 (which covered mofussil areas).

● Parliamentary Passage - Introduced as The Presidency-Towns Insolvency Bill, 1908 in the Council of the Governor General of India for the purpose of making Laws and Regulations, referred to an expert Select Committee for detailed review, and debated and passed in March 1909 at Calcutta.

● Governor-General's Assent - Received the assent of the Governor-General of India (Lord Minto) on March 12, 1909.

● Enforcement - Brought into force on January 1, 1910 (pursuant to Section 1(3) of the Act).

Sources - Official Records of the Council of the Governor General of India, India Code, and Ministry of Corporate Affairs.

Key Features
•	Registration of Co-operative Societies: Provides for the registration of co-operative societies and confers legal status upon them. 
•	Democratic Governance: Prescribes the management and administration of societies through elected governing bodies in accordance with their bye-laws.

•	Financial Management: Contains provisions relating to funds, accounts, audit, and proper financial administration of societies.

meta.dc.legislation.history:
Legislative History:

The Co-operative Societies Act, 1912

● Act Title - The Co-operative Societies Act, 1912

● Act Number / Year - 2 of 1912

● Act ID (India Code) - 191202

● Assent Date - March 1, 1912

● Enforcement Date - March 1, 1912

● Nodal Ministry - Ministry of Cooperation

Precedent & Historical Rationale

● Deficiencies and Narrow Scope of the Co-operative Credit Societies Act, 1904 - Prior to 1912, the co-operative movement in India was governed strictly by the Co-operative Credit Societies Act, 1904 (Act X of 1904). The 1904 framework was confined solely to agricultural and urban credit societies, offering no legal recognition or statutory protection for non-credit co-operative ventures such as production, marketing, distribution, housing, or consumer stores. Furthermore, it lacked statutory provisions for creating central financing agencies, provincial apex co-operative banks, or supervising unions.

● Expanded Statutory Scope, Federal Structures, and Non-Credit Co-operatives - Formulated to facilitate the formation of co-operative societies for the promotion of thrift and self-help among agriculturists, artisans, and other persons with common economic needs. The Act broadened registration eligibility to all types of co-operative enterprises (both credit and non-credit), established a legal framework for federal structures (enabling primary societies to federate into Central and Provincial Co-operative Banks and Unions), regulated audit and inspection through the Registrar of Co-operative Societies, and conferred tax exemptions and priority of claims over debtor assets.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

● Formulation - Drafted by the Revenue and Agriculture Department and the Legislative Department of the Government of India, incorporating the recommendations of the Registrars' Conferences (1906–1911) and the Maclagan Committee findings on co-operative expansion.

● Parliamentary Passage - Introduced as The Co-operative Societies Bill, 1911 in the Council of the Governor General of India for the purpose of making Laws and Regulations, referred to a Select Committee for detailed clause-by-clause examination, and passed in early 1912 at Calcutta.

● Governor-General's Assent - Received the assent of the Governor-General of India (Lord Hardinge of Penshurst) on March 1, 1912.

● Enforcement - Enforced on March 1, 1912 (later transferred to provincial legislative lists under the Government of India Act, 1919, forming the blueprint for subsequent State Co-operative Societies Acts).

Sources - Official Records of the Council of the Governor General of India, India Code, and Ministry of Cooperation.

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of the Administrators-General Act, 1963 
Objectives of the Act
•	To consolidate the law relating to Administrators-General. 
•	To provide for the appointment and jurisdiction of Administrators-General. 
•	To ensure the efficient administration and protection of the estates of deceased persons where no competent person is available to administer them. 
•	To safeguard the interests of heirs, beneficiaries, creditors, and other persons entitled to the estate. 
Key Provisions
•	Appointment of Administrators-General: The Act provides for the appointment of an Administrator-General for specified States or territories by the Central Government. 
•	Administration of Estates: An Administrator-General may administer the estate of a deceased person in accordance with the Act and other applicable succession laws, particularly where no executor or administrator has been appointed or is willing or competent to act. 
•	Powers and Duties: The Administrator-General has powers to take possession of estate assets, realise and manage property, pay debts and liabilities, represent the estate in legal proceedings, and distribute the remaining assets to the lawful beneficiaries. 
•	Grant of Letters of Administration: The Act lays down the circumstances in which an Administrator-General may obtain or be granted letters of administration by the competent court. 
•	Accounts and Supervision: The Administrator-General is required to maintain proper accounts, administer estates in a fiduciary capacity, and comply with statutory requirements relating to reporting, audit, and court supervision. 
•	Rule-making Power: The Central Government is empowered to make rules for carrying out the provisions of the Act.

title: The Chief Election Commissioner And Other Election Commissioners (Appointment, Conditions of Service And Term of Office) Act, 2023

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of chief election commissioner and other election commissioners (appointment, conditions of service and term of office), act 2023
The Act regulates the appointment, conditions of service, and term of office of the Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) and other Election Commissioners (ECs) in India, ensuring transparency and standardizing their service conditions with those of Supreme Court Judges.
Key Provisions
1.	Appointment
•	By: President of India
•	Recommendation: Selection Committee consisting of:
•	Prime Minister (Chairperson)
•	Leader of Opposition in the House of the People (Member)
•	A Union Cabinet Minister (Member)
•	Search Committee: Prepares a panel of 5 persons, headed by the Minister of Law and Justice.
2.	Qualifications
•	Persons of integrity with knowledge and experience in election management.
•	Holding or have held a post equivalent to the rank of Secretary to the Government of India.
3.	Term of Office
•	Duration: 6 years from the date of assuming office or until attaining 65 years, whichever is earlier.
•	Re-appointment: Not eligible for re-appointment.
•	Aggregate Term for EC appointed as CEC: Not more than 6 years in total.
4.	Conditions of Service
•	Salary: Equal to a Judge of the Supreme Court.
•	Dearness Allowance: As admissible to Supreme Court Judges.
•	Leave: Governed by rules applicable to their previous service or IAS rules; leave encashment up to 50%.
•	Pension:
•	Equivalent to a Supreme Court Judge’s pension.
•	Option to draw previous service pension with benefits.
•	General Provident Fund: Eligible to subscribe.
•	Other Benefits: Travel allowance, medical facilities, etc., similar to Supreme Court Judges.
5.	Resignation and Removal
•	Resignation: By writing to the President.
•	Removal of CEC: Similar grounds as for a Supreme Court Judge.
•	Removal of ECs: On recommendation of the CEC.
6.	Transaction of Business
•	Unanimous Decision: Preferred.
•	Majority Opinion: In case of differing opinions.
7.	Protection
•	Legal Protection: No civil or criminal proceedings for acts done in official capacity.

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of Boilers Act, 2025
The Act enforces stringent boiler safety and environmental regulations, emphasizing immediate reporting and response to emissions, alongside defined penalty structures and appeal processes, ensuring public safety and regulatory adherence.
Key Provisions
1.	Immediate Reporting and Response to Emissions
•	Duty to Inform: Person in charge must immediately notify the State Board and prescribed authorities upon emission occurrence or apprehension.
•	Remedial Measures: State Board and authorities must take prompt mitigating actions.
2.	Regulatory Framework and Penalty
•	Rule Making Power: Central and State Governments empowered to make rules for various aspects, including qualifications, appeals, and penalties.
•	Penalty for non-compliance:
•	First Contravention: Up to one thousand rupees.
•	Subsequent Contraventions: Up to one lakh rupees.
3.	Operational Compliance
•	Boiler Registration and Certification: Mandatory, with fees payable for registration.
•	Qualified Personnel: Boilers must be under the charge of certified persons.
4.	Appeal and Adjudication Process
•	Appeal Mechanism: Defined procedure for preferring appeals against decisions, with specified fees and timelines.
•	Adjudicating Officers: Empowered to impose penalties after due hearing.
5.	Exemptions and Emergency Provisions
•	State Government Powers: Can exempt certain boilers under specific conditions or in emergencies through general or special orders.
•	Rapid Industrialisation Exemption: Possible for boilers/components if deemed necessary for the country’s rapid industrialisation, subject to conditions.

Precedent & Historical Rationale
●	Overhaul and Repeal of Century-Old Framework: Repeals the colonial-era Indian Boilers Act, 1923 (5 of 1923) in its entirety to modernize pressure vessel safety norms, align compliance with global engineering practices, and remove archaic provisions.

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of Immigration and Foreigners Act, 2025 

The  Immigration and Foreigners Act, 2025 consolidates and modernizes India's immigration laws 
Key Provisions
1. Entry and Exit Requirements
Valid Travel Documents: Every person entering or leaving India must possess a valid passport or other travel document, and foreigners must also possess a valid visa unless exempted.
Designated Immigration Posts: Entry into and exit from India is permitted only through notified immigration check posts. 
2. Registration and Reporting
Registration of Foreigners: Specified categories of foreigners are required to register with the prescribed Registration Officer.
Mandatory Information: Hotels, educational institutions, hospitals, and other prescribed establishments must furnish information regarding foreign nationals staying or receiving services. 
3. Powers of the Central Government
Regulation of Foreigners: The Central Government may regulate the entry, stay, movement, departure, and activities of foreigners in India.
Immigration Officers: Authorises immigration officers to examine travel documents, grant or refuse entry, and enforce the provisions of the Act. ([India Code][1])
4. Offences and Penalties
Illegal Entry and Overstay: Prescribes penalties for entering India without valid documents, overstaying visas, or violating conditions of stay.
Forged Documents: Imposes stringent punishment for using forged passports, visas, or other travel documents and for aiding illegal immigration.

title: The Promotion and Regulation of Online Gaming Act, 2025

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of Promotion and Regulation of Online Gaming Act, 2025
The Act promotes e-sports and online social games, prohibits online money games, and seeks to ensure consumer protection, responsible gaming, and a safe digital gaming ecosystem while preventing gambling, fraud, and financial harm. 
Key Provisions
1. Promotion of E-Sports and Online Social Games
•	Recognition of E-Sports: Recognises and promotes e-sports as a legitimate competitive sporting activity. 
•	Development of Online Social Games: Encourages the growth and regulation of online social games through a structured legal framework. 
2. Prohibition of Online Money Games
•	Ban on Money Games: Prohibits online games involving betting, wagering, or monetary stakes. 
•	Advertising Restrictions: Prohibits advertisements promoting online money games or related gaming services. 
3. Regulatory Authority
•	Establishment of Authority: Establishes an Online Gaming Authority of India to regulate and oversee the online gaming sector. 
•	Licensing and Compliance: The Authority is empowered to monitor compliance, issue directions, and enforce the provisions of the Act. 
4. Consumer Protection and Financial Safeguards
•	Protection of Users: Provides safeguards against fraud, addiction, and unfair gaming practices. 
•	Restriction on Fund Transfers: Prohibits financial transactions relating to prohibited online money games and mandates compliance with applicable financial laws.

meta.dc.identifier.preamble_description:
THE PROMOTION AND REGULATION OF ONLINE GAMING ACT, 2025
ACT NO. 32 OF 2025

[22nd August, 2025.]


An Act to promote and regulate the online gaming sector including e-sports, educational games and social gaming; to provide for the appointment of an Authority for coordinated policy support, strategic development and regulatory oversight of the sector; to prohibit the offering, operation, facilitation, advertisement, *[promotion] and participation in online money games through any computer resource, mobile device or the internet, particularly where such activities operate across State borders or from foreign jurisdictions; to protect individuals, especially youth and vulnerable populations, from the adverse social, economic, psychological and privacy-related impacts of such games; to ensure the responsible use of digital technologies; to maintain public order and protect public health; to safeguard the integrity of financial systems and the security and sovereignty of the State; to establish a uniform national-level legal framework in the public interest; and for matters connected therewith or incidental thereto.
WHEREAS the online gaming sector has rapidly evolved into one of the most dynamic and fastest-growing segments of the digital and creative economy, offering significant opportunities for innovation, cognitive development, employment generation, technological advancement and global competitiveness;
AND WHEREAS India possesses a large and growing pool of young professionals with technological capabilities and rapidly expanding domestic market, which together enable the country to assume a leadership role in the global online gaming value chain;
AND WHEREAS the online gaming ecosystem comprises diverse segments, including e-sports, casual and social games, educational games and online money games, and is currently operating in the absence of a dedicated institutional and legal framework necessary for strategic coordination, capacity building, common infrastructure, research and responsible innovation;
AND WHEREAS the lack of a coherent and enabling legal framework has hindered the sector’s structured development and the promotion of responsible gaming practices, requiring urgent policy intervention and support mechanisms;
AND WHEREAS the parallel proliferation of online money games accessible through mobile phones, computers and the internet, and offering monetary returns against user deposits has led to serious social, financial, psychological and public health harms, particularly among young individuals and economically disadvantaged groups;
AND WHEREAS such games often use manipulative design features, addictive algorithms, bots and undisclosed agents, undermining fairness, transparency and user protection, while promoting compulsive behaviour leading to financial ruin;
AND WHEREAS platforms offering online gaming system are often aggressively marketed through pervasive advertising campaigns, including celebrity and influencer endorsements, thereby amplifying their reach and impact especially among the youth and vulnerable groups;
AND WHEREAS the unchecked expansion of online money gaming services has been linked to unlawful activities including financial fraud, money-laundering, tax evasion, and in some cases, the financing of terrorism, thereby posing threats to national security, public order and the integrity of the State;
AND WHEREAS considering the deleterious and negative impact of online money games on the individuals, families, society and the nation and given the technical aspects including the very nature of the electronic medium used for online money games, the algorithms applied and the national and transnational networks involved therein;
AND WHEREAS many such services operate from offshore jurisdictions, bypassing domestic laws, undermining state-level regulations, and presenting significant enforcement challenges in terms of extra-territorial jurisdiction and inter-State inconsistencies;
AND WHEREAS it is expedient in the public interest for the Union Government to assume legislative competence over the online gaming sector to ensure the creation of a secure, structured and innovation-friendly digital environment, while addressing the associated risks to public health, consumer safety, public morality and financial sovereignty;
AND WHEREAS it is necessary to clearly delineate and categorise the various forms of online games and to provide a tailored legal framework to govern each sub-sector of the industry appropriately.
BE it enacted by Parliament in the Seventy-sixth Year of the Republic of India as follows:---

title: The Coal Bearing Areas (Acquisition and Development) Act, 1957

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of the Coal Bearing Areas (Acquisition and Development) Act, 1957

Key Provisions:
1.	Acquisition of Coal Bearing Land 
o	The Act empowers the Central Government to acquire land containing coal deposits or land considered necessary for coal mining and related activities. 
o	Acquisition is carried out through notifications published in the Official Gazette. 
2.	Preliminary Investigation 
o	Before acquisition, the Central Government may authorise surveys, drilling, and other investigations to determine the existence and extent of coal deposits. 
o	Authorised officers may enter the land for conducting such investigations. 
3.	Declaration of Acquisition 
o	If the land is required for coal mining or development, the Central Government may issue a declaration acquiring the land or rights over the land. 
o	Upon publication of the declaration, the land or specified rights vest in the Central Government free from encumbrances. 
4.	Compensation 
o	The Act provides for payment of compensation to landowners and other persons whose land or rights are acquired. 
o	It also provides a mechanism for determining compensation and resolving disputes relating to its amount. 
5.	Management and Development 
o	The Central Government may utilise the acquired land directly or transfer it to a Government company, corporation, or other authorised entity for coal mining and development. 
6.	Dispute Resolution 
o	The Act provides for reference of disputes relating to compensation and other specified matters to the appropriate authority or tribunal in accordance with its provisions. 
7.	Rule-Making Power 
o	The Central Government is empowered to make rules for carrying out the purposes of the Act, including procedures for acquisition, compensation, and administration.

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of the River Boards Act, 1956

Key Provisions:
1.	Establishment of River Boards 
o	The Central Government may establish a River Board by notification for any inter-State river or river valley. 
o	A River Board may be constituted when the Central Government considers it necessary in the public interest. 
2.	Composition of River Boards 
o	A River Board consists of a Chairman and other members appointed by the Central Government. 
o	The Board may include experts in fields such as water resources, engineering, agriculture, and administration. 
3.	Functions of River Boards
River Boards may perform functions including: 
o	Advising State Governments on the development and utilisation of river waters. 
o	Preparing plans for conservation, control, and utilisation of water resources. 
o	Coordinating activities related to irrigation, flood control, drainage, and hydroelectric power generation. 
o	Promoting efficient use of water resources. 
4.	Powers and Duties 
o	The Board provides technical advice and assistance to States. 
o	It helps coordinate development projects involving inter-State rivers and river valleys. 
o	It may collect and analyse data relating to water resources. 
5.	Cooperation with State Governments 
o	River Boards work in consultation with concerned State Governments. 
o	The Act encourages cooperative management of shared river resources. 
6.	Rule-Making Power 
o	The Central Government is empowered to make rules for carrying out the purposes of the Act. 
o	Rules may prescribe procedures relating to the functioning of River Boards.

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of the Faridabad Development Corporation Act, 1956

Key Provisions:
1.	Establishment of the Corporation 
o	The Act established the Faridabad Development Corporation as a body corporate with perpetual succession and a common seal. 
o	The Corporation was empowered to acquire, hold, and dispose of property, enter into contracts, and sue or be sued in its corporate name. 
2.	Functions of the Corporation 
o	The Corporation was entrusted with: 
	Planning and developing the township. 
	Constructing and maintaining roads, buildings, water supply, drainage, and other civic infrastructure. 
	Developing residential, commercial, and industrial areas. 
	Providing public amenities and essential services. 
3.	Powers of the Corporation 
o	The Corporation was authorised to acquire land, execute development schemes, construct public works, and undertake activities necessary for the development of Faridabad. 
4.	Management and Administration 
o	The Act provided for the constitution of the Corporation, including the appointment of a Chairman, and other members not less than or and not more than eight. 
o	It prescribed their powers, duties and the manner in which the Corporation's affairs were to be managed. 
5.	Financial Provisions 
o	The Corporation was empowered to receive grants, loans, and other financial assistance from the Central Government and other sources. 
o	It was required to maintain proper accounts, prepare annual budgets and reports, and have its accounts audited. 
6.	Rule-Making Power 
o	The Central Government was empowered to make rules for carrying out the purposes of the Act. 
o	The Corporation could also frame regulations for its internal administration, subject to the provisions of the Act.

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of the Central Sales Tax Act, 1956

Key Provisions:
1.	Inter-State Sale and Purchase of Goods 
o	The Act defines when a sale or purchase of goods takes place in the course of inter-State trade or commerce. 
o	A sale is considered inter-State when it involves the movement of goods from one State to another or when documents of title are transferred during movement. 
2.	Levy and Collection of Central Sales Tax (CST) 
o	The Act provides for the levy of Central Sales Tax on inter-State sales. 
o	Although imposed by the Central Government, the tax is collected and retained by the State Governments as per the provisions of the Act. 
3.	Registration of Dealers 
o	Dealers engaged in inter-State trade are required to register under the Act. 
o	Registered dealers are entitled to certain benefits, including concessional tax rates on specified transactions. 
4.	Declaration Forms and Concessional Rates 
o	The Act provides for the use of prescribed forms, such as Form C, for claiming concessional rates of tax on inter-State purchases. 
o	Dealers must comply with prescribed conditions to avail such benefits. 
5.	Restrictions on State Tax Laws 
o	The Act places restrictions on State Governments regarding taxation of certain goods declared to be of special importance in inter-State trade. 
o	It ensures that such goods are taxed uniformly. 
6.	Goods of Special Importance 
o	The Act identifies certain goods as being of special importance in inter-State trade or commerce. 
o	States cannot impose taxes on these goods beyond prescribed limits. 
7.	Filing of Returns and Maintenance of Records 
o	Dealers are required to maintain accounts, submit returns, and comply with procedures prescribed under the Act and relevant State rules.

title: The Manipur (Village Authorities in Hill Areas) Act, 1956

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of the Manipur (Village Authorities in Hill Areas) Act, 1956

Key Provisions:
1.	Constitution of Village Authorities 
o	The Act provides for the constitution of a Village Authority for each recognised village in the hill areas of Manipur. 
o	It prescribes the composition, election or nomination of members, and the appointment of the Chairman. 
2.	Powers and Functions 
o	Village Authorities are entrusted with the administration of village affairs, including: 
	Maintenance of public order and village discipline. 
	Management of village property and community resources. 
	Promotion of sanitation, public health, and welfare. 
	Assistance in implementing government programmes and development activities. 
3.	Meetings and Procedure 
o	The Act lays down procedures for convening meetings of the Village Authority, conducting its business, and recording decisions. 
o	Decisions are generally taken by a majority of members present. 
4.	Financial Powers 
o	Village Authorities may collect prescribed fees, manage village funds, and utilise resources for community welfare and development in accordance with the Act and applicable rules. 
5.	Supervision and Control 
o	The functioning of Village Authorities is subject to the supervision of the prescribed government authorities. 
o	The Act empowers the Government to issue directions and take appropriate action in cases of non-compliance or misconduct. 
6.	Rule-Making Power 
o	The appropriate Government is empowered to make rules for carrying out the provisions of the Act, including matters relating to elections, administration, and financial management.

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of the Inter-State Corporation Act, 1957

Key Provisions:
1.	Extension of Corporate Powers 
o	The Act enables the objects and powers of a corporation established under a State law to be extended to another State or States. 
o	Such extension requires the consent of the Governments of the States concerned. 
2.	Inter-State Agreements 
o	The participating States may enter into agreements specifying the terms and conditions for extending the corporation's jurisdiction and operations. 
o	These agreements may provide for administration, management, financial arrangements, and other related matters. 
3.	Approval by Parliament 
o	The extension of a corporation's powers takes effect through a law enacted by Parliament under Article 252 of the Constitution, after resolutions are passed by the Legislatures of the participating States. 
4.	Administration and Governance 
o	The Act provides for the continued functioning of the corporation in accordance with the law under which it was established, subject to modifications made through the inter-State arrangement. 
5.	Rights and Liabilities 
o	The corporation retains its legal identity, and its rights, obligations, assets, liabilities, and contracts continue to operate in the extended area as provided by the Act and the relevant agreement. 
6.	Supplementary Provisions 
o	The Act contains provisions to facilitate the effective implementation of inter-State arrangements, including matters relating to administration, finance, and legal proceedings.

Summary of the Lok Sahayak Sena Act, 1956

Key Provisions:
1.	Establishment of Lok Sahayak Sena 
o	The Act provided for the establishment of the Lok Sahayak Sena under the authority of the Central Government. 
o	It enabled eligible citizens to voluntarily join and receive military training. 
2.	Membership and Enrolment 
o	The Act provided rules regarding the enrolment, service conditions, and obligations of members of the Lok Sahayak Sena. 
o	Members were required to undergo prescribed training and follow applicable discipline and regulations. 
3.	Training and Duties 
o	The organisation was intended to provide basic military training and prepare volunteers for assistance during: 
	National emergencies. 
	Defence requirements. 
	Other situations requiring support to civil and military authorities. 
4.	Control and Administration 
o	The Central Government was empowered to make provisions regarding the administration, organisation, and functioning of the Lok Sahayak Sena. 
o	Rules could be framed relating to training, discipline, and service conditions. 
5.	Protection and Legal Provisions 
o	The Act provided legal protection for actions taken in good faith while performing duties under the Act. 
o	It also authorised the Government to make rules for effective implementation.

1. 2. Establishment of Statutory Auxiliary Corps: Enacted to constitute a statutory force named the Lok Sahayak Sena (National Volunteer Force). title: The Women’s and Children’s Institutions (Licensing) Act, 1956.

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of the Women's and Children's Institutions (Licensing) Act, 1956

Key Provisions:
1.	Licensing of Institutions 
o	The Act requires institutions established for the care, protection, maintenance, or reception of women and children to obtain a licence from the prescribed authority before commencing or continuing operations. 
o	Licences are granted subject to compliance with prescribed conditions. 
2.	Inspection and Supervision 
o	The competent authority is empowered to inspect licensed institutions to ensure compliance with the provisions of the Act and applicable rules. 
o	Inspections may cover accommodation, sanitation, health, nutrition, safety, records, and overall management. 
3.	Suspension or Cancellation of Licence 
o	The licensing authority may suspend or cancel a licence if an institution fails to comply with the provisions of the Act or the conditions of the licence. 
o	The institution is generally given an opportunity to be heard before such action is taken. 
4.	Penalties 
o	The Act prescribes penalties for: 
	Operating an institution without a valid licence. 
	Violating licence conditions. 
5.	Rule-Making Power 
o	The Central Government is empowered to make rules for carrying out the purposes of the Act, including matters relating to licensing, inspection, administration, and standards for institutions.

Precedent & Historical Rationale

1. Proliferation of Unregulated Shelter Homes: In the 1950s, numerous private, non-statutory orphanages, rescue homes, and shelters for destitute women operated without regulatory oversight, giving rise to instances of physical exploitation, sub-standard living conditions, and illegal adoption practices.

2. Mandatory Statutory Licensing & Inspection Standards: Enacted to prevent commercial exploitation and neglect of vulnerable inmates by making it illegal to establish or maintain an institution for women or children without a valid statutory license granted by the State Government. It empowered authorities to inspect homes, prescribe minimal maintenance standards, and revoke licenses for non-compliance.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

● Formulation: Initiated as a social reform measure to enforce baseline welfare and safety norms across private social welfare institutions.

● Parliamentary passage: Debated and passed by both Houses of Parliament (First Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha) in December 1956.

● Presidential Assent: Received Presidential Assent on December 30, 1956.

● Enforcement: Brought into force on January 15, 1958. (Note: Applicable to areas where state-specific institutional licensing statutes were not enacted; later supplemented by the Orphanages and Other Charitable Homes (Supervision and Control) Act, 1960).

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of the States Reorganisation Act, 1956

Key Provisions:
1.	Reorganisation of States 
o	The Act provided for the alteration of boundaries and the formation of new States. 
o	The existing classification of States into Part A, Part B, Part C, and Part D States was abolished. 
o	India was reorganised into 14 States and 6 Union Territories. 
2.	Formation and Alteration of States 
o	Several States were created, merged, or their boundaries were modified. 
o	Major changes included: 
	Formation of Andhra Pradesh by merging Andhra State with Telugu-speaking areas of Hyderabad State. 
	Formation of Kerala by integrating Malayalam-speaking regions. 
	Creation of Mysore State (later Karnataka) through the merger of Kannada-speaking areas. 
	Reorganisation of Bombay, Madhya Pradesh, Punjab and Rajasthan. 
3.	Establishment of Union Territories 
o	Certain territories were designated as Union Territories to be administered directly by the Central Government. 
o	Examples included Delhi, Himachal Pradesh, Manipur, Tripura, and others. 
4.	Changes in High Courts and Administration 
o	The Act provided for adjustments in the jurisdiction and functioning of High Courts due to territorial changes. 
o	Administrative arrangements, including transfer of officers and assets, were also provided. 
5.	Representation in Parliament 
o	The Act made necessary changes to the allocation of seats in the Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha following the reorganisation of States. 
o	It provided for adjustments in parliamentary and legislative representation. 
6.	Territorial Adjustments 
o	The Act contained provisions relating to the transfer of territories, assets, liabilities, and administrative arrangements between reorganised States.

o Disputes regarding ownership, custody, and administration of state properties, private properties of rulers, and revenue assets required immediate, specialized legislative intervention to prevent asset dissipation and maintain civil order.

Central Silk Board Act, 1948

5.	Financial Provisions: 
o	The Act provides for the constitution and management of funds required for carrying out the functions of the Board. 
6.	Rule-Making Powers: 
o	The Central Government is empowered to make rules for implementing the provisions of the Act.

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of the Census Act, 1948

Key Provisions:
1.	Conduct of Census 
o	The Central Government may declare its intention to conduct a census through notification. 
o	The census may include the collection of information relating to population, households, occupations, and other prescribed matters. 
2.	Appointment of Census Officers 
o	The Government may appoint: 
	Census Commissioner. 
	Census officers. 
	Supervisory and other staff required for conducting census operations. 
o	These officers are responsible for carrying out census activities. 
3.	Power to Require Information 
o	Census officers are authorised to collect information from individuals and households for census purposes. 
o	Persons are required to provide true information as demanded under the Act. 
4.	Duties of Citizens 
o	Individuals are required to cooperate with census officials and provide necessary information. 
o	Failure to provide information or providing false information may attract penalties. 
5.	Confidentiality of Census Information 
o	Information collected during the census is treated as confidential. 
o	Census records are not used as evidence against individuals in legal proceedings except as provided under the Act. 
6.	Offences and Penalties 
o	The Act provides penalties for: 
	Refusing to provide required information. 
	Giving false information. 
	Obstructing census officials in performing their duties. 
	Misconduct by census officers. 
7.	Rule-Making Power 
o	The Central Government is empowered to make rules regarding: 
	Census procedures. 
	Collection and recording of information. 
	Duties of census officers. 
	Forms and methods used during census operations.

Act Number / Year 37 of 1948

Presidential Assent / Enactment Date September 3, 1948

Nodal Ministry Ministry of Home Affairs

Precedent & Statutory Rationale

1. Inadequacy of Periodic Colonial Frameworks:

o Prior to 1948, population censuses in British India were conducted under short-term enactments or temporary administrative orders issued for specific decennial years, lacking a permanent, unified statutory framework applicable across the entire sovereign dominion.

o Following partition and independence, the immediate necessity to collect accurate demographic, social, and economic data for national planning, resource allocation, and democratic delimitation required a robust, permanent statutory backing.

2. Establishment of Permanent Enumeration Authority:

o The 1948 Act was enacted to provide a permanent legislative framework for conducting population censuses throughout India or any part thereof.

o It officially empowers the Central Government to notify and declare census operations, appoints the administrative machinery (including the Census Commissioner and local enumerators), imposes a legal obligation on citizens to provide truthful answers, and guarantees the confidentiality of individual census records.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

• Formulation: Drafted and piloted by the Ministry of Home Affairs to secure a dependable legislative instrument for handling large-scale post-independence demographic profiling.

• Parliamentary Passage: Tabled, debated, and passed by the Constituent Assembly of India (Legislative), receiving formal Presidential Assent on September 3, 1948.

• Enforcement: Enforced on September 3, 1948.

o	Authorizes the restriction or prohibition of the movement of ships, boats, fishing vessels, and other craft within notified danger areas during artillery practice. 
o	Requires compliance with directions issued by the competent authorities.
