title: The National Institute of Mental Health and Neuro-Sciences, Bangalore Act, 2012

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of the National Institute of Mental Health and Neuro-Sciences, Bangalore Act 2012 
Key Provisions
1. Regulatory Alignment for Mental Health Establishments
•	Registration Requirement: The Institute, as a mental health establishment, must register with the State Authority under the Act, submitting proof of existing registration (if any) under the Clinical Establishments (Registration and Regulation) Act, 2010, or other state laws.
•	Exemption Clause Awareness: Acknowledges the Central Government's power to exempt certain categories of existing establishments from registration requirements.
2. Compliance with Minimum Standards
•	Facilities and Services: Must fulfill minimum standards specified by the Authority for its category, with periodic updates to meet newly specified standards.
•	Personnel Qualifications: Ensures all staff meet the minimum qualifications set by the Authority's regulations.
•	Record Keeping and Reporting: Maintains and reports as per the Authority's specifications for mental health establishments.
3. Governance and Oversight in the Context of Mental Health Regulations
•	Central Oversight Alignment: The Institute's governance structure is aligned with broader regulatory frameworks, facilitating compliance with mental health establishment regulations.
•	Regulatory Directives: Empowered to receive and implement directives from the Central Government for maintaining operational and academic standards in line with mental health establishment regulations.
4. Operational Functions with Regulatory Compliance
•	Education and Research: Conducts programs and research with consideration for regulatory standards impacting mental health education and practice.
•	Healthcare Services: Provides care adhering to the specified minimum standards for mental health establishments.
•	Accreditation and Recognition: Ensures degrees and diplomas are recognized, reflecting compliance with national standards for mental health education.
5. Financial and Administrative Accountability
•	Transparent Funding: Central Government funding with potential for additional sources, all subject to audit for transparency and compliance.
•	Audit and Oversight: Subject to the Comptroller and Auditor-General of India for financial transparency and regulatory adherence.
6. Transitional and Employee Provisions
•	Employee Protection: Employees are protected under the Amendment Act, with benefits retained, ensuring stability in compliance efforts.
•	Legislative Validity and Compliance: All institutional actions remain valid despite governance flaws, ensuring continuous regulatory compliance.

title: The Street Vendors (Protection of Livelihood and Regulation of Street Vending) Act, 2014

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of the Street Vendors (Protection of Livelihood and Regulation of Street Vending) Act, 2014 
Key Provisions
I. Regulation & Protection of Street Vending
Mandatory Survey: - Identification of existing street vendors.
•	Protection from eviction until the survey and vending certificate process is completed.
Certificate of Vending: - Issuance post-survey, with categories (e.g., stationary, mobile).
•	Includes identity cards; non-transferable.
Conditions & Fees:
•	Undertaking for personal/family operation.
•	Fees and validity periods as per the scheme.
Cancellation/Suspension:
•	Grounds: Breach of conditions or fraud.
•	Procedure: After providing an opportunity for hearing.
Appeal Mechanism: - Against Town Vending Committee decisions to the local authority.
III. Rights & Responsibilities of Street Vendors
Rights: - To vend as per certificate.
•	Entitlement to a new site upon relocation.
Duties: - Maintain public hygiene and cleanliness.
•	Preserve civic amenities.
•	Pay specified maintenance charges.
IV. Relocation, Eviction, & Asset Protection
Relocation/Eviction:
•	Only for public purposes with provision for rehabilitation.
•	Notice period: 30 days.
Seizure & Reclaiming of Goods:
•	Procedure for seizure in case of non-compliance.
•	Reclaiming process with fees (differentiated for perishable and non-perishable goods).
V. Governance & Dispute Resolution
Town Vending Committee (TVC):
•	Composition: Includes municipal, medical, planning, and vendor representatives.
•	Functions: Survey, certificate issuance, relocation decisions.
Dispute Redressal: - Mechanism for grievance resolution.
Rule Making Power: - For appropriate Government and local authorities to frame rules, bye-laws, and schemes.
VI. Miscellaneous Provisions
No Ownership Rights: - Vending rights do not confer land ownership.
Overriding Clause: - This Act supersedes inconsistent provisions in other laws.
Power to Address Difficulties: - Temporary power to the Central Government to remove operational difficulties.
VII. Schedules
First Schedule: Outlines the Plan for Street Vending (accommodation, facilities).
Second Schedule: Details for the Scheme for Street Vendors (survey, certification, relocation principles).

Short Title The Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013

Presidential Assent Date January 1, 2014

Nodal Ministry Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions

Precedent & Statutory Rationale

1. Decades of Institutional Advocacy and Lapsed Bills:

o The concept of an anti-corruption ombudsman (Lokpal at the Centre and Lokayukta in the States) was first proposed in Parliament in 1968, followed by multiple attempts across decades (in 1971, 1977, 1985, 1989, 1996, 1998, and 2001) that repeatedly lapsed due to the dissolution of successive Lok Sabhas.

2. The Anti-Corruption Movement and International Commitments:

o The legislative momentum culminated following widespread national public protests against institutional corruption. Simultaneously, the legislation aligned India's domestic framework with its obligations under the United Nations Convention against Corruption (UNCAC) to establish transparent investigative bodies for public functionaries.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

• Formulation: Developed and piloted by the Department of Personnel and Training (DoPT) under the Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions.

• Parliamentary Passage: Tabled as the Lokpal and Lokayuktas Bill, 2011, scrutinized by a Parliamentary Standing Committee and a subsequent Rajya Sabha Select Committee, and eventually passed by the Lok Sabha on December 27, 2011. Following extensive revisions, it was passed by the Rajya Sabha on December 17, 2013, and by the Lok Sabha on December 18, 2013.

• Presidential Assent: Received formal Presidential Assent from President Pranab Mukherjee on January 1, 2014, entering the statute book as Act No. 1 of 2014.

• Enforcement: Enforced on January 16, 2014.

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of the Repealing and Amending (Second) Act, 2015
Objectives of the Act
•	To repeal obsolete, redundant, and spent Central Acts that no longer serve any practical purpose. 
•	To make minor consequential amendments to existing laws, including corrections of statutory references, drafting errors, and inconsistencies. 
•	To simplify and modernise the corpus of Central legislation. 
•	To improve the clarity, accessibility, and efficiency of the legal framework. 
Key Provisions
•	Repeal of Enactments: The Act repeals a number of Central Acts and amending Acts that had become obsolete, fully implemented, superseded, or otherwise unnecessary. 
•	Consequential Amendments: It makes limited amendments to certain existing enactments to update references, rectify drafting errors, and ensure consistency in statutory language. 
•	Saving Clause: The repeal of any enactment does not affect its previous operation or any rights, obligations, liabilities, penalties, investigations, or legal proceedings arising under it, unless expressly provided otherwise. 
•	Schedules: The Acts repealed and the amendments made are specified in the Schedules to the Act.

title: The Civil Liability for Nuclear Damage Act, 2010

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of the Civil Liability for Nuclear Damage Act, 2010
Key Provisions
1.	Liability Framework
•	Operator's Liability: Strict and no-fault for nuclear damage, with capped limits.
•	Nuclear Reactors (≥10 MW): ₹1,500 crores
•	Spent Fuel Reprocessing Plants: ₹300 crores
•	Others: ₹100 crores
•	Joint and Several Liability for multiple operators.
•	Central Government's Liability: For excess damages, government-owned installations, and special causes (natural disasters, war, etc.).
2.	Exemptions
•	Damage from natural disasters, armed conflict, victim’s negligence, or damage to the installation itself.
Claims and Compensation
•	Claims Commissioner: Oversees claims process.
•	Eligible Claimants: Victims, property owners, and their representatives.
•	Time Limits:
•	Property Damage: 10 years
•	Personal Injury: 20 years
•	Award Process: Final award by the Claims Commissioner within 3 months.
Financial and Regulatory
•	Mandatory Insurance/Fiscal Security for operators.
•	Potential Nuclear Liability Fund, funded by operator levies.
Definitions and Integration
•	Broad Definitions for key nuclear terms.
•	Integration with Atomic Energy Act, 1962 for operational and regulatory frameworks.

Act Number / Year Act No. 38 of 2010

Presidential Assent Date September 21, 2010

Precedent & Statutory Rationale

1. Indo-US Civil Nuclear Agreement and International Obligations:

o Following the Indo-US Civil Nuclear Agreement (2005–2008) and India's separation of civilian and military nuclear facilities, India sought to integrate into global nuclear commerce. A prerequisite for this was establishing a domestic nuclear liability regime to enable international trade and movement toward ratifying the international Convention on Supplementary Compensation for Nuclear Damage (CSC).

2. Addressing Liability Gaps and Ensuring Victim Compensation:

o Prior to 2010, India lacked a specialized legal framework to handle catastrophic industrial accidents in the nuclear sector. The law was designed to create a predictable, "no-fault" liability mechanism that guarantees prompt and adequate compensation to victims of a nuclear incident without forcing them to undergo protracted civil litigation to prove negligence.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

• Formulation: Drafted and piloted by the Department of Atomic Energy to align India's domestic laws with international civil nuclear standards while addressing unique national security and public safety priorities.

• Parliamentary Passage: Tabled in Parliament in May 2010, subjected to intense political debate and scrutiny by a Parliamentary Standing Committee, and subsequently passed by both the Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha in August 2010.

• Presidential Assent: Received formal Presidential Assent on September 21, 2010, entering the statute book as Act No. 38 of 2010.

• Enforcement: Enforced on November 11, 2011.

Precedent & Historical Rationale

● Deficiencies of the Society and Deemed-to-be-University Framework - The Rajiv Gandhi National Institute of Youth Development (RGNIYD) was initially set up in 1993 at Sriperumbudur, Tamil Nadu, as an autonomous society registered under the Societies Registration Act, 1860, and later conferred the status of a 'Deemed-to-be-University' under Section 3 of the UGC Act, 1956 in 2008. Operating under these intermediate administrative models restricted the institute's statutory authority to function as an apex national body for policy research, formulate nationwide youth development curricula, establish regional centers across the country, and award specialized degrees with statutory autonomy.

● Statutory Elevation to an Institution of National Importance - Formulated to declare the Rajiv Gandhi National Institute of Youth Development to be an Institution of National Importance and to provide for its incorporation and matters connected therewith. Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

● Formulation & Introduction - Drafted by the Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports to establish a premier apex institute for youth policy; introduced as The Rajiv Gandhi National Institute of Youth Development Bill, 2011 (Bill No. 120 of 2011) by Minister of State (Independent Charge) for Youth Affairs and Sports Ajay Maken in the Lok Sabha on December 21, 2011.

● Enforcement - Enforced on November 19, 2012.

Summary of  Press and Registration of Periodicals Act, 2023
The Press and Registration of Periodicals Act regulate the printing and publication of periodicals across India, ensuring transparency and accountability. It applies uniformly across all languages within the same State or Union territory.

1.	Scope and Extent
•	Applies uniformly across all languages within the same State or Union territory in India.
2.	Definitions
•	Periodical/Newspaper: Includes publications in any language within a State/Union territory.
3.	Registration of Periodicals
•	Mandatory Registration: With the Press Registrar, applicable to all languages within a State/Union territory.
•	Unique Title Requirement: Across languages within the same geographical jurisdiction.
4.	Obligations on Publishers
•	Annual Statement: Must include language-specific circulation and readership details.

5.	Penalties
•	Uniform Penalties: Apply equally to all language publications within a State/Union territory for non-compliance.
6.	Authorities and Powers
•	Press Registrar: Oversees registrations, verifications, and penalties across all languages in a jurisdiction.

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of the Delhi Sales Tax Act, 1975
Objective
The Delhi Sales Tax Act, 1975 was enacted to consolidate and amend the law relating to the levy of tax on the sale of goods in the Union Territory of Delhi. The Act provides a comprehensive framework for the assessment, collection, recovery, and administration of sales tax while ensuring effective regulation of dealers and tax compliance. 
Key Provisions
•	Levy of Sales Tax: Provides for the levy of sales tax on the sale of goods in Delhi and prescribes the rates of tax, taxable turnover, exemptions, and tax-free goods. 
•	Registration of Dealers: Requires eligible dealers to obtain registration and provides for voluntary, provisional, special registration, amendment, and cancellation of registration certificates. 
•	Returns and Assessment: Prescribes filing of tax returns, assessment and reassessment of tax, recovery of tax, payment of interest, refunds, and set-off of tax. 
•	Sales Tax Authorities: Establishes sales tax authorities, including the Commissioner of Sales Tax and the Appellate Tribunal, and defines their powers and functions. 
•	Accounts and Inspection: Requires dealers to maintain accounts and records and empowers tax authorities to inspect premises, examine documents, conduct searches, and collect information. 
•	Appeals and Revisions: Provides for appeals, revisions, rectification of mistakes, and references to the High Court against specified orders. 
•	Offences and Penalties: Prescribes penalties and prosecution for offences such as tax evasion, concealment of sales, false declarations, and unauthorised collection of tax. 
•	Rule-making Power: Empowers the Administrator/Government to make rules for carrying out the provisions of the Act.

Summary of the Mental Health Care Act, 2017
•	Act Name: The Mental Healthcare Act, 2017
•	Extent: Whole of India
•	Objective: Provide mental healthcare and services, protect, promote, and fulfill the rights of persons with mental illness, with a structured governance framework.
Governance & Decision Making
•	Central Mental Health Authority (CMHA) & State Mental Health Authorities: Oversee mental healthcare, register establishments, and set norms. Decision Making: Authorities may have a presiding member with a second or casting vote to ensure decisive governance.
•	Mental Health Review Boards (MHRBs): Review admissions, treatments, and decisions, ensuring patient rights.
Key Provisions
•	Advance Directives: Allowed for mental healthcare decisions.
•	Nominated Representatives: Can be appointed for decision-making in the patient's best interest.
•	Emergency Treatment: Permitted without consent in life-threatening situations, with strict limitations.
•	Prohibited Procedures: Electro-convulsive therapy without anesthesia, for minors, and psychosurgery without consent and Board approval.
Penalties & Protections
•	Penalties: For unauthorized mental health establishments and violations.
•	Protection of Action Taken in Good Faith: For professionals acting in good faith.
•	Overriding Effect: This Act supersedes conflicting laws.

Summary of the School of Planning and Architecture Act, 2014 
Objectives 
•	To declare specified Schools of Planning and Architecture as Institutions of National Importance. 
•	To provide for their incorporation, administration, and governance. 
•	To promote high standards of education, research, and professional training in architecture, planning, and allied fields. 
•	To support innovation and capacity building for sustainable urban, regional, and environmental development. 
Key Provisions
•	Institutions of National Importance: The Act declares the Schools of Planning and Architecture at New Delhi, Bhopal, and Vijayawada as Institutions of National Importance. 
•	Incorporation of Institutions: Each School is constituted as a body corporate with perpetual succession, having the power to acquire, hold, and dispose of property, enter into contracts, and sue or be sued. 
•	Governance Structure: The Act provides for the constitution of a Board of Governors, a Senate, and other statutory authorities responsible for the administration, academic affairs, finance, and management of each School. 
•	Academic Functions: The Schools are empowered to provide instruction, conduct research, award degrees, diplomas, and other academic distinctions, establish centres of excellence, and collaborate with national and international institutions. 
•	Faculty and Administration: The Act contains provisions relating to the appointment, service conditions, and responsibilities of the Director, faculty members, officers, and employees. 
•	Finance and Accountability: It provides for grants from the Central Government, maintenance of funds, preparation of budgets, audit of accounts, and submission of annual reports to ensure financial transparency and accountability. 
•	Statutes, Ordinances, and Regulations: The Schools are empowered to frame statutes, ordinances, and regulations, with the approval of the appropriate authorities, for carrying out the purposes of the Act.

title: The Specified Bank Notes (Cessation of Liabilities) Act, 2017

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of the Specified Bank Notes (Cessation of Liabilities) Act, 2017
*Act Name: Specified Bank Notes (Cessation of Liabilities) Act, 2017 
*Enactment: By Parliament in the Sixty-eighth Year of the Republic of India 
*Commencement: Deemed to have come into force on 31st December, 2016 
*Primary Objective: To provide in the public interest for the cessation of liabilities on specified bank notes (₹500 and ₹1000 series existing on or before 8th November, 2016) and related matters.
Key Provisions
1.	Cessation of Liability: - Specified bank notes ceased to be legal tender as per a notification dated 8th November, 2016.
•	These notes ceased to be liabilities of the Reserve Bank of India and lost the guarantee of the Central Government from 31st December, 2016.
2.	Exchange of Specified Bank Notes: - Eligible Persons:
•	Citizens of India who were outside India between 9th November, 2016 to 30th December, 2016 (with conditions).
•	Classes of persons specified by the Central Government for valid reasons.
•	Process: Tender within a specified "grace period" with declarations/statements at designated Reserve Bank offices.
•	Outcome for Genuine Cases: Value of notes credited to a Know Your Customer (KYC) compliant bank account after verification.
3.	Prohibitions and Penalties: - Prohibition: Holding, transferring, or receiving specified bank notes after the appointed day, with exceptions (e.g., up to 10 notes in total for individuals, more for study/research/numismatics, and for authorized entities).
•	Penalties:
•	For false declarations under Section 4: Fine up to ₹50,000 or 5 times the face value of the notes, whichever is higher.
•	For contravening Section 5 (holding/transferring/receiving beyond allowed limits): Fine up to ₹10,000 or 5 times the face value of the notes involved, whichever is higher.
4.	Corporate Liability: - Companies found guilty under Sections 6 or 7, along with responsible directors/managers, are liable for punishment.
•	Provision for appeal against the Reserve Bank's decisions.

Precedent & Statutory Rationale

1. Formal Extinction of Central Bank & Government Liabilities:

o Legally terminated the statutory guarantee of the Central Government and the liability of the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) under Sections 26 and 34 of the RBI Act, 1934 for the demonetized ₹500 and ₹1,000 currency notes existing prior to November 8, 2016.

2. Prohibition and Penal Framework for Holding/Parallel Circulation:

o Imposed a strict legal ban on holding, transferring, or receiving specified high-denomination notes beyond permissible threshold limits post the designated cutoff period, penalizing violations to prevent the re-entry of unaccounted cash into informal channels.

3. Statutory Grace Period & Exempted Declarations:

o Created a formal mechanism permitting certain categories of individuals—such as Non-Resident Indians (NRIs) and citizens traveling abroad during the demonetization window—to deposit/exchange specified notes at designated RBI branches subject to verification.

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of the National Judicial Appointments Commission Act, 2014
Key Provisions:
1.	Establishment and Headquarters: - Establishes the National Judicial Appointments Commission (NJC).
•	Headquarters in Delhi.
2.	Composition and Reference for Vacancies: - Composition not detailed in the provided excerpt.
•	Central Government to intimate vacancies to the NJC for recommendations.
3.	Appointment Procedures: - Supreme Court Judges:
•	Senior-most Judge for Chief Justice of India if fit.
•	Selection based on ability, merit, and other criteria for other Judges.
•	High Court Judges:
•	Chief Justice selection based on inter se seniority, ability, and merit.
•	Involves nominations from the High Court's Chief Justice and consideration of ability and merit for other Judges.
4.	Decision Making and Oversight: - President's Power to Reconsider: Can require the NJC to reconsider its recommendations.
•	Quorum and Voting: Not specified in the provided excerpt for the NJC, but mentioned for another context (possibly not relevant due to different file path).
5.	Operational and Administrative: - Officers and Employees: Appointed by the Central Government in consultation with the NJC.
•	Rules and Regulations: Power to make rules (Central Government) and regulations (NJC).
•	Parliamentary Oversight: Rules and regulations to be laid before Parliament.
6.	Judicial and Administrative Actions: - Transfer of Judges: NJC to recommend transfers with specified procedures via regulations.
•	Removal of Difficulties: Central Government can issue orders to remove difficulties in implementing the Act, valid for 5 years from commencement.

Legislative History:

The National Judicial Appointments Commission Act, 2014

Short Title The National Judicial Appointments Commission Act, 2014

Act Number / Year Act No. 40 of 2014

India Code Act ID 201440

Presidential Assent Date December 31, 2014

Enforcement Date April 13, 2015

Nodal Ministry Ministry of Law and Justice

Precedent & Statutory Rationale

1. The Limitations of the Collegium System:

o Prior to 2014, the appointment and transfer of judges to the Supreme Court and High Courts were handled by the "Collegium System"—an administrative mechanism evolved via judicial interpretation rather than a statutory enactment. This system faced sustained criticism from various stakeholders for opacity, lack of institutional accountability, and the total exclusion of the executive branch from the selection loop.

2. Ensuring Transparency and Broad-Based Representation:

o Enacted alongside the Constitution (Ninety-Ninth Amendment) Act, 2014, the legislation aimed to establish a transparent, accountable, and participatory institutional framework for judicial appointments, balancing judicial independence with democratic checks and balances.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

• Formulation: Developed and piloted by the Ministry of Law and Justice to completely overhaul the judicial appointment architecture in India.

• Parliamentary Passage: Introduced as the National Judicial Appointments Commission Bill, 2014, alongside the Constitution (121st Amendment) Bill, in August 2014; passed unanimously by the Lok Sabha on August 13, 2014, and by the Rajya Sabha on August 14, 2014, followed by swift ratification by more than half of the State Legislatures.

• Presidential Assent: Received formal Presidential Assent on December 31, 2014.

• Enforcement: Enforced on April 13, 2015.

• Source: India Code Official Repository (indiacode.gov.in) and Ministry of Law and Justice Official Records

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of the Coinage Act, 2011
Key Provisions
Definitions
•	Coin: Encompasses any coin made of metal or other material stamped by the Government, including legal tender, commemorative coins, and notably, the Government of India one rupee note, with exclusions for credit and debit cards.
•	Deface: Defined as the alteration of a coin's surface or shape that is distinguishable from reasonable wear.
•	Mint: Refers to the Security Printing and Minting Corporation of India Limited or any other organisation authorised by the Government.
Coinage Provisions
•	Specifications and Legal Tender:
•	Denominations, Dimensions, Designs, and Composition: Prescribed by the Government.
•	Legal Tender: Specifies the maximum sums for which different coin denominations are legally acceptable.
•	Decimal System: Mandates the rupee to be divided into 100 units.
Offences and Penalties
•	Prohibited Activities:
•	Making, melting, destruction, or unlawful possession of coins.
•	Penalties:
•	Up to 7 years imprisonment and a fine for melting, destruction, or unlawful possession.
•	Penalties for other prohibited activities, including making or bringing in unauthorized metal pieces for use as money.
Regulatory and Protective Provisions
•	Rule Making Power: The Government is empowered to make rules to carry out the Act's purposes.
•	Good Faith Protection: Shields persons acting in good faith under the Act from legal proceedings.
•	Repeal and Savings: Repeals preceding enactments while preserving existing rights and proceedings.

ACT NO. 11 OF 2011

[1st September, 2011.]

An Act to consolidate the laws relating to coinage and the Mints, the protection of coinage and to provide for the prohibition of melting or destruction of coins and prohibit the making or the possession thereof for issue and for matters connected therewith or incidental thereto.

meta.dc.legislation.history:
Legislative History:

The Coinage Act, 2011

Short Title The Coinage Act, 2011

Act Number / Year Act No. 11 of 2011

Act ID (India Code) 201111

Presidential Assent Date September 1, 2011

Enforcement Date March 28, 2012

Nodal Ministry Ministry of Finance

Precedent & Statutory Rationale

1. Obsolescence and Fragmentation of Legacy Laws:

o Prior to 2012, laws governing coin production, legal tender limits, and mint management were split across archaic frameworks, principally the Indian Coinage Act of 1906 and the Small Coins (Offences) Act of 1971. These legacy texts failed to address contemporary economic realities, modern minting capabilities, and robust security demands.

2. Combating Illegal Melting and Hoarding:

o Fluctuations in global metal prices frequently caused the intrinsic metal value of certain coins to exceed their face value, triggering widespread illegal melting, destruction, and hoarding. The legislation was unified and tightened to introduce stringent safeguards and penal measures against the destruction of currency.

3. Comprehensive Definition and Modernization:

o The legislature sought to clarify the legal definition of a "coin" (explicitly encompassing commemorative issues and one-rupee notes while excluding digital/e-money instruments, credit cards, and postal orders) and streamline the operational framework for India's mints.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

• Formulation: Developed and piloted by the Department of Economic Affairs within the Ministry of Finance to consolidate and overhaul the legal framework governing currency and minting.

• Parliamentary Passage: Tabled, debated, and passed by both Houses of Parliament during the monsoon session of 2011.

• Presidential Assent: Received formal Presidential Assent on September 1, 2011, entering the statute book as Act No. 11 of 2011.

• Enforcement: Brought into active operational force on March 28, 2012.

title: The Smugglers and Foreign Exchange Manipulators (Forfeiture of Property) Act, 1976

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of the Smugglers and Foreign Exchange Manipulators (Forfeiture of Property) Act, 1976 (SAFEMA)
Objective
The Smugglers and Foreign Exchange Manipulators (Forfeiture of Property) Act, 1976 (SAFEMA) was enacted to provide for the forfeiture of illegally acquired properties of smugglers and foreign exchange manipulators. The Act aims to deprive such persons of the proceeds of unlawful activities, thereby protecting the national economy and deterring smuggling and foreign exchange violations. 
Key Provisions
•	Applicability: Applies to specified persons, including certain convicted smugglers, foreign exchange offenders, persons detained under the COFEPOSA Act, 1974, and, in certain circumstances, their relatives, associates, and holders of illegally acquired property. 
•	Prohibition of Holding Illegal Property: Prohibits persons covered by the Act from holding illegally acquired property, whether movable or immovable. 
•	Forfeiture of Property: Empowers the competent authority to identify, investigate, and forfeit illegally acquired property to the Central Government after following the prescribed procedure. 
•	Burden of Proof: Places the burden of proving that the property was lawfully acquired on the person affected by the proceedings. 
•	Appellate Tribunal: Provides for an Appellate Tribunal to hear appeals against orders of the competent authority. 
•	Powers of Authorities: Confers powers of a civil court on the competent authority and the Appellate Tribunal for summoning witnesses, requiring documents, and conducting inquiries. 
•	Rule-making Power: Empowers the Central Government to make rules for carrying out the provisions of the Act.
meta.dc.identifier.preamble_description:
THE SMUGGLERS AND FOREIGN EXCHANGE MANIPULATORS (FORFEITURE OF PROPERTY) ACT, 1976
ACT NO. 13 OF1976

[25th January, 1976.]

An Act to provide for the forfeiture of illegally acquired properties of smugglers and foreign exchange manipulators and for matters connected therewith or incidental thereto.
WHEREAS for the effective prevention of smuggling activities and foreign exchange manipulations which are having a deleterious effect on the national economy it is necessary to deprive persons engaged in such activities and manipulations of their ill-gotten gains;
AND WHEREAS such persons have been augmenting such gains by violations of wealth-tax, income-tax or other laws or by other means and have thereby been increasing their resources for operating in a clandestine manner;
AND WHEREAS such persons have in many cases been holding the properties acquired by them through such gains in the names of their relatives, associates and confidants;
BE it enacted by Parliament in the Twenty-sixth Year of the Republic of India as follows:--

Legislative History:

The Smugglers and Foreign Exchange Manipulators (Forfeiture of Property) Act, 1976

● Act Title - The Smugglers and Foreign Exchange Manipulators (Forfeiture of Property) Act, 1976 (SAFEMA)

● Act Number / Year - 13 of 1976

● Act ID (India Code) - 197613

● Presidential Assent Date - January 25, 1976

● Enforcement Date - November 5, 1975

● Nodal Ministry - Ministry of Finance

Precedent & Historical Rationale

● Targeting Ill-Gotten Assets of Economic Offenders - Enacted to deprive persons engaged in smuggling activities and foreign exchange manipulations, as well as their relatives and associates, of illegally acquired properties accumulated through economic crimes.

● Complementary Framework to COFEPOSA - Formulated to strengthen preventive detention laws like the Conservation of Foreign Exchange and Prevention of Smuggling Activities Act, 1974 (COFEPOSA). While COFEPOSA focused on personal detention, SAFEMA provided for the statutory attachment, tracking, and forfeiture to the Central Government of properties acquired through illicit economic operations, shifting the burden of proof onto the property holder to show legitimate sources of income.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

● Formulation - Introduced by the Ministry of Finance to replace the Smugglers and Foreign Exchange Manipulators (Forfeiture of Property) Ordinance, 1975 (Ordinance 14 of 1975) promulgated by the President during the Emergency period to crack down on the parallel shadow economy.

● Parliamentary Passage - Debated and passed by both Houses of Parliament (Fifth Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha) during the winter session in January 1976.

● Presidential Assent - Received Presidential Assent on January 25, 1976.

● Enforcement - Enforced on November 5, 1975.

title: The National Capital Territory of Delhi Laws (Special Provisions) Second Act, 2011

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of the National Capital Territory of Delhi Laws (Special Provisions) Act, 2011
The National Capital Territory of Delhi Laws (Special Provisions) Act, 2011 was enacted as a temporary measure to address the large number of unauthorised developments in Delhi while the Government worked towards a comprehensive and planned solution. The Act provides protection against punitive action in respect of specified categories of unauthorised developments for a limited period, subject to certain conditions.
Key Objectives
•	To provide temporary relief from demolition, sealing, and eviction in respect of specified unauthorised developments in Delhi. 
•	To maintain the status quo while policies for regularisation and planned development are formulated and implemented. 
•	To facilitate orderly urban development through planned measures. 
•	To protect the interests of residents and businesses affected by unauthorised constructions and settlements during the transitional period.

9* * * * *
AND WHEREAS in view of the foregoing paragraphs, it is expedient and in public interest that no hardship be caused (whether by way of sealing or demolition of the structures or otherwise), to the public until the revision of Master Plan as stated in the preceding paragraph is undertaken to facilitate the smooth review of the Master Plan;

The National Capital Territory of Delhi Laws (Special Provisions) Second Act, 2009

Short Title The National Capital Territory of Delhi Laws (Special Provisions) Second Act, 2009

Presidential Assent / Enactment Date December 22, 2009

Nodal Ministry Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs

Precedent & Statutory Rationale

1. Extended Timeline for Comprehensive Urban Policy Implementation:

o Although initial special provisions acts and the early 2009 legislation provided short-term reprieves against sealing and demolition, the massive administrative tasks of regularizing unauthorized colonies, village abadis, slum clusters, and mixed-use commercial activities required an extended runway.

o Local bodies and the Delhi Development Authority (DDA) required sustained statutory protection to finalize complex policy frameworks, alignment guidelines, and infrastructural upgrades under the Master Plan for Delhi (MPD) 2021 without abrupt disruptions.

2. Longer-Term Moratorium on Punitive Actions:

o The Second Act of 2009 was enacted to provide a continuous, expanded moratorium lasting through December 31, 2011, keeping coercive actions like sealing and unauthorized construction demolitions in abeyance for specified categories.

o It established clear legal parameters for orderly policy implementation regarding hawkers, urban village developments, and informal settlements while preventing chaotic large-scale displacements.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

• Formulation: Framed and piloted by the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs to create a stable, longer-term legislative bridge for managing Delhi's complex urban anomalies.

• Parliamentary Passage: Tabled, debated, and passed by both Houses of Parliament, receiving Presidential Assent on December 22, 2009.

• Enforcement: Enforced on January 1, 2010.

o For decades, civil society organizations, cultural bodies, and the public advocated for reverting the colonial-era, Anglicized spellings "Orissa" and "Oriya" to their authentic local forms—"Odisha" and "Odia"—which accurately reflect the native pronunciation and linguistic heritage of the region.

2. Constitutional Process under Article 3:

o Pursuant to Article 3 of the Constitution of India, which empowers Parliament to alter the name of any State, the Odisha Legislative Assembly unanimously passed a formal resolution on August 28, 2008, requesting the change, which was subsequently forwarded to the Union Government for statutory enactment.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

• Formulation: Developed and piloted by the Ministry of Home Affairs to give legal effect to the resolution passed by the Odisha State Legislature.

• Parliamentary Passage: Introduced in the Lok Sabha in March 2010, passed by the Lok Sabha in November 2010, passed by the Rajya Sabha in March 2011, and finally cleared across both houses in September 2011.

• Presidential Assent: Received formal Presidential Assent on September 23, 2011, entering the statute book as Act No. 15 of 2011.

• Enforcement: Enforced on November 1, 2011.

• Source: India Code and Ministry of Home Affairs Official Records

title: The Prevention of Blackmarketing and Maintenance of Supplies of Essential Commodities Act, 1980

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of The Prevention of Black marketing and Maintenance of Supplies of Essential Commodities Act, 1980 
Purpose:
•	To prevent black marketing, hoarding, and profiteering, and maintain uninterrupted supplies of essential commodities (including foodstuffs, edible oilseeds, oil, and drugs) as per regulatory orders.
Key Provisions:
1.	Offences and Trials: - Contraventions of special orders regarding essential commodities (e.g., food, drugs) are triable summarily by a Judicial Magistrate of the First Class or a Metropolitan Magistrate.
•	Sentence Limit in Summary Trials: Up to 1 year imprisonment.
2.	Detention and Regulatory Powers: - Authorities empowered to detain individuals suspected of disrupting essential commodity supplies or violating related laws.
•	Regulatory Scope: Includes control over goods movement, possession of dangerous substances, and prevention of unfair practices.
3.	Procedure and Legal Safeguards: - Detailed detention and trial procedures with emphasis on minimizing procedural challenges.
•	Appeal Limitations: No appeal for sentences ≤ 1 month imprisonment and/or fine ≤ ₹2,000, unless additional penalties are imposed.
4.	Advisory and Oversight Mechanisms: - Advisory Boards for detention review, ensuring due process.
•	Provisions for Rehearing: If a summary trial appears insufficient due to the potential need for a longer sentence or other reasons.
5.	Legal Protections and Compliance: - Immunity for actions in good faith.
•	Comprehensive clauses for legal transitions and compliance with broader regulatory frameworks (e.g., Essential Commodities Act, 1955; Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973).

title: The Indira Gandhi National Tribal University Act, 2007

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of the Indira Gandhi National Tribal University Act, 2007
Key Provisions
1.	Establishment: - A teaching and affiliating University at Amarkantak with potential Regional Centres and Campuses in tribal areas.
2.	Objects: - Provide higher education and research for tribal populations.
•	Focus on tribal art, culture, traditions, languages, medicinal systems, and technologies related to natural resources.
•	Collaborate with national and international institutions for cultural studies and research.
•	Develop tribal-centric development models and contribute to policy matters.
•	Improve social, educational, and economic conditions of Scheduled Tribes.
3.	Powers of the University: - Provide instruction in various branches of learning.
•	Grant degrees, diplomas, and certificates.
•	Organize extra-mural studies, training, and extension services.
•	Confer honorary degrees.
•	Utilize distance education systems.
•	Establish positions, appoint staff, and recognize institutions.
4.	Definitions and Governance Structure: - Defined roles for Academic Board, Academic Council, Chancellor, Vice-Chancellor, Pro-Vice-Chancellor, etc.
•	Structure includes a Court, Executive Council, Finance Committee, and College Development Council.
    5. Governance and Administration 
•	Body Corporate: The University has perpetual succession and a common seal. 
•	Management: Led by a Chancellor, Vice-Chancellor, and Pro-Vice-Chancellor, with support from various councils and committees. 
•	Academic and Administrative Autonomy: Empowered to make Statutes, Ordinances, and Regulations for its governance and academic affairs.

Legislative History:

The Rajiv Gandhi University Act, 2006

● Act Title - The Rajiv Gandhi University Act, 2006

Precedent & Historical Rationale

● Elevation of Arunachal University from a State University to a Central University - Arunachal University was established at Rono Hills, Doimukh (Itanagar) in 1984 under the Arunachal University Act, 1984 (Arunachal Pradesh Act No. 1 of 1984) to serve as the premier institution of higher learning in the state. In 2005, the state government renamed it Rajiv Gandhi University. However, operating as a state university severely constrained its financial resources, specialized faculty recruitment, and research infrastructure, necessitating central intervention to upgrade it into a fully funded Central University to meet the higher educational aspirations of the tribal-dominated border state.

● Statutory Incorporation as a Teaching and Affiliating Central University - Formulated to establish and incorporate a teaching and affiliating Central University in Arunachal Pradesh, dissolve the erstwhile state university, and vest all its properties, assets, rights, and liabilities into the newly incorporated central statutory body. The Act mandated the university to provide instructional and research facilities in emerging disciplines (including tribal culture, folklore, and regional development), conferred autonomous degree-granting powers across the state of Arunachal Pradesh, and designated the President of India as the Visitor.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

● Formulation & Introduction - Drafted by the Ministry of Human Resource Development (now Ministry of Education) as part of the national initiative to establish Central Universities in northeastern border states lacking central higher educational infrastructure; introduced as The Rajiv Gandhi University Bill, 2006 in the Rajya Sabha on August 18, 2006.

title: The Sports Broadcasting Signals (Mandatory Sharing with PrasarBharati) Act, 2007

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of the Sports Broadcasting Signals (Mandatory Sharing with Prasar Bharati) Act, 2007
Key Provisions
1.	Mandatory Signal Sharing: - Applicability: Live TV (cable/DTH) and radio broadcasts of national importance sporting events.
•	Requirement: Content owners/providers must share signals (TV without ads) with Prasar Bharati.
2.	Revenue Sharing: - TV: 75% to Content Rights Owner, 25% to Prasar Bharati.
•	Radio: 50% split.
3.	Prasar Bharati’s Revenue Utilization:
•	A specified percentage used for broadcasting other sports events.
4.	Penalties for Non-Compliance:
•	Specified by the Central Government, including potential licence actions and fines up to ₹1 crore.
•	Exemption: Pre-Ordinance (2005-2007) actions are exempt.
5.	Regulatory and Legislative Provisions: - Central Government Guidelines: Authority to issue.
•	Rule Making Power: For implementation, to be tabled in Parliament.
•	Validation and Repeal: Previous guidelines validated; Ordinance repealed with savings.

ACT NO. 11 OF 2007

[19th March, 2007.]

An Act to provide access to the largest number of listeners and viewers, on a free to air basis, of sporting events of national importance through mandatory sharing of sports broadcasting signals with Prasar Bharati and for matters connected therewith or incidental thereto.
BE it enacted by Parliament in the Fifty-eighth Year of the Republic of India as follows:--

meta.dc.legislation.history:
Legislative History:

The Sports Broadcasting Signals (Mandatory Sharing with PrasarBharati) Act, 2007

● Act Title - The Sports Broadcasting Signals (Mandatory Sharing with Prasar Bharati) Act, 2007

● Act Number / Year - 11 of 2007

● Act ID (India Code) - 200711

● Assent Date - March 19, 2007

● Enforcement Date - November 11, 2005

● Nodal Ministry - Ministry of Information and Broadcasting

Precedent & Historical Rationale

● Privatization of Sports Rights and Inaccessibility on Free-to-Air Networks - With the rapid expansion of satellite and cable television in India, private commercial broadcasters acquired exclusive telecast and commentary rights for major sporting events, particularly international cricket matches. Because the vast majority of the Indian population—especially in rural, remote, and socio-economically weaker regions—relied exclusively on the free-to-air terrestrial network and Direct-to-Home (DD Free Dish) platforms of the public broadcaster (Prasar Bharati / Doordarshan), millions of citizens were effectively excluded from viewing sporting events of national importance without expensive private pay-TV subscriptions.

● Statutory Signal-Sharing Architecture and Revenue Distribution - While the Union Government issued Downlinking and Uplinking Guidelines in November/December 2005 to mandate signal sharing, the guidelines faced legal challenges from private broadcasters questioning executive competence. The Act was formulated to provide dedicated statutory backing mandating that all content rights owners and broadcast service providers must simultaneously share live broadcasting signals (free of their own advertisements) of notified sporting events of national importance with Prasar Bharati, while establishing a statutory advertisement revenue-sharing ratio (not less than 75:25 for television and 50:50 for radio).

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

● Formulation & Promulgation of Ordinance - Drafted by the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting; to ensure uninterrupted public telecast of the ICC Cricket World Cup 2007, the President promulgated The Sports Broadcasting Signals (Mandatory Sharing with Prasar Bharati) Ordinance, 2007 (Ordinance No. 4 of 2007) on February 7, 2007.

● Parliamentary Passage - Introduced as a statutory replacement bill, The Sports Broadcasting Signals (Mandatory Sharing with Prasar Bharati) Bill, 2007, by Information and Broadcasting Minister Priyaranjan Dasmunsi; debated and passed by the Lok Sabha on March 8, 2007, and considered and passed by the Rajya Sabha on March 9, 2007, during the Budget Session.

● President's Assent - Received the assent of the President of India (Dr. A.P.J. Abdul Kalam) on March 19, 2007, and was published in the Gazette of India on March 20, 2007.

● Enforcement - Enforced on November 11, 2005.

Sources - Parliamentary Debates (Lok Sabha & Rajya Sabha), The Gazette of India, India Code, and Ministry of Information and Broadcasting.

Legislative History:

The Presidency Small Cause Courts Act, 1882

● Act Title - The Presidency Small Cause Courts Act, 1882

● Act Number / Year - 15 of 1882

● Act ID (India Code) - 188215

● Presidential Assent Date - March 17, 1882

● Enforcement Date - July 1, 1882

● Nodal Ministry - Ministry of Law and Justice

Precedent & Historical Rationale

● Deficiencies & High Costs of Presidency Civil Litigation - Prior to 1882, the administration of small commercial and civil disputes within the Presidency Towns (Calcutta, Madras, and Bombay) was governed under an outdated framework rooted in the Charter of Justice and Act IX of 1850 (Courts of Small Causes in Presidency Towns). The existing courts suffered from jurisdictional confusion with the Ordinary Original Civil Jurisdiction of the Chartered High Courts, restrictive pecuniary ceilings, and procedural complexities that made the recovery of modest debts and commercial claims excessively expensive and slow.

● Consolidation of Summary Jurisdictions & Expansion of Pecuniary Powers - Formulated to consolidate and amend the law relating to the Courts of Small Causes established in the Presidency Towns of Calcutta, Madras, and Bombay. The Act:

○ Overhauled the constitution, powers, and procedures of Presidency Small Cause Courts to ensure speedy, summary adjudication of money suits, personal property claims, and simple contractual disputes.

○ Enhanced the pecuniary jurisdiction of these courts (initially up to ₹1,000, and up to ₹2,000 with consent of parties or by subsequent local amendments), providing an accessible forum for mercantile disputes.

○ Excluded complex matters—such as suits concerning title to immovable property, partition, dissolution of partnership, specific performance, and defamation—from their cognizance to preserve their summary nature.

○ Provided summary procedures for distress warrants (recovery of rent) and summary recovery of possession of immovable property from tenants and licensees under Chapter VII.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

● Formulation - Introduced by the colonial government to modernize, streamline, and codify the jurisdiction and procedural mechanics of the Small Cause Courts in the commercial hubs of Calcutta, Madras, and Bombay.

● Parliamentary Passage - Considered and passed by the Council of the Governor General of India for making Laws and Regulations in early 1882.

● Presidential Assent - Received the assent of the Governor General of India on March 17, 1882.

● Enforcement - Enforced on July 1, 1882.

Sources - Official Records of the Governor General in Council, India Code, and Ministry of Law and Justice.

The Government Savings Promotion Act, 1873

● Act Title - The Government Savings Promotion Act, 1873

● Act Number / Year - 5 of 1873

● Act ID (India Code) - 187305

● Enforcement Date - January 28, 1873

● Nodal Ministry - Ministry of Finance

Precedent & Historical Rationale

● Encouraging Small Domestic Savings & Resolving Probate Bottlenecks - In the 19th century, the expansion of government and Post Office savings banks sought to cultivate habits of thrift among small depositors and lower-income families. However, under the general succession laws of the time, the heirs of a deceased depositor were required to obtain costly and time-consuming Letters of Administration or Probate certificates to claim even modest bank balances, effectively trapping small family savings.

● Simplified Succession, Minor Accounts, & Streamlined Payouts - Formulated to amend the law relating to Government Savings Banks and protect depositors. The Act established a summary administrative procedure empowering savings bank authorities to pay out deposits below a specified monetary threshold to legal heirs or nominees without requiring mandatory probate or succession certificates, provided statutory protection for deposits held in the names of minors and married women, and granted full indemnity to the government for bona fide payments made under the statute. (Note: The Act was substantially amended and renamed as the Government Savings Promotion Act, 1873 via the Finance Act, 2018 to consolidate small savings schemes).

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

● Formulation - Introduced to simplify payout and administration procedures for government savings banks and facilitate easy access to funds for deceased depositors' families.

● Parliamentary Passage - Considered and passed by the Council of the Governor General of India for making Laws and Regulations in early 1873.

● Presidential Assent - Received the assent of the Governor General of India on January 28, 1873.

Summary of The Married Women's Property Act, 1874 

Key Aspects

1.	Legal Proceedings by and Against Married Women
•	Right to Sue and Be Sued: A married woman can maintain a suit in her own name for the recovery of her separate property.
•	Remedies: Same civil and criminal remedies as if unmarried for the protection of her separate property.
2.	Wife's Liability for Postnuptial Debts
•	Contractual Liability: For contracts related to her separate property, a married woman can be sued to the extent of her separate property.
•	Exceptions:
•	Property transferred with conditions restricting her power to transfer or charge during marriage.
•	Does not affect the husband's liability for debts contracted by his wife's agency.
3.	Insurances by Wives and Husbands
•	Married Women's Insurance: Can independently effect a policy, considered her separate property.
•	Husband's Insurance for Wife/Children: Deemed a trust, not under the husband's control, with proceeds managed by the Official Trustee if no special trustees are appointed.

The Married Women's Property Act, 1874

● Act Title - The Married Women's Property Act, 1874

● Act Number / Year - 3 of 1874

● Act ID (India Code) - 187403

● Presidential Assent Date -February 24, 1874

● Enforcement Date - February 24, 1874

● Nodal Ministry - Ministry of Law and Justice

Precedent & Historical Rationale

● Doctrine of Coverture & Lack of Independent Property Rights - Under traditional English common law principles applicable to non-native residents in colonial India (the doctrine of coverture), a woman's legal personality merged with that of her husband upon marriage. As a consequence, a married woman could not independently hold, manage, or dispose of personal property, retain her own separate wages and earnings, or contract in her individual capacity without her husband's control and liability to his creditors.

● Securing Separate Wages, Insurance Policies, & Contractual Independence - Formulated to explain and extend certain aspects of the Indian Succession Act, 1865 and protect the separate property of married women (modeled after the UK Married Women's Property Act, 1870). The Act established that a married woman’s wages, earnings, and investments acquired through her separate skill or employment were her separate property, empowered her to effect insurance policies on her own or her husband’s life for her separate benefit (creating a statutory trust under Section 6 that shields insurance proceeds from creditors), and conferred the legal capacity to institute civil proceedings and enter into contracts in her own name.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

● Formulation - Introduced to define the independent property rights, earnings protection, and contractual status of married women across British India.

● Parliamentary Passage - Considered and passed by the Council of the Governor General of India for making Laws and Regulations in early 1874.

● Presidential Assent - Received the assent of the Governor General of India on February 24, 1874.

● Enforcement - Came into force on February 24, 1874.

Sources - Official Records of the Governor General in Council, India Code, and Ministry of Law and Justice.

The Oudh Laws Act, 1876

● Act Title - The Oudh Laws Act, 1876

● Act Number / Year - 18 of 1876

● Act ID (India Code) - 187618

● Presidential Assent Date - October 10, 1876

● Enforcement Date - October 10, 1876

● Nodal Ministry - Ministry of Home Affairs

Precedent & Historical Rationale

● Non-Regulation Status & Legal Uncertainty in Post-Annexation Oudh - Following the annexation of Oudh in 1856 and the post-1857 pacification, the province was administered as a Non-Regulation territory through executive circulars, notifications, and administrative rules. This raised doubts about which central Regulations and statutory enactments retained formal legal validity in Oudh courts.

● Declaration of Substantive Laws, Custom, Pre-emption, & Dower - Formulated to declare and amend the laws to be administered by the courts of Oudh. Modeled closely after the Punjab Laws Act, 1872, the statute:

○ Established valid local custom as the primary rule of decision in family and succession disputes (superseding personal laws where proven).

○ Regulated excessive Muhammadan dower contracts, giving courts equitable discretion to reduce disproportionate mahr claims relative to the husband’s means (Section 5).

○ Codified the statutory law of pre-emption (haq-i-shufa) to protect village communities and prevent land alienation to strangers (Sections 6–15).

○ Preserved the residual rule of decision according to "justice, equity, and good conscience" (Section 3(g)).

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

● Formulation - Introduced to define the statutory corpus, judicial hierarchy, and specific customary adaptations applicable across the Province of Oudh.

● Parliamentary Passage - Considered and passed by the Council of the Governor General of India for making Laws and Regulations in late 1876.

● Presidential Assent - Received the assent of the Governor General of India on October 10, 1876.

● Enforcement - Came into force on October 10, 1876.

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of the Bombay Revenue Jurisdiction Act 1876
.
Summary Points

1.	Short Title & Commencement:
•	Short Title: "The Bombay Revenue Jurisdiction Act, 1876"
•	Commencement: Immediate for most parts, with a specific section to commence on a date directed by the Governor General in Council.
2.	Extent: - Applies to all of the State of Maharashtra (then referred to by other names in amendments).
•	Exceptions include suits regarding revenue assessment in the City of Bombay and certain specified Acts.
3.	Definitions: - Land and Land-Revenue broadly defined to include various rights, payments, and sums related to land.
4.	Bar of Certain Suits (Section 4):
•	Prohibited Matters in Civil Courts:
•	Claims against the Government related to hereditary officer properties, certain land grants, and more.
•	Objections to land-revenue assessments, mode, or notifications.
•	Claims arising from land-revenue realization proceedings.
•	Specific entry, omission, or amendment claims in revenue records.
•	Distribution of land on estate partition under certain Acts.
•	Claims for land free from land-revenue payment, certain payments, and waste land occupation.
•	Boundary disputes under specific Acts.
•	Exceptions (Proviso): Allows civil court jurisdiction for claims based on explicit exemptions by enactment, specific grants, or judicial/adjudicative decisions.
5.	Other Provisions: - Bar of Suits against Revenue Officers (Section 6) for bona fide acts.
•	Punishment/Prosecution of Revenue Officers does not bar civil remedies (Section 7).
•	Requirement to Exhaust Appeal Rights before suing (Section 11).
•	Power of State Government to Refer Questions to the High Court (Section 12).

meta.dc.legislation.history:
Legislative History:

The Bombay Revenue Jurisdiction Act, 1876

● Act Title - The Bombay Revenue Jurisdiction Act, 1876

● Act Number / Year - 10 of 1876

● Act ID (India Code) - 187610

● Presidential Assent Date - March 28, 1876

● Enforcement Date - March 28, 1876

● Nodal Ministry - Ministry of Law and Justice

Precedent & Historical Rationale

● Civil Court Interference in Land Revenue Administration - Prior to 1876, civil courts across the Bombay Presidency frequently entertained suits challenging government land revenue assessments, inam (rent-free) grants, watan (hereditary office) tenures, and administrative recovery proceedings. This persistent judicial intervention disrupted revenue collection, created administrative friction between civil judges and executive revenue officers, and threatened colonial fiscal stability.

● Barring Civil Court Jurisdiction & Strengthening Revenue Authority - Formulated to limit the jurisdiction of Civil Courts in matters relating to the land revenue throughout the Bombay Presidency. The Act placed an explicit statutory bar preventing civil courts from entertaining suits concerning the determination and assessment of land revenue, realization of revenue arrears, claims against government officers regarding official land settlements, and disputes over village hereditary offices. It also instituted a mandatory rule requiring litigants to exhaust all administrative appeals before revenue authorities prior to instituting any permitted civil action.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

● Formulation - Introduced to define and circumscribe the boundaries between civil judicial authority and executive revenue administration across the Bombay Presidency.

● Parliamentary Passage - Considered and passed by the Council of the Governor General of India for making Laws and Regulations in early 1876.

● Presidential Assent - Received the assent of the Governor General of India on March 28, 1876.

● Enforcement - Enforced on March 28, 1876.

Sources - Official Records of the Governor General in Council, India Code, and Ministry of Law and Justice.

title: The Chutia Nagpur Encumbered Estates Act, 1876

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of the Chutia Nagpur Encumbered Estates Act, 1876:

Key Features
•	Purpose: To protect indebted estate owners from losing their estates and to ensure proper management of such estates. 
•	Government Intervention: The Act empowered the government to take over the management of an encumbered estate upon application or under specified conditions. 
•	Debt Settlement: The appointed manager was responsible for collecting revenue, paying government dues, settling creditors' claims, and reducing debts. 
•	Protection from Creditors: Once an estate came under the Act, creditors could not freely enforce claims or sell the estate without following the procedures laid down in the Act. 
•	Restoration of Estate: After debts were substantially cleared and the estate's finances stabilized, management could be returned to the rightful owner. 
•	Revenue Administration: The Act helped ensure regular payment of land revenue to the government while preventing the fragmentation or forced sale of estates.

meta.dc.legislation.history:
Legislative History:

The Chutia Nagpur Encumbered Estates Act, 1876

● Act Title - The Chutia Nagpur Encumbered Estates Act, 1876

● Act Number / Year - 6 of 1876

● Act ID (India Code) - 187606

● Presidential Assent Date - March 14, 1876

● Enforcement Date - March 14, 1876

● Nodal Ministry - Ministry of Home Affairs

Precedent & Historical Rationale

● Widespread Indebtedness & Agrarian Discontent in Chota Nagpur - During the 19th century, indigenous tribal chiefs, local rajas, and large landholders (zamindars) across the Chota Nagpur Division (in present-day Jharkhand) fell into severe debt to money-lenders and non-local creditors. Under ordinary civil execution procedures, their estates were subject to attachment and forced auction sales. This systemic alienation of ancestral land to outsider creditors triggered intense tribal unrest and posed a severe threat to agrarian stability and colonial peace in the region.

● Statutory Debt Protection & Management by Appointed Officers - Formulated to relieve encumbered estates in the Chota Nagpur Division from debt and prevent their permanent alienation through court-ordered sales. The Act empowered the Lieutenant-Governor to vest the management of an indebted landholder's estate in an appointed statutory "Manager" upon application. During management, the Act barred all civil suits, stays of execution, and attachments against the land, froze fresh liabilities, and empowered the Manager to determine valid claims, settle with creditors on reduced terms, and restore the estate to the proprietor once debts were liquidated.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

● Formulation - Introduced to provide special agrarian relief and prevent the displacement of traditional landed proprietors in the Non-Regulation territory of Chota Nagpur.

● Parliamentary Passage - Considered and passed by the Council of the Governor General of India for making Laws and Regulations in early 1876.

● Presidential Assent - Received the assent of the Governor General of India on March 14, 1876.

● Enforcement - Enforced on March 14, 1876.

Sources - Official Records of the Governor General in Council, India Code, and Ministry of Home Affairs.

Summary of the Majority Act, 1875

Key Details
•	Act No.: 9 of 1875
•	Enactment Date: 2nd March, 1875
•	Local Extent: Whole of India (with specified exceptions and updates for certain territories)
•	Commencement: Three months after passing.
Provisions
1.	Short Title: The Majority Act, 1875
2.	Age of Majority: - Section 3: Every person domiciled in India attains majority upon completing 18 years.
•	Calculation: The day of birth is counted as a whole day, and majority is attained at the beginning of the 18th anniversary of the birth day.
3.	Savings (Exceptions):
•	(a) Does not affect capacity in matters of marriage, dower, divorce, and adoption.
•	(b) Does not impact the religion or religious rites and usages of any class of citizens.
•	(c) Does not affect persons who attained majority under applicable law before this Act's commencement.

meta.dc.legislation.history:
Legislative History:

The Majority Act, 1875

● Act Title - The Majority Act, 1875

● Act Number / Year - 9 of 1875

● Act ID (India Code) - 187509

● Presidential Assent Date - March 2, 1875

● Enforcement Date - March 2, 1875

● Nodal Ministry - Ministry of Law and Justice

Precedent & Historical Rationale

● Discrepancy in the Age of Majority Across Personal Laws - Prior to 1875, there was no uniform age of majority across British India. Under Hindu law, majority was generally attained at the age of 15 or 16 (end of minority/poganda age); under Islamic law, majority was tied to the onset of puberty (bulugh); and English common law observed 21 years. This lack of uniformity created extreme legal uncertainty regarding contractual capacity, property conveyances, litigation competency, and estate administration.

● Establishment of a Uniform Standard for Legal Capacity - Formulated to establish a uniform, secular age of majority for all persons domiciled in India. The Act fixed the general age of majority at 18 years, while extending it to 21 years in cases where a guardian had been appointed by a court of justice or where an estate was administered by the Court of Wards (a distinction later streamlined by the Majority (Amendment) Act, 1999 to establish a uniform age of 18 across all categories). The Act specifically preserved personal laws in matters concerning marriage, dower, divorce, and adoption.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

● Formulation - Introduced to codify and establish a uniform age of majority across British India, resolving conflicts between divergent customary rules and commercial transactions.

● Parliamentary Passage - Considered and passed by the Council of the Governor General of India for making Laws and Regulations in early 1875.

● Presidential Assent - Received the assent of the Governor General of India on March 2, 1875.

● Enforcement - Enforced on March 2, 1875.

Sources - Official Records of the Governor General in Council, India Code, and Ministry of Law and Justice.

title: The Petroleum and Natural Gas Regulatory Board Act, 2006

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of the Petroleum and Natural Gas Regulatory Board Act,2006
Key Provisions 
1. Governance and Finance
•	Grants by Central Government (Section 38): The Central Government may provide grants to the Board for salaries, allowances, and administrative expenses.
•	Constitution: Includes grants, fees, penalties, and approved external sources.
•	Application: For salaries, administrative expenses, and expenses under the Act.
•	Accounts and Audit (Section 40): Maintenance and Preparation.
•	Audit: By the Comptroller and Auditor-General of India.
•	Reporting: Annual accounts and audit report to be laid before Parliament.
•	Annual Report (Section 41): The Board prepares an annual report on its activities and accounts, to be laid before Parliament.
2. Operational Powers and Directives
•	Power of Central Government to Issue Directions (Section 42): In the interest of sovereignty, security, foreign relations, or public order.
•	Policy Directives for Public Interest: Ensuring supply, equitable distribution, and availability of petroleum, petroleum products, or natural gas.
•	Taking Over Control in Public Interest (Section 43):
•	Trigger: War, natural calamity, or similar disruptions to supply.
•	Action: Take over control and management of entities, suspend operations, or entrust to government agencies.
3. Operational and Regulatory Provisions : 000Power of Inspection (Section 11): Right to Inspect, Enter, inspect oilfields, order production of documents, and examine persons.
•	Status of Officers: Authorized officers are deemed public servants.
•	Relaxation of Rules (Section 12): The Central Government may authorize deviations from rules in the public interest.

Legislative History:

The Petroleum and Natural Gas Regulatory Board Act, 2006

Short Title The Petroleum and Natural Gas Regulatory Board Act, 2006

Act Number / Year Act No. 19 of 2006

Act ID (India Code) 200619

Presidential Assent Date March 31, 2006

Enforcement Date October 1, 2007

Nodal Ministry Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas

Precedent & Strategic Rationale

1. Dismantling of the Administered Pricing Mechanism (APM):

o Following the government decision to phase out the Administered Pricing Mechanism and deregulate the petroleum sector starting in April 2002, downstream activities transitioned from a heavily controlled state-monopoly framework to a competitive market environment.

2. Need for an Independent Regulatory Body:

o To protect consumer interests, foster fair competition, ensure uninterrupted and adequate supplies, and regulate downstream activities such as refining, processing, storage, transportation, distribution, and marketing of petroleum and natural gas (excluding upstream crude oil and natural gas production) a specialized statutory regulator became essential.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

• Formulation: Prepared by the Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas to provide a comprehensive legal framework for downstream petroleum and natural gas infrastructure and market operations.

• Parliamentary Passage: Tabled, debated, and passed by both Houses of Parliament during the budget session of 2006.

• Presidential Assent: Received formal Presidential Assent on March 31, 2006, entering the statute book as Act No. 19 of 2006.

• Enforcement: Enforced on October 1, 2007.

Source: Official Records of Parliament, India Code, and Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of the Guardians and Wards Act, 1890

Key Provisions
•	Empowers the competent court to appoint or declare a guardian of the person or property of a minor where necessary. 
•	Provides that the welfare of the minor shall be the paramount consideration in appointing or removing a guardian. 
•	Prescribes the qualifications, powers, duties, and responsibilities of guardians appointed under the Act. 
•	Regulates the management, protection, and disposal of a minor's property, subject to the supervision and permission of the court where required. 
•	Empowers the court to remove or discharge a guardian for misconduct, incapacity, neglect of duty, or other sufficient cause. 
•	Provides for the jurisdiction of courts, appeals, and other procedural matters relating to guardianship proceedings. 
•	Ensures judicial supervision over the actions of guardians to safeguard the interests of minors.

meta.dc.legislation.history:
Legislative History:

The Guardians and Wards Act, 1890

● Act Title - The Guardians and Wards Act, 1890

● Act Number / Year - 8 of 1890

● Act ID (India Code) - 189008

● Presidential Assent Date - March 21, 1890

● Enforcement Date - March 21, 1890

● Nodal Ministry - Ministry of Law and Justice

Precedent & Historical Rationale

● Fragmented and Inconsistent Laws on Minors and Guardianship - Prior to 1890, the law relating to the guardianship and custody of minors was scattered across diverse, uncoordinated enactments, including Act XL of 1858 (Minors Act for Bengal), Act XX of 1864 (Bombay Minors Act), Act IX of 1861, and varied local regulations. This fragmentation created severe jurisdictional conflicts between provincial civil courts and the Chartered High Courts, while offering inconsistent protections for a minor's person and estate.

● Unified Statutory Code & Primacy of the Welfare of the Minor - Formulated to consolidate and amend the entire law relating to guardians and wards throughout British India. The Act established a uniform procedural framework for the District Court to appoint or declare guardians of a minor's person and property, regulated the duties, liabilities, and removal of guardians, and codified the paramount principle that all judicial orders concerning custody and guardianship must prioritize the welfare of the minor (Section 17), consistent with applicable personal laws.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

● Formulation - Introduced to repeal scattered provincial guardianship statutes and enact a comprehensive, secular procedural code for appointing, declaring, and supervising guardians of minors across British India.

● Parliamentary Passage - Considered, examined in detail by a Select Committee, and passed by the Council of the Governor General of India for making Laws and Regulations in early 1890.

● Presidential Assent - Received the assent of the Governor General of India on March 21, 1890.

● Enforcement - Enforced on March 21, 1890

Sources - Official Records of the Governor General in Council, India Code, and Ministry of Law and Justice.

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of the General Clauses Act, 1897

Key Features
•	Definitions: Explains terms such as "Central Government," "State Government," "person," "immovable property," "movable property," "document," "month," and others.
•	Computation of Time: Sets rules for calculating time periods prescribed under laws.
•	Powers and Appointments: States that the power to appoint a person generally includes the power to suspend or dismiss that person, unless a law provides otherwise.
•	Power to Issue Orders: A power to issue notifications, rules, or orders generally includes the power to amend, vary, or rescind them.
•	Repeal and Re-enactment: Provides rules on what happens when a law is repealed or replaced, including protection of rights, liabilities, penalties, and legal proceedings that arose under the repealed law unless the new law indicates otherwise.
•	Gender and Number: Unless the context requires otherwise:
•	Words in the masculine gender include females.
•	Words in the singular include the plural, and vice versa.
•	Meaning of "Person": Includes individuals, companies, associations, and bodies of individuals.
•	Official Powers: Clarifies how powers conferred on public authorities should be exercised.

Legislative History:

The General Clauses Act, 1897

Short Title The General Clauses Act, 1897

Act Number / Year Act No. 10 of 1897

India Code Act ID 189710

Enactment / Assent Date March 11, 1897

Enforcement Date March 11, 1897

Nodal Ministry Ministry of Law and Justice

Precedent & Statutory Rationale

1. Consolidation and Uniformity of Statutory Interpretation:

o Grounded in the administrative necessity to shorten the length of Central Acts, avoid repetitive boilerplate phrasing across legislation, and provide standard legal definitions and rules of construction for all future Central Acts and Regulations.

2. Standardization of Legal and Administrative Terminology:

o Designed to establish definitive statutory meanings for recurring terms (such as "affidavit", "district judge", "financial year", "good faith", "local authority", "Immovable/Movable property", and "person") across the entire framework of British Indian law.

3. Legal Safeguards on Repeal and Construction:

o Incorporated core provisions governing the effect of repeals (Section 6), the commencement and termination of time (Section 9), powers of conferment, and the operational timeline of enactments to prevent legal ambiguity when laws are amended or replaced.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

• Formulation: Developed by the central colonial administration under the direction of the Governor-General’s Council to streamline legislative drafting standards and judicial interpretation rules.

• Legislative Passage: Debated and passed by the Imperial Legislative Council of India.

• Enactment: Received formal assent from the Governor-General on March 11, 1897, entering the statute book as Act No. 10 of 1897.

• Enforcement: Enforced on March 11, 1897.

• Source: India Code Official Repository (indiacode.gov.in) and Ministry of Law and Justice Records
