Legislative History:

The Government Buildings Act, 1899

● Act Title - The Government Buildings Act, 1899

● Act Number / Year - 4 of 1899

● Act ID (India Code) - 189904

● Assent Date - February 3, 1899

● Enforcement Date - February 3, 1899

● Nodal Ministry - Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs

Precedent & Historical Rationale

● Municipal Interference and Secrecy Risks in Public and Defence Works - In late nineteenth-century British India, local municipal committees exercised sweeping, discretionary statutory powers under various municipal enactments to sanction building plans, regulate alterations, and conduct mandatory on-site inspections. Subjecting crown infrastructure, military establishments, arsenals, and state public works to ordinary municipal bye-laws caused severe administrative friction, unnecessary execution delays, and raised acute security concerns regarding the compulsory exposure of confidential defence plans and structural designs to local municipal bodies.

● Statutory Immunity from Municipal Building Bye-Laws and Structured Objection Mechanism - Formulated to exempt lands and buildings used or required for public service or public purposes (which are owned or occupied by the Government) from the operation of municipal building regulations governing erection, re-erection, construction, alteration, or maintenance. The Act replaced municipal control with an institutional consultative procedure requiring the government to give reasonable prior notice to municipal authorities (except for defence or confidential buildings) and allowing municipal bodies—with prior permission—to inspect plans and submit objections directly to the Government for executive adjudication rather than through local building sanctions.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

● Formulation - Drafted by the Public Works and Legislative Departments of the Government of India to protect imperial infrastructure, defence installations, and government public works from local municipal regulation and scrutiny.

● Parliamentary Passage - Introduced as The Government Buildings Bill, 1898 in the Council of the Governor General of India for the purpose of making Laws and Regulations, reviewed, debated, and passed in early 1899.

● Governor-General's Assent - Received the assent of the Governor-General of India (Lord Curzon) on February 3, 1899.

● Enforcement - Enforced on February 3, 1899.

Sources - Official Records of the Council of the Governor General of India, India Code, and Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs.

•	Penalties: Stipulated for unauthorized toll collection and extortion.
•	Toll Rates and Proceeds: Originally referenced a schedule (now repealed); proceeds are public revenue.

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of the Fatal Accidents Act, 1855
Key Provisions 
1.	Right to Compensation for Fatal Accidents
•	Cause: Whenever a person's death is caused by a wrongful act, neglect, or default that would have entitled the deceased to an action for damages if death had not occurred.
•	Liability: The party liable for the wrongful act, etc., is liable for an action or suit for damages despite the death.
2.	Beneficiaries of the Action
•	Benefit For: Wife, husband, parent, and child of the deceased.
•	Initiator of the Action: To be brought by and in the name of the executor, administrator, or representative of the deceased.
3.	Damages and Distribution
•	Award: Court may give damages proportioned to the loss suffered by the beneficiaries.
•	Distribution: Amount recovered (after costs) to be divided amongst the beneficiaries as directed by the Court.
4.	Procedure
•	Single Suit: Not more than one action or suit to be brought for the same subject-matter.
•	Claim for Estate Loss: Executor, etc., may also claim for pecuniary loss to the deceased's estate.
•	Particulars in Plaint: Must give full particulars of the beneficiaries and the nature of the claim.

Legislative History:

The Fatal Accidents Act, 1855

● Act Title - The Fatal Accidents Act, 1855

● Act Number / Year - 13 of 1855

● Act ID (India Code) - 185513

● Presidential Assent Date - March 27, 1855

● Enforcement Date - March 27, 1855

● Nodal Ministry - Ministry of Law and Justice

Precedent & Historical Rationale

● Overcoming Common Law Limits on Fatal Injury Claims - At English common law, the maxim actio personalis moritur cum persona (a personal right of action dies with the person) prevented dependents from claiming damages when a person died due to a wrongful act, neglect, or default. Modeled on the UK Fatal Accidents Act 1846 (Lord Campbell’s Act), statutory reform was necessary in British India to provide financial redress to surviving families.

● Providing Compensation to Families for Death Caused by Actionable Wrong - Formulated to grant a statutory cause of action to specified representative family members (such as the spouse, parent, and children) of a person whose death was caused by a wrongful act, neglect, or default. The Act established the foundation for tortious liability and wrongful death claims in Indian law, serving as the statutory precursor to modern personal injury and motor vehicle accident compensation frameworks.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

● Formulation - Introduced to provide statutory compensation rights to surviving families for financial loss resulting from wrongful or negligent acts causing death.

● Parliamentary Passage - Considered and passed by the Legislative Council of India in early 1855.

● Presidential Assent - Received the assent of the Governor General of India on March 27, 1855.

● Enforcement - Enforced on March 27, 1855.

Sources - Official Records of the Governor General in Council, India Code, and Ministry of Law and Justice.

Legislative History:

The Prisons Act, 1894

Short Title The Prisons Act, 1894

Act Number / Year Act No. 9 of 1894

India Code Act ID 189409

Enactment / Assent Date March 22, 1894

Enforcement Date July 1, 1894

Nodal Ministry Ministry of Home Affairs

Precedent & Statutory Rationale

1. Consolidation and Uniformity of Prison Administration:

o Grounded in the recommendations of the Prison Conference and subsequent Jail Commission reports to replace fragmented, localized penal regulations with a standardized statutory framework governing prison management, security, and discipline across the country.

2. Regulation of Prisoner Classification and Labor:

o Designed to establish formal rules regarding the classification of prisoners (civil, criminal, under-trial, and convicted), separation of genders and age groups, and the systematic regulation of penal labor, food, clothing, and bedding.

3. Health, Sanitation, and Discipline Standards:

o Instituted mandatory statutory provisions concerning prison sanitation, medical inspections, hospital accommodations, disciplinary offenses, punishments (including solitary confinement and whipping, which were later amended or repealed post-independence), and the responsibilities of prison officers.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

• Formulation: Developed and piloted by the home department under the direction of the Governor-General’s Council to address administrative irregularities and reform penal oversight across colonial correctional facilities.

• Legislative Passage: Debated and passed by the Imperial Legislative Council of India.

• Enactment: Received formal assent from the Governor-General on March 22, 1894.

• Enforcement: Enforced on July 1, 1894.

Legislative History:

The Ancient Monuments Preservation Act, 1904

● Act Title - The Ancient Monuments Preservation Act, 1904

● Act Number / Year - 7 of 1904

● Act ID (India Code) - 190407

● Assent Date - March 18, 1904

● Enforcement Date - March 18, 1904

● Nodal Ministry - Ministry of Culture

Precedent & Historical Rationale

● Decades of Vandalism, Neglect, and the Inadequacy of the Treasure Trove Act, 1878 - Prior to 1904, historic monuments, stupas, temples, and archaeological sites across British India suffered from widespread neglect, despoliation, unscientific excavations, and illegal trafficking of antiquities. Existing enactments—primarily the Bengal Regulation XIX of 1810, Madras Regulation VII of 1817, and the Indian Treasure Trove Act, 1878 (Act VI of 1878)—offered no legal mechanism to declare standing structures as protected monuments, regulate private owners of heritage sites, or protect ancient immovable structures from destruction.

● Comprehensive Statutory Architecture for Heritage Conservation and Antiquities Control - Formulated to provide for the preservation of ancient monuments, for the exercise of control over traffic in antiquities and over excavation in certain places, and for the protection and acquisition in certain cases of ancient monuments and of objects of archaeological, historical, or artistic interest. The Act empowered the government to notify protected monuments, execute binding conservation agreements with private owners, compulsorily acquire endangered structures under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, prohibit unauthorized excavations, and restrict or ban the export and inter-provincial movement of historical antiquities.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

● Formulation - Drafted by the Revenue and Agriculture Department and the Legislative Department of the Government of India under the personal initiative and leadership of Viceroy Lord Curzon and the first Director General of the reconstituted Archaeological Survey of India, Sir John Marshall.

● Parliamentary Passage - Introduced as The Ancient Monuments Preservation Bill, 1903 in the Council of the Governor General of India for the purpose of making Laws and Regulations on September 11, 1903, referred to a Select Committee for clause-by-clause examination, and debated and passed in March 1904 at Calcutta.

● Governor-General's Assent - Received the assent of the Governor-General of India (Lord Curzon) on March 18, 1904.

● Enforcement - Enforced on March 18, 1904 (later largely superseded at the central level for national heritage by the Ancient Monuments and Archaeological Sites and Remains Act, 1958).

Sources - Official Records of the Council of the Governor General of India, India Code, and Ministry of Culture.

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of the Bengal, Agra and Assam Civil Courts Act, 1887 

Key Provisions 

1.	Title, Extent, and Commencement
•	Title: The Bengal, Agra and Assam Civil Courts Act, 1887.
•	Extent: Applied to territories administered by the Lieutenant-Governors of Bengal and the North-Western Provinces, and the Chief Commissioner of Assam, with exceptions.
•	Commencement: Came into force on July 1, 1887.
2.	Repeal and Continuation of Previous Acts
•	Repealed previous acts but continued the validity of courts, appointments, and proceedings under those acts as if made under this Act.
3.	Jurisdiction and Court Hierarchy
•	District Judge: Highest in the hierarchy mentioned, with administrative control.
•	Subordinate Judges (later referred to as Civil Judges Senior/Junior Division): Below District Judges, with specified jurisdictions.
•	Munsifs (later referred to as Civil Judges Junior Division): Lowest in the mentioned hierarchy, with jurisdiction over smaller value suits.
4.	Amendments Over Time 
•	Substitution of Titles:
•	"Civil Judge (Senior Division)" for "Civil Judge".
•	"Civil Judge (Junior Division)" for "Munsif".
•	Jurisdictional Changes:
•	Amendments to the jurisdictional limits of Civil Judges (Senior and Junior Divisions) and Munsifs over time, increasing the value of suits they could handle.
•	Specific amendments for Uttar Pradesh, notably:
•	Increasing jurisdictional limits for Munsifs/Civil Judges (Junior Division) from 5,000 to 10,000 rupees (U.P. Act 57 of 1976), then to 1 lakh rupees (U.P. Act 14 of 2015).
•	Allowing for the delegation of powers to the High Court.
•	Provisions for Temporary Charges and Transfers
•	Temporary charge of District Court by Additional Judge or Senior Subordinate Judge in the absence of the District Judge.
•	Transfer of proceedings from a Subordinate Judge's Court to another competent Court in case of vacancy or incapacity.
5.	Small Causes Court Jurisdiction
•	Power to confer Small Causes Court jurisdiction on Civil Judges and Munsifs, with specified value limits for suits, which were amended over time.

The Bengal, Agra and Assam Civil Courts Act, 1887

● Act Title - The Bengal, Agra and Assam Civil Courts Act, 1887

● Act Number / Year - 12 of 1887

● Act ID (India Code) - 188712

● Presidential Assent Date - March 11, 1887

● Enforcement Date - July 1, 1887

● Nodal Ministry - Ministry of Law and Justice

Precedent & Historical Rationale

● Inadequacy of the Bengal Civil Courts Act, 1871 - Prior to 1887, the constitution and hierarchy of subordinate civil courts in the Bengal Presidency, the North-Western Provinces, and Assam were regulated by the Bengal Civil Courts Act, 1871 (Act VI of 1871). Increased litigation, jurisdictional conflicts between intermediate judicial officers, and procedural updates required after the enactment of the Civil Procedure Code and Suits Valuation Act rendered the 1871 framework obsolete.

● Consolidation of Subordinate Judicial Hierarchy & Pecuniary Limits - Formulated to consolidate and amend the law relating to civil courts in Bengal, the North-Western Provinces (later Agra), and Assam. The Act formally categorized four classes of civil courts (District Judge, Additional Judge, Subordinate Judge/Civil Judge Senior Division, and Munsif/Civil Judge Junior Division), defined their territorial and pecuniary jurisdictions, regulated appellate pathways to the District Court and High Court, and laid down administrative powers for local judicial management.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

● Formulation - Drafted to replace Act VI of 1871 and establish a structured, uniform hierarchy of subordinate civil courts across northern and eastern British India.

● Parliamentary Passage - Considered, reviewed by a Select Committee, and passed by the Council of the Governor General of India for making Laws and Regulations in early 1887.

● Presidential Assent - Received the assent of the Governor General of India on March 11, 1887.

● Enforcement - Enforced on July 1, 1887

Sources - Official Records of the Governor General in Council, India Code and Ministry of Law and Justice.

meta.dc.legislation.history:
Legislative History:

The Punjab Tenancy Act, 1887

● Act Title - The Punjab Tenancy Act, 1887

● Act Number / Year - 16 of 1887

● Act ID (India Code) - 188716

● Presidential Assent Date - September 23, 1887

● Enforcement Date - September 23, 1887

● Nodal Ministry - Ministry of Rural Development

Precedent & Historical Rationale

● Deficiencies and Agrarian Friction under the Punjab Tenancy Act, 1868 - Prior to 1887, agrarian relations between landlords and tenants in the Punjab were regulated by the Punjab Tenancy Act, 1868 (Act XXVIII of 1868). Rapid economic changes, agricultural commercialization, rising land values, and widespread litigation revealed severe defects in the 1868 statute, particularly concerning the determination of occupancy rights, arbitrary rent enhancements, and the summary eviction of customary cultivators.

● Comprehensive Regulation of Occupancy Rights, Rent Fixation, and Revenue Courts - Formulated to consolidate and amend the law relating to the tenancy of land in the Punjab. The Act clearly defined four distinct classes of occupancy tenants, established strict statutory grounds and procedures for rent enhancement and reduction, regulated ejectment and compensation for tenant improvements, and conferred exclusive jurisdiction over landlord-tenant disputes on specialized Revenue Courts and Revenue Officers (barring the jurisdiction of ordinary civil courts).

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

● Formulation - Introduced alongside the Punjab Land-Revenue Act, 1887 to overhaul provincial agrarian and revenue laws, drafted under the guidance of Sir Lyall and the Punjab administration.

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of The Punjab Land-revenue Act, 1887:

Scope and Commencement
•	Title & Extent: Known as the Punjab Land-revenue Act, 1887, extending to territories administered by the Lieutenant-Governor of the Punjab, including Spiti.
•	Commencement: Came into force on a day appointed by the Local Government with the Governor General's sanction.

Key Definitions
•	Estate: Area with a separate record-of-right, separately assessed for land-revenue, or declared as such by the Local Government.
•	Landowner: Excludes tenants and assignees of land-revenue but includes those in possession of an estate or its profits.
•	Holding: Share/portion of an estate held by one or more landowners.
•	Land-Revenue: Includes assigned land-revenue, quit-rent, and commutation for service.
•	Arrear of Land-Revenue: Unpaid land-revenue after the due date.
•	Defaulter: Person liable for an arrear, including sureties.

Provisions Highlighted in the Context
1.	Repeal and Continuity: - Repeals specified enactments, with continuity for actions taken under them.
•	References to repealed enactments are construed as referring to this Act.
2.	Enforcement and Recovery
•	Arrest and Detention of Defaulter (Section 69): Allows for the arrest of defaulters (excluding females, minors, lunatics, or idiots) and their detention up to one month.
•	Distress and Sale of Moveable Property and Crops (Section 70): Permits distraint and sale, with exemptions for subsistence needs.
•	Transfer of Holding (Section 71): Enables the Collector to transfer a holding to another landowner to recover arrears, with conditions.
•	Attachment of Estate or Holding (Section 72): Allows for attachment and management by the Collector or an agent until arrears are cleared.

Legislative History:

The Punjab Land-Revenue Act, 1887

● Act Title - The Punjab Land-Revenue Act, 1887

● Act Number / Year - 17 of 1887

● Act ID (India Code) - 188717

● Presidential Assent Date - September 23, 1887

● Enforcement Date - eptember 23, 1887

●

● Nodal Ministry - Ministry of Rural Development

Precedent & Historical Rationale

● Inadequacy of the Punjab Land Revenue Act, 1871 - Prior to 1887, land revenue administration in the Punjab was governed under the Punjab Land Revenue Act, 1871 (Act XXXIII of 1871). Extensive settlement operations, agricultural expansion, and practical administrative experience highlighted significant deficiencies in the 1871 framework, especially concerning the periodic revision of land records, partition of joint agricultural estates, and the precise hierarchy and powers of revenue officers.

● Comprehensive Code for Survey, Record of Rights, Revenue Assessment, and Partition - Formulated as a companion statute to the Punjab Tenancy Act, 1887 to consolidate and declare the law relating to land revenue and revenue officers across the Punjab. The Act established a structured administrative hierarchy (Financial Commissioner, Commissioners, Collectors, Assistant Collectors, and Tahsildars), regulated survey operations and periodic settlements, codified the preparation and maintenance of annual records of rights (jamabandi and khasra girdawari), and provided detailed procedures for the partition of holdings and summary recovery of revenue arrears.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

● Formulation - Drafted under the direction of the Punjab Government to replace Act XXXIII of 1871 with a modern, exhaustive revenue code tailored to the province's agrarian and village tenures (Mahalwari system).

● Parliamentary Passage - Considered, debated, and passed by the Council of the Governor General of India for making Laws and Regulations in late 1887.

● Presidential Assent - Received the assent of the Governor General of India on September 23, 1887.

● Enforcement - Enforced on eptember 23, 1887

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of the Charitable Endowments Act, 1890

Key Provisions and Definitions
•	"Charitable Purpose": Encompasses relief of the poor, education, medical relief, and public utility objectives, excluding religious teaching or worship.
•	Treasurer of Charitable Endowments:
•	Appointed by the Government
•	Operates as a Corporation Sole with perpetual succession and a corporate seal
•	Empowered to sue and be sued
Main Provisions
1.	Property Vesting
•	The Government can vest charitable property in the Treasurer upon application, with predefined terms for its use or income distribution.
•	Vesting does not mandate active administration by the Treasurer.
2.	Administration Schemes
•	The Government, with the applicant's concurrence, can establish, alter, or replace schemes for managing vested properties.
•	Established schemes override conflicting judicial decrees or directives.
3.	Application and Administration
•	Eligible Applicants: Trustees of existing charitable trusts or proposers of new trusts.
•	Treasurer’s Responsibilities:
•	Role: Acts as a bare trustee without administrative responsibilities unless specified.
•	Accounting: Maintains separate financial records for each property.
•	Transparency: Publishes an annual list of vested properties and a summary of accounts.
4.	Powers and Limitations
•	Powers: Authorized to sell or dispose of property in accordance with sanctioned directives or investment strategies.
•	Limitations: Restricted to sole trusteeship; cannot hold or transfer property outside the Act’s stipulations.
5.	Protection and Savings Clauses
•	Indemnity: Shields the Government and Treasurer from legal liabilities, except in cases of willful negligence.
•	Savings Clause: Ensures the Act does not undermine the efficacy of other relevant legislation.
6.	Amendments and State-Specific Modifications
•	Subject to various amendments and state-level adaptations altering its scope or adding provisions.

Legislative History:

The Charitable Endowments Act, 1890

● Act Title - The Charitable Endowments Act, 1890

● Act Number / Year - 6 of 1890

● Act ID (India Code) - 189006

● Presidential Assent Date - March 17, 1890

● Enforcement Date - October 1, 1890

● Nodal Ministry - Ministry of Law and Justice

Precedent & Historical Rationale

● Mismanagement, Loss of Trust Funds, and Succession Gaps in Public Charities - Prior to 1890, numerous private donors and non-governmental bodies established endowments for education, medical relief, and public utility, but lacked a secure and cost-free mechanism to protect trust corpora. Properties and securities held by private trustees were frequently dissipated, mismanaged, or tied up in costly conveyancing and legal disputes whenever private trustees died, retired, or became insolvent.

● Creation of the Treasurer of Charitable Endowments as a Corporate Bare Trustee - Formulated to provide for the vesting and administration of property held in trust for charitable purposes (expressly excluding exclusively religious purposes). The Act created the statutory office of the Treasurer of Charitable Endowments as a corporation sole with perpetual succession, acting as a secure "bare trustee" to hold invested securities and properties without interfering with the day-to-day administration, which remained vested in managers operating under government-approved schemes of administration.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

● Formulation - Introduced to provide donors of non-religious charitable funds with a reliable, permanent government-backed custody mechanism to secure the preservation and intended application of trust assets.

● Parliamentary Passage - Considered, reviewed by a Select Committee, and passed by the Council of the Governor General of India for making Laws and Regulations in early 1890.

● Presidential Assent - Received the assent of the Governor General of India on March 17, 1890.

● Enforcement - Enforced on October 1, 1890

Sources - Official Records of the Governor General in Council, India Code, and Ministry of Law and Justice.

Legislative History:

The Deo Estate Act, 1886

● Act Title - The Deo Estate Act, 1886

● Act Number / Year - 9 of 1886

● Act ID (India Code) - 188609

● Presidential Assent Date - March 10, 1886

● Enforcement Date - March 10, 1886

● Nodal Ministry - Ministry of Home Affairs

Precedent & Historical Rationale

● Indebtedness and Protection of the Historic Deo Raj - The Deo Estate (in the Gaya district of the Bengal Presidency, now in Bihar) was a prominent and historic landed estate held by the Rajas of Deo, a family that had rendered notable loyalty and military assistance to the British Crown during regional uprisings, including the Santhal Rebellion and the events of 1857. By the 1880s, the estate had become heavily encumbered with private debts and contractual liabilities, threatening the total dissolution and court auction of this historically significant zamindari.

● Extension of the Chutia Nagpur Encumbered Estates Framework - Formulated to apply the protective administrative regime of the Chutia Nagpur Encumbered Estates Act, 1876 to the Deo Estate. Although the Deo Estate was situated in the Gaya district (outside the geographic limits of the Chutia Nagpur Division), this special enactment statutorily applied the provisions of Act VI of 1876 to the estate. It vested the management of the property in a government-appointed statutory Manager, barred civil court executions and attachments against the estate's lands, provided a mechanism to determine and liquidate lawful claims, and preserved the estate intact for the Raja and his successors.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

● Formulation - Introduced as a special relief measure to prevent the disintegration and judicial sale of the encumbered Deo Estate in Gaya.

● Parliamentary Passage - Considered and passed by the Council of the Governor General of India for making Laws and Regulations in early 1886.

● Presidential Assent - Received the assent of the Governor General of India on March 10, 1886.

● Enforcement - Enforced on March 10, 1886

Sources - Official Records of the Governor General in Council, India Code, and Ministry of Home Affairs .

Legislative History:

The City of Bombay Municipal (Supplementary) Act, 1888

● Act Title - The City of Bombay Municipal (Supplementary) Act, 1888

● Act Number / Year - 12 of 1888

● Act ID (India Code) - 188812

● Presidential Assent Date - October 12, 1888

● Enforcement Date - October 12, 1888

● Nodal Ministry - Ministry of Home Affairs

Precedent & Historical Rationale

● Constitutional Limitations of the Bombay Provincial Legislature - When the Bombay Legislative Council enacted the City of Bombay Municipal Act, 1888 (Bombay Act III of 1888), it sought to establish special magisterial benches, confer specific civil adjudicatory powers on the Court of Small Causes, and regulate appellate pathways to the High Court of Judicature at Bombay. However, under the Indian Councils Act, 1861, a provincial legislature lacked the constitutional competence to alter, extend, or regulate the jurisdiction, appellate authority, or procedures of the Chartered High Courts and other judicial bodies governed by Central legislation.

● Statutory Validation and Appellate Jurisdiction via Central Enactment - Formulated by the Governor General in Council to validate and supplement the judicial and magisterial provisions of the Bombay municipal statute. The Act formally confirmed the judicial powers conferred on municipal benches, Presidency Magistrates, and the Small Cause Court, and provided a direct statutory route of appeal to the Bombay High Court against decisions of the Chief Judge of the Court of Small Causes and orders of Presidency Magistrates in municipal disputes.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

● Formulation - Introduced in the central legislature to cure the constitutional and jurisdictional incapacity of the local Bombay legislature regarding the powers of the High Court and subordinate judiciary.

● Parliamentary Passage - Considered, debated, and passed by the Council of the Governor General of India for making Laws and Regulations in late 1888.

● Presidential Assent - Received the assent of the Governor General of India on October 12, 1888.

● Enforcement - Enforced on October 12, 1888

Sources - Official Records of the Governor General in Council, India Code, and Ministry of Home Affairs.

The King of Oudh's Estate Act, 1888

● Act Title - The King of Oudh's Estate Act, 1888

● Act Number / Year - 14 of 1888

● Act ID (India Code) - 188814

● Presidential Assent Date - October 26, 1888

● Enforcement Date - October 26, 1888

● Nodal Ministry - Ministry of Home Affairs

Precedent & Historical Rationale

● Operational Difficulties under the King of Oudh's Estate Act, 1887 - Following the death of Nawab Wajid Ali Shah in September 1887, the King of Oudh's Estate Act, 1887 (Act XIX of 1887) had empowered the Governor-General in Council to appoint an Agent to administer the estate, but it lacked detailed machinery regarding the Agent's corporate capacity to institute suits, hold title, and convey landed properties. The designated Agent encountered severe procedural barriers when attempting to execute property conveyances, recover estate assets, and defend against conflicting adverse possession or title suits brought by third parties in civil courts.

● Statutory Vesting, Legal Succession, and Litigational Powers of the Agent - Formulated to make further and more effective provision for the administration and liquidation of the late King’s estate. The Act statutorily authorized the Agent to the Governor-General in Council to institute, conduct, and defend legal proceedings relating to the estate in his official name, validated all transfers of immovable and movable property executed by or to the Agent, and ensured continuous succession so that all pending actions, rights, and vested properties automatically devolved upon successor Agents without abatement or the need for formal assignments.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

● Formulation - Introduced as supplementary legislation to cure administrative and conveyancing defects in the 1887 statute and empower the Agent to effectively manage, sell, and litigate on behalf of the late King of Oudh's estate.

● Parliamentary Passage - Considered, debated, and passed by the Council of the Governor General of India for making Laws and Regulations in late 1888.

● Presidential Assent - Received the assent of the Governor General of India on October 26, 1888.

● Enforcement - Enforced on October 26, 1888

Precedent & Historical Rationale

● Demise of Nawab Wajid Ali Shah & Estate Complications - Following the annexation of Awadh (Oudh) in 1856, the deposed King of Oudh, Nawab Wajid Ali Shah, was relocated and resided in exile at Metiabruz, Garden Reach, near Calcutta, receiving a substantial political stipend and maintaining an extensive royal household. Upon his death in September 1887, he left behind vast immovable and movable properties, numerous surviving wives, dependants, children, and complex liabilities that could not be adequately administered under ordinary civil courts without severe delays and public disputes.

● Special Administrative Machinery for Liquidation and Distribution - Formulated to enable the Governor-General in Council to appoint an Agent or Commissioner to take charge of, manage, and liquidate the affairs and estate of the late King. The Act barred ordinary civil court jurisdiction over the estate, established a summary procedure to determine genuine debts, settled maintenance allowances and pensions for the royal family and retinue, and provided for the orderly distribution of remaining assets in accordance with Mohammedan law.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

● Formulation - Introduced as urgent special legislation by the colonial administration immediately following the death of Nawab Wajid Ali Shah to prevent litigation, waste, and distress among his dependants.

Summary of the Asian Development Bank Act, 1966 
Objectives of the Act
•	To give effect in India to the Agreement Establishing the Asian Development Bank. 
•	To enable India to become and continue as a member of the ADB. 
•	To authorize the Central Government to subscribe to the Bank's capital stock and meet India's financial obligations under the Agreement. 
•	To confer on the ADB the privileges, immunities, exemptions, and facilities required for the performance of its functions in India. 
Key Provisions
•	Implementation of the ADB Agreement: The Act gives statutory effect to the Agreement Establishing the Asian Development Bank. 
•	Capital Subscription: It authorizes the Central Government to make payments towards India's subscription to the Bank's capital and to fulfil other financial commitments arising from India's membership. 
•	Privileges and Immunities: The Act grants the ADB, its property, assets, officials, and representatives certain privileges and immunities, including legal protection, tax exemptions, and other facilities, in accordance with the Agreement. 
•	Power to Make Rules: The Central Government is empowered to make rules for carrying out the provisions of the Act.

THE BIOLOGICAL DIVERSITY ACT, 2002
ACT NO. 18 OF 2003

[5th February, 2003.]

An Act to provide for conservation of biological diversity, sustainable use of its components and fair and equitable sharing of the benefits arising out of the use of biological resources, knowledge and for matters connected therewith or incidental thereto.
WHEREAS India is rich in biological diversity and associated traditional and contemporary knowledge system relating thereto.
AND WHEREAS India is a 1[Party] to the United Nations Convention on Biological Diversity signed at Rio de Janeiro on the 5th day of June, 1992;
AND WHEREAS the said Convention came into force on the 29th December, 1993;
AND WHEREAS the said Convention reaffirms the sovereign rights of the States over their biological resources;
AND WHEREAS the said Convention has the main objective of conservation of biological diversity, sustainable use of its components and fair and equitable sharing of the benefits arising out of utilisation of genetic resources;
2[AND WHEREAS India is a Party to the Nagoya Protocol on access to genetic resources and the fair and equitable sharing of benefits arising from their utilisation to the convention on Biological Diversity which was adopted on the 29th October, 2010 in Nagoya, Japan;
AND WHEREAS it is considered necessary to provide for conservation, sustainable utilisation, fair and equitable sharing of the benefits arising out of utilisation of biological resources and also to give effect to the said Convention.]
BE it enacted by Parliament in the Fifty-third Year of the Republic of India as follows:--

meta.dc.legislation.history:
Legislative History:

The Biological Diversity Act, 2002

Short Title- The Biological Diversity Act, 2002

Act Number / Year-18 of 2003

Act ID (India Code)-200318

Presidential Assent / Enactment Date-February 5, 2003

Enforcement Date-Phased Enforcement: October 1, 2003 (initial administrative provisions) and July 1, 2004 (substantive regulatory and enforcement sections)

Nodal Ministry-Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change

Precedent & Statutory Rationale

1. Fulfillment of International Obligations (CBD):

o India signed and ratified the United Nations Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD) in 1994, which affirmed sovereign rights over national biological resources while mandating the conservation of biodiversity, sustainable use of its components, and fair and equitable sharing of benefits arising from commercial utilization.

o Prior to this enactment, India lacked comprehensive regulatory machinery to prevent bio-piracy, regulate foreign access to indigenous genetic resources, and protect traditional knowledge held by local communities.

2. Establishment of a Three-Tier Regulatory Architecture:

o The 2002 Act was enacted to create an institutional mechanism comprising the National Biodiversity Authority (NBA) at the central level, State Biodiversity Boards (SBBs) at the state level, and Biodiversity Management Committees (BMCs) at local body levels.

o It instituted stringent approval requirements for obtaining biological resources for commercial utilization or research, mandated the documentation of traditional knowledge through People's Biodiversity Registers (PBRs), and established mechanisms for benefit-sharing with local creators and holders of biological assets.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

• Formulation: Extensively deliberated through joint parliamentary committees and consultations led by the Ministry of Environment and Forests, drawing inputs from scientists, legal experts, and indigenous communities.

• Parliamentary Passage: Tabled, debated, and passed by both Houses of Parliament, receiving Presidential Assent on February 5, 2003.

• Enforcement: Phased Enforcement: October 1, 2003 (initial administrative provisions) and July 1, 2004 (substantive regulatory and enforcement sections)

Source: India Code (indiacode.gov.in) and Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change Official Records

title: The Suppression of Unlawful Acts Against Safety of Maritime Navigation and Fixed Platforms on Continental Shelf Act, 2002

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of the Suppression of Unlawful Acts Against safety of Maritime of Navigation and Fixed platforms on Continental Shelf Act, 2002
Key Provisions
1.	Jurisdiction
•	Applies to the whole of India, including its maritime zones (territorial waters, continental shelf, exclusive economic zone).
•	Extends to offences committed outside India involving Indian ships, citizens, or stateless persons with a habitual Indian residence.
2.	Offences
•	Acts Punishable:
•	Violence or intimidation against persons on ships or fixed platforms.
•	Destruction, damage, or seizure of ships, fixed platforms, or their cargo.
•	Placing explosive devices to destroy ships or platforms.
•	Damaging maritime navigational facilities.
•	Transmitting false information to endanger navigation.
•	Penalties: Imprisonment (up to life imprisonment for severe offences, including those resulting in death).
•	Fines for less severe violations.
3.	Investigation & Prosecution
•	Investigative Powers: Granted to specified Coast Guard or Central Government officers.
•	Court Jurisdiction:
•	Exclusive Trial Courts: Offences under this Act can only be tried by a Metropolitan Magistrate or a Judicial Magistrate of the first class or higher courts.
•	No Lower Courts: Courts inferior to the aforementioned are barred from trying offences under this Act.
•	Special Courts: Designated for swift trials, with provisions for continuous hearings.
•	Bail Restrictions: Mandatory hearing of the Public Prosecutor before bail can be granted.
•	Requires a written report from an authorised officer for cognizance.
•	Empowers Metropolitan Magistrates or Judicial Magistrates of the first class to impose enhanced penalties.
•	Place of Trial: Can be directed by the Central Government through official gazette notifications.

title: The Deposit Insurance and Credit Guarantee Corporation Act, 1961

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of the Deposit Insurance and Credit Guarantee Corporation Act, 1961 
Key Components
1.	Establishment & Management
•	Name: Deposit Insurance and Credit Guarantee Corporation
•	Governance: Board of Directors with representatives from the Reserve Bank of India (RBI), Central Government, and experts.
•	Operations: Head Office in Mumbai with potential branches.
2.	Deposit Insurance
•	Registration: Mandatory for banking companies (existing, new, defunct) and co-operative banks.
•	Premium: Insured banks pay premiums; provisions for default and interest.
•	Liability: Corporation pays up to a specified limit per depositor in case of bank failure, with adjustable limits.
•	Special Provisions:
•	(a): Extension of payment liability up to 90 days for amalgamation, compromise, or reconstruction schemes.
•	(b): No liability if RBI removes payment restrictions and the bank can pay depositors without restrictions.
3.	Credit Guarantee Functions
•	Role: Guarantees credit facilities and indemnifies credit institutions on behalf of the Central Government.
4.	Financial Provisions
•	Funds:
•	Deposit Insurance Fund: Premiums, receipts, and investments.
•	Credit Guarantee Fund: Transferred assets, fees, and investments.
•	General Fund: Other receipts for operational expenses.
•	Investments: Primarily in Central Government securities and RBI deposits.
5.	Operational & Regulatory
•	Staff Utilization: Can utilize RBI staff.
•	Reporting: Annual accounts and reports to RBI and Central Government.
•	Regulations & Penalties: Board makes regulations with RBI approval; penalties for false statements and non-compliance.
6.	Miscellaneous
•	Liquidation: Only by Central Government order.
•	Tax Exemptions & Reserves: As specified, with a focus on reserve funds for liabilities.
•	Amendments: Reflects changes in management, liability, and operational aspects over time.

title: The Recovery Of Debts And Bankruptcy Act, 1993

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of the Recovery of Debts Due to (Banks and Financial Institutions) Act, 1993
1. Objective
The Act was enacted to provide for the speedy adjudication and recovery of debts due to banks and financial institutions by establishing Debts Recovery Tribunals (DRTs) and Debts Recovery Appellate Tribunals (DRATs). Before this Act, banks had to approach ordinary civil courts, resulting in prolonged delays in debt recovery. 
2. Scope and Application
•	Applies throughout India. 
•	Covers debts owed to banks and financial institutions above the minimum monetary threshold prescribed by the Central Government. 
•	Initially called the Recovery of Debts Due to Banks and Financial Institutions Act, 1993; renamed as the Recovery of Debts and Bankruptcy Act, 1993 by the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016. 
3. Establishment of Tribunals
(a) Debts Recovery Tribunal (DRT)
•	Established by the Central Government. 
•	Headed by a Presiding Officer. 
•	Has exclusive jurisdiction over applications by banks and financial institutions for recovery of debts. 
(b) Debts Recovery Appellate Tribunal (DRAT)
•	Hears appeals against orders of DRTs. 
•	Headed by a Chairperson. 
4. Jurisdiction of DRT
The DRT has the power to:
•	Entertain applications from banks and financial institutions for recovery of debts. 
•	Determine the amount due. 
•	Issue recovery certificates. 
•	Exercise powers similar to those of a civil court in relation to summoning witnesses, receiving evidence, and enforcing attendance. 
5. Recovery Officer
After the DRT determines the amount payable, a Recovery Officer executes the recovery certificate and may recover the amount by:
•	Attachment and sale of movable or immovable property. 
•	Arrest and detention of the debtor (where permitted by law). 
•	Appointment of a receiver. 
•	Other modes prescribed under the Act. 
6. Appeals
•	Any person aggrieved by an order of the DRT may appeal to the DRAT. 
•	Appeals must generally be filed within the prescribed limitation period. 
•	The Act also contains provisions regarding pre-deposit requirements, subject to statutory conditions and discretion available under the Act. 
7. Powers of the Tribunal
The DRT has powers to:
•	Summon and examine witnesses. 
•	Receive evidence on affidavit. 
•	Compel production of documents. 
•	Review its own orders in specified circumstances. 
•	Grant interim orders, injunctions, and appoint receivers where necessary.

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of the Railway Claims Tribunal Act, 1987
Overview
*Act Name: The Railway Claims Tribunal Act, 1987 *Purpose: Establishes the Railway Claims Tribunal to adjudicate claims against railway administrations for various losses or incidents.
Key Provisions
1.	Jurisdiction and Eligibility to Claim: - Eligible Claimants:
•	The person who sustained injury or loss.
•	An authorised agent of such person.
•	The guardian of a minor claimant.
•	A dependant of the deceased (in case of death), including minor dependants through their guardian.
•	Claims Scope:
•	Loss, destruction, damage, deterioration, or non-delivery of goods.
•	Refund of overcharges for goods carriage.
•	Compensation for personal injury or loss of life to passengers.
2.	Procedure for Claims: - Application Filing:
•	Against the relevant railway administration based on ticket purchase, destination, or incident location.
•	Requirement for prior notice for goods claims within six months.
•	Burden of Proof:
•	Claimant must prove monetary loss or declared value of goods, without needing to prove causation.
3.	Tribunal Operations: - Decision Finality and Enforcement:
•	Decisions of the Tribunal are final.
•	Courts barred from jurisdiction over Tribunal matters.
•	Regulatory Powers:
•	Tribunal may make its own regulations.
•	Central Government's oversight through rule-making and parliamentary scrutiny.
4.	Integration with Other Legislation: - Railways Act, 1989: Defines "untoward incidents" and liability for accidents.
•	Merchant Shipping Act, 1958: Applies to sea carriage liabilities when part of a railway contract.

Legislative History:

The Railway Claims Tribunal Act, 1987

Act Title - The Railway Claims Tribunal Act, 1987

Act Number - 54 of 1987

Act ID (India Code) - 198754

Presidential Assent Date - December 23, 1987

Enforcement Date - November 8, 1989

Nodal Ministry - Ministry of Railways

Precedent & Historical Rationale

Severe Court Backlog and Delays in Railway Claims:

Prior to 1987, all legal claims arising from accidents involving railways, loss, destruction, damage, deterioration, or non-delivery of animals and goods entrusted to the railways, as well as passenger refund claims, had to be litigated through regular civil courts. This traditional judicial route resulted in massive procedural delays, exorbitant legal costs, and heavy backlogs, leaving claimants—often ordinary passengers or small merchants—waiting years for compensation.

Creation of Specialized Adjudication:

To provide a speedy, cost-effective, and specialized mechanism for the prompt settlement of compensation and refund claims against the railway administration, Parliament enacted the Railway Claims Tribunal Act. Modeled along the lines of administrative tribunals under Article 323A of the Constitution, the statute established the Railway Claims Tribunal with nationwide benches equipped to handle specialized transport-related litigation without the technicalities of ordinary civil procedure.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

Formulation:

Drafted by the Ministry of Railways to establish a dedicated multi-bench tribunal system for inquiring into and determining claims against railway administrations, outlining the composition, powers, procedures, and appellate mechanisms.

Parliamentary Passage:

Introduced, debated, and passed by both Houses of Parliament (Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha) during the winter session of 1987.

Presidential Assent: Received Presidential Assent on December 23, 1987.

Enforcement: Enforced on November 8, 1989.

Source: Official Records of Parliament, India Code, and Ministry of Railways.

Summary of Bengal Embankment Act, 1855 
Key Provisions
1.	Governance and Reforms: -
•	Consolidates and repeals earlier Bengal Regulations (VI of 1806, XI of 1829), enhancing administrative clarity.
•	Empowers a Superintendent of Embankments with wide-ranging authority for enforcement, maintenance, and strategic directives.

2.	Scope and Definitions: - Defines "embankment" broadly to encompass all water management structures, ensuring uniform regulatory oversight regardless of ownership.
3.	Procedural Framework for Modifications: - Mandates detailed notification processes for embankment alterations, including public notices and structured appeal mechanisms to facilitate transparency and stakeholder participation.
4.	Maintenance and Financial Responsibilities: - Legally obligates proprietors to maintain embankments and contribute financially, with state intervention provisions for negligence.
5.	Infrastructure Development and Dispute Resolution:-Specifies requirements for sluice gate construction at the applicant's expense, temporary water diversion structures, and road access, balancing infrastructure needs with environmental and community considerations.
Establishes compensation procedures for affected parties, including arbitration and judicial recourse.
6.	Enforcement and Penal Provisions:- Imposes penalties for obstructing authorized works, damaging embankments, and other harmful actions to ensure compliance.
7.	Judicial and Administrative Oversight: - Grants jurisdiction to Deputy/Assistant Magistrates for dispute resolution, with defined appeal processes, and outlines police protocols for enforcement actions.

meta.dc.description.abstract:
The Border Security Force Act, 1968
Objective
The main objectives of the Act are to:
•	Constitute the Border Security Force (BSF) as an armed force of the Union.
•	Ensure the security and integrity of India's international borders.
•	Prevent illegal infiltration, cross-border crimes, smuggling, and unauthorized entry or exit.
•	Maintain discipline, efficiency, and professionalism within the Force.
•	Provide a legal framework for the administration, deployment, and functioning of the BSF in the interest of national security.
Key Provisions
•	Constitution of the BSF: Establishes the Border Security Force as an armed force of the Union under the control of the Central Government.
•	Organisation and Command: Provides for the appointment of the Director General and other officers responsible for the command, administration, and supervision of the Force.
•	Functions and Duties: Assigns the BSF the responsibility of guarding India's international borders, preventing trans-border crimes, checking illegal immigration, combating smuggling, and assisting civil authorities in maintaining public order when required.
•	Powers of BSF Personnel: Empowers members of the Force to perform security duties, conduct searches, make arrests, seize property, and use reasonable force in accordance with the Act and other applicable laws.
•	Discipline and Service Conditions: Prescribes provisions relating to recruitment, training, duties, discipline, leave, pay, and other service conditions of BSF personnel.
•	Offences and Punishments: Defines offences such as mutiny, desertion, insubordination, absence without leave, disobedience of lawful commands, and other misconduct, and prescribes punishments, including imprisonment, dismissal, reduction in rank, or other disciplinary measures.
•	Security Force Courts: Provides for the establishment of Security Force Courts to try offences committed by members of the BSF and lays down the procedures for trial, sentencing, and appeals.
•	Rule-Making Power: Empowers the Central Government to make rules for implementing the provisions of the Act relating to the administration, discipline, and functioning of the Force.

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of the Boundary-marks, Bombay Act, 1846

Purpose
•	The primary objective is to establish and maintain field boundary marks within the Presidency of Bombay. This aims to secure landed property, prevent encroachments and disputes, and facilitate the identification of lands for revenue collection purposes.

Key Provisions
1.	Authority and Compliance
•	Designated Revenue Officers, empowered by the Governor in Council, have the authority to mandate Landowners/Occupants to erect or maintain boundary marks using specified materials and in designated quantities.
2.	Notification Process
•	A formal requisition, adhering to the Prescribed Format, must be served on the responsible party. If the individual cannot be found, the notice is posted at a Prominent Village Location.
3.	Non-Compliance and Recovery
•	In the event of non-compliance, the Revenue Authority will undertake the necessary work. The costs incurred are then equitably distributed among the benefiting land parcels and recovered from the Owners/Occupants. If this is not feasible, the costs are deducted from the Village Revenue.
4.	Ownership Claims and Outstanding Debts
•	No claims to ownership or occupancy can be validated until all outstanding debts related to boundary mark construction or repair are fully settled.
5.	Intentional Damage to Marks
•	Penalty for Wilful Destruction/Alteration: A maximum fine of Fifty Rupees per affected mark is imposed. The penalty is split, with half allocated to the Informant and the remainder used for Restoration.
6.	Assessment and Appeal
•	Revenue Officers are vested with the power to assess and realize these costs, following standard revenue collection procedures. Appeal Rights are afforded to Superior Revenue Authorities.

title: The National Dairy Development Board Act, 1987

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of the National Dairy Development Board Act, 1987
Objective:
•	Declare the National Dairy Development Board (NDDB) as an institution of national importance.
•	Incorporate NDDB and vest the undertakings of the Indian Dairy Corporation (IDC) in NDDB, leading to IDC's dissolution.
Key Provisions:
1.	Incorporation & Declaration:
•	NDDB is constituted as a body corporate with perpetual succession and a common seal.
•	Declared an institution of national importance.
2.	Vesting and Dissolution: - All undertakings of the Indian Dairy Corporation vest in NDDB.
•	Indian Dairy Corporation is dissolved.
3.	Effect of Incorporation: - Assets, liabilities, rights, and obligations of the society (original NDDB form) and IDC transfer to the new NDDB body corporate.
•	Subsidiaries of the society and IDC become subsidiaries of NDDB.
4.	Powers and Functions of NDDB: - Broad Mandate: Promote, plan, and organize dairy and allied industries development nationwide.
•	Specific Powers:
•	Adopt co-operative strategies.
•	Facilitate research, training, and technological know-how.
•	Design, develop, and finance dairy industries.
•	Provide consultancy, managerial services, and project execution.
•	Regulate dairy and allied industries (if directed by the Central Government).
•	Engage in import/export, buffer stock management, and export promotion.
•	Acquire, hold, dispose of property; borrow and lend money.
•	Participate in other organisations with Central Government approval.
5.	Governance and Protection: - Protection: Acts done in good faith are protected from legal proceedings.
•	Indemnity: Directors are indemnified against losses except for wilful acts/default.
•	Secrecy: Obligations regarding fidelity and secrecy for board members and employees.
6.	Miscellaneous Provisions: - Liquidation: Only possible by order of the Central Government.
•	Delegation of Powers: Central Government can delegate activities related to dairy development to NDDB.
•	Transitional Provisions: For auditors, Chairman, Board, and ongoing management/assistance activities.
•	Mother Dairy: Becomes a subsidiary unit of NDDB, retaining its separate character unless decided otherwise.
•	Formation of Companies: NDDB can form companies with previous Central Government approval.
•	Returns and Reports: To be furnished to the Central Government.
•	Overriding Effect: Act's provisions override other inconsistent laws.
•	Regulatory Powers: NDDB can make regulations and schemes as necessary.
7.	Financial and Administrative: - Borrowing Powers: Detailed in Section 23 (context not provided).
•	Grants and Loans: From the Central Government (Sections 24, 25, context not provided).
•	National Dairy Development Board Fund: Established (Section 26, context not provided).
•	Accounting, Audit, and Reporting: Mandatory with specifications 

Effective Date:
•	Came into force on 12th October, 1987, as notified by the Central Government.

meta.dc.identifier.preamble_description:
THE NATIONAL DAIRY DEVELOPMENT BOARD ACT, 1987
ACT NO. 37 OF 1987

[15th September, 1987.]

An Act to declare the institution known as the National Dairy Development Board in the State of Gujarat to be an institution of national importance and to provide for its incorporation and for the vesting in that body corporate of the undertakings of the Indian Dairy Corporation with a view to provide for the administration and the carrying on of the functions to be performed by the body corporate more effectively throughout the country and for matters connected therewith and incidental thereto.
WHEREAS the National Dairy Development Board, a society formed and registered under the Societies Registration Act, 1860 (21 of 1860) has been serving the country by the adoption of a co-operative strategy, being a strategy evolved at Anand (Gujarat), for the economic development of the rural masses and has been playing a vital role in improving the quality of life of the people through co-operative effort;
AND WHEREAS the objects of the National Dairy Development Board are such as to make it an institution of national importance and to constitute it as a body corporate;
AND WHEREAS the functions of the Indian Dairy Corporation, a company formed and registered under the Companies Act, 1956 (1 of 1956), and the functions of the National Dairy Development Board are complementary to each other and aimed at achieving common objectives;
AND WHEREAS it is necessary that the freedom and flexibility of operation hitherto available to the National Dairy Development Board should continue to be available to it so as to enable it to perform its functions more effectively and to play a wider and increasingly important role in serving the nation;
AND WHEREAS it is considered necessary to vest the undertakings of the Indian Dairy Corporation in the National Dairy Development Board and to dissolve the said Corporation with a view to provide for the administration and the carrying on of the functions to be performed by the body corporate more effectively.
BE it enacted by Parliament in the Thirty-eighth Year of the Republic of India as follows:--

meta.dc.legislation.history:
Legislative History:

The National Dairy Development Board Act, 1987

Act Title - The National Dairy Development Board Act, 1987

Act Number/Year - 37 of 1987

Act ID (India Code) - 198737

Presidential Assent Date - September 15, 1987

Enforcement Date - October 12, 1987

Nodal Ministry - Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare

Precedent & Historical Rationale

From Registered Society to National Institution:

The National Dairy Development Board (NDDB) was originally established and registered as a society under the Societies Registration Act, 1860, in 1965 at Anand, Gujarat, largely inspired by the vision of Verghese Kurien to replicate the "Anand pattern" of dairy cooperatives across India. Over the next two decades, NDDB spearheaded monumental national initiatives—most notably Operation Flood (the world's largest agricultural dairy development program)—which transformed India from a milk-deficient nation into one of the world's largest milk producers.

Integration with the Indian Dairy Corporation and Statutory Autonomy:

Prior to 1987, the commercial and international food-aid implementation aspects of dairy development were handled alongside the Indian Dairy Corporation (IDC), a company registered under the Companies Act, 1956. To streamline operations, eliminate administrative duality, provide absolute structural flexibility, and grant permanent statutory standing, Parliament enacted the 1987 Act. The statute formally dissolved the IDC, merged its undertakings into NDDB, and elevated NDDB to a body corporate declared explicitly as an institution of national importance.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

Formulation:

Drafted by the Ministry of Agriculture to provide statutory incorporation to NDDB, vesting all assets and liabilities of the erstwhile Indian Dairy Corporation into the board, and empowering it with nationwide authority to promote dairy, oilseeds, and other allied agricultural cooperatives.

Parliamentary Passage:

Introduced, debated, and passed by both Houses of Parliament (Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha) during the monsoon session of 1987.

Presidential Assent: Received Presidential Assent on September 15, 1987.

Enforcement: Enforced on October 12, 1987.

Source: Official Records of Parliament, India Code, and Ministry of Fisheries, Animal Husbandry and Dairying.

title: The Governors (Emoluments, Allowances and Privileges) Act, 1982

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of The Governors (Emoluments, Allowances and Privileges) Act, 1982
Key Provisions
1. Definitions
•	Ex-Governor: A person who has been the Governor of a State or more.
•	Governor: Includes any person discharging the Governor's functions.
•	Maintenance, Members of the Family, Official Residences, Rules, State (defined in Section 2)
•	Emoluments- Governors are paid ₹3,50,000 per month (as of the last amendment provided, 2018).
•	Reductions apply if the Governor receives a pension or contributory provident fund benefits from previous government service.
2.	Allowances and Privileges
•	Leave Allowance: Determined by the President.
•	Official Residences: Use without rent, with furnished and maintained residences.
•	Household Establishment: No personal charge for staff emoluments.
•	Medical Treatment: Free for the Governor and family, both during and after tenure.
•	Conveyance: Use of motor vehicles without rent or hire, with maintenance covered.
•	Traveling Allowance: For assuming/vacating office.
•	Renewal and Maintenance Allowances: For official residences.
•	Other Privileges and Allowances: Entertainment, hospitality, etc., as determined by the President.
•	Additional Expenses: The President may sanction increased expenses or new ones not covered by rules.
•	Secretarial Assistance for Ex-Governors: One Personal Assistant on a reimbursement basis, unless re-appointed to certain offices.
3. Administrative Provisions
•	Power to Make Rules: By the President, to give effect to the Act's provisions.
•	Validation: Validates past special orders on allowances, expenses, and privileges.
•	Saving: Ensures the Act does not reduce emoluments and allowances of Governors during their term.

o Under Article 158(3) of the Constitution of India, the emoluments, allowances, and privileges of a State Governor are determined by Parliament by law, and until such provision is made, they are specified in the Second Schedule.

o Prior to 1982, Governor emoluments and allowances were largely governed by colonial-era statutory orders and colonial precedents under the Government of India Act, which had become obsolete in independent India's democratic framework.

2. Standardization and Institutional Dignity:

o The legislative intent centered on replacing antiquated provisions with a comprehensive, modern central statute to regulate the salary, official residences, medical facilities, travel privileges, and pensionary benefits of Governors in a uniform and transparent manner across all states.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

• Formulation: Drafted by the Ministry of Home Affairs to fulfill the explicit mandate under Article 158(3) of the Constitution, rationalizing executive perks while maintaining the dignity of constitutional officeholders.

Precedent & Historical Rationale

1. Expansion and Protection of Institutional Confidentiality:

o During the early 1980s, India’s public financial institutions (such as ICICI, IRCI, and other designated term-lending bodies) managed expansive industrial portfolios, corporate financing data, and sensitive commercial records.

o While traditional commercial banks were bound by statutory obligations of fidelity and secrecy under their respective founding acts or banking regulations, several specialized public financial institutions lacked explicit, uniform statutory mandates protecting customer and corporate confidentiality.

2. Standardizing Professional Secrecy and Declarations:

o The legislative intent centered on imposing a formal, statutory duty of fidelity and secrecy upon directors, committee members, auditors, officers, and employees of public financial institutions.

o It also required these officials to make formal declarations of fidelity and secrecy, ensuring that sensitive financial and credit information of constituents was protected from unauthorized disclosure while permitting necessary information-sharing between regulatory bodies and scheduled banks.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

• Formulation: Drafted by the Ministry of Finance to plug gaps in institutional governance and secrecy standards across public financial lending companies.

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of the Cardamom Act, 1965
The Cardamom Act, 1965 was enacted to regulate and promote the cultivation, production, processing, quality improvement, and marketing of cardamom in India. The Act provided for the establishment of the Cardamom Board, which was responsible for the development of the cardamom industry, improving production standards, promoting exports, supporting research, and protecting the interests of cardamom growers. The Act aimed to strengthen India's position as a leading producer and exporter of cardamom.
Note: The Cardamom Board was subsequently merged into the Spices Board under the Spices Board Act, 1986, and the Cardamom Act, 1965 was repealed.
Objective
The main objectives of the Act are:
•	To regulate the development of the cardamom industry.
•	To promote scientific cultivation and increase the production of quality cardamom.
•	To improve processing, grading, and marketing practices.
•	To encourage the export of Indian cardamom.
•	To establish a statutory authority for the development and regulation of the cardamom sector.
•	To safeguard the interests of cardamom growers and traders.
Key Provisions
1.	Establishment of the Cardamom Board
o	The Act provided for the constitution of the Cardamom Board to oversee the development and regulation of the cardamom industry.
2.	Functions of the Board
o	The Board was entrusted with promoting cultivation, conducting research, improving quality, collecting industry statistics, providing technical assistance, and encouraging exports.
3.	Registration of Growers and Dealers
o	The Act empowered the Board to maintain records and regulate registered growers, dealers, and exporters involved in the cardamom trade.
 
4.	Development Programmes
o	The Board could implement schemes for improving cultivation techniques, pest and disease control, irrigation, and post-harvest management.
5.	Financial Powers
o	The Board was authorized to receive grants from the Central Government and utilize funds for the development of the cardamom industry.
6.	Inspection and Enforcement
o	The Act empowered authorized officers to inspect records and ensure compliance with the provisions of the Act and the rules made thereunder.
7.	Rule-Making Powers
o	The Central Government was empowered to make rules for carrying out the purposes of the Act.
