1

The Central Armed Police Forces (General Administration) Act, 2026

(ACT NO. 9 OF 2026)

[As on the 8th October, 2026]

2

LIST OF ABBREVIATIONS USED

G.S.R. . . . . . for General Statutory Rules.

S.O. . . . . . ,, Statutory Order.

Notifn. . . . . . ,, Notification.

3

THE CENTRAL ARMED POLICE FORCES (GENERAL ADMINISTRATION) ACT, 2026

_______

ARRANGEMENT OF SECTIONS

______

SECTIONS

1. Short title and commencement.

2. Definitions.

3. Regulation of recruitment and conditions of service.

4. Power to amend Schedules.

5. Savings.

6. Power to make rules.

7. Provisions of Act to have overriding effect.

8. Power to remove difficulties.

THE FIRST SCHEDULE.

THE SECOND SCHEDULE.

4

THE CENTRAL ARMED POLICE FORCES (GENERAL ADMINISTRATION) ACT, 2026

ACT NO. 9 OF 2026

[9th April, 2026.]

An Act to regulate the general rules governing the recruitment and conditions of service of

Group A General Duty Officers and other officers in the Central Armed Police Forces and

other rules regarding these forces, and for matters connected therewith or incidental thereto.

WHEREAS the Central Armed Police Forces are performing important functions of national security

and are deployed for securing borders and maintaining internal security of the Union and the States and

connected matters;

AND WHEREAS the Central Armed Police Forces are primarily armed troops performing armed

duties in the field with strict command and control mechanism and a functional hierarchy;

AND WHEREAS the operational and functional requirements of the Central Armed Police Forces

are distinct from other organisations;

AND WHEREAS the recruitment and conditions of service of Group A General Duty Officers and

other officers and members of the Central Armed Police Forces are governed by the rules made under

the respective Acts specified in the First Schedule;

AND WHEREAS the Central Armed Police Forces perform functions of national security in close

coordination with State authorities;

AND WHEREAS in the interest of maintaining Centre-State relationship and ensuring close

coordination between the Union and the States, the Indian Police Service Officers are necessary for

effective functioning of these forces;

AND WHEREAS it is considered necessary to enact an umbrella law to regulate the recruitment and

conditions of service of Group A General Duty Officers and other officers appointed to the Central

Armed Police Forces and other rules regarding these forces, with a view to ensuring legislative clarity,

preserving its operational distinctiveness, and harmonising judicial directions with administrative and

federal requirements.

BE it enacted by Parliament in the Seventy-seventh Year of the Republic of India as follows:–

1. Short title and commencement.—(1) This Act may be called the Central Armed Police Forces

(General Administration) Act, 2026.

(2) It shall come into force on such date1

as the Central Government may, by notification in the

Official Gazette, appoint.

2. Definitions.—(1) In this Act, unless the context otherwise requires,—

(a) “Central Armed Police Force” means an armed force of the Union constituted under any of

the Acts specified in the First Schedule;

(b) “Central Government” means the Ministry of Home Affairs in the Government of India;

(c) “Group A General Duty Officer” means Group A (general duty or executive) officer of the

rank of Assistant Commandant and above in the Central Armed Police Force;

1. 08th day of October, 2026, vide Notifn. No. G.S.R. 870 (E), dated 08th October, 2026, see Gazette of India, Extraordinary,

Part II, s. 3 (ii).

5

(d) “notification” means a notification published in the Official Gazette and the expression

“notify” or “notified” shall be construed accordingly;

(e) “officer” means Group A General Duty Officer and includes—

(i) an officer of the Indian Police Service on deputation; or

(ii) an officer of the Indian Army on deputation or re-employment; or

(iii) such other officers recruited under the rules specified in the Second Schedule,

in the Central Armed Police Force;

(f) “Order” means any instruction issued by any department of the Government of India whether

called as Office Memorandum or by any other name.

(2) Words and expressions used and not defined in this Act but defined in the Acts specified in the

First Schedule shall have the meanings respectively assigned to them in those Acts.

3. Regulation of recruitment and conditions of service.—(1) Notwithstanding anything contained

in any other law for the time being in force, or in—

(a) any judgment, decree or order of any court; or

(b) any Order issued from time to time,

the Central Government may, by notification, make rules to provide for the method, manner and mode

of recruitment including promotion and deputation and the conditions of service of officers in the

Central Armed Police Force:

Provided that the rules regulating the recruitment of Group A General Duty Officers as specified in

the Second Schedule, shall continue to be in force unless and until they are modified, amended,

rescinded or superseded, keeping in view the functional and operational requirements of the Central

Armed Police Force:

Provided further that for the purposes of appointment of officers from the Indian Police Service in

the ranks of Inspector General and above, such rules shall provide for––

(a) fifty per cent. of the posts to be filled by deputation in the rank of Inspector General; and

(b) a minimum of sixty-seven per cent. of the posts to be filled by deputation in the rank of

Additional Director General:

Provided also that the posts in the ranks of Special Director General and Director General shall be

filled by deputation only.

(2) The Central Government may, by notification, make such other rules for the Central Armed

Police Forces for achieving the objectives of this Act.

(3) In case of any inconsistency between any rule made under this Act with any other rule or Order,

whether made or issued before or after the commencement of this Act, the rules made under this Act

shall prevail.

4. Power to amend Schedules.—(1) The Central Government may, if it is of the opinion that it is

necessary or expedient in the public interest so to do, by notification,—

(a) add any other Act governing a new armed force of the Union or any existing armed force of

the Union in the First Schedule, or alter or amend the said Schedule; or

(b) add a new rule in the Second Schedule or alter or amend the said Schedule,

6

and thereupon, the First Schedule or the Second Schedule shall be deemed to be amended accordingly.

(2) Every notification issued under sub-section (1) shall be laid, as soon as may be after it is made,

before each House of Parliament.

5. Savings.—Any financial benefits granted to Group A General Duty Officers under any Order

issued before the date of commencement of this Act shall continue to be so granted till such time new

Orders are issued in this regard.

6. Power to make rules.—(1) The Central Government may, by notification, make rules for carrying

out the purposes of this Act.

(2) Every rule made under this Act shall be laid, as soon as may be after it is made, before each

House of Parliament, while it is in session for a total period of thirty days which may be comprised in

one session or in two or more successive sessions, and if, before the expiry of the session immediately

following the session or the successive sessions aforesaid, both Houses agree in making any

modification in the rule, or both Houses agree that the rule should not be made, the rule shall thereafter

have effect only in such modified form or be of no effect, as the case may be; so, however, that any such

modification or annulment shall be without prejudice to the validity of anything previously done under

that rule.

7. Provisions of Act to have overriding effect.—The provisions of this Act shall have effect,

notwithstanding anything inconsistent therewith contained in any other law for the time being in force

or any instrument having effect by virtue of any such law.

8. Power to remove difficulties.— (1) If any difficulty arises in giving effect to the provisions of

this Act, the Central Government may, by order published in the Official Gazette, make such provisions,

not inconsistent with the provisions of this Act, as may appear to it to be necessary or expedient for

removing the difficulty:

Provided that no order shall be made under this section after the expiry of three years from the

commencement of this Act.

(2) Every order made under this section shall be laid, as soon as may be after it is made, before each

House of Parliament.

7

THE FIRST SCHEDULE

[See sections 2(1)(a), 2(2) and 4(1)]

Sl. No. Central Armed Police Force Acts

1. The Central Reserve Police Force Act, 1949 (66 of 1949).

2. The Border Security Force Act, 1968 (47 of 1968).

3. The Central Industrial Security Force Act, 1968 (50 of 1968).

4. The Indo-Tibetan Border Police Act, 1992 (35 of 1992).

5. The Sashastra Seema Bal Act, 2007 (53 of 2007).

8

THE SECOND SCHEDULE

[See sections 2(e)(iii), 3(1) and 4(1)]

Sl. No. Name of the rules

1. (i) The Central Reserve Police Force Group “A” (General Duty) Officers Recruitment Rules,

2010.

2. (i) The Border Security Force Group ‘A’ (General Duty Officers) Recruitment Rules, 2017.

(ii) The Border Security Force Group ‘A’ (General Duty Officers) Recruitment Rules, 2015.

3. (i) The Central Industrial Security Force, Assistant Commandant (Executive), Recruitment

Rules, 2009.

(ii) The Central Industrial Security Force (Group ‘A’ Executive Cadre Recruitment Rules,

2002).

(iii) The Central Industrial Security Force, Group ‘A’ posts (Executive Cadre) Recruitment

Rules, 2010.

(iv) The Central Industrial Security Force, Additional Director General, Recruitment Rules,

2020.

(v) The Central Industrial Security Force, Director General, Recruitment Rules, 2003.

4. (i) The Indo-Tibetan Border Police Force, General Duty Cadre (Group ‘A’ Posts) Recruitment

Rules, 2018.

(ii) The Indo-Tibetan Border Police Force, Additional Director General (General Duty)

Recruitment Rules, 2020.

5. (i) The Sashastra Seema Bal Group ‘A’ Combatised (General Duty) Director General,

Additional Director General, Inspector General, Deputy Inspector General and Commandant

Posts Recruitment Rules, 2013.

(ii) The Sashastra Seema Bal Group ‘A’ Combatised (General Duty) Second-in-Command,

Deputy Commandant and Assistant Commandant Posts Recruitment Rules, 2012.

9

STATEMENT OF OBJECTS AND REASONS

The Central Armed Police Forces play a vital role in maintaining national security and discharging

important functions such as securing the borders of the country, undertaking anti-insurgency operations

and maintaining internal security of the Union and the States and matters connected therewith. These

Forces are also designed to supplement Armed Forces of the Union during war.

2. The Central Armed Police Forces primarily comprise ground troops who perform armed duties in

the field. Owing to the nature of armed duties performed by these Forces, they are required to have

strict command and control mechanism and functional hierarchy. Accordingly, they are structured as

Sections/Platoons/Companies/Battalions and higher field formations. Having regard to the requirement

of their operational command structure, the organisational framework of the Central Armed Police

Forces differs from that of other organisations.

3. Under article 312 of the Constitution, the Indian Police Service is an All India Service, and the

officers of the Service are posted in the Union and the States. Historically, Indian Police Service officers

are an integral and important part of the Central Armed Police Forces, who have been serving on

deputation along with officers and members of these Forces. The Central Armed Police Forces perform

functions relating to national security and anti-insurgency in close coordination with the State

authorities. Therefore, in the interest of maintaining Centre-State relations by ensuring close

coordination between the Union and the States for effective operational functioning, it is essential to

maintain the existing system of deputation of the Indian Police Service Officers in the Central Armed

Police Forces.

4. The Central Armed Police Forces are governed by the respective Acts of the Parliament. The

recruitment and conditions of service of Group A General Duty Officers and other officers and members

in the Central Armed Police Forces are governed by the rules made under these Acts.

5. In view of expanding functional and operational requirements, the distinct organisational structure

of these Forces have evolved over a period of time. In recent years, due to absence of an umbrella law,

regulatory provisions have evolved in a fragmented manner resulting in several litigations on

service-related matters, leading to some functional and administrative difficulties. Considering the

nature and purposes of the Central Armed Police Forces and to avoid unnecessary litigations, there is a

need to lay down an umbrella law to regulate the recruitment, deputation, promotion and other

conditions of services of Group A General Duty Officers and other officers appointed in these Central

Armed Police Forces and other rules regarding these Forces, to ensure legislative clarity, preserving

their distinct operational and functional requirements and harmonising judicial directions with

administrative and federal requirements.

6. The Bill seeks to achieve the above objectives.

AMIT SHAH.

NEW DELHI;

The 16th March, 2026.

 THE KERALA (ALTERATION OF NAME) ACT, 2026

_______

ARRANGEMENT OF SECTIONS

______

SECTIONS

1. Short title and commencement.

2. Definitions.

3. Alteration of name of State of Kerala.

4. Amendment of article 31A.

5. Amendment of article 290A.

6. Amendment of First Schedule to Constitution.

7. Amendment of Fourth Schedule to Constitution.

8. Power to adapt laws.

9. Power to construe laws.

10. Legal proceedings.

 THE KERALA (ALTERATION OF NAME) ACT, 2026

ACT NO. 18 OF 2026

[14th August, 2026.]

An Act to alter the name of the State of Kerala.

    BE it enacted by Parliament in the Seventy-seventh Year of the Republic of India as follows:—

    1. Short title and commencement.—(1) This Act may be called the Kerala (Alteration of Name) Act, 2026.

     (2) It shall come into force on such date[1] as the Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, appoint.

 2. Definitions.—In this Act, unless the context otherwise requires,––

 (a) “appointed day” means the date appointed under sub-section (2) of section 1;

     (b) “appropriate Government” means, as respects a law relating to a matter enumerated in List I in the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution, the Central Government, and as respects any other law, the State Government;

    (c) “law” includes any enactment, Ordinance, regulation, order, bye-law, rule, scheme, notification or other instrument having the force of law in the whole or any part of the State of Kerala.

    3. Alteration of name of State of Kerala.—On and from the appointed day, the State of Kerala shall be known as the State of Keralam.

    4. Amendment of article 31A.—In article 31A of the Constitution, in clause (2), in sub-clause (a), in item (i), for the word “Kerala”, the word “Keralam” shall be substituted.

    5. Amendment of article 290A.—In article 290A of the Constitution, for the word “Kerala”, the word “Keralam” shall be substituted.

    6. Amendment of First Schedule to Constitution.—In the First Schedule to the Constitution, under the heading “I. THE STATES”, in entry 5, under the column “Name”, for the word “Kerala”, the word “Keralam” shall be substituted.

     7. Amendment of Fourth Schedule to Constitution.—In the Fourth Schedule to the Constitution, under the heading “TABLE”, in entry 9, in the second column, for the word “Kerala”, the word “Keralam” shall be substituted.

    8. Power to adapt laws.—(1) For the purpose of giving effect to the alteration of the name of the State of Kerala by section 3, the appropriate Government may, before the expiration of one year from the appointed day, by order, make such adaptations and modifications of any law made before the appointed day, whether by way of repeal or amendment, as may be necessary or expedient, and thereupon every such law shall have effect subject to the adaptations and modifications so made.

    (2) Nothing in sub-section (1) shall be deemed to prevent a competent Legislature or other competent authority from repealing or amending any law adapted or modified by the appropriate Government under the said sub-section.

1. 25th day of August, 2026, vide Notifn. No. S.O. 4712 (E), dated 25th August, 2026, see Gazette of India, Extraordinary, Part II, s. 3 (ii).

    9. Power to construe laws.—Notwithstanding that no provision or insufficient provision has been made under section 8 for the adaptation of a law made before the appointed day, any court, tribunal or authority, required or empowered to enforce such law, may construe the law in such manner, without affecting the substance, as may be necessary or proper in regard to the matter before the court, tribunal or authority.

    10. Legal proceedings.—Where immediately before the appointed day any legal proceedings are pending to which the State of Kerala is a party, the State of Keralam shall be deemed to have been substituted for the State of Kerala in those proceedings. 

    STATEMENT OF OBJECTS AND REASONS

    The Government of Kerala forwarded to the Central Government, the resolution passed by the Legislative Assembly of Kerala on 24th June, 2024 stating, inter alia, that necessary steps may be taken to amend the First Schedule to the Constitution by modifying the name of State of “Kerala” as “Keralam” in accordance with article 3 of the Constitution.

    2. As required by the proviso to article 3 of the Constitution, the President referred the Bill to the Legislature of the State of Kerala for expressing its views thereon. The

Legislative Assembly of Kerala considered the Kerala (Alteration of Name) Bill, 2026 and adopted a unanimous Resolution agreeing with the Bill.

    3. The Kerala (Alteration of Name) Bill, 2026 provides for such alteration of name of the State of Kerala and contains necessary amendments to the provisions of the Constitution and also consequential provisions.     

    AMIT SHAH.

    NEW DELHI;

The 29th July, 2026.

The Atomic Energy Act, 1962

Key Provisions

1.	Entitlement & Application
•	Eligibility: Recorded proprietors of joint undivided revenue-paying estates
•	Process: Written application to Collector with detailed estate information, potentially leading to separate account openings for shares.
2.	Partition Process & Dispute Resolution
•	Modes: Private Agreement, Arbitration, or Official Partition by appointed Officer
•	Procedure: Includes publication, potential objections, and mandatory Civil Court referral for title disputes or challenges to claimed shares/interests.
•	Sale of Shares in Arrears: Collector may sell specific shares in arrears, exempting others from sale if separately accounted for, with provisions for the entire estate sale under certain conditions.
3.	Financial Considerations & Income Calculation
•	Deductions from Gross Income:
•	Local rates or rent to the Government
•	Agricultural Income-tax or Indian Income-tax Act liabilities
•	Management and collection charges at tiered rates based on gross income levels
•	Net Income Calculation: After deductions, ensuring a minimum net income threshold across similar estate categories
•	Apportionment & Compensation:
•	Net income distributed among intermediaries in proportion to their shares.
•	Compensation Table: Specifies total compensation as a multiple of the intermediary's net income from one or more estates.
4.	Post Partition & Default Mechanisms
•	Outcome: Compact, individually assessed revenue estates, potentially sold partially or wholly for unpaid arrears.
•	Deposit for Protection: Option for recorded proprietors to deposit money/securities to exempt the estate from sale for arrears, with withdrawal rights.
•	Exemptions & Exceptions: Estates under Court of Wards or attachment are not liable for sale.
5.	Administration & Interpretation
•	Collector's Powers & Oversight: By Commissioner and Board of Revenue
•	Language & Interpretation: Inclusive for gender and number, ensuring broad applicability
•	Judicial Determinations: Final resort for unresolved disputes, with provisions for civil court involvement.

Precedent & Historical Rationale

● Resolving Co-Sharer Disputes in Jointly Assessed Estates - Under the land revenue system established by the Permanent Settlement, large agricultural estates were frequently held jointly by multiple co-sharers (pattidars). Earlier regulations governing the division of joint estates (Batwara) proved slow and cumbersome, leaving co-sharers collectively liable for the entire revenue demand. If one co-sharer defaulted, the entire estate was subject to summary auction sale, unfairly penalizing non-defaulting owners.

● Simplifying Partition (Batwara) and Apportionment of Land Revenue - Formulated to streamline and accelerate the partition of revenue-paying estates into separate, independent holdings (mahals). The Act enabled individual co-sharers to apply to the Revenue Collector for a formal partition, established clear survey and valuation procedures, and provided for the distinct apportionment of land revenue responsibilities to protect individual property rights from collective default forfeitures.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

● Formulation - Introduced to consolidate, amend, and simplify the procedures for partitioning revenue-paying lands across the North-Western Provinces and the Bengal Presidency.

● Parliamentary Passage - Considered and passed by the Council of the Governor General of India for making Laws and Regulations in early 1863.

● Presidential Assent - Received the assent of the Governor General of India on March 10, 1863.

● Enforcement - Enforced on March 10, 1863.

title: The Terrorist Affected Areas (Special Courts) Act, 1984

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of the  Terrorist Affected Areas (Special Courts) Act, 1984
The Terrorist Affected Areas (Special Courts) Act, 1984 was enacted to provide for the establishment of Special Courts for the speedy trial of specified offences committed in areas affected by terrorist and extremist activities. The Act aimed to ensure swift justice in regions experiencing serious threats to public order and national security, particularly in parts of Punjab during the 1980s. It empowered the Central Government to declare certain regions as "terrorist affected areas" and establish Special Courts to deal with offences arising in those areas.
Objective
The main objectives of the Act are:
•	To ensure the speedy trial of offences connected with terrorism in notified areas.
•	To maintain public order and safeguard national security.
•	To provide a special judicial mechanism for dealing with serious terrorist-related crimes.
•	To strengthen the criminal justice system in areas affected by terrorism.
•	To deter terrorist activities through prompt investigation and adjudication.
Key Provisions
1.	Declaration of Terrorist Affected Areas
o	The Central Government was empowered to declare any area as a terrorist affected area if terrorist activities posed a serious threat to public order and security.
2.	Establishment of Special Courts
o	Special Courts could be established for the trial of specified offences committed in terrorist affected areas.
3.	Appointment of Judges
o	Judges of the Special Courts were appointed by the Central Government in consultation with the Chief Justice of the concerned High Court.
4.	Exclusive Jurisdiction
o	Special Courts had exclusive jurisdiction to try notified offences arising within terrorist affected areas.
5.	Speedy Trial
o	The Act provided simplified procedures to ensure the expeditious disposal of cases involving terrorist offences.
6.	Direct Cognizance of Offences
o	Special Courts could take direct cognizance of offences without requiring committal proceedings by a Magistrate, thereby reducing delays.
7.	Appeals
o	Appeals against the judgments of Special Courts lay directly to the Supreme Court of India within the prescribed period.
8.	Overriding Effect
o	The provisions of the Act prevailed over inconsistent provisions contained in other laws to the extent of such inconsistency.

Precedent & Historical Rationale

1. Surge of Terrorism and Stalled Judicial Prosecution:

o During the early 1980s, escalating extremist violence and militancy—particularly connected to the Punjab crisis—led to widespread fear, disruption of essential services, and challenges to state sovereignty.

o Standard criminal judicial proceedings under the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, faced severe bottlenecks, including witness intimidation, prolonged trial durations, and security risks to judicial officers and prosecutors operating in high-threat environments.

2. Framework for Speedy Trials and Special Jurisdiction:

o The legislative intent centered on creating a robust legal mechanism to establish Special Courts and Additional Special Courts for the expeditious trial of specified "scheduled offences" committed in notified terrorist-affected zones.

o The Act introduced modified procedural rules, provisions for holding trials in camera, measures for the protection and anonymity of witnesses, and direct appeals to the Supreme Court of India, bypassing normal High Court appellate tiers to ensure swift and decisive dispensation of justice.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

• Formulation:

Drafted by the Ministry of Home Affairs as an exceptional counter-terrorism measure during a period of acute national security crisis.

• Parliamentary Passage:

Initially promulgated as an ordinance before being formally introduced, debated, and passed by both Houses of Parliament (Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha) during the monsoon session of 1984.

• Presidential Assent: Received Presidential Assent on August 31, 1984 (with statutory retrospective enforcement from July 14, 1984).

• Enforcement: Enforced on July 14, 1984.

title: The Bengal Land Holder's Attendance Act, 1848

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of the Bengal Land-Holders' Attendance Act, 1848

Introduction

The Bengal Land-Holders' Attendance Act, 1848 was enacted during British rule to regulate the obligation of landholders (zamindars) in Bengal to attend the civil courts. It aimed to reduce inconvenience to important landowners while ensuring the smooth administration of justice.

Objectives
•	To exempt certain landholders from personally attending civil courts.
•	To allow legal proceedings to continue through authorized representatives.
•	To protect influential landholders from unnecessary disruption of estate management.

Key Provisions
•	Selected landholders were exempted from compulsory personal appearance in civil courts.
•	They could appear through a recognized agent or legal representative.
•	Courts retained the power to require personal attendance if it was considered necessary for the interests of justice.

Significance
•	Reduced the burden of frequent court appearances on major landholders.
•	Improved the administration of large estates by allowing owners to continue managing their properties.
•	Balanced the convenience of landholders with the authority of the courts.

Conclusion
The Bengal Land-Holders' Attendance Act, 1848 was an administrative reform that granted specified landholders the privilege of appearing in court through representatives instead of attending personally, while preserving the courts' power to require personal attendance when necessary.

meta.dc.legislation.history:
Legislative History:

The Special Economic Zones Act, 2005

● Act Title - The Special Economic Zones Act, 2005

● Act Number / Year - 28 of 2005

● Act ID (India Code) - 200528

● Assent Date - June 23, 2005

● Enforcement Date - February 10, 2006

● Nodal Ministry - Ministry of Commerce and Industry

Precedent & Historical Rationale

● Limitations of the Export Processing Zones (EPZ) Model and Exim Policy Regime - India established Asia's first Export Processing Zone (EPZ) at Kandla in 1965, later converting existing EPZs into Special Economic Zones under the Foreign Trade Policy in April 2000. However, these zones operated primarily under administrative circulars and fragmented regulatory orders without an overarching statutory backing. This absence of a dedicated central statute generated legal uncertainties regarding long-term fiscal stability, created multi-agency bureaucratic friction, and discouraged large-scale domestic and foreign private investments in zone infrastructure.

● Dedicated Statutory Architecture for Export Promotion and Single-Window Governance - Formulated to provide a comprehensive, stable statutory framework for the establishment, development, and management of Special Economic Zones for export promotion. The Act designated SEZs as deemed duty-free enclaves outside the customs territory of India, instituted an apex Board of Approval (BoA) and zone-level Approval Committees for single-window clearances, provided statutory tax holidays and duty drawbacks, permitted the establishment of Offshore Banking Units (OBUs) and International Financial Services Centres (IFSCs), and decentralized zone administration through Development Commissioners.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

● Formulation & Introduction - Drafted by the Ministry of Commerce and Industry to replace executive guidelines with an overarching legislative enactment; introduced as The Special Economic Zones Bill, 2005 by Commerce and Industry Minister Kamal Nath in the Lok Sabha during the Budget Session.

● Parliamentary Passage - Debated and passed by the Lok Sabha on May 10, 2005 (after key official amendments addressing labour provisions were incorporated), and considered and passed by the Rajya Sabha on May 12, 2005.

● President's Assent - Received the assent of the President of India (Dr. A.P.J. Abdul Kalam) on June 23, 2005, and was published in the Gazette of India on the same day.

● Enforcement - Enforced on February 10, 2006.

Sources - Parliamentary Debates (Lok Sabha & Rajya Sabha), Press Information Bureau (PIB Delhi), The Gazette of India, India Code, and the Ministry of Commerce and Industry.

Act Title - The Judges (Protection) Act, 1985

Act Number/Year - 59 of 1985

Precedent & Historical Rationale

Need for Judicial Independence:

The foundational requirement of a democratic and impartial justice system mandates that judges must be able to deliver decisions and judgments strictly based on law and facts, entirely free from the threat of personal litigation, malicious civil or criminal prosecution, or harassment by dissatisfied litigants.

Inadequacy of Existing Frameworks:

Prior to this enactment, judicial immunity relied heavily on older colonial-era statutes such as the Judicial Officers' Protection Act, 1850. To provide a more comprehensive, modern, and robust statutory shield specifically tailored to protect judicial officers and persons acting in a judicial capacity from vexatious proceedings arising from the discharge of their official duties, Parliament found it necessary to enact a dedicated law.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

Formulation:

Drafted by the Ministry of Law and Justice to extend clear and statutory immunity to judges, ensuring that courts are barred from entertaining or continuing civil or criminal proceedings against them for acts done in the course of their official judicial functions (while preserving the powers of higher courts and governments to initiate legal or departmental action where legally warranted).

Parliamentary Passage:

Introduced, deliberated, and passed by both Houses of Parliament (Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha) in 1985.

Presidential Assent: Received Presidential Assent on September 6, 1985.

Enforcement: Enforced on September 6, 1985.

Source: Official Records of Parliament, India Code, and Ministry of Law and Justice (Department of Justice).

title: Extending certain Acts to Straits Settlement , 1852

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of the Extending Certain Acts to Straits Settlements Act, 1852

Objectives
•	To extend the provisions of Acts XXIV of 1841 and XVII of 1843 to the Straits Settlements.
•	To ensure uniform administration of justice in these British territories.
•	To clarify the legal status of existing laws and eliminate uncertainty regarding their application. 

Key Provisions
•	Declared that the provisions of the two earlier Acts would apply to the Straits Settlements.
•	Provided that references in those Acts to the Supreme Courts of the Indian Presidencies would be interpreted as references to the Court of Judicature of Prince of Wales' Island, Singapore, and Malacca.
•	Ensured that the same legal procedures and judicial powers operated in the Straits Settlements as intended under the earlier Acts. 

Significance
•	Promoted legal uniformity across British-administered territories.
•	Clarified the jurisdiction and powers of the Court of Judicature in the Straits Settlements.
•	Strengthened the administration of justice in the expanding British colonial system. 

Conclusion
The Extending Certain Acts to Straits Settlements Act, 1852 was a clarifying measure that extended earlier Indian laws to the Straits Settlements and adapted them to the local Court of Judicature, ensuring consistent legal administration throughout these British territories.

•	Title: The Geneva Conventions Act, 1960

6.	Miscellaneous Provisions
•	Rule Making Power: Central Government can make rules, to be laid before Parliament.

Summary of Madras District Police Act, 1859

Validity and Continuity of Previous Actions
•	Relevance of Previous Acts: The Act's provisions implicitly validate actions taken under previous regulations, ensuring continuity in policing practices unless explicitly contradicted by the new Act's stipulations.
•	Operational Continuity: Despite the enactment of the Madras District Police Act, 1859, the legitimacy of prior police operations, appointments, and judicial actions under previous rules remains intact, provided they do not conflict with the new Act.

Structure and Governance (Unchanged from Original Context)
•	Act Title & Enactment: The Madras District Police Act, 1859 (24 of 1859), enacted to better regulate police within the Madras Presidency.
•	Governance:
•	Superintendence: Vested in the Governor in Council.
•	Inspector-General of Police: Appointed by the Governor in Council, with powers to frame orders and regulations for the Police Force.
•	District Superintendents: May be appointed as Magistrates with specified powers.

Police Force (Unchanged)

•	Constitution: The entire Police establishment of the Madras Presidency is deemed one Police Force, formally enrolled and constituted as ordered by the Governor in Council.
•	Appointment & Dismissal: Rests with the Inspector-General and Deputy Superintendents, under sanctioned rules.
•	Certification: Police Officers receive certificates of office, which cease to be effective upon suspension, dismissal, or removal.

Powers and Responsibilities (Unchanged)

•	Inspector-General & District Superintendents:
•	Inspector-General has full powers of a Magistrate throughout the General Police District, exercisable under Government orders.
•	District Superintendents may act as Magistrates for specific cases related to peace, crime prevention, and offender detention.
•	General Powers:
•	All powers not inconsistent with the Act, previously belonging to existing police authorities, are vested in the new police authorities.
•	Police functionaries cannot possess or exercise judicial or revenue authority.

Financial Provisions (Unchanged)
•	Police Superannuation Fund: Established through deductions from Police Officers' pay and other specified sources, for superannuation or retiring allowances.

Other Provisions (Updated for New Context)
•	Repeal and Continuity: While the Act repeals previous Regulations and Acts within the General Police District's limits, it ensures that all actions, proceedings, and rules made under the repealed Acts are deemed valid and continued under this Act, to the extent they are not inconsistent with its provisions.
•	Additional Police & Other: (Remains unchanged due to lack of new context relevance)

Precedent & Historical Rationale

● Torture Commission Report (1855) & Reorganisation Need - Following the revelatory findings of the Madras Torture Commission Report of 1855, severe abuses were exposed in the dual role played by revenue officials who also exercised police authority. There was an urgent administrative necessity to separate police functions from revenue collection and place policing under a distinct, disciplined statutory authority.

● Establishment of a Professional Police Force - Formulated to replace fragmented village and district watch systems with a single, disciplined, and uniformed police force under the Madras Presidency. Serving as a crucial precursor to the general Police Act of 1861, the Act established a structured hierarchy under an Inspector-General of Police, defined police powers, regulated conditions of service, and instituted strict penalties for police misconduct and corruption.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

● Formulation - Introduced to reorganize and better regulate the police force throughout the mofussil (districts) of the Presidency of Fort St. George (Madras).

● Parliamentary Passage - Considered and passed by the Legislative Council of India in mid-1859.

Summary of the Salar Jung Museum Act, 1961
Key Provisions
1.	Establishment of the Museum
•	Constitutes the Salar Jung Museum as a statutory institution under the Central Government.
•	Provides for its continued functioning as a national museum dedicated to preserving the Salar Jung collection.
2.	Board of Trustees
•	Establishes a Board to administer and manage the museum.
•	The Board is responsible for:
•	Managing the museum's affairs.
•	Preserving and expanding the collections.
•	Administering finances and property.
•	Framing policies for the museum's development.
3.	Director and Staff
•	Provides for the appointment of a Director and other officers and employees.
•	The Director is responsible for the day-to-day administration and implementation of the Board's decisions.
4.	Museum Collections
•	Vests the museum's collections, assets, and properties in the institution.
•	Requires the preservation, cataloguing, conservation, and display of valuable objects of historical, artistic, archaeological, and cultural significance.
5.	Functions of the Museum
•	Collect, preserve, and exhibit works of art and antiquities.
•	Promote research and scholarship in art, history, archaeology, and culture.
•	Organize exhibitions, educational programmes, and publications.
•	Acquire objects of artistic or historical value through lawful means.
6.	Finance
•	Provides for grants from the Central Government and other lawful sources.
•	Authorizes the Board to maintain accounts, prepare budgets, and ensure proper financial management.
•	Requires auditing of the museum's accounts in accordance with applicable law.
7.	Rule-making Powers
•	Empowers the Central Government to make rules for carrying out the provisions of the Act.
•	The Board may also frame regulations on matters relating to administration and museum management, subject to the Act and rules.

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of The Enemy Property Act, 1968 
Objective
•	Protect and preserve enemy properties situated in India. 
•	Vest enemy properties in the Custodian of Enemy Property for India for proper management and administration. 
•	Prevent unauthorized transfer, inheritance, disposal, or misuse of enemy property. 
•	Ensure that such properties are managed in accordance with the law and in the national interest. 
•	Provide a legal framework for the identification, control, and disposal of enemy properties. 
Key Provisions
•	Definition of Enemy and Enemy Property: Defines "enemy," "enemy subject," "enemy firm," and "enemy property" for the purposes of the Act. 
•	Vesting of Property: Provides that all enemy property shall vest in the Custodian of Enemy Property for India, who exercises control and management over such property. 
•	Powers of the Custodian: Empowers the Custodian to take possession, manage, preserve, maintain, and protect enemy properties, and to collect rent, income, or other dues arising from them. 
•	Restriction on Transfer: Declares that transfers of enemy property made in contravention of the Act are void, and prohibits unauthorized sale, mortgage, lease, gift, or other forms of transfer. 
•	Succession and Inheritance: Clarifies that enemy property continues to remain vested in the Custodian notwithstanding the death of the enemy or claims based on succession or inheritance, as reinforced by the 2017 amendments. 
•	Powers of the Central Government: Authorizes the Central Government to issue directions regarding the management, preservation, and disposal of enemy property in accordance with the Act. 
•	Appeals and Legal Proceedings: Provides mechanisms for addressing disputes and bars civil courts from entertaining matters that fall within the authority of the Custodian or the Central Government under the Act. 
•	Penalties: Prescribes penalties for unauthorized possession, transfer, concealment, or interference with enemy property and for contravention of the provisions of the Act.

•	Commencement: Dates appointed by the Central Government through notifications (e.g., 1st January 1982, for most provisions, and 1st March 1982, for Section 26)
2.	Purpose
•	Establish the Export-Import Bank of India (Exim Bank)
•	Provide financial assistance to exporters and importers
•	Function as the principal financial institution for coordinating export and import financing
•	Promote the country's international trade
3.	Establishment and Structure
•	Exim Bank: A corporation with perpetual succession and a common seal
•	Head Office: Initially at Bombay (now Mumbai), potentially relocatable by Central Government notification
•	Offices/Branches: Can be established in or outside India as necessary
4.	Capital
•	Authorised Capital: Ten thousand crores of rupees (subject to increase by the Central Government)
•	Issued Capital: Wholly subscribed by the Central Government
5.	Business Operations
•	Primary:
•	Grant loans and advances for export/import
•	Coordinate financing institutions for export/import
•	Additional Businesses (non-exhaustive list from Section 10):
•	Refinance to scheduled banks
•	Underwriting stocks/shares for export/import companies
•	Issuing bid bonds/guarantees
•	Discounting bills of exchange for export/import
•	Letters of credit
•	Lines of credit to foreign governments/institutions
•	Financing joint ventures and equipment leases
•	Foreign exchange dealings
•	Research and development for international trade
•	Technical/administrative/financial assistance for export/import
6.	Resources
•	Loans from Central Government
•	Borrowings:
•	Issue bonds/debentures (with or without Central Government guarantee)
•	Borrow from the Reserve Bank of India
•	Borrow from approved authorities/institutions in India
•	Accept deposits (repayable after 12 months)
•	Foreign Currency Loans: With previous consent of the Central Government
•	Grants/Donations: Can be received from any source
7.	Export Development Fund (EDF)
•	Establishment: By Exim Bank, as notified by the Central Government
•	Credits to EDF:
•	Loans, gifts, grants, etc.
•	Repayments from EDF-funded loans
•	Income from investments
•	Interest/income from EDF applications
•	Utilisation:
•	For specific loan/advance arrangements under Section 10, with Central Government approval
•	Prior approval required, ensuring no ordinary financial institution would provide the facility
•	Debits to EDF:
•	Disbursed/spent amounts
•	Liability discharges for EDF loans
•	Investment losses
•	Administrative expenses determined by the Board
•	Accounts and Audit:
•	Prepared in a prescribed form
•	Audited by Central Government-appointed auditors
•	Reports to be laid before Parliament
8.	Miscellaneous
•	Definitions: Provided for key terms (e.g., Board, Exim Bank, Export, Import, Goods, Services)
•	Amendments: Reference to an amendment (e.g., by Act 11 of 2012)

THE EXPORT-IMPORT BANK OF INDIA ACT, 1981
ACT NO. 28 OF 1981

[11th September, 1981.]

An Act to establish a corporation to be known as the Export-Import Bank of India for providing financial assistance to exporters and importers, and for functioning as the principal financial institution for co-ordinating the working of institutions engaged in financing export and import of goods and services with a view to promoting the countrys international trade and for matters connected therewith or incidental thereto.

meta.dc.legislation.history:
Legislative History:

The Export-Import Bank of India Act, 1981

● Act Title - The Export-Import Bank of India Act, 1981

● Act Number / Year - 28 of 1981

● Act ID (India Code) - 198128

● Presidential Assent Date - September 11, 1981

● Enforcement Date - January 1, 1982

● Nodal Ministry - Ministry of Finance

Precedent & Historical Rationale

● Specialized Apex Financial Institution for International Trade - Prior to 1981, international trade financing and export credit operations were managed directly by the Industrial Development Bank of India (IDBI) through its International Finance Wing, alongside commercial banks. As India’s foreign trade expanded, there arose an urgent structural need for a dedicated, apex export credit agency to support cross-border trade, project exports, and joint ventures.

● Establishment of Exim Bank of India - Formulated to establish the Export-Import Bank of India (Exim Bank) as a principal statutory financial institution. The Act empowered the bank to finance, facilitate, and promote India’s international trade, provide lines of credit to foreign governments and financial institutions, refinance commercial banks for export-import transactions, and offer advisory services to exporters to enhance global competitiveness.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

● Formulation - Introduced by the Union Ministry of Finance to provide a specialized statutory foundation and capital base for international trade financing, transferring the international finance operations of IDBI to the newly created Exim Bank.

● Parliamentary Passage - Debated and passed by both Houses of Parliament (Seventh Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha) during the monsoon session in August–September 1981.

● Presidential Assent - Received Presidential Assent on September 11, 1981.

● Enforcement - Enforced on January 1, 1982.

Source - Official Record of Parliament, India Code, and Ministry of Finance .

meta.dc.identifier.preamble_description:
THE BIRD AND COMPANY LIMITED (ACQUISITION AND TRANSFER OF UNDERTAKINGS AND OTHER PROPERTIES) ACT, 1980
ACT NO. 67 OF 1980

[27th December, 1980.]

An Act to provide for the acquisition and transfer of the undertakings of the Bird and Company Limited for the purpose of ensuring the continuity of production of goods which are vital to the needs of the country and for the acquisition of shares held by the Bird and Company Limited in the specified companies for the purpose of securing to those undertakings the facilities and advantages derived by reason of such shareholding with respect to the operation and functioning of those undertakings and also to enable the Central Government to exercise such control over the affairs of the specified companies as is necessary to ensure that the affairs of those companies are not mismanaged and for matters connected therewith or incidental thereto.
WHEREAS the Bird and Company Limited were engaged in the manufacture of E.O.T. cranes and other varieties of cranes; polystyrene based cation exchange resin; equipment for fertilizers, oil refineries, steel plants, petro-chemical and other industries; tanks and vessels of various shapes and sizes, water treatment equipment and other types of equipment for the control of water pollution and were also engaged in various other activities;
AND WHEREAS the top management of the Bird and Company Limited had so mismanaged the affairs of that Company as to cause heavy losses to the Company and had also managed the affairs of the Company in a manner prejudicial to the interests of the Company and the public interest;
AND WHEREAS in view of the mismanagement aforesaid, the Central Government had, in pursuance of the provisions of section 408 of the Companies Act, 1956 (1 of 1956), appointed six directors on the Board of directors of the Bird and Company Limited;
AND WHEREAS investment of a large amount is necessary for the maintenance and development of the production of the undertakings of the Company;
AND WHEREAS it is necessary in the public interest to acquire the undertakings of the Bird and Company Limited to enable the Central Government to have such investment made and to ensure that the interests of the general public are served by the continuance, by the undertakings of the Company, of the manufacture, production and distribution of goods or articles which are essential to the needs of the economy of the country;
AND WHEREAS the Bird and Company Limited is holding shares in the specified companies which are either engaged in the production, distribution or marketing of goods which are vital to the needs of the country or are engaged in providing finance to other companies which are so engaged and it is expedient in the public interest to acquire the said shares to secure for the undertakings of the Company the facilities and advantages derived by reason of such shareholding with respect to the operation and functioning of such undertakings and also to enable the Central Government to exercise, through such shareholdings, such control on the affairs of those companies as may be necessary to prevent their mismanagement;
BE it enacted by Parliament in the Thirty-first Year of the Republic of India as follows:--

Precedent & Historical Rationale

● Restructuring of Historical Industrial Conglomerates - Bird & Company (originally a prominent British-era managing agency conglomerate founded in the 19th century) controlled vast interests in engineering, coal, jute, mining, and trading. Following post-independence financial mismanagement, severe liquidity crises, and mounting liabilities, the management of the company was initially taken over under the Industries (Development and Regulation) Act, 1951.

● Nationalisation for Industrial Recovery - Formulated to acquire the undertakings and properties of Bird and Company Limited to ensure effective utilization of production assets, safeguard employment, and protect public sector financial institution investments. ● Presidential Assent - Received Presidential Assent on December 27, 1980.

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of the Rent Recovery Act, 1853

The Rent Recovery Act, 1853 (Act No. 8 of 1853) was enacted to provide a summary and expeditious procedure for the recovery of rent payable by tenants to landlords in certain cases. The Act aimed to simplify the process of recovering arrears of rent through designated authorities, thereby reducing delays associated with ordinary civil litigation.

Objectives
•	To provide a speedy and simplified procedure for the recovery of arrears of rent. 
•	To facilitate the enforcement of landlords' rights to recover rent lawfully due from tenants. 
•	To reduce the burden on civil courts by introducing a summary mechanism for rent recovery. 
•	To promote certainty and efficiency in landlord–tenant relations. 
Key Provisions
•	Provided a summary procedure for landlords to recover arrears of rent from tenants. 
•	Empowered designated judicial or revenue authorities to hear and determine applications for rent recovery. 
•	Prescribed the procedure for filing claims, issuing notices, hearing parties, and passing recovery orders. 
•	Authorized the recovery of rent in accordance with the provisions of the Act, including enforcement measures where applicable. 
•	Included safeguards to ensure that tenants were given an opportunity to contest claims before recovery orders were made.

meta.dc.legislation.history:
Legislative History:

The Rent Recovery Act, 1853

● Act Title - The Rent Recovery Act, 1853

● Act Number / Year - 6 of 1853

● Act ID (India Code) - 185306

● Enactment Date - April 15, 1853

● Enforcement Date - April 15, 1853

● Nodal Ministry - Ministry of Home Affairs

Precedent & Historical Rationale

● Clarification of Jurisdictional Conflicts in Summary Rent Suits - Under earlier Bengal Regulations (specifically Bengal Regulation VIII of 1831 and Regulation VII of 1832), jurisdiction over summary suits for arrears of rent and the power to conduct sales of Patni (Putnee) Taluks and saleable tenures were transferred from Zilla and City Courts to Revenue Collectors. However, procedural ambiguity arose regarding which Revenue Collector had jurisdiction when tenures, leases, or revenue-paying lands stretched across multiple Collectorates (districts).

● Streamlining Tenure Sales & Protecting Historical Titles - Formulated to clearly define territorial jurisdiction for summary rent suits and land sales. The Act established that the Collector of the district containing the greater part of the land held under one rent/lease had the sole authority to hear summary rent claims and execute land sales to satisfy rent decrees. It also validated past actions and sales made prior to April 1853 to prevent titling disputes arising solely from minor administrative or district boundary irregularities.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

● Formulation - Introduced to streamline administrative jurisdiction for summary rent recoveries and land sales where estate boundaries traversed multiple administrative districts within the Presidency of Fort William.

● Parliamentary Passage - Considered and passed by the Council of the Governor General of India in early 1853.

● Presidential Assent - Received the assent of the Governor General of India on April 15, 1853.

● Enforcement - Enforced on April 15, 1853.

Sources - Official Records of the Governor General in Council, India Code, and Ministry of Home Affairs

Historical Context and Legacy

1. Reorganizing Revenue Administration in the Bombay Presidency:

o During the expansion of British territorial administration in western India, the Bombay Presidency required decentralized yet tightly controlled supervisory machinery to manage land revenue collection, settlement operations, and administrative accountability.

o Prior legislative measures had established varying configurations of Revenue Commissioners. This 1842 Act was brought forth to formally regulate and clarify the precise number of Commissioners required for the Presidency and to legally delineate their jurisdictional powers and authority over subordinate collectors and revenue officials.

o Delegation of Powers: Empowered the appointed Revenue Commissioners to exercise comprehensive supervisory, appellate, and administrative control over revenue departments, land assessments, and fiscal administration across assigned regional collectorates.

o Legal Force of Orders: Ensured that official directives and decisions issued by the Revenue Commissioners within their statutory purview possessed binding legal execution over local revenue officers.

• Formulation: Drafted under the British East India Company administration to reorganize and expedite revenue management and administrative oversight across the districts of the Bombay Presidency.

• Parliamentary Passage: Passed by the Governor-General of India in Council pursuant to the legislative powers under the Charter Act of 1833.

• Presidential Assent: Not applicable (Enacted by the Governor-General-in-Council on September 23, 1842)

meta.dc.legislation.history:
Legislative History:

The Insurance Act, 1938

● Act Title - The Insurance Act, 1938

● Act Number / Year - 4 of 1938

● Act ID (India Code) - 193804

● Presidential Assent Date - February 26, 1938

● Enforcement Date - July 1, 1939

● Nodal Ministry - Ministry of Finance

Precedent & Historical Rationale

● Inadequacies of the Indian Life Assurance Companies Act, 1912 & Provident Insurance Societies Act, 1912 - Prior to 1938, the regulation of the domestic insurance sector was fragmented between the Indian Life Assurance Companies Act, 1912 and the Provident Insurance Societies Act, 1912, while non-life insurance (fire, marine, and general accident) remained largely unregulated by dedicated statutes. Following the Swadeshi movement and rapid expansion in the 1920s and 1930s, numerous undercapitalized insurance ventures emerged, characterized by reckless financial management, excessive agency commissions, inadequate actuarial reserves, and predatory competition from established foreign insurers, leading to frequent company failures and significant losses for policyholders.

● Recommendations of the Clauson Committee & the Sen Committee (1935) - The Government of India appointed a special consultative committee headed by Susil Chandra Sen in 1935 (which drew heavily upon the contemporary Clauson Committee recommendations in the UK) to overhaul insurance laws. The committee underscored the imperative need for comprehensive legislation covering life and non-life insurance, mandatory statutory deposits, strict investment norms, regulation of intermediaries, and supervisory oversight by a central statutory authority.

● Comprehensive Statutory Architecture for the Indian Insurance Industry - Formulated to consolidate and amend the law relating to the business of insurance in India. The Act established the office of the Superintendent of Insurance (later the Controller of Insurance), mandated compulsory registration and substantial security deposits with the Reserve Bank of India, regulated investments of life fund assets into government securities, capped managerial remuneration and agency commissions, instituted mandatory periodic actuarial investigations, and introduced stringent provisions governing mergers, amalgamations, and assignments of insurance policies to protect policyholders' interests.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

● Formulation - Drafted by the Department of Commerce of the Government of India based on the Sen Committee Report (1935) and introduced in the Indian Legislative Assembly in January 1937 by the Law Member, Sir Nripendra Nath Sircar.

● Parliamentary Passage - Referred to an exhaustive Joint Select Committee, intensely debated across the Simla and Delhi sessions over issues of domestic protectionism and foreign insurer regulation, and passed by the Indian Legislative Assembly in October 1937 and the Council of State in early 1938.

● Presidential Assent - Received the assent of the Governor General of India on February 26, 1938.

● Enforcement - Enforced on July 1, 1939.

Sources - Official Records of the Governor General in Council, India Code, and Ministry of Finance.

title: The National Capital Region Planning Board Act, 1985

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of The National Capital Region Planning Board Act, 1985 
Act Name: National Capital Region Planning Board Act, 1985 
Objective: Establish a planning framework for the National Capital Region (NCR) to ensure coordinated and balanced development. 
Key Components
1.	Constitution of the Board
•	Name: National Capital Region Planning Board
•	Composition: Up to 21 members, including Union Ministers, Chief Ministers of participating states (Haryana, Rajasthan, Uttar Pradesh), the Administrator of the Union Territory (Delhi), and nominated experts.
•	Chairman: The Union Minister for Works and Housing.
2.	Planning Committee
•	Role: Assists the Board in discharge of its functions.
•	Membership: Includes the Member-Secretary of the Board, representatives from the Ministry of Works and Housing, Secretaries of participating states, and urban development experts.
3.	Functions and Powers of the Board
•	Prepare Regional and Functional Plans for NCR.
•	Coordinate Implementation across participating states and the Union Territory.
•	Powers: Include calling for reports, ensuring plan conformity, reviewing implementations, and approving projects.
4.	The Regional Plan
•	Mandatory Elements:
•	Land-use policy
•	Urban settlement patterns
•	Economic base proposals
•	Transport and communications plans
•	Water supply and drainage proposals
•	Priority areas for development
•	Preparation and Amendment Process: Involves public consultation, publication, and consideration of objections.
5.	Miscellaneous Provisions
•	Overriding Clause: Act's provisions override conflicting laws.
•	Central Government Directions: Can issue directions to the Board.
•	Protection of Actions: Good faith actions under the Act are legally protected.
•	Rule and Regulation Making Powers: For effective implementation. Operational Aspects
•	Coming into Operation of the Plan: Upon notified publication.
•	Modifications: Non-substantial changes can be made after public notice and consideration of objections.
•	Dissolution: The Board can be dissolved by the Central Government if objectives are met or failed, with assets transferring accordingly. Governance and Compliance
•	Participating Entities: Haryana, Rajasthan, Uttar Pradesh, and the Union Territory of Delhi.
•	Public Servants: Board members and employees are deemed public servants.
•	Acquisition of Land: Responsibility of the respective state or Union Territory government for plan implementation.

Legislative History:

The National Capital Region Planning Board Act, 1985

Act Title - The National Capital Region Planning Board Act, 1985

Act Number/Year - 2 of 1985

Act ID (India Code)- 198502

Presidential Assent Date - February 9, 1985

Enforcement Date - October 19, 1984.

Nodal Ministry - Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs

Precedent & Historical Rationale

1. Unchecked Population Growth and Congestion in Delhi:

o By the late 1970s and early 1980s, India's capital city, Delhi, experienced unprecedented population explosion, rapid urbanization, and mounting pressure on civic infrastructure, housing, transport, and basic utilities.

o Recognizing that Delhi alone could not absorb the continuous influx of migrants without triggering total urban decay, urban planners and policymakers emphasized the necessity of a coordinated, regional approach to development across neighbouring states.

2. Establishment of a Statutory Inter-State Regional Planning Board:

o The legislative intent centered on establishing a statutory body—the National Capital Region Planning Board (NCRPB)—to systematically plan, harmonize, and coordinate the development of the National Capital Region (NCR) spanning the Union Territory of Delhi and parts of the surrounding states of Haryana, Uttar Pradesh, and later Rajasthan.

o The Act empowered the Board to formulate a comprehensive Regional Plan, functional plans, and coordinated land-use policies to deflect population pressures from the core capital by developing counter-magnet towns and integrated satellite urban centers.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

• Formulation: Drafted by the Ministry of Works and Housing (now Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs) in close consultation with the planning commissions and participating state governments.

• Parliamentary Passage:

Introduced, debated, and passed by both Houses of Parliament (Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha) during the winter/budget session of Parliament.

• Presidential Assent: Received Presidential Assent on February 11, 1985.

• Enforcement: Enforced March 28, 1985.

Source: Official Records of Parliament, India Code, and Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs.

Summary of the Compensatory Afforestation Fund Act, 2016
Title & Extent
•	Act Name: The Compensatory Afforestation Fund Act, 2016
•	Act No.: 38 of 2016
•	Extent: Whole of India, including Union Territory Administrations
Purpose
•	Establish funds for compensatory afforestation and related activities across all territories.
•	Utilize monies from user agencies for forest land diversion under the Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980, uniformly applied.
Key Provisions
1.	Funds Establishment & Administration
•	National Compensatory Afforestation Fund (National Fund): Centralized, overseeing all territories.
•	State/Union Territory Compensatory Afforestation Fund (State/UT Fund): Established in each, with clear administration guidelines for Union Territories.
2.	Management Authorities & Coordination
•	National Authority: Oversees National Fund, coordinates with State and Union Territory Authorities.
•	State/Union Territory Authority: Manages respective funds, with specified roles for Union Territory Administrations.
3.	Fund Utilisation & Territory Considerations
•	National Fund: 90% distributed to State/UT Funds; 10% for overarching management, ecological projects, and inter-territory initiatives.
•	State/UT Fund: Prioritizes local compensatory afforestation, forest and wildlife protection, tailored infrastructure, and community projects, with adjustments for Union Territory specific needs.

meta.dc.identifier.preamble_description:
THE COMPENSATORY AFFORESTATION FUND ACT, 2016
ACT NO. 38 OF 2016

[3rd August, 2016.]

An Act to provide for the establishment of funds under the public accounts of India and the public accounts of each State and crediting thereto the monies received from the user agencies towards compensatory afforestation, additional compensatory afforestation, penal compensatory afforestation, net present value and all other amounts recovered from such agencies under the Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980; constitution of an authority at national level and at each of the State and Union territory Administration for administration of the funds and to utilise the monies so collected for undertaking artificial regeneration (plantations), assisted natural regeneration, protection of forests, forest related infrastructure development, Green India Programme, wildlife protection and other related activities and for matters connected therewith or incidental thereto.
WHEREAS the Supreme Court in its order in T.N. Godavarman Thirumulpad vs. Union of India and Others [Writ Petition (Civil) No. 202 of 1995], dated the 30th October, 2002, observed that a Compensatory Afforestation Fund be created in which all the monies received from the user agencies towards compensatory afforestation, additional compensatory afforestation, penal compensatory afforestation, net present value of the diverted forest land or catchment area treatment plan shall be deposited;
AND WHEREAS it had also been observed that the money received from the user agencies in cases where forest land diverted falls within protected areas, that is, the areas notified under the Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972 (35 of 1972) for undertaking activities related to protection of biodiversity or wildlife shall also be deposited in the Fund;
AND WHEREAS the Supreme Court has directed that, besides artificial regeneration (Plantations), the Fund shall also be utilised for undertaking assisted natural regeneration, protection of forests, infrastructure development, wildlife protection and other related activities and an independent system of concurrent monitoring and evaluation should be evolved and implemented through the Compensatory Afforestation Fund to ensure effective and proper utilisation of funds;
AND WHEREAS the Supreme Court in its judgment dated 26th September, 2005 in the said Writ Petition observed that the Fund generated for protecting ecology and providing regeneration should not be treated as a Fund under article 266 and article 283 of the Constitution;
AND WHEREAS in its direction dated the 5th May, 2006, the Supreme Court had directed that since the Government has not constituted a Compensatory Afforestation Fund Management and Planning Authority (hereinafter referred to as Authority), an ad hoc Authority should be constituted till the Compensatory Afforestation Fund Management and Planning Authority becomes operational and directed to centrally pool the money recovered on behalf of the said Authority lying in the States and Union territories into the ad hoc Compensatory Afforestation Fund Management and Planning Authority;
AND WHEREAS Central Government formulated guidelines dated the 2nd July, 2009 on the subject of State Authority for utilisation of funds lying with the ad hoc Authority;
AND WHEREAS in its direction dated the 10th July, 2009, the Supreme Court had directed that the guidelines and structure of the State Authority prepared by the Central Government may be notified and implemented;
AND WHEREAS in its directions dated the 10th July, 2009, the Supreme Court further directed that till an alternative system is put in place, after obtaining permission from the Supreme Court, the money towards compensatory afforestation, net present value and protected areas (national parks, wildlife sanctuaries) shall continue to be deposited in the ad hoc Authority;
AND WHEREAS in compliance of the directions of the Supreme Court including its order dated the 5th May, 2006, over rupees thirty eight thousand crores as collected by the State Governments and Union territory Administrations have been placed under the ad hoc Authority, and deposited in the nationalised banks;
AND WHEREAS absence of permanent institutional mechanism for utilisation of funds collected by the State Governments and Union territory Administrations is the main reason for accumulation of huge unspent funds in the ad hoc Authority;
NOW, THEREFORE, based on the above orders, directions and observations of the Supreme Court to ensure safety, security and expeditious utilisation in a transparent manner of funds accumulated with the ad hoc Authority and the funds to be collected by the State Governments and Union territory Administrations, it is proposed to create a National Compensatory Afforestation Fund and a National Compensatory Afforestation Fund Management and Planning Authority at the national level, and a State Compensatory Afforestation Fund and a State Compensatory Afforestation Fund Management and Planning Authority in each State and Union territory, by an Act of Parliament.
BE it enacted by Parliament in the Sixty-seventh Year of the Republic of India as follows:---

meta.dc.legislation.history:
Legislative History:

The Compensatory Afforestation Fund Act, 2016

● Act Title - The Compensatory Afforestation Fund Act, 2016

● Act Number / Year - 38 of 2016

● Act ID (India Code) - 201638

● Assent Date - August 3, 2016

● Enforcement Date - September 30, 2017

● Nodal Ministry - Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change

Precedent & Historical Rationale

● Ad-Hoc CAMPA and Accumulation of Unspent Funds under Supreme Court Orders - Under the Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980, when forest land is diverted for non-forest purposes, the user agency must pay for compensatory afforestation, Net Present Value (NPV), and catchment area treatment. In 2002, the Supreme Court of India in T.N. Godavarman Thirumulpad v. Union of India directed the creation of a specialized body, leading to the creation of the ad-hoc Compensatory Afforestation Fund Management and Planning Authority (CAMPA) in 2006. Over the years, massive compensatory levies (exceeding ₹40,000 crore) accumulated in ad-hoc bank accounts outside the Consolidated Fund of India, lacking a permanent institutional mechanism for statutory allocation and transparent expenditure by States.

● Permanent Statutory Architecture for Fund Management and Afforestation - Formulated to provide for the establishment of funds under the public accounts of India and the public accounts of each State, and the crediting of monies received from user agencies for compensatory afforestation. The Act established the National Compensatory Afforestation Fund Management and Planning Authority (National CAMPA) and State CAMPAs, mandating a permanent statutory formula where 90% of collected funds are transferred directly to the respective State Funds and 10% retained in the National Fund to expedite reforestation, assisted natural regeneration, wildlife habitat protection, and forest infrastructure management.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

● Formulation & Re-introduction - Drafted by the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change following an earlier lapsed measure from 2008 (The Compensatory Afforestation Fund Bill, 2008); re-introduced as The Compensatory Afforestation Fund Bill, 2015 (Bill No. 147 of 2015) by Minister of State (Independent Charge) Prakash Javadekar in the Lok Sabha on May 8, 2015.

● Parliamentary Passage - Debated and passed by the Lok Sabha on May 3, 2016, and considered and passed by the Rajya Sabha on July 28, 2016, during the Monsoon Session.

● President's Assent - Received the assent of the President of India (Pranab Mukherjee) on August 3, 2016, and was published in the Gazette of India on the same day.

● Enforcement - Enforced on September 30, 2017.

Sources - Parliamentary Debates (Lok Sabha & Rajya Sabha), The Gazette of India, India Code, and Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change..

The Bombay Civil Courts Act, 1869

● Act Title - The Bombay Civil Courts Act, 1869

● Act Number / Year - 14 of 1869

● Act ID (India Code) - 186914

● Presidential Assent Date - March 19, 1869

● Enforcement Date - March 19, 1869

● Nodal Ministry - Ministry of Law and Justice

Precedent & Historical Rationale

● Overhauling the Mofussil Civil Judicial Architecture - Prior to 1869, the administration of civil justice outside the Presidency Town of Bombay (in the mofussil districts) was governed by an patchwork of old Bombay Regulations (such as Regulation II of 1827) and subsequent scattered acts. This resulted in jurisdictional overlaps, inconsistent pecuniary limits for local judges, and inefficient appellate hierarchies across civil courts.

● Streamlining Judicial Hierarchy & Pecuniary Limits - Formulated to consolidate and amend the law relating to the constitution, powers, and jurisdiction of Civil Courts in the Bombay Presidency. The Act established a structured, three-tiered civil court hierarchy—District Courts, Subordinate Courts (later categorized as Civil Judges of Senior and Junior Divisions), and Courts of Small Causes—defining their respective original, pecuniary, and appellate jurisdictions to ensure efficient judicial administration.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

● Formulation - Introduced to reorganize the system of civil courts, define judicial cadres, and establish clear territorial and pecuniary limits for civil litigation across the Bombay Presidency.

● Parliamentary Passage - Considered and passed by the Council of the Governor General of India for making Laws and Regulations in early 1869.

● Presidential Assent - Received the assent of the Governor General of India on March 19, 1869.

● Enforcement - Enforced on March 19, 1869.

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of the Advocates Act, 1961
Key Provisions
1.	Bar Council of India (BCI)
•	Establishes the Bar Council of India, the apex statutory body for the legal profession.
•	Its functions include:
•	Prescribing standards of professional conduct and etiquette.
•	Promoting and supervising legal education.
•	Recognizing law degrees for enrolment.
•	Protecting the rights and interests of advocates.
•	Exercising disciplinary and supervisory powers over State Bar Councils.
2.	State Bar Councils
•	Constitutes State Bar Councils for each State or group of States.
•	Their functions include:
•	Enrolling advocates.
•	Maintaining the State roll of advocates.
•	Safeguarding the rights and welfare of advocates.
•	Conducting disciplinary proceedings against advocates.
3.	Enrolment of Advocates
•	Prescribes the qualifications and conditions for enrolment as an advocate.
•	A person enrolled with a State Bar Council becomes entitled to practice law, subject to the provisions of the Act and the rules made under it.
4.	Right to Practice
•	Advocates enrolled under the Act have the right to practice before:
•	All courts in India.
•	Tribunals.
•	Any authority legally authorized to take evidence.
•	The exercise of this right is subject to the Act and applicable rules.
5.	Professional Conduct and Discipline
•	Advocates are required to maintain high standards of professional ethics.
•	Complaints of professional or other misconduct are inquired into by the disciplinary committees of the State Bar Councils.
•	Appeals against disciplinary orders may lie to the Bar Council of India and, in appropriate cases, to the Supreme Court.
6.	Legal Education
•	The Bar Council of India is empowered to:
•	Lay down standards of legal education.
•	Recognize universities and law degrees for enrolment.
•	Conduct inspections of law institutions.
7.	Senior Advocates
•	Provides for the designation of distinguished advocates as Senior Advocates by the Supreme Court or High Courts.
•	Senior Advocates are subject to certain restrictions regarding legal practice as prescribed by the rules.
8.	Rule-making Powers
•	The Bar Council of India and State Bar Councils may frame rules on:
•	Professional conduct and etiquette.
•	Legal education.
•	Enrolment procedures.
•	Disciplinary proceedings.

Act ID (India Code) 200638

Presidential Assent Date August 30, 2006

Nodal Ministry Ministry of Finance

Precedent & Statutory Rationale

1. Obsolescence of Colonial Frameworks:

o Prior to 2006, the legal mechanisms governing the issuance, holding, transfer, and servicing of government debt in India were anchored in legacy enactments specifically the Indian Securities Act, 1920 and the Public Debt Act, 1944.

o These historical statutes were inherently paper-based, rigid, and inadequate for supporting modern electronic trading systems, dematerialized book-entry structures, and efficient secondary market clearing managed by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI).

2. Modernization of Public Debt Administration:

o The legislation was enacted to create a flexible, efficient, and transparent legal framework capable of accommodating electronic record-keeping, simplifying ownership transfers, lowering transaction friction, and strengthening the overall market integrity of government securities.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

• Formulation: Developed by the Ministry of Finance in coordination with the Reserve Bank of India to structurally reform public debt legislation.

• Parliamentary Passage: Tabled, debated, and passed by both Houses of Parliament during the monsoon session of 2006.

• Presidential Assent: Received formal Presidential Assent on August 30, 2006, entering the statute book as Act No. 38 of 2006.

• Enforcement: Enforced on December 1, 2007.

• Source: India Code and Ministry of Finance Official Gazette Notifications
