meta.dc.legislation.history:
Legislative History:

The Indian Stamp Act, 1899

● Act Title - The Indian Stamp Act, 1899

● Act Number / Year - 2 of 1899

● Act ID (India Code) - 189902

● Assent Date - January 27, 1899

● Enforcement Date - July 1, 1899

● Nodal Ministry - Ministry of Finance

Precedent & Historical Rationale

● Deficiencies and Ambiguities of the Indian Stamp Act, 1879 - Prior to 1899, the fiscal levy on formal instruments was governed by the Indian Stamp Act, 1879 (Act I of 1879). Over two decades of judicial interpretation and commercial expansion, the 1879 statute revealed significant ambiguities concerning the definition of taxable instruments, valuation of fluctuating securities, enforcement against un-stamped documents, and loopholes enabling widespread duty evasion in commercial transactions.

● Comprehensive Re-codification of Fiscal Duties on Instruments and Evidentiary Admissibility Rules - Formulated to consolidate and amend the law relating to stamps into a comprehensive, uniform code for British India. The Act standardized the categorization and rates of stamp duties across commercial and conveyancing instruments (Schedule I), codified rules for impounding and penalty adjudication of insufficiently stamped documents, and established the fundamental evidentiary rule (Section 35) barring the admission in evidence or registration of instruments not duly stamped.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

● Formulation - Drafted by the Finance and Legislative Departments of the Government of India, incorporating recommendations from provincial revenue administrations, High Court decisions, and Chambers of Commerce to replace the 1879 Act.

● Parliamentary Passage - Introduced as The Indian Stamp Bill, 1898 in the Council of the Governor General of India for the purpose of making Laws and Regulations, referred to a Select Committee for detailed clause-by-clause scrutiny, and passed in January 1899.

● Governor-General's Assent - Received the assent of the Governor-General of India (Lord Curzon) on January 27, 1899.

● Enforcement - Brought into force on July 1, 1899 (pursuant to Section 1(3) of the Act).

Sources - Official Records of the Council of the Governor General of India, India Code, and Ministry of Finance.

Summary of the Energy Conservation Act, 2001 

Key Provisions
1.	Central Authority and National Jurisdiction
•	Bureau of Energy Efficiency (BEE): Established under Section 3, operating under central government oversight.
•	National Energy Efficiency Enforcement: Central Government's role in setting and enforcing national energy efficiency norms.
2.	State Jurisdiction and Powers
•	State-Level Enforcement: Under Section 15, states are empowered to enforce energy conservation within their territorial boundaries.
•	State Energy Conservation Fund: Each state manages its fund for local initiatives, highlighting decentralized financial authority.
3.	Shared and Overlapping Jurisdictions
4.	Designated Consumers and Energy Audits: While the designation of consumers is a national standard, the oversight and audit enforcement can involve both central and state authorities.
5.	Energy Efficiency Standards: National standards apply, but states may enforce additional, stricter regulations within their jurisdictions.
6.	Regulatory Framework Across Jurisdictions
•	Central Government Rules: Apply uniformly across India, covering national energy policies.
•	State Government Rules: Allow for tailored regulations to address local energy conservation needs.
7.	Bureau’s Regulations: Operate within the national framework, with potential for state-specific adaptations.

meta.dc.legislation.history:
Legislative History:

The Geographical Indications of Goods (Registration and Protection) Act, 1999

Short Title The Geographical Indications of Goods (Registration and Protection) Act, 1999

Act Number / Year 48 of 1999

Act ID (India Code) 199948

Presidential Assent / Enactment Date December 30, 1999

Enforcement Date September 15, 2003

Nodal Ministry Ministry of Commerce and Industry

Precedent & Statutory Rationale

• Vulnerability of Indigenous Products to Misappropriation:

o Prior to 1999, India lacked a specific statutory registration and protection mechanism for geographical indications (such as Darjeeling Tea, Pochampally Ikat, or Kanchipuram Silk).

o This legislative gap left unique agricultural, natural, and manufactured goods originating from specific geographical regions vulnerable to counterfeiting, unfair competition, and misappropriation by domestic and international entities without safeguarding the economic interests of local artisan and farming communities.

• Legislative Intervention and Regularization:

o Enacted to comply with India's obligations under the World Trade Organization's Trade-Related Aspects of Intellectual Property Rights (TRIPS) Agreement, which mandates the protection of geographical indications to prevent unfair trade practices.

o The core objective was to provide for the registration and better protection of geographical indications relating to goods, prevent the unauthorized use of registered indications by third parties, secure legal remedies for infringement, and preserve the unique reputation tied to a region's heritage, soil, climate, or traditional craftsmanship.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

• Formulation: Framed by the Central Government as part of a sweeping modernization of India's intellectual property rights regime (alongside reforms to trademark, patent, and copyright laws) following global trade agreements.

title: The Semiconductor Integrated Circuits Layout-Design Act, 2000

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of the Semiconductor Integrated Circuit Layout-Design Act, 2000
Key Provisions  
1.	Definitions (Section 2)
•	Layout-Design: A layout of transistors and other circuitry elements in a semiconductor integrated circuit. 
•	Commercial Exploitation: Selling, leasing, offering for sale, or distributing for commercial purposes.
•	 Registered Proprietor: The person entered in the register as the proprietor of the layout-design.
2.	Registration Process (Sections 8-14)
Application: By the creator in the prescribed manner to the Registrar.
Filing: At the appropriate Semiconductor Integrated Circuits Layout-Design Registry office based on the applicant's location.
Advertisement: Of the application after acceptance.
Opposition: Allowed within three months of advertisement, with a counter-statement required from the applicant.
Registration: Upon successful opposition process or lack thereof, with a certificate issued.
Duration: Registration is for 10 years from the date of application filing or first commercial exploitation, whichever is earlier.
3. Conditions of Registration (Section 7)
*Originality: The layout-design must be original, not commonly known, and the result of the creator's intellectual efforts. *Non-Prior Commercial Exploitation: Except for up to two years before application in India or a convention country. *Distinctiveness: Must be inherently distinctive and distinguishable from other registered layouts.
4. Effects of Registration (Section 16-18)
Exclusive Rights: The registered proprietor has exclusive rights to use the layout-design and seek relief for infringement. 
Infringement: Defined as reproducing, importing, selling, or distributing without permission, with exceptions for scientific evaluation, analysis, research, or teaching.
5. Offences, Penalties, and Procedure (Sections 56-62)
•	Infringement Penalty: Up to 3 years imprisonment, or a fine of ₹50,000 to ₹10,000,000, or both. 
•	Falsely Representing Registration: Up to 6 months imprisonment, or a fine up to ₹50,000, or both. 
•	Forfeiture of Goods: Court may direct forfeiture of goods used in the commission of an offence.
•	Exemptions and Procedures: For certain employees, and procedures for pleading invalid registration.
6. Appellate and Judicial Procedures (Sections 52-55)
Appellate Board: Established under the Act, with transitional provisions until its setup, the Intellectual Property Appellate Board (under the Trade Marks Act, 1999) exercises jurisdiction. 
Appeals to High Court: Against decisions of the Appellate Board, with the High Court having the power to make rules.

Precedent & Statutory Rationale

• Gaps in Support Systems for Severe and Developmental Disabilities:

o Prior to 1999, existing disability frameworks (such as the Persons with Disabilities Act, 1995) focused primarily on physical and sensory impairments, leaving a severe institutional void for persons with autism, cerebral palsy, mental retardation, and multiple disabilities.

o Families of individuals with severe developmental disabilities faced intense vulnerability regarding long-term care, legal guardianship, residential support, and financial security after the demise or incapacitation of parents or primary caregivers.

• Legislative Intervention and Regularization:

o Enacted to set up a national corporate body—The National Trust—equipped with statutory powers to protect and promote the rights of persons with specific developmental and multiple disabilities.

o The core objective was to provide legal guardianship through local-level committees, promote independent living, facilitate the creation of residential group homes and care centers, and financially support registered non-governmental organizations working for the welfare of severely disabled individuals.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

• Formulation: Framed by the Central Government following extensive consultations with disability rights advocates, parents' associations, and social welfare organizations to address the safety nets required for profoundly disabled citizens.

• Parliamentary Passage: Passed by both houses of Parliament, receiving formal presidential assent on December 30, 1999.

• Enforcement: Enforced on December 30.

Precedent & Historical Rationale

Modernization and Consolidation of Intellectual Property Laws:

Prior to this enactment, industrial designs in India were governed by the outdated The Patents and Designs Act, 1911. With rapid economic globalization, advancements in industrial design, and changing technological landscapes, the old law became inadequate to address modern standards of design protection and piracy prevention.

The absence of updated provisions hindered effective safeguards for creators regarding the shape, configuration, pattern, or ornament applied to manufactured articles, creating a need for a comprehensive and independent legal framework.

Creation of a Robust Legal and Registration Regime:

The legislative intent centered on repealing the 1911 Act in relation to designs to establish a self-contained, modern statute that aligns with international intellectual property trends, broadens the definition of designs, expands scope for protection, enhances penalties for infringement, and simplifies the registration process.

Drafted and introduced by the Ministry of Commerce and Industry to overhaul and modernize the legal regime governing industrial designs, aligning domestic law with international practices and strengthening enforcement mechanisms.

ACT NO. 29 OF 1981

[11th September, 1981.]

meta.dc.legislation.history:
Legislative History:

The British India Corporation Limited (Acquisition of Shares) Act, 1981

● Presidential Assent Date - September 11, 1981

● Enforcement Date - June 11, 1981

● Nodal Ministry - Ministry of Textiles

Precedent & Historical Rationale

● Nationalisation of Historical Textile Conglomerate - The British India Corporation (BIC) Limited, Kanpur, was a premier colonial-era industrial conglomerate controlling major woolen and cotton textile mills, including Cawnpore Woollen Mills (Lalimli) and New Egerton Woollen Mills (Dhariwal). Financial mismanagement, mounting debts, and severe operational sickness threatened the total collapse of these manufacturing centers.

● Public Investment Protection & Worker Rehabilitation - Prior to 1981, the Central Government and public financial institutions already held a significant minority stake in the corporation. To prevent liquidation, protect the employment of thousands of textile workers, secure national wool manufacture capacity, and enable direct state capital infusion for modernization, the Act provided for the compulsory acquisition of all privately held shares, turning BIC into a wholly owned Central Public Sector Undertaking (CPSU).

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

● Parliamentary Passage - Debated and passed by both Houses of Parliament (Seventh Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha) during the monsoon session in August–September 1981.

● Presidential Assent - Received Presidential Assent on September 11, 1981.

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of the National Security Guard Act, 1986
The National Security Guard (NSG) Act, 1986 was enacted to provide for the constitution and regulation of the National Security Guard (NSG), a specialised armed force of the Union established to combat terrorist activities and protect the nation against internal security threats. The Act was enacted on 22 September 1986 and came into force on 16 October 1986. 
1. Objective
The Act aims to:
•	Constitute the National Security Guard as a specialised armed force of the Union. 
•	Combat terrorism and counter hijacking, hostage situations, and other high-risk operations. 
•	Assist in protecting States against internal disturbances. 
•	Regulate the service conditions, discipline, and administration of NSG personnel. 
2. Constitution of the National Security Guard (Sections 3–5)
•	The Act specifies the persons who are subject to it and formally establishes the National Security Guard. 
•	The NSG functions under the Central Government and is headed by a Director-General. 
•	The Central Government exercises overall control, direction, and administration of the Force. 
3. Service Conditions
The Act contains provisions relating to:
•	Appointment and tenure of members. 
•	Liability for service, including service outside India where authorised. 
•	Resignation and termination of service. 
•	Dismissal, removal, or reduction in rank. 
•	Restrictions on forming associations, participating in political activities, and certain aspects of freedom of speech to maintain discipline. 
4. Discipline and Offences
The Act prescribes offences specific to NSG personnel, including:
•	Mutiny. 
•	Desertion. 
•	Absence without leave. 
•	Disobedience of lawful commands. 
•	Assault or insubordination towards superior officers. 
•	Ill-treatment of subordinates. 
•	Drunkenness while on duty. 
•	Conduct prejudicial to good order and discipline. 
5. Punishments
Depending on the nature of the offence, punishments may include:
•	Death (for specified grave offences). 
•	Imprisonment. 
•	Dismissal or removal from service. 
•	Reduction in rank. 
•	Detention, forfeiture of pay, or other disciplinary punishments authorised by the Act. 
6. Security Guard Courts
The Act establishes three types of Security Guard Courts to try offences committed by persons subject to the Act:
•	General Security Guard Court 
•	Petty Security Guard Court 
•	Summary Security Guard Court

meta.dc.legislation.history:
Legislative History:

The National Security Guard Act, 1986

Act Title - The National Security Guard Act, 1986

Act Number/Year - 47 of 1986

Act ID (India Code) - 198647

Presidential Assent Date - September 22, 1986

Enforcement Date - October 16, 1986

Nodal Ministry - Ministry of Home Affairs

Precedent & Historical Rationale

Rising Terrorism and the Need for a Specialized Counter-Terror Force:

During the early and mid-1980s, India faced an unprecedented surge in violent militancy, cross-border terrorism, and high-risk internal security threats (including high-profile hostage crises and airplane hijackings) that exceeded the operational capabilities of standard civil police and regular paramilitary forces. The government recognized the critical necessity for a specialized, highly trained, and agile federal contingency force capable of rapid response to acts of terrorism and internal disturbances.

Creation of the "Black Cats":

To provide a dedicated legal mandate, disciplinary framework, and clear command structure for this elite force—popularly known as the Black Cats—Parliament enacted the National Security Guard Act, 1986. This statute formally established and governed the National Security Guard (NSG) as a federal strike force designed exclusively for counter-terrorism and counter-hijacking operations across the country.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

Formulation:

Drafted by the Ministry of Home Affairs to provide for the constitution, regulation, discipline, and command structure of the National Security Guard, modeling its legal framework and penal provisions similarly to other premier central armed police and defense statutes.

Precedent & Historical Rationale

Rapid Urbanization and Vertical Housing Growth:

During the 1970s and 1980s, the Union Territory of Delhi experienced massive demographic expansion, leading to a severe scarcity of land and a rapid shift from traditional independent horizontal housing to multi-storied apartment complexes and group housing societies.

Legal Gaps in Ownership Rights and Common Areas:

Prior to this enactment, property laws in Delhi lacked a dedicated legal framework to govern multi-story ownership structures. Individual apartment buyers faced deep legal ambiguities regarding the clear title of their specific units, undivided interests in common areas and facilities (such as stairs, elevators, corridors, and compounds), formation of apartment owners' associations, and liability for common expenses and maintenance. To protect apartment buyers from exploitation by builders and to provide heritable and transferable clear titles for individual units alongside shared management structures, Parliament enacted this dedicated regulatory statute.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

Formulation:

Drafted by the Ministry of Works and Housing (now Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs) to provide statutory recognition for individual apartment ownership, define common areas and facilities, mandate the execution and registration of declarations by property owners, and outline provisions for the creation of associations of apartment owners to manage common affairs.

Parliamentary Passage:

Introduced, deliberated, and passed by both Houses of Parliament (Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha) during the winter session of 1986.

Presidential Assent: Received Presidential Assent on December 16, 1986.

Enforcement: Enforced on September 15, 1987.

Precedent & Historical Rationale

Industrial Distress and Mismanagement:

Prior to the mid-1980s, the textile undertakings belonging to the Swadeshi Cotton Mills Company Limited suffered from severe operational mismanagement, financial distress, and accumulating liabilities. This led to widespread closures or under-production, threatening large-scale unemployment for thousands of textile workers and causing a severe shortage in the production and distribution of controlled varieties of cloth vital to the general public.

Government Intervention and Public Interest:

To protect the interests of workers, prevent economic disruption, and secure the proper management and revitalization of the sick textile undertakings, the Central Government had previously taken over management control. To provide a permanent statutory footing, nationalize the undertakings, vest them securely under the National Textile Corporation (NTC), and ensure the continued manufacture and distribution of essential textiles, Parliament enacted the formal acquisition legislation.

Formulation:

Drafted by the Ministry of Textiles to supersede preceding emergency ordinances, formally providing for the acquisition and transfer of certain textile undertakings of Swadeshi Cotton Mills Company Limited, vesting them in the Central Government and subsequently transferring them to the National Textile Corporation, alongside provisions for settling prior claims and compensating the company.

Parliamentary Passage:

Introduced and passed by both Houses of Parliament (Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha) during the budget session of 1986 to replace the Swadeshi Cotton Mills Company Limited (Acquisition and Transfer of Undertakings) Ordinance, 1986.

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of The State of Mizoram Act, 1986:
Key Objectives:
1.	Establishment: Establish the State of Mizoram.
2.	Territorial Composition: Comprise territories of the existing Union territory of Mizoram.
3.	Governance & Legislative Framework: Outline the initial governance, legislative assembly setup, and legal continuance/adaptations.
Summary Points:
1.	Establishment of Mizoram: - Section 3: Establishes Mizoram as a new State from the appointed day, comprising the existing Union territory of Mizoram.
2.	Legislative Assembly: - Section 10: The Legislative Assembly of Mizoram to have 40 seats, filled by direct election.
•	Section 11: Delimitation of constituencies by the Election Commission, considering geographical compactness, administrative boundaries, and Scheduled Tribes population concentration.
3.	Governance & Administration:
•	Definitions (Section 2): Defines key terms including "Administrator", "appointed day", and "law".
•	Section 29: Allowances and privileges of the Governor of Mizoram to be determined by the President until Parliament legislates otherwise.
•	Section 30: The President to determine grants-in-aid and Mizoram's share in Union duties.
4.	Legal & Financial Provisions:
•	Section 43: Continuance of existing laws in Mizoram until altered or repealed.
•	Section 44: Empowers courts, tribunals, and authorities to construe laws for application in Mizoram if necessary adaptations aren’t made.
•	Sections 27 & 28: Authorisation of expenditure and management of financial accounts transition.
5.	Judicial & Electoral:
•	Election Commission’s Role: Delimitation of constituencies and associated processes.
•	Implications for Judicial Bodies: Though detailed amendments to other acts (e.g., Manipur, Tripura Courts Orders) are provided, direct implications on Mizoram’s judicial setup aren’t explicitly summarized here due to the focus on the State of Mizoram Act, 1986, itself.

Act Number/Year - 34 of 1986

Presidential Assent Date - August 14, 1986

Enforcement Date - February 20, 1987

Nodal Ministry - Ministry of Home Affairs

Precedent & Historical Rationale

The Mizo Insurgency and the Historic Mizoram Accord:

For decades following Indian independence, the region of Mizoram—initially part of Assam as the Mizo Hills district and later transformed into a Union Territory under the North-Eastern Areas (Reorganisation) Act, 1971—witnessed deep political unrest and an armed insurgency led by the Mizo National Front (MNF) demanding sovereignty. Following prolonged negotiations between the Government of India and the MNF leadership, the historic Mizoram Peace Accord was signed on June 30, 1986, bringing an end to two decades of conflict.

Fulfillment of Constitutional Aspirations:

As a core commitment under the Accord to restore lasting peace, democracy, and normal political life, the Central Government agreed to confer full statehood upon the Union Territory of Mizoram. This necessitated a formal constitutional amendment (the Constitution (Fifty-third Amendment) Act, 1986) alongside this specific reorganisation statute to establish Mizoram as the 23rd State of the Indian Union with its own Legislative Assembly.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

Formulation:

Drafted by the Ministry of Home Affairs to provide for the establishment of the State of Mizoram by separating the territories of the existing Union Territory of Mizoram, detailing provisions for a bicameral or unicameral legislative assembly, allocation of seats in Parliament, distribution of assets, liabilities, financial adjustments, and representation of judicial and administrative machinery.

Parliamentary Passage:

Introduced, debated, and passed by both Houses of Parliament (Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha) during the monsoon session of August 1986 alongside the corresponding constitutional amendment bill.

Presidential Assent:

Received Presidential Assent on August 14, 1986.

Enforcement: Enforced on February 20, 1987.

Source: Official Records of Parliament, India Code, and Ministry of Home Affairs.

Precedent & Historical Rationale

Diversification and Promotion of Agricultural Exports:

Prior to the mid-1980s, India’s export framework heavily emphasized traditional commodities, while potential high-value segments like processed foods, fruits, vegetables, meat products, and poultry lacked an organized, dedicated export promotion council or statutory board. The export of agricultural items was governed largely by fragmented institutional setups that could not adequately address modern quality control, packaging standards, or market research needs.

Transition from Processed Food Export Promotion Council:

Recognizing the shifting global trade environment and the vital need to boost foreign exchange earnings through value-added agricultural exports, the government felt it necessary to replace the old Processed Foods Export Promotion Council with a powerful, statutory apex board. This led to the conception of the Agricultural and Processed Food Products Export Development Authority (APEDA) to systematically handle market intelligence, quality standardization, and infrastructure development for scheduled agro-products.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

Formulation:

Drafted by the Ministry of Commerce to establish a statutory authority tasked with developing, promoting, and regulating the export of specific scheduled agricultural and processed food items, alongside setting up a dedicated export development fund.

Parliamentary Passage:

Introduced and deliberated through both Houses of Parliament in late 1985, securing formal enactment heading into the new year.

Precedent & Historical Rationale

Proliferation of Objectifying Media:

Prior to the mid-1980s, the rapid expansion of print media, advertisements, billboards, and cinema saw an increasing trend of portraying women in an overtly derogatory, explicit, and indecent manner. Existing laws, such as general provisions under the Indian Penal Code (like obscenity under Section 292), were found to be broad, reactive, and insufficient to deal specifically with the commercial exploitation and objectification of women's figures and bodies in public media.

Social Advocacy and Legislative Intent:

Responding to persistent demands from women's rights organizations, social reformers, and public opinion, the government recognized that indecent representation undermines human dignity, promotes voyeurism, and negatively impacts societal attitudes toward gender equality. Consequently, Parliament enacted a specialized statute to outrightly ban the indecent representation of women through advertisements, publications, writings, paintings, figures, or any other media.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

Formulation:

Drafted by the government to establish clear statutory definitions prohibiting advertisements, publications, and public displays that contain indecent depictions of women, while empowering law enforcement authorities to search premises, seize offending material, and impose stringent penalties and imprisonment for violations.

Parliamentary Passage:

Introduced, debated, and passed by both Houses of Parliament (Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha) during the winter session of 1986.

Presidential Assent: Received Presidential Assent on December 23, 1986.

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of the Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act, 1976
Objective
The Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act, 1976 was enacted to abolish the bonded labour system, prevent the economic and physical exploitation of weaker sections of society, and free bonded labourers from debt bondage. The Act also provides for their rehabilitation and the enforcement of measures to eliminate bonded labour throughout India. 
Key Provisions
•	Abolition of Bonded Labour: Abolishes the bonded labour system and declares all forms of bonded labour illegal. 
•	Extinguishment of Bonded Debt: Cancels all bonded debts, and bonded labourers are no longer liable to repay such debts. 
•	Void Agreements: Declares all agreements, customs, or practices requiring bonded labour to be void and unenforceable. 
•	Protection of Freed Labourers: Protects freed bonded labourers from eviction from their homesteads or other residential premises provided under the bonded labour system. 
•	Implementing Authorities and Vigilance Committees: Provides for the appointment of implementing authorities and the constitution of Vigilance Committees at the district and sub-divisional levels to identify, release, rehabilitate, and protect bonded labourers. 
•	Offences and Penalties: Prescribes imprisonment and fines for compelling any person to render bonded labour or for enforcing bonded debt. 
•	Overriding Effect: Gives the Act overriding effect over any inconsistent law, custom, contract, or agreement relating to bonded labour.

● Abolition of Debt Bondage & Feudal Servitude - Formulated to abolish the centuries-old custom of bonded labor (Kamiuti, Gothi, Vetti, etc.), under which impoverished individuals and marginalized communities were forced to provide labor or service to creditors without wages or at nominal rates to liquidate inherited or nominal advances/debts. meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of the Disturbed Areas (Special Courts) Act, 1976
Objective
The Disturbed Areas (Special Courts) Act, 1976 was enacted to provide for the speedy trial of specified offences committed in areas declared as "disturbed areas." The Act aims to ensure the prompt administration of criminal justice in regions affected by serious disturbances by establishing Special Courts with exclusive jurisdiction over notified offences. 
Key Provisions
•	Declaration of Disturbed Areas: Empowers the Central Government to declare any area as a disturbed area where the use of criminal force or violence by groups or bodies of persons creates a grave public order situation. 
•	Establishment of Special Courts: Provides for the constitution of Special Courts to conduct the speedy trial of scheduled offences committed in disturbed areas. 
•	Exclusive Jurisdiction: Confers exclusive jurisdiction on Special Courts to try offences specified in the Schedule that arise out of or are connected with disturbances in the notified area. 
•	Special Procedure and Powers: Authorises Special Courts to follow expedited procedures while exercising powers under the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, to ensure prompt disposal of cases. 
•	Transfer of Cases: Empowers the appropriate authority to transfer cases from Special Courts to ordinary criminal courts where considered necessary. 
•	Appeals and Revisions: Provides for appeals and revision of judgments and orders passed by Special Courts in accordance with the Act. 
•	Overriding Effect: Gives the Act overriding effect over inconsistent provisions of other laws to ensure effective implementation in disturbed areas.

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of the Interest Act, 1978
1. Objective
•	To enable courts to award interest on debts or damages for the period before a lawsuit is filed (pre-suit interest), in appropriate cases. 
•	To ensure fairness by compensating a person who has been deprived of money that was due to them. 
2. Scope
•	Applies throughout India. 
•	Covers proceedings before courts and certain tribunals or arbitrators that function like courts. 
3. Key Definitions
•	Court: Includes tribunals and arbitrators in specified circumstances. 
•	Current rate of interest: The highest of the maximum lending rates of scheduled banks as notified according to the Act. 
4. Power of Courts to Award Interest
A court may award interest if:
•	A debt or a specific sum of money was payable at a certain time. 
•	The payment was wrongfully withheld. 
•	There is no contractual or statutory provision governing interest. 
•	Interest is awarded at a rate not exceeding the current rate of interest. 
5. Interest Before Institution of Suit
Interest may be awarded:
•	From the date the debt became payable until the date the suit is filed. 
•	If the amount is payable by virtue of a written instrument, from the date specified in the instrument. 
•	In other cases, from the date a written notice demanding payment is served, provided the notice states that interest will be claimed. 
6. Saving of Existing Rights
The Act does not affect:
•	Any right to recover interest under a contract. 
•	Interest payable under any other law. 
•	The powers of courts under other statutes, such as the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (particularly Section 34 regarding interest after the institution of a suit).

title: The Parliamentary Proceedings (Protection of Publication) Act, 1977

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of the Parliamentary Proceedings (Protection of Publication) Act, 1977
Objective
The Parliamentary Proceedings (Protection of Publication) Act, 1977 was enacted to protect the publication of substantially true reports of the proceedings of Parliament. The Act ensures that newspapers, news agencies, and broadcasting organisations can report parliamentary proceedings without fear of civil or criminal liability, provided such publication is made in good faith, is substantially accurate, and is in the public interest. It restored the protection that had been withdrawn during the Emergency. 
Key Provisions
•	Protection for Publication: Grants immunity from civil or criminal proceedings for publishing a substantially true report of the proceedings of either House of Parliament, unless the publication is proved to have been made with malice. 
•	Public Good Limitation: The protection does not extend to the publication of any matter that is not for the public good. 
•	Definition of Newspaper: Defines "newspaper" to include any printed periodical containing public news or comments on public news, and includes news agencies supplying material for publication. 
•	Broadcast Coverage: Extends the same legal protection to reports of parliamentary proceedings broadcast by wireless telegraphy (now applicable to broadcasting services). 
•	Retrospective Commencement: The Act was enacted on 18 April 1977 but is deemed to have come into force retrospectively from 25 March 1977.

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of the High Court at Patna (Establishment of a Permanent Bench at Ranchi) Act, 1976
Objective
The High Court at Patna (Establishment of a Permanent Bench at Ranchi) Act, 1976 was enacted to establish a permanent Bench of the Patna High Court at Ranchi. The Act aimed to improve access to justice for litigants in the Chotanagpur region by enabling the Bench to exercise the jurisdiction of the Patna High Court over specified districts. 
Key Provisions
•	Establishment of Permanent Bench: Establishes a permanent Bench of the Patna High Court at Ranchi. 
•	Appointment of Judges: Provides that not less than three Judges of the Patna High Court, nominated by the Chief Justice, shall sit at the Ranchi Bench. 
•	Territorial Jurisdiction: Confers jurisdiction on the Ranchi Bench over cases arising from the districts of Hazaribagh, Giridih, Dhanbad, Ranchi, Palamau, and Singhbhum. 
•	Power of the Chief Justice: Empowers the Chief Justice of the Patna High Court to direct that any case or class of cases arising from these districts may instead be heard at Patna. 
•	Exercise of High Court Powers: Authorises the Ranchi Bench to exercise the same jurisdiction and powers as the Patna High Court in respect of matters within its territorial jurisdiction.

Precedent & Historical Rationale

● Geographic Isolation and Inaccessibility of Patna for the Chota Nagpur Region - Prior to 1976, litigants and advocates residing in the mineral-rich, predominantly tribal southern districts of Bihar (the Chota Nagpur Division and Santhal Parganas) faced severe hardship, high travel costs, and prolonged travel times to access the principal seat of the High Court at Patna. Although a temporary circuit bench had operated periodically at Ranchi under Clause 36 of the Letters Patent of the Patna High Court, it lacked continuity, permanent judicial infrastructure, and the capacity to handle the growing volume of local writ petitions and appeals.

● Statutory Establishment of a Permanent High Court Bench at Ranchi - Formulated to provide for the establishment of a permanent bench of the High Court of Judicature at Patna at Ranchi to serve the southern districts of Bihar. The Act statutorily mandated that not less than three judges of the Patna High Court would sit permanently at Ranchi, conferred exclusive territorial jurisdiction over matters arising in the districts of the Chota Nagpur Division (and adjoining notified areas), and empowered the Chief Justice to transfer cases between Patna and Ranchi to ensure the efficient administration of justice (a bench that subsequently became the seat of the Jharkhand High Court in 2000).

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

● Formulation - Drafted and introduced by the Union Minister of Law and Justice in Parliament to fulfill the long-standing demand for a permanent High Court bench in southern Bihar and improve access to justice for the tribal and industrial populace of Chota Nagpur.

● Presidential Assent - Received the assent of the President of India on April 8, 1976.

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of the National Service Act, 1972
Objective
The National Service Act, 1972 was enacted to provide for the registration of qualified persons (doctors and engineers) and to require them, when necessary, to render national service in the Armed Forces or other services of national importance. The Act also provides for enlistment, training, postponement on grounds of hardship, reinstatement after service, and related matters. 
Key Provisions
•	Liability for National Service: Makes qualified doctors and engineers below 30 years of age liable to be called for national service for a period of up to four years. 
•	Registration and Enlistment: Requires eligible persons to register in the National Service Register and empowers the Central Government to issue enlistment notices after assessing their physical and mental fitness. 
•	Service and Training: Empowers the Central Government to assign qualified persons to the Armed Forces or other notified national services and require them to undergo training. 
•	Hardship Relief: Establishes a National Service (Hardship) Committee to consider applications for postponement of national service on grounds of exceptional hardship, with a right of appeal to the High Court on substantial questions of law. 
•	Protection of Employees: Provides for payment of salary, allowances, and other benefits during national service and guarantees reinstatement in the former employment after completion of service, subject to the Act. 
•	Offences and Penalties: Prescribes penalties for failure to render national service, making false statements, forgery, and other violations of the Act. 
•	Rule-making Power: Empowers the Central Government to make rules and regulations for carrying out the provisions of the Act.

Precedent & Statutory Rationale

1. Mobilizing Skilled Professional Talent for National Needs:

o In the wake of intense geopolitical developments and national security pressures in the early 1970s, the Government of India sought a formal statutory mechanism to ensure that highly trained technical professionals could be legally registered and systematically called upon to support defense, civil defense, and critical public infrastructure.

o The core policy intent was to mandate that young citizens possessing critical technical skills contribute directly to national defense or essential public services for a designated term.

2. Core Statutory Scope and Target Demographics:

o Definition of "Qualified Persons": The Act targeted Indian citizens ordinarily residing in India under the age of 30 who held recognized medical qualifications (under the Indian Medical Council Act, 1956) or university degrees/equivalent qualifications in engineering or technology.

o Registration and Conscription Framework: Mandated eligible professionals to register in a National Service Register. It empowered the Central Government to issue enlistment notices requiring qualified individuals to render national service either within the Armed Forces of the Union or in other designated civil/social national service roles.

o Protections and Safeguards: Included provisions for National Service (Hardship) Committees to review postponement applications, regulated employer release obligations, and set parameters for wages, service continuity, and post-service reinstatement.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

• Formulation: Drafted to pilot a universal civic-military readiness framework targeting specialized medical and technical graduates.

• Parliamentary Passage: Tabled, debated, and passed by both Houses of Parliament, receiving Presidential Assent on June 9, 1972.

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of the North-Eastern Hill University Act, 1973
Objective
The North-Eastern Hill University Act, 1973 was enacted to establish and incorporate the North-Eastern Hill University (NEHU) for the advancement and dissemination of knowledge in the North-Eastern region of India. The Act aims to promote higher education, research, and regional development through a Central University. 
Key Provisions
•	Establishment of the University: Establishes the North-Eastern Hill University (NEHU) as a Central University with perpetual succession and a common seal. 
•	Powers and Functions: Empowers the University to provide instruction, conduct research, confer degrees, establish colleges and institutions, and promote higher education in the North-Eastern region. 
•	University Authorities: Provides for authorities such as the Visitor, Chancellor, Vice-Chancellor, Court, Executive Council, Academic Council, Finance Committee, and Planning Board to administer the University. 
•	Academic Administration: Authorises the establishment of Schools of Studies, Departments, Boards of Studies, and Committees for academic planning, teaching, and research. 
•	Appointments and Service Conditions: Prescribes the appointment, powers, duties, and service conditions of the Vice-Chancellor, teachers, officers, and other employees of the University. 
•	Affiliation and Student Welfare: Provides for admission of colleges and institutions to the privileges of the University, regulation of examinations, discipline, scholarships, and welfare of students. 
•	Finance and Rule-making: Provides for the University's finances, accounts, audit, statutes, ordinances, regulations, and empowers the Central Government and University authorities to frame rules for effective administration.

1. Rationale & Context: Prior to 1973, higher education infrastructure in the northeastern region of India was sparse, and existing institutions struggled to meet the specialized developmental, linguistic, and cultural needs of the diverse tribal and hill communities.

2. The Legislative Problem: The unique geopolitical and socioeconomic landscape of the northeastern hill areas required an academic institution specifically structured to foster regional intellectual growth without diluting local cultural identities, which ordinary state universities or distant mainland institutions could not adequately provide.

3. The Remedy: Pursuant to resolutions passed by the Legislatures of the States of Meghalaya and Nagaland under Article 252(1) of the Constitution, Parliament enacted the North-Eastern Hill University Act, 1973. This established a central teaching and affiliating university designed to accelerate social and economic welfare through targeted higher education and research across the hill regions.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

● Formulation: Conceived as a landmark federal initiative to promote regional equity in higher education across the northeastern states and Union Territories, requiring formal state-level enabling resolutions under constitutional provisions for centralized legislation

● Parliamentary Passage: Tabled and debated in both Houses of Parliament during the early part of 1973 to fulfill federal commitments toward educational expansion in the northeast.

● Presidential Assent:Received assent from the President of India on May 26, 1973, and was brought into force via official notification on July 19, 1973 .

● Enforcement: Enforced on July 19, 1973.

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summay of The General Insurance Business (Nationalisation) Act, 1972
Objective
The General Insurance Business (Nationalisation) Act, 1972 was enacted to nationalise the general insurance business in India and reorganize it to serve the needs of the economy and the public. The Act aimed to ensure the orderly growth of the insurance sector, protect policyholders' interests, and promote the development of general insurance under public ownership and control.
Key Provisions
•	Nationalisation of General Insurance: Provides for the acquisition and transfer of the shares of Indian insurance companies engaged in general insurance business to the Central Government. 
•	General Insurance Corporation (GIC): Establishes the General Insurance Corporation of India (GIC) as the holding company to supervise and manage the nationalised general insurance business. 
•	Transfer and Reorganisation: Provides for the transfer, merger, and restructuring of insurance companies into Government-owned entities for efficient management. 
•	Management and Administration: Vests the management of nationalised insurance companies in Government-appointed Boards and provides for their administration and supervision. 
•	Protection of Employees: Safeguards the service conditions, salaries, and other benefits of employees affected by nationalisation. 
•	Accounts and Audit: Prescribes provisions relating to the maintenance of accounts, audit, annual reports, and submission of financial statements. 
•	Rule-making Power: Empowers the Central Government to make rules and the Corporation to frame regulations for implementing the provisions of the Act.

Precedent & Statutory Rationale

1. Social Control and Consolidation of Economic Resources:

o Following the nationalization of life insurance in 1956 through the Life Insurance Corporation Act, the general insurance sector remained under private ownership and control. By the early 1970s, the government identified widespread malpractices, unhealthy competition, siphoning of funds, and a lack of adequate insurance coverage for rural and weaker sections of society among private general insurers.

o To serve socio-economic objectives, mobilize public savings for national development, and ensure risk protection across all sectors of the economy, the government promulgated an ordinance in May 1972, which was subsequently enacted into this permanent statute.

2. Core Structural Innovations of the 1972 Act:

o Acquisition and Transfer: Provided for the acquisition and transfer of shares of Indian general insurance companies and undertakings of foreign insurers to the Central Government, bringing them under public ownership.

o Creation of the General Insurance Corporation (GIC): Established the General Insurance Corporation of India (GIC) as a government company to superintend, control, and carry on general insurance business.

o Restructuring into Subsidiary Companies: Initially amalgamated over 100 private entities and subsequently organized them into four major public sector subsidiary companies:

 National Insurance Company Limited

 The New India Assurance Company Limited

 The Oriental Insurance Company Limited

 The United India Insurance Company Limited

o Subsequent Reforms (2000 Amendment): Restructured GIC's operational mandate to transition it exclusively into a national reinsurer (GIC Re), while severing the statutory links between GIC and the four subsidiary companies, thereby paving the way for the re-opening of the general insurance sector to private and foreign competition following recommendations of the Malhotra Committee.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

• Formulation: Drafted and piloted by the Ministry of Finance to execute a major socialist economic reform under the Indira Gandhi administration.

• Parliamentary Passage: Tabled, debated, and passed by both Houses of Parliament, receiving Presidential Assent on September 20, 1972.

• Enforcement: Enforced on September 20, 1972.

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of the  Architects Act, 1972
Objective
The Architects Act, 1972 was enacted to regulate the architectural profession in India by providing for the registration of architects, establishing the Council of Architecture (CoA), prescribing standards of architectural education and professional conduct, and preventing unqualified persons from using the title "Architect." 
Key Provisions
•	Council of Architecture (CoA): Establishes the Council of Architecture as the statutory body to regulate the profession and maintain standards of architectural education and practice. 
•	Registration of Architects: Provides for the preparation and maintenance of a Register of Architects. Only persons possessing recognized qualifications and registered under the Act are entitled to be registered. 
•	Recognition of Qualifications: Recognizes architectural qualifications awarded by approved institutions in India and certain foreign institutions, and empowers the Central Government to amend the Schedule of recognized qualifications. 
Standards of Education: Empowers the Council to prescribe minimum standards of architectural education, inspect institutions, and recommend withdrawal of recognition where standards are not maintained. 
•	Professional Conduct: Authorizes the Council to prescribe a code of ethics and inquire into cases of professional misconduct, with powers to reprimand, suspend, or remove architects from the register. 
•	•Protection of Title: Prohibits any unregistered person from using the title "Architect" and prescribes penalties for false representation or unauthorized use of the title. 
•	 Rule and Regulation Making: Empowers the Central Government to make rules and the Council to frame regulations for implementing the Act.

1. Regulating the Architectural Profession and Protecting Public Interest:

o Prior to 1972, there was no comprehensive all-India statutory framework governing the professional practice, title, and educational standards of architects. Anyone could practice architecture or use the title, exposing clients and the public to structural safety risks from unqualified individuals.

o Professional bodies like the Indian Institute of Education and the Indian Institute of Architects (IIA) strongly lobbied for statutory regulation to maintain high educational benchmarks, establish professional ethics, and protect the integrity of the profession.

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of the Delhi School Education Act, 1973
Objective
The Delhi School Education Act, 1973 was enacted to provide for the better organisation, development, regulation, and management of school education in Delhi. It aims to ensure quality education, proper administration of schools, protection of teachers' service conditions, and effective Government supervision over recognized schools. 
Key Provisions
•	Establishment and Recognition of Schools: Regulates the establishment, recognition, management, and grant of aid to schools and prescribes conditions for recognition. 
•	Management of Schools: Requires recognized schools to have an approved scheme of management and empowers the Administrator to regulate school education. 
•	Service Conditions of Employees: Prescribes qualifications, service conditions, pay, disciplinary procedures, and safeguards against arbitrary dismissal of school employees. 
•	Admissions and Fees: Regulates admission of students, school fees, school funds, and financial management of recognized schools. 
•	Delhi School Tribunal: Establishes the Delhi School Tribunal to hear appeals relating to dismissal, removal, or reduction in rank of school employees. 
•	Government Supervision: Empowers the Administrator to inspect schools, withdraw recognition or aid, and, in certain cases, take over the management of schools in the interest of education. 
•	Advisory Board and Rule-making: Provides for the Delhi School Education Advisory Board and empowers the Administrator to make rules for implementing the Act.

title: The Antiquities and Art Treasures Act, 1972

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of The Antiquities and Art Treasures Act, 1972
Objective
The Antiquities and Art Treasures Act, 1972 was enacted to preserve and protect India's cultural heritage by regulating the export, trade, ownership, and movement of antiquities and art treasures. It seeks to prevent the illegal export and trafficking of valuable cultural objects and ensure their conservation in the national interest.
Key Provisions
•	Regulation of Export: Prohibits the export of antiquities and art treasures except in accordance with the provisions of the Act. 
•	Registration of Antiquities: Requires the registration of specified antiquities with the prescribed authority to facilitate their identification and protection. 
•	Licensing of Dealers: Mandates that persons engaged in the business of buying or selling antiquities obtain a licence and comply with prescribed conditions. 
•	Control over Trade: Regulates the sale, purchase, transfer, and possession of antiquities and art treasures to prevent illegal transactions. 
•	Search, Seizure and Confiscation: Empowers authorized officers to inspect premises, search, seize, and confiscate antiquities involved in violations of the Act. 
•	Penalties: Prescribes penalties, including imprisonment and fines, for offences such as illegal export, unlicensed dealing, and contravention of the Act. 
•	Rule-making Power: Empowers the Central Government to make rules for implementing the provisions of the Act.

THE ANTIQUITIES AND ART TREASURES ACT, 1972
ACT NO. 52 OF 1972

[9th September, 1972.]

An Act to regulate the export trade in antiquities and art treasures, to provide for the prevention of smuggling of, and fraudulent dealings in, antiquities, to provide for the compulsory acquisition of antiquities and art treasures for preservation in public places and to provide for certain other matters connected therewith or incidental or ancillary thereto.
BE it enacted by Parliament in the Twenty-third Year of the Republic of India as follows:--

Legislative History: The Antiquities and Art Treasures Act, 1972

Source: India Code (indiacode.gov.in) and Archaeological Survey of India (ASI) / Ministry of Culture Official Records

Key Legislative Metadata

Legislative Stage / Attribute Official Details

Short Title The Antiquities and Art Treasures Act, 1972

Act Number / Year Act No. 52 of 1972

Act ID (India Code) 197252

Presidential Assent / Enactment Date September 9, 1972

Official Gazette Publication September 1972

Enforcement Date April 5, 1976

Administrative Nodal Ministry Ministry of Culture

Precedent & Statutory Rationale

1. Curbing Illegal Smuggling and Protecting Cultural Heritage:

o In the decades following independence, India witnessed a massive surge in the illicit smuggling, theft, and unauthorized export of priceless ancient idols, sculptures, paintings, and historical artifacts from temples, archaeological sites, and private collections to international art markets.

o The earlier Antiquities (Export Control) Act, 1947 proved entirely inadequate because it only regulated exports and lacked mechanisms to track or control internal trade, possession, and movement. To plug these loopholes, protect India's rich cultural heritage from being plundered, and establish strict penal accountability, Parliament enacted the 1972 Act.

2. Core Structural Innovations of the 1972 Act:

o Mandatory Registration of Antiquities: Required all persons who owned, controlled, or possessed "antiquities" (such as sculptures, paintings, and manuscripts older than a prescribed period—generally 100 years, or 75 years for manuscripts) to register them with the registering authority and obtain registration certificates.

o Regulation of Trade and Dealing: Restricted the business of trading in antiquities exclusively to licensed dealers, prohibiting unauthorized private commercial transactions.

o Absolute Export Ban: Imposed a strict statutory prohibition on the export of any antiquity or art treasure by private individuals, allowing exports solely under the authority of the Central Government.

o Compulsory Acquisition: Empowered the Central Government to compulsorily acquire any antiquity or art treasure for preservation in a public museum or institution, ensuring state oversight over rare heritage assets.

o Penal Consequences: Introduced stringent penal provisions—including rigorous imprisonment and heavy fines—for illegal export, smuggling, fraudulent transfers, and failure to register antiquities.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

• Formulation: Drafted and piloted by the Ministry of Education and Social Welfare (under which the Archaeological Survey of India functioned) to fulfill international commitments and curb rampant cultural heritage theft.

• Parliamentary Passage: Tabled, debated, and passed by both Houses of Parliament, receiving Presidential Assent on September 9, 1972.

• Enforcement: Enforced on April 5, 1976.

title: The Delhi Lands (Restrictions on Transfer) Act, 1972

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of the Delhi Lands (Restrictions on Transfer) Act, 1972
Objective
The Delhi Lands (Restrictions on Transfer) Act, 1972 was enacted to prevent the transfer of lands acquired or proposed to be acquired by the Central Government in the Union Territory of Delhi without prior Government permission. The Act aims to curb unauthorized transactions, prevent speculation, and facilitate planned development of Delhi. 
Key Provisions
•	Restriction on Transfer: Prohibits the transfer, sale, gift, mortgage, lease, or any other transfer of land that has been acquired or is proposed to be acquired by the Central Government, except with the previous permission of the competent authority. 
•	Void Transfers: Declares any transfer made in contravention of the Act as null and void, having no legal effect. 
•	Permission by Competent Authority: Empowers the competent authority to grant or refuse permission for transfer, subject to the provisions of the Act. 
•	Penalties: Prescribes penalties for contravention of the Act, including unauthorized transfers of restricted lands. 
•	Protection and Rule-making: Provides protection for actions taken in good faith and empowers the Central Government to make rules for carrying out the provisions of the Act.

ACT NO. 30 OF 1972

[14th June, 1972.]

An Act to impose certain restrictions on transfer of lands which have been acquired by the Central Government or in respect of which acquisition proceedings have been initiated by that Government, with a view to preventing large-scale transactions of purported transfers or, as the case may be, transfers of such lands to unwary public.

Legislative History: The Delhi Lands (Restrictions on Transfer) Act, 1972

Source: India Code (indiacode.gov.in) and Ministry of Home Affairs Official Records

Key Legislative Metadata

Legislative Stage / Attribute Official Details

Short Title The Delhi Lands (Restrictions on Transfer) Act, 1972

Act Number / Year Act No. 30 of 1972

Act ID (India Code) 197230

Introduced In Parliament

Presidential Assent / Enactment Date June 14, 1972

Official Gazette Publication June 1972

Enforcement Date June 14, 1972

Administrative Nodal Ministry Ministry of Home Affairs

Precedent & Statutory Rationale

1. Combating Fraudulent Land Transactions and Protecting Unwary Public:

o Rapid urbanization and planned development in the capital territory during the late 1950s and 1960s triggered widespread land acquisition initiatives by the Central Government under the master plan framework (such as the scheme for "Large Scale Acquisition, Development, and Disposal of Land in Delhi").

o Unscrupulous landowners and speculators frequently attempted to dupe the unwary public by selling, gifting, or mortgaging plots of land that had already been officially acquired by the government or were actively facing acquisition proceedings. To suppress these fraudulent transactions, prevent illegal real estate splintering, and protect buyers from severe financial fraud, Parliament intervened with this dedicated penal statute.

2. Core Statutory Restraints and Regulatory Design:

o Absolute Prohibition on Acquired Lands: Under Section 3, the Act strictly prohibits any person from purporting to transfer (by sale, mortgage, gift, lease, or otherwise) any land that has already been acquired by the Central Government.

o Conditional Regulation on Notified Lands: Under Section 4, transfers of land in respect of which acquisition proceedings have been initiated require prior written permission from a designated Competent Authority.

o Subregistrar Restraints: Under Section 8, registering officers (Sub-registrars) are legally barred from registering any document transferring such restricted lands unless proof of competent authority clearance or non-applicability is established.

o Penal Consequences: Section 9 establishes punitive measures, including imprisonment and fines, for individuals executing illegal transfers in violation of statutory notifications.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

• Formulation: Drafted and piloted by the Ministry of Home Affairs to safeguard public interests and reinforce state control over notified urban development zones in Delhi.

• Parliamentary Passage: Tabled, debated, and passed by both Houses of Parliament, receiving Presidential Assent on June 14, 1972.

• Enforcement: Enforced on June 14, 1972.

title: The Former Secretary of State Service Officers (Conditions of Service) Act, 1972

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of the Former Secretary of State Service Officers (Conditions of Service) Act, 1972
Objective
The Former Secretary of State Service Officers (Conditions of Service) Act, 1972 was enacted to regulate the conditions of service, retirement benefits, pension, leave, disciplinary matters, and other service-related rights of officers belonging to the former Secretary of State's Services after Independence. The Act ensures uniformity and legal certainty regarding their service conditions under the Government of India.
Key Provisions
•	Regulation of Service Conditions: Governs the pay, allowances, leave, pension, provident fund, retirement benefits, and other service conditions of former Secretary of State Service officers. 
•	Continuation of Existing Rights: Protects the service rights and privileges of eligible officers in accordance with the provisions of the Act. 
•	Disciplinary Matters: Prescribes the authority and procedure for disciplinary action, suspension, dismissal, removal, and compulsory retirement of such officers. 
•	Pension and Retirement Benefits: Provides for the grant, regulation, and payment of pension and other retirement benefits. 
•	Rule-making Power: Empowers the Central Government to make rules for carrying out the provisions of the Act. 
•	Repeal and Savings: Repeals the earlier legal provisions governing these officers while saving actions already taken under the previous law.

ACT NO. 59 OF 1972

Source: India Code (indiacode.gov.in) and Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions Official Records

Key Legislative Metadata

Legislative Stage / Attribute Official Details

Short Title The Former Secretary of State Service Officers (Conditions of Service) Act, 1972

Act Number / Year Act No. 59 of 1972

Act ID (India Code) 1972-59

Introduced In Parliament

Presidential Assent / Enactment Date September 21, 1972

Official Gazette Publication September 1972

Enforcement Date October 1, 1972

Administrative Nodal Ministry Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions (Department of Personnel and Training)

Precedent & Statutory Rationale

1. Transitioning Legacy Colonial Services into Modern Frameworks:

o Prior to India's independence, senior civil servants belonging to the Indian Civil Service (ICS) and the Indian Police (IP) were appointed directly by the Secretary of State for India and enjoyed special constitutional guarantees, protective covenants, and privileges concerning remuneration, leave, and pensions (often pegged or payable in sterling).

o Following independence, these officers were absorbed into the newly created Indian Administrative Service (IAS) and Indian Police Service (IPS). While Article 314 of the Constitution originally protected their pre-independence service conditions, Parliament subsequently repealed Article 314 and inserted Article 312A via the Constitution (Twenty-eighth Amendment) Act, 1972. This empowered Parliament to vary or revoke these special rights to ensure administrative uniformity and parity with contemporary public service standards.

2. Core Structural Innovations of the 1972 Act:

o Parity in Service Conditions: Brought the remuneration, leave, pension, and disciplinary rights of former Secretary of State service officers broadly in line with regular members of the IAS and IPS governed by the All India Services Act, 1951.

o Compulsory Retirement and Tenure Rules: Standardized retirement terms, empowering the government to mandate retirement in public interest upon completing 30 years of qualifying service or attaining 50 years of age, matching modern civil service guidelines.

o Currency and Pension Adjustments: Explicitly restricted pension payouts to Indian currency only, removing statutory entitlements to claim pensions in sterling or have them computed and paid outside India beyond specified legacy exchange thresholds.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

• Formulation: Drafted and piloted by the Department of Personnel to give domestic legislative effect to constitutional changes authorizing the rationalization of legacy colonial service contracts.

• Parliamentary Passage: Tabled, debated, and passed by both Houses of Parliament, receiving Presidential Assent on September 21, 1972.

• Enforcement: Brought into active operational force on October 1, 1972.

title: The Banking Companies (Acquisition and Transfer of Undertakings) Act, 1980

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of The Banking Companies (Acquisition and Transfer of Undertakings) Act, 1980
Purpose:
•	To provide for the acquisition and transfer of undertakings of certain banking companies.
•	To control the heights of the economy, serve the development needs of the economy, and promote public welfare in line with the Constitution's Article 39 (b) and (c).
Key Provisions:
1.	Acquisition and Transfer: - Enables the Central Government to acquire and transfer the undertakings of specified banking companies.
•	Undertakings, assets, and liabilities of acquired banks vest in the Central Government or a designated transferee bank.
2.	Existing and Corresponding New Banks: - Existing Bank: A banking company with total demand and time liabilities in India of not less than ₹200 crores as of March 14, 1980.
•	Corresponding New Bank: A body corporate established under the Act, corresponding to an existing bank, with an initial paid-up capital equal to that of the existing bank.
3.	Management and Capital: - Corresponding new banks are guided by the Central Government's directions.
•	Authorised capital of corresponding new banks initially set at ₹3,000 crores, with provisions for adjustment and capital increase through various means, ensuring the Central Government holds at least 51% of the paid-up equity capital.
4.	Miscellaneous: - Provisions for the management of undertakings, payment of amounts, employee continuance, and indemnity.
•	Amendments to various enactments and repeal/saving clauses.

Precedent & Historical Rationale

● Second Phase of Bank Nationalisation - Enacted to carry out the second major wave of commercial bank nationalisation in India, following the first phase under the Banking Companies (Acquisition and Transfer of Undertakings) Act, 1969.

● Socio-Economic Development & Credit Expansion - Formulated to acquire six major private sector commercial banks whose demand and time liabilities exceeded ₹200 crores (including Andhra Bank, Corporation Bank, New Bank of India, Oriental Bank of Commerce, Punjab & Sind Bank, and Vijaya Bank). meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of the Press Council Act, 1978 
Objective
•	Establish a Press Council of India to preserve the freedom of the Press.
•	Maintain and improve the standards of newspapers and news agencies in India.
Key Provisions
1.	Establishment of the Press Council
•	Body Corporate: The Press Council of India is a body corporate with perpetual succession.
•	Composition:
•	Chairman (nominated by a Committee consisting of the Chairman of Rajya Sabha, Speaker of Lok Sabha, and a member elected by the Council).
•	28 other members, including:
•	13 working journalists (6 editors, 7 non-editors, with a minimum of 3 editors and 4 non-editors from Indian language newspapers).
•	6 from the newspaper management sector (2 each from big, medium, and small newspapers).
•	1 from news agencies.
•	3 with expertise in education/science, law, and literature/culture.
•	5 Members of Parliament.
2.	Term and Conditions of Service
•	Term: 3 years for members, with the Chairman potentially serving up to 6 months after the Council's reconstitution.
•	Conditions: Chairman is a whole-time officer with a salary determined by the Central Government; other members receive allowances/fees.
3.	Powers and Functions
•	Objects:
•	Preserve Press freedom.
•	Maintain/improve newspaper and news agency standards.
•	Functions:
•	Help newspapers maintain independence.
•	Establish a code of conduct.
•	Ensure high standards of public taste and citizenship.
•	Review developments restricting news supply.
•	Study foreign newspapers' impact.
•	Promote a functional relationship among press professionals.
•	Address ownership concentration affecting Press independence.
•	Powers:
•	Censure newspapers/news agencies/editors/journalists for unethical behavior.
•	General powers similar to a civil court for inquiries.
•	Levy fees from registered newspapers/news agencies.
4.	Financial and Administrative Provisions
•	Funding: Through fees, Central Government grants, and other contributions.
•	Staff: Appointed by the Council, with terms and conditions determined by regulations.
•	Reports: Annual reports and budgets to be submitted to the Central Government.
5.	Miscellaneous
•	Protection: Actions in good faith under the Act are protected from legal proceedings.
•	Public Servants: Members and employees of the Council are deemed public servants.
•	Rule Making: Central Government can make rules, with the Council's consultation once established.
•	Regulations: The Council can make regulations, subject to the Act and rules, with certain requiring Central Government approval.

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of the Prize Chits and Money Circulation Schemes (Banning) Act, 1978
Objective
•	To prohibit and regulate prize chits, money circulation schemes, and explicitly, Unregulated Deposit Schemes in India, protecting the public from fraudulent activities.
Key Provisions
1.	Definitions & Scope:
•	Prize Chit & Money Circulation Scheme: Includes schemes promising returns without regulatory oversight.
•	Deposit Taker: Entities collecting deposits outside regulated frameworks.
2.	Banning and Penalties: - Prohibition: Strictly bans all unregulated schemes.
•	Penalties:
•	Contravention: Up to 3 years imprisonment or ₹5,000 fine (or both). Minimum 1 year imprisonment and ₹1,000 fine if no special reasons.
•	Related Offences: Up to 2 years imprisonment or ₹3,000 fine (or both). Minimum 1 year imprisonment and ₹1,000 fine if no special reasons.
3.	Enforcement Mechanisms: - Competent Authority: Empowered to impound records and provisionally attach properties.
•	Designated Court: Exclusive jurisdiction for trying offences.
4.	Liability: - Corporate and Officer Liability: Companies and their officers held liable.
5.	Jurisdiction and Procedure: - Exclusive Courts: Specialized handling of offences.
•	Cognizable & Non-Bailable Offences: Immediate police action.
•	Investigation Powers: Robust powers for investigations.
6.	Exemptions: - Exempts government schemes, banks, and specified institutions.
7.	Procedural Provisions: - Existing Schemes: Subject to winding-up and enforcement.
•	Record Keeping: Stricter rules.
8.	Governance and Repeal: - Central & State Oversight: Rules in consultation with the RBI.

Summary of The Brahmaputra Board Act, 1980
Key Provisions 
1. Title, Commencement, and Declaration
•	Title & Commencement: The Act may be called the Brahmaputra Board Act, 1980, coming into force on a date notified by the Central Government.
2. Key Definitions
•	Board: Brahmaputra Board established under Section 4.
•	Brahmaputra Valley: Inter-State Brahmaputra river valley demarcated under Section 11.
•	Fund: Brahmaputra Board Fund constituted under Section 19.
•	Master Plan: Plan for controlling floods, bank erosion, and improving drainage in the Brahmaputra Valley.
3. Establishment of the Board
•	Establishment & Incorporation: The Brahmaputra Board is established as a body corporate with perpetual succession and a common seal (Section 4).
•	Composition:
•	Chairman and Vice-Chairman appointed by the Central Government.
•	Ex officio members (General Manager, Financial Adviser).
•	Representatives from various State Governments and Central Ministries.
•	Representatives from Central Water Commission, Central Electricity Authority, etc.
•	Conditions of Service & Powers: Defined for members, Chairman, Vice-Chairman, General Manager, and other officers (Sections 5, 6, 7).
4. Functions and Powers of the Board
•	Limits of the Brahmaputra Valley: To be demarcated by the Central Government (Section 11).
•	Master Plan Preparation: For control of floods, bank erosion, and drainage improvement, considering water resources development (Section 12).
•	Other Functions:
•	Preparing reports, estimates, standards for projects.
•	Constructing, maintaining, and operating multi-purpose dams and works.
•	Phased programme for State Governments’ projects (Section 13).
•	General Powers: To do anything necessary for performing its functions, with specific powers to publish statistics, require information from State Governments (Section 15).
•	Conditions for Performing Functions: Including land provision by State Governments, assistance, and cost sharing (Section 14).
5. Finance, Accounts, and Audit
•	Grants and Loans: From the Central Government (Section 18).
•	Brahmaputra Board Fund: Composition and application purposes (Section 19).
•	Budget and Annual Report: To be prepared and forwarded to the Central Government (Sections 20, 21).
•	Accounts and Audit: Maintained and audited as prescribed (Section 22).
•	Allocation of Water Resources & Project Declarations: Specific to other rivers/projects (e.g., Polavaram Irrigation Project, Tungabhadra Board).

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of The Banking Companies (Acquisition and Transfer of Undertakings) Act, 1970
Purpose
•	Acquisition and transfer of undertakings of specified banking companies to control the economy's heights and align with national development policies and constitutional principles (Article 39, clauses b & c).
Key Provisions
1.	Acquisition & Transfer:
•	Central Government acquires undertakings of "existing banks" (with deposits ≥ Rs. 50 crores as of a specified date).
•	Transfer to "corresponding new banks" (constituted as per the First Schedule).
2.	Vesting of Assets & Liabilities:
•	All assets, liabilities, rights, and obligations of existing banks vest in corresponding new banks.
•	Global transfer includes books, records, borrowings, and all obligations, both within and outside India.
3.	Management & Control:
•	New banks' head offices and management structures are defined.
•	Guided by the Central Government with the power to make management schemes.
4.	International Assets/Liabilities:
•	If foreign laws hinder direct transfer, the Chief Executive Officer of the new bank manages these assets/liabilities to ensure effective transfer and discharge.
5.	Exemptions: - Credit information under the Credit Information Companies (Regulation) Act, 2005, is exempt from the Act's provisions.
Definitions & Scope
•	Existing Bank: Defined by deposit size (≥ Rs. 50 crores) and excludes foreign companies.
•	Corresponding New Bank: Takes over an existing bank's undertaking as per the First Schedule.

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of the Public Premises (Eviction of Unauthorised Occupants) Act, 1971
The Public Premises (Eviction of Unauthorised Occupants) Act, 1971 was enacted to provide a speedy and effective mechanism for evicting persons who occupy public premises without legal authority. The Act applies to premises owned or controlled by the Central Government, government companies, statutory corporations, public sector undertakings, and certain autonomous bodies. It aims to protect public property from illegal occupation and ensure its proper use. 
Objective:
The primary objective of the Act is to ensure the prompt eviction of unauthorized occupants from government and other public premises, prevent misuse of public property, and facilitate its efficient management in the public interest.
Key Features:
•	Defines "public premises" and "unauthorised occupation" under the Act. 
•	Empowers the Central Government to appoint Estate Officers to conduct eviction proceedings. 
•	Requires the Estate Officer to issue a show-cause notice before ordering eviction, ensuring the occupant has an opportunity to be heard. 
•	Authorizes the Estate Officer to order the eviction of unauthorized occupants and remove unauthorized constructions or encroachments. 
•	Permits recovery of arrears of rent, damages for unauthorized occupation, and disposal of property left behind after eviction. 
•	Provides powers similar to those of a civil court to Estate Officers for summoning witnesses, examining evidence, and enforcing attendance. 
•	Allows an appeal against the Estate Officer's order before the designated appellate authority within the prescribed period. 
•	The Act has been amended from time to time to make the eviction process more efficient, particularly for unauthorized occupation of government residential accommodation.
