AND WHEREAS for accelerated agricultural development in the country, it is necessary to protect plant breeders' rights to stimulate investment for research and development, both in the public and private sector, for the development of new plant varieties;

meta.dc.legislation.history:
Legislative History:

The Protection of Plant Varieties and Farmers' Rights Act, 2001

Act Title The Protection of Plant Varieties and Farmers' Rights Act, 2001

Act Number 53 of 2001

Act ID (India Code) 200153

Presidential Assent Date October 30, 2001

Enforcement Dates Phase 1 (Sections 2–13, 95–97): November 11, 2005

Phase 2 (Sections 1, 14–94): October 19, 2006

Nodal Ministry Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare

Precedent & Historical Context

1. International Obligations (TRIPS Agreement & UPOV):

o India’s ratification of the WTO Trade-Related Aspects of Intellectual Property Rights (TRIPS) Agreement required establishing an effective sui generis system for protecting plant varieties under Article 27.3(b).

o While the UPOV (International Union for the Protection of New Varieties of Plants) model emphasized plant breeders' rights, India formulated a unique sui generis framework balancing breeders' rights with comprehensive protection for traditional farmers' rights.

2. Domestic Rationale:

o Aimed to stimulate research and investment in seed development across public and private sectors while recognizing rural and tribal farmers' traditional contributions as conservers and improvers of plant genetic resources.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

• December 14, 1999: Introduced in the Lok Sabha as The Protection of Plant Varieties and Farmers' Rights Bill, 1999.

• December 1999 – August 2000: Referred to a Joint Parliamentary Committee (JPC) of both Houses chaired by Sahib Singh Verma for detailed nationwide consultations and report formulation.

• August 25, 2000: The Joint Parliamentary Committee submitted its report recommending substantial safeguards for farmers' traditional practices of saving, using, sowing, re-sowing, exchanging, sharing, or selling farm produce.

• August 2001: Passed by the Lok Sabha and subsequently agreed to by the Rajya Sabha with official amendments.

• Enactment: Received Presidential Assent on October 30, 2001.

• Enforcement: Enforced on November 11, 2005.

Summary of The Khuda Bakhsh Oriental Public Library Act, 1969:
Objective:
To declare the Khuda Bakhsh Oriental Public Library at Patna, Bihar, as an institution of national importance and to provide for its administration.
Key Provisions:
1.	Declaration: - Declares the Khuda Bakhsh Oriental Public Library as an institution of national importance.

3.	Board's Responsibilities and Powers:
•	Duties:
•	Manage the Library.
•	Implement development programs on modern scientific lines.
•	Advise Central and State Governments on library matters.
•	Preserve and conserve manuscripts, books, and other articles.
•	Publish bibliographies, assist in publications, and promote symposia/seminars.
•	Powers:
•	Acquire, hold, dispose of property.
•	Contract and sue/be sued.
•	Purchase/acquire manuscripts, books, etc., for the Library.
4.	Financial and Administrative Provisions: - Fund: Establishment and management of the Board's Fund.
•	Grants: From the Central Government.
•	Accounts, Audit, and Reports: Detailed provisions for transparency and oversight.
5.	Miscellaneous: - Protection of Actions: Immunity for actions taken in good faith under the Act.
•	Power to Make Rules and Regulations:

title: The High Court at Bombay (Extension of Jurisdiction to Goa, Daman and Diu) Act, 1981

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of The High Court at Bombay (Extension of Jurisdiction to Goa, Daman and Diu) Act, 1981
Key Provisions
1.	Extension of Jurisdiction: - The High Court at Bombay's jurisdiction extends to the Union territory of Goa, Daman, and Diu from the appointed day.
•	The Court of the Judicial Commissioner for Goa, Daman, and Diu ceases to function and is abolished.
2.	Jurisdiction and Powers: - The High Court at Bombay assumes all jurisdiction, powers, and authority previously held by the Court of the Judicial Commissioner over the territory.
3.	Constitutional Application: - Chapter VI of Part VI of the Constitution applies to the High Court at Bombay in relation to Goa, Daman, and Diu, with specified exceptions and modifications (e.g., references to "State" are construed as references to the Union territory, and "Governor" as "Administrator").
4.	Practical Arrangements
•	Permanent Bench: Established at Panaji with at least two Judges nominated by the Chief Justice.
•	Advocates: Those practicing in the Court of the Judicial Commissioner before the appointed day can practice in the High Court at Bombay.
•	Pending Proceedings: Transferred from the Court of the Judicial Commissioner to the High Court at Bombay.
•	Right to Appear: Advocates authorized in transferred proceedings retain their right to appear before the High Court at Bombay.
5.	Financial and Administrative
•	Expenditure Allocation: Between the State of Maharashtra and the Union, proportion to be determined by the President.
•	Rule of Construction: References to the Court of the Judicial Commissioner in laws are construed as references to the High Court at Bombay.
6.	Miscellaneous
•	Power to Remove Difficulties: The Central Government can make provisions to address difficulties in implementing the Act, within two years of the appointed day.
•	Power to Adapt Laws: The Central Government can adapt or modify laws for better application in Goa, Daman, and Diu, within two years of the appointed day.

Precedent & Historical Rationale

Precedent & Historical Rationale

● Accession to the African Development Fund Agreement - In 1972, an international agreement was established to constitute the African Development Fund (ADF) as the concessional lending arm of the African Development Bank Group, aimed at fostering economic and social development across African member states. India, seeking to expand South-South cooperation, deepen economic and technical partnerships with African nations, and contribute to international development finance, decided to become a non-regional state participant in the Fund.

● Statutory Authorization of Financial Contributions, Immunities, and Privileges - Formulated to implement the international Agreement establishing the African Development Fund and give effect to India’s participation therein. The Act statutorily authorized the Central Government to make initial and periodic subscription payments to the Fund out of the Consolidated Fund of India, issue non-negotiable, non-interest-bearing promissory notes in lieu of payments, and confer legal capacity, judicial immunities, exemptions from taxation, and privileges upon the Fund, its Governors, Directors, and personnel within the territory of India in accordance with the international treaty.

● Formulation - Introduced by the Union Minister of Finance in Parliament to fulfill India's treaty obligations and provide domestic legislative sanction for financial contributions and diplomatic immunities relating to the African Development Fund.

Summary of The Oaths Act, 1969
Overview The Oaths Act, 1969, is a legislative act aimed at consolidating and amending the laws related to the administration of oaths in judicial proceedings across India, with certain exemptions.
Key Provisions
1.	Jurisdiction and Commencement
•	Applies to the whole of India.
•	Came into effect on 26th December, 1969.
2.	Administration of Oaths
•	Empowers designated courts and officials to administer oaths.
•	Includes provisions for military personnel under specific circumstances.
3.	Mandatory Oaths/Affirmations
•	For witnesses, interpreters, and jurors in judicial proceedings.
•	Exception for minors under 12 who cannot comprehend the oath's significance.
4.	Option for Affirmation
•	Allows individuals to opt for an affirmation instead of taking an oath.
5.	Standardized Forms
•	Prescribes specific forms for oaths and affirmations (outlined in The Schedule).
•	Permits alternative forms under defined conditions.
6.	Validity of Proceedings
•	Irregularities in oath administration do not invalidate legal proceedings or evidence.
7.	Truth Binding
•	Mandates that all individuals providing evidence must state the truth.
8.	Repeal and Transition
•	Repeals the Indian Oaths Act, 1873, with provisions to safeguard ongoing proceedings.
The Schedule: Forms of Oaths and Affirmations
•	Witnesses
•	Jurors
•	Interpreters
•	Affidavits

● Law Commission Modernization Recommendations - Enacted following the 28th Report of the Law Commission of India to consolidate, simplify, and modernize the law relating to judicial oaths and solemn affirmations, replacing the colonial Indian Oaths Act, 1873.

● Secularization & Uniformity in Judicial Proceedings - Formulated to establish a uniform rule across all courts and tribunals in India, allowing witnesses, interpreters, and persons making affidavits the option to make a solemn affirmation instead of taking a religious oath, ensuring religious neutrality and constitutional values under Article 25.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

● Formulation - Introduced by the Ministry of Law and Justice to streamline procedure, clarify authority for administering oaths (including courts, tribunals, and authorized persons), and declare that omissions or irregularities in administering oaths do not invalidate proceedings.

● Parliamentary Passage - Debated and passed by both Houses of Parliament (Fourth Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha) during the December 1969 winter session.

● Presidential Assent - Received Presidential Assent on December 26, 1969.

● Enforcement - Enforced on December 26, 1969.

Source - Official Record of Parliament, India Code, and Ministry of Law and Justice.

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of the Sugar Development Fund Act, 1982 
The Sugar Development Fund Act, 1982 was enacted by the Parliament of India to establish the Sugar Development Fund (SDF) for promoting the development and modernization of the sugar industry. The Act provides financial assistance to sugar factories for rehabilitation, modernization, expansion, research, and other developmental activities. It came into force on 1 April 1982.
Objectives
The main objectives of the Act are to:
•	Promote the development and modernization of the sugar industry. 
•	Improve the efficiency and productivity of sugar factories. 
•	Support rehabilitation and replacement of obsolete machinery. 
•	Encourage research and development in sugar production and by-products. 
•	Provide financial assistance for activities benefiting sugarcane growers and the sugar industry. 
Key Provisions 
1.	Establishment of the Sugar Development Fund
The Act establishes the Sugar Development Fund (SDF) under the control of the Central Government. The Fund consists mainly of:
•	Amounts credited by the Central Government. 
•	Proceeds of duties of excise or cesses, as provided by law. 
•	Interest received on loans granted from the Fund. 
•	Repayments of loans and other receipts. 
2.	Utilization of the Fund
The Fund may be used for:
•	Granting loans to sugar factories for modernization, expansion, rehabilitation, and technological upgradation. 
•	Financing research projects related to sugarcane cultivation, sugar production, and value-added products. 
•	Supporting the development of improved sugar manufacturing techniques. 
•	Assisting schemes for the welfare and development of sugarcane growers. 
•	Funding activities that promote the long-term growth and competitiveness of the sugar industry. 
3.	Financial Assistance
The Central Government may provide:
•	Loans for approved development projects. 
•	Grants for research, training, and specified developmental activities. 
•	Assistance subject to prescribed terms and conditions, including repayment schedules and interest where applicable. 
4.	Administration
The Central Government is responsible for:
•	Administering the Fund. 
•	Sanctioning loans and grants. 
•	Monitoring the utilization of financial assistance. 
•	Ensuring that the Fund is used only for purposes specified under the Act. 
5.	Recovery of Loans
The Act provides for:
•	Recovery of loans advanced from the Fund. 
•	Payment of interest on loans, where applicable. 
•	Measures for recovery in the event of default, in accordance with the provisions of the Act and applicable rules. 
6.	Rule-making Powers
The Central Government may make rules regarding:
•	The administration and management of the Fund. 
•	Eligibility for loans and grants. 
•	Conditions for financial assistance. 
•	Procedures for application, approval, repayment, and monitoring. 
•	Any other matter necessary for implementing the Act.

Summary of The Anti-Apartheid (United Nations Convention) Act, 1981:
Title & Extent: The Anti-Apartheid (United Nations Convention) Act, 1981 (Act No. 48 of 1981), extends to the whole of India.
 Purpose: To give effect to the International Convention on the Suppression and Punishment of the Crime of Apartheid, ratified by India. 
Key Provisions:
1.	Application of the Convention: Specified provisions of the International Convention on the Suppression and Punishment of the Crime of Apartheid have the force of law in India (Schedule, not fully provided in the context).
2.	Punishment for International Criminal Responsibility: - Offence: Acts under Article III of the Convention (reference to Article II for context).
•	Penalties: Death, imprisonment for life, or up to 10 years, plus a fine.
3.	Corporate/Institutional Liability:
•	Responsibility: Persons in charge of companies/institutions committing offences under this Act.
•	Defence: Proof of lack of knowledge or due diligence to prevent the offence.
4.	Jurisdiction & Procedure:
•	Place of Trial: Any place in India where the offender is found, or as directed by the Central Government.
•	Previous Sanction for Prosecution: Required from the Central Government.
5.	Extradition: Offences under this Act are not considered political for the purposes of the Extradition Act, 1962.

Precedent & Historical Rationale

● Legislative Curing Post-Baij Nath Kedia Judgment - Enacted directly in response to the landmark Supreme Court ruling in Baij Nath Kedia v. State of Bihar (1969). This protected the state exchequer from mass claims for refunds of royalties and rents previously collected under invalidated state provisions.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

● Formulation - Introduced by the Union Government to re-enact and validate specified provisions of the Bihar State laws as if they had been enacted by Parliament itself, thereby overcoming the constitutional lack of state legislative competence.

● Parliamentary Passage - Debated and passed by both Houses of Parliament (Fourth Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha) during the winter session in December 1969.

THE GOA, DAMAN AND DIU MINING CONCESSIONS (ABOLITION AND DECLARATION AS MINING LEASES) ACT, 1987
ACT NO. 16 OF 1987

[23rd May, 1987.]

An Act to provide for the abolition of the mining concessions in operation in the Union territory of Goa, Daman and Diu and specified in the First and the Second Schedules, and for the declaration of such mining concessions as mining leases under the Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957 with a view to the regulation of the mines to which such concessions relate and for the development of minerals under the control of the Union and for matters connected therewith or incidental thereto.
WHEREAS certain mining concessions have been granted in perpetuity under the former Portuguese Mining Laws (Decree of 20th day of September, 1906) in the territories now included in the Union territory of Goa, Daman and Diu by the former Portuguese Government and by the Government of Goa, Daman and Diu:
AND WHEREAS the aforesaid mining laws have ceased to be in force and doubts have been expressed as to whether such mining concessions are mining leases within the meaning of the Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act 1957 (67 of 1957):
AND WHEREAS it is expedient in the public interest to abolish such mining concessions and declare them as mining leases under the aforesaid Act for the purpose of making the provisions of that Act applicable to the mines to which such concessions relate with a view to the regulation of such mines and for the development of minerals under the control of the Union so as to subserve the common good:
BE it enacted by Parliament in the Thirty-eighth Year of the Republic of India as follows:--
meta.dc.legislation.history:
Legislative History:

The Goa, Daman and Diu Mining Concessions (Abolition and Declaration as Mining Leases) Act, 1987

Act Title - The Goa, Daman and Diu Mining Concessions (Abolition and Declaration as Mining Leases) Act, 1987

Act Number/Year - 18 of 1987

Act ID (India Code) - 198718

Presidential Assent Date - May 23, 1987

Enforcement Date - May 23, 1987

Nodal Ministry - Ministry of Mines

Precedent & Historical Rationale

Portuguese Colonial Legacy and Unique Concession System:

Prior to the liberation of Goa, Daman, and Diu in 1961, mining operations in the region were governed by colonial Portuguese laws (specifically the Regulamento de Concessao de Terceiros and related mining decrees). Under this system, perpetual or long-term "concessions" (concessões mineradoras) were granted to private operators rather than standard, regulated mining leases under regular Indian mineral legislation like the Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957. Post-liberation, these concessions continued to operate under a protected transitional legal framework.

Need for Uniform National Mineral Regulation:

Decades after liberation, the continuation of colonial-era concessions created administrative anomalies, environmental degradation, and a lack of systematic revenue control compared to the rest of India. To bring mineral administration in Goa into conformity with the national regulatory regime, abolish archaic perpetual rights, and convert these concessions into regulated mining leases under the MMDR Act, Parliament enacted this specific statutory measure.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

Formulation:

Drafted by the Ministry of Mines to abolish old colonial mining concessions granted in Goa, Daman, and Diu, convert them into regular mining leases under Indian statutory law for a limited transitional period, and establish provisions for compensation and regulatory oversight.

Parliamentary Passage:

Introduced, debated, and passed by both Houses of Parliament (Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha) during the budget session of 1987.

Presidential Assent: Received Presidential Assent on May 23, 1987.

Enforcement: Enforced on October 1, 1987.

Source: Official Records of Parliament, India Code, and Ministry of Mines.

title: The Maritime Zones of India (Regulation of Fishing by Foreign Vessels) Act, 1981

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of the  Maritime Zones of India (Regulation of Fishing by Foreign Vessels) Act, 1981 
The Maritime Zones of India (Regulation of Fishing by Foreign Vessels) Act, 1981 was enacted by the Parliament of India to regulate fishing activities by foreign vessels in India's maritime zones. The Act aims to protect India's marine resources, prevent unauthorized fishing, conserve fish stocks, and safeguard the interests of Indian fishermen. It came into force on 2 November 1981.
Objectives
The main objectives of the Act are to:
•	Regulate fishing by foreign fishing vessels in India's maritime zones. 
•	Conserve and sustainably manage marine fishery resources. 
•	Prevent illegal, unreported, and unregulated (IUU) fishing by foreign vessels. 
•	Protect the livelihood and interests of Indian fishermen. 
•	Ensure that foreign fishing operations are carried out only with the permission of the Central Government. 
Scope of the Act
The Act applies to foreign fishing vessels operating in the maritime zones of India, including:
•	The territorial waters. 
•	The contiguous zone. 
•	The exclusive economic zone (EEZ). 
•	Other maritime zones declared under Indian law. 
It does not generally regulate fishing by Indian fishing vessels, which are governed by other laws.
Licensing of Foreign Fishing Vessels
The Act requires that:
•	No foreign fishing vessel may fish in India's maritime zones without a valid licence issued by the Central Government. 
•	Licences are granted subject to prescribed conditions, including: 
o	Area of operation. 
o	Type of fishing. 
o	Duration of the licence. 
o	Reporting and operational requirements. 
•	The Government may suspend, cancel, or refuse to renew a licence if licence conditions or legal requirements are violated. 
Powers of Enforcement
The Act authorizes designated officers to:
•	Board and inspect foreign fishing vessels. 
•	Examine licences and related documents. 
•	Search vessels suspected of violations. 
•	Seize fishing gear, catch, equipment, or the vessel where necessary. 
•	Arrest persons involved in offences under the Act. 
•	Detain vessels pending legal proceedings. 
Offences and Penalties
The Act prescribes penalties for offences such as:
•	Fishing without a valid licence. 
•	Violating licence conditions. 
•	Obstructing authorized officers in the performance of their duties. 
•	Providing false information or documents. 
•	Engaging in unauthorized fishing activities. 
Penalties may include:
•	Imprisonment. 
•	Monetary fines. 
•	Confiscation of the vessel, fishing gear, catch, or equipment. 
•	Cancellation or suspension of licences.

Summary of The Asiatic Society Act, 1984
Key Provisions
1.	Declaration: - Declares the Asiatic Society (with its registered office in Calcutta) as an institution of national importance.
2.	Definitions: - Defines key terms such as "memorandum", "prescribed", "regulations", and "Society".
3.	Financial Provisions: - Grants, Loans, etc. (Section 4): The Central Government may provide financial assistance to the Society for its activities.
•	Audit of Accounts (Section 5): Mandates the Society to maintain accounts, audited by the Comptroller and Auditor-General of India, with reports submitted to the Central Government and laid before Parliament.
4.	Reporting and Oversight: - Annual Report (Section 6): The Society must submit an annual report of its activities to the Central Government, to be laid before Parliament.
5.	Restrictions and Approvals: - Prior Approval Necessary (Section 7): The Society requires prior Central Government approval for altering its purposes, memorandum, regulations, selling/disposing of certain properties, or dissolution.
6.	Governance and Advisory Bodies: - Planning Board (Section 8): The Central Government may establish a Planning Board to advise on the Society’s developmental programmes.
•	Committees (Section 9): The Central Government can constitute committees for specific duties related to the Society’s work and financial planning.
7.	Operational Oversight: - Review, Inspection, and Evaluation (Section 10): The Central Government can form a Committee for reviewing the Society’s work, inspecting assets, and evaluating its performance, with the Society entitled to representation.

Precedent & Historical Rationale

1. Preservation of Priceless Heritage and Historical Legacy:

o The Asiatic Society, originally founded in Calcutta in 1784 by Sir William Jones, is one of the world's premier institutions for Oriental research, housing an invaluable collection of rare manuscripts, ancient texts, coins, artifacts, and a vast library of historical literature.

o Despite its immense cultural and historical significance, the Society faced severe financial constraints, administrative challenges, and deteriorating infrastructure for preserving its archival treasures under its existing society registration framework.

2. Declaration of National Importance and Statutory Reorganization:

o The legislative intent centered on declaring the Asiatic Society in Calcutta as an institution of national importance to ensure direct financial backing and patronage from the Central Government.

o The Act provided for the incorporation of the Society under a statutory framework, vested its management in a designated council, and empowered it with a secure administrative and financial structure to protect, preserve, and promote research in humanities and oriental studies.

• Formulation: Drafted by the Ministry of Education and Culture (now Ministry of Culture) to commemorate the bicentenary of the institution and safeguard its unique repository of knowledge and historical heritage.

• Parliamentary Passage: Introduced, deliberated, and passed by both Houses of Parliament (Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha) during the budget session of 1984.

• Presidential Assent: Received Presidential Assent on March 19, 1984.

• Enforcement: Enforced on June 1, 1984.

Summary of The Chandigarh Disturbed Areas Act, 1983 (Act No. 33 of 1983):
Purpose
•	To make better provision for the suppression of disorder and for the restoration and maintenance of public order in disturbed areas in Chandigarh.
Key Provisions
1.	Short Title, Extent, and Commencement
•	Title: Chandigarh Disturbed Areas Act, 1983
•	Extent: Whole of the Union territory of Chandigarh
•	Commencement: Deemed to have come into force on 7th October, 1983
2.	Definitions
•	"Administrator": The Administrator of the Union territory of Chandigarh.
•	"Disturbed Area": An area declared as such by notification under Section 3.
3.	Operational Provisions
•	Section 3: Empowers the Administrator to declare any part of Chandigarh a "disturbed area" via notification.
•	Section 4: Authorizes Magistrates or Police Officers (not below Sub-Inspector/Havildar in Armed Branch) to fire upon or use force (up to causing death) against persons contravening orders related to assembly, weapons, etc., after due warning.
•	Section 5: Empowers authorized officers to destroy arms dumps, fortified positions, etc., used for or likely to be used for armed attacks or as hide-outs.
4.	Protection and Legal Aspects
•	Section 6: Protects persons acting under Sections 4 and 5 from legal proceedings without the previous sanction of the Central Government.

Legislative History:

Act Title - The Chandigarh Disturbed Areas Act, 1983

Act Number/Year - 34 of 1983

Presidential Assent Date - December 8, 1983

Enforcement Date - October 7, 1983

Nodal Ministry - Ministry of Home Affairs

Precedent & Historical Rationale

1. Escalation of Militancy and Law and Order Breakdown in Punjab:

o By the early 1980s, the Union Territory of Chandigarh and the surrounding State of Punjab experienced a severe escalation of extremist violence, terrorist activities, and communal unrest, posing a grave threat to the security of the state and public order.

o Because Chandigarh served as the shared administrative capital of both Punjab and Haryana, ensuring its absolute security and stability was of paramount national importance.

2. Special Powers for Security Forces to Maintain Public Order:

o Standard law enforcement mechanisms under the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, were deemed insufficient to cope with the extraordinary security crisis.

o The legislative intent centered on empowering the Central Government or the local administration to declare Chandigarh a "disturbed area," thereby vesting armed forces and police officers with special statutory powers—such as the power to fire upon persons violating prohibitory orders or carrying unauthorized weapons, and to conduct search and arrest operations without warrants—to suppress terrorist activities and restore peace.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

• Formulation:

Drafted by the Ministry of Home Affairs as an emergency counter-terrorism measure to arm law enforcement and security agencies in Chandigarh with robust legal powers analogous to those provided under the Armed Forces (Punjab and Chandigarh) Special Powers Act.

• Parliamentary Passage:

Initially promulgated as an ordinance, it was introduced, deliberated, and passed by both Houses of Parliament (Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha) during the autumn session of 1983.

• Presidential Assent: Received Presidential Assent on October 1, 1983.

• Enforcement: Enforced on October 7, 1983.

Source: Official Records of Parliament, India Code, and Ministry of Home Affairs

Summary of The Registration of Births and Deaths Act, 1969 
*Title: The Registration of Births and Deaths Act, 1969 *Act No.: 18 of 1969 *Extent & Commencement: Applies to the whole of India with varied commencement dates for different states/UTs.
Key Provisions
1.	Registration Hierarchy
•	Registrar General of India: Oversees national registration and maintains a unified database of births and deaths.
•	Chief Registrar (State Level): Manages state-level registrations and database.
•	District Registrar & Registrars: Handle district and local area registrations.

•	Mandatory Reporting: Specified individuals (parents, medical officers, etc.) must report births and deaths within a prescribed timeframe.

•	Delayed Registrations: Possible with approvals and fees.
•	New Additions (2023 Amendment): Provisions for surrogacy, single parents, and foundlings.
3.	Data Management & Statistics
•	Unified National & State Databases: For registered births and deaths, shareable with other national databases (e.g., electoral rolls, Aadhaar) with approvals.
•	Periodical Statistical Reports: Submitted to Central/State Governments.
4.	Compliance & Enforcement
•	Penalties for Non-Compliance: Fines for failure to report or provide false information (varied amounts for different offenders).
•	Powers of Registrars: Can demand information from locals; special powers during disasters/epidemics.
5.	Amendments & Updates
•	2023 Amendments: Significant updates including digital registration, surrogacy, single parent registrations, and integration with national databases.

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of The President (Discharge of Functions) Act, 1969
Overview
Purpose: To outline the protocol for the discharge of the President of India's functions during specific contingencies, ensuring continuity of governance.
Key Provisions
1.	Vacancy in Both President and Vice-President Offices:
•	Interim Authority: The Chief Justice of India (or the senior-most Supreme Court Judge if the Chief Justice is unavailable).
•	Duration: Until the election and assumption of office by a new President or the commencement of duties by a new Vice-President acting as President, whichever occurs first.
2.	Incumbent Vice-President Discharging Presidential Duties but Unable to Continue:
•	Interim Authority: Same as above.
•	Duration:
•	If acting as President: Until a new President takes office or the Vice-President resumes duties.
•	Otherwise: Until the President resumes duties or the Vice-President does, whichever is sooner.
3.	Powers, Immunities, and Emoluments of the Interim Authority:
•	Powers & Immunities: Equivalent to those of the President during the tenure.
•	Emoluments & Allowances: As prescribed by Parliament, or interim, as per the Constitution's Second Schedule.
•	Section 3: Discharge of Presidential Functions in Specified Contingencies (Subsections addressing different scenarios of vacancy or incapacity)

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of the National Waterways Act, 2016 
Objectives of the Act
•	To declare specified inland waterways as National Waterways. 
•	To facilitate the development and maintenance of inland water transport infrastructure. 
•	To promote safe, efficient, and sustainable movement of passengers and cargo. 
•	To improve multimodal connectivity and support economic and regional development. 
Key Provisions
•	Declaration of National Waterways: The Act declares 111 inland waterways as National Waterways, as specified in the Schedule to the Act. 
•	Unified Legal Framework: It repeals the five earlier Acts that separately declared individual waterways as National Waterways, thereby creating a single, comprehensive legislative framework. 
•	Development of Waterways: The declaration enables the Central Government, principally through the Inland Waterways Authority of India (IWAI), to undertake the development, regulation, and maintenance of National Waterways for navigation. 
•	Infrastructure Development: The Act facilitates the development of navigation channels, terminals, jetties, navigational aids, and other infrastructure required for inland water transport. 
•	No Automatic Development or Land Acquisition: The declaration of a waterway as a National Waterway does not by itself mandate its development or authorize land acquisition. Such activities are undertaken separately in accordance with applicable laws and subject to technical, environmental, and financial feasibility.

THE NATIONAL WATERWAYS ACT, 2016
ACT NO. 17 OF 2016

[25th March, 2016.]

An Act to make provisions for existing national waterways and to provide for the declaration of certain inland waterways to be national waterways and also to provide for the regulation and development of the said waterways for the purposes of shipping and navigation and for matters connected therewith or incidental thereto.
BE it enacted by Parliament in the Sixty-seventh Year of the Republic of India as follows:--
meta.dc.legislation.history:
Legislative History:

The National Waterways Act, 2016

Short Title The National Waterways Act, 2016

Act Number / Year Act No. 17 of 2016

India Code Act ID 201617

Presidential Assent Date March 25, 2016

Enforcement Date April 12, 2016

Nodal Ministry Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways

Precedent & Statutory Rationale

1. Underutilization of Eco-Friendly and Cost-Effective Inland Transport:

o Prior to 2016, India possessed thousands of kilometers of navigable rivers, canals, backwaters, and creeks, yet inland water transport accounted for a minuscule fraction of national freight and passenger movement. High logistics costs, fragmented state regulations, and a lack of centralized funding hampered sector growth compared to roads and railways.

2. Comprehensive Expansion under Entry 24 of the Union List:

o Grounded in the constitutional mandate under Entry 24 of the Union List (Seventh Schedule)—which empowers Parliament to legislate on shipping and navigation on inland waterways declared to be national waterways—the legislation was enacted to drastically scale up infrastructure, reduce carbon footprints, and lower freight transit costs across industrial corridors.

• Formulation: Developed and piloted by the Ministry of Shipping under Minister Nitin Gadkari to formulate an integrated policy for nationwide river and canal transport.

• Parliamentary Passage: Introduced in the Lok Sabha as the National Waterways Bill on May 5, 2015; reviewed extensively by the Parliamentary Standing Committee; passed by the Lok Sabha in December 2015, passed with amendments by the Rajya Sabha in March 2016; and finally cleared by the Lok Sabha on March 15, 2016.

• Presidential Assent: Received formal Presidential Assent from President Pranab Mukherjee on March 25, 2016, entering the statute book as Act No. 17 of 2016.

• Enforcement: Brought into active operational force on April 12, 2016.

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of the Anti Hijacking Act, 2016

The Anti-Hijacking Act, 2016 was enacted to strengthen India's legal framework for preventing and punishing the unlawful seizure of aircraft. It replaced the Anti-Hijacking Act, 1982 and implements India's obligations under the Hague Convention, 1970 and the 2010 Beijing Protocol. The Act broadens the definition of hijacking to include seizure or control of an aircraft through technological means, prescribes stringent punishments, and provides for designated courts to ensure the speedy trial of hijacking-related offences.
Objective
The main objectives of the Act are:
•	To prevent and punish the unlawful seizure or control of aircraft.
•	To implement India's international obligations under the Hague Convention and the Beijing Protocol.
•	To strengthen aviation security against emerging forms of hijacking and terrorism.
•	To provide for effective investigation, prosecution, and speedy trial of hijacking offences.
•	To safeguard the lives of passengers, crew members, and the security of civil aviation.
Key Provisions
1.	Expanded Definition of Hijacking
o	Defines hijacking to include the unlawful seizure or exercise of control over an aircraft by force, threat, coercion, intimidation, or technological means, even if the offender is not physically on board the aircraft.
2.	Severe Punishments
o	Provides life imprisonment and fine for hijacking.
o	If the hijacking results in the death of any person, the offender may be punished with the death penalty.
3.	Acts of Violence Connected with Hijacking
o	Punishes acts of violence against passengers, crew, or airport personnel that are connected with the commission of hijacking.
4.	Jurisdiction
o	Extends jurisdiction to offences committed within India and, in specified circumstances, outside India involving Indian aircraft, Indian nationals, or aircraft landing in India.
5.	Designated Courts
o	Provides for the establishment of Designated Courts for the speedy trial of offences under the Act.
6.	Investigation and Prosecution
o	Empowers designated investigating agencies to investigate offences and requires prior sanction of the Central Government before prosecution in specified cases.
7.	Bail and Extradition
o	Contains special provisions relating to bail and treats hijacking offences as extraditable offences in accordance with international obligations.
8.	Attachment and Confiscation of Property
o	Authorizes the seizure, attachment, confiscation, and forfeiture of property connected with hijacking offences.
9.	Repeal of the 1982 Act
o	Repeals the Anti-Hijacking Act, 1982 while preserving actions already taken under the earlier law through saving provisions.

meta.dc.identifier.preamble_description:
THE ANTI-HIJACKING ACT, 2016
ACT NO. 30 OF 2016

[13th May, 2016.]

An Act to give effect to the Convention for the Suppression of Unlawful Seizure of Aircraft and for matters connected therewith.
WHEREAS a Convention for the Suppression of Unlawful Seizure of Aircraft was signed at The Hague on the 16th day of December, 1970;
AND WHEREAS India acceded to the said Convention and enacted the Anti-Hijacking Act, 1982 (65 of 1982) to give effect to the provisions of the Convention;
AND WHEREAS India has signed the Protocol Supplementary to the Convention at Beijing on the 10th day of September, 2010 which deals with unlawful acts against Civil Aviation by new types of threats which require comprehensive amendments to the said Act;
AND WHEREAS it is considered expedient that the unlawful acts of seizure or exercise of control of aircraft which jeopardize safety of persons and property is a matter of great concern to be addressed effectively by making suitable provisions for giving effect to the Convention and the Protocol and for matters connected therewith.
BE it enacted by Parliament in the Sixty-seventh Year of the Republic of India as follows:---
meta.dc.legislation.history:
Legislative History:

The Anti-Hijacking Act, 2016

Short Title The Anti-Hijacking Act, 2016

Act Number / Year Act No. 30 of 2016

India Code Act ID 201630

Presidential Assent Date May 13, 2016

Enforcement Date July 5, 2017

Administrative Nodal Ministry Ministry of Civil Aviation

Precedent & Statutory Rationale

1. Alignment with International Legal Frameworks (Beijing Protocol, 2010):

o The 1982 Act gave effect solely to The Hague Convention (1970). The 2016 legislation incorporated provisions of the Beijing Protocol (2010) supplementary to the Hague Convention, updating the statutory framework to combat modern security threats to civil aviation.

2. Expanded Scope of the Offence:

o Broadened the definition of hijacking beyond physical in-flight control to include technological threats, coercion, intimidation, and unlawful control exercised while an aircraft is "in service" (from pre-flight preparations until 24 hours after landing).

3. Stringent Penal Mechanisms & Asset Confiscation:

o Introduced capital punishment (death penalty) where an act of hijacking results in the death of a hostage, security personnel, or any uninvolved person. For all other instances, it mandated life imprisonment for the remainder of natural life alongside confiscation of movable and immovable properties.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

• Formulation: Drafted and piloted by the Ministry of Civil Aviation to strengthen anti-terror laws following global standards and recommendations from national security agencies.

Legislative History:

The Bhopal Gas Leak Disaster (Processing of Claims) Act, 1985

Act Title - The Bhopal Gas Leak Disaster (Processing of Claims) Act, 1985

Act Number/Year - 21 of 1985

Act ID (India Code) - 198521

Presidential Assent Date - March 29, 1985

Enforcement Date - February 20, 1985

Nodal Ministry - Ministry of Chemicals and Fertilizers

Precedent & Historical Rationale

1. The World's Worst Industrial Disaster and Exploitation Risks:

o On the night of December 2-3, 1984, a catastrophic leak of highly toxic Methyl Isocyanate (MIC) gas from the Union Carbide India Limited (UCIL) pesticide plant in Bhopal, Madhya Pradesh, resulted in the immediate death of thousands of citizens and caused severe, long-term injuries to hundreds of thousands more.

o In the aftermath, destitute, traumatized victims faced the immediate danger of being exploited by predatory domestic and foreign lawyers or coerced into accepting hasty, out-of-court, low-value settlements by the multinational corporation, Union Carbide Corporation (UCC).

2. Exclusive Representation by the Sovereign State:

o The legislative intent centered on conferring an exclusive, sovereign right upon the Central Government to represent all Indian citizens affected by the disaster in any legal proceedings inside or outside India.

o By stepping into the shoes of the victims as their sole legal representative, the Government aimed to streamline the processing of compensation claims, prevent multi-forum litigation chaos, and ensure that justice was pursued collectively and effectively against corporate negligence on a global scale.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

• Formulation:

Drafted urgently by the Ministry of Law and Justice and the Ministry of Chemicals and Fertilizers under the Rajiv Gandhi administration to respond to the unprecedented legal vacuum created by the catastrophe.

• Parliamentary Passage: Introduced as an emergency legislative measure, debated swiftly, and passed by both Houses of Parliament (Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha) during the budget session of 1985.

• Presidential Assent: Enforced on March 29, 1985.

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of The National Commission for Homoeopathy Act, 2020
Overview
*Act Name: The National Commission for Homoeopathy Act, 2020 *Key Focus: Regulating Homoeopathy education, practice, and research in India, emphasizing standardized quality and ethical practices. *Governance: Establishes the National Commission for Homoeopathy (NCH) with autonomous boards, under the Central Government's regulatory oversight.
Core Objectives
1.	Quality Education: Ensure uniform, quality Homoeopathy education nationwide.
2.	Standardized Practice: Set and enforce standards for Homoeopathy professionals.
3.	Ethical Compliance: Promote and regulate ethical practices in Homoeopathy.
4.	Integrated Healthcare Contribution: Strengthen Homoeopathy's role in India's healthcare system.
5.	Structured Governance: With clear roles for NCH, autonomous boards, and the Central Government.
Governance Structure
1.	National Commission for Homoeopathy (NCH):
•	Appointment: By the Central Government, with defined eligibility.
•	Roles: Oversight, policy, regulation, and standard setting in Homoeopathy.
2.	Autonomous Boards: - Education Board: For curriculum and education standards.
•	Medical Assessment & Rating Board: For institution evaluation.
•	Ethics & Registration Board: For practitioner ethics and registration.
•	Specific Responsibilities: Outlined for each, ensuring comprehensive coverage.
Key Provisions
•	Membership & Elections:
•	Clear Eligibility: For Central Council members, with succession planning allowed within three months before term expiry.
•	Term Management: Defined terms, ensuring continuity and preventing gaps.
•	Meetings & Decision Making:
•	Scheduled Meetings: At least annually for the Central Council, with defined quorum and majority voting.
•	Committee Operations: Similar structure for committees, ensuring efficiency.
•	Registration & Practice:
•	Mandatory Registration: For all practitioners, with national and state registers.
•	Continuous Professional Development: Encouraged for updated practices.
•	Disciplinary & Ethical Framework:
•	Clear Procedures: For addressing unethical practice or misconduct.
•	Appeal Mechanisms: Ensuring fairness in disciplinary actions.
•	Administrative & Transitional:
•	Rule Making Authority: Rests with the Central Government, with parliamentary oversight.
•	Smooth Transition: From the repealed Homoeopathy Central Council Act, 1973, protecting existing rights.
Transition & Repeal
•	Repeal of Old Act: With protective clauses for existing registrations and seamless transition.
•	Transitory Measures: Ensuring no gap in regulatory and governance functions during the transition.

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of the Voluntary Surrender of Salaries (Exemption from Taxation) Act, 1961
Key Provisions
1.	Exemption from Income Tax: - Salaries Surrendered in Public Interest: No income-tax or super-tax shall be payable on the portion of the salary voluntarily surrendered in the public interest by an individual, if:
•	Paid out of the Consolidated Fund of India or a State, and surrendered after 31st March 1961 via a written declaration.
•	Surrendered to the Central Government in accordance with rules, in other cases.
•	Such surrendered salary shall not be included in the total income for taxation purposes.
2.	Application to Allowances: - Provisions of Section 2 (regarding exemption) also apply to allowances due after 31st March 1961.

•	Power to Make Rules: Central Government can make rules to carry out the Act's purposes, subject to parliamentary oversight.
•	Repeal: Repeals the Voluntary Surrender of Salaries (Exemption from Taxation) Act, 1950, with a provision for declarations under the repealed Act to be deemed valid under this Act.

Summary of the Central Universities Act, 2009 
Key Provisions
1. Establishment of Universities: The Act establishes Central Universities in various states, transforming existing universities or establishing new ones.

2. Governance Structure:
•	Chancellor: Usually a dignitary (e.g., the Minister of Education).
•	Vice-Chancellor: The chief executive officer, appointed by the Visitor (typically the President of India) from a panel.
•	Authorities: Include the Court (the supreme governing body), Executive Council, Academic Council, and Finance Committee.
3. Academic and Administrative Autonomy: Universities have the power to make Statutes, Ordinances, and Regulations for their governance and academic affairs.
4. Financial Provisions: Universities are funded by the Central Government, with provisions for fund management and annual reporting.
5. Transitional Provisions: For the smooth transition of existing universities to the new framework, including the continuation of students, staff, and ongoing academic programs.
6. Protection and Miscellaneous:
•	Protection of Action Taken in Good Faith.
•	Power to Remove Difficulties: Temporarily, to address unforeseen challenges.
7. Repeal and Savings: Repeals previous acts (where applicable) with savings for actions taken under those acts.

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of the Depositories Act, 1996 
Key Provisions
•	Establishment and Regulation of Depositories: The Act provides for the establishment and regulation of depositories, which hold securities in electronic form and facilitate their transfer. A depository can commence business only after obtaining a certificate of registration from the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI). 
•	Dematerialisation and Rematerialisation: The Act enables investors to convert physical securities into electronic form (dematerialisation) and, where permitted, reconvert electronic holdings into physical certificates (rematerialisation). 
•	Depository Participants (DPs): Investors access depository services through Depository Participants, who act as intermediaries between the depository and the beneficial owner. 
•	Rights of Beneficial Owners: While the depository is recorded as the registered owner of the securities for the limited purpose of effecting transfers, the beneficial owner retains all rights and benefits attached to the securities, including voting rights, dividends, and other entitlements. 
•	Transfer of Securities: The Act provides for the transfer of securities through electronic book entries, eliminating the need for physical transfer deeds and certificates. 
•	Pledge and Hypothecation: It enables securities held in a depository to be pledged or hypothecated in accordance with prescribed procedures. 
•	Records and Inspection: Depositories are required to maintain accurate records, and SEBI is empowered to inspect and regulate their operations. 
•	Rule-making and Regulations: The Central Government may make rules, while SEBI may make regulations for implementing the provisions of the Act.

ACT NO. 22 OF 1996

[10th August, 1996.]

An Act to provide for regulation of depositories in securities and for matters connected therewith or incidental thereto.

meta.dc.legislation.history:
Legislative History:

The Depositories Act, 1996

Short Title The Depositories Act, 1996

Act Number / Year 22 of 1996

Act ID (India Code) 199622

Presidential Assent / Enactment Date August 10, 1996

Enforcement Date September 20, 1995

Nodal Ministry Ministry of Finance

Precedent & Statutory Rationale

• Inefficiencies and Risks of Physical Paper Trading:

o Prior to the mid-1990s, India’s securities market relied entirely on physical paper documentation. Every share transfer required manual handling, physical delivery, and re-registration with corporate issuers.

o This manual workflow resulted in chronic settlement delays, high transaction costs, rampant risks of document loss, theft, mutilation, signature mismatches, and fraudulent or forged share certificates.

• Legislative Intervention and Regularization:

o Enacted to overhaul financial market infrastructure, the 1996 Act created a robust legal framework enabling securities to be held, traded, and transferred in electronic, fungible form through registered depositories (such as NSDL and CSDL).

o The core objectives include eliminating paper-based settlement backlogs, granting full legal recognition to "beneficial owners," protecting investors from fraud, and aligning India’s capital market standards with advanced global electronic clearing networks.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

• Formulation: Conceived by the Ministry of Finance and regulatory authorities to support economic liberalization policies and modernize India's rapidly growing capital markets. Prior to the formal parliamentary statute, the framework was given early legal effect via successive ordinances (culminating in the Depositories Third Ordinance, 1996).

• Parliamentary Passage: Introduced as the Depositories Bill in the Lok Sabha, passed by both houses of Parliament in July 1996, and granted formal presidential assent on August 10, 1996.

• Enforcement: Enforced on September 20, 1995.

• Source: India Code (indiacode.gov.in), Ministry of Finance Official Records, and Parliament of India Records.

Key Provisions
•	Acquisition of Textile Undertakings: The Act provides for the acquisition of the specified textile undertakings by the Central Government, free from encumbrances, on the appointed day. 
•	Transfer to the National Textile Corporation: The acquired undertakings are vested in the National Textile Corporation (NTC) or in a government company nominated by the Central Government for their management and operation. 
•	Management and Administration: The NTC is empowered to manage, operate, modernise, and develop the acquired undertakings to ensure their efficient functioning and revival. 
•	Compensation: The Act provides for the payment of compensation to the owners of the acquired undertakings in the manner specified under the Act. 
•	Protection of Employees: The services of employees of the acquired undertakings generally continue without interruption, subject to the terms and conditions specified in the Act. 
•	Pending Liabilities and Legal Proceedings: The Act contains provisions regarding the treatment of liabilities, contracts, legal proceedings, and obligations relating to the acquired undertakings. 
•	Rule-making Power: The Central Government is empowered to make rules for carrying out the provisions of the Act.

THE TEXTILE UNDERTAKINGS (NATIONALISATION) ACT, 1995
ACT NO. 39 OF 1995

[8th September, 1995.]

An Act to provide for the acquisition and transfer of the textile undertakings, and the right, title and interest of the owners in respect of the textile undertakings, specified in the First Schedule with a view to augmenting the production and distribution of different varieties of cloth and yarn so as to subserve the interests of the general public and for matters connected therewith or incidental thereto.
WHEREAS the textile companies specified in column (3) of the First Schedule have, through their undertakings specified in column (2) of the said Schedule, been engaged in the manufacture and production of different varieties of cloth and yarn;
AND WHEREAS, pending acquisition, the management of the said textile undertakings was taken over by the Central Government under section 3 of the Textile Undertakings (Taking Over of Management) Act, 1983 (40 of 1983)or under section 3 of the Laxmirattan and Atherton West Cotton Mills (Taking Over of Management) Act, 1976 (98 of 1976), as the case may be;
AND WHEREAS large sums of money have been invested with a view to making the said textile undertakings viable;
AND WHEREAS further investment of very large sums of money is necessary for the purpose of securing the optimum utilisation of the available facilities for the manufacture, production and distribution of cloth and yarn by the said textile undertakings of the companies;
AND WHEREAS such investment is also necessary for securing the continued employment of the workmen employed in the said textile undertakings;
AND WHEREAS it is necessary in the public interest to acquire the said textile undertakings of the textile companies to ensure that the interest of the general public are served by the continuance by the said undertakings of the companies of the manufacture, production and distribution of different varieties of cloth and yarn which are vital to the needs of the country;
BE it enacted by Parliament in the Forty-sixth Year of the Republic of India as follows:--

The Textile Undertakings (Nationalisation) Act, 1995

Act Title The Textile Undertakings (Nationalisation) Act, 1995

Act Number 39 of 1995

Act ID (India Code) 199539

Presidential Assent Date September 8, 1995

Enforcement Date Sections 31 and 32 came into force at once; remaining provisions deemed effective from April 1, 1994

Nodal Ministry Ministry of Textiles

Precedent & Historical Rationale

1. Prolonged Management Takeover:

o Prior to 1995, the management of several financially distressed or sick textile undertakings across the country had been taken over by the Central Government under specific preceding laws, such as the Textile Undertakings (Taking Over of Management) Act, 1983, and the Laxmirattan and Atherton West Cotton Mills (Taking Over of Management) Act, 1976.

2. Augmenting Production and Protecting Public Interest:

o To secure the long-term viability of these sick mills, protect employment, and systematically augment the production and distribution of mass-varieties of cloth and yarn at fair prices, the government transitioned from temporary management takeover to outright nationalization. The Act transferred ownership, rights, and interests of specified textile undertakings directly to the Central Government, which subsequently vested them in the National Textile Corporation (NTC).

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

• Formulation: Preceded by an Ordinance framework (The Textile Undertakings (Nationalisation) Ordinance, 1995), the Bill was drafted by the Ministry of Textiles to formalize the acquisition of specific sick textile mills listed in its schedules.

• Parliamentary Passage: Introduced and debated during the monsoon session of Parliament, securing passage in both the Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha in September 1995.

• Presidential Assent: Received Presidential Assent on September 8, 1995.

• Enforcement: Enforced on April 1, 1994.

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of the Technology Development Board Act, 1995 
Key Provisions
•	Establishment of the Technology Development Board: The Act provides for the incorporation of the Technology Development Board as a body corporate with perpetual succession and a common seal. 
•	Functions of the Board: The Board is empowered to promote the development and commercial application of indigenous technology and the adaptation of imported technology by providing financial and other support. 
•	Financial Assistance: The Board may provide assistance in the form of loans, equity participation, grants, or other financial support to industrial concerns, research institutions, and other eligible entities for technology development and commercialisation projects. 
•	Management of the Board: The Act provides for the composition of the Board, including its Chairperson and members representing the Government, scientific community, industry, and financial institutions, and prescribes their powers and functions. 
•	Fund of the Board: The Act establishes a dedicated fund for the Board, consisting of grants, loans, recoveries, and other receipts, to finance its activities. 
•	Accounts and Audit: The Board is required to maintain proper accounts, prepare annual statements, and have its accounts audited in accordance with the Act. 
•	Rule-making Power: The Central Government is empowered to make rules for carrying out the provisions of the Act.

title: The Provisions of the Panchayats (Extension to the Scheduled Areas) Act, 1996

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of the Provisions of the Panchayats (Extension to the Scheduled Areas) Act, 1996 
Objectives of the Act
•	To extend the provisions of Part IX of the Constitution to the Scheduled Areas with appropriate modifications. 
•	To promote self-governance and democratic decentralisation in tribal areas. 
•	To safeguard the traditions, customs, cultural identity, and customary rights of Scheduled Tribes. 
•	To empower Gram Sabhas in the management of natural resources and local development. 
Key Provisions
•	Extension of Panchayati Raj: The Act extends the provisions of Part IX of the Constitution to the Scheduled Areas, subject to modifications specified in the Act. 
•	Empowerment of Gram Sabhas: The Gram Sabha is recognised as the foundational institution of local self-government and is vested with significant powers to safeguard and preserve community resources, traditions, customs, and cultural identity. 
•	Consultation and Consent: The Act requires consultation with, or in specified cases the recommendation of, the Gram Sabha or Panchayats before matters such as land acquisition, rehabilitation of displaced persons, grant of mining leases, and development projects in Scheduled Areas are undertaken, as provided under the Act and applicable laws. 
•	Control over Community Resources: Gram Sabhas and Panchayats are entrusted with powers relating to the management of community resources, minor water bodies, minor forest produce, village markets, and local institutions, in accordance with State laws. 
•	Customary Laws and Practices: The Act recognises and seeks to preserve customary law, social and religious practices, and traditional methods of dispute resolution of tribal communities, provided they are consistent with the Constitution. 
•	State Legislation: States having Scheduled Areas are required to amend their Panchayati Raj laws to bring them into conformity with the provisions of the Act.

Legislative History:

The Provisions of the Panchayats (Extension to the Scheduled Areas) Act, 1996

Short Title The Provisions of the Panchayats (Extension to the Scheduled Areas) Act, 1996 (PESA)

Act Number / Year 40 of 1996

Act ID (India Code) 199640

Presidential Assent / Enactment Date December 24, 1996

Enforcement Date December 24, 1996

Nodal Ministry Ministry of Panchayati Raj

Precedent & Statutory Rationale

• Marginalization and Exclusion of Tribal Self-Governance:

o Following the landmark 73rd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1992 which established the three-tier Panchayati Raj system, Article 243M explicitly excluded the Scheduled Areas (Fifth Schedule areas) from its routine purview due to distinct cultural, social, and traditional management practices of indigenous tribal communities.

o Without a tailored framework, tribal populations faced systemic disconnects, lacking formal statutory backing to run local governance through their traditional village assemblies.

• Legislative Intervention and Regularization:

o Enacted following the recommendations of the Bhuria Committee, the 1948-successor spirit culminated in an empowering mechanism ensuring self-governance for people living in Scheduled Areas.

o The core objective was to vest supreme authority in the Gram Sabha regarding the preservation of community resources, management of minor forest produce, prevention of land alienation, enforcement of local excise regulations, and approval of social/economic development plans.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

• Formulation: Conceptualized via constitutional provisions (Article 243M(4)(b)) and structured through extensive committee reviews to safeguard indigenous customary laws and social practices.

• Parliamentary Passage: Processed and passed by both houses of Parliament, securing formal presidential assent on December 24, 1996.

• Enforcement: Enforced on December 24, 1996.

Source: India Code and Ministry of Panchayati Raj Official Records.

Summary of the Manipur Municipalities Act, 1994 
Key Provisions
•	Constitution of Municipalities: The Act provides for the constitution of Municipal Councils and Nagar Panchayats for different categories of urban areas in the State, based on population and other prescribed criteria. 
•	Composition and Elections: Members of Municipalities are elected through direct elections from territorial wards. The Act also provides for the election of Chairpersons and Vice-Chairpersons in accordance with its provisions. 
•	Reservation of Seats: It provides for reservation of seats and offices for Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes, women, and other categories, in accordance with constitutional requirements. 
•	Powers and Functions: Municipalities are entrusted with responsibilities relating to urban planning, regulation of land use, roads and bridges, water supply, public health, sanitation, solid waste management, street lighting, environmental protection, urban poverty alleviation, and other matters specified in the Twelfth Schedule to the Constitution. 
•	Municipal Finance: The Act provides for municipal funds, taxation powers, fees, grants, budgeting, maintenance of accounts, and audit to ensure financial sustainability and accountability. 
•	Committees and Administration: It contains provisions relating to municipal committees, officers, employees, meetings, decision-making processes, and administrative procedures. 
•	State Election Commission and State Finance Commission: The Act gives effect to the constitutional provisions regarding the conduct of municipal elections by the State Election Commission and financial devolution based on the recommendations of the State Finance Commission.

THE MANIPUR MUNICIPALITIES ACT, 1994
ACT NO. 43 OF 1994

[8th July, 1994.]

An Act to provide for constitution and organisation of municipalities in the Urban areas of Manipur and for matters connected therewith and incidental thereto.
BE it enacted by Parliament in the Forty-fifth Year of the Republic of India as follows:--
meta.dc.legislation.history:
Legislative History:

The Manipur Municipalities Act, 1994

● Act Title - The Manipur Municipalities Act, 1994

● Act Number / Year - 43 of 1994

● Act ID (India Code) - 199443

● Assent Date - July 8, 1994

● Enforcement Date - May 24, 1994

● Nodal Ministry - Ministry of Home Affairs

Precedent & Historical Rationale

● Constitutional Mandate of the 74th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1992 - With the enactment of the Constitution (Seventy-fourth Amendment) Act, 1992, Part IXA was inserted into the Constitution of India, creating a mandatory constitutional architecture for urban local governance. State laws were constitutionally required to conform to Part IXA by introducing a three-tier municipal system (Nagar Panchayats, Municipal Councils, and Municipal Corporations), ensuring fixed five-year tenures, mandating statutory reservations for Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes, and women (not less than one-third of seats), and providing for independent State Election Commissions and State Finance Commissions.

● Parliamentary Enactment for Manipur under President's Rule (Article 356) - Manipur was under President's Rule under Article 356 of the Constitution from December 31, 1993, to December 13, 1994, which vested the legislative powers of the State Legislature in the Parliament of India pursuant to Article 357. To replace the outdated Assam Municipal Act, 1956 (as previously extended and adapted in Manipur) with a modern municipal code conforming to Part IXA within the mandatory constitutional deadline, Parliament directly formulated and enacted a comprehensive municipal law for the State of Manipur.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

● Formulation & Introduction - Drafted by the Ministry of Home Affairs in coordination with the Ministry of Urban Development and the Administration of Manipur to satisfy constitutional obligations under Part IXA during President's Rule; introduced as The Manipur Municipalities Bill, 1994 in the Rajya Sabha during the Budget Session of 1994.

● Parliamentary Passage - Debated and passed by the Rajya Sabha on June 14, 1994, and considered, debated, and passed by the Lok Sabha on June 15, 1994.

● President's Assent - Received the assent of the President of India (Dr. Shankar Dayal Sharma) on July 8, 1994, and was published in the Gazette of India on July 11, 1994.

● Enforcement - Enforced on May 24, 1994.

Sources - Parliamentary Debates (Lok Sabha & Rajya Sabha), The Gazette of India, India Code, and Ministry of Home Affairs.

title: The Prasar Bharati (Broadcasting Corporation of India) Act, 1990

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of the Prasar Bharati (Broadcasting Corporation of India) Act, 1990:
Objective
•	Establish the Prasar Bharati (Broadcasting Corporation of India)
•	Define its composition, functions, and powers
Key Provisions
1.	Establishment
•	Prasar Bharati (Broadcasting Corporation of India) established by the Central Government
•	Body corporate with perpetual succession and a common seal
•	Headquarters in New Delhi with potential offices elsewhere in India and abroad (with Central Government approval)
2.	Composition of the Board
•	Chairman
•	Executive Member
•	Member (Finance)
•	Member (Personnel)
•	6 Part-time Members
•	Ex Officio Members:
•	Director-General (Akashvani)
•	Director-General (Doordarshan)
•	Representatives:
•	1 from the Union Ministry of Information and Broadcasting
•	2 from the employees of the Corporation (elected)
3.	Appointments
•	Chairman and other Members (except ex officio, nominated, and elected members) appointed by the President of India on the recommendation of a committee.
•	Committee for Recommendations consists of:
•	Chairman of the Council of States (Chairman of the Committee)
•	Chairman of the Press Council of India
•	Nominee of the President of India
4.	Term of Office
•	Chairman: Part-time, 3 years or until 70 years of age, whichever is earlier.
•	Whole-time Members (Executive, Finance, Personnel): 6 years or until 62 years of age (for Finance and Personnel), 5 years or until 65 years of age (for Executive, as amended).
•	Part-time Members: 6 years, with one-third retiring every 2 years.
•	Elected Members: 2 years or until they cease to be employees.
5.	Powers and Functions
•	Executive Member: Chief Executive, exercises powers delegated by the Board.
•	Board: General superintendence, direction, and management of the Corporation.
6.	Removal and Suspension
•	Chairman and Members (except ex officio, nominated, and elected) can only be removed by the President of India on the ground of misbehavior after a Supreme Court inquiry.
•	Suspension possible pending inquiry.
7.	Other
•	Committees and Associations: Corporation can form committees and associate persons for advice.
•	Immunity of Proceedings: No act of the Board or committee invalidated by vacancies, defects in constitution, or appointment irregularities (unless affecting the merits of the case).

THE PRASAR BHARATI (BROADCASTING CORPORATION OF INDIA) ACT, 1990
ACT NO. 25 OF 1990

[12th September, 1990.]

An Act to provide for the establishment of a Broadcasting Corporation for India, to be known as Prasar Bharati, to define its composition, functions and powers and to provide for matters connected therewith or incidental thereto.
BE it enacted by Parliament in the Forty-first Year of the Republic of India as follows:--
meta.dc.identifier.reference_sites: Ministry of Information and Broadcasting https://mib.gov.in/en
meta.dc.legislation.history:
Legislative History:

The Prasar Bharati (Broadcasting Corporation of India) Act, 1990

Short Title The Prasar Bharati (Broadcasting Corporation of India) Act, 1990

Act Number / Year 25 of 1990

Act ID (India Code) 199025

Presidential Assent Date September 12, 1990

Enforcement Date September 15, 1997

Nodal Ministry Ministry of Information and Broadcasting, Government of India

Precedent & Statutory Rationale

• Background/Transition:

Prior to 1990, India's public broadcasting networks—All India Radio and Doordarshan—operated directly under government control as media units of the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting. Following growing demands from civil society, media experts, and various parliamentary committees (such as the Verghese Committee) for editorial autonomy, freedom from political executive interference, and credible public service broadcasting akin to the BBC, Parliament sought to establish an independent statutory corporation.

• Rationale/Objectives:

The Act was enacted by Parliament to provide for the establishment of a Broadcasting Corporation of India, to be known as Prasar Bharati, and to define its composition, functions, and powers. Its core purpose was to transform state-controlled media into an autonomous public service broadcaster tasked with informing, educating, and entertaining the public impartially, while ensuring balance, objectivity, and freedom of expression.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Legislative Milestones

• Formulation/Introduction:

Introduced by the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting to grant statutory autonomy to state broadcasting media, fulfilling long-standing democratic aspirations for independent public media.

• Legislative Passage & Assent:

Passed by both Houses of Parliament and received presidential assent on September 12, 1990. (Note: Although enacted in 1990, due to subsequent political shifts and administrative reviews, the Act was brought into formal force only on September 15, 1997).

• Statutory Mechanics & Provisions:

o Establishment of Prasar Bharati: Created Prasar Bharati as a body corporate having perpetual succession and a common seal, comprising All India Radio and Doordarshan as its constituent units.

o Composition of the Board: Structured the Prasar Bharati Board to include a Chairperson, an Executive Member, a Member (Finance), a Member (Personnel), six part-time members, representing diverse public interests, alongside ex-officio representatives.

o Objectives and Charter: Mandated the Corporation to uphold the unity and integrity of the country, safeguard democratic values, provide balanced news coverage, promote social justice, and foster national integration.

o Broadcasting Council: Provided for the establishment of a Parliamentary Committee and a Broadcasting Council to receive and consider public complaints regarding the content and quality of broadcasts.

• Presidential Assent: Received Presidential Assent on September 12, 1990.

• Enforcement: Enforced on September 15, 1990.

Source: India Code Official Repository (indiacode.gov.in) and Ministry of Information and Broadcasting, Government of India Official Records.

title: The Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of the Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992
Overview
Enactment: By Parliament in the Forty-third Year of the Republic of India Commencement:
•	Sections 11 to 14 came into force at once.
•	Remaining provisions deemed to have come into force on 19th June, 1992.
Key Provisions 
1.	Powers of Central Government
•	Make Orders for developing and regulating foreign trade (Imports & Exports).
•	Prohibit, restrict, or regulate imports/exports of goods, services, or technology.
•	Formulate and announce Foreign Trade Policy (FTP) and amend it.
2.	Director General of Foreign Trade
•	Appointment by Central Government.
•	Advises on FTP formulation and is responsible for its implementation.
•	May be delegated certain powers by the Central Government.
3.	Definitions
•	Import/Export: Broadly defined for goods, services, and technology, with specific clauses for services and technology.
•	Services/Technology: Defined with clarity on what constitutes supply/import/export.
•	Other key definitions: Adjudicating Authority, Appellate Authority, Conveyance, etc.
4.	Regulatory Framework
•	Licenses: Not necessary unless required under this Act or its rules/orders.
•	Prohibitions/Restrictions: Goods under prohibition/regulation deemed so under the Customs Act, 1962.
•	Continuance of Existing Orders: Orders under the Imports and Exports (Control) Act, 1947, continue unless inconsistent.
5.	Repeal and Savings
•	Repeals the Imports and Exports (Control) Act, 1947, and the Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Ordinance, 1992.
•	Savings clause for previous operations, rights, and liabilities under the repealed Acts.
6.	Penalty, Confiscation, and Adjudication
•	Power of Search and Seizure (mentioned but details not provided in the context).
•	Contraventions: Lead to penalty/confiscation (details not provided).
•	Adjudicating Authority: Established for deciding on contraventions.
•	Owner's Opportunity: Right to be heard before action on seized goods.

The Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992

Short Title The Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992

Act Number / Year 22 of 1992

Act ID (India Code) 199222

Presidential Assent / Enactment Date August 7, 1992

Enforcement Date June 19, 1992

Nodal Ministry Ministry of Commerce and Industry

Precedent & Statutory Rationale

• Transition from Control-Oriented Regime to Liberalization:

o Prior to 1992, India’s foreign trade was stringently controlled under the Imports and Exports (Control) Act, 1947, a restrictive framework designed primarily for a command-style economy with absolute government oversight over physical imports and exports.

o Following the sweeping economic reforms of 1991, India shifted its policy paradigm toward globalization, export-led growth, and integration with the world economy, rendering the old control-centric framework obsolete.

• Legislative Intervention and Regularization:

o Enacted to provide a modern statutory foundation focused on the development and regulation of foreign trade rather than mere restrictions.

o The core objective was to empower the Central Government to formulate and announce the Foreign Trade Policy (FTP), facilitate imports, augment exports, introduce the mandatory Importer-Exporter Code (IEC), and regulate specific cross-border transactions smoothly.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

• Formulation: Developed by the Ministry of Commerce to institutionalize structural trade reforms and provide legal teeth to export promotion schemes and trade facilitation procedures.

• Parliamentary Passage: Passed by both houses of Parliament, receiving formal presidential assent on August 7, 1992.

• Enforcement: Enforced on June 19, 1992.

• Source: India Code and Ministry of Commerce and Industry Official Records.

ACT NO. 1 OF 1992

[2nd January, 1992.]

meta.dc.legislation.history:
Legislative History:

The Government of National Capital Territory of Delhi Act, 1991

Short Title The Government of National Capital Territory of Delhi Act, 1991

Act Number / Year Act No. 1 of 1992 (Passed in late 1991, assented to in January 1992)

Act ID (India Code) 199201

Presidential Assent / Enactment Date January 2, 1992

Enforcement Date February 1, 1992

Nodal Ministry Ministry of Home Affairs

Precedent & Statutory Rationale

• Evolution of Delhi's Governance and the 69th Amendment:

o Prior to 1992, the Union Territory of Delhi was administered by the Central Government through a Chief Commissioner or Lieutenant Governor, operating under advisory assemblies or metropolitan councils with limited legislative power (such as the Delhi Administration Act, 1966).

o To satisfy long-standing democratic aspirations for representative self-governance, Parliament enacted the Constitution (Sixty-Ninth Amendment) Act, 1991, inserting Article 239AA into the Constitution to designate Delhi as the "National Capital Territory of Delhi" (NCT).

• Legislative Intervention and Regularization:

o Enacted to give statutory effect to Article 239AA, the 1991 Act established the legislative assembly, council of ministers, and executive administrative machinery for the NCT of Delhi.

o The core objectives include defining the powers of the Legislative Assembly to make laws for matters in the State and Concurrent Lists (except specific reserved subjects like public order, land, and police), establishing the Chief Minister and Council of Ministers to aid and advise the Lieutenant Governor, and setting mechanisms for resolving differences between the Lieutenant Governor and the elected government.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

• Formulation: Drafted by the Ministry of Home Affairs to operationalize the federal and administrative architecture mandated by the 69th Constitutional Amendment, balancing Delhi's dual identity as both a national capital and a representative local state.

• Parliamentary Passage: Introduced in Parliament during the winter session of 1991, reviewed by legislative committees, passed by both the Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha, and granted formal presidential assent on January 2, 1992.

• Enforcement: Brought into force on February 1, 1992, marking the formal institutional birth of the modern elected legislative assembly and government administration for the National Capital Territory of Delhi.

• Presidential Assent: Received Presidential Assent on January 2, 1992.

• Enforcement: Enforced on February 1, 1992.
