title: The Medical Termination of Pregnancy Act, 1971

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of The Medical Termination of Pregnancy Act, 1971
Purpose
•	To legally regulate the termination of pregnancies under specified conditions and by registered medical practitioners.
Key Provisions
1.	Gestational Limits for Termination: - Up to 20 weeks: Requires the opinion of one registered medical practitioner.
•	20-24 weeks: Needs the opinion of two registered medical practitioners, limited to prescribed categories of women.
•	Beyond 24 weeks: Only permissible if substantial foetal abnormalities are confirmed by a constituted Medical Board.
2.	Medical Board: - Established by each State/Union Territory.
•	Comprises specialists (Gynaecologist, Paediatrician, Radiologist/Sonologist, etc.).
•	Mandated to diagnose substantial foetal abnormalities for late-term terminations.
3.	Authorized Facilities: - Government hospitals.
•	Places approved by the Government or a District Level Committee.
4.	Consent Requirements: - Minors/Mentally Ill: Written consent from a guardian.
•	Others: Consent of the pregnant woman.
5.	Confidentiality: - Practitioners must maintain patient confidentiality.
•	Breach punishable by up to 1 year imprisonment, fine, or both.
6.	Legal Safeguards: - Good Faith Protection: Immunity for actions taken in good faith.
•	Penalties for Illegal Terminations: 2-7 years imprisonment for unauthorized practitioners or unapproved locations.
7.	Administrative Framework: - Central Government: Empowered to make rules.
•	State Governments: Authority to make regulations and form Medical Boards.
Important Provisions
•	Section 3: Outlines conditions for legal termination.
•	Section 4: Specifies approved locations for the procedure.
•	Section 5A: Ensures patient privacy.
•	Section 8: Protects good faith actions.

title: The Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of The Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985 
Overview
•	The Act harmonizes the regulation, control, and prohibition of narcotic drugs and psychotropic substances in India, ensuring consistency between central and state government oversight. Ensures that any restrictions or punishments imposed under this Act for the cultivation of cannabis, consumption of, or traffic in, any narcotic drug or psychotropic substance within India are not less stringent than those for corresponding offenses, reflecting a unified approach to drug regulation.
Key Provisions 
1.	Unified Enforcement Framework: - Sections 82 & 83: While repealing predecessor acts and providing for the resolution of implementation difficulties, these sections underscore the Act's role in standardizing regulatory practices across the country.
2.	Integrated Legislation with Enhanced Consistency: - Sections 79, 80, & 81: These ensure seamless integration with the Customs Act, 1962, the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940, and the validation of stricter state laws, all aligned with the principle of not imposing less stringent measures than those for comparable offenses under this Act.
3.	State Government's Aligned Rule-Making Power (Section 78):
•	Empowers States to make rules that are consistent with the central framework, for supply of substances for medical necessity and management of treatment centres, avoiding discrepancies.
Substance Regulation and Scheduling with Penalty Alignment
•	The Schedule & General Provisions: Together, they list and regulate specific psychotropic substances and all narcotic drugs, with controls on cultivation, manufacture, possession, and trade, where penalties for violations are calibrated to ensure they are not less severe than those for analogous offenses under the Act.
Penalties and Judicial Aspects with Enhanced Uniformity
•	Penal Provisions: Imposing uniform and stringent penalties across the board for violations, including external dealings and repeated offenses, to maintain national regulatory coherence.
•	Judicial and Procedural Measures: Establishment of special courts and standardized procedures for seized substance disposal, reflecting a consistent judicial approach.

Legislative History:

The Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985

Act Title - The Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985

Act Number/Year - 61 of 1985

Presidential Assent Date - September 16, 1985

Precedent & Historical Rationale

International Obligations and Conventions:

Prior to the mid-1980s, the legal framework governing addictive substances in India was archaic and fragmented, primarily regulated by colonial-era legislations such as the Opium Act, 1857, the Opium Act, 1878, and the Dangerous Drugs Act, 1930. These laws proved inadequate to combat modern, highly organized international drug trafficking networks. Furthermore, India was a signatory to key global treaties, including the Single Convention on Narcotic Drugs (1961) and the Convention on Psychotropic Substances (1971), which necessitated comprehensive and stringent domestic legislation to fulfill international commitments.

Surge in Illicit Drug Trafficking and Abuse:

The evolving dynamics of transit drug trafficking (such as the shifting routes of the "Golden Crescent") and rising domestic addiction rates highlighted systemic loopholes in older statutes, which carried relatively lenient penalties and lacked provisions for asset forfeiture. Addressing these loopholes required a consolidated, heavy-handed statutory deterrent.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

Formulation:

Drafted comprehensively by the executive branch to consolidate multiple obsolete laws, introduce severe deterrent penalties, empower specialized enforcement agencies, and establish strict controls over the production, manufacture, possession, sale, purchase, and transport of narcotic drugs and psychotropic substances.

Parliamentary Passage: Introduced in the Lok Sabha on August 23, 1985, and subsequently debated and passed by both Houses of Parliament.

Presidential Assent: Received Presidential Assent on September 16, 1985.

Enforcement: Enforced on November 14, 1985.

Source: Official Records of Parliament, India Code, and Ministry of Finance (Department of Revenue).

title: The Representation of the People Act, 1951

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of Representation of the People Act, 1951 

Summary 

Purpose
•	To provide for the conduct of elections to the Houses of Parliament and the House(s) of the Legislature of each State.
•	To outline qualifications and disqualifications for membership in these Houses.
•	To define corrupt practices and other election-related offenses.
•	To establish the process for resolving election-related doubts and disputes.

Key Components 

1.	Structure: - Part I: Preliminary - Short title, Interpretation.
•	Part II: Qualifications and Disqualifications - For Parliament, State Legislatures, and Voting.
•	Part III: Notification of General Elections.
•	Other Sections (referenced): Power to make rules, Jurisdiction of civil courts barred.
2.	Qualifications and Disqualifications: - Qualifications for Membership:
•	Parliament (Council of States, House of the People).
•	State Legislatures (Legislative Assembly, Legislative Council).
•	Disqualifications:
•	For Membership of Parliament and State Legislatures (e.g., conviction for certain offenses, corrupt practices, government contracts).
•	For Voting (conviction, corrupt practices).
3.	Corrupt Practices: - Defined in Section 123 (context not fully provided, but mentioned in interpretations).
•	Includes propagation or glorification of "sati" as a corrupt practice (as per the amendment in a1958_03.pdf).
4.	Election-Related:
•	Notification for Elections (e.g., biennial election to the Council of States).
•	Amendments (referenced in other documents) to provide for disqualification periods post-conviction and for glorification of "sati" as a corrupt practice.
Limitations of the Summary 

•	The provided context is fragmented across multiple files, focusing more on amendments and related acts rather than the entirety of the RAPI, 1951.
•	Key sections (e.g., detailed corrupt practices in Section 123, full scope of Part III) are not fully contextualized.

Amendments and Related Acts Referenced

•	Representation of the People (Amendment) Act, 1966.
•	Representation of the People (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act, 1956.
•	Impacts from The Delimitation Act, 2002, and others, indicating the Act's evolution over time.

title: The Securities and Exchange Board of India Act, 1992

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of the Securities and Exchange Board of India Act, 1992
1. Securities and Exchange Board of India Act, 1992 (SEBI Act, 1992)
*Purpose: Establishes the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) to regulate and develop the securities market, protect investor interests, and ensure fair market practices. *Key Provisions:
•	Establishment & Management: SEBI is a body corporate with a Chairman, whole-time members, and part-time members, overseeing market regulation.
•	Powers & Functions: Includes regulating securities markets, issuing directions, conducting investigations, and imposing penalties for non-compliance.
•	Penalties & Offences: Specifies penalties for various violations (e.g., failure to furnish returns, insider trading), with amounts detailed in amendments (e.g., ₹5 lakh to ₹25 crore for certain offences).
•	Judicial Mechanism: References the establishment of Special Courts for securities-related offences.
2. Securities Contracts (Regulation) Act, 1956 (SCR Act, 1956)
*Relevant Summary from Context: *Key Provisions (Penalties & Regulations):
•	Penalties for Non-Compliance:
•	Failure to furnish periodical returns or comply with SEBI directions: ₹5 lakh to ₹25 crore.
•	Failure to conduct business as per SEBI rules: ₹5 crore to ₹25 crore or 3 times the gains.
•	Stock Exchange Governance: Regulations for recognition, corporatisation, and demutualisation of stock exchanges.
3. Special Court (Trial of Offences Relating to Transactions in Securities) Act, 1992
*Summary: *Key Provisions:
•	Establishment of Special Court: Comprises sitting High Court Judges for trial of securities offences.
•	Hearing and Orders: Special Court hears parties and makes orders as deemed fit, especially concerning notifications, cancellations, or orders related to securities transactions.
•	Timeframe for Action: Actions must be taken within thirty days of the issuance of such notifications, cancellations, or orders.

The Securities and Exchange Board of India Act, 1992

Short Title The Securities and Exchange Board of India Act, 1992 (SEBI Act)

Act Number / Year 15 of 1992

Presidential Assent / Enactment Date April 4, 1992

Enforcement Date January 30, 1992

Administrative Nodal Ministry Ministry of Finance

Precedent & Statutory Rationale

• Market Malpractices and Absence of Independent Regulation:

o Prior to 1992, the Indian capital market lacked an independent, statutory regulator, leaving investor protection, stock exchanges, and merchant banking largely under fragmented control or self-regulation prone to rampant market manipulation, fraud, and severe systemic scams.

o The initial non-statutory setup of SEBI established in 1988 lacked statutory teeth, penal powers, and investigative authority to effectively discipline market intermediaries and safeguard public investors.

• Legislative Intervention and Regularization:

o Enacted to establish the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) as a statutory body equipped with comprehensive regulatory, supervisory, and penal powers over securities markets.

o The core objective was to protect the interests of investors in securities, promote the orderly development of the securities market, regulate stock exchanges, mutual funds, merchant bankers, and other intermediaries, and curb insider trading and fraudulent trade practices.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

• Formulation: Framed by the Central Government during the peak of 1991–1992 economic reforms to instill confidence in liberalized capital markets and establish international standard transparency.

• Parliamentary Passage: Passed by both houses of Parliament, receiving formal presidential assent on April 4, 1992.

• Enforcement: Enforced on January 30, 1992.

• Source: India Code and Ministry of Finance Official Records.

Precedent & Historical Context

1. High Non-Performing Assets (NPAs) & Pre-Existing Legal Bottlenecks:

o Prior to 2002, financial institutions in India had to rely primarily on civil suits or Debt Recovery Tribunals (DRTs) established under the Recovery of Debts Due to Banks and Financial Institutions Act, 1993 (RDDBFI).

o Civil courts and DRTs suffered from severe litigation delays, preventing banks from seizing and realizing collateral security without prolonged judicial intervention.

2. Expert Committee Recommendations:

o Narasimham Committee II (1998): Recommended the enactment of a dedicated law empowering banks to enforce security interests without court intervention and establishing Asset Reconstruction Companies (ARCs).

o Andhyarujina Committee (2000): Drafted specific statutory proposals enabling secured creditors to take possession and sell secured assets directly upon default.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Promulgation

• June 21, 2002: The President of India promulgated the Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Ordinance, 2002 (Ordinance No. 2 of 2002) to give immediate effect to recovery measures.

• Enactment: Received Presidential Assent on December 17, 2002.

• Enforcement: Enforced on June 21, 2002.

Legislative History:

The Real Estate (Regulation and Development) Act, 2016

Short Title The Real Estate (Regulation and Development) Act, 2016

Act Number / Year Act No. 16 of 2016

India Code Act ID 201616

Presidential Assent Date March 25, 2016

Enforcement Date Phased enforcement: May 1, 2016 (61 sections notified) and May 1, 2017 (remaining provisions fully operationalized)

Nodal Ministry Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs

Precedent & Statutory Rationale

1. Rampant Consumer Exploitation and Systemic Delays:

o Prior to 2016, India's real estate sector was largely unregulated and heavily tilted in favor of developers. Homebuyers faced chronic, unpenalized project delays, arbitrary changes to building plans, unilateral builder-buyer agreement terms, and a total lack of transparency regarding project approvals.

2. Diversion of Funds and Financial Vulnerability:

o Developers frequently diverted capital collected from advance bookings of one project to acquire land banks or finance other projects, leaving thousands of residential projects stalled. The legislation was enacted to establish financial discipline, accountability, and a robust consumer grievance redressal mechanism.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

• Formulation: Developed and piloted by the Ministry of Housing and Urban Poverty Alleviation to bring uniformity and consumer protection to the national property market.

• Parliamentary Passage: Originally introduced as the Real Estate (Regulation and Development) Bill in the Rajya Sabha on August 14, 2013, scrutinized extensively by a Parliamentary Standing Committee, and ultimately passed by the Rajya Sabha on March 10, 2016, and the Lok Sabha on March 15, 2016.

• Presidential Assent: Received formal Presidential Assent from President Pranab Mukherjee on March 25, 2016, entering the statute book as Act No. 16 of 2016.

• Enforcement: Enforced in two phases—initially bringing 61 sections into effect on May 1, 2016, and fully operationalizing the remaining provisions (including mandatory project registration) on May 1, 2017

Summary of the Goods and Services Tax (Compensation to States) Act, 2017
Objective: Compensate Indian States for revenue losses due to GST implementation, alongside ensuring anti-profiteering measures are indirectly supported by maintaining state financial stability.

1.	Stable Revenue for States *Compensation Framework: Ensures states do not face significant revenue shortfalls, potentially allowing for more consistent policy-making, including those related to anti-profiteering.
2.	Calculation of Compensation *Projected vs. Actual Revenue: Mechanism to adjust for shortfalls, which could indirectly influence states' ability to regulate and enforce anti-profiteering laws effectively.
3.	Funding Mechanism and Its Implications *GST Compensation Cess: While not directly an anti-profiteering tool, the cess on specified goods/services could influence pricing strategies, with the intent of preventing undue profit at the consumer's expense. *GST Compensation Fund: Management of funds ensures transparency, a principle also crucial in anti-profiteering enforcement.
4.	Duration and Settlement in Relation to Market Stability *5-Year Compensation Period: Provides a timeframe for states to adjust and potentially implement more effective anti-profiteering measures as the GST ecosystem matures.

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987
The Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987 was enacted to establish legal services authorities at the national, state, district, and taluk levels to provide free and competent legal services to eligible persons and to organise Lok Adalats for the amicable settlement of disputes. The Act was enacted on 11 October 1987 and came into force on 9 November 1995. It gives effect to the constitutional mandate of equal access to justice, particularly under Articles 14 and 39A of the Constitution. 
1. Objective
The Act aims to:
•	Provide free and competent legal services to weaker sections of society. 
•	Ensure that no person is denied justice due to economic or other disabilities. 
•	Promote equal access to justice. 
•	Organise Lok Adalats for speedy and amicable settlement of disputes. 
2. National Legal Services Authority (NALSA) (Sections 3–5)
The Act establishes the National Legal Services Authority (NALSA) to:
•	Lay down policies and principles for legal aid. 
•	Frame effective legal services programmes. 
•	Monitor and coordinate the implementation of legal aid schemes. 
•	Promote legal literacy and legal awareness. 
•	Coordinate with State Legal Services Authorities and other agencies. 
3. State, District and Taluk Legal Services Authorities
The Act provides for:
•	State Legal Services Authorities (SLSAs). 
•	High Court Legal Services Committees. 
•	District Legal Services Authorities (DLSAs). 
•	Taluk Legal Services Committees (TLSCs). 
These authorities implement legal aid programmes, organise Lok Adalats, spread legal awareness, and provide legal assistance at their respective levels. 
4. Persons Entitled to Free Legal Services (Section 12)
Free legal services are available to, among others:
•	Members of Scheduled Castes (SCs) and Scheduled Tribes (STs). 
•	Women and children. 
•	Victims of trafficking or begar. 
•	Persons with disabilities or mental illness. 
•	Victims of mass disasters, ethnic violence, caste atrocities, floods, droughts, earthquakes, or industrial disasters. 
•	Industrial workmen. 
•	Persons in custody (including prisons, protective homes, juvenile homes, and psychiatric hospitals). 
•	Persons whose annual income is below the prescribed limit. 
5. Lok Adalats (Chapter VI)
The Act provides for the organisation of Lok Adalats to settle:
•	Pending court cases. 
•	Pre-litigation disputes. 
Features of Lok Adalats:
•	Proceedings are based on compromise and conciliation. 
•	No court fee is payable; any fee already paid is refunded if the matter is settled. 
•	The award is deemed to be a decree of a civil court. 
•	The award is final and binding on the parties, and ordinarily no appeal lies against it.

THE LEGAL SERVICES AUTHORITIES ACT, 1987
ACT NO. 39 OF 1987

[11th October, 1987.]

An Act to constitute legal services authorities to provide free and competent legal services to the weaker sections of the society to ensure that opportunities for securing justice are not denied to any citizen by reason of economic or other disabilities, and to organise Lok Adalats to secure that the operation of the legal system promotes justice on a basis of equal opportunity.

Legislative History:

The Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987

Act Title - The Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987

Act Number/Year - 39 of 1987

Act ID (India Code) - 198739

Presidential Assent Date - October 11, 1987

Enforcement Date - November 9, 1995

Nodal Ministry - Ministry of Law and Justice

Precedent & Historical Rationale

Constitutional Mandate and Access to Justice:

Article 39A of the Constitution of India (inserted by the 42nd Amendment Act, 1976) directs the State to secure that the operation of the legal system promotes justice on a basis of equal opportunity, and to ensure, by suitable legislation or schemes, that opportunities for securing justice are not denied to any citizen by reason of economic or other disabilities. Prior to 1987, free legal aid programs existed largely as voluntary, fragmented state-level schemes or advisory committees without a uniform statutory backbone or guaranteed financial backing.

Institutionalizing Lok Adalats and Legal Aid:

To fulfill this constitutional promise, reduce mounting pendency in regular courts, and provide an economical, accessible forum for marginalized and weaker sections of society, Parliament enacted the Legal Services Authorities Act. The statute established a nationwide network of statutory bodies—from the National Legal Services Authority (NALSA) down to State, District, and Taluk Legal Services Authorities—and formalized Lok Adalats (People's Courts) as a recognized alternative dispute resolution mechanism with statutory binding force.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

Formulation:

Drafted by the Ministry of Law and Justice to constitute legal services authorities for providing free and competent legal services to weaker sections of the society and to organize Lok Adalats to secure that the operation of the legal system promotes justice on a basis of equal opportunity.

Parliamentary Passage:

Introduced, debated, and passed by both Houses of Parliament (Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha) during the autumn session of 1987, receiving Presidential assent in October 1987.

Presidential Assent:

Received Presidential Assent on October 11, 1987.

Enforcement: Enforced on November 9, 1995.

Source: Official Records of Parliament, India Code, and Department of Legal Affairs, Ministry of Law and Justice.

Legislative History:

The National Institutes of Technology, Science Education and Research Act, 2007

● Act Title - The National Institutes of Technology, Science Education and Research Act, 2007

● Act Number / Year - 29 of 2007

● Act ID (India Code) - 200729

● Assent Date - June 5, 2007

● Enforcement Date - August 15, 2007

● Nodal Ministry - Ministry of Education

Precedent & Historical Rationale

● Deficiencies and Dual Control of the REC System under Registered Societies - The Regional Engineering Colleges (RECs) were originally established between 1959 and 1986 as joint ventures between the Central Government and respective State Governments, functioning as autonomous societies registered under the Societies Registration Act, 1860. Operating as non-statutory societies under dual central-state administrative control restricted academic innovation, created disparities in infrastructure and funding across states, and required affiliation with state universities for degree-granting powers.

● Statutory Elevation to Institutes of National Importance (INIs) and Academic Autonomy - Formulated to declare the National Institutes of Technology (and later extended by amendments to IISERs and IIEST) to be Institutions of National Importance. The Act established a unified statutory governance framework modeled after the IIT system, dissolved the individual governing societies, vested their assets in newly incorporated statutory bodies with direct central funding, conferred autonomous degree-granting powers, established a central Council for NITSER under the Union Education Minister for national policy coordination, and appointed the President of India as the Visitor.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

● Formulation & Standing Committee Review - Drafted by the Ministry of Human Resource Development (now Ministry of Education) following the 2002 decision to upgrade RECs into NITs; introduced as The National Institutes of Technology Bill, 2006 in the Lok Sabha and referred to the Parliamentary Standing Committee on Human Resource Development for clause-by-clause scrutiny.

● Parliamentary Passage - Debated and passed by the Lok Sabha on May 14, 2007, and considered and passed by the Rajya Sabha on May 16, 2007, during the Budget Session.

● President's Assent - Received the assent of the President of India (Dr. A.P.J. Abdul Kalam) on June 5, 2007, and was published in the Gazette of India on June 6, 2007.

● Enforcement - Enforced on August 15, 2007.

Act Number/Year - 35 of 1987

Act ID (India Code) - 198735

Presidential Assent Date - September 14, 1987

Enforcement Date - November 1, 1987

Nodal Ministry - Ministry of Finance

Precedent & Historical Rationale

Fiscal Policy and Conspicuous Consumption:

During the 1980s, the Government of India sought to broaden its tax base, curb ostentatious and extravagant spending, and mobilize additional revenue to address fiscal deficits. Following budget proposals aimed at targeting high-end luxury consumption, the government felt a specific need to levy a direct tax on expenditures incurred in luxury hotels and, subsequently, restaurants.

Targeting High-End Tourism and Luxury Services:

Prior to 1987, income tax alone did not adequately capture lavish discretionary spending by affluent individuals in top-tier commercial establishments. The Expenditure-tax Act was introduced as a fiscal measure to impose a tax on chargeable expenditure incurred in hotels where the room tariff exceeded a specified monetary limit, ensuring that luxury consumption contributed directly to national revenue streams.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

Formulation:

Drafted by the Ministry of Finance to provide for the levy of a tax on chargeable expenditure incurred by individuals in certain luxury hotels, detailing assessment procedures, collection machinery, penalties for evasion, and appellate mechanisms.

Parliamentary Passage:

Introduced, debated, and passed by both Houses of Parliament (Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha) during the monsoon session of 1987 as part of the broader financial and taxation legislative agenda.

Presidential Assent: Received Presidential Assent on September 14, 1987.

Enforcement: Enforced on October 1, 1987.

Act Title The Foreign Aircraft (Exemption from Taxes and Duties on Fuel and Lubricants) Act, 2002

Act Number 36 of 2002

Act ID (India Code) 200236

Presidential Assent Date June 11, 2002

Enforcement Date June 30, 2002

Nodal Ministry Ministry of Civil Aviation

Precedent & International Rationale

1. International Obligations (Chicago Convention & Bilateral Air Services Agreements):

o India is a signatory to the Convention on International Civil Aviation (Chicago Convention, 1944).

o Under Article 24 of the Chicago Convention and standard Bilateral Air Services Agreements (BASAs) executed between India and sovereign foreign nations, reciprocal tax exemptions are mandated on fuel, lubricating oils, and spare parts loaded on aircraft operating international routes.

2. Domestic Statutory Requirement:

o Prior to 2002, central customs duties were exempted under custom notifications, but sales taxes/VAT levied by various State Governments on aviation turbine fuel (ATF) supplied to foreign designated airlines created legal ambiguities and international reciprocal disputes.

o Central legislation was necessary to give statutory effect to international obligations and enforce nationwide exemptions across state tax domains.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

• May 9, 2000: Introduced in the Lok Sabha as The Foreign Aircraft (Exemption from Taxes and Duties on Fuel and Lubricants) Bill, 2000.

• May 2000 – March 2001: Referred to the Department-Related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Transport, Tourism and Culture for detailed examination and stakeholder consultation.

• Enactment: Received Presidential Assent on June 11, 2002.

• Enforcement: Enforced on June 30, 2002.

Act Number / Year 24 of 1997

Presidential Assent / Enactment Date March 28, 1997

Nodal Ministry Ministry of Communications

Precedent & Statutory Rationale

• Post-Liberalization Market Evolution and Conflicts of Interest:

o Following the sweeping economic reforms of 1991 and the opening up of the telecommunications sector to private players, the Department of Telecommunications (DoT) acted simultaneously as a policymaker, service provider (via MTNL and BSNL), and licensing authority.

o This created severe conflicts of interest, regulatory uncertainty, arbitrary tariff structures, and friction between private operators and the government, necessitating an independent statutory referee.

• Legislative Intervention and Regularization:

o Enacted in the 48th Year of the Republic of India, the 1997 Act established the Telecom Regulatory Authority of India (TRAI) to regulate telecommunication services, fix tariffs, protect consumer interests, and ensure fair competition.

o The core objectives include ensuring transparent licensing conditions, resolving disputes between service providers and consumers (later restructured via the 2000 amendment to separate quasi-judicial powers into the Telecom Disputes Settlement and Appellate Tribunal - TDSAT), and promoting rapid, high-quality telecom infrastructure growth.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

• Formulation: Conceived by the Central Government to facilitate smooth market entry for private telecommunications operators and build investor confidence. The legislative framework was initially promulgated via the TRAI Ordinance on January 25, 1997, before being introduced for parliamentary approval.

• Parliamentary Passage: Introduced in Parliament during the budget session, debated, and passed by both houses, receiving formal presidential assent on March 28, 1997.

• Enforcement: Enforced on January 25, 1997.

title: The Babasaheb Bhimrao Ambedkar University Act, 1994

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of the Babasaheb Bhimrao Ambedkar University Act, 1994 
Key Provisions
•	Establishment of the University: The Act establishes the Babasaheb Bhimrao Ambedkar University, Lucknow, as a body corporate with perpetual succession and a common seal, having the power to acquire, hold, and dispose of property, enter into contracts, and sue or be sued. 
•	Powers and Functions: The University is empowered to provide instruction, conduct research, establish departments and centres, award degrees, diplomas, and other academic distinctions, collaborate with other institutions, and undertake extension and community development programmes. 
•	Authorities of the University: The Act provides for the constitution of the Court, Executive Council, Academic Council, Board of Management, Finance Committee, and other statutory authorities responsible for the governance and administration of the University. 
•	Officers of the University: It lays down provisions relating to the appointment, powers, and functions of the Visitor, Chancellor, Vice-Chancellor, Registrar, Finance Officer, and other officers. 
•	Finance and Accountability: The Act provides for grants from the Central Government, maintenance of the University's funds, preparation of budgets, maintenance and audit of accounts, and submission of annual reports.

Summary of Provisional Collection of Taxes Act, 2023
The Provisional Collection of Taxes Act, 2023, enables the Central Government to immediately impose or increase customs or excise duties through a declaration in a Bill, effective for a limited period until the Bill's enactment, amendment, rejection, or expiration of a specified period.
Key Provisions
1.	Immediate Effect 
 Declared provisions in a Bill come into force the day after introduction. 
2. Duration  
 Until the Bill is enacted (with/without amendments), notified to cease by the Central Government, or 75 days after introduction, whichever is earlier. 
3. Refunds 
Enacted in Amended Form Before 75 Days: Refunds for excess duties based on rate differences. Declaration Ceases Otherwise: Full refund of duties collected under the declaration.
 Repeals the Provisional Collection of Taxes Act, 1931

THE PROHIBITION OF BENAMI PROPERTY TRANSACTIONS ACT, 1988
ACT NO. 45 OF 1988

[5th September, 1988.]

An Act to prohibit benami transactions and the right to recover property held benami and for matters connected therewith or incidental thereto.
BE it enacted by Parliament in the Thirty-ninth Year of the Republic of India as follows:--
meta.dc.legislation.history:
Legislative History:

The Prohibition of Benami Property Transactions Act, 1988

Short Title The Prohibition of Benami Property Transactions Act, 1988 (Originally enacted as the Benami Transactions (Prohibition) Act, 1988)

Act Number / Year 45 of 1988

Act ID (India Code) 198845

Presidential Assent Date May 19, 1988

Enforcement Date September 5, 1988

Nodal Ministry Ministry of Finance

Precedent & Statutory Rationale

• Background/Transition:

Prior to 1988, "benami" transactions—where property is held by one person but has been provided or paid for by another—were widely utilized in India. While English common law concepts of resulting trusts were partially codified under Sections 81 and 82 of the Indian Trusts Act, 1882, the legal framework lacked an absolute prohibition or a mechanism to penalize the practice, leading to massive accumulations of undisclosed wealth and unrecorded real estate holdings used for tax evasion. The Law Commission of India in its 57th Report recommended comprehensive legislation to outlaw benami transactions.

• Rationale/Objectives:

The Act was enacted by Parliament to prohibit benami transactions and the right to recover benami property. Its core purpose was to curb the proliferation of black money, prevent the evasion of taxes, deter the laundering of disproportionate assets through fictitious names, and empower the state to confiscate benami properties without compensation.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Legislative Milestones

• Formulation/Introduction:

Introduced as a short, preemptive legislative instrument by the Central Government in 1988 to abolish the legal enforceability of benami claims and penalize violators.

• Legislative Passage & Assent:

Passed by both Houses of Parliament and received presidential assent on September 5, 1988. (Note: Because the original 1988 law suffered from procedural loopholes and lacked operational machinery for attachment and adjudication, Parliament drastically revamped and strengthened the statute via the Benami Transactions (Prohibition) Amendment Act, 2016, renaming it the Prohibition of Benami Property Transactions Act, 1988).

• Statutory Mechanics & Provisions:

o Prohibition of Benami Transactions: Declared all benami transactions illegal, barring any suits, claims, or actions to enforce rights in respect of any property held benami against the person in whose name the property is held or against any other person.

o Confiscation of Property: Empowered the government to confiscate any property held benami without payment of compensation to the beneficial owner or the benamidar.

o Penalties and Prosecution: Imposed severe terms of rigorous imprisonment and heavy financial penalties for persons entering into benami transactions to defeat revenue laws or conceal assets.

o Institutional Authorities: Established specialized administrative and adjudicating machinery—including Initiating Officers, Approving Authorities, and Adjudicating Authorities—to trace, attach, and confiscate benami properties, subject to appellate review by the Appellate Tribunal.

• Presidential Assent: Received Presidential Assent on May 19, 2988.

• Enforcement: Enforced on September 5, 1988.

• Source: India Code Official Repository (indiacode.gov.in) and Ministry of Finance (Department of Revenue), Government of India Official Records.

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of the Repealing and Amending Act, 2019
Brief Summary
The Repealing and Amending Act, 2019 was enacted to simplify and streamline India's statute book by repealing obsolete, redundant, and spent laws that had become unnecessary. It also made minor amendments and corrections to certain existing Acts to remove inconsistencies, update references, and improve legislative clarity. The Act did not introduce any major policy changes but was intended to improve the efficiency and accessibility of the legal framework.
Objective
The main objectives of the Act are:
•	To repeal obsolete and redundant laws that are no longer in force or have become unnecessary.
•	To simplify and modernize India's legal framework.
•	To remove inconsistencies, errors, and outdated references in existing legislation.
•	To improve the clarity and accessibility of statutory laws.
•	To facilitate better governance by maintaining an updated and coherent body of laws.
Key Provisions
1.	Repeal of Obsolete Acts
o	The Act repeals a number of Central Acts that had become obsolete, spent, or redundant and no longer served any legal purpose.
2.	Minor Amendments
o	It makes minor textual amendments, corrections, and updates to certain existing laws, including correcting drafting errors and updating statutory references.
3.	Savings Clause
o	The repeal of an Act does not affect any rights, liabilities, obligations, penalties, investigations, legal proceedings, or actions already taken under the repealed law unless expressly provided otherwise.
4.	Removal of Redundant Provisions
o	The Act removes unnecessary legislative provisions that have become ineffective due to the passage of time or subsequent legal developments.
5.	No Substantive Policy Changes
o	The amendments made under the Act are technical and consequential in nature and do not alter the substantive rights, duties, or legal effect of the principal Acts.
6.	Legislative Housekeeping
o	The Act forms part of the Government's ongoing legislative reform initiative to keep the statute book concise, current, and free from outdated enactments.

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of The Goa, Daman and Diu Reorganisation Act, 1987
Key Objective
•	To facilitate the reorganisation of the Union Territory of Goa, Daman and Diu into the State of Goa and the Union Territory of Daman and Diu, effective from the appointed day.
Main Provisions
1.	Territorial Reorganisation
•	State of Goa: Established from the Goa district.
•	Union Territory of Daman and Diu: Comprises Daman and Diu districts.
2.	Judicial Adjustments
•	High Court of Bombay's Jurisdiction: Exercises jurisdiction over the new Union Territory of Daman and Diu, with a permanent bench at Panaji for Goa, Daman, and Diu cases.
•	Transfer of Proceedings: Proceedings from the Court of the Judicial Commissioner are transferred to and disposed of by the High Court at Bombay.
3.	Legal and Administrative Continuity
•	Right to Appear in Proceedings: Advocates authorised before the appointed day can appear in the High Court at Bombay for transferred proceedings.
•	Expenditure Allocation: Expenses of the High Court at Bombay, including salaries, are allocated between Maharashtra and the Union as determined by the President.
•	Rule of Construction: References to the Court of the Judicial Commissioner in laws are construed as references to the High Court at Bombay for the Union Territory.
4.	Power and Adaptation Provisions
•	Power to Remove Difficulties: The Central Government (and later the President in a similar provision) may issue orders to address difficulties in implementing the Act, subject to parliamentary scrutiny.
•	Power to Adapt Laws: The Central Government and appropriate state governments can adapt laws for better application in Goa and Daman and Diu within two years from the appointed day.
5.	Continuity and Override
•	Continuance of Courts and Authorities: Unless inconsistent with the Act, all courts, tribunals, and authorities continue their functions.
•	Supremacy of the Act: Provisions of this Act override any inconsistent laws.

ACT NO. 18 OF 1987

meta.dc.legislation.history:
Legislative History:

The Goa, Daman and Diu Reorganisation Act, 1987

Act Title - The Goa, Daman and Diu Reorganisation Act, 1987

Act Number/Year - 18 of 1987

Act ID (India Code) - 198718

Presidential Assent Date - May 23, 1987

Enforcement Date - May 30, 1987

Nodal Ministry - Ministry of Home Affairs

Precedent & Historical Rationale

Liberation Legacy and Union Territory Status:

Following the liberation of Goa, Daman, and Diu from Portuguese colonial rule in December 1961 (via Operation Vijay), the territories were initially governed under military administration and subsequently constituted into a single Union Territory administered by the President through an administrator under the Constitution (Twelfth Amendment) Act, 1962. Over the succeeding two decades, vibrant political, cultural, and linguistic movements grew, demanding full-fledged statehood and distinct administrative identities for the separate regions.

Geographic Division and Fulfillment of Statehood:

Because Goa and Daman & Diu possessed distinct cultural identities and geographic separation, the reorganization framework was structured to split the territories: elevating Goa to full statehood as the 25th State of the Indian Union, while keeping Daman and Diu as a separate Union Territory. This required a corresponding constitutional amendment alongside this specific reorganisation statute to establish the new political and administrative apparatus.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

Formulation:

Drafted by the Ministry of Home Affairs to provide for the reorganization of the Union Territory of Goa, Daman, and Diu, detailing the formation of the State of Goa, the constitution of Daman and Diu as a separate Union Territory, allocation of seats in Parliament, creation of the new Legislative Assembly for Goa, and the distribution of assets, liabilities, and judicial machinery (including the establishment of a common High Court or extension of jurisdiction).

Parliamentary Passage:

Introduced, debated, and passed by both Houses of Parliament (Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha) during the budget session of 1987.

Presidential Assent: Received Presidential Assent on May 23, 1987.

Enforcement: Enforced on May 30, 1987.

Source: Official Records of Parliament, India Code, and Ministry of Home Affairs

Summary of Protection of Interests in Aircraft Objects Act, 2025
 *Primary Objective: To safeguard interests in aircraft objects in alignment with international conventions, ensuring clarity in ownership, security, dispute resolution, and regulated oversight by the Central Government. 
Key Provisions 
1. Central Oversight & International Alignment:
•	Central Government ensures implementation of the Convention on International Interests in Mobile Equipment and its Protocol concerning Aircraft Equipment in India.
•	Regulatory Powers: Empowered to make rules for operational compliance, security, and dispute resolution under the Act.
2.	Regulatory Framework & Central Authority:
•	DGCA (Directorate General of Civil Aviation): Acts under Central Government's oversight for managing the registry and ensuring compliance.
•	Rule Making Authority: Central Government authorized to make rules, including those governing operational standards, security protocols, and dispute resolutions.
3.	Compliance & Central Enforcement:
•	Operators & Stakeholders: Must comply with regulations set by the Central Government.
•	Non-Compliance Penalties: Central Government can impose penalties, including fines, for non-compliance, especially in cases involving national security or aggression.
4.	Remedies, Resolutions, & Central Jurisdiction:
•	Default Remedies: Mechanisms for resolution are established under Central Government's regulations.
•	Time Limits: Specified time limits for seeking remedies apply, with Central Government overseeing enforcement.
5.	Jurisdiction, Enforcement, & Central Oversight:
•	High Courts: Have jurisdiction over disputes, with the Central Government's regulations guiding the process.
•	Override Clause: Act’s provisions, under Central Government's authority, take precedence over other laws in cases of conflict.
6.	Additional Powers & Central Amendments:
•	Declaration Amendments: Central Government can amend India’s declarations under the international conventions.
•	Penalty Enhancements: For serious offences, including those against national security, the Central Government can enforce enhanced penalties

ACT NO. 17 OF 2025

[16th April, 2025.]


An Act to provide for protection of interests in aircraft objects and to implement the Convention on International Interests in Mobile Equipment and the Protocol to the Convention on International Interests in Mobile Equipment on Matters Specific to Aircraft Equipment signed at Cape Town on 16th November, 2001 and for matters connected therewith or incidental thereto.

Legislative History:
The Protection of Interests in Aircraft Objects Act, 2025

Source: Official Record of Parliament, India Code, and Ministry of Civil Aviation 
 
Act Title - The Protection of Interests in Aircraft Objects Act, 2025
Act Number - Act No. 17 of 2025 
Act ID (India Code) - 202517 
 Presidential Assent date -April 16, 2025 
 Enforcement Date -May 01, 2025 
Nodal Ministry -Ministry of Civil Aviation 

Precedent & Historical Rationale
●	Implementation of the Cape Town Convention & Protocol: Gives full statutory effect to the Convention on International Interests in Mobile Equipment and the Protocol on Matters Specific to Aircraft Equipment (signed at Cape Town in 2001), resolving long-standing domestic enforceability gaps due to India's dualist legal framework.
●	Protection of Lessors & Reduction of Capital Costs: Overrides conflicting local insolvency and procedural laws to provide robust non-judicial remedies, streamlined IDERA (Irrevocable De-registration and Export Request Authorisation) processes, and predictable repossession timelines. This lowers jurisdiction risk for global aircraft financiers, significantly reducing leasing costs for Indian airlines.
 
Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment
●	Formulation: Introduced as the Protection of Interests in Aircraft Objects Bill, 2025 by the Union Minister of Civil Aviation, Shri Ram Mohan Naidu, to strengthen India's aviation leasing ecosystem and align with global aviation standards.
●	Parliamentary Passage: Passed by the Rajya Sabha on April 1, 2025, and subsequently passed by the Lok Sabha on April 3, 2025.
●	Presidential Assent: Received the assent of the President of India on April 16, 2025.
●	Enforcement: Enforced on May 01, 2025 .

Legislative History:

The National Commission for Backward Classes (Repeal) Act, 2018

Short Title - The National Commission for Backward Classes (Repeal) Act, 2018

Act Number / Year - Act No. 24 of 2018

Act ID (India Code) - A2018-24

Presidential Assent / Enactment Date - August 14, 2018

Enforcement Date - August 15, 2018

Nodal Ministry - Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment

Precedent & Statutory Rationale

1. Constitutional Empowerment of the Backward Classes Commission:

o Prior to 2018, the National Commission for Backward Classes (NCBC) operated as a statutory body established under the National Commission for Backward Classes Act, 1993, with limited oversight powers.

o Following the passage of the landmark 102nd Constitution Amendment Act, 2018, which inserted Article 338B into the Constitution of India, the Commission was granted a prestigious constitutional status akin to the National Commission for Scheduled Castes (NCSC) and National Commission for Scheduled Tribes (NCST).

2. Abolition of Statutory Duplication:

o The Act was formulated to repeal the National Commission for Backward Classes Act, 1993, to prevent legal duplication and streamline institutional frameworks now that the commission derived its direct powers, duties, and mandate from the Constitution itself.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

• Formulation: Prepared by the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment to operationalize the structural changes mandated by the constitutional elevation of the NCBC.

• Parliamentary Passage: Tabled alongside constitutional reform bills, thoroughly reviewed, and passed by both houses of the Parliament of India, receiving presidential assent on August 14, 2018.

• Enforcement: Enforced on August 15, 2018.

Source: India Code (indiacode.gov.in) and Ministry of Law and Justice Official Records.

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of the  University of Allahabad Act, 2005
Key Provisions
1.	Commencement: - Declaration: Establishes the University of Allahabad as an Institution of National Importance, incorporating it as a body corporate.
2.	Core Objectives and Powers: - Objectives: Disseminate knowledge, advance learning through integrated courses, foster innovation, and drive social progress.
•	Powers: Includes providing educational and research facilities, awarding degrees (including honorary degrees), and collaborating with other institutions.
3.	Governance Structure: - Visitor: The President of India, overseeing the University.
•	Key Officers:
•	Chancellor: Appointed by the Visitor from a panel (of at least three) recommended by the Executive Council for a 5-year term, with the possibility of continuation until a successor takes office.
•	Vice-Chancellor: Selected from a panel of at least three, recommended by a specially constituted committee, serving a 5-year term or until the age of 65, whichever is earlier.
•	Pro-Vice-Chancellor, Registrar, and Finance Officer: Defined roles within the University's hierarchy.
•	Authorities: The Court (highest statutory body), The Executive Council (principal executive body), The Academic Council (overseeing academic matters), The Finance Committee (managing financial affairs).
4.	Regulatory and Operational Framework: - Statutes: Initially, relevant provisions from the Uttar Pradesh State Universities Act, 1973, apply until new Statutes are made; thereafter, made under the Act with Central Government approval.
•	Ordinances: To be made under the Act and Statutes, covering operational aspects like admission, courses, and examinations.
•	Regulations: Detailed operational guidelines to be published in the Official Gazette.

Summary of The Emigration Act, 1983:
Overview
*Title: The Emigration Act, 1983 *Extent & Application: Whole of India, also applies to citizens of India outside India *Commencement: Came into force on 30th December, 1983 (with provisions for different commencement dates for different provisions)
Key Definitions (Selected)
*Emigrant: A citizen of India intending to, emigrating, or having emigrated, excluding dependents and those who have lived outside India for 3+ years after turning 18. *Emigration: Departure from India for employment outside India. *Employer: Person providing employment outside India. *Emigrant Conveyance: Conveyance specially chartered for emigrants or exceeding a prescribed number of emigrants.
Provisions Summary
Emigration Process
*Emigration Clearance: Mandatory for citizens of India emigrating (Section 22).
•	Application to Protector of Emigrants with prescribed documents (agreement, security for repatriation, fee, etc.).
•	Protector may reject based on exploitative terms, unlawful work, sub-standard conditions, or insufficient repatriation provisions.
Authorities
*Protectors of Emigrants: Appointed by the Central Government (Section 3). *Protector General of Emigrants: Oversees Protectors of Emigrants. *Emigration Check-posts: Can be set up by the Central Government (Section 6). *Emigration Officers/Staff: Appointed to assist (Section 7). *Public Servants: Status of all emigration authorities (Section 8).
Regulatory Powers
*Prohibition of Emigration:
•	To any country in the interests of the general public, etc. (Section 30).
•	Due to epidemics, civil disturbances, etc., in a country (Section 31).
•	Of any class/category of persons (Section 32). *Security Provisions: Reasonable security for repatriation expenses, subject to forfeiture or renewal as necessary (Section 33).
Offences & Penalties
*Offences: Emigrating without clearance, contravening provisions, furnishing false info, altering documents, disobeying orders, excess charges, cheating (Section 24). *Penalties: Up to 2 years imprisonment and/or up to ₹2,000 fine for primary offences, with increased penalties for subsequent offences. *Corporate Liability: Companies and their directors/managers can be held liable (Section 25). *Cognizable Offences: All offences under this Act are cognizable (Section 26). *Sanction for Prosecution: Generally required from the Central Government, except for complaints by affected emigrants or their immediate relatives (Section 27).
Miscellaneous
*Determination of Emigrant Status: By Protector of Emigrants through inquiry (Section 29). *Refund of Security: When no longer required (Section 34, partially provided).

meta.dc.legislation.history:
Legislative History:

The Emigration Act, 1983

Act Title - The Emigration Act, 1983

Act Number/Year - 31 of 1983

Act ID (India Code) - 198331

Presidential Assent Date- September 10, 1983

Enforcement Date - December 30, 1983

Nodal Ministry - Ministry of External Affairs

Precedent & Historical Rationale

1. Boom in Overseas Migration and Exploitation by Unscrupulous Agents:

o Following the massive economic boom in the Gulf region during the 1970s and early 1980s, hundreds of thousands of Indian workers migrated abroad for employment.

o This rapid surge exposed vulnerable migrant workers—particularly semi-skilled and unskilled laborers—to widespread exploitation, exorbitant service fees, fraudulent job offers, and substandard working conditions perpetrated by unscrupulous and unregistered recruiting agents.

2. Repeal of Obsolete Colonial Frameworks:

o Prior to 1983, emigration was governed by the archaic Indian Emigration Act, 1922, which was fundamentally designed for colonial-era labor export rather than safeguarding modern emigrant workers.

o The legislative intent centered on enacting a comprehensive, modern statute to regulate emigration processes, establish a mandatory licensing system for recruitment agencies, protect the rights and welfare of Indian workers abroad, and set up the office of the Protector General of Emigrants.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

• Formulation: Drafted by the Ministry of External Affairs and the Ministry of Labour to build a robust regulatory mechanism ensuring strict oversight on recruitment practices and safeguarding the socio-economic interests of Indian diaspora workers.

• Parliamentary Passage: Introduced, deliberated, and passed by both Houses of Parliament (Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha) during the monsoon session of 1983.

• Presidential Assent: Received Presidential Assent on September 10, 1983.

• Enforcement: Enforced on December 30, 1983.

• Source: Official Records of Parliament, India Code, and Ministry of External Affairs

Summary of the Warehousing Corporations Act, 1962 
Key Components
1.	Definitions: - Agricultural Produce: Includes foodstuffs, cattle fodder, raw cotton, raw jute, and vegetable oils.
•	Notified Commodity: Any commodity (other than agricultural produce) declared by the Central Government.
•	Appropriate Government: Central Government for the Central Warehousing Corporation, State Government for State Warehousing Corporations.
2.	Corporations: - Central Warehousing Corporation (CWC): Established under Section 3.
•	State Warehousing Corporations (SWCs): Established by State Governments with CWC's approval.
3.	Management and Structure: - CWC & SWCs: Body corporates with perpetual succession and a common seal.
•	Board of Directors:
•	CWC: Composition not detailed in the provided context.
•	SWCs: 5 directors nominated by CWC, 5 by the State Government, and a Managing Director appointed by the State Government with CWC's approval.
4.	Financial Provisions: - Share Capital:
•	CWC: Not detailed in the provided context.
•	SWCs:
•	Authorized Capital: Up to 2 crores of rupees, with the Central Government empowered to increase this limit as determined, reflecting the new context's emphasis on flexible capital adjustment.
•	Subscription and Issue:
•	Initial and subsequent share capital issues require a 50% subscription by the State Government, with the CWC subscribing to the remaining 50%.
•	Borrowing Powers: From Reserve Bank, State Bank, scheduled banks, nationalised banks, and approved financial institutions, with limits.
•	Investment of Funds: In government securities or as prescribed.
•	Disposal of Profits: Establishment of a reserve fund, with dividend rates regulated.
5.	Accounts, Audit, and Governance:
•	Annual Accounts and Audit: By a qualified auditor, with oversight by the Comptroller and Auditor-General of India.
•	Returns and Reports: To the appropriate Government as required.
6.	Miscellaneous Provisions: - Delegation of Powers: By the Corporation to its officers.
•	Voting Rights: One vote per share in shareholders' meetings.
•	Disputes: Between CWC and SWCs resolved by the Central Government.
•	Winding Up: Only by order of the appropriate Government.
•	Repeal and Savings: Repeals the Agricultural Produce (Development and Warehousing) Corporations Act, 1956, with savings for existing provisions and actions.

title: The Weapons of Mass Destruction and their Delivery Systems (Prohibition of Unlawful Activities) Act, 2005

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of the Weapons of Mass Destruction and Their Delivery Systems (Prohibition of Unlawful Activities) Act, 2005
Key Provisions
1. Definitions: - Covers Biological, Chemical, and Nuclear Weapons, Fissile Material, Radioactive Material, Non-State Actors, and Terrorists (referencing the Unlawful Activities Prevention Act, 1967).
2. Prohibitions: - Manufacture, Acquisition, Possession, and Transport of WMDs and their delivery systems.
•	Transfer to Non-State Actors or Terrorists of specified materials, technology, or equipment.
•	Intimidation using Fissile/Radioactive Material.
•	Export for WMD Design/Manufacture.
•	Brokering of Prohibited Transactions and Financing of Prohibited Activities.
3. Regulations: - Control over Export, Transfer, and Transit of notified items by the Central Government.
4. Penalties: - Imprisonment (5 years to Life) and Fines for violating core provisions (Sections 8, 9, 10).
5. Miscellaneous: - Rule Making Power with the Central Government.
•	Good Faith Protection for actions taken under the Act.

THE WEAPONS OF MASS DESTRUCTION AND THEIR DELIVERY SYSTEMS (PROHIBITION OF UNLAWFUL ACTIVITIES) ACT, 2005
ACT NO. 21 OF 2005

[6th June, 2005.]

An Act to prohibit unlawful activities, in relation to weapons of mass destruction and their delivery systems and for matters connected therewith or incidental thereto.
WHEREAS India is determined to safeguard its national security as a Nuclear Weapon State;
AND WHEREAS India is committed not to transfer nuclear weapons or other nuclear explosive devices, or to transfer control over such weapons or explosive devices, and not in any way to assist, encourage, or induce any other country to manufacture nuclear weapons or other nuclear explosive devices;
AND WHEREAS India is committed to prevent a non-State actor and a terrorist from acquiring weapons of mass destruction and their delivery systems;
AND WHEREAS India is committed to the objective of global nuclear disarmament;
AND WHEREAS India is committed to its obligations as a State Party to the Convention on the Prohibition of the Development, Production, Stockpiling and Use of Chemical Weapons and on their Destruction and the Convention on the Prohibition of the Development, Production and Stockpiling of Bacteriological (Biological) and Toxin Weapons and on their Destruction;
AND WHEREAS India is exercising controls over the export of chemicals, organisms, materials, equipment and technologies in relation to weapons of mass destruction and their delivery systems under other relevant Acts;
AND WHEREAS it is considered necessary to provide for integrated legal measures to exercise controls over the export of materials, equipment and technologies and to prohibit unlawful activities in relation to weapons of mass destruction and their means of delivery.
BE it enacted by Parliament in the Fifty-sixth Year of the Republic of India as follows:--

Precedent & International Rationale

1. International Non-Proliferation Obligations:

o Enacted to fulfill India's international obligations under international conventions, treaties, and United Nations Security Council resolutions (such as UNSC Resolution 1540), ensuring that non-State actors and terrorists do not acquire weapons of mass destruction (WMD) or their means of delivery.

2. Integrated Export Controls:

o Prior to 2005, export controls over dual-use chemicals, biological agents, equipment, and technologies were governed across multiple fragmented laws and trade policies. The Act established a unified statutory regime to prohibit illicit transfers, re-transfers, trans-shipments, and brokering activities relating to WMDs.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

• Formulation: Developed jointly by the Ministry of External Affairs, Ministry of Defence, and the Department of Revenue to plug legal loopholes concerning the transit and export of sensitive dual-use technologies.

• Parliamentary Passage: Tabled, debated, and passed by both the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha during the budget/monsoon sessions of Parliament in 2005.

• Presidential Assent: Received Presidential Assent on June 6, 2005, entering the statute book as Act No. 21 of 2005.

• Enforcement: Enforced on November 17, 2006.

• Source: Official Records of Parliament, India Code, and Ministry of External Affairs

THE PAREL INVESTMENTS AND TRADING PRIVATE LIMITED AND DOMESTIC GAS PRIVATE LIMITED (TAKING OVER OF MANAGEMENT) REPEAL ACT, 2005
ACT NO. 14 OF 2005

[31st March, 2005.]

An Act to repeal the Parel Investments and Trading Private Limited and Domestic Gas Private Limited (Taking Over of Management) Act, 1979.
WHEREAS for giving effect to the policy of the State towards securing the principle specified in clause (b) of article 39 of the Constitution, it was proposed to acquire the undertakings of the Parel Investments and Trading Private Limited (hereinafter referred to as PITCL) as well as Domestic Gas Private Limited (hereinafter referred to as DGPL) and collectively referred to as the said Companies so that the means and resources as to bottling, transporting, marketing and distribution of liquefied petroleum gas of the said Companies become vested in the State and thereby, are so distributed as best to sub-serve the common good;
AND WHEREAS pending the acquisition of the undertakings of the said Companies for the purpose of nationalisation of the business of bottling, transporting, marketing and distribution of liquid petroleum gas carried on by them, the management of the undertakings of the said Companies was taken over by the Central Government by the Parel Investments and Trading Private Limited and Domestic Gas Private Limited (Taking Over of Management) Act, 1979 (29 of 1979), and the Hindustan Petroleum Corporation Limited was appointed as the Custodian of the said undertakings;
And whereas in terms of a Memorandum of Compromise entered into on the 11th April, 2002 by the said Companies and its certain shareholders on the one part and the Central Government and the Custodian on the other part, two separate Deeds of Assignment both dated the 2nd April, 2004 were executed between PITCL and DGPL respectively through the Custodian as the Assignors and the Central Government as the Assignee and registered with the Sub- Registrar of Assurances at Mumbai on the 2nd August, 2004, to assign, transfer and vest in the Central Government, the undertakings and business of the said Companies together with their assets and properties and more particularly described in sub- section (2) of section 3 of the said Act and in the manner set out in the said Memorandum of Compromise, but excluding the assets not to be taken over and to be handed over back to PITCL and DGPL respectively for the consideration and in the manner set out in the said Deeds;
And whereas in terms of the said Memorandum of Compromise two other separate Deeds of Assignment both dated the 2nd April, 2004 were executed between the Central Government and the Hindustan Petroleum Corporation Limited and registered with the Sub- Registrar of Assurances at Mumbai on the 2nd August, 2004, to assign, transfer and vest in the Hindustan Petroleum Corporation Limited the undertakings and business of the said Companies together with their assets and properties excluding the assets not to be taken over and to be handed over back to PITCL and DGPL respectively for the consideration and in the manner set out in the said Deeds;
AND WHEREAS in pursuance of the execution of the aforesaid Deeds of Assignment and acquisition of undertakings of the said Companies by the Central Government and thereafter by the Hindustan Petroleum Corporation Limited, it has become necessary to repeal the said Act and to revest the management of the said Companies in respect of their business and assets other than those relating to liquefied petroleum gas through their respective board of directors, as may be appointed in accordance with the law for the time being in force.
BE it enacted by Parliament in the Fifty-sixth Year of the Republic of India as follows:--

Legislative History:

The Parel Investments and Trading Private Limited and Domestic Gas Private Limited (Taking Over of Management) Repeal Act, 2005

Short Title The Parel Investments and Trading Private Limited and Domestic Gas Private Limited (Taking Over of Management) Repeal Act, 2005

Act Number / Year Act No. 14 of 2005

Act ID (India Code) 200514

Presidential Assent Date March 31, 2005

Enforcement Date March 31, 2005

Nodal Ministry Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas

Precedent & Statutory Rationale

1. Origins of the 1979 Takeover Act:

o In 1979, Parliament enacted The Parel Investments and Trading Private Limited and Domestic Gas Private Limited (Taking Over of Management) Act, 1979 (Act No. 29 of 1979) to take over the management of the undertakings of Parel Investments and Trading Private Limited (PITCL) and Domestic Gas Private Limited (DGPL).

o The primary objective was to maintain an essential service vital to the life of the community—specifically, the bottling, transporting, marketing, and distribution of liquefied petroleum gas (LPG)—pending full nationalization of their business undertakings.

2. Memorandum of Compromise & Assignment to HPCL:

o On April 11, 2002, a formal Memorandum of Compromise was entered into by the two companies, certain key shareholders, the Central Government, and the designated Custodian.

o Pursuant to this compromise, two separate Deeds of Assignment (both dated April 2, 2004) were executed between PITCL, DGPL, the Central Government, and Hindustan Petroleum Corporation Limited (HPCL), and subsequently registered with the Sub-Registrar of Assurances at Mumbai on August 2, 2004.

3. Redundancy of the Legacy Framework:

o With the execution of the assignment deeds and the formal integration of the undertakings into HPCL under government acquisition structures, the continued existence of the 1979 management takeover legislation became legally obsolete, necessitating a dedicated repeal statute.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

• Formulation: Prepared by the Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas to formally wind up the statutory management takeover framework following corporate settlement and asset vesting.

• Parliamentary Passage: Tabled, debated, and passed by both Houses of Parliament during the Budget Session of 2005.

• Presidential Assent: Received Presidential Assent on March 31, 2005, entering the statute book as Act No. 14 of 2005.

• Source: Official Records of Parliament, India Code, and Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas

Presidential Assent / Enactment Date December 30, 1999

Precedent & Statutory Rationale

• Outdated Legal Standards and Expansion of Commercial Trade:

o Prior to 2000, trademark protection in India was governed by the Trade and Merchandise Marks Act, 1958, which lagged behind rapid industrial growth, international trade expansion, and modern marketing practices.

o The old law lacked provisions for the registration of services, contemporary digital trade markers, collective marks, and international treaties, leaving brand owners vulnerable to counterfeiting and inadequate legal remedies.

• Legislative Intervention and Regularization:

o Enacted to overhaul and streamline trademark protection, aligning Indian intellectual property laws with international standards and obligations under the World Trade Organization's TRIPS Agreement.

o The core objective was to provide for the registration and better protection of trademarks for goods as well as services, prevent the deceptive use of marks by unauthorized entities, simplify registration procedures, enhance penalties for infringement and counterfeiting, and establish the Intellectual Property Appellate Board (IPAB) for speedy dispute resolution.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

• Formulation: Developed by the Central Government as part of a comprehensive legislative modernization of India's intellectual property regime to attract foreign investment and protect domestic brand equity.

• Parliamentary Passage: Passed by both houses of Parliament, receiving formal presidential assent on December 30, 1999.

• Enforcement: Enforced on September 15, 2003.

Summary of Essential Commodities Act, 1955 

Key Provisions 

1.	Financial Handling by Authorities (Railway Administration Context)
•	Retention of Sums: Authorities may deduct freight, charges, and expenses from the sale of seized/abandoned goods before refunding the surplus.
•	Priority of Claims: Retained sums take precedence over other encumbrances on the goods.
2.	Government Oversight and Rule Making
•	Central Government's Power: To make rules for carrying out the Act's purposes, including specifics on auctions, payments, and encumbrance priorities.
•	State Amendments and Precedence: Recent amendments (e.g., Uttar Pradesh Acts) highlight the evolving nature of the Act; earlier directives generally prevail unless superseded.
3.	Penal and Regulatory Framework Enhancements
•	Severe Penalties for Non-Compliance: Imprisonment (up to 7 years) and fines for violations, with reduced minimums for special reasons.
•	Forfeiture and Confiscation: Applicable to offending property and conveyances.
•	Bar on Jurisdiction: Specific provisions (like Section 6E) grant exclusive jurisdiction to the Collector or State Government over seized essentials, overriding other laws.
4.	Essential Commodities List and Protections
•	Extensive List: Now includes over 30 categories (e.g., cereals, pulses, specific fabrics, educational materials, and more), with detailed specifications for some items.
•	Good Faith Protection: Continued emphasis on protecting actions taken in good faith.
5.	Additional Provisions for Public and National Interest
•	Civil Defence and Security Measures: Provisions for emergencies, including evacuation, property control, and information security, though not directly linked to essential commodities, reflect the Act's place within broader public interest legislation.
•	Requisitioning and Compensation: Principles for movable property requisition, ensuring fair compensation.

title: The Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act, 2009

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of the  Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act, 2009 
The Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act, 2009, ensures free and compulsory elementary education for children aged 6-14, emphasizing accessibility, quality, and protection against discrimination, with specific provisions for disadvantaged groups and children with disabilities.
 Key Provisions 
1. Infrastructure Norms 
•	Barrier-Free Access: Mandatory for all schools to ensure inclusivity. 
•	Separate Toilets for Boys and Girls: Essential for hygiene and dignity. 
•	Safe and Adequate Drinking Water Facility: Accessible to all children. 
•	Kitchen for Mid-Day Meals: Ensuring nutritional support within the school premises.
•	Playground and Secured Fencing: For safety and recreational purposes. 
•	Operational Norms: Minimum Working Days/ Instructional Hours: 200 working days for 1st to 5th class, with 800 instructional hours. 220 working days for 6th to 8th class, with 1,000 instructional hours. 
•	Teacher Working Hours: 45 hours per week, including preparation time. 
•	Teaching-Learning Equipment, Library, and Play Material: To be provided as required for each class. 
2. Transfer Rights and Support: Inter/Intra-State Transfers: Facilitated with immediate transfer certificates and no admission delays. 
•	Special Training for Age-Appropriate Admissions: To integrate children into their age-appropriate classes seamlessly. 
3. Governance and Amendments: 
•	Parliamentary and Legislative Oversight: For transparency and accountability. 
•	Power to Remove Difficulties: Granted to the Central Government for smooth implementation. Key Points (Updated for Clarity): 
4. Core Objective: Free and Compulsory Education for 6-14 year olds. 
5. Responsibilities: Governments: Funding, Infrastructure, Teacher Training. *
•	Local Authorities: Oversight, Attendance Monitoring, Special Provisions. 
6. Prohibitions: Against Capitation Fees, Admission Screening, and Corporal Punishment.

THE RIGHT OF CHILDREN TO FREE AND COMPULSORY EDUCATION ACT, 2009
ACT NO. 35 OF 2009

[26th August, 2009.]

An Act to provide for free and compulsory education to all children of the age of six to fourteen years.
BE it enacted by Parliament in the Sixtieth Year of the Republic of India as follows:--
meta.dc.legislation.history:
Legislative History:

The Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act, 2009

● Act Title - The Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act, 2009

● Act Number / Year - 35 of 2009

● Act ID (India Code) - 200935

● Assent Date - August 26, 2009

● Enforcement Date - April 1, 2010

● Nodal Ministry - Ministry of Education

Precedent & Historical Rationale

● Constitutional Mandate under Article 21A and Supreme Court Jurisprudence - Following landmark Supreme Court rulings in Mohini Jain v. State of Karnataka (1992) and Unni Krishnan, J.P. v. State of Andhra Pradesh (1993), which recognized the right to education as an integral part of the right to life under Article 21, Parliament enacted the Constitution (Eighty-sixth Amendment) Act, 2002. This amendment inserted Article 21A into the Constitution, obligating the State to provide free and compulsory education to all children aged 6 to 14 years "in such manner as the State may, by law, determine." However, the realization of this fundamental right remained non-enforceable until an overarching central enabling statute was enacted.

● Universal Statutory Framework for Elementary Education and Child Rights - Formulated to give domestic statutory effect to Article 21A of the Constitution and the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child. The Act established a binding legal entitlement for every child aged 6 to 14 to full-time elementary education of satisfactory and equitable quality in a neighborhood school, mandated a 25% reservation for children from economically weaker sections and disadvantaged groups in private unaided schools (Section 12(1)(c)), laid down legally binding norms for Pupil-Teacher Ratios (PTR), physical school infrastructure, and teacher qualifications, and prohibited physical punishment, screening procedures, capitation fees, and private tuition by teachers.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

● Formulation & Introduction - Drafted by the Ministry of Human Resource Development (now Ministry of Education) following extensive recommendations by the Central Advisory Board of Education (CABE) and expert drafting committees; introduced as The Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Bill, 2008 in the Rajya Sabha by Human Resource Development Minister Kapil Sibal on December 15, 2008.

● Parliamentary Passage - Debated and passed by the Rajya Sabha on July 20, 2009, and considered, debated, and passed by the Lok Sabha on August 4, 2009, during the Monsoon Session.

● President's Assent - Received the assent of the President of India (Pratibha Devisingh Patil) on August 26, 2009, and was published in the Gazette of India on August 27, 2009.

● Enforcement - Enforced on April 1, 2010.

Sources - Parliamentary Debates (Lok Sabha & Rajya Sabha), The Gazette of India, India Code, and Ministry of Education.

title: The Prevention and Control of Infectious and Contagious Diseases in Animals Act, 2009

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of the Prevention and Control of Infectious and Contagious Diseases in Animals Act, 2009
To prevent, control, and eradicate infectious and contagious diseases in animals, ensuring international trade compliance and adherence to OIE (Office International Des Epizooties) membership obligations. 
Key Provisions
1. Administrative & Regulatory Framework
•	Definitions: Comprehensive, including "animal," "Competent Officer," and "scheduled disease."
•	Appointments: State Governments to appoint Veterinarians, Veterinary Officers, and Competent Officers for enforcement.
2. Disease Management
•	Mandatory Reporting: Owners/persons in charge must report suspected scheduled diseases.
•	Control Measures: Segregation of infected animals, Compulsory Vaccination in designated areas.
•	Declaration of Controlled and Free Areas with movement restrictions.
•	Quarantine and Check Posts for detention, inspection, and vaccination.
3. Handling Infected Animals
•	Segregation, Examination, and Treatment protocols. 
•	Euthanasia: Under specified conditions, with Humane Disposal of carcasses. 
•	Post-Mortem Examinations and Seizure of non-compliant or unclaimed infected animals.
4. Governance and Compliance
•	Delegation of Powers: State Governments can delegate authorities. 
•	Schedule Amendment: Central Government may add/remove diseases from the schedule.
•	Direction and Rule Making: Powers for Central and State Governments to issue directives and formulate rules. 
•	Public Servant Status: Accorded to specified officers under the Act.
5. Enforcement and Penalties
•	Specific Penalty Provisions:
•	Issuing Unauthorized Vaccination Certificates or Defective Vaccines: Up to ₹5,000 fine or 1 month imprisonment (first offence), increasing to ₹10,000 or 3 months for subsequent offences.
•	General Non-Compliance or Obstruction: Up to ₹1,000 fine or 1 month imprisonment (first offence), increasing to ₹2,000 or 2 months for subsequent offences.
•	Placing Infected Carcasses in Water Bodies: Up to ₹2,000 fine or 1 month imprisonment (first offence), increasing to ₹5,000 or 3 months for subsequent offences. *Corporate Liability: Companies and their responsible officers liable for offences, with defences for due diligence and lack of knowledge.
