THE PREVENTION AND CONTROL OF INFECTIOUS AND CONTAGIOUS DISEASES IN ANIMALS ACT, 2009
ACT NO. 27 OF 2009

[20th March, 2009.]

An Act to provide for the prevention, control and eradication of infectious and contagious diseases affecting animals, for prevention of outbreak or spreading of such diseases from one State to another, and to meet the international obligations of India for facilitating import and export of animals and animal products and for matters connected therewith or incidental thereto.
WHEREAS economic losses due to infectious and contagious diseases of animals are enormous in the country with some of these diseases constituting a serious threat to the public;
AND WHEREAS many of such animal diseases can be largely prevented by judicious implementation of vaccination programmes or by taking other appropriate and timely measures on scientific lines;
AND WHEREAS such measures are necessary to facilitate the import and export of animals and animal products and to keep in tune with international practices;
AND WHEREAS it has been realised that the prevention, control and eradication of infectious and contagious diseases of animals from India has to be tackled on a national basis so as to avoid adverse impact of such diseases on the economy of the country and for this purpose harmonise the control procedures and to prevent inter-State transmission of animal diseases;
AND WHEREAS the national level handling has to be done with the active involvement of the State Governments, particularly in regard to the precautionary measures required to be taken within their jurisdiction in respect of certain infectious and contagious diseases and the regulation of movement of animals outside their respective areas by timely adoption of appropriate measures;
AND WHEREAS India is a Member Country of the Office International Des Epizooties, Paris and it is necessary to implement the general obligations, decisions and recommendations of the said Organisation and abide by the International Animal Health Code stipulated by the said Organisation;

The Prevention and Control of Infectious and Contagious Diseases in Animals Act, 2009

Act Number / Year Act No. 27 of 2009

Act ID (India Code) 200927

Presidential Assent Date March 20, 2009

Enforcement Date August 25, 2009

Precedent & Statutory Rationale

1. Obsolescence of Colonial Frameworks:

o Prior to 2009, legal measures for controlling livestock diseases relied heavily on fragmented and archaic statutes like the Glanders and Farcy Act, 1899, which were narrowly focused on specific equines and completely inadequate for modern livestock management, multi-species disease vectors, and intensive farming systems.

2. Fulfilling International Obligations and Global Trade Compliance:

o With the globalization of trade in livestock and animal products, India needed a robust legal framework aligned with international sanitary standards set by international bodies (such as the World Organisation for Animal Health / OIE).

o The legislation was enacted to prevent the interstate spread of contagious animal diseases, safeguard livestock wealth, protect public health from zoonotic spillovers, and satisfy international export compliance obligations.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

• Formulation: Developed by the Department of Animal Husbandry and Dairying to overhaul animal health governance.

• Parliamentary Passage: Originally introduced as a Bill in late 2005, scrutinized by the Parliamentary Standing Committee on Agriculture, and subsequently passed by both Houses of Parliament.

• Presidential Assent: Received formal Presidential Assent on March 20, 2009, entering the statute book as Act No. 27 of 2009.

• Enforcement: Brought into active operational force on August 25, 2009.

Precedent & Historical Rationale

Consolidation of Spice and Cardamom Administration:

Prior to 1986, the institutional structure governing the promotion and regulation of Indian spices was fragmented. Specifically, the Cardamom Board (established under the Cardamom Act, 1968) focused narrowly on cardamom, while the Spices Export Promotion Council (established in 1960) handled broader spice export marketing.

Need for a Unified Apex Body:

Recognizing the vast global market potential for Indian spices and the necessity for uniform quality control, unified export strategies, and centralized research and development, the government moved to amalgamate these separate entities. The objective was to create a single statutory board capable of overseeing the entire lifecycle—from cultivation and processing standardization to global export promotion—for an expanded list of scheduled spices.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

Formulation:

Drafted by the Ministry of Commerce to provide for the constitution of the Spices Board, merging the erstwhile Cardamom Board and the Spices Export Promotion Council, and vesting it with statutory powers to regulate production, control the cardamom industry, and drive aggressive international export marketing.

Parliamentary Passage:

Introduced, debated, and passed by both Houses of Parliament (Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha) in early 1986.

Presidential Assent: Received Presidential Assent on March 20, 1986.

Enforcement: Enforced on February 26, 1987.

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of The Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Divorce) Act, 1986
Overview
1.	Title & Extent:
•	Title: Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Divorce) Act, 1986
•	Extent: Applies uniformly across India
Key Provisions
2.	Definitions: - Divorced Woman: A Muslim woman divorced under Muslim law.
•	Iddat Period: The specified period for a divorced woman as per Muslim law.
•	Magistrate: A First Class Magistrate as defined by the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973.
3.	Rights and Entitlements of a Divorced Woman: - Maintenance and Provision: Entitled to reasonable maintenance during the Iddat period.
•	Child Support: Up to two years from birth.
•	Return of Personal Properties and Mahr (Dower): Mandatory return of all personal effects and the agreed-upon Mahr.
•	Iddat Maintenance: Covers essential living expenses.
4.	Enforcement Mechanisms: - Application to Magistrate: For enforcement of rights under the Act.
•	Penalty for Non-Compliance: Imprisonment or until compliance is achieved.
5.	Post-Iddat Support:
•	If unable to support herself and remains unmarried, support may be sought from:
1.	Financially Capable Children.
2.	Parents, if children are unable.
3.	State Wakf Board as a last resort.
4.	Option to Invoke Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973:
•	A declaration at the first hearing allows opting for Sections 125-128 for maintenance.
7.	Rule Making Authority: - The Central Government has the power to make rules for effective implementation.
8.	Transitional Provisions: - Pending applications under the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, to be disposed of under this Act.
Significance and Recent Developments
•	Enhanced Protection: Ensures comprehensive rights for divorced Muslim women.
•	Legislative Updates: Complemented by newer laws addressing the divorce process, while this Act focuses on post-divorce rights.
•	Uniform Application: Now applies uniformly across India, including Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh.

[19th May, 1986.]

meta.dc.legislation.history:
Legislative History:

The Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Divorce) Act, 1986

Act Title - The Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Divorce) Act, 1986

Act Number/Year - 25 of 1986

Act ID (India Code) - 198625

Presidential Assent Date - May 19, 1986

Enforcement Date - May 19, 1986

Nodal Ministry - Ministry of Law and Justice

Precedent & Historical Rationale

Judicial Controversy and the Shah Bano Case:

The enactment of this legislation was a direct legislative response to the landmark Supreme Court judgment in Mohd. Ahmed Khan v. Shah Bano Begum (1985). In that case, the Supreme Court ruled that a Muslim divorced woman was entitled to claim maintenance from her former husband under Section 125 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, sparking an intense nationwide debate on personal law, secular criminal jurisprudence, and women's rights.

Legislative Intent and Protection of Personal Law:

The socio-political landscape following the judgment witnessed sharp divisions regarding the applicability of secular maintenance laws to Muslim personal law. To address the financial security of divorced Muslim women while respecting traditional Islamic jurisprudence (specifically regarding the iddat period and provisions to be made by the husband), the government introduced the Act to delineate and safeguard the rights of Muslim women upon divorce outside the scope of general criminal maintenance provisions, shifting financial responsibility during and after the iddat period primarily to the former husband or, subsequently, relatives and the Wakf Board.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

Formulation:

Drafted by the Ministry of Law and Justice to specify the rights of Muslim women upon being divorced by their husbands, outlining provisions for a reasonable and fair provision and maintenance to be made and paid within the iddat period, along with mechanisms involving the State Wakf Boards for destitute women.

Parliamentary Passage:Introduced, fiercely debated, and passed by both Houses of Parliament (Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha) amid widespread national discourse during the early summer session of 1986.

Presidential Assent: Received Presidential Assent on May 19, 1986.

Enforcement: Enforced on May 19, 1986.

Source: Official Records of Parliament, India Code, and Ministry of Law and Justice (Department of Legal Affairs).

THE PROTECTION OF CHILDREN FROM SEXUAL OFFENCES ACT, 2012
ACT NO. 32 OF 2012

[19th June, 2012.]

An Act to protect children from offences of sexual assault, sexual harassment and pornography and provide for establishment of Special Courts for trial of such offences and for matters connected therewith or incidental thereto.
WHEREAS clause (3) of article 15 of the Constitution, inter alia, empowers the State to make special provisions for children;
AND WHEREAS, the Government of India has acceded on the 11th December, 1992 to the Convention on the Rights of the Child, adopted by the General Assembly of the United Nations, which has prescribed a set of standards to be followed by all State parties in securing the best interests of the child;
AND WHEREAS it is necessary for the proper development of the child that his or her right to privacy and confidentiality be protected and respected by every person by all means and through all stages of a judicial process involving the child;
AND WHEREAS it is imperative that the law operates in a manner that the best interest and well being of the child are regarded as being of paramount importance at every stage, to ensure the healthy physical, emotional, intellectual and social development of the child;
AND WHEREAS the State parties to the Convention on the Rights of the Child are required to undertake all appropriate national, bilateral and multilateral measures to prevent--
(a) the inducement or coercion of a child to engage in any unlawful sexual activity;
(b) the exploitative use of children in prostitution or other unlawful sexual practices;
(c) the exploitative use of children in pornographic performances and materials;
AND WHEREAS sexual exploitation and sexual abuse of children are heinous crimes and need to be effectively addressed.
BE it enacted by Parliament in the Sixty-third Year of the Republic of India as follows:--

Legislative Framework:

The Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012

Short Title The Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012 (POCSO Act)

Act Number / Year Act No. 32 of 2012

India Code Act ID 201232

Presidential Assent Date June 19, 2012

Enforcement Date November 14, 2012

Nodal Ministry Ministry of Women and Child Development

Precedent & Statutory Rationale

1. Inadequacies in General Penal Laws for Child Sexual Abuse:

o Prior to the enactment, child sexual offences were predominantly prosecuted under generic provisions of the Indian Penal Code (IPC), such as sections dealing with rape and outraging modesty. These laws contained critical loopholes: they lacked gender neutrality, failed to cover non-penetrative or diverse forms of assault, did not distinguish between adult and child victims, and lacked specialized mechanisms to shield minor victims from secondary trauma.

2. Dedicated Child-Centric Legal Architecture:

o The legislation was formulated to establish a robust, comprehensive framework specifically dedicated to safeguarding individuals below the age of 18 years from sexual assault, sexual harassment, and pornography. Its goals include defining clear-cut offences with graded punishments, instituting child-friendly investigation and trial protocols via designated Special Courts, and prioritizing the best interests, safety, and rehabilitation of the child at every stage of the judicial process.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

• Formulation: Prepared and piloted by the Ministry of Women and Child Development to address systemic gaps in child protection and fulfill India's constitutional mandates and international commitments under the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child.

• Parliamentary Passage: Tabled, debated, and passed by both Houses of Parliament (Rajya Sabha on May 10, 2012, and Lok Sabha on May 22, 2012) during the budget session.

• Presidential Assent: Received formal Presidential Assent on June 19, 2012, entering the statute book as Act No. 32 of 2012.

• Enforcement: Enforced on November 14, 2012.

Source: India Code and Ministry of Women and Child Development, Government of India

Precedent & Statutory Rationale

1. Aftermath of the 2008 Mumbai Terror Attacks:

o Prior to 2008, India lacked a dedicated, federal counter-terrorism investigative agency. Cross-border terror conspiracies, multi-state organized crimes, and threats to national sovereignty were primarily investigated by respective State police forces, which faced jurisdictional constraints, limited inter-state intelligence sharing, and resource gaps.

o The devastating 2008 Mumbai terror attacks exposed critical vulnerabilities in national security architecture and underscored the urgent necessity for a centralized, specialized agency capable of seamless pan-India investigations.

2. Imperative for Federal Counter-Terrorism Response:

o The legislation was enacted to create a premier federal investigation agency to handle terror-related crimes, cyber-terrorism, atomic/nuclear facility threats, and offenses affecting India's sovereignty, security, and integrity, unhindered by state borders.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

• Formulation: Developed and fast-tracked by the Ministry of Home Affairs in the immediate wake of the November 2008 Mumbai attacks as part of a sweeping counter-terrorism legislative overhaul (alongside amendments to the Unlawful Activities Prevention Act).

• Parliamentary Passage: Tabled, debated, and swiftly passed by both Houses of Parliament during a special session in December 2008.

• Presidential Assent: Received formal Presidential Assent on December 31, 2008, entering the statute book as Act No. 34 of 2008.

• Enforcement: Enforced on December 31, 2008.

meta.dc.legislation.history:
Legislative History:

The National Security Act, 1980

● Act Title - The National Security Act, 1980

● Act Number / Year - 65 of 1980

● Act ID (India Code) - 198065

● Presidential Assent Date - December 27, 1980

● Enforcement Date - December 27, 1980

● Nodal Ministry - Ministry of Home Affairs

Precedent & Historical Rationale

● Constitutional Framework under Article 22(3)–(7) - Enacted pursuant to the constitutional provisions under Article 22, which allow Parliament to make laws providing for preventive detention for reasons connected with the Defence of India, foreign affairs, security of India, or the maintenance of public order and essential services.

● Replacement of Prior Preventive Detention Laws - Formulated to fill the legislative vacuum left by the expiration of the Maintenance of Internal Security Act (MISA), 1971, and the repeal of earlier preventive detention measures post-Emergency. The Act empowered the Central Government and State Governments (as well as District Magistrates and Commissioners of Police) to detain individuals without formal charge or trial to prevent them from acting in any manner prejudicial to the defence of India, public order, or the maintenance of supplies and services essential to the community.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

● Formulation - Introduced by the Union Ministry of Home Affairs to replace the National Security Ordinance, 1980 (Ordinance 11 of 1980) promulgated by President N. Sanjiva Reddy on September 23, 1980.

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949

Key Provisions:
1.	Licensing of Banking Companies: 
o	Requires every banking company to obtain a licence from the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) before commencing or carrying on banking business. 
o	Empowers the RBI to grant, refuse, suspend, or cancel licences subject to prescribed conditions. 
2.	Regulation of Banking Business: 
o	Prescribes the forms of business that banking companies may undertake and restricts activities not related to banking. 
o	Regulates the opening, shifting, and closing of branches with the approval of the RBI where required. 
3.	Capital and Reserve Requirements: 
o	Prescribes minimum capital and reserve requirements for banking companies. 
o	Requires banks to maintain adequate reserves and comply with prudential norms to ensure financial stability. 
4.	Management and Governance: 
o	Regulates the appointment, qualifications, and remuneration of directors and key managerial personnel. 
o	Empowers the RBI to issue directions relating to the management and administration of banking companies. 
5.	Inspection and Supervision: 
o	Authorizes the RBI to inspect banking companies, examine their books and accounts, and issue directions in the interest of banking policy, depositors, or the public. 
o	Requires banks to furnish returns, statements, and other information to the RBI. 
6.	Amalgamation, Reconstruction, and Winding Up: 
o	Provides procedures for the amalgamation, reconstruction, or voluntary winding up of banking companies. 
o	Empowers the RBI to prepare schemes for amalgamation or reconstruction in appropriate cases. 
7.	Moratorium and Suspension of Business: 
o	Enables the Central Government, on the recommendation of the RBI, to impose a moratorium on a banking company under specified circumstances. 
o	Facilitates measures for the revival or orderly resolution of financially distressed banks. 
8.	Restrictions on Loans and Investments: 
o	Imposes restrictions on loans and advances to directors and related parties to prevent conflicts of interest. 
o	Regulates investments and exposure to safeguard depositors' funds. 
9.	Accounts, Audit, and Disclosure: 
o	Requires banking companies to maintain proper books of account, prepare financial statements, and have their accounts audited. 
o	Prescribes disclosure and reporting requirements to ensure transparency. 
10.	Penalties and Enforcement: 
o	Prescribes penalties for contraventions of the Act, rules, directions, or orders issued by the RBI. 
o	Empowers the RBI to take corrective and supervisory action against defaulting banking companies.

The Banking Regulation Act, 1949

Short Title The Banking Regulation Act, 1949

Act Number / Year 10 of 1949

Act ID (India Code) 194910

Presidential Assent / Enactment Date March 10, 1949

Enforcement Date March 16, 1949

Nodal Ministry Ministry of Finance

Precedent & Statutory Rationale

1. Vulnerabilities and Failures in the Pre-Independence Banking Sector:

o Prior to 1949, banking companies in British India operated under the general provisions of the Indian Companies Act, 1913, which lacked specialized prudential norms, liquidity requirements, or robust regulatory oversight.

o The absence of a dedicated legal framework led to a high frequency of bank failures, speculative management practices, inadequate capital reserves, and severe risks to public deposits, which became especially acute during the economic turbulence following the Second World War and partition.

2. Establishment of Comprehensive Statutory Regulation:

o The 1949 Act was enacted to consolidate and amend the law relating to banking companies, empowering the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) with sweeping statutory authority to regulate, supervise, and inspect the banking sector.

o The core statutory objective was to protect public savings, ensure minimum capital and liquid asset requirements (such as the Cash Reserve Ratio and Statutory Liquidity Ratio frameworks), regulate branch expansion, prevent fraudulent management, and secure the stability and orderly growth of India's financial system.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

• Formulation: Drafted and piloted by the Ministry of Finance in close collaboration with the Reserve Bank of India to establish a stable, centralized legal architecture for national banking operations.

• Parliamentary Passage: Tabled, debated, and passed by the Constituent Assembly of India (Legislative), receiving formal assent from the Governor-General on March 10, 1949.

• Enforcement: Enforced on March 16, 1949.

meta.dc.legislation.history:
Legislative History:

The Indian Contract Act, 1872

● Act Title - The Indian Contract Act, 1872

● Act Number / Year - 9 of 1872

● Act ID (India Code) - 187209

● Presidential Assent Date - April 25, 1872

● Enforcement Date - September 1, 1872

● Nodal Ministry - Ministry of Law and Justice

Precedent & Historical Rationale

● Inconsistencies and Fragmented Commercial Law in British India - Prior to 1872, contract law across British India was governed by a patchwork system. In the Presidency Towns (Calcutta, Bombay, and Madras), English common law applied to Europeans, while Hindu and Muslim personal laws governed contract disputes between natives. In the mofussil (rural areas), courts relied on broad notions of "justice, equity, and good conscience." This fragmented structure caused immense uncertainty for growing commercial trade and interstate business.

● Codification Based on English Common Law Principles - Drafted by the Third Law Commission of India (led by Sir James Fitzjames Stephen and heavily influenced by Lord Romilly’s earlier drafts), the Act sought to establish a single, comprehensive statutory framework for commercial agreements. It adapted principles of English common law to Indian conditions, codifying fundamental rules regarding offer and acceptance, consideration, free consent, performance, breach, and damages. (Note: Special branches originally included, such as Sales of Goods and Partnership, were later carved out into separate statutes in 1930 and 1932).

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

● Formulation - Prepared by the Law Commission in England, subsequently revised by the Legislative Council of India to better suit local socio-economic contexts.

● Parliamentary Passage - Considered and passed by the Council of the Governor General of India for making Laws and Regulations in April 1872.

● Presidential Assent - Received the assent of the Governor General of India on April 25, 1872.

● Enforcement - Came into force on September 1, 1872.

Sources - Official Records of the Governor General in Council, India Code, Law Commission of India Reports, and Ministry of Law and Justice.

Legislative History:

The Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881

● Act Title - The Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881

● Act Number / Year - 26 of 1881

● Act ID (India Code) - 188126

● Presidential Assent Date - December 9, 1881

● Enforcement Date - March 1, 1882

● Nodal Ministry - Ministry of Finance

Precedent & Historical Rationale

● Multiplicity of Mercantile Customs & Legal Uncertainty - Prior to 1881, commercial credit transactions across British India lacked a unified statutory code. In Presidency Towns, English mercantile common law governed European traders, while indigenous commercial instruments—such as traditional bills of exchange (hundis, shah-jog hundis, and darshani hundis)—were regulated entirely by customary usage and merchant guild practices. In rural districts (mofussil), courts resolved payment and endorsement disputes by applying variable notions of "equity and good conscience." This statutory void hindered inter-regional commerce, credit discounting, and banking operations.

● Codification of Negotiable Commercial Paper - Originally drafted by the Third Indian Law Commission in 1867 and subsequently revised by a Select Committee and the Fourth Law Commission (led by Sir Arthur Hobhouse and Sir James Fitzjames Stephen), the Act codified the law relating to Promissory Notes, Bills of Exchange, and Cheques. It established core commercial principles:

○ Freedom of negotiation by delivery or endorsement.

○ Protections for a "holder in due course" against underlying defects of title.

○ Presumptions as to consideration, date, and order of endorsements.

○ Formal rules for presentment, notice of dishonour, protest by Notaries Public, and banker duties.

○ Preservation of indigenous hundi customs unless excluded by the terms of the instrument (Section 1).

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

● Formulation - Introduced to define and amend the substantive law of negotiable instruments, balancing English codification principles with local commercial trade practices across India.

● Parliamentary Passage - Underwent extensive committee revisions and was passed by the Imperial Legislative Council of India in late 1881.

● Presidential Assent - Received the assent of the Governor General of India on December 9, 1881.

● Enforcement - Enforced on March 1, 1882.

Sources - Official Records of the Governor General in Council, India Code and Ministry of Finance.

Precedent & Statutory Rationale

1. Limitations of Traditional Partnerships and Companies:

It combined the organizational and operational flexibility of a traditional partnership with the legal protection of limited liability typically reserved for companies.

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955

The Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 (Act No. 25 of 1955) was enacted to codify and reform the law relating to marriage among Hindus. It provides a comprehensive legal framework governing the solemnization of Hindu marriages, matrimonial rights and obligations, judicial separation, divorce, maintenance, and the legitimacy of children.

Key Provisions

•	Applies to Hindus, Buddhists, Jains, and Sikhs, and to other persons to whom the Act is made applicable, subject to its provisions. 
•	Prescribes the essential conditions for a valid marriage, including: 
o	Monogamy. 
o	Soundness of mind of both parties. 
o	Minimum marriageable age prescribed by law. 
o	Absence of prohibited relationships or sapinda relationships, unless permitted by custom. 
•	Recognizes marriages solemnized in accordance with customary rites and ceremonies. 
•	Provides for the registration of Hindu marriages. 
•	Prescribes grounds for void and voidable marriages. 
•	Provides for restitution of conjugal rights, judicial separation, and divorce on specified grounds such as cruelty, desertion, conversion, incurable mental disorder, renunciation, and presumed death, among others. 
•	Provides for interim maintenance, permanent alimony, child custody, and maintenance during matrimonial proceedings. 
•	Declares children born of void and voidable marriages to be legitimate, subject to the provisions of the Act. 
•	Confers jurisdiction on family courts and other competent courts to adjudicate matrimonial disputes.

•	Objection Period: 30 days from notice publication.
•	Solemnization Post-Objection Clearance: Not detailed in provided context.

Additional Insights from Context

•	The Prohibition of Child Marriage Act, 2006: Separate legislation dealing with child marriages, punishments, and rights.
•	Amendments and Extensions: Historical updates to the Special Marriage Act, applying to various territories.

Precedent & Historical Rationale

1. Replacement of the Special Marriage Act, 1872: The earlier colonial legislation (Act III of 1872) required parties of different faiths to explicitly renounce their respective religions before solemnizing a civil marriage, creating severe social and personal hardship.

2. Establishment of a Civil, Secular Matrimonial Code: Enacted to provide a universal, secular form of civil marriage available to all citizens of India regardless of religion, faith, or caste, without requiring religious conversion. It also established statutory provisions for civil registration of marriages celebrated under other personal laws, restitution of conjugal rights, judicial separation, and divorce by mutual consent or specified grounds.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

● Formulation: Introduced by the Law Ministry to enact progressive personal law reforms post-independence and fulfill the spirit of a uniform secular civil standard under the Constitution of India.

● Parliamentary passage: Examined by a Joint Select Committee of Parliament, extensively debated, and passed by both Houses (First Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha) in late 1954.

● Presidential Assent: Received Presidential Assent on October 9, 1954.

● Enforcement: Enforced on January 1, 1955.

Summary of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956

Key Provisions:

1.	Application of the Act 
o	The Act applies to Hindus, Buddhists, Jains, and Sikhs. 
o	It governs succession to the property of a person who dies without making a will (intestate succession). 
2.	General Rules of Succession 
o	The Act lays down rules for determining the legal heirs of a deceased person. 
o	It classifies heirs into different categories for distribution of property. 
3.	Succession to the Property of a Male Hindu 
o	The property of a deceased male Hindu devolves upon heirs according to the order specified in the Act. 
o	Class I heirs (such as widow, children, and mother) receive priority over other heirs. 
o	If no Class I heirs exist, succession passes to Class II heirs, agnates, and cognates. 
4.	Succession to the Property of a Female Hindu 
o	The Act provides rules for inheritance of property owned by a female Hindu. 
o	Property generally devolves upon her sons, daughters, husband, and other specified heirs according to the order prescribed. 
5.	Rights of Daughters in Coparcenary Property 
o	Originally, the Act recognised only male members as coparceners in a Hindu joint family. 
o	The Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005 granted daughters equal rights as sons in ancestral property, making them coparceners by birth with the same rights and liabilities. 
6.	Devolution of Interest in Coparcenary Property 
o	The Act provides rules regarding the transfer of interest in joint family property. 
o	After the 2005 amendment, the principle of survivorship was modified to ensure equal rights for daughters. 
7.	Disqualifications from Succession 
o	The Act specifies circumstances where a person may be disqualified from inheriting property, such as certain cases involving murder of the deceased. 
8.	Testamentary Succession 
o	The Act does not restrict a Hindu from disposing of property through a valid will, subject to applicable legal provisions.

Summary of Repealing and Amending Act,2025

The Act aims to simplify the statute book, improve legal clarity, and remove enactments that have become unnecessary without affecting accrued rights, liabilities, or pending proceedings. 
It repeals 71 obsolete Acts and amends 4 existing Acts. 
Key Provisions
1. Repeal of Obsolete Laws
•	Repeal of 71 Acts: Removes enactments that have become obsolete, spent, or whose purpose has already been fulfilled. 
•	Removal of Amendment Acts: Repeals several amending Acts whose amendments have already been incorporated into the principal legislation. 
2. Amendment of Existing Laws
•	Four Acts Amended: Makes technical and consequential amendments to the General Clauses Act, 1897, Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Indian Succession Act, 1925, and Disaster Management Act, 2005. 
•	Legislative Clarity: Updates terminology, corrects drafting errors, and removes obsolete provisions. 
3. Savings Clause
•	Protection of Existing Rights: The repeal does not affect accrued rights, liabilities, obligations, penalties, or pending legal proceedings. 
•	Continuity of Law: Ensures that actions taken under the repealed enactments remain legally valid. 
4. Simplification of the Statute Book
•	Removal of Redundant Laws: Eliminates unnecessary legislation to reduce complexity and improve accessibility. 
•	Ease of Governance: Facilitates efficient legal administration by maintaining a cleaner and more coherent body of laws. 
5. Modernisation of the Legal Framework
•	Improved Legislative Drafting: Promotes consistency and modern legal terminology across statutes. 
•	No Substantive Policy Change: The Act primarily performs legislative housekeeping without introducing major policy reforms.

Precedent & Historical Rationale

●	Statutory Cleanup & Removal of Obsolete Enactments: Formally repeals 71 redundant, spent, and obsolete Acts enacted between 1886 and 2023, continuing periodic legislative exercise to purge outdated laws and reduce statutory congestion.

Precedent & Statutory Rationale

1. Working Capital Bottlenecks for MSMEs:

o Prior to 2012, micro, small, and medium enterprises (MSMEs) frequently suffered from severe liquidity crunches and working capital delays caused by extended payment cycles from commercial purchasers, impacting their operational viability.

2. Lack of Legal Clarity on Assignment of Receivables:

o The absence of a formal legal framework for the assignment of receivables, multi-agency registration mechanisms, and clear rights and obligations of factors, assignors, and debtors constrained the growth of the domestic factoring industry.

3. Fulfilling Recommendations of Expert Committees:

o The legislation was enacted following comprehensive recommendations by expert panels (such as the Kalyankrishnan Committee and the Standing Committee on Finance) to institutionalize factoring as an effective tool for trade finance and prompt liquidity realization.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

• Formulation: Developed and piloted by the Department of Financial Services within the Ministry of Finance to establish a robust regulatory framework for factoring and assignment of receivables.

• Parliamentary Passage: Introduced in Parliament in March 2011, examined in detail by the Parliamentary Standing Committee on Finance, and subsequently passed by both Houses of Parliament.

• Presidential Assent: Received formal Presidential Assent on January 22, 2012, entering the statute book as Act No. 12 of 2012.

Enforcement: Enforced on February 1, 2012 (and April 2, 2012 for specific sections)

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of The Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, 1967 
Objective
The main objectives of the Act are to:
•	Safeguard the sovereignty, unity, integrity, and security of India. 
•	Prevent and prohibit unlawful activities and terrorist acts. 
•	Declare and ban organizations and individuals involved in terrorism or activities threatening national security. 
•	Prevent the financing of terrorism and disrupt terrorist networks. 
•	Provide a legal framework for the investigation, prosecution, and punishment of offences relating to terrorism and unlawful activities. 
•	Enable cooperation with international obligations relating to the prevention and suppression of terrorism. 
Key Provisions
•	Unlawful Activities: Defines and prohibits activities that seek to bring about the cession or secession of any part of India or that otherwise threaten the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the country. 
•	Terrorist Acts: Defines terrorist acts, including acts intended to threaten the unity, integrity, security, economic security, or sovereignty of India, or to terrorize the public through the use of violence or other specified means. 
•	Unlawful Associations: Empowers the Central Government to declare an association as an unlawful association if it is involved in activities prohibited under the Act. 
•	Designation of Terrorists: Authorizes the Central Government to designate organizations and individuals as terrorists if they are involved in terrorism. The Act also provides a mechanism for seeking review of such designation. 
•	Terrorist Funding: Criminalizes the raising, collection, provision, or use of funds and other assets intended for terrorist activities and provides for the attachment and forfeiture of property connected with terrorism. 
•	Investigation: Permits investigation of offences by designated agencies, including the National Investigation Agency (NIA) where applicable, and provides special procedural powers for investigating terrorist offences. 
•	Arrest and Bail: Prescribes stringent provisions relating to arrest, detention, and bail. Courts may grant bail only after considering the statutory conditions laid down in the Act. 
•	Punishments: Provides severe penalties, including imprisonment for varying terms, life imprisonment, or, in certain cases involving terrorist acts resulting in death, the death penalty. 
•	Forfeiture of Property: Enables attachment, seizure, and forfeiture of property derived from or used in connection with terrorist activities. 
•	Jurisdiction and Procedure: Provides for the constitution of Special Courts for the speedy trial of offences under the Act and prescribes special procedures for investigation and prosecution

Legislative History:

The Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, 1967

● Act Title - The Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, 1967

● Act Number / Year - 37 of 1967

● Act ID (India Code) - 196737

● Presidential Assent Date - December 30, 1967

● Enforcement Date - December 30, 1967

● Nodal Ministry - Ministry of Home Affairs

Precedent & Historical Rationale

● Constitutional Authorization under the 16th Amendment - Enacted pursuant to the Constitution (Sixteenth Amendment) Act, 1963, which allowed Parliament to impose reasonable restrictions on fundamental rights (specifically freedom of speech, assembly, and association) in the interests of the sovereignty and integrity of India.

● Prevention of Unlawful Associations & Secessionist Activities - Formulated to provide a statutory mechanism to prevent, declare unlawful, and penalize associations and activities directed against the territorial integrity and sovereignty of the Union of India.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

● Formulation - Introduced by the Ministry of Home Affairs to establish permanent national security powers following national security challenges and secessionist demands in the 1960s.

● Parliamentary Passage - Debated extensively in both Houses of Parliament (Fourth Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha) and referred to a Joint Committee before being passed in December 1967.

● Presidential Assent - Received Presidential Assent on December 30, 1967.

● Enforcement - Enforced on December 30, 1967.

Summary of Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023:
1. Jurisdiction and Procedure
*Applicability: Every person liable under this Sanhita for acts within India or beyond, with specific provisions for citizens abroad and offenses targeting Indian computer resources (Section 1). 
*Trial Procedure: Governed by the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, for all offences under it and other laws, unless specified otherwise. 
2. Court Structure
*Classes of Criminal Courts: Courts of Session, Judicial Magistrates (1st & 2nd class), and Executive Magistrates in every State. 
*Court of Session: Establishment, composition, and operational provisions. 
3. Offences and Punishments
*Punishment Nature: All offences under the Act are cognizable, non-bailable, and non-compoundable. 
*Specific Punishments:
•	Unfair Means: 3-5 years’ imprisonment and up to 10 lakh rupees fine, with additional penalties . 
•	Organised Crimes: 5-10 years’ imprisonment, significant fines, and asset forfeiture.
•	Defamation (Section 222): Special conditions for prosecuting public officials.
4. Compoundable Offences
*List and Conditions: Specified offences can be compounded with Court permission, detailing who can compound them.
*Special Cases: Provisions for minors, persons of unsound mind, etc. 

5. General Exceptions
*Acts Covered: Includes acts done under law, by mistake, accident, by children, persons of unsound mind, etc. (Chapter III) 
6. Prosecution Conditions
*Offences Against State & Public Servants: Requires previous sanction from Central/State Government or District Magistrate for prosecution 
 *Defamation Against Public Officials: Specific conditions for prosecution

THE EMPLOYMENT OF MANUAL SCAVENGERS AND CONSTRUCTION OF DRY LATRINES (PROHIBITION) ACT, 1993
ACT NO. 46 OF 1993

[5th June, 1993.]

An Act to provide for the prohibition of employment of manual scavengers as well as construction or continuance of dry latrines and for the regulation of construction and maintenance of water-seal latrines and for matters connected therewith or incidental thereto.
WHEREAS fraternity assuring the dignity of the individual has been enshrined in the Preamble to the Constitution;
AND WHEREAS article 47 of the Constitution, inter alia, provides that the State shall regard raising the standard of living of its people and the improvement of public health as among its primary duties; AND WHEREAS the dehumanizing practice of manual scavenging of human excreta still continues in many parts of the country;
AND WHEREAS the municipal laws by themselves as a measure for conversion of dry latrines into water-seal latrines and prevention of construction of dry latrines are not stringent enough to eliminate this practice;
AND WHEREAS it is necessary to enact a uniform legislation for the whole of India for abolishing manual scavenging by declaring employment of manual scavengers for removal of human excreta an offence and thereby ban the further proliferation of dry latrines in the country;
AND WHEREAS it is desirable for eliminating the dehumanising practice of employment of manual scavengers and for protecting and improving the human environment to make it obligatory to convert dry latrines into water-seal latrines or to construct water-seal latrines in new construction;
AND WHEREAS Parliament has no power to make laws for the States with respect to the matters aforesaid, except as provided in articles 249 and 250 of the Constitution;
AND WHEREAS in pursuance of clause (1) of article 252 of the Constitution, resolutions have been passed by all the Houses of the Legislatures of the States of Andhra Pradesh, Goa, Karnataka, Maharashtra, Tripura and West Bengal that the matters aforesaid should be regulated in those States by Parliament by law;
BE it enacted by Parliament in the Forty-fourth Year of the Republic of India as follows:--

Precedent & Historical Rationale

1. Persistence of Dehumanizing Practices:

o Despite Constitutional commitments under the Preamble (assuring individual dignity) and Article 47 (raising public health standards), the practice of manual removal of human excreta from dry latrines continued across various parts of the country.

2. Inadequacy of Municipal Laws:

o Pre-existing municipal legislations lacked uniform stringency and nationwide enforcement capabilities to completely eliminate dry latrines and penalize the employment of manual scavengers, necessitating a dedicated central framework enacted via state-adopted resolutions under Article 252 of the Constitution.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

• Formulation: Drafted by the Central Government to create a standardized national mechanism prohibiting the employment of manual scavengers, banning new dry latrines, and compelling their conversion into water-seal latrines.

• Parliamentary Passage: Introduced in Parliament after receiving enabling resolutions from participating State Legislatures under Article 252(1), subsequently passing both Houses.

• Presidential Assent: Received Presidential Assent on June 5, 1993.

• Enforcement: Enforced on January 26, 1997.

Legislative History:

The Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015

Short Title The Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015

Act Number / Year Act No. 2 of 2016

India Code Act ID 201602

Presidential Assent Date December 31, 2015

Enforcement Date January 15, 2016

Nodal Ministry Ministry of Women and Child Development

Precedent & Statutory Rationale

1. Public Outcry and Response to Heinous Crimes:

o Prior to 2015, the juvenile justice system treated all individuals under 18 uniformly as juveniles, regardless of the severity of the offense. Following intense public debate and national outrage catalyzed by the 2012 Delhi gang rape case—where one of the primary convicts was just months short of 18 and received the maximum reformatory term under the 2000 Act—the legislature recognized an urgent need to address rising violent crimes involving older adolescents.

2. Balancing Restorative Justice with Deterrence:

o Grounded in child rights and constitutional obligations under Articles 15(3), 39(e), 39(f), and 47, the legislation sought to overhaul the framework by introducing a differential justice system that separates reformative rehabilitation for younger children from criminal culpability and adult trial mechanisms for minors aged 16 to 18 involved in heinous crimes.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

• Formulation: Developed and piloted by the Ministry of Women and Child Development, spearheaded by then-Minister Maneka Gandhi.

• Parliamentary Passage: Introduced in the Lok Sabha in August 2014, subjected to extensive parliamentary scrutiny, passed by the Lok Sabha on May 7, 2015, and subsequently passed by the Rajya Sabha on December 22, 2015.

• Presidential Assent: Received formal Presidential Assent on December 31, 2015, entering the statute book as Act No. 2 of 2016.

• Enforcement: Brought into active operational force on January 15, 2016

• Source: India Code and Ministry of Women and Child Development Official Records

meta.dc.legislation.history:
Legislative History:

The Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989

Short Title The Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989

Act Number / Year 33 of 1989

Act ID (India Code) 198933

Presidential Assent Date September 11, 1989

Enforcement Date January 30, 1990

Nodal Ministry Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment

Precedent & Statutory Rationale

• Background/Transition:

Despite constitutional safeguards under Articles 15, 17, and 46, and the enactment of the Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955, members of Scheduled Castes (SCs) and Scheduled Tribes (STs) continued to face severe social discrimination, indignities, humiliation, and targeted violence across various parts of India. General penal provisions under the Indian Penal Code were often found inadequate to address caste-based atrocities, systemic marginalization, and the social impunity enjoyed by perpetrators. Recognizing that existing laws lacked sufficient deterrent value and specialized institutional mechanisms, Parliament resolved to enact a comprehensive special statute.

• Rationale/Objectives:

The Act was enacted by Parliament to prevent the commission of offenses of atrocities against members of the Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes, to provide for special courts for the trial of such offenses and for the relief and rehabilitation of the victims of such offenses and for matters connected therewith. Its core purpose was to instill a sense of security, punish specific caste-based crimes with heightened severity, dismantle structural discrimination, and ensure state accountability in protecting vulnerable communities.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Legislative Milestones

• Formulation/Introduction:

Formulated by the Ministry of Welfare (now Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment) to address widespread social injustices and deliver an uncompromising legal instrument against caste-based violence.

• Legislative Passage & Assent:

Passed by both Houses of Parliament and received presidential assent on September 11, 1989. (Note: The Act was comprehensively amended by the Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Amendment Act, 2015, which expanded the definition of atrocities, added new offenses, established exclusive special courts, and strengthened procedural safeguards for victims and witnesses).

• Statutory Mechanics & Provisions:

o Definition and Specification of Atrocities: Categorized and criminalized distinct acts of indignity, humiliation, harassment, forced labor, sexual exploitation, wrongful dispossession of land, and physical violence directed against members of SCs and STs.

o Special Courts and Exclusive Special Courts: Mandated the creation of Special Courts by State Governments (in concurrence with Chief Justices of High Courts) for the speedy trial of atrocity cases.

o Exclusion of Anticipatory Bail: Barred the application of Section 438 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (anticipatory bail) for persons accused of committing offenses under the Act, ensuring stricter pre-trial custody.

o Relief, Rehabilitation, and Collective Fines: Empowered authorities to provide immediate financial relief, travel allowances, and protective rehabilitation to victims and witnesses, while enabling imposition of collective fines on areas harboring perpetrators of atrocities.

• Presidential Assent: Received Presidential Assent on September 11, 1989.

• Enforcement: Enforced on January 30, 1990.

• Source: India Code Official Repository (indiacode.gov.in) and Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment, Government of India Official Records.

title: The Pre-conception and Pre-natal Diagnostic Techniques (Prohibition of Sex Selection) Act, 1994

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of the Pre-conception and Pre-natal Diagnostic Techniques (Prohibition of Sex Selection) Act, 1994 
Key Provisions
•	Prohibition of Sex Selection: The Act prohibits sex selection before or after conception and bans the communication or disclosure of the sex of the foetus to any person. 
•	Regulation of Diagnostic Techniques: Pre-conception and pre-natal diagnostic techniques may be used only for specified medical purposes and under the conditions prescribed by the Act. 
•	Registration of Centres: All genetic counselling centres, genetic laboratories, genetic clinics, ultrasound clinics, and imaging centres must be registered with the Appropriate Authority before carrying out any procedures covered by the Act. 
•	Appropriate Authorities: The Act provides for the appointment of Appropriate Authorities to register, monitor, inspect, investigate, suspend, or cancel the registration of centres and enforce compliance with the Act. 
•	Advisory Committees: Central, State, and Union Territory Supervisory Boards and Advisory Committees are constituted to oversee implementation, monitor compliance, and advise the Governments on matters relating to the Act. 
•	Prohibition of Advertisement: The Act prohibits advertisements relating to sex selection or facilities for sex determination and prescribes penalties for such advertisements. 
•	Offences and Penalties: The Act prescribes stringent penalties, including imprisonment, fines, suspension or cancellation of registration, and action against medical practitioners for contraventions such as conducting or facilitating sex selection or sex determination. 
•	Record Maintenance: Registered centres are required to maintain prescribed records and furnish information to the authorities, enabling effective monitoring and enforcement.

Act Title The Pre-conception and Pre-natal Diagnostic Techniques (Prohibition of Sex Selection) Act, 1994 (Originally enacted as The Pre-natal Diagnostic Techniques (Regulation and Prevention of Misuse) Act, 1994)

Precedent & Historical Rationale

1. Combating Female Foeticide and Skewed Sex Ratios:

o With the widespread commercial availability of ultra-sonography and prenatal diagnostic techniques in the 1980s and early 1990s, these technologies began to be heavily misused for illegal sex determination, leading to a sharp rise in female foeticide and a severely declining child sex ratio in India.

2. Regulatory Vacuum in Medical Ethics:

o Pre-existing medical codes were inadequate to curb the clandestine commercial practice of sex selective abortion. A robust statutory framework was required to regulate genetic counselling centers, laboratories, and clinics, completely prohibiting pre-natal sex determination and penalizing violations.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

• Formulation: Drafted by the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare to legally regulate the use of diagnostic techniques and ban any form of sex selection prior to or after conception.

• Parliamentary Passage: Introduced in Parliament, rigorously debated across both houses, and successfully passed during the Monsoon Session of 1994.

• Presidential Assent: Received Presidential Assent on September 20, 1994.

• Enforcement: Enforced on January 1, 1996.

Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (CPC)

Objective
•	To provide a uniform procedure for the adjudication of civil disputes.
•	To ensure fair, speedy, and effective delivery of civil justice.
•	To regulate the powers and jurisdiction of civil courts.
•	To facilitate the execution and enforcement of civil decrees and orders.
Key Provisions
•	Defines the jurisdiction and powers of civil courts.

•	Regulates the execution of decrees and orders passed by civil courts.
•	Contains provisions relating to temporary injunctions, attachment before judgment, appointment of receivers, and other interim reliefs.
•	Recognizes alternative dispute resolution (ADR) mechanisms, including arbitration, conciliation, mediation, and judicial settlement, to encourage amicable resolution of disputes.
•	Includes provisions for representative suits, suits by or against the Government, and matters involving foreign judgments.

The Code of Civil Procedure, 1908

Legislative History: The Code of Civil Procedure, 1908

● Act Title - The Code of Civil Procedure, 1908

● Act Number / Year - 5 of 1908

● Act ID (India Code) - 190805

● Assent Date - March 21, 1908

● Enforcement Date - January 1, 1909

● Nodal Ministry - Ministry of Law and Justice

Precedent & Historical Rationale

● Procedural Rigidity, Delays, and Judicial Conflicts under the 1882 Code - The predecessor Code of Civil Procedure, 1882 (Act XIV of 1882)—which had succeeded the Codes of 1859 and 1877—proved excessively rigid, formalistic, and prone to protracted procedural delays. Because every minute procedural rule was codified into primary statutory sections, amending even minor procedural defects required formal legislative enactments, resulting in severe backlogs, conflicting High Court interpretations, and an inability of courts to adapt trial procedures to local requirements.

● Bifurcated Structural Architecture of Substantive Sections and Delegated Rules - Formulated to consolidate and amend the laws relating to the procedure of the Courts of Civil Judicature into a durable, flexible, two-part code. The Act established unalterable substantive principles in the main body (Sections 1 to 158) dealing with jurisdiction, res judicata, execution, appeals, and inherent powers (Section 151), while relegating detailed procedural machinery to the First Schedule (Orders I to LI), crucially empowering High Courts (under Sections 122–131) to alter, annul, or frame new rules via Rule Committees without awaiting parliamentary amendment.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

● Formulation - Drafted by the Legislative Department of the Government of India under the direction of Law Member Sir Henry Erle Richards, building upon the exhaustive recommendations and revision bills prepared by the Special Civil Procedure Code Revision Committees and High Court Chief Justices (1901–1907).

● Parliamentary Passage - Introduced as The Code of Civil Procedure Bill, 1907 in the Council of the Governor General of India for the purpose of making Laws and Regulations on September 6, 1907, subjected to comprehensive clause-by-clause scrutiny by a Special Select Committee, and passed on March 20, 1908 at Calcutta.

● Governor-General's Assent - Received the assent of the Governor-General of India (Lord Minto) on March 21, 1908.

● Enforcement - Enforced on January 1, 1909.

Sources - Official Records of the Council of the Governor General of India, India Code, and Ministry of Law and Justice.

THE DELHI URBAN ART COMMISSION ACT, 1973

ACT NO. 1 OF 1974

[1st January, 1974.]

An Act to provide for the establishment of the Delhi Urban Art Commission with a view to preserving, developing and maintaining the aesthetic quality of urban and environmental design within Delhi.

BE it enacted by Parliament in the Twenty-fourth Year of the Republic of India as follows:—

CHAPTER I

PRELIMINARY

1. Short title, extent and commencement.—(1) This Act may be called the Delhi Urban Art Commission Act, 1973.

(2) It extends to the whole of the Union territory of Delhi.

(3) It shall come into force on such date1 as the Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, appoint.

2. Definitions.—In this Act, unless the context otherwise requires,—

(a) “building” includes any structure or erection or part of a structure or erection which is intended to be used for residential, industrial, commercial or other purposes, whether in actual use or not;

(b) “building operations” includes rebuilding operations, structural alterations of, or additions to, buildings and other operations normally undertaken in connection with the construction of buildings;

(c) “Commission” means the Delhi Urban Art Commission established under section 3;

(d) “Delhi” means the Union territory of Delhi;

(e) “development” with its grammatical variations means the carrying out of building, engineering, mining or other operations in, on, over or under, land or the making of any material change in any building or land and includes re-development;

(f) “engineering operations” includes the formation or laying out of means of access to a road or the laying out of means of water supply;

(g) “local body” means the Delhi Municipal Corporation established under the Delhi Municipal Corporation Act, 1957 (66 of 1957), the New Delhi Municipal Committee constituted under the Punjab Municipal Act, 1911 (Punjab Act III of 1911), as in force in Delhi, the Delhi Development Authority constituted under the Delhi Development Act, 1957 (61 of 1957), or any other local authority concerned with urban development of Delhi;

(h) “member” means a member of the Commission and includes its Chairman;

(i) “public amenity” includes road, water supply, street lighting, drainage, sewerage, public works and such other convenience as the Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, specify to be a public amenity for the purposes of this Act;

(j) “regulation” means a regulation made under this Act by the Commission;

(k) “rule” means a rule made under this Act by the Central Government.

1. 1st May, 1974, vide notification No. G.S.R. 189(E), dated the 27th April, 1974, see Gazette of India, Extraordinary, Part II, s. 3(i).

6

CHAPTER II

ESTABLISHMENT OF THE COMMISSION

3. Establishment of the Commission.—(1) With effect from such date as the Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, appoint, there shall be established a Commission by the name of the Delhi Urban Art Commission.

(2) The Commission shall be a body corporate having perpetual succession and a common seal with power to acquire, hold and dispose of property and to contract and shall by the said name sue or be sued.

4. Composition of the Commission.—The Commission shall consist of a Chairman and such number of other members, being not less than two and not more than four as the Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, appoint from amongst persons who, in the opinion of the Central Government, have sensibility and interest in the plastic and visual arts and urban environment, or possess special knowledge or practical experience in respect of architecture or art.

5. Terms and conditions of service of members.—(1) A member shall, unless his appointment is terminated earlier by the Central Government, hold office for a term of three years from the date of his appointment.

(2) A person who holds, or who has held, office as Chairman or member shall be eligible for re-appointment to that office once, but only once.

(3) A member may resign his office by writing under his hand addressed to the Central Government, but he shall continue in office until his resignation is accepted by the Central Government.

(4) A casual vacancy caused by the resignation of a member under sub-section (3) or for any other reason, shall be filled by fresh appointment.

(5) A member may be appointed either as a whole-time or part-time member as the Central Government thinks fit.

(6) Subject to the foregoing provisions, the terms and conditions of service of the Chairman and other members shall be such as may be prescribed by rules.

6. Meetings of the Commission.—The Commission shall meet at such times and places and shall observe such rules of procedure in regard to the transaction of business at its meetings as may be prescribed by regulations.

7. Vacancies amongst members or defect in constitution not to invalidate acts or proceedings of the Commission.—No act or proceeding of the Commission shall be deemed to be invalid by reason merely of any vacancy in, or any defect in the constitution of, the Commission.

8. Temporary association of persons with the Commission for particular purposes.—(1) The Commission may associate with itself, in such manner and for such purposes as may be determined by regulations, any person whose assistance or advice it may desire in carrying out any of the provisions of this Act.

(2) A person associated with it by the Commission under sub-section (1) for any purpose shall have a right to take part in the discussions relevant to that purpose, but shall not have a right to vote at a meeting of the Commission, and shall not be a member for any other purpose.

9. Appointment of staff of the Commission.—(1) The Central Government shall, in consultation with the Commission, appoint a Secretary of the Commission who shall hold office during the pleasure of the Central Government:

Provided that the first appointment of the Secretary may be made by the Central Government without consultation with the Commission.

(2) The terms and conditions of service of the Secretary shall be such as may be prescribed by rules.

7

(3) Subject to any rules, the Commission may appoint such other employees as it may think necessary for the efficient performance of its functions under this Act, and the terms and conditions of service of the employees so appointed shall be such as may be determined by regulations.

10. Authentication of orders and other instrument of the Commission.—All orders and decisions and other instruments of the Commission shall be authenticated by the signature of the Secretary or any other officer of the Commission duly authorised by it in this behalf.

CHAPTER III

FUNCTIONS AND POWERS OF THE COMMISSION

11. Functions of the Commission.—(1) It shall be the general duty of the Commission to advise the Central Government in the matter of preserving, developing and maintaining the aesthetic quality of urban and environmental design within Delhi and to provide advice and guidance to any local body in respect of any project of building operations or engineering operations or any development proposal which affects or is likely to affect the sky-line or the aesthetic quality of surroundings or any public amenity provided therein.

(2) Subject to the provisions of sub-section (1), it shall be the duty of the Commission to scrutinise, approve, reject or modify proposals in respect of the following matters, namely:—

(a) development of district centres, civic centres, areas earmarked for Government administrative buildings and for residential complexes, public parks and public gardens;

(b) re-development of the area within the jurisdiction of New Delhi Municipal Committee including Connaught Place Complex and its environs, Central Vista, the entire bungalow area of Lutyen’s New Delhi, and such other areas as the Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, specify;

(c) plans, architectural expressions and visual appearance of new buildings in the centres, areas, parks and gardens specified in clauses (a) and (b) including selections of models for statues and fountains therein;

(d) re-development of areas in the vicinity of Jama Masjid, Red Fort, Qutab, Humayun’s Tomb, Old Fort, Tuglakabad and of such other places of historical importance as the Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, specify;

(e) conservation, preservation and beautification of monumental buildings, public parks and public gardens including location or installation of statues or fountains therein;

(f) under passes, over-passes and regulations of street furniture and hoardings;

(g) location and plans of power houses, water towers, television and other communication towers and other allied structures;

(h) any other projects or lay-out which is calculated to beautify Delhi or to add to its cultural vitality or to enhance the quality of the surroundings thereof;

(i) such other matters as may be prescribed by rules.

Explanation.—For the purposes of this sub-section,—

(i) “civic centre” means the headquarters of a local body comprising therein its office buildings and buildings intended for cultural activities;

(ii) “Connaught Place Complex” means the area comprising Connaught Place and its extension measuring approximately 140 hectares, being the area described as Zone D-I (Revised) in the Delhi Master Plan;

(iii) “district centre” means a self-contained unit created in the Delhi Master Plan comprising areas for retail shopping, general business, commercial and professional offices, forwarding, booking and Government offices, cinemas, restaurants and other places of entertainment.

8

(3) Without prejudice to the provisions contained in sub-section (1) and sub-section (2), the Commission may suo motu promote and secure the development, re-development or beautification of any areas in Delhi in respect of which no proposals in that behalf have been received from any local body.

12. Duty of local bodies to refer development proposals, etc., to the Commission.— Notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force, every local body shall, before according approval in respect of any building operations, engineering operations or development proposals referred to in sub-section (1) of section 11 or intended to be undertaken in any area or locality specified in sub-section (2) of that section, refer the same to the Commission for scrutiny and the decision of the Commission in respect thereof shall be binding on such local body.

13. Appeal to the Central Government in certain cases.—If any local body is aggrieved by a decision of the Commission in respect of any building operation, engineering operation or development proposal intended to be undertaken or notified, as the case may be, by that local body and referred to the Commission under section 12, the local body may, within sixty days from the date of such decision, prefer an appeal to the Central Government, and the Central Government may pass such order thereon as it deems fit.

14. Power to revise decision in certain cases.—Nothing contained in this Act shall preclude the Central Government from calling for and examining, on its own motion, if it considers it necessary so to do in the public interest, any case in which a decision has been made by the Commission under section 12 but no appeal lies thereto, and passing such order thereon as it thinks fit:

Provided that no such order shall be made prejudicially affecting any person except after giving him an opportunity of making a representation in the matter.

15. Powers of the Commission.—for the purpose of performing its functions under this Act, the Commission shall have the same powers as are vested in a civil court while trying a suit under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (5 of 1908), in respect of the following matters, namely:—

(a) summoning and enforcing the attendance of any person and examining him;

(b) requiring discovery and production of any documents;

(c) receiving evidence on affidavits;

(d) requisitioning any public record or copies thereof from any office;

(e) any other matter which may be prescribed by rules.

CHAPTER IV

FUND, ACCOUNTS AND AUDIT

16. Payment to the Commission.—The Central Government may, after due appropriation made by Parliament by law in this behalf, pay to the Commission in each financial year such sums as the Central Government may consider necessary for the performance of the functions of the Commission under this Act.

17. Fund of the Commission.—(1) The Commission shall have its own fund, and all sums which may, from time to time, be paid to it by the Central Government shall be carried to the fund of the Commission and all payments by the Commission shall be made therefrom.

(2) The Commission may spend such sums as it thinks fit for performing its functions under this Act, and such sums shall be treated as expenditure payable out of the fund of the Commission.

(3) All moneys in the fund shall be deposited in such bank or invested in such manner as may, subject to the approval of the Central Government, be decided by the Commission.

18. Budget.—The Commission shall prepare, in such form and within such time, each year as may be prescribed by rules, a budget in respect of the financial year next ensuing showing the estimated receipts and expenditure, and copies thereof shall be forwarded to the Central Government.

9

19. Annual report.—The Commission shall prepare once every year, in such form and within such time as may be prescribed by rules, an annual report giving a true and full account of its activities during the previous year, and copies thereof shall be forwarded to the Central Government, and the Central Government shall cause every such report to be laid before both Houses of Parliament.

20. Accounts and audit.—(1) The Commission shall cause to be maintained such books of accounts and other books in relation to its accounts in such form and in such manner as may, in consultation with the Comptroller and Auditor-General of India, be prescribed by rules.

(2) The Commission shall, as soon as may be after closing its annual accounts, prepare a statement of accounts in such form as may be prescribed by rules, and forward the same to the Comptroller and Auditor-General of India by such date, as the Central Government may, in consultation with the Comptroller and Auditor-General of India, determine.

(3) The accounts of the Commission shall be audited by the Comptroller and Auditor-General of India at such times and in such manner as he thinks fit.

(4) The annual accounts of the Commission together with the audit report thereon shall be forwarded to the Central Government, and the Central Government shall cause the same to be laid before both Houses of Parliament and shall also forward a copy of the audit report to the Commission for taking appropriate action on the matters arising out of the audit report.

CHAPTER V

MISCELLANEOUS

21. Returns and information.—The Commission shall furnish to the Central Government such returns or other information with respect to its fund or activities as the Central Government may, from time to time, require.

22. Power to exempt.—The Central Government may, subject to such conditions as may be prescribed by rules in this behalf, exempt any building, building operation or engineering operation which has been designed as a result of an architectural competition, from the operation of all or any of the provisions of this Act.

23. Delegation of powers.—The Commission may, by general or special order in writing, delegate to the Chairman or any other member or any officer of the Commission, subject to such conditions and limitations, if any, as may be specified in the order, such of its powers and functions under this Act as it may deem necessary for the efficient running of the day-to-day administration of the Commission.

24. Members and officers of the Commission to be public servants.—All members and officers of the Commission shall, when acting or purporting to act in pursuance of any of the provisions of this Act, be deemed to be public servants within the meaning of section 21 of the Indian Penal Code (45 of 1860).

25. Protection of action taken in good faith.—No suit or other legal proceeding shall lie against any member or officer of the Commission in respect of anything which is in good faith done or intended to be done in pursuance of this Act.

26. Power to make rules.—(1) The Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, make rules to carry out the purposes of this Act.

(2) In particular, and without prejudice to the generality of the foregoing power, such rules may provide for all or any of the following matters, namely:—

(a) the salaries, if any, allowances and other terms and conditions of service of members of the Commission;

(b) the terms and conditions of service of the Secretary of the Commission;

(c) the matters in respect of which the Commission may tender advice to the Central Government under clause (i) of sub-section (2) of section 11;

(d) the form in which, and the time within which, the budget and annual report of the Commission may be prepared and forwarded to the Central Government;

10

(e) the form and manner in which the accounts of the Commission may be maintained, and the time at which, and the manner in which, such accounts may be audited;

(f) the returns and information which the Commission may be required to furnish to the Central Government;

(g) the conditions subject to which any building, building operation or engineering operation, designed as a result of an architectural competition, may be exempted;

(h) any other matter which has to be or may be prescribed by rules.

(3) Every rule made by the Central Government under this Act shall be laid, as soon as may be after it is made, before each House of Parliament while it is in session, for a total period of thirty days which may be comprised in one session or in two or more successive sessions, and if, before the expiry of the session immediately following the session or the successive sessions aforesaid, both Houses agree in making any modification in the rule or both Houses agree that the rule should not be made, the rule shall thereafter have effect only in such modified form or be of no effect, as the case may be; so, however, that any such modification or annulment shall be without prejudice to the validity of anything previously done under that rule.

27. Power to make regulations.—1[(1)] The Commission may, with the previous approval of the Central Government, by notification in the Official Gazette, make regulations consistent with this Act and the rules made thereunder for—

(a) regulating the meetings of the Commission and the procedure for conducting business thereat;

(b) regulating the manner in which and the purposes for which persons may be associated with the Commission under section 8:

(c) determining the terms and conditions of service of persons appointed by the Commission under sub-section (3) of section 9;

(d) any other matter which has to be or may be prescribed by regulations.

2[(2) Every regulation made under this section shall be laid, as soon as may be after it is made, before each House of Parliament, while it is in session, for a total period of thirty days which may be comprised in one session or in two or more successive sessions, and if, before the expiry of the session immediately following the session or the successive sessions aforesaid, both Houses agree in making any modification in the regulation or both Houses agree that the regulation should not be made the regulation shall thereafter have effect only in such modified form or be of no effect, as the case may be; so, however, that any such modification or annulment shall be without prejudice to the validity of anything previously done under that regulation.]

1. S. 27 renumbered as sub-section (1) thereof by Act 4 of 1986, s. 2 and the Sch. (w.e.f. 15-5-1986).

2. Ins. by s. 2 and the Schedule, ibid. (w.e.f. 15-5-1986).

11

STATEMENT OF OBJECTS AND REASONS

In large metropolitan cities, such as Washington, Paris, London, etc., Art Commissions have been set up to ensure the aesthetics of major public or governmental buildings when they come up in important streets or areas of the city. These buildings, in addition to conforming to the local building bye-laws, must pass the “Muster” of the Art Commission which is an independent authority.

2. It has been recommended in the National Building Code of India, 1970, that for major public building complexes or buildings coming up in important areas or monumental buildings in metropolitan cities, the aesthetics of the whole scheme vis-a-vis existing structures may be examined by an Art Commission. Accordingly, it is proposed to set up an Art Commission for the metropolitan area of Delhi. This is particularly necessary because the quality of urban designing emerging in Delhi has been a matter of great concern for some time as adequate thought is not being given to the aesthetics of the fresh constructions or lay-outs. The proposed Art Commission in addition to ensuring the aesthetics of new construction in areas mentioned above will also provide high level advice to Government, Semi-Government, and local bodies on any project or developmental proposals or schemes which will beautify the city and add to its cultural vitality.

NEW DELHI;

BHOLA PASWAN SHASTRI.

The 12th December, 1973.
