Source:

Key Legislative Metadata

Legislative Stage / Attribute Official Details

Act Title The Delhi Urban Art Commission Act, 1973

Act Number Act No. 1 of 1974

Act ID (India Code) 197401

Presidential Assent Date January 1, 1974

Enforcement Date May 1, 1974

Nodal Ministry Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs

Precedent & Historical Rationale

1. Rationale & Context: Following rapid post-independence urbanization, industrial growth, and large-scale public and private construction projects in the National Capital Territory of Delhi, concerns grew regarding the degradation of the city's unique architectural landscape, green covers, historical precincts, and open skylines.

2. The Legislative Problem: Existing municipal bodies and town planning laws (such as the Delhi Development Act, 1957) primarily focused on land-use zoning, spatial planning, and civic infrastructure, but lacked a specialized expert statutory advisory body dedicated exclusively to safeguarding, evaluating, and enhancing the aesthetic and environmental design quality of urban spaces.

3. The Remedy: Parliament enacted the Delhi Urban Art Commission Act, 1973 to establish an independent, expert statutory body the Delhi Urban Art Commission (DUAC) charged with the responsibility of advising the Central Government and local bodies on preserving, developing, and maintaining the aesthetic quality of urban and environmental design within Delhi

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

● Formulation: Conceived by the central government to institutionalize aesthetic and architectural scrutiny for major public buildings, infrastructural layouts, and urban redevelopment schemes in Delhi.

● Parliamentary Passage: Debated and enacted by both Houses of Parliament in late 1973, receiving formal statutory establishment at the start of 1974.

● Presidential Assent:Received assent from the President of India on January 1, 1974, and was brought into force on May 1, 1974

● Enforcement date: Enforced on May 1, 1974.

An Act to provide for the adjudication or trial by Armed Forces Tribunal of disputes and complaints with respect to commission, appointments, enrolment and conditions of service in respect of persons subject to the Army Act, 1950, the Navy Act, 1957 and the Air Force Act, 1950 and also to provide for appeals arising out of orders, findings or sentences of court martial held under the said Acts and for matters connected therewith or incidental thereto.

Precedent & Statutory Rationale

1. Backlog of Service Litigations and Judicial Recommendations:

o Prior to 2007, a large volume of service disputes and appeals arising from court-martial verdicts concerning personnel of the Indian Army, Navy, and Air Force remained pending in regular civil courts and High Courts for extended periods.

o Dating back to 1982, the Supreme Court of India urged the Central Government to establish specialized judicial mechanisms to ensure accessible review for military personnel, a recommendation reinforced by the Parliamentary Estimates Committee in 1992.

2. Dedicated, Timely, and Cost-Effective Dispute Resolution:

o The legislation was enacted to create an independent, expert statutory tribunal capable of handling military service matters and court-martial appeals with greater speed, specialized expertise, and confidentiality than traditional civilian judicial forums.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

• Formulation: Prepared and piloted by the Ministry of Defence to institute a dedicated military justice and grievance redressal tier.

• Parliamentary Passage: Introduced in the Rajya Sabha (Bill No. CXXIX of 2005) in December 2005, reviewed by the Standing Committee on Defence, and subsequently passed by both Houses of Parliament in December 2007.

• Presidential Assent: Received formal Presidential Assent on December 25, 2007, entering the statute book as Act No. 55 of 2007.

• Enforcement: Brought into active operational force on June 15, 2008.

An Act to provide for the regulation of chit funds and for matters connected therewith.

meta.dc.legislation.history:
Legislative History:

The Chit Funds Act, 1982

Act Title The Chit Funds Act, 1982

Act Number/Year 40 of 1982

Act ID (India Code) 198240

Presidential Assent Date August 19, 1982

Enforcement Date April 2, 1984

Nodal Ministry Ministry of Finance

Precedent & Historical Rationale

1. Regional Disparities and Multiplicity of State Laws:

o Prior to 1982, chit fund businesses were governed by a diverse patchwork of state-level enactments (such as the Madras Chit Funds Act, 1961, and the Kerala Chitties Act, 1975) or operated in a legislative vacuum in states without specific regulations.

o This multiplicity of laws created severe operational difficulties for multi-state chit operators and left subscribers vulnerable to malpractices, fraudulent defaults, and lack of uniform consumer protection.

2. Recommendations of the Banking Commission and Select Committee:

o Following the recommendations of the Banking Commission (1972) and subsequent extensive studies on indigenous savings and credit mechanisms, the Central Government recognized the need for a uniform, comprehensive central legislation.

o The legislative intent centered on regulating chit funds nationwide, safeguarding the interests of subscribers, prohibiting unauthorized or prize chits that resembled lottery schemes, and establishing standard operational guidelines for foremen.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

• Formulation:

Drafted by the Ministry of Finance in consultation with the Reserve Bank of India to provide a uniform legal framework that could be adopted or enforced smoothly across all states and union territories.

• Parliamentary Passage:

Referred to a Joint Committee of Parliament for detailed scrutiny, and subsequently deliberated and passed by both Houses of Parliament (Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha) during the monsoon session of 1982.

• Presidential Assent: Received Presidential Assent on August 19, 1982.

• Enforcement: Enforced on April 2, 1984.

Source: Official Records of Parliament, India Code, and Ministry of Finance (Department of Financial Services).

Summary of the Central Vigilance Commission Act, 2003
Key Provisions
1. Establishment & Governance
•	Central Vigilance Commission (CVC): Constituted under Section 3, led by a Central Vigilance Commissioner and up to two Vigilance Commissioners, appointed by the President on a committee's recommendation.
•	Tenure & Eligibility: 4-year term or until 65, with backgrounds emphasizing vigilance, administration, finance, law, etc.
2. Core Responsibilities & Authorities
•	Oversight Responsibilities: - Supervision over the Delhi Special Police Establishment (DSPE) in corruption cases.
•	Vigilance administration oversight in Central Ministries and Government entities.
•	Investigative Powers: - Authority to direct DSPE investigations.
•	Inquiry into corruption allegations against high-ranking public servants.
•	Advisory & Review Roles: Review of investigation progress.
•	Civil court powers during inquiries for evidence and testimony.
3. Operational Safeguards & Protections
•	Appointment Integrity:
•	Committee-driven appointments for key enforcement and DSPE positions ensuring experience and integrity.
•	Good Faith Protection:
•	Actions taken in good faith under the Act or its rules/orders are protected.
•	Members and officers are deemed public servants under the Indian Penal Code for legal protection.
4. Legislative Framework & Accountability
•	Rule Making Authority: Empowerment of the Central Government to create rules for operationalizing the Act.
•	Parliamentary scrutiny and potential amendment/annulment of rules.
•	Transparency & Oversight: Mandatory laying of orders and rules before Parliament.
5. Administrative & Judicial Provisions
•	Financial & Reporting: Expenses are borne by the Consolidated Fund of India.
•	Annual reporting to the President, subsequently tabled in Parliament.

Precedent & Supreme Court Directives

1. Executive Origin (1964):

o The Central Vigilance Commission (CVC) was originally established by a Government Resolution on February 11, 1964, upon the recommendations of the Committee on Prevention of Corruption (Santhanam Committee). However, it lacked statutory backing and operated merely as an advisory executive body.

2. The Vineet Narain v. Union of India (1997) Landmark Judgment:

o In the historic Hawala case (Vineet Narain v. Union of India, 1998), the Supreme Court of India mandated that the CVC be given statutory status to ensure institutional independence, insulate investigating agencies (CBI and Enforcement Directorate) from political interference, and supervise their functioning.

3. Ordinance Interregnum:

o Prior to the 2003 Act, the Government had promulgated successive Ordinances (first in 1999) to establish the statutory CVC, which eventually culminated in the enactment of the comprehensive 2003 legislation.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

• July 21, 2003: Introduced in the Lok Sabha as The Central Vigilance Commission Bill, 2003 by the Minister of State for Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions.

• August 2003: Bypassed standard committee referral due to pre-existing judicial mandates and prior parliamentary vetting of earlier drafts, being taken up directly for floor debate.

• September 11, 2003: Received Presidential Assent as Act No. 45 of 2003, coming into immediate legal effect.

THE ALL INDIA COUNCIL FOR TECHNICAL EDUCATION ACT, 1987
ACT NO. 52 OF 1987

[23rd December, 1987.]

An Act to provide for the establishment of an All India Council for Technical Education with a view to the proper planning and co-ordinated development of the technical education system throughout the country, the promotion of qualitative improvement of such education in relation to planned quantitative growth and the regulation and proper maintenance of norms and standards in the technical education system and for matters connected therewith.

Legislative History:

The All India Council for Technical Education Act, 1987

Act Title - The All India Council for Technical Education Act, 1987

Act Number/Year - 52 of 1987

Act ID (India Code) - 198752

Presidential Assent Date - December 23, 1987

Enforcement Date - March 28, 1988

Nodal Ministry - Ministry of Education

Precedent & Historical Rationale

Transition from an Advisory Body to a Statutory Authority:

The All India Council for Technical Education (AICTE) was originally established in November 1945 by a government resolution as a national-level advisory body to oversee and coordinate facilities for technical education across India. Over the subsequent four decades, explosive quantitative growth in engineering, technology, management, and architecture institutions led to widespread concerns regarding declining educational standards, unmonitored commercial expansion, and infrastructure deficiencies.

National Policy on Education (1986) Recommendations:

Recognizing these systemic challenges, the National Policy on Education (NPE), 1986, strongly emphasized the need for a statutory, empowered national body capable of enforcing rigorous quality standards, proper planning, and coordinated development. To operationalize this vision, Parliament enacted the All India Council for Technical Education Act, 1987, granting AICTE full statutory status, financial autonomy, and binding regulatory powers to inspect, accredit, and approve new and existing technical institutions.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

Formulation:

Drafted by the Ministry of Human Resource Development (now Ministry of Education) to provide statutory backing to AICTE, defining its powers and functions regarding the maintenance of norms, prevention of sub-standard institutions, and promotion of research and training in engineering, technology, architecture, town planning, management, pharmacy, and applied arts.

Parliamentary Passage:

Introduced, debated, and passed by both Houses of Parliament (Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha) during the winter session of December 1987.

Presidential Assent: Received Presidential Assent on December 23, 1987.

Enforcement: Enforced on March 28, 1988.

Source: Official Records of Parliament, India Code, and Ministry of Education (Department of Higher Education).

Precedent & Statutory Rationale

1. Shift from Development Finance to Commercial Banking:

o Established under the Industrial Development Bank of India Act, 1964 as an apex Development Finance Institution (DFI), IDBI historically focused on providing long-term project finance for industrial growth.

o With financial sector reforms and the evolution of capital markets, the traditional DFI model faced structural limitations in raising low-cost retail funds. Transforming IDBI into a commercial banking entity became imperative to ensure operational viability and market competitiveness.

2. Corporate Restructuring:

o The legislative framework was designed to corporatize IDBI by transferring its undertaking to a company registered under the Companies Act, 1956, enabling it to function as a full-fledged universal commercial bank while preserving existing statutory protections for bondholders, assets, and employees.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

• Formulation: Developed by the Ministry of Finance to restructure public sector financial institutions and align them with modern banking regulations.

title: The Slum Areas (Improvement and Clearance) Act, 1956

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of the Slum Areas (Improvement and Clearance) Act, 1956

Key Provisions:
1.	Declaration of Slum Areas 
o	The competent authority may declare an area as a slum area if buildings are unfit for human habitation or the area is overcrowded, insanitary, or detrimental to public health, safety, or convenience. 
2.	Improvement of Slum Areas 
o	The competent authority may prepare and implement improvement schemes, including: 
	Provision of basic civic amenities. 
	Repair and improvement of buildings. 
	Construction of roads, drainage, water supply, sanitation, and other public facilities. 
3.	Clearance of Slum Areas 
o	Where improvement is not feasible, the authority may declare the area as a slum clearance area. 
o	Buildings that are unsafe or unfit for habitation may be demolished, and redevelopment measures may be undertaken. 
4.	Acquisition of Land 
o	The Act empowers the Government to acquire land required for slum improvement or redevelopment projects in accordance with the prescribed procedure. 
5.	Protection of Tenants 
o	A landlord cannot evict a tenant from a building situated in a notified slum area without obtaining prior permission from the competent authority. 
o	This provision is intended to prevent displacement of vulnerable residents without due process. 
6.	Powers of the Competent Authority 
o	The competent authority may inspect properties, issue notices, require repairs, order demolition of unsafe structures, and take other measures necessary for implementing the Act. 
7.	Appeals and Rule-Making 
o	The Act provides for appeals against specified orders of the competent authority. 
o	The Central Government is empowered to make rules for carrying out the provisions of the Act.

Summary of the Prize Competitions Act, 1955

Key Provisions:
1.	Definition of Prize Competition 
o	The Act defines a prize competition as a competition where prizes are offered for solving puzzles or problems based upon the arrangement, combination, or permutation of letters, words, or figures (such as crossword and similar competitions). 

2.	Restriction on Prize Competitions 
o	Prize competitions offering prizes beyond the prescribed limit were prohibited. 
o	Competitions within the permitted limit required a valid licence from the competent authority. 
3.	Licensing of Competitions 
o	The Act provided for granting, suspension, and cancellation of licences for conducting prize competitions. 
o	Promoters were required to comply with conditions imposed by the licensing authority. 
4.	Maintenance of Accounts 
o	Organisers of prize competitions were required to maintain proper accounts and submit them to the licensing authority for inspection. 
5.	Penalties 
o	The Act prescribed penalties for: 
	Conducting illegal prize competitions. 
	Failure to maintain or submit accounts. 
	Other violations connected with prize competitions. 
6.	Powers of Authorities 
o	Licensing authorities were empowered to inspect records, call for documents, conduct searches, and take action against violations.

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of the Prisoners (Attendance in Courts) Act, 1955

Core Provisions
1.	Definitions: - Prison: Includes subsidiary jails, reformatories, and similar institutions.
•	Confinement in a Prison: Encompasses preventive detention.
2.	Court's Power to Summon Prisoners:
•	Authority: Civil and Criminal Courts can order a prisoner's production to give evidence if deemed material.
•	Geographical Limitation for Civil Courts: Cannot summon from prisons outside the court's state.
•	Procedure: Involves specific forms (e.g., Form No. 38 for contempt, Form No. 39 for uncooperative witnesses) and, for subordinate courts, requires countersignature.
3.	Exemptions by State Government: - Criteria for Exemption:
•	Nature of the offence or detention grounds.
•	Potential for public order disruption.
•	Broader public interest.
4.	Production and Detention in Court: - Procedure for Bringing Prisoners to Court: Ensures safe transit and custody until the court releases them.
•	Forms for Warrants: Utilizes specific legal forms (e.g., Warrant of Commitment, Form No. 40 for death sentences, Form No. 41 for commuted sentences).
5.	Exceptions for Prison Officer: - Valid Reasons to Abstain:
•	Prisoner's medical unfitness.
•	Pending trial or short detention period.
•	State Government exemption.
•	Specific procedural exemptions for certain court types.
6.	Commission for Prisoner Examination: - Alternative to Physical Appearance: Under specific circumstances, allows for in-prison examination via commission.
7.	Rule Making & Repeal:
•	State Government Powers: To make rules for the Act’s implementation.
•	Repeal of Preceding Laws: Repealed relevant sections of the Prisoners Act, 1900.

Legislative History: The Prisoners (Attendance in Courts) Act, 1955

Source: Official Record of Parliament, India Code, and Ministry of Home Affairs

Key Legislative Metadata

Legislative Stage /Attribute Official Details

Act Title The Prisoners (Attendance in Courts) Act, 1955

Act Number Act No. 32 of 1955

Act ID (India Code) 195532

Presidential Assent date September 20, 1955

Enforcement Date January 1, 1956

Nodal Ministry Ministry of Home Affairs

Precedent & Historical Rationale

1. Replacement of Outdated & Cumbersome Colonial Procedures: Prior to this Act, the production of incarcerated individuals before civil and criminal courts was governed by Part IX (Sections 34–52) of the Prisoners Act, 1900. The older procedure was notoriously cumbersome, requiring court orders to be routed through District or Sub-Divisional Magistrates or State Governments, causing severe delays in trials and unnecessary extended detentions.

2. Establishment of Direct Judicial Attendance Orders: Enacted to repeal Part IX of the Prisoners Act, 1900 and create a streamlined, standalone statutory framework. The Act empowered civil and criminal courts to issue direct attendance orders to prison officers-in-charge to produce prisoners for giving evidence or answering criminal charges, while establishing statutory exemptions (e.g., public order, safety, or severe illness) under which prison authorities could abstain from carrying out such orders.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

● Formulation: Introduced by the Ministry of Home Affairs in the First Lok Sabha as a procedural law reform measure to reduce trial delays across the Indian judicial system.

● Parliamentary passage: Debated and passed by both Houses of Parliament (First Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha) in August–September 1955.

● Presidential Assent: Received Presidential Assent on September 20, 1955.

● Enforcement: Enforced on January 1, 1956.

meta.dc.description.abstract:
summary of Himachal Pradesh and Bilaspur (New State) Act,1954

Key Provisions of the Act

1.	Formation of New State 
o	Himachal Pradesh and Bilaspur merged to form a new state called Himachal Pradesh.
o	Effective date: 1 July 1954.
2.	Constitutional Amendments
o	The First and Fourth Schedules of the Constitution were amended to reflect the new boundaries and representation.
3.	Representation
o	Adjustments made for representation in the Council of States (Rajya Sabha) and the House of the People (Lok Sabha).
o	Parliamentary constituencies were redefined and sitting members reassigned.
4.	Legislature & Administration
o	A Legislative Assembly was constituted for the new state.
o	The Governor held executive powers, including ordinance-making authority.
5.	Judiciary & Laws
o	A Court of the Judicial Commissioner was established for the new state.
o	Subordinate courts and existing laws continued until modified.
6.	Continuity & Transition
o	Existing authorities, officers, and taxes continued.
o	Special provisions safeguarded the Central Government’s control over the Bhakra-Nangal Project.

7.	Legislative Assembly: - Continuity for Sitting Members.
•	Validation: Later validated by The Himachal Pradesh Legislative Assembly (Constitution and Proceedings) Validation Act, 1958.

8.	Judicial System: - Unified Judicial Court: Formed by amalgamating the Courts of the Judicial Commissioners.
•	Subordinate Courts: Placed under the new Court’s superintendence.

title: The Delivery of Books and Newspapers (Public Libraries) Act, 1954

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of the Delivery of Books and Newspapers (Public Libraries) Act, 1954

Key Provisions: 
1. Scope: - Extends to the whole of India (initially except Jammu and Kashmir, but now applicable as per notification S.O. 3912(E), dated 30th October, 2019).
•	Applies to the National Library at Calcutta and up to three other libraries specified by the Central Government.

2.	Delivery Requirements: - Books: Publishers must deliver a copy of every newly published book to the National Library and one copy to each of the other specified public libraries within 30 days, free of cost.
•	Copy for the National Library: Complete with all maps and illustrations, on the best paper, and properly bound.
•	Copies for other libraries: On the paper used for the largest print run, in the condition prepared for sale.
•	Exemption: Second or subsequent editions without changes, if a previous edition was already delivered.
•	Newspapers: Publishers must deliver one copy of each issue to specified public libraries as soon as published, free of cost.

3.	Receipt and Penalty: - Receipt: Public libraries must provide a written receipt for delivered books.
•	Penalty for Non-compliance: Fine up to fifty rupees (potentially plus the book's value for book non-delivery), with possible compensation to the affected library.

4.	Jurisdiction and Rules: - Cognizance of Offences: Only courts of presidency magistrates or magistrates of the first class and above, on complaint from an officer empowered by the Central Government.
•	Power to Make Rules: Central Government can make rules to carry out the Act's provisions, with rules laid before Parliament.

5.	Special Provisions: - Government Publications: Act applies to books and newspapers published by the Government, except those for official use only.

•	To assimilate and extend specified laws to the Rifle Range and Umlong Cantonments in Shillong. 
•	To establish legal uniformity in the administration of these cantonments. 
•	To facilitate effective governance and judicial administration in the cantonment areas. 
•	To provide for consequential and transitional matters arising from the extension of laws.

•	Extended specified Central and State laws to the Rifle Range and Umlong Cantonments. 
•	Provided for the adaptation and modification of existing laws, where necessary, to suit the circumstances of the cantonments. 
•	Ensured that rights, liabilities, legal proceedings, and administrative actions existing before the commencement of the Act remained valid unless otherwise provided. 
•	Included transitional provisions to ensure the smooth implementation of the assimilated legal framework. 
•	Empowered the appropriate authorities to administer the extended laws within the cantonment areas.

title: The Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934
Key Features
•	Establishment of the RBI: Establishes the Reserve Bank of India as the central bank of the country and defines its constitution, management, and functions. 
•	Issue of Banknotes: Confers upon the RBI the sole authority to issue banknotes in India, except as otherwise provided by law. 
•	Monetary Policy: Empowers the RBI to formulate and implement monetary policy to maintain price stability while supporting economic growth. 
•	Banker to Government: Provides for the RBI to act as the banker, agent, and adviser to the Central and State Governments. 
•	Bankers' Bank: Authorises the RBI to regulate and supervise banks, maintain reserves, and provide financial assistance to scheduled banks when necessary. 
•	Management of Currency and Reserves: Entrusts the RBI with the management of currency circulation and the country's foreign exchange and reserve assets in accordance with applicable laws. 
•	Financial Stability and Regulation: Empowers the RBI to promote financial stability, regulate banking operations, and perform functions assigned under the Act and other financial laws.

meta.dc.legislation.history:
Legislative History:

The Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934

● Act Title - The Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934

● Act Number / Year - 2 of 1934

● Act ID (India Code) - 193402

● Presidential Assent Date - March 6, 1934

● Enforcement Date - March 6, 1934

● Nodal Ministry - Ministry of Finance

Precedent & Historical Rationale

● Dichotomy between Currency Control and Commercial Credit Administration - Prior to 1934, India lacked a unified central banking authority. Currency issuance and exchange management were controlled directly by the Government of India through its Finance Department, whereas commercial banking and government treasury operations were handled by the Imperial Bank of India (formed in 1921). This structural dichotomy created chronic inelasticity in the money supply, seasonal credit crunches, and an inability to manage exchange rates effectively.

● Recommendations of the Hilton Young Commission & Constitutional Prerequisite - In 1926, the Royal Commission on Indian Currency and Finance (Hilton Young Commission) recommended the establishment of an independent central bank—to be called the "Reserve Bank of India"—to separate the control of currency and credit from the political government. Furthermore, the British Government made the establishment of a financially sound, non-political Reserve Bank a fundamental prerequisite for constitutional reforms and the devolution of financial responsibility to a responsible federal government under the subsequent Government of India Act, 1935.

● Statutory Mandate for Monetary Stability, Currency Monopoly, and Banker to the State - Formulated to constitute a central bank to regulate the issue of banknotes, keep reserves with a view to securing monetary stability in India, and operate the currency and credit system of the country to its advantage. The Act conferred upon the Reserve Bank the sole monopoly of banknote issuance, designated it as the banker and debt manager to the government, mandated scheduled commercial banks to maintain cash reserves with it, and established its lender-of-last-resort functions.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

● Formulation - Following the withdrawal of an earlier 1927–1928 Bill over disagreements regarding state versus private shareholder ownership, a revised Bill was drafted based on the report of the London Committee on Reserve Bank Legislation (1933) and introduced in the Indian Legislative Assembly by the Finance Member, Sir George Schuster, in September 1933.

● Parliamentary Passage - Examined extensively by a Joint Select Committee, debated across sessions, and passed by the Indian Legislative Assembly in December 1933 and the Council of State in February 1934.

● Presidential Assent - Received the assent of the Governor General of India on March 6, 1934.

● Enforcement - Enforced on March 6, 1934

Sources - Official Records of the Governor General in Council, India Code, and Ministry of Finance.

Legislative History:

The Indian Succession Act, 1925

● Act Title - The Indian Succession Act, 1925

● Act Number / Year - 39 of 1925

● Act ID (India Code) - 192539

● Assent Date - September 30, 1925

● Enforcement Date - September 30, 1925

● Nodal Ministry - Ministry of Law and Justice

Precedent & Historical Rationale

● Fragmentation of Testamentary and Intestate Jurisprudence - Prior to 1925, the law governing succession, wills, and the administration of estates in British India was scattered across numerous community-specific and procedural enactments. These included the Indian Succession Act, 1865 (which excluded Hindus, Muslims, and Buddhists), the Parsi Intestate Succession Act, 1865, the Hindu Wills Act, 1870, the Probate and Administration Act, 1881, the District Delegates Act, 1881, and the Succession Certificate Act, 1889. This piecemeal legislative landscape created immense judicial confusion regarding the applicable rules for granting probates, letters of administration, and succession certificates across different religious denominations.

● Consolidated Statutory Code Preserving Substantive Personal Laws - Formulated as a pure consolidating measure by the Statute Law Revision Committee to unify the scattered enactments into a single comprehensive code. The Act harmonized the procedural machinery for testamentary and intestate succession—standardizing the jurisdiction of District Judges, High Courts, and district delegates over estate administration—while strictly preserving the distinct substantive personal laws of Hindus, Muslims, Christians, and Parsis without introducing new legal liabilities or altering existing community rights.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

● Formulation - Drafted by the Legislative Department of the Government of India upon the specific recommendations of the Statute Law Revision Committee, which was tasked with cleaning up the unwieldy Indian statute book and reducing overlapping procedural laws.

● Parliamentary Passage - Introduced as The Indian Succession Bill, 1925 in the Council of State, referred to a Joint Select Committee of both Houses for meticulous verification against the repealed parent acts to ensure no substantive changes were inadvertently made, passed by the Council of State, and concurred in by the Central Legislative Assembly during the Autumn Session of 1925 at Simla.

● Governor-General's Assent - Received the assent of the Governor-General of India (Lord Reading) on September 30, 1925.

● Enforcement - Enforced on September 30, 1925.

Sources - Debates of the Indian Legislative Assembly and Council of State, India Code, and Ministry of Law and Justice.

Legislative History:

The Sale of Goods Act, 1930

● Act Title - The Sale of Goods Act, 1930

● Act Number / Year - 3 of 1930

● Act ID (India Code) - 193003

● Assent Date - March 15, 1930

● Enforcement Date - July 1, 1930

● Nodal Ministry - Ministry of Law and Justice

Precedent & Historical Rationale

● Deficiencies and Inadequacy of Chapter VII of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 - Commercial transactions relating to the sale of movable property in British India were originally governed by Chapter VII (Sections 76 to 123) of the Indian Contract Act, 1872. Over five decades of rapid industrial and international commercial expansion, these concise provisions proved overly rigid and incomplete. In contrast, English commercial jurisprudence had been modernized comprehensively under the English Sale of Goods Act, 1893 (56 & 57 Vict. c. 71) drafted by Sir Mackenzie Chalmers. The 1872 provisions lacked clear statutory rules regarding the passing of property in unascertained goods, statutory implied conditions and warranties, the doctrine of caveat emptor and its exceptions, rights and remedies of unpaid sellers, and performance standards in mercantile contracts.

● Codification of a Dedicated, Self-Contained Mercantile Code - Formulated to define and amend the law relating to the sale of goods by carving it out of the general contract law framework. The Act established a dedicated statutory code governing the formation and subject matter of contracts of sale, codified the critical distinction between conditions and warranties (and implied statutory undertakings as to title, description, and quality), framed precise default rules regarding the transfer of property and risk between buyer and seller, defined the rights of an unpaid seller (including lien, stoppage in transit, and resale), and prescribed remedies and measures of damages for breach of contract.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

● Formulation - Drafted by the Special Committee appointed by the Government of India under the chairmanship of Law Member Sir Brojendra Lal Mitter, adapting the proven framework of the English Sale of Goods Act, 1893 to Indian commercial conditions and merchant customs.

● Parliamentary Passage - Introduced as The Indian Sale of Goods Bill, 1929 in the Central Legislative Assembly in September 1929, referred to a Select Committee for detailed clause-by-clause mercantile examination, debated and passed by the Legislative Assembly, and agreed to by the Council of State during the Budget Session in February 1930 at Delhi.

● Governor-General's Assent - Received the assent of the Governor-General of India (Lord Irwin) on March 15, 1930.

● Enforcement - Enforced on July 1, 1930.

Sources - Debates of the Indian Legislative Assembly and Council of State, India Code, and Ministry of Law and Justice.

Legislative History:

The Murshidabad Estate Administration Act, 1933

● Act Title - The Murshidabad Estate Administration Act, 1933

● Act Number / Year - 23 of 1933

● Act ID (India Code) - 193323

● Assent Date - September 21, 1933

● Enforcement Date - September 21, 1933

● Nodal Ministry - Ministry of Home Affairs

Precedent & Historical Rationale

● The Murshidabad Act, 1891 and the Nawab Bahadur's Settled Estate - Following the formal abdication of hereditary sovereign claims by the Nawabs of Bengal, the imperial administration entered into an Indenture of Settlement in 1891 confirmed by The Murshidabad Act, 1891 (Act XV of 1891). This settlement created the hereditary title of the Nawab Bahadur of Murshidabad, guaranteed a state political pension, and settled vast landed estates and properties in Bengal to descend impartibly to successive Nawabs to support the dignity of the title.

● Severe Financial Distress, Incumbrances, and Inadequacy of the 1891 Framework - By the early 1930s, the current Nawab Bahadur (Sir Wasif Ali Mirza) had accumulated massive personal debts and liabilities exceeding the estate’s immediate revenue. The statutory framework under the 1891 Act lacked practical administrative machinery to protect the settled estate from widespread creditor litigation, attachment of rents, and forced liquidation of unencumbered portions, threatening the financial collapse of the historic house.

● Statutory Machinery for State Management and Debt Liquidation - Formulated to provide for the appointment of a Manager on behalf of the Secretary of State for India in Council to take charge of the administration of the properties of the Nawab Bahadur of Murshidabad and for the liquidation of his debts and liabilities. The Act empowered the Local Government of Bengal to appoint a statutory Manager of the Murshidabad Estate, vested complete managerial control, custody of properties, and collection of rents in the Manager, imposed a statutory moratorium barring civil courts from entertaining suits or executing decrees against the Nawab Bahadur or the settled estate without sanction, and established a summary mechanism for the investigation, determination, and phased liquidation of valid creditor claims.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

● Formulation - Drafted by the Legislative Department of the Government of India in close consultation with the Government of Bengal and the Nawab Bahadur of Murshidabad, following the Nawab's formal petition for government intervention to rescue the estate from insolvency.

● Parliamentary Passage - Introduced as The Murshidabad Estate Administration Bill, 1933 in the Central Legislative Assembly, referred to a Select Committee for detailed clause-by-clause scrutiny, debated, passed by the Legislative Assembly, and concurred in by the Council of State during the Autumn Session of 1933 at Simla.

● Governor-General's Assent - Received the assent of the Governor-General of India (Lord Willingdon) on September 21, 1933.

● Enforcement - Enforced on September 21, 1933.

Sources - Debates of the Indian Legislative Assembly and Council of State, India Code, and Ministry of Home Affairs.

title: The Hindu Gains of Learning Act, 1930

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Key Features of the Hindu Gains of Learning Act, 1930
•	Separate Property: Declares that gains acquired by a Hindu through learning, education, training, science, art, or professional skill are the individual's separate property. 
•	Recognition of Personal Skill and Effort: Recognises that income and assets earned through personal knowledge, qualifications, and abilities belong exclusively to the individual who acquired them. 
•	Modification of Traditional Hindu Law: Abolishes the rule under traditional Hindu law that treated gains of learning as joint family property merely because joint family funds were used for education or training. 
•	Protection of Individual Property Rights: Safeguards the ownership rights of individuals over property and earnings derived from their personal learning and professional expertise. 
•	Applicability: Applies to Hindus and clarifies the legal status of property acquired through personal learning and skill. 
•	Legal Certainty: Removes ambiguity regarding the ownership of gains from learning and reduces disputes concerning joint family property.

Legislative History:

The Hindu Gains of Learning Act, 1930

● Act Title - The Hindu Gains of Learning Act, 1930

● Act Number / Year - 30 of 1930

● Act ID (India Code) - 193030

● Assent Date - September 25, 1930

● Enforcement Date - September 25, 1930

● Nodal Ministry - Ministry of Law and Justice

Precedent & Historical Rationale

● Traditional Hindu Law Rules and Judicial Uncertainty Regarding "Gains of Science" - Under classical Hindu coparcenary law and conflicting interpretations by the High Courts and the Privy Council (notably Gokal Chand v. Hukum Chand (1921)), if an individual member of a Hindu Undivided Family (HUF) acquired specialized education, professional training, or "learning" at the expense of joint family funds, all professional earnings and properties acquired through such training were legally deemed joint family property (partible), rather than the earner's separate self-acquired property (impartible). This doctrine disincentivized individual ambition, penalized educated professionals (such as lawyers, doctors, and civil servants), and created pervasive intra-family litigation over claims of coparceners to the personal professional earnings of family members.

● Statutory Declaration of Professional Income as Self-Acquired Property - Formulated to remove all doubts as to the rights of a member of a Hindu undivided family in property acquired by him by means of his learning. The Act unequivocally declared that all "gains of learning"—defined broadly to include all education, training, and specialization of whatever kind—shall be the sole and separate property of the person who acquired them, regardless of whether the education or maintenance during education was provided from joint family funds or by other family members.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

● Formulation - Spearheaded and drafted as a landmark private member's legislative measure by Dr. Mukund Ramrao Jayakar (M. R. Jayakar), an eminent jurist, constitutionalist, and legislator, to reform outdated property doctrines in Hindu law.

● Parliamentary Passage - Introduced as The Hindu Gains of Learning Bill, 1929 by Dr. M. R. Jayakar in the Central Legislative Assembly, referred to a Select Committee for clause-by-clause scrutiny, debated extensively on social and property law implications, passed by the Legislative Assembly, and agreed to by the Council of State during the Autumn Session of 1930 at Simla.

● Governor-General's Assent - Received the assent of the Governor-General of India (Lord Irwin) on September 25, 1930.

● Enforcement - Enforced on September 25, 1930.

Sources - Debates of the Indian Legislative Assembly and Council of State, India Code, and Ministry of Law and Justice.

Legislative History:

The Indian Wireless Telegraphy Act, 1933

● Act Title - The Indian Wireless Telegraphy Act, 1933

● Act Number / Year - 17 of 1933

● Act ID (India Code) - 193317

● Assent Date - September 11, 1933

● Enforcement Date - January 1, 1934

● Nodal Ministry - Ministry of Communications

Precedent & Historical Rationale

● Deficiencies and Regulatory Lacunae under the Indian Telegraph Act, 1885 - Prior to 1933, the establishment, maintenance, and operation of telegraphic and radio-transmission apparatus were regulated primarily under the Indian Telegraph Act, 1885 (Act XIII of 1885). While the 1885 statute effectively governed the establishment and operation of transmitting stations and line infrastructure by the government or licensed operators, it did not provide adequate statutory machinery to regulate or penalize the mere possession of unauthorized wireless receiving apparatus (radio receiving sets, valves, and components).

● Rapid Proliferation of Broadcast Receivers and Radio License Fee Evasion - Following the growth of public and private sound broadcasting in India in the late 1920s (including the formation of the Indian State Broadcasting Service, later All India Radio), broadcast receiver sets were increasingly imported and acquired by private individuals. Because the 1885 Act lacked enforcement mechanisms targeting simple unregistered possession, widespread evasion of broadcast receiver licensing fees eroded state revenues necessary to sustain the national broadcasting service.

● Statutory Regulation of Wireless Apparatus Possession and Anti-Evasion Architecture - Formulated to regulate the possession of wireless telegraphy apparatus throughout British India. The Act prohibited the possession of any wireless telegraphy apparatus (including domestic radio sets and designated components) by any person without a valid license granted by the Telegraph Authority, conferred powers of search, inspection, and seizure upon authorized officers to detect unlicensed equipment, and established criminal penalties and apparatus forfeiture provisions for unlawful possession.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

● Formulation - Drafted by the Department of Industries and Labour (Posts and Telegraphs Branch) and the Legislative Department of the Government of India to curb broadcast license evasion and establish comprehensive control over wireless receiving gear.

● Parliamentary Passage - Introduced as The Indian Wireless Telegraphy Bill, 1933 in the Central Legislative Assembly by Sir Frank Noyce (Member for Industries and Labour), reviewed by a Select Committee, debated and passed by the Legislative Assembly, and agreed to by the Council of State during the Autumn Session of 1933 at Simla.

● Governor-General's Assent - Received the assent of the Governor-General of India (Lord Willingdon) on September 11, 1933.

● Enforcement - Brought into force on January 1, 1934 (notified via Gazette Notification No. 17-T/33 issued by the Department of Industries and Labour).

Sources - Debates of the Indian Legislative Assembly and Council of State, India Code, and Ministry of Communications.

Precedent & Historical Rationale

● Constitutional Limitations of the Punjab Legislative Council under the Government of India Act, 1919 - Following the historic Gurdwara Reform Movement (Akali Movement) to liberate historical Sikh shrines from the control of hereditary mahants, the Punjab Legislative Council enacted the landmark Sikh Gurdwaras Act, 1925 (Punjab Act VIII of 1925). To adjudicate disputed claims over gurdwara properties, hereditary offices, and compensation, the Punjab Act constituted specialized Sikh Gurdwaras Tribunals and provided for direct statutory appeals from these Tribunals to the High Court of Judicature at Lahore. However, under the Devolution Rules and Section 80A of the Government of India Act, 1919, a provincial legislature lacked the constitutional competence to alter, expand, or regulate the appellate jurisdiction and procedure of a Chartered High Court established under the Letters Patent.

● Central Statutory Validation of High Court Jurisdiction and Appellate Procedures - Formulated to supplement certain provisions of the Sikh Gurdwaras Act, 1925 through central parliamentary legislation. The Act provided the essential central legal authority validating all provisions of Punjab Act VIII of 1925 in so far as they conferred appellate jurisdiction on, regulated the proceedings before, or affected the powers of the High Court of Judicature at Lahore (now the High Court of Punjab and Haryana), curing any potential ultra vires infirmities in the provincial enactment.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

● Formulation - Drafted by the Legislative Department and Home Department of the Government of India in close coordination with the Government of the Punjab under Governor Sir Malcolm Hailey, to provide seamless central legislative concurrence to the provincial settlement.

● Governor-General's Assent - Received the assent of the Governor-General of India (Lord Reading) on September 11, 1925.

● Nodal Ministry - Ministry of Home Affairs

Precedent & Historical Rationale

● Constitutional Limitations of Provincial Legislatures under the Government of India Act, 1919 - Following the Indian Jails Committee Report (1919–1920) recommending specialized juvenile justice administration, the provincial legislatures enacted progressive regional child welfare laws: the Madras Children Act, 1920, the Bengal Children Act, 1922, and the Bombay Children Act, 1924. However, under the Government of India Act, 1919, a provincial legislature lacked the constitutional competence to alter, expand, or regulate the appellate or revisionary jurisdiction of the Chartered High Courts established under the Letters Patent, or to amend procedures prescribed in central all-India codes such as the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898.

● Statutory Conferment of Appellate and Revisionary Jurisdiction on High Courts - Formulated to supplement the child welfare enactments passed by the local legislatures of Madras, Bengal, and Bombay. The Act provided the necessary central legislative sanction by formally conferring appellate and revisionary powers upon the High Courts of Judicature at Madras, Fort William in Bengal, and Bombay with respect to orders passed by juvenile courts, magistrates, or district courts under the respective provincial Children Acts, ensuring full legal harmony between central procedural law and provincial juvenile justice reforms.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

● Formulation - Drafted by the Home Department and the Legislative Department of the Government of India in consultation with the provincial governments and the Presidency High Courts to provide the enabling central statutory umbrella for provincial juvenile statutes.

● Parliamentary Passage - Introduced as The Madras, Bengal and Bombay Children (Supplementary) Bill, 1925 in the Central Legislative Assembly, considered and passed during the Budget Session, and agreed to by the Council of State in February 1925 at Delhi.

● Governor-General's Assent - Received the assent of the Governor-General of India (Lord Reading) on September 23, 1925.

● Enforcement - Enforced on September 23, 1925.

Sources - Debates of the Indian Legislative Assembly and Council of State, India Code, and Ministry of Home Affairs.

Summary of Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023
1. Preliminary
Title, Commencement, and Application: Applies to all persons in India and beyond under specific conditions.
2. Summary Trials
Eligible Offences: Not punishable by death, life imprisonment, or imprisonment over 3 years.
Procedure:
Magistrate's Powers: Try summarily with the accused's opportunity to be heard.
Record and Judgment: In the language of the Court, with substance of evidence and brief reasons.
3. Punishments for Offences 
•	Cognizable, Non-Bailable, Non-Compoundable:
•	Unfair Means in Exams: 3-5 years’ imprisonment, up to ₹10 lakh fine.
•	Service Providers: Up to ₹1 crore fine, 4-year ban from exam responsibilities.
•	Senior Management Involvement: 3-10 years’ imprisonment, ₹1 crore fine.
4. Other Procedural Aspects 
Arrest and Summons Procedures
Powers of Police and Magistrates
Public Responsibilities

CHAPTER II

CONSTITUTION OF CRIMINAL COURTS AND OFFICES

6. Classes of Criminal Courts.— Besides the High Courts and the Courts constituted under any law,

other than this Sanhita, there shall be, in every State, the following classes of Criminal Courts, namely:—

(i) Courts of Session;

(ii) Judicial Magistrates of the first class;

(iii) Judicial Magistrates of the second class; and

(iv) Executive Magistrates.

7. Territorial divisions.—(1) Every State shall be a sessions division or shall consist of sessions

divisions; and every sessions divisions shall, for the purposes of this Sanhita, be a district or consist of

districts.

(2) The State Government may, after consultation with the High Court, alter the limits or the number

of such divisions and districts.

(3) The State Government may, after consultation with the High Court, divide any district into

sub-divisions and may alter the limits or the number of such sub-divisions.

(4) The sessions divisions, districts and sub-divisions existing in a State at the commencement of this

Sanhita, shall be deemed to have been formed under this section.

8. Court of Session.—(1) The State Government shall establish a Court of Session for every sessions

division.

(2) Every Court of Session shall be presided over by a Judge, to be appointed by the High Court.

(3) The High Court may also appoint Additional Sessions Judges to exercise jurisdiction in a Court of

Session.

(4) The Sessions Judge of one sessions division may be appointed by the High Court to be also an

Additional Sessions Judge of another division, and in such case, he may sit for the disposal of cases at such

place or places in the other division as the High Court may direct.

(5) Where the office of the Sessions Judge is vacant, the High Court may make arrangements for the

disposal of any urgent application which is, or may be, made or pending before such Court of Session by

an Additional Sessions Judge or if there be no Additional Sessions Judge, by a Chief Judicial Magistrate,

in the sessions division; and every such Judge or Magistrate shall have jurisdiction to deal with any such

application.

(6) The Court of Session shall ordinarily hold its sitting at such place or places as the High Court may,

by notification, specify; but, if, in any particular case, the Court of Session is of opinion that it will tend to

the general convenience of the parties and witnesses to hold its sittings at any other place in the sessions

division, it may, with the consent of the prosecution and the accused, sit at that place for the disposal of the

case or the examination of any witness or witnesses therein.

(7) The Sessions Judge may, from time to time, make orders consistent with this Sanhita, as to the

distribution of business among such Additional Sessions Judges.

(8) The Sessions Judge may also make provision for the disposal of any urgent application, in the event

of his absence or inability to act, by an Additional Sessions Judge or if there be no Additional Sessions

Judge, by the Chief Judicial Magistrate, and such Judge or Magistrate shall be deemed to have jurisdiction

to deal with any such application.

experience in relation to legal affairs as the High Court may, by rules, specify.
