THE ELECTRICITY ACT, 2003
ACT NO. 36 OF 2003

[26th May, 2003.]

An Act to consolidate the laws relating to generation, transmission, distribution, trading and use of electricity and generally for taking measures conducive to development of electricity industry, promoting competition therein, protecting interest of consumers and supply of electricity to all areas, rationalisation of electricity tariff, ensuring transparent policies regarding subsidies, promotion of efficient and environmentally benign policies, constitution of Central Electricity Authority, Regulatory Commissions and establishment of Appellate Tribunal and for matters connected therewith or incidental thereto.

meta.dc.legislation.history:
Legislative History:

The Electricity Act, 2003

Short Title The Electricity Act, 2003

Act Number / Year Act No. 36 of 2003

Act ID (India Code) 200336

Presidential Assent / Enactment Date May 26, 2003

Enforcement Date June 10, 2003

Nodal Ministry Ministry of Power

Precedent & Statutory Rationale

1. Overhauling a Fragmented and State-Monopolized Sector:

o Prior to 2003, India's power sector was governed by colonial-era legislation (1910 Act) and post-independence supply laws (1948 Act) that heavily relied on state-run State Electricity Boards (SEBs). These boards suffered from massive commercial losses, operational inefficiencies, severe power shortages, and lack of private investment.

o The economic liberalization of the 1990s demanded a modern legislative framework to unbundle state electricity boards, separate generation, transmission, and distribution, and introduce market competition.

2. Establishment of Independent Regulation and Market Opening:

o The 2003 Act was enacted as a landmark reform statute to consolidate laws relating to generation, transmission, distribution, trading, and use of electricity.

o It abolished licensing requirements for power generation (except for hydro projects above a certain capacity), mandated the unbundling of SEBs, established independent regulatory bodies (the Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (CERC) and State Electricity Regulatory Commissions (SERCs)), set up the Appellate Tribunal for Electricity (APTEL), and introduced strict legal provisions against electricity theft.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

• Formulation: Extensively drafted and debated over several years by the Ministry of Power in consultation with state governments, industry stakeholders, and consumer groups to transform the structural architecture of India's energy grid.

• Parliamentary Passage: Tabled, rigorously debated, and passed by both Houses of Parliament, receiving Presidential Assent on May 26, 2003.

• Enforcement: Enforced on June 10, 2003.

Source: India Code (indiacode.gov.in) and Ministry of Power Official Records

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of the Bombay Reorganisation Act, 1960

Key Outcomes
1.	Formation of New States
•	Maharashtra: The residuary State of Bombay, primarily for Marathi-speaking populations.
•	Gujarat: Comprising areas with predominantly Gujarati-speaking populations.

2.	Effective Implementation Date
•	Appointed Day for Reorganisation: 1st May 1960.

3.	Constitutional Implications
•	Amendment to the Constitution of India: Specifically, an update to the First Schedule to reflect the creation of Maharashtra and Gujarat.

4.	Administrative Provisions
•	Flexibility for State Governments: Empowerment to make adjustments to district, taluka, or village boundaries, names, or extents post-reorganisation.
•	Provisions for State-Owned Corporations:
•	Temporary Operation and Dissolution: For entities like the Bombay State Electricity Board, State Warehousing Corporation, and Financial Corporation, with defined timelines for dissolution (e.g., October 1, 1960, for some) and protocols for dividing assets and liabilities between the new states.
•	Special Provisions for Transition: Including the framing of schemes for reorganisation of corporations and the power of the Central Government to sanction these schemes.

Summary of the Customs Act, 1962 
Objectives of the Act
•	To regulate the import and export of goods into and out of India. 
•	To provide for the levy, assessment, and collection of customs duties. 
•	To prevent smuggling and customs-related offences. 
•	To facilitate legitimate international trade while ensuring compliance with customs laws. 
•	To protect the economic interests and security of the country. 
Key Provisions
•	Levy and Collection of Customs Duty: The Act provides for the assessment, levy, and collection of customs duties on imported and exported goods in accordance with the applicable tariff laws. 
•	Import and Export Procedures: It prescribes procedures for the arrival, clearance, warehousing, transit, transhipment, and export of goods through customs stations. 
•	Powers of Customs Officers: Customs officers are empowered to inspect, search, seize, detain, and confiscate goods, conveyances, and documents, and to arrest persons involved in customs offences where authorized by law. 
•	Warehousing: The Act provides for the storage of imported goods in bonded warehouses without immediate payment of duty, subject to prescribed conditions. 
•	Confiscation and Penalties: Goods imported or exported in violation of the Act may be confiscated, and penalties may be imposed on persons responsible for contraventions. 
•	Adjudication and Appeals: The Act establishes procedures for adjudication of customs disputes and provides for appeals against orders of customs authorities before appellate forums and courts. 
•	Search, Seizure, and Investigation: It confers investigative powers on customs authorities to detect and prevent smuggling and other customs violations. 
•	Rule-making Power: The Central Government is empowered to make rules, and the CBIC may issue regulations and notifications for implementing the Act.

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of the National Co-operative Development Corporation Act, 1962 
Objectives of the Act
•	To promote the development of the cooperative sector as an instrument of economic and rural development. 
•	To provide financial assistance and support for cooperative projects and programmes. 
•	To strengthen agricultural production, processing, storage, marketing, and other cooperative activities. 
Key Provisions
•	Establishment of the Corporation: The Act provides for the incorporation of the National Co-operative Development Corporation as a body corporate with perpetual succession and a common seal. 
•	Functions of the Corporation: The Corporation is empowered to plan, promote, finance, and implement programmes for the production, processing, storage, marketing, distribution, and export of agricultural produce and other notified cooperative activities. 
•	Financial Assistance: The Corporation may provide loans, grants, subsidies, guarantees, and other forms of financial assistance to cooperative societies, State Governments, and other eligible institutions in accordance with the Act. 
•	Management: The Act provides for the composition of the Corporation's Board of Management, including its Chairperson, Managing Director, and other members, and specifies their powers and functions. 
•	Funds and Accounts: The Act provides for the Corporation's capital, borrowing powers, maintenance of accounts, audit, preparation of annual reports, and submission of reports to the Central Government. 
•	Rule-making Power: The Central Government is empowered to make rules, and the Corporation may make regulations, consistent with the Act, for carrying out its provisions.

Summary of the  Coconut Development Board Act, 1979 
The Coconut Development Board Act, 1979 was enacted by the Parliament of India to promote the planned development of the coconut industry under the control of the Central Government. The Act provides for the establishment of the Coconut Development Board (CDB) as a statutory body responsible for improving coconut cultivation, production, processing, marketing, and overall industry development. The Act was passed on 17 March 1979 and came into force on 12 January 1981. 
Objectives
The main objectives of the Act are to:
•	Promote the integrated development of the coconut industry. 
•	Increase coconut production and improve quality. 
•	Encourage scientific cultivation and modern farming practices. 
•	Support processing, marketing, and export of coconut and coconut products. 
•	Coordinate efforts between the Central Government, State Governments, research institutions, and growers. 
Establishment of the Coconut Development Board
The Act establishes the Coconut Development Board as a body corporate with perpetual succession. It can:
•	Acquire, hold, and dispose of property. 
•	Enter into contracts. 
•	Sue and be sued in its own name. 
Composition of the Board
The Board consists of representatives from:
•	The Central Government. 
•	State Governments of coconut-growing regions. 
•	Members of Parliament. 
•	Research institutions. 
•	Coconut growers. 
•	Coconut processing industry. 
•	Other stakeholders connected with the coconut sector. 
The 2021 Amendment introduced a non-executive Chairman and a Chief Executive Officer (CEO) to improve governance and administration. 
Functions of the Board
The Board is responsible for:
•	Recommending measures for coconut cultivation and production. 
•	Financing development schemes. 
•	Promoting research, extension, and training. 
•	Improving processing and marketing of coconut products. 
•	Collecting and publishing industry statistics. 
•	Advising the Central and State Governments on coconut-related matters. 
•	Encouraging domestic and international marketing of coconut products. 
Finance
The Act provides for:
•	Grants and loans from the Central Government. 
•	Creation of the Coconut Development Fund. 
•	Borrowing powers of the Board with Central Government approval. 
•	Maintenance of accounts and annual audits. 
Government Control
The Central Government has the power to:
•	Issue policy directions to the Board. 
•	Approve rules and regulations. 
•	Require reports and returns from the Board. 
•	Dissolve the Board under specified circumstances.

● Integrated Development of the Coconut Industry - Enacted to provide for the integrated development of the coconut industry in India, which serves as a major source of livelihood for millions of small and marginal farmers across coastal and southern states.

● Establishment of a Statutory Development Board - Formulated to create the Coconut Development Board (CDB) as a statutory body under the Central Government. The Act empowered the Board to implement schemes for boosting coconut productivity, promoting product diversification and value-addition (such as coir, coconut water, virgin coconut oil, and desiccated coconut), assisting farmers with credit and marketing facilities, and supporting scientific research for disease management (e.g., Root (Wilt) disease).

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

● Formulation - Introduced by the Ministry of Agriculture and Irrigation to fulfill long-standing demands from coconut-growing states (particularly Kerala, Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, and Andhra Pradesh) for a dedicated central commodity board similar to those for Rubber, Tea, and Coffee.

● Parliamentary Passage - Debated and passed by both Houses of Parliament (Sixth Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha) during the budget session in February–March 1979.

● Presidential Assent - Received Presidential Assent on March 17, 1979.

● Enforcement - Enforced on January 12, 1981.

title: The Suppression of Unlawful Acts against Safety of Civil Aviation Act, 1982

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of the Suppression of Unlawful Acts Against Safety of Civil Aviation Act, 1982 
Purpose
•	To implement the Convention for the Suppression of Unlawful Acts against the Safety of Civil Aviation (Montreal Convention, 1971) in India, ensuring alignment with recent legal amendments (notably, Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023).
Key Provisions
1.	Scope, Application, and Jurisdiction
•	Nationwide applicability in India.
•	Extends to offences committed outside India under specified conditions.
•	Cognizance of Offences now strictly requires a complaint by or with the previous sanction of designated Directors General (Section 31).
2.	Definitions and Regulatory Framework
•	Exclusions for certain aircraft types remain.
•	Convention Country definitions aligned with international treaties in force.
3.	Offences and Penalties
•	Specific Offences (e.g., flying to cause danger, non-compliance with directions) punishable by up to 2 years imprisonment or a fine up to 1 crore rupees, or both.
•	Abetment and Attempted Offences liable to the same punishment as the main offence (Section 29).
4.	Procedural Framework and Enforcement
•	Compounding of Offences possible for non-imprisonment-only offences, up to 1 crore rupees, with specific conditions and exclusions for repeat offenders (Section 30).
•	Investigation and Prosecution norms, including time limits for complaints (1 year, Section 31(2)).
5.	Miscellaneous and Updated Provisions
•	Extradition, Bail, and Previous Sanction for Prosecution norms.
•	Protection for Actions in Good Faith.
•	Cognizance by Courts limited to those of Judicial Magistrate of the first class or higher for certain offences, reflecting recent legal harmonizations.

meta.dc.identifier.preamble_description:
THE SUPPRESSION OF UNLAWFUL ACTS AGAINST SAFETY OF CIVIL AVIATION ACT, 1982
ACT NO. 66 OF 1982

[6th November, 1982.]

An Act to give effect to the Convention for the Suppression of Unlawful Acts against the Safety of Civil Aviation and for matters connected therewith.
WHEREAS a Convention for the Suppression of Unlawful Acts against the Safety of Civil Aviation was, on the 23rd day of September, 1971, signed at Montreal;
AND WHEREAS it is expedient that India should accede to the said Convention and make provisions for giving effect thereto and for matters connected therewith;
BE it enacted by Parliament in the Thirty-third Year of the Republic of India as follows:--
meta.dc.legislation.history:
Legislative History:

The Suppression of Unlawful Acts against Safety of Civil Aviation Act, 1982

Key Legislative Metadata

Legislative Stage / Attribute Official Details

Act Title - The Suppression of Unlawful Acts against Safety of Civil Aviation Act, 1982

Act Number/Year - Act No. 66 of 1982

Act ID (India Code) - 198266

Presidential Assent Date - November 6, 1982

Enforcement Date - November 15, 1982 (vide Notification No. S.O. 759(E))

Nodal Ministry - Ministry of Civil Aviation

Precedent & Historical Rationale

1. International Conventions (Montreal Convention of 1971):

o Following a sharp rise in global incidents of aircraft sabotage, bombings, and attacks on civil aviation infrastructure during the 1970s, the international community adopted the Convention for the Suppression of Unlawful Acts against the Safety of Civil Aviation at Montreal in September 1971.

o India, as a signatory to the Montreal Convention, was internationally obligated to enact municipal legislation to give effect to its provisions, establishing universal penal jurisdiction over acts endangering civil aviation safety.

2. Combating Terrorist Threats and Ensuring Aviation Security:

o Prior to 1982, domestic penal codes (such as the Indian Penal Code) lacked specialized or sufficiently rigorous extra-territorial provisions tailored to modern acts of air sabotage, destruction of navigational facilities, and onboard violence.

o The legislative intent centered on creating stringent criminal penalties, fast-track trial mechanisms, and extra-territorial jurisdiction to deter and punish acts threatening the safety of operational aircraft and international civil aviation.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

• Formulation:

Drafted by the Ministry of Civil Aviation in coordination with the Ministry of Law and Justice to align domestic criminal law precisely with the anti-sabotage mandates of the Montreal Convention.

• Parliamentary Passage:

• Introduced, deliberated, and passed by both Houses of Parliament (Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha) during the autumn session of 1982.

• Presidential Assent:

• Received Presidential Assent on November 6, 1982.

• Enforcement:

• Enforced on November 15, 1982.

Source: Official Records of Parliament, India Code, and Ministry of Civil Aviation

Key Provisions

1.	Repeal
•	Repeals specific chapters of Regulation XXI of 1827 and Act XXIV of 1850.

2.	Municipal Duty on Tobacco
•	Rate: 7 Rupees and 8 annas per maund.
•	Payment: Either on importation or upon removal from a licensed warehouse for consumption.
•	Remission: Applies if warehoused Tobacco is re-exported.

3.	Warehousing
•	Bombay declared a warehousing port under Act XXV of 1836.

4.	Collection & Enforcement
•	Managed by the Commissioner of Customs, Salt, and Opium, and Customs Officers.

5.	Import & Retail Regulations
•	Import: Must be by sea, with designated landing places.
•	Retail Sale:
•	License: Mandatory, with a 1 Rupee fee, valid for 12 months.
•	Quantity Limit for Retail: Not exceeding 14 seers of 80 tolas.
•	Operational Requirements:
•	Sales only at licensed premises.
•	Display of dealer’s name and license in multiple languages.
•	Record Keeping: Monthly stock returns and daily entry books.

6.	Penalties & Enforcement
•	Search & Seizure Powers.
•	Penalties: Confiscation and fines up to 10 times the Tobacco’s value for violations.
•	License Revocation for guilty dealers.

7.	Interpretation
•	Defines "Town of Bombay" and clarifies singular/plural and gender neutrality.

An Act to consolidate and amend the law relating to the governance of the Assam Rifles, an Armed Force of the Union for ensuring the security of the borders of India, to carry out Counter Insurgency Operations in the specified areas and to act in aid of civil authorities for the maintenance of the law and order and for matters connected therewith.

Act Number / Year Act No. 47 of 2006

Act ID (India Code) 200647

Presidential Assent / Enactment Date November 3, 2006

Nodal Ministry Ministry of Home Affairs

Precedent & Statutory Rationale

1. Obsolescence of the 1941 Framework:

o Prior to 2006, the governance, regulation, and discipline of the Assam Rifles—India's oldest paramilitary/central armed police force—were structured under the colonial-era Assam Rifles Act, 1941.

o Over decades of changing geopolitical environments, internal security challenges, and structural developments in national defense architecture, the 1941 framework became inadequate for modern operational mandates, legal procedures, and administrative requirements.

2. Modernization and Clarification of Force Mandate:

o The 2006 legislation was enacted to comprehensively consolidate and update the law relating to the governance of the Assam Rifles as an Armed Force of the Union. It officially codified its multi-faceted responsibilities, including international border security, counter-insurgency operations in specified areas, and acting in aid of civil authorities for maintaining law and order.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

• Formulation: Drafted and piloted by the Ministry of Home Affairs to restructure the statutory foundation of the Assam Rifles.

• Parliamentary Passage: Tabled, debated, and passed by both Houses of Parliament, receiving Presidential Assent on November 3, 2006.

• Enforcement: Enforced on February 20, 2009.

meta.dc.legislation.history:
Legislative History:

The Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016

Short Title - The Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016

Act Number / Year - Act No. 49 of 2016

India Code Act ID - 201649

Introduced In - Parliament Rajya Sabha

Presidential Assent Date - December 27, 2016

Official Gazette Publication - December 28, 2016

Enforcement Date - April 19, 2017

Nodal Ministry - Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment (Department of Empowerment of Persons with Disabilities)

Precedent & Statutory Rationale

1. Fulfilling International Obligations under UNCRPD:

o Enacted to give full effect to the United Nations Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (UNCRPD), which India signed and ratified in 2007.

2. Expansion of Recognized Disability Categories:

o Expanded the recognized categories of disabilities from 7 (under the 1995 Act) to 21 conditions (including speech/language disabilities, autism spectrum disorder, cerebral palsy, muscular dystrophy, acid attack victims, chronic neurological conditions like Parkinson's/Multiple Sclerosis, and blood disorders like Thalassemia, Sickle Cell Disease, and Haemophilia).

3. Rights-Based Enforcement & Increased Reservation Mandates:

o Replaced the welfare approach with a rights-based framework, increasing government job reservations for persons with benchmark disabilities from 3% to 4% and higher education institution allocations to 5%. It also introduced statutory rights to non-discrimination, accessibility, inclusive education, and severe penalties for offences against persons with disabilities.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

• Formulation: Drafted and piloted by the Department of Empowerment of Persons with Disabilities (DEPwD) under the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment following extensive consultation with disability rights organizations.

• Parliamentary Passage: Introduced in the Rajya Sabha on February 7, 2014; referred to the Parliamentary Standing Committee on Social Justice and Empowerment; debated and passed by the Rajya Sabha on December 14, 2016, and subsequently passed by the Lok Sabha on December 16, 2016.

• Presidential Assent: Received formal Presidential Assent on December 27, 2016, entering the statute book as Act No. 49 of 2016.

• Enforcement: Brought into active operational force across India on April 19, 2017 via Official Gazette notification, with the accompanying national statutory rules notified on June 15, 2017.

Summary of the Improvements in Towns Act, 1850

Purpose
•	Enables town improvements under the East India Company's governance, repealing the ineffectual Act X of 1842.

•	Repeals Act X of 1842.

•	Annual accounts must be submitted to the Local Government.

Summary of the Foreigners Law (Application and Amendment) Act, 1962 
Objectives of the Act
•	To extend the application of laws relating to foreigners to specified territories. 
•	To amend existing laws governing the regulation and control of foreigners. 
•	To ensure uniform administration and enforcement of laws relating to the entry, stay, movement, and departure of foreigners in India. 
•	To strengthen the Central Government's powers in matters concerning foreigners. 
Key Provisions
•	Application of Foreigners Laws: The Act extends the operation of specified laws relating to foreigners to the territories covered by the Act, ensuring that such laws apply uniformly. 
•	Amendment of Existing Laws: It amends provisions of existing legislation concerning foreigners to remove inconsistencies and facilitate effective implementation. 
•	Regulation of Foreigners: The Act supports the legal framework under which the Central Government may regulate the entry into, presence in, movement within, and departure from India of foreigners. 
•	Administrative Continuity: It ensures that the legal regime governing foreigners continues to operate effectively in newly integrated or reorganised territories without disruption.

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of the Calcutta Land-Revenue Act, 1856

1.	Recovery and Jurisdiction
•	Recovery of Amounts Due: Amounts due to the Government (costs, penalties, etc.) are recoverable as an arrear of land revenue.
•	Special Provision Regarding Scheduled Tribes: Transfers of land by Scheduled Tribes members require either transfer to another member, previous permission for transfers outside the tribe, or a mortgage to a co-operative society.

2. Legal and Administrative Provisions
•	Jurisdiction of Civil Courts Excluded: Generally, civil courts have no jurisdiction over matters under this Act, except for disputes involving questions of title.
•	Act to Override Contract and Other Laws: This Act's provisions supersede other laws, customs, usages, agreements, decrees, or court orders, unless otherwise specified.
•	Court-Fees: Prescribed court-fee stamps are required for applications, appeals, or proceedings under this Act, notwithstanding the Court-fees Act, 1870.

3. Official Capacities and Powers
•	Village Officers as Public Servants: Amins and other village officers are deemed public servants under the Indian Penal Code.
•	Power to Exempt: The Administrator, with Government approval, may exempt classes of lands from the Act's provisions.
•	General Provision as to Penalties: Contraventions without specified penalties incur a fine up to 500 rupees.

4. Protection, Delegation, and Rule Making Protection of Action Taken in Good Faith: Officers and the Government are protected from suits/prosecutions for actions done in good faith under this Act.
	Delegation of Powers: The Administrator can delegate powers (except rule-making) to subordinate officers/authorities.
•	Power to Remove Difficulties: The Government can take necessary actions to resolve difficulties in implementing the Act.
•	General Power to Make Rules: The Administrator can make rules to carry out the Act's purposes.
•	Laying of Rules Before Parliament: Rules must be laid before Parliament, subject to potential modification or annulment.
•	Repeal and Savings: Enactments specified in the Schedule are repealed in areas where this Act's provisions are enforced, with savings for previous actions.

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of The Marine Insurance Act, 1963 
Key Components Summary
1.	Foundational Provisions & Scope
•	Definitions and Scope: Outlines core marine insurance terms and applies to all marine insurance contracts in India.
•	International Alignment: Reflects adherence to global maritime standards, ensuring consistency in practices.
2.	Contractual Foundations
•	Insurable Interest: Mandatory at the time of loss; void if absent.
•	Utmost Good Faith: Emphasized as a foundational principle in contracts.
3.	Policy and Contract Specifications
•	Policy Requirements: Detailed, written policies are essential.
•	Contractual Integrity: Covers various policy types, ensuring flexibility.
4.	Financial and Assignment Aspects
•	Premium Payment: A critical concurrent condition for contract validity.
•	Assignability: Policies are generally assignable.
5.	Loss and Liability Framework
•	Insurer Liability: For direct losses from insured perils, excluding wilful misconduct.
•	Peril Coverage: Aligns with international standards on maritime perils.
6.	Total Loss, Abandonment, and Salvage
•	Abandonment Conditions: Clearly defined for total losses.
•	Salvage and Total Loss Distinctions: Guides insurance payouts with clarity.
7.	Shared Risks and Contributions
•	General Average: Defined with the right to contribution.
•	Salvage Expenses: Explained to promote cooperative risk management.
8.	Payout Mechanisms
•	Indemnity Measurement: Specifies liability for total and partial losses.
•	Policy Valuation Types: Differentiates between valued and unvalued policies.
9.	Jurisdiction and Integrated Framework
•	Admiralty Jurisdiction: Links for dispute resolution.
•	Broader Maritime Law Integration: Part of India’s maritime legal framework.

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of the Orphanages and Other Charitable Homes (Supervision and Control) Act, 1960 
Key Components in the Context of Child Welfare with New Context Emphasis
1.	Relevant Definitions (Inferred and Aligned with New Context)
•	Child in Need: Explicitly implies a child requiring humane and considerate care, potentially aligning with states of vulnerability (e.g., orphaned, abandoned) where the child's best interest is paramount.
•	Institutional Care: Refers to regulated, child-friendly environments (e.g., Children's Homes, as defined in contemporary laws) providing necessary care and protection.
2.	Governance and Oversight with a Child-Centric Approach
•	Board of Control/Equivalent Oversight Body: Suggests a structured approach to managing and inspecting homes, ensuring best interests of the child are met, similar to the roles of Child Welfare Committees or District Child Protection Units in modern legislation.
•	Functions & Powers: Imply ensuring humane treatment and considerate standards in care, potentially mirroring the oversight for fit facilities and fit persons in contemporary child protection frameworks.
3.	Operational Requirements for Homes with Emphasis on Child Welfare
•	Licensing/Certification: Mandatory for operation, underlining the importance of accredited, child-friendly care environments.
•	Management and Care Standards: Explicitly implies a focus on the well-being and best interests of the child, akin to emphasizing non-corporal punishment and childline services in modern laws.
4.	Compliance and Enforcement with a Focus on Child Protection
•	Penalties for Non-Compliance: Indicates seriousness in ensuring humane and considerate treatment, similar to penalties for violating corporal punishment norms or neglecting child welfare in contemporary legislation.
•	Appeals and Protection Clauses: Suggests a balanced approach to governance, potentially safeguarding the best interests of the child in decision-making processes.

Precedent & Historical Rationale

Geopolitical Strategic Significance and Transition from NEFA:

Arunachal Pradesh, historically known as the North-East Frontier Agency (NEFA) and administered directly by the Governor of Assam, held immense strategic sensitivity along India's international border. Following the Sino-Indian conflict of 1962 and subsequent administrative reorganization, it was constituted as the Union Territory of Arunachal Pradesh under the North-Eastern Areas (Reorganisation) Act, 1971, with its own Legislative Assembly established later in 1975.

Fulfillment of Regional Aspirations and Full Statehood:

As part of the central government's sustained policy to foster democratic governance, fulfill regional political aspirations, and accelerate socio-economic development in the Northeast, the Union Territory was deemed ready for full self-governance. Granting statehood required a formal constitutional amendment (the Constitution (Fifty-fifth Amendment) Act, 1986) to insert special provisions for the state, alongside this specific reorganisation statute to formally establish Arunachal Pradesh as the 24th State of the Indian Union.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

Formulation:

Drafted by the Ministry of Home Affairs to provide for the erection of the Union Territory of Arunachal Pradesh into a full-fledged State, detailing provisions for the allocation of seats in Parliament, the structure and strength of the new State Legislative Assembly, distribution of assets, financial adjustments, and transition of judicial and administrative machinery.

Parliamentary Passage:

Introduced, debated, and passed by both Houses of Parliament (Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha) during the winter session of December 1986 alongside the corresponding constitutional amendment bill.

Presidential Assent: Received Presidential Assent on December 24, 1986.

Enforcement: Enforced on February 20, 1987.

Source: Official Records of Parliament, India Code, and Ministry of Home Affairs.

Summary of the Bengal Indigo Contracts Act, 1836


Key Provisions 

1.	Repeal of Clause: - Repeals Clause Third, Section V, Regulation VI, 1823, of the Bengal Code.

2.	Disputed Indigo Plant Delivery: - When the right to Indigo Plant is contested, the party to whom delivery is ordered must provide sufficient security before cutting or removing the plant, to cover potential claims.

3.	Contract Breach by Third Party Interference: - If a third party induces a ryut to break a lawful Indigo contract (after the contractor has advanced money), the contractor can sue both the third party and the ryut for damages.

4.	Court Proceedings: - Courts can examine both plaintiff and defendant as necessary.

•	Defendants may receive compensation for expenses if the award is in their favor.

5.	Jurisdiction and Reference: - Empowers Zillah or City Judges to refer suits under this Act or Regulation VI, 1823, to Principal Sudder Ameen or Sudder Ameen for inquiry and decision.

Source: Official Record of Parliament, India Code, and Ministry of Home Affairs

Key Legislative Metadata

Legislative Stage / Attribute Official Details

Act Number / Year Act No. 10 of 1836

Act ID (India Code) 183610

Presidential Assent Date April 11, 1836

Precedent & Statutory Rationale

• Background/Transition: Prior to this 1836 enactment, disputes surrounding the cultivation and delivery of indigo particularly regarding the recovery of financial advances made by planters to local cultivators (ryots) were primarily governed by Regulation VI of 1823 of the Bengal Code. The earlier framework proved inefficient for planters, as crops were often removed or disposed of before summary suits could be finalized.

• Rationale/Objectives: The primary objective of the Act was to establish strict, enforceable legal procedures for contesting the rights to Indigo Plants. It aimed to legally bind ryots to specific performance when they had accepted cash advances to cultivate or deliver indigo. Furthermore, the Act mandated that if the right to an indigo crop was contested, the claiming party could not cut or remove the plant without providing sufficient financial security to the court to cover any potential claims or land rent arrears.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Legislative Milestones

• Formulation: Drafted and enacted under the British East India Company regime to amend Bengal Regulation VI of 1823 and secure British planters' investments in commercial indigo cultivation.

• Parliamentary Passage: Enacted by the Governor-General of India in Council under the legislative powers granted by the Charter Act of 1833.

• Presidential Assent: Not applicable (Passed by the Governor-General-in-Council on April 11, 1836).

• Enforcement: Enforced On April 11,1835

title: The National Bank for Agriculture and Rural Development Act, 1981

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of the National Bank for Agriculture and Rural Development Act, 1981 
The National Bank for Agriculture and Rural Development (NABARD) Act, 1981 was enacted by the Parliament of India to establish the National Bank for Agriculture and Rural Development (NABARD) as the apex development financial institution for agriculture, rural development, and allied sectors. The Act came into force on 12 July 1982, and NABARD commenced operations on 15 July 1982, taking over the agricultural credit functions of the Reserve Bank of India and the Agricultural Refinance and Development Corporation (ARDC).
Objectives
The main objectives of the Act are to:
•	Promote sustainable agriculture and rural development. 
•	Provide and regulate credit for agriculture, cottage and village industries, handicrafts, small-scale industries, and other rural economic activities. 
•	Strengthen rural financial institutions. 
•	Support integrated rural development through refinance, planning, and policy initiatives. 
•	Improve rural infrastructure and enhance financial inclusion. 
Key Provisions 
1.	Establishment of NABARD
The Act establishes NABARD as a statutory body corporate with perpetual succession. It has the power to:
•	Acquire, hold, and dispose of property. 
•	Enter into contracts. 
•	Sue and be sued in its own name. 
2.	Management of the Bank
The affairs of NABARD are managed by a Board of Directors, comprising:
•	A Chairperson. 
•	A Managing Director (or Managing Directors, as provided by later amendments). 
•	Directors nominated by the Central Government. 
•	Directors representing the Reserve Bank of India (RBI), State Governments, cooperative institutions, commercial banks, and experts in agriculture, economics, rural development, and finance. 
The Central Government appoints the Chairperson and Managing Director(s) in consultation with the RBI.
3.	Functions of NABARD
The Act assigns NABARD several important functions, including:
•	Providing refinance to cooperative banks, regional rural banks (RRBs), commercial banks, and other eligible financial institutions for agricultural and rural lending. 
•	Promoting institutional development and strengthening rural credit systems. 
•	Preparing rural credit plans and coordinating rural financing. 
•	Supporting agriculture, allied activities, rural industries, self-help groups (SHGs), microfinance, and farmer-producer organisations (FPOs). 
•	Financing rural infrastructure projects through dedicated funds. 
•	Undertaking research, training, consultancy, and capacity-building in agriculture and rural development. 
•	Monitoring and evaluating rural development programmes. 
4.	Financial Resources
The Act provides for NABARD's financial resources through:
•	Initial capital subscribed by the Central Government and the RBI (with subsequent amendments enabling changes in shareholding). 
•	Borrowings from the Central Government, RBI, financial institutions, and international agencies. 
•	Issue of bonds and debentures. 
•	Deposits and other approved sources of funds. 
5.	Powers of NABARD
NABARD is empowered to:
•	Grant loans and advances. 
•	Provide refinance facilities. 
•	Inspect and supervise eligible financial institutions receiving its assistance. 
•	Advise the Central and State Governments on rural credit and development policies. 
•	Promote innovation and institutional reforms in rural finance.

Precedent & Historical Rationale

1. Fulfilling Regional Educational Aspirations:

o Following the integration of the former French colonial territory of Puducherry (then Pondicherry) into the Indian Union, the Union Territory experienced a steady rise in the demand for advanced higher education and specialized academic research facilities suited to its distinct cultural and academic environment.

o Prior to 1985, colleges in Puducherry were predominantly affiliated with the University of Madras, limiting local academic autonomy, curriculum tailoring, and regional research orientation.

2. Establishment of a Central University:

o The legislative intent centered on establishing a teaching and affiliating Central University in the Union Territory of Pondicherry to facilitate and promote higher education and research in various academic disciplines.

o The Act provided for the incorporation of Pondicherry University, established its administrative structure (including the Visitor, Chancellor, Vice-Chancellor, Court, Executive Council, and Academic Council), and empowered it to affiliate colleges within the Union Territories of Pondicherry and Andaman and Nicobar Islands.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

• Formulation: Drafted by the Ministry of Education in response to long-standing public and parliamentary demands for a central institution of higher learning in the Union Territory.

• Parliamentary Passage: Introduced, debated, and passed by both Houses of Parliament (Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha) during the monsoon session of 1985.

• Presidential Assent: Received Presidential Assent on September 4, 1985.

• Enforcement: Brought into force on October 16, 1985, paving the way for the establishment of the university campus and academic administration.

The Delimitation Act, 2002

Act Title The Delimitation Act, 2002 (enacted as Act No. 33 of 2002)

Act ID (India Code) 200233

Presidential Assent Date June 3, 2002

Enforcement Date June 3, 2002

Nodal Ministry Ministry of Law and Justice

Precedent & Historical Context

1. Constitutional Mandate:

o Under Article 82 and Article 170 of the Constitution of India, Parliament is required to enact a Delimitation Act after every decennial census to readjust the territorial boundaries of Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assembly constituencies.

o Prior Delimitation Commissions had been constituted under the Delimitation Commission Acts of 1952, 1962, and 1972.

2. The 84th Constitutional Amendment (2001):

o The Constitution (Eighty-Fourth Amendment) Act, 2001 maintained the freeze on the overall total number of seats in the Lok Sabha and State Assemblies until the first census taken after 2026.

o However, it permitted the readjustment and rationalization of constituency boundaries within each State based on the 1991 Census figures (later updated to the 2001 Census via the 87th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2003).

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

• Introduction & Formulation: Drafted by the Ministry of Law and Justice to constitute a new high-powered Delimitation Commission.

• Parliamentary Passage: Considered and passed by both Houses of Parliament (Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha) during the Budget Session of 2002.

• Presidential Assent: Received Presidential Assent on June 3, 2002, and came into force immediately.

• Enforcement: Enforced on June 3, 2002.

Source: Official Records of Parliament, India Code, and Election Commission of India.

Summary  of Bharatiya Vayuan Adhiniyam , 2024
To consolidate and provide general rules and principles of evidence for a fair trial. 
Key Provisions
1.	Application and Scope
•	Applies to all judicial proceedings in or before any Court in India, excluding affidavits and arbitrator proceedings.
2.	Definitions
•	Court: Includes all Judges, Magistrates, and legally authorized persons to take evidence.
•	Conclusive Proof, Disproved, Document (including electronic/digital records), Evidence (oral and documentary), and Fact are defined with detailed illustrations for clarity.
3.	Evidence and Documentation
•	Recognizes electronic and digital records (e.g., emails, server logs, digital messages) as documents.
•	Evidence includes all statements (oral and electronic) and documents permitted or required by the Court.
4.	Provisions on Facts and Evidence
•	Defines how facts are to be proven or disproven, with explanations on conclusive proof and its implications.
•	Specifies "facts in issue" and their determination in legal proceedings.

Summary of the Haj Committee Act, 2002 
Key Provisions
1.	Constitution, Leadership, & Decision Finality
•	Composition & Leadership: Bodies corporate with perpetual succession, led by elected, nominated, and ex officio members, serving 3-year terms with potential extensions.
•	Decision Finality: The Board of Arbitration's decisions, comprising a Central Government-appointed district judge, are final and not subject to judicial challenge.
2.	Oversight Mechanisms
•	Central Government: Exercises oversight through bye-law approval, modification, or cancellation powers, ensuring national policy alignment.
•	Parliamentary Scrutiny: Bye-laws and orders are laid before Parliament, enhancing transparency and accountability.
2. Financial Governance & Transparency
•	Central Haj Fund & State Haj Funds:
•	Sources: Fees, service charges, pilgrim contributions, investments, and government loans.
•	Management & Transparency: Centrally audited, with detailed accounting and budgeting practices, ensuring financial integrity.
     3. Regulatory, Protective, & Dispute Resolution Provisions
•	Judicial Finality: No legal proceedings can question matters decided by the Board of Arbitration.
•	Operational Continuity: Defects in constitution or vacancies do not invalidate Committee actions.
•	Enforcement: Final orders enforceable as civil court decrees.
4. Transition, Repeal, & Legacy
•	Repeal & Transition: Supersedes the Haj Committee Act, 1959, with provisions for seamless continuity and validation of prior actions.

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of the Repatriation of Prisoners Act, 2003
Key Provisions
1.  Definitions
•	Contracting State: A country with which India has a prisoner transfer agreement.
•	Prisoner: Includes individuals serving sentences in India or in a contracting state, eligible for transfer under the Act.
2. Eligibility and Application
•	Eligibility: Prisoners who are citizens of the contracting state and have consented to the transfer.
•	Application Process: Prisoners apply to the Central Government, which forwards the application to the contracting state after verifying eligibility.
3. Transfer Mechanism
•	Warrant Issuance: Upon receiving consent from the contracting state, the Central Government issues a warrant for the prisoner's transfer, which serves as a sufficient legal document for the execution of the transfer.
•	Transfer Process: The warrant authorizes the delivery of the prisoner, along with their records and personal effects, to the contracting state, ensuring a lawful handover.
4. Consequences of Transfer
•	Custody and Conveyance: Authorized personnel from the contracting state can lawfully receive, hold, and convey the prisoner out of India.
•	Escape Liability: If a prisoner escapes during transfer within India, they can be retaken and are liable under Indian law.
5. Receiving Prisoners into India
•	Applicability: For Indian citizens imprisoned in contracting states who are transferred back to India.
•	Detention and Sentence Adaptation: Transferred prisoners are detained in an Indian prison, with their sentence adapted to comply with Indian penal laws if necessary, ensuring continuity of justice.
6. Administrative Provisions
•	Rule Making Power: The Central Government can make rules to implement the Act, including specifying forms and procedures for transfer warrants.
•	Difficulty Resolution: Temporary orders can be issued to address implementation challenges, maintaining operational flexibility.

THE REPATRIATION OF PRISONERS ACT, 2003
ACT NO. 49 OF 2003

[28th September, 2003.]

An Act to provide for the transfer of certain prisoners from India to country or place outside India and reception in India of certain prisoners from country or place outside India.
BE it enacted by Parliament in the Fifty-fourth Year of the Republic of India as follows:--
meta.dc.legislation.history:
Legislative History:

The Repatriation of Prisoners Act, 2003

Short Title The Repatriation of Prisoners Act, 2003

Act Number / Year Act No. 49 of 2003

Act ID (India Code) 200349

Presidential Assent Date September 28, 2003

Enforcement Date January 1, 2004

Nodal Ministry Ministry of Home Affairs

Precedent & Statutory Rationale

1. Absence of Domestic Legal Mechanism:

o Prior to 2003, India lacked a municipal statutory framework allowing foreign nationals convicted by Indian courts to serve their sentences in their home countries, or enabling Indian citizens imprisoned abroad to be transferred back to India.

o Humanitarian considerations and the rehabilitative objective of modern penology dictated that offenders should serve sentences within their own linguistic, cultural, and social environments.

2. Fulfillment of International Conventions:

o Enabled India to formally enter into bilateral and multilateral treaties (such as the Transfer of Sentenced Persons agreements) and provide the necessary domestic legal backing under Article 253 of the Constitution of India to execute mutual prisoner exchanges with "contracting States".

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

• Formulation: Prepared by the Ministry of Home Affairs to establish uniform legal protocols governing outbound and inbound transfer requests.

• Parliamentary Passage: Debated and passed by both the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha during the Monsoon Session of Parliament in 2003.

• Presidential Assent: Received Presidential Assent on September 28, 2003, entering the statute book as Act No. 49 of 2003.

• Enforcement: Brought into effect on January 1, 2004.

Source: Official Records of Parliament, India Code, and Ministry of Home Affairs

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of Companies (Profits) Surtax Act, 1964
The Companies (Profits) Surtax Act, 1964 was enacted to levy a surtax (an additional tax) on the chargeable profits of certain companies exceeding the statutory deduction prescribed under the Act. The objective was to ensure that highly profitable companies contributed an additional share of revenue to the Government. The Act prescribed the method for computing chargeable profits, determining statutory deductions, assessment, collection, and recovery of surtax.

Objective
The main objectives of the Act are:
•	To impose an additional tax (surtax) on the excess profits of companies.
•	To augment Government revenue from highly profitable companies.
•	To prescribe a uniform method for computing chargeable profits.
•	To provide for the assessment, collection, and recovery of surtax.
•	To ensure equitable taxation of corporate profits exceeding the prescribed statutory deduction.
Key Provisions
1.	Levy of Surtax
o	The Act imposed surtax on the chargeable profits of companies that exceeded the statutory deduction calculated under the Act.
2.	Chargeable Profits
o	Chargeable profits were determined on the basis of the company's taxable income, subject to the adjustments specified in the Act.
3.	Statutory Deduction
o	Companies were allowed a statutory deduction, generally calculated with reference to their capital, before surtax became payable.
4.	Computation of Capital
o	The Act laid down detailed rules for computing the capital of a company for determining the statutory deduction.
5.	Assessment and Collection
o	Surtax was assessed, collected, and recovered by the income tax authorities in accordance with the procedures prescribed under the Act.
6.	Returns and Compliance
o	Companies liable to surtax were required to file returns, maintain records, and furnish information necessary for assessment.
7.	Penalties and Interest
o	The Act provided for the levy of interest and penalties in cases of non-payment, delayed payment, concealment of income, or failure to comply with statutory requirements.
8.	Appeals
o	Companies aggrieved by assessment orders could file appeals before the prescribed appellate authorities under the tax laws.
9.	Rule-Making Power
o	The Central Government was empowered to make rules for carrying out the provisions of the Act.

title: The Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act, 1960

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act, 1960 
Key Provisions
•	Definitions
•	Defines important terms such as animal, captive animal, domestic animal, owner, and phooka (an illegal practice used to increase milk production).
•	Animal Welfare Board of India (AWBI)
•	Establishes the Animal Welfare Board of India to:
•	Advise the Government on animal welfare laws and policies.
•	Promote animal welfare organizations.
•	Spread awareness about the humane treatment of animals.
•	Recommend measures to prevent cruelty.
•	Cruelty to Animals
•	Declares various acts as cruelty, including:
•	Beating, kicking, overloading, or torturing animals.
•	Keeping animals in inadequate shelter or without sufficient food and water.
•	Abandoning animals.
•	Using injured or unfit animals for work.
•	Organizing or promoting animal fights.
•	Administering harmful substances to animals.
•	Experiments on Animals
•	Permits scientific experiments on animals only under prescribed conditions and regulations.
•	Provides for oversight through rules framed under the Act.
•	Performing Animals
•	Requires the registration of certain performing animals.
•	Empowers authorities to prohibit or regulate performances that involve cruelty.
•	Prohibition of Certain Practices
•	Prohibits cruel practices such as phooka and doom dev, which involve causing pain to milch animals to increase milk production.
•	Penalties
•	Prescribes penalties for acts of cruelty, including fines and, in certain cases, imprisonment.
•	Penalties increase for repeat offenders, though many of the original fines under the Act have been criticized as being too low.
•	Power to Make Rules
•	Empowers the Central Government to make rules for carrying out the provisions of the Act, including rules relating to transport, housing, breeding, experimentation, and the welfare of animals.

title: The Illegal Migrants (Determination by Tribunals) Act, 1983

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of The Illegal Migrants (Determination by Tribunals) Act, 1983
Purpose and Scope
•	Purpose: To establish a framework for determining whether a person is an illegal migrant and to facilitate their expulsion from India.
•	Scope: Applies to the entire territory of India, with specific commencement dates for different regions.
Key Definitions
•	Illegal Migrant: Defined as a foreigner who entered India after 25th March 1971 without a valid passport or lawful authority.
Tribunal Structure and Procedure
1.	Illegal Migrants (Determination) Tribunals:
•	Established by the Central Government.
•	Comprise two members, with one designated as Chairman, both of whom must be or have been District/Additional District Judges.
2.	Appellate Tribunal: - Established at the state level.
•	Composed of 2 to 6 members, all of whom must be or have been Judges of a High Court, with a President appointed by the Central Government.
Determination Procedure
1.	Initiation: - References or applications can be made by the Central Government or any individual.
•	Must be accompanied by an affidavit and a prescribed fee (between 10 to 100 rupees).
2.	Tribunal Powers and Procedure: - Empowered with powers similar to those of a civil court under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908.
•	Decisions based on evidence and inquiries, with a mandated disposal timeframe of six months.
Appeal, Enforcement, and Legal Implications
1.	Appeal Process: - Appeals against Tribunal decisions can be made to the Appellate Tribunal within thirty days, with provision for extension under sufficient cause.
2.	Enforcement of Orders: - The Central Government issues directives for the removal of individuals determined to be illegal migrants.
•	Enforcement Authority: Police officers of the rank of Superintendent of Police or above.
3.	Legal Status and Overrides: - Overriding Clause: This Act takes precedence over other relevant laws (e.g., Foreigners Act, 1946; Passports Act, 1967).
•	Judicial Outcome: The Act was struck down by the Supreme Court of India in 2006 due to constitutional violations, specifically for infringing upon the principles of natural justice and the right to equality.

THE ILLEGAL MIGRANTS (DETERMINATION BY TRIBUNALS) ACT, 1983
ACT NO. 39 OF 1983

[25th December, 1983.]

An Act to provide for the establishment of Tribunals for the determination, in a fair manner, of the question whether a person is an illegal migrant to enable the Central Government to expel illegal migrants from India and for matters connected therewith or incidental thereto.
WHEREAS a good number of the foreigners who migrated into India across the borders of the eastern and north-eastern regions of the country on and after the 25th day of March, 1971, have, by taking advantage of the circumstances of such migration and their ethnic similarities and other connections with the people of India and without having in their possession any lawful authority so to do, illegally remained in India;
AND WHEREAS the continuance of such foreigners in India is detrimental to the interests of the public of India;
AND WHEREAS on account of the number of such foreigners and the manner in which such foreigners have clandestinely been trying to pass off as citizens of India and all other relevant circumstances, it is necessary for the protection of the citizens of India to make special provisions for the detection of such foreigners in Assam and also in any other part of India in which such foreigners may be found to have remained illegally;
BE it enacted by Parliament in the Thirty-fourth Year of the Republic of India as follows:--
meta.dc.legislation.history:
Legislative History:

The Illegal Migrants (Determination by Tribunals) Act, 1983

Act Title - The Illegal Migrants (Determination by Tribunals) Act, 1983 (IMDT Act)

Act Number/Year - 39 of 1983

Act ID (India Code) - 198339

Presidential Assent Date- December 25, 1983

Enforcement Date - October 15, 1983

Nodal Ministry - Ministry of Home Affairs

Precedent & Historical Rationale

1. The Assam Agitation and Post-1971 Migration Concerns:

o Following the Bangladesh Liberation War of 1971, the state of Assam experienced large-scale cross-border migration. This triggered the historic Assam Movement (Assam Agitation) led by student bodies and local organizations demanding the identification and deportation of undocumented immigrants.

o While the central Foreigners Act, 1946 applied nationwide and placed the burden of proving citizenship squarely on the accused person, minority groups and regional stakeholders in Assam expressed deep concerns regarding potential harassment during mass detection drives.

2. Creation of a Separate Legal Procedure and Tribunals:

o The legislative intent centered on establishing specialized quasi-judicial tribunals specifically for Assam (though extending technically to the country) to detect individuals who had illegally entered India on or after March 25, 1971.

o Uniquely, the IMDT Act shifted the legal burden of proof away from the accused individual, requiring instead that the complainant or the state police establish the person's status as an illegal migrant under stringent procedural limitations.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

• Formulation:

Drafted by the Ministry of Home Affairs under the Indira Gandhi administration to balance the demands of the Assam Accord movement with safeguards for genuine citizens residing in the state.

• Parliamentary Passage:

Introduced, debated, and passed by both Houses of Parliament (Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha) during the winter session of 1983.

• Presidential Assent: Received Presidential Assent on December 25, 1983.

• Enforcement Date: Enforced on October 15, 1983.

Source: Official Records of Parliament, India Code, and Ministry of Home Affairs.

Summary of The Brahmaputra Board Act, 1980
Key Provisions 
1. Title, Commencement, and Declaration
•	Title & Commencement: The Act may be called the Brahmaputra Board Act, 1980, coming into force on a date notified by the Central Government.
2. Key Definitions
•	Board: Brahmaputra Board established under Section 4.
•	Brahmaputra Valley: Inter-State Brahmaputra river valley demarcated under Section 11.
•	Fund: Brahmaputra Board Fund constituted under Section 19.
•	Master Plan: Plan for controlling floods, bank erosion, and improving drainage in the Brahmaputra Valley.
3. Establishment of the Board
•	Establishment & Incorporation: The Brahmaputra Board is established as a body corporate with perpetual succession and a common seal (Section 4).
•	Composition:
•	Chairman and Vice-Chairman appointed by the Central Government.
•	Ex officio members (General Manager, Financial Adviser).
•	Representatives from various State Governments and Central Ministries.
•	Representatives from Central Water Commission, Central Electricity Authority, etc.
•	Conditions of Service & Powers: Defined for members, Chairman, Vice-Chairman, General Manager, and other officers (Sections 5, 6, 7).
4. Functions and Powers of the Board
•	Limits of the Brahmaputra Valley: To be demarcated by the Central Government (Section 11).
•	Master Plan Preparation: For control of floods, bank erosion, and drainage improvement, considering water resources development (Section 12).
•	Other Functions:
•	Preparing reports, estimates, standards for projects.
•	Constructing, maintaining, and operating multi-purpose dams and works.
•	Phased programme for State Governments’ projects (Section 13).
•	General Powers: To do anything necessary for performing its functions, with specific powers to publish statistics, require information from State Governments (Section 15).
•	Conditions for Performing Functions: Including land provision by State Governments, assistance, and cost sharing (Section 14).
5. Finance, Accounts, and Audit
•	Grants and Loans: From the Central Government (Section 18).
•	Brahmaputra Board Fund: Composition and application purposes (Section 19).
•	Budget and Annual Report: To be prepared and forwarded to the Central Government (Sections 20, 21).
•	Accounts and Audit: Maintained and audited as prescribed (Section 22).
•	Allocation of Water Resources & Project Declarations: Specific to other rivers/projects (e.g., Polavaram Irrigation Project, Tungabhadra Board).

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of the Madras Rent and Revenue Sales Act, 1839

Summary
*Act Title: The Madras Rent and Revenue Sales Act, 1839 
*Enactment Date: 18th March, 1839 

Key Provisions 

1.	Authority and Jurisdiction: - The Act's authority in the Lower Provinces of Bengal is noted to cease, implying its primary jurisdiction was outside this area or its application was region-specific.
•	No Direct Impact on Summary: Since the new context regarding the cessation of authority in the Lower Provinces of Bengal does not alter the operational provisions of the Act itself but rather its geographical applicability, the core summary remains unchanged.
2.	Empowerment of Tahsildars: - Tahsildars are vested with powers of Commissioners for selling property distrained for arrears of rent or revenue.
•	Subject to the same rules and provisions as Commissioners.
3.	Control and Superintendence: - Tahsildars are subject to the control and superintendence of the Collector.
•	Not subject to the Zila Judge's authority except in judicial proceedings.
4.	Fees and Commissions: - Tahsildars are not entitled to fees or commissions for selling distrained property.
•	Such fees/commissions to be credited to the Government.
5.	Delegation of Powers: - Tahsildars can delegate their powers (under Section 2) to public servants under their authority, subject to the Collector's orders.
•	Provisions of Sections 3 and 5 apply equally to delegated public servants.

Precedent & Statutory Rationale

• Background/Transition: Prior to this Act, the sale of property distrained (seized) for the recovery of rent or revenue arrears within the Presidency of Fort St. George (Madras Presidency) was governed by older administrative regulations (Regulation XXVIII of 1802). The existing framework lacked an efficient mechanism at the local administrative level, necessitating the direct empowerment of Tahsildars.

• Rationale/Objectives: The primary objective was to formally vest Tahsildars with the powers of Commissioners to conduct the sale of property distrained for arrears of rent or revenue. It aimed to streamline local revenue collection, ensuring Tahsildars operated under the direct supervision of the District Collector rather than the authority of the Zila (District) Judge, thereby expediting executive actions outside formal judicial proceedings.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Legislative Milestones

• Formulation: Enacted under the British East India Company administration to improve the efficiency and speed of land revenue collection and rent recovery across the Madras Presidency.

• Parliamentary Passage: Passed by the Governor-General of India in Council pursuant to legislative powers under the Charter Act of 1833.

• Presidential Assent: Not applicable (Enacted by the Governor-General-in-Council on March 18, 1839)

THE RIGHT TO INFORMATION ACT, 2005
ACT NO. 22 OF 2005

[15th June, 2005.]

An Act to provide for setting out the practical regime of right to information for citizens to secure access to information under the control of public authorities, in order to promote transparency and accountability in the working of every public authority, the constitution of a Central Information Commission and State Information Commissions and for matters connected therewith or incidental thereto.
WHEREAS the Constitution of India has established democratic Republic;
AND WHEREAS democracy requires an informed citizenry and transparency of information which are vital to its functioning and also to contain corruption and to hold Governments are their instrumentalities accountable to the governed;
AND WHEREAS revelation of information in actual practice is likely to conflict with other public interests including efficient operations of the Governments, optimum use of limited fiscal resources and the preservation of confidentiality of sensitive information;
AND WHEREAS it is necessary to harmonise these conflicting interests while preserving the paramountcy of the democratic ideal;
Now, THEREFORE, it is expendient to provide for furnishing certain information to citizens who desire to have it.
BE it enacted by Parliament in the Fifty-sixth Year of the Republic of India as follows:--

meta.dc.legislation.history:
Legislative History:

The Right to Information Act, 2005

Short Title - The Right to Information Act, 2005

Act Number / Year - Act No. 22 of 2005

Act ID (India Code) - 200522 (Internal ID: 2005-22)

Introduced In - Lok Sabha (as The Right to Information Bill, 2004)

Presidential Assent Date - June 15, 2005

Official Gazette Publication - June 21, 2005

Enforcement Strategy - Phase 1 (Immediate provisions): June 15, 2005 (Ss. 4(1), 5(1)-(2), 12, 13, 15, 16, 24, 27, 28); Phase 2 (Full Enforcement): October 12, 2005 (120th day of enactment)

Nodal Ministry - Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions

Precedent & Statutory Rationale

1. Replacement of the Weak 2002 Framework:

o The preceding Freedom of Information Act, 2002 was widely criticized for containing excessive exemptions, weak enforcement mechanisms, and lacking proactive disclosure mandates. It was never notified into force.

2. Promotion of Transparency and Accountability:

o Enacted to provide a practical regime for citizens to secure access to information under the control of public authorities, thereby combating systemic corruption, promoting governmental transparency, and establishing independent appeal bodies.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

• December 2004: The Right to Information Bill, 2004 was introduced in the Lok Sabha, reflecting wide inputs from the National Advisory Council (NAC) and civil society organizations.

• May 2005: Passed by the Lok Sabha (May 11, 2005) and Rajya Sabha (May 12, 2005) with significant amendments strengthening penalty structures and disclosure rules.

• June 15, 2005: Received Presidential Assent as Act No. 22 of 2005.

• October 12, 2005: Came into full operational effect across India upon the completion of the 120-day statutory transition window.

Core Statutory Framework Established

1. Obligation of Public Authorities (Section 4): Mandates every public authority to maintain records duly cataloged and proactively publish vast categories of administrative data.

2. Public Information Officers (Section 5): Requires public authorities to designate Central/State Public Information Officers (CPIOs/SPIOs) to process information requests within strict timeframes (typically 30 days).

3. Information Commissions (Sections 12 & 15): Establishes the autonomous Central Information Commission (CIC) and State Information Commissions (SICs) vested with powers of a civil court to penalize non-compliance and hear second appeals

Source: Official Records of Parliament, India Code, and Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of the National Green Tribunal Act, 2010
To establish a National Green Tribunal (NGT) for the effective and expeditious disposal of environmental protection and conservation cases, ensuring a balanced approach through judicial and expert oversight.
Key Provisions
1.	Establishment & Composition
•	Established By: Central Government through official notification.
•	Members:
•	Chairperson: Retired Judge of the Supreme Court of India or former Chief Justice of a High Court.
•	Judicial Members: Experienced Judges from High Courts.
•	Expert Members: Professionals with at least 15 years of experience in environmental science, ecology, conservation, or administration.
2.	Jurisdiction, Powers, & Proceedings
•	Jurisdiction: Covers environmental and ecological disputes, including compensation for environmental damage under specified laws.
•	Appellate Jurisdiction: Handles appeals from decisions of lower environmental authorities.
•	Powers: Empowered with the powers of a civil court, with decisions made by a majority, ensuring a blend of legal and environmental expertise in each case.
3.	Penalty & Offences
•	Non-Compliance Penalties: Imposes penalties for ignoring NGT orders or violating environmental laws.
•	Liability: Holds corporations and government entities liable, with directors/officers personally liable unless they can prove no negligence.
4.	Miscellaneous Provisions
•	Exclusion of Civil Court Jurisdiction: Bars civil courts from entertaining cases within NGT’s jurisdiction.
•	Offence Cognizance: Requires specific complaints or a 60-day notice before cognizance of offences.
•	Good Faith Actions: Provides immunity for actions taken in good faith under the Act.
•	Rule Making: Authorizes the Central Government to make rules for implementation.
5.	Repeal, Savings, & Schedules
•	Repeals: Replaces the National Environment Tribunal Act, 1995, and the National Environment Appellate Authority Act, 1997.
•	Schedules:
•	I: Enumerates Acts under NGT’s purview.
•	II: Outlines criteria for compensation (including death, injury, property, and environmental damage).
•	III: Lists amendments to other Acts for alignment.

[2nd June, 2010.]

An Act to provide for the establishment of a National Green Tribunal for the effective and expeditious disposal of cases relating to environmental protection and conservation of forests and other natural resources including enforcement of any legal right relating to environment and giving relief and compensation for damages to persons and property and for matters connected therewith or incidental thereto.
AND WHEREAS India is a party to the decisions taken at the United Nations Conference on the Human Environment held at Stockholm in June, 1972, in which India participated, calling upon the States to take appropriate steps for the protection and improvement of the human environment;
AND WHEREAS decisions were taken at the United Nations Conference on Environment and Development held at Rio de Janeiro in June, 1992, in which India participated, calling upon the States to provide effective access to judicial and administrative proceedings, including redress and remedy and to develop national laws regarding liability and compensation for the victims of pollution and other environmental damage;
AND WHEREAS in the judicial pronouncement in India, the right to healthy environment has been construed as a part of the right to life under article 21 of the Constitution;
AND WHEREAS it is considered expedient to implement the decisions taken at the aforesaid conferences and to have a National Green Tribunal in view of the involvement of multi-disciplinary issues relating to the environment.
BE it enacted by Parliament in the Sixty-first Year of the Republic of India as follows:--

meta.dc.legislation.history:
Legislative History:

The National Green Tribunal Act, 2010

Short Title The National Green Tribunal Act, 2010

Act Number / Year Act No. 19 of 2010

Act ID (India Code) 201019

Presidential Assent Date June 2, 2010

Enforcement Date October 18, 2010

Nodal Ministry Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change

Precedent & Statutory Rationale

1. Overburdened Traditional Judiciary and Technical Complexity:

o Prior to 2010, civil disputes and writ petitions concerning environmental degradation were adjudicated by regular civil courts and High Courts, which faced severe backlogs and lacked the specialized, multi-disciplinary scientific expertise required to evaluate complex ecological, chemical, and environmental impact assessments.

2. Fulfilling International Environmental Jurisprudence and Rio Declaration:

o Grounded in international commitments undertaken at the United Nations Conference on the Human Environment (Stockholm, 1972) and the United Nations Conference on Environment and Development (Rio de Janeiro, 1992), India sought to create an independent, dedicated judicial forum to guarantee effective access to justice, swift redress, and standardized liability and compensation frameworks for victims of environmental harm.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

• Formulation: Developed and piloted by the Ministry of Environment and Forests to overhaul environmental litigation and compliance enforcement.

• Parliamentary Passage: Tabled, debated, and passed by both Houses of Parliament during the budget/monsoon sessions of 2010.

• Presidential Assent: Received formal Presidential Assent on June 2, 2010, entering the statute book as Act No. 19 of 2010.

• Enforcement: Enforced on October 18, 2010.

• Source: India Code and Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change Official Records

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of the Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Act, 2010
Key Provisions
1.	Definitions 
•	Foreign Contribution: Donations, currency, securities, or hospitality from foreign sources.
•	Foreign Hospitality: Non-casual offers of travel, boarding, etc., from foreign sources.
•	Foreign Source: Includes foreign governments, international agencies, foreign companies, etc.
2.	Regulation of Foreign Contribution & Hospitality
•	Prohibitions and Restrictions:
•	Organisations of Political Nature: Designation process outlined, emphasizing transparency and due process.
•	Restrictions on Foreign Hospitality: Prohibits acceptance without prior Central Government permission, with exceptions for emergency medical aid.
•	Prohibition on Transfer of Foreign Contributions: Strict ban on transferring received foreign contributions to other persons.
•	Limitations on Administrative Expenses : Caps administrative expenses to 20% of foreign contributions, with possibilities for approval of excess.
3.	Registration, Prior Permission, and Reporting
•	Registration Requirement: Mandatory for consistent foreign contribution recipients, with a streamlined 5-year renewal process.
•	Prior Permission: Required for non-registered entities, with a clarified application process for specific purposes or sources.
•	FCRA Account and Reporting: Mandatory account with specified banking channels; tightened reporting timelines, especially for election candidates (within 180 days before nomination).
4.	Power of Central Government
•	Specification of Organisations of Political Nature: Detailed process for designation, including notice, representation, and decision timelines (up to 180 days).
•	Prohibition and Regulation Powers: Authority to prohibit foreign contributions or hospitality based on national interest, public interest, electoral fairness, foreign relations, or social harmony.
•	Exemption Power: Central Government can exempt entities in the public interest.
5.	Compliance and Penalties
•	Enhanced Audit Powers: With confidentiality for information obtained.
•	Penalties for Non-Compliance: Includes suspension, cancellation of registration, and legal action for violations.

THE FOREIGN CONTRIBUTION (REGULATION) ACT, 2010
ACT NO. 42 OF 2010

[26th September, 2010.]

An Act to consolidate the law to regulate the acceptance and utilisation of foreign contribution or foreign hospitality by certain individuals or associations or companies and to prohibit acceptance and utilisation of foreign contribution or foreign hospitality for any activities detrimental to the national interest and for matters connected therewith or incidental thereto.
BE it enacted by Parliament in the Sixty-first Year of the Republic of India as follows:--
meta.dc.legislation.history:
Legislative History:

The Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Act, 2010

● Act Title - The Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Act, 2010

● Act Number / Year - 42 of 2010

● Act ID (India Code) - 201042

● Assent Date - September 26, 2010

● Enforcement Date - May 1, 2011

● Nodal Ministry - Ministry of Home Affairs

Precedent & Historical Rationale

● Deficiencies and Lacunae in the Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Act, 1976 - Foreign donations in India were previously governed by the Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Act, 1976 (Act 49 of 1976), enacted during the Emergency primarily to curb covert foreign political influence during elections. Over the decades, massive increases in foreign inflows to non-governmental organizations (NGOs) and associations exposed major loopholes in the 1976 law, including permanent/perpetual registrations with no statutory renewal mechanism, lack of statutory caps on administrative expenses, and inadequate tracking of diverted funds affecting national security.

● Modernized Statutory Framework for Transparency and National Security - Formulated to consolidate the law to regulate the acceptance and utilization of foreign contribution or foreign hospitality by certain individuals or associations or companies and to prohibit the acceptance and utilization of foreign contribution or foreign hospitality for any activities detrimental to the national interest. The Act introduced a 5-year validity and mandatory renewal regime for FCRA registrations, prohibited political parties, candidates, judges, journalists, and public servants from receiving foreign funds, capped administrative expenses funded by foreign donations, mandated maintenance of separate accounts, and expanded inspection and audit powers of the Union Government.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

● Formulation & Standing Committee Review - Drafted by the Ministry of Home Affairs to replace the outdated 1976 statute; introduced as The Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Bill, 2006 in the Rajya Sabha on December 18, 2006, and examined by the Parliamentary Standing Committee on Home Affairs, which presented its report in October 2008.

● Parliamentary Passage - Incorporating the Standing Committee's recommendations, the Bill was debated and passed by the Rajya Sabha on August 19, 2010, and considered and passed by the Lok Sabha on August 31, 2010, during the Monsoon Session.

● President's Assent - Received the assent of the President of India (Pratibha Devisingh Patil) on September 26, 2010, and was published in the Gazette of India on September 27, 2010.

● Enforcement - Enforced on May 1, 2011.

Sources - Parliamentary Debates (Lok Sabha & Rajya Sabha), Reports of the Department-Related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Home Affairs, The Gazette of India, India Code, and Ministry of Home Affairs.
