meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of the Immoral Traffic (Prevention) Act, 1956

Key Provisions:
1.	Prohibition of Trafficking and Exploitation 
o	The Act criminalises trafficking of persons for the purpose of prostitution and prohibits commercial sexual exploitation. 
2.	Punishment for Keeping or Managing a Brothel 
o	Keeping, managing, or assisting in the management of a brothel is an offence punishable under the Act. 
3.	Living on the Earnings of Prostitution 
o	Any person who knowingly lives wholly or partly on the earnings of the prostitution of another person commits an offence. 
4.	Procuring, Inducing or Trafficking Persons 
o	Procuring, inducing, taking, or attempting to take a person for the purpose of prostitution is punishable under the Act. 
o	Enhanced penalties apply where children or minors are involved. 
5.	Prostitution in or Near Public Places 
o	The Act prohibits prostitution in the vicinity of public places such as schools, places of worship, hospitals, and other notified areas. 
6.	Rescue and Protective Homes 
o	Magistrates may order the rescue of victims from brothels and place them in protective homes or rehabilitation institutions. 
o	The Act provides for the care, protection, and rehabilitation of rescued persons. 
7.	Special Police Officers 
o	The Act authorises the appointment of Special Police Officers to investigate offences and enforce its provisions. 
o	It also provides for search, rescue, and investigation procedures. 
8.	Punishments 
o	The Act prescribes penalties for offences such as: 
	Keeping or managing a brothel. 
	Living on the earnings of prostitution. 
	Procuring or trafficking persons. 
	Detaining a person in premises where prostitution is carried on. 
	Other related offences.

THE ENVIRONMENT (PROTECTION) ACT, 1986
ACT NO. 29 OF 1986

[23rd May, 1986.]

An Act to provide for the protection and improvement of environment and for matters connected therewith.
WHEREAS decisions were taken at the United Nations Conference on the Human Environment held at Stockholm in June, 1972, in which India participated, to take appropriate steps for the protection and improvement of human environment;
AND WHEREAS it is considered necessary further to implement the decisions aforesaid in so far as they relate to the protection and improvement of environment and the prevention of hazards to human beings, other living creatures, plants and property;
BE it enacted by Parliament in the Thirty-seventh Year of the Republic of India as follows:--

meta.dc.legislation.history:
Legislative History:

The Environment (Protection) Act, 1986

Act Title - The Environment (Protection) Act, 1986

Act Number /Year- 29 of 1986

Act ID (India Code) - 198629

Presidential Assent Date - May 23, 1986

Enforcement Date - November 19, 1986

Nodal Ministry - Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change

Precedent & Historical Rationale

International Commitments and the Bhopal Disaster:

Following the United Nations Conference on the Human Environment held in Stockholm in June 1972, India committed to broad-scale environmental preservation. However, the immediate catalyst for comprehensive framework legislation was the tragic Bhopal gas leak disaster of December 1984. The catastrophe starkly exposed severe gaps, fragmentation, and enforcement weaknesses in existing environmental laws (such as the Water Act, 1974 and the Air Act, 1981), which dealt with specific mediums rather than providing an overarching national umbrella for environmental safety.

Need for an Omnibus Environmental Law:

Prior to 1986, there was no centralized statute empowering the central government to coordinate the activities of various regulatory agencies, lay down comprehensive national standards for emission or discharge of environmental pollutants, and handle industrial accidents or hazardous substances uniformly. The government felt an urgent imperative to enact an umbrella legislation under Article 253 of the Constitution to implement decisions reached at international conferences and establish strict preventive and penal mechanisms for environmental safety.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

Formulation:

Drafted by the Ministry of Environment and Forests as an overarching umbrella legislation to plug legislative gaps, granting sweeping powers to the Central Government to take all necessary measures for protecting and improving the quality of the environment, setting standards for emissions and discharges, inspecting industrial units, and restricting hazardous operations.

Parliamentary Passage:

Introduced, debated, and passed by both Houses of Parliament (Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha) in the spring session of 1986.

Presidential Assent: Received Presidential Assent on May 23, 1986.

Enforcement: Enforced on November 19, 1986.

Source: Official Records of Parliament, India Code, and Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change.

meta.dc.identifier.preamble_description:
THE SCHEDULED TRIBES AND OTHER TRADITIONAL FOREST DWELLERS (RECOGNITION OF FOREST RIGHTS) ACT, 2006
ACT NO. 2 OF 2007

[29th December, 2006.]

An Act to recognise and vest the forest rights and occupation in forest land in forest dwelling Scheduled Tribes and other traditional forest dwellers who have been residing in such forests for generations but whose rights could not be recorded; to provide for a framework for recording the forest rights so vested and the nature of evidence required for such recognition and vesting in respect of forest land.
WHEREAS the recognised rights of the forest dwelling Scheduled Tribes and other traditional forest dwellers include the responsibilities and authority for sustainable use, conservation of biodiversity and maintenance of ecological balance and thereby strengthening the conservation regime of the forests while ensuring livelihood and food security of the forest dwelling Scheduled Tribes and other traditional forest dwellers;
AND WHEREAS the forest rights on ancestral lands and their habitat were not adequately recognised in the consolidation of State forests during the colonial period as well as in independent India resulting in historical injustice to the forest dwelling Scheduled Tribes and other traditional forest dwellers who are integral to the very survival and sustainability of the forest ecosystem;
AND WHEREAS it has become necessary to address the long standing insecurity of tenurial and access rights of forest dwelling Scheduled Tribes and other traditional forest dwellers including those who were forced to relocate their dwelling due to State development interventions.
BE it enacted by Parliament in the Fifty-seventh Year of the Republic of India as follows:--
meta.dc.legislation.history:
Legislative History:

The Scheduled Tribes and Other Traditional Forest Dwellers (Recognition of Forest Rights) Act, 2006

Short Title The Scheduled Tribes and Other Traditional Forest Dwellers (Recognition of Forest Rights) Act, 2006

Act Number / Year Act No. 2 of 2007

Act ID (India Code) 200702

Presidential Assent / Enactment Date December 29, 2006

Enforcement Date December 31, 2007

Administrative Nodal Ministry Ministry of Tribal Affairs

Precedent & Statutory Rationale

1. Redressing Historical Injustice:

o Prior to the enactment of the 2006 legislation, forest management frameworks in India largely rooted in colonial-era legislations such as the Indian Forest Act, 1927 failed to recognize the symbiotic relationship between forest-dwelling communities and forest ecosystems.

o Forest-dwelling Scheduled Tribes (FDSTs) and Other Traditional Forest Dwellers (OTFDs) were systematically treated as encroachers on their ancestral lands, resulting in widespread tenurial insecurity, arbitrary evictions, and a failure to record customary rights during the consolidation of state forests.

2. Constitutional and Livelihood Mandate:

o The law was formulated to correct these historical injustices, guarantee livelihood and food security, and legally vest forest rights recognizing that the conservation regime is strengthened when local communities are empowered as stewards of biodiversity and ecological balance.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

• Formulation: Piloted and finalized by the Ministry of Tribal Affairs following extensive legislative deliberations, civil society advocacy, and inputs from a Joint Parliamentary Committee.

• Parliamentary Passage: Tabled, rigorously debated, and passed by both Houses of Parliament in December 2006.

• Presidential Assent: Received formal Presidential Assent on December 29, 2006, entering the statute book as Act No. 2 of 2007.

• Enforcement: Enforced on December 31, 2007.

• Source: India Code (indiacode.gov.in) and Ministry of Tribal Affairs Official Records

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of the Companies Act, 2013 
Objectives of the Act
•	To regulate the incorporation, management, and dissolution of companies. 
•	To promote good corporate governance, transparency, and accountability. 
•	To protect the interests of shareholders, creditors, employees, and other stakeholders. 
•	To strengthen compliance, disclosures, and corporate responsibility. 
•	To facilitate a business-friendly legal environment while safeguarding public interest. 
Key Provisions
•	Incorporation of Companies: The Act lays down the procedures for the formation, registration, and classification of companies, including private companies, public companies, one-person companies (OPCs), and companies incorporated for charitable purposes. 
•	Corporate Governance: It prescribes provisions relating to the composition and responsibilities of the Board of Directors, independent directors, key managerial personnel, board committees, and directors' duties. 
•	Share Capital and Securities: The Act regulates the issue, allotment, transfer, buy-back, and reduction of share capital, as well as the issuance of debentures and other securities. 
•	Meetings and Administration: It governs the conduct of shareholders' meetings, board meetings, maintenance of statutory registers and records, filing requirements, and corporate disclosures. 
•	Accounts and Audit: The Act provides for the preparation of financial statements, statutory audits, appointment and rotation of auditors, internal audit, and enhanced financial reporting standards. 
•	Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR): It introduced mandatory Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) obligations for specified classes of companies, requiring them to spend a prescribed percentage of their average net profits on eligible social welfare activities. 
•	Prevention of Fraud: The Act strengthens measures against corporate fraud, establishes responsibilities for auditors and directors, and provides for investigation into the affairs of companies. 
•	Mergers, Amalgamations, and Compromises: It lays down procedures for corporate restructuring, including mergers, amalgamations, arrangements, and compromises. 
•	Revival and Winding Up: The Act provides mechanisms for the revival, rehabilitation, and winding up of companies in accordance with applicable laws. 
•	National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT): The Act provides for the constitution and functioning of the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT) and the National Company Law Appellate Tribunal (NCLAT) for adjudication of company law matters. 
•	Rule-making Power: The Central Government is empowered to make rules for implementing the provisions of the Act.

meta.dc.legislation.history:
Legislative History:

The Companies Act, 2013

Short Title The Companies Act, 2013

Act Number / Year Act No. 18 of 2013

Act ID (India Code) 201318

Presidential Assent Date August 29, 2013

Enforcement Date Brought into force in phased stages (initial provisions on August 30, 2013; 98 sections on September 12, 2013; and a major batch of 183 sections on April 1, 2014)

Nodal Ministry Ministry of Corporate Affairs

Precedent & Statutory Rationale

1. Inadequacies of the Legacy 1956 Framework:

o Operating for nearly six decades, the Companies Act, 1956 became outdated in the face of rapid globalization, complex corporate structures, cross-border mergers, and electronic commerce, lacking modern governance mandates and quick dispute-resolution mechanisms.

2. Aligning with Global Corporate Governance Standards:

o Grounded in extensive recommendations by expert panels—most notably the J.J. Irani Committee on Company Law—the legislation was enacted to overhaul India's corporate regulatory framework, enhance transparency, protect minority shareholder rights, curb corporate malpractices, and facilitate ease of doing business.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

• Formulation: Developed and piloted by the Ministry of Corporate Affairs to replace the archaic 1956 statute with a dynamic, self-regulatory, and disclosure-based framework.

• Parliamentary Passage: Originally introduced as the Companies Bill, 2011, examined comprehensively by the Parliamentary Standing Committee on Finance, passed by the Lok Sabha in December 2012, and subsequently passed by the Rajya Sabha in August 2013.

• Presidential Assent: Received formal Presidential Assent on August 29, 2013, entering the statute book as Act No. 18 of 2013.

• Enforcement: Enforced progressively through multiple phased government notifications between late 2013 and mid-2016 to allow corporate entities smooth structural transition.

• Source: India Code and Ministry of Corporate Affairs Official Records

meta.dc.legislation.history:
Legislative History:

The Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017

Short Title The Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017

Act Number / Year Act No. 12 of 2017

India Code Act ID 201712

Presidential Assent Date April 12, 2017

Enforcement Date June 22, 2017 (for preliminary/registration provisions vide S.O. 1972(E)); July 1, 2017 (for full operational levy and collections vide S.O. 2068(E))

Nodal Ministry Ministry of Finance

Precedent & Statutory Rationale

1. Unification of Indirect Tax Architecture ("One Nation, One Tax"):

o Enacted pursuant to the historic Constitution (One Hundred and First Amendment) Act, 2016, which inserted Article 246A to grant simultaneous taxation powers to Parliament and State Legislatures. The Act replaced a fragmented indirect tax system with a unified central tax framework on the intra-State supply of goods and services.

2. Elimination of Tax Cascading & Seamless Input Tax Credit (ITC):

o Established a comprehensive statutory framework for levying tax at every stage of the supply chain while allowing registered taxpayers to claim an Input Tax Credit (ITC) on taxes paid on inputs, thereby removing the "tax-on-tax" cascading effect.

3. Cooperative Federalism & GST Council Consensus:

o Functionally anchored in the decisions of the GST Council (established under Article 279A of the Constitution), ensuring that legislative rules, tax slabs, threshold exemptions, and compliance mechanics are harmonized across the Union and the States.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

• Formulation: Drafted under the guidance of the GST Council chaired by Union Finance Minister Arun Jaitley, with representation from Finance Ministers of all States and Union Territories.

• Parliamentary Passage: Introduced in the Lok Sabha as a Money Bill on March 27, 2017; debated and passed by the Lok Sabha on March 29, 2017; returned without amendments by the Rajya Sabha on April 6, 2017.

• Presidential Assent: Received formal Presidential Assent on April 12, 2017, entering the statute book as Act No. 12 of 2017.

• Enforcement: Phased rollout commencing June 22, 2017 (for registration and procedural sections) and coming into full operational force nationwide on July 1, 2017.

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of the Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013 
Key Provisions
I. Determination of Social Impact & Public Purpose
Social Impact Assessment (SIA) Study:
•	Mandatory before land acquisition (except in specified exemptions).
•	Public hearing for SIA.
•	Publication of SIA report.
Expert Group Appraisal of SIA report.
Exemption from SIA in specified cases (e.g., national security, public health emergencies).
II. Special Provisions
Safeguarding Food Security: Provisions to ensure minimal impact on agricultural land and food security.
III. Notification & Acquisition
Preliminary Notification & Survey:
•	Publication and power of officers to survey.
•	Pre-Acquisition Procedures: Certain actions (e.g., SIA) must be undertaken prior to initiation of acquisition proceedings.
•	Extendable Period for Proceedings Initiation: The appropriate Government can extend the 12-month period for initiating acquisition proceedings if justified, with written record and public notification.
Hearing of Objections within 60 days of notification, covering:
•	Area and suitability of land.
•	Justification for public purpose.
•	SIA report findings.
•	Collector's Role: Receives objections, provides hearing, and submits recommendations to the appropriate Government.
iV. Rehabilitation & Resettlement (R&R)
Preparation of R&R Scheme by the Administrator post preliminary notification:
•	Includes survey, census of affected families, and details on livelihoods, public utilities, and amenities.
•	Draft Scheme Contents:
•	Rehabilitation and resettlement entitlements.
•	List of Government buildings and public amenities in the Resettlement Area.
•	Time-Bound Implementation: Scheme includes a time limit for implementation.
•	Public Participation:
•	Wide publicity and discussion in Gram Sabhas/Municipalities.
•	Mandatory Public Hearing: With adequate publicity, and in every affected Gram Sabha/Municipality if ≥25% of their land is acquired, considering special provisions for Scheduled Areas.
Review of R&R Scheme by the Collector.
V. Compensation
Components of Compensation: - Market value of land.
•	Multiplication factor based on location (rural/urban).
•	Value of assets attached.
•	Solatium (100% of the calculated value).
Determination of Market Value by the Collector.
VI. Judicial & Administrative Provisions
Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Authority:
•	Establishment.
•	Powers and procedure.
Appeal to High Court from Authority's decisions.
Rules and Regulations: - Power of appropriate Government to make rules.
•	Previous publication of rules.
Power to Remove Difficulties within 2 years of commencement.
Schedules 
•	The First Schedule: Details the minimum compensation package.
•	Provisions for Affected Families: Including those in Scheduled Areas and special considerations for Scheduled Castes and Tribes.
•	Awards and Resettlement Areas: Provisions for infrastructural amenities and corrections to awards.

THE RIGHT TO FAIR COMPENSATION AND TRANSPARENCY IN LAND ACQUISITION, REHABILITATION AND RESETTLEMENT ACT, 2013
ACT No. 30 OF 2013

[26th September, 2013.]

An Act to ensure, in consultation with institutions of local self-government and Gram Sabhas established under the Constitution, a humane, participative, informed and transparent process for land acquisition for industrialisation, development of essential infrastructural facilities and urbanisation with the least disturbance to the owners of the land and other affected families and provide just and fair compensation to the affected families whose land has been acquired or proposed to be acquired or are affected by such acquisition and make adequate provisions for such affected persons for their rehabilitation and resettlement and for ensuring that the cumulative outcome of compulsory acquisition should be that affected persons become partners in development leading to an improvement in their post acquisition social and economic status and for matters connected therewith or incidental thereto.

meta.dc.legislation.history:
Legislative History:

The Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013

Short Title The Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013

Act Number / Year Act No. 30 of 2013

Act ID (India Code) 201330

Presidential Assent Date September 26, 2013

Enforcement Date January 1, 2014

Nodal Ministry Ministry of Rural Development

Precedent & Statutory Rationale

1. Inadequacies and Archaic Nature of the Legacy 1894 Framework:

o For over a century, compulsory land acquisition across British and independent India was governed by the Land Acquisition Act, 1894. This colonial-era framework focused narrowly on state acquisition for public purposes against minimal cash compensation, completely lacking statutory mandates for rehabilitation, resettlement, transparency, or public consultation.

2. Balancing Industrial Growth with Social Justice:

o Grounded in constitutional welfare commitments, the legislation was enacted to replace arbitrary acquisition practices with a transparent, participative, and informed process. It sought to ensure that families losing land are treated as partners in development, protecting vulnerable agrarian communities, livelihood dependencies, and rural food security from unmitigated displacement.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

• Formulation: Developed and piloted by the Department of Land Resources under the Ministry of Rural Development to overhaul the national land acquisition regime.

• Parliamentary Passage: Introduced in the Lok Sabha as the Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Bill, 2011, on September 7, 2011; extensively scrutinized by the Parliamentary Standing Committee on Rural Development; and subsequently passed by the Lok Sabha on August 29, 2013, and the Rajya Sabha on September 4, 2013.

• Presidential Assent: Received formal Presidential Assent on September 26, 2013, entering the statute book as Act No. 30 of 2013.

• Enforcement: Enforced on January 1, 2014.

• Source: India Code Official Repository (indiacode.gov.in) and Ministry of Rural Development Official Records

ACT NO. 35 OF 2019

[9th August, 2019.]

An Act to provide for protection of the interests of consumers and for the said purpose, to establish authorities for timely and effective administration and settlement of consumers' disputes and for matters connected therewith or incidentalthereto.

Legislative History:

The Consumer Protection Act, 2019

Short Title - The Consumer Protection Act, 2019

Act Number / Year - Act No. 35 of 2019

Act ID (India Code) - 201935

Presidential Assent / Enactment Date - August 9, 2019

Enforcement Date - Phased enforcement commencing with specific provisions on July 20, 2020.

Nodal Ministry - Ministry of Consumer Affairs, Food and Public Distribution

Precedent & Statutory Rationale

1. Modernizing Consumer Rights for the Digital Age:

o Prior to 2019, consumer disputes were adjudicated under the Consumer Protection Act, 1986. However, rapid globalization, a surge in e-commerce transactions, digital marketing, telemarketing, and multi-layered supply chains exposed severe limitations in the old legal framework, particularly regarding swift grievance redressal and digital marketplace accountability.

o Comprehensive legislative overhaul was required to safeguard consumers against increasingly complex unfair trade practices, fraudulent online sellers, and sub-standard or hazardous products.

2. Establishment of Central Regulatory Authorities and Product Liability:

o The Act was formulated to provide for the protection of the interests of consumers and for that purpose to establish authorities for timely and effective administration and settlement of consumer disputes.

o It establishes the Central Consumer Protection Authority (CCPA) to regulate unfair trade practices, curb misleading ads, issue class-action safety recalls, and introduce strict Product Liability provisions holding manufacturers and sellers financially liable for harm caused by defective goods or services.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

• Formulation: Developed by the Department of Consumer Affairs following intensive stakeholder consultations, parliamentary committee scrutiny, and policy reviews of emerging global consumer protection standards.

• Parliamentary Passage: Tabled, debated, and successfully passed by both houses of the Parliament of India, receiving the formal assent of the President of India on August 9, 2019.

• Enforcement: Enforced on July 20, 2020.

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 
Objectives of the Act
•	To provide a comprehensive legal framework for domestic and international commercial arbitration. 
•	To facilitate the speedy and efficient resolution of disputes through arbitration and conciliation. 
•	To minimise judicial intervention in arbitral proceedings. 
•	To ensure the recognition and enforcement of domestic and foreign arbitral awards. 
•	To promote India as an arbitration-friendly jurisdiction. 
Key Provisions
•	Arbitration Agreement: The Act recognises and enforces written arbitration agreements, under which parties agree to refer disputes to arbitration instead of litigation. 
•	Appointment of Arbitrators: It lays down the procedure for the appointment, challenge, replacement, and termination of arbitrators, while ensuring their independence and impartiality. 
•	Conduct of Arbitral Proceedings: The Act provides flexibility to parties in determining the procedure for arbitration, subject to the principles of fairness, equality, and natural justice. 
•	Arbitral Award: Arbitral tribunals are empowered to make final and binding awards. The Act specifies the form, contents, and grounds for correction, interpretation, and challenge of awards. 
•	Court Assistance and Limited Judicial Intervention: Courts may assist in matters such as appointment of arbitrators, grant of interim measures, and enforcement of awards, but judicial intervention is otherwise limited to the circumstances expressly provided in the Act. 
•	Enforcement of Awards: Domestic arbitral awards are enforceable as decrees of a court. The Act also provides for the recognition and enforcement of foreign arbitral awards under the New York Convention and the Geneva Convention, subject to specified conditions. 
•	Conciliation: The Act establishes a statutory framework for conciliation, enabling parties to resolve disputes amicably with the assistance of an impartial conciliator. A settlement agreement reached through conciliation has the same status and effect as an arbitral award on agreed terms. 
•	Rule-making Power: The Central Government is empowered to make rules for carrying out the provisions of the Act.

meta.dc.identifier.preamble_description:
THE ARBITRATION AND CONCILIATION ACT, 1996
ACT No. 26 OF 1996

[16th August, 1996.]

An Act to consolidate and amend the law relating to domestic arbitration, international commercial arbitration and enforcement of foreign arbitral awards as also to define the law relating to conciliation and for matters connected therewith or incidental thereto.
Preamble.--WHEREAS the United Nations Commission on International Trade Law (UNCITRAL) has adopted the UNCITRAL Model Law on International Commercial Arbitration in 1985; AND WHEREAS the General Assembly of the United Nations has recommended that all countries give due consideration to the said Model Law, in view of the desirability of uniformity of the law of arbitral procedures and the specific needs of international commercial arbitration practice;
AND WHEREAS the UNCITRAL has adopted the UNCITRAL Conciliation Rules in 1980;
AND WHEREAS the General Assembly of the United Nations has recommended the use of the said Rules in cases where a dispute arises in the context of international commercial relations and the parties seek an amicable settlement of that dispute by recourse to conciliation;
AND WHEREAS the said Model Law and Rules make significant contribution to the establishment of a unified legal framework for the fair and efficient settlement of disputes arising in international commercial relations;
AND WHEREAS it is expedient to make law respecting arbitration and conciliation, taking into account the aforesaid Model Law and Rules;
BE it enacted by Parliament in the Forty-seventh Year of the Republic of India as follows:--

meta.dc.legislation.history:
Legislative History:

The Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996

Short Title The Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996

Act Number / Year 26 of 1996

Act ID (India Code) 199626

Presidential Assent / Enactment Date August 16, 1996

Enforcement Date August 22, 1996

Nodal Ministry Ministry of Law and Justice

Precedent & Statutory Rationale

• Deficiencies of the 1940 Framework:

o Prior to 1996, domestic arbitration in India was governed by the Arbitration Act of 1940, which was heavily criticized for fostering judicial intervention, excessive delays, and high litigation costs.

o Awards could easily be challenged or stalled in court, defeating the entire purpose of alternative dispute resolution (ADR) and deterring foreign commercial investment following the 1991 economic reforms.

• Legislative Intervention and Regularization:

o Enacted to modernize and harmonize India's dispute resolution regime with international standards, the 1996 Act was based on the United Nations Commission on International Trade Law (UNCITRAL) Model Law on International Commercial Arbitration, 1985 and the UNCITRAL Conciliation Rules, 1980.

o The core objectives include minimizing judicial intervention in arbitral proceedings, ensuring party autonomy, providing a binding legal framework for international commercial arbitrations and enforcement of foreign awards, and introducing statutory recognition for conciliation as an amicable settlement tool.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

• Formulation: Drafted following widespread legal consultations and recommendations to replace a trifecta of obsolete pre-independence and fragmented post-independence statutes. The framework was initially promulgated via ordinance (The Arbitration and Conciliation Ordinance, 1996) before being enacted into law.

• Parliamentary Passage: Introduced in Parliament, debated, and passed by both houses during the monsoon session, receiving formal presidential assent on August 16, 1996.

• Enforcement: Enforced on August 22, 1996.

• Source: India Code (indiacode.gov.in), Ministry of Law and Justice Official Records, and Parliament of India Records.

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of the National Highways Act, 1956

Key Provisions:
1.	Declaration of National Highways 
o	The Act empowers the Central Government to declare any highway or part thereof as a National Highway through notification in the Official Gazette. 
o	National Highways are highways considered necessary for national importance. 
2.	Responsibility of Central Government 
o	The Central Government is responsible for the development and maintenance of National Highways. 
o	It may undertake construction, improvement, widening, and repair works either directly or through authorised agencies. 
3.	Acquisition of Land 
o	The Act provides a procedure for acquiring land required for the construction or development of National Highways. 
o	The Central Government may appoint competent authorities for land acquisition purposes. 
4.	Compensation for Acquired Land 
o	The Act provides for payment of compensation to landowners whose land is acquired for highway projects. 
o	The procedure for determining compensation and resolving disputes is prescribed under the Act. 
5.	Leasing and Transfer of Land 
o	The Central Government may acquire, hold, and manage land required for National Highways. 
o	It may also permit the use of highway land for specified purposes. 
6.	Control and Regulation of Highways 
o	The Act provides powers to authorities for regulating activities affecting National Highways. 
o	It enables measures for ensuring proper maintenance and safe use of highways. 
7.	National Highways Authority of India (NHAI) 
o	The Act was later supplemented by the National Highways Authority of India Act, 1988, which established NHAI for the development, maintenance, and management of National Highways.

title: The Airports Authority of India Act, 1994

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of the Airports Authority of India Act, 1994 
Key Provisions
•	Establishment of the Airports Authority of India: The Act provides for the incorporation of the Airports Authority of India as a body corporate with perpetual succession and a common seal. 
•	Functions of the Authority: The AAI is entrusted with the planning, development, operation, maintenance, and management of airports, civil enclaves, air traffic management services, communication, navigation and surveillance systems, passenger terminals, cargo facilities, and other airport infrastructure. 
•	Powers of the Authority: The Authority is empowered to acquire, hold, and dispose of property, enter into contracts, levy and collect fees and charges for airport and air navigation services, undertake infrastructure projects, and perform all acts necessary for carrying out its functions. 
•	Management: The Act provides for the composition of the Authority, including the Chairperson and other members appointed by the Central Government, and lays down their powers, functions, and service conditions. 
•	Finance and Accounts: The Act provides for the Authority's funds, budget, borrowing powers, maintenance of accounts, audit by the Comptroller and Auditor General of India (CAG), and submission of annual reports to the Central Government. 
•	Rule-making Power: The Central Government is empowered to make rules, and the Authority may make regulations, consistent with the Act, for carrying out its functions.

Act Number 55 of 1994

Precedent & Historical Rationale

1. Fragmentation of Airport Management:

o Prior to 1994, civil aviation infrastructure in India was managed separately by two distinct statutory bodies: the International Airports Authority of India (IAAI), which handled major international hubs, and the National Airports Authority (NAA), which managed domestic airports and civil aviation communication systems.

2. Need for Administrative Synergy and Modernization:

o To streamline operations, eliminate administrative overlap, pool financial and technical resources, and create a single unified agency capable of accelerating airport development to meet the demands of economic liberalization, the merger of NAA and IAAI into a single overarching body became essential.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

• Formulation: Drafted by the Ministry of Civil Aviation to dissolve the NAA and IAAI and establish a consolidated corporate statutory entity—the Airports Authority of India (AAI).

• Parliamentary Passage: Introduced as a comprehensive legislative bill, debated, and passed by both Houses of Parliament (Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha) during the Monsoon Session of 1994.

• Presidential Assent: Received Presidential Assent on September 12, 1994.

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of the Limitation Act, 1963 
Objectives of the Act
•	To prescribe limitation periods for filing suits, appeals, and applications. 
•	To ensure that legal claims are pursued within a reasonable time. 
•	To promote certainty, finality, and efficiency in the administration of justice. 
•	To provide for extension or exclusion of limitation in specified circumstances. 
Key Provisions
•	Schedules of Limitation: The Act contains a Schedule prescribing different limitation periods for various types of civil suits, appeals, and applications, along with the point from which the limitation period begins to run. 
•	Bar of Limitation: A suit, appeal, or application filed after the prescribed limitation period is generally barred, even though the underlying right may continue to exist. 
•	Extension of Time: Courts may condone delays in filing certain appeals and applications if the applicant shows sufficient cause for not filing within the prescribed period. 
•	Exclusion of Time: The Act provides for exclusion of certain periods in computing limitation, such as time spent prosecuting proceedings in good faith before a court without jurisdiction, or where legal proceedings are stayed by injunction or order. 
•	Disability: Special provisions apply where the person entitled to sue is a minor, of unsound mind, or otherwise under a legal disability at the time the right to sue accrues. 
•	Acknowledgment and Part Payment: A written acknowledgment of liability or part payment made before the expiry of the limitation period may give rise to a fresh limitation period in specified cases. 
•	Acquisition of Ownership by Prescription: The Act also lays down the law relating to the acquisition of rights by prescription, including easements and, in certain circumstances, ownership through adverse possession.

● Act ID (India Code) - 196336

● Presidential Assent Date - October 5, 1963

● Enforcement Date - January 1, 1964

● Nodal Ministry - Ministry of Law and Justice

Precedent & Historical Rationale

● Codification and Restructuring of Prescription Standards - Enacted to consolidate and amend the law for the limitation of suits, appeals, and applications to civil courts, replacing the outdated Indian Limitation Act, 1908 based on recommendations of the Law Commission of India (3rd Report).

● Statutory Certainty and Equity Mechanisms - Formulated to enforce the principles of public policy (interest reipublicae ut sit finis litium and vigilantibus non dormientibus jura subveniunt) by setting fixed periods for litigation while embedding statutory provisions for condonation of delay (Section 5), legal disability (Section 6), and exclusion of time in legal proceedings.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

● Formulation - Introduced by the Ministry of Law following extensive revision of limitation periods across distinct categories of civil suits, property claims, and contractual obligations.

● Parliamentary Passage - Debated and passed by both Houses of Parliament (Third Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha) during the August–September session of 1963.

● Presidential Assent - Received Presidential Assent on October 5, 1963.

● Enforcement - Enforced on January 1, 1964.

title: The Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act, 1956

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of the Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act, 1956

Key Provisions:

1.	Application of the Act 
o	The Act applies to Hindus, Buddhists, Jains, and Sikhs. 
2.	Definition of Minor 
o	A minor is a person who has not completed the age of eighteen years. 
3.	Natural Guardians
The Act specifies natural guardians for different categories of Hindu minors: 
o	For a Hindu boy or an unmarried Hindu girl: The father is the natural guardian, and after him, the mother. However, the custody of a child below five years of age is ordinarily with the mother. 
o	For an illegitimate child: The mother is the natural guardian, followed by the father. 
o	For a married girl: The husband is considered the natural guardian. 
4.	Rights and Powers of Natural Guardians 
o	A natural guardian may take necessary decisions for the benefit and welfare of the minor. 
o	The guardian cannot act in a manner harmful to the minor’s interests. 
o	The guardian cannot transfer, mortgage, or dispose of the minor’s immovable property without prior permission of the court. 
5.	Welfare of the Minor 
o	The Act establishes that the welfare of the minor shall be the paramount consideration in appointing or recognising a guardian. 
o	Personal preferences or legal rights of guardians are subordinate to the child’s welfare. 
6.	Disqualification of Natural Guardian 
o	A person who has renounced the world or ceased to be a Hindu is not eligible to act as a natural guardian. 
o	A guardian who acts against the interest of the minor may lose guardianship rights. 
7.	Testamentary Guardians 
o	The Act allows a Hindu father or mother to appoint a guardian for their minor child through a will. 
o	The testamentary guardian has powers subject to the provisions of the Act and the welfare of the minor.

Summary of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 (IBC)
Overview
*Act Name: Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 
*Coverage: Corporate Persons, Individuals, and Partnership Firms
Key Components
1.	Initiation of Insolvency Process
•	Initiators: Financial Creditors (Section 7), Operational Creditors (Section 8), and Corporate Applicants (Section 10)
•	Outcome: Appointment of Interim Resolution Professional and Public Announcement (Section 13)
2.	Moratorium
•	Provisions (Sections 13-14):
•	Halt on legal proceedings against the corporate debtor
•	Restriction on asset transfer or encumbrance by the corporate debtor
•	Exceptions for critical supply of goods/services and notified transactions
•	Duration: From insolvency commencement date until process completion, approval of resolution plan, or liquidation order (Section 15)
3.	Resolution Process Governance
•	Resolution Professional’s Role (Sections 16-18): Management of debtor’s business, asset valuation, and facilitation of resolution plan
•	Timeline (Section 12): 180 days for resolution, extendable
•	Oversight: By the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India (IBBI)
4.	Liquidation
•	Trigger: Failure of resolution process or direct order (Section 33)
•	Liquidator’s Role: Asset realization and distribution according to IBC hierarchy
5.	Distribution Hierarchy
•	Priority Order (Inferred, not directly provided): Secured Creditors, Operational Creditors, etc., guided by principles akin to Section 60 for insolvency resolution

THE INSOLVENCY AND BANKRUPTCY CODE, 2016
ACT NO. 31 OF 2016

[28th May, 2016.]

An Act to consolidate and amend the laws relating to reorganisation and insolvency resolution of corporate persons, partnership firms and individuals in a time bound manner for maximisation of value of assets of such persons, to promote entrepreneurship, availability of credit and balance the interests of all the stakeholders including alteration in the order of priority of payment of Government dues and to establish an Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India, and for matters connected therewith or incidental thereto.
BE it enacted by Parliament in the Sixty-seventh Year of the Republic of India as follows:---
meta.dc.legislation.history:
"Legislative History:

The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016

Short Title - The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016

Act Number / Year - Act No. 31 of 2016

India Code Act ID - 201631

Introduced In - Parliament Lok Sabha

Presidential Assent Date - May 28, 2016

Official Gazette Publication - May 28, 2016 (Extraordinary Gazette Part II, Section 1)

Enforcement Date - 5th August, 2016

Nodal Ministry - Ministry of Corporate Affairs

Precedent & Statutory Rationale

1. Consolidation of Fragmented Insolvency Frameworks:

o Prior to 2016, insolvency and debt recovery were governed by overlapping, disparate statutes (such as SICA, SARFAESI, and winding-up under Companies Act), resulting in parallel judicial proceedings, multi-year delays, and severe value erosion for creditors.

2. Shift to ""Creditor-in-Control"" Model & Time-Bound Resolution:

o Replaced the outdated debtor-in-possession regime with a creditor-driven resolution process (CIRP). The Code instituted a mandatory time-bound matrix (180 days, extendable up to 330 days including litigation) to resolve distressed assets or proceed to liquidation.

3. Establishment of Dedicated Ecosystem and Regulators:

o Created a specialized multi-pillar institutional architecture comprising the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India (IBBI) as the regulator, Insolvency Professionals (IPs), Information Utilities (IUs), and dedicated adjudicating authorities (NCLT for corporates/LLPs and DRT for individuals/partnerships).

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

• Formulation: Developed based on the Bankruptcy Law Reforms Committee (BLRC) report chaired by Dr. T. K. Viswanathan, and introduced by Finance Minister Arun Jaitley.

• Parliamentary Passage: Introduced in the Lok Sabha on December 21, 2015; referred to a Joint Parliamentary Committee (JPC), which submitted its report on April 28, 2016. Passed by the Lok Sabha on May 5, 2016, and subsequently passed by the Rajya Sabha on May 11, 2016.

• Presidential Assent: Received formal Presidential Assent on May 28, 2016, entering the statute book as Act No. 31 of 2016.

Source: India Code Official Repository (indiacode.nic.in) and Ministry of Corporate Affairs / Ministry of Finance Official Records

title: The Army and Air Force (Disposal of Private Property) Act, 1950

meta.dc.description.abstract:
summary of Army and Air Force (Disposal of Private Property) Act, 1950

Key Provisions 

1.	Decision Finality & Judicial Oversight:
•	Decisions on debts by the prescribed person are final, implying minimal court intervention in these specific determinations.
•	Court Involvement: Not directly outlined for the disposal process, suggesting the Act operates largely independently of court proceedings for its primary objectives.
2.	Representative Powers & Legal Implications:
•	Commanding officers/Committees act with powers similar to having taken out representation, which typically would involve court proceedings in civil contexts, but here is authorized by the Act.
•	Implication for Courts: The Act grants specific legal powers without necessitating court intervention, streamlining the process for armed forces personnel.
3.	Protection of Actions & Good Faith:
•	Payments and dispositions made in good faith are considered full discharge, protecting authorized persons from legal (court) challenges, barring fraud or negligence.
4.	Saving Provisions & Rights:
•	Court Recognition: While not seeking to derogate from other laws (as per principles like those in Section 60 of the provided context for another Act), the Act saves the rights of representatives, implying that in disputes, court resolution might be sought based on general law.

Precedent & Statutory Rationale

1. Regulating Disposal of Private Property of Military Personnel:

o To provide a uniform and clear statutory mechanism for the safe custody, inventory, and lawful disposal of private property belonging to persons subject to the Army Act, 1950 or the Air Force Act, 1950 who die, desert, are declared of unsound mind, or are officially reported missing while on active service.

o Grounded in administrative necessity to protect the financial interests of legal heirs and prevent unauthorized handling or loss of service members' personal belongings.

2. Committees of Adjustment and Creditor Claims:

o Empowers military authorities to establish specialized committees of adjustment to manage inventories, liquidate outstanding service debts, meet legitimate expenses, and disburse remaining assets to rightful claimants or legal heirs.

o Establishes formal safeguards to resolve claims transparently and protect against legal liability for actions taken in good faith.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

Formulation: Drafted by the Ministry of Defence as part of the post-independence legislative overhaul of military law following the enactment of the comprehensive Army Act and Air Force Act of 1950.

Parliamentary Passage: Passed by Parliament, receiving formal presidential assent on April 28, 1950.

Enforcement: Brought into force on July 22, 1950, via notification No. S.R.O. 123 published in the Gazette of India.

THE BANKERS’ BOOKS EVIDENCE ACT, 2026

ACT NO. 15 OF 2026

[13th August, 2026.]

An Act to provide for law relating to evidence with respect to bankers’ books and to align it

with contemporary digital banking practices and for matters connected therewith or

incidental thereto.

BE it enacted by Parliament in the Seventy-seventh Year of the Republic of India as follows:—

1. Short title and commencement.—(1) This Act may be called the Bankers’ Books Evidence

Act, 2026.

(2) It shall come into force on such date1

as the Central Government may, by notification in the

Official Gazette, appoint.

2. Definitions.—(1) In this Act, unless the context otherwise requires,––

(a) “bank” and “banker” mean—

(i) any company or corporation carrying on the business of banking;

(ii) any entity or class of entities operating in financial sector, to whose books the provisions

of this Act shall have been extended as hereinafter provided;

(iii) any post office savings bank or money order office;

(b) “bankers’ books” include ledgers, day-books, cash-books, account books and all other records

used in the ordinary course of business of the bank, whether kept in written or physical form or

stored in any form of data storage mechanisms such as electronic or digital form, or otherwise, either

onsite or at any offsite or virtual or cloud location, including a back-up or disaster recovery site, or

both;

(c) “certified copy”, in relation to any entry or information contained in the bankers’ book, shall

mean the following, namely:—

(i) where the bankers’ book is maintained in written or physical form, a copy of any entry or

information in such books together with a certificate referred to in sub-section (1) of section 3; and

(ii) where the bankers’ book is maintained in any other mode of data storage mechanisms,

such as, electronic or digital form or otherwise, a copy of any entry or information in such

bankers’ book, which is printed on paper, stored, recorded or copied in optical or magnetic media

or semi-conductor memory, or otherwise stored, recorded or copied in any electronic or digital

form, together with the certificate in accordance with the provisions of sub-section (2) of

section 3;

(d) “company” means any company as defined in clause (20) of section 2 of the Companies Act,

2013 (18 of 2013) and includes a foreign company within the meaning of clause (42) of the said

section;

(e) “corporation” means any body corporate established by or under any law for the time being

in force in India and includes the Reserve Bank of India, the State Bank of India or any corresponding

1. 1st day of October, 2026, vide Notifn. No. S.O. 5041 (E), dated 10th September, 2026, see Gazette of India, Extraordinary,

Part II, s. 3 (ii).

5

new bank constituted under the Banking Companies (Acquisition and Transfer of Undertakings) Act,

1970 (5 of 1970) and the Banking Companies (Acquisition and Transfer of Undertakings) Act, 1980

(40 of 1980);

(f) “legal proceeding” means—

(i) any proceeding or inquiry in which evidence is or may be taken;

(ii) an arbitration; and

(iii) any investigation or inquiry under the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023

(46 of 2023), or under any other law for the time being in force for the collection of evidence,

conducted by a police officer, or by any other person (not being a Magistrate) authorised in this

behalf by a Magistrate or by any law for the time being in force;

(g) “notification” means a notification published in the Gazette of India and the expression

“notify” with its grammatical variation and cognate expressions shall be construed accordingly; and

(h) “trial” means any hearing before the Court at which evidence is taken.

(2) Words and expressions used herein and not defined but defined in the Arbitration and

Conciliation Act, 1996 (26 of 1996), the Information Technology Act, 2000 (21 of 2000), the Bharatiya

Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (46 of 2023) and the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (47 of 2023),

shall have the same meanings as assigned to them in the said Acts.

3. Conditions for a certified copy.—(1) Every copy of any entry or information of the bankers’

books, maintained in written or physical form, as referred to in sub-clause (i) of clause (c) of

sub-section (1) of section 2, shall be accompanied by a certificate stating the following, namely:—

(a) that the said copy is a true and correct copy of such entry or information;

(b) that such entry or information is contained in one of the ordinary books of the bank and was

made in the usual and ordinary course of business of the bank;

(c) that such books are still in the custody of the bank, but where the book from which such copy

was prepared was destroyed, it was destroyed in the usual course of business of the bank after the

date on which the copy had been so prepared;

(d) that such copy itself ensures its accuracy, if that copy was obtained by mechanical or other

process; and

(e) such other conditions as may be notified by the Central Government,

in such form as specified in the First Schedule.

(2) Every copy of any entry or information of the bankers’ books, maintained in any mode of data

storage mechanisms, such as, electronic or digital form or otherwise, as referred to in sub-clause (ii) of

clause (c) of sub-section (1) of section 2, shall be accompanied by a certificate stating the following,

namely:––

(a) the particulars of the computer system or device involved in the production of the said copy

from bankers’ books as may be appropriate for the purpose of showing that the said copy was

produced by a computer system or device referred to in clauses (a) to (e) of sub-section (2) of

section 7; and

(b) specifying any of the matters to which the conditions mentioned in section 7 relate,

in such form as specified in the Second Schedule.

6

(3) Every certificate referred to in sub-sections (1) and (2) shall bear the date of its issue, be signed

or authenticated, either manually or by means of digital or electronic signature in accordance with the

provisions of the Information Technology Act, 2000 (21 of 2000), by the branch head or the office head

or any other officer of the bank duly authorised by the bank in this behalf, and shall state therein the

full name and official designation of the officer so signing or authenticating:

Provided that for the purposes of this section it shall be sufficient for a matter to be stated to the best

of the knowledge and belief of the person stating it in the certificates specified in the respective

Schedule.

4. Power to extend provisions of Act.—The Central Government may, if it considers necessary or

expedient so to do, from time to time, by notification, extend the application of the provisions of this

Act to the books of any entity or class of entities operating in the financial sector, subject to such

conditions, exceptions or modifications as may be specified in the notification, and the Central

Government may, in like manner, rescind, vary or modify any such notification.

5. Mode of proof of entries in bankers’ books.—Subject to the provisions of this Act, a certified

copy of any entry in a banker’s book shall in all legal proceedings be received as prima facie evidence

of the existence of such entry and shall be admitted as evidence of the matters, transactions and accounts

therein recorded in every case where, and to the same extent as, the original entry itself is now

admissible by law, but not further or otherwise.

6. Admissibility of electronic or digital records.—Notwithstanding anything contained in any

other law for the time being in force, the admissibility of an electronic or digital record of a banker’s

book in evidence, shall not be denied on the ground that it is an electronic or digital record and such

record shall, subject to the conditions specified in section 7, be admissible, valid and legally enforceable,

as other evidence.

7. Conditions for admissibility of records maintained in electronic or digital form.—(1) The

conditions to be satisfied, in relation to the information or record of banker’s book maintained in

electronic or digital form, for its admissibility, validity and enforceability as evidence, shall be

following, namely:—

(a) the copy of the record was produced by a computer system or communication device during

the period over which such computer system or communication device was used regularly to create,

store, or process information for the purposes of any activity regularly carried on over that period

by the person having lawful control over the use of the computer system or communication device;

(b) during the said period, information of the kind contained in such copy of the record or, of the

kind from which the information so contained is derived, was regularly fed into the computer system

or communication device in the ordinary course of the said activities;

(c) throughout the material part of the said period, the computer system or communication device

was operating properly, or, if not, then in respect of any period in which it was not operating properly

or was out of operation during that part of the period, was not such as to affect the said record or the

accuracy of its contents;

(d) the information contained in such copy of the record reproduces, or was derived from, such

information fed into the computer system or communication device in the ordinary course of the

said activities;

(e) the said copy is a true copy of such entry or information and was prepared from all the relevant

records, and it correctly represents, or is appropriately derived from, such records;

7

(f) the data entry or any other operation had been performed only by authorised persons after

taking adequate safeguards and no unauthorised alteration or change of the data is observed or

detected during the relevant time;

(g) adequate safeguards were taken to transfer the data relating to such entry or the information

accurately from the computer system or communication device to an identifiable removable media,

including but not limited to optical or magnetic media, semiconductor memory, discs or otherwise,

in any electronic or digital form, and all steps for safe storage and custody of such removable device

were taken;

(h) no tampering with the system or other event which may be essential for establishing the

integrity and accuracy of the system is observed or detected;

(i) the network, devices and the data contained therein were secure and equipped to meet the

challenge of cyber risks or threats; and

(j) such other conditions as may be notified by the Central Government.

(2) Where over any period, the function of creating, storing or processing entry or information for

the purposes of any activity regularly carried on over that period as mentioned in clause (a) of

sub-section (1) was regularly performed by means of one or more computer systems or communication

devices, whether––

(a) in standalone mode; or

(b) on a computer system; or

(c) on a computer network; or

(d) on a computer resource enabling information creation or providing information processing

and storage; or

(e) through an intermediary,

all such computer system or communication device used for that purpose during that period shall be

treated for the purposes of this section as constituting a single computer system or communication

device and the references in this Act to a computer system or communication device shall be construed

accordingly.

8. Case in which officer of bank not compellable to produce books.—(1) No officer of a bank

shall, in any legal proceeding to which the bank is not a party, be compelled to produce any banker’s

book, the contents of which may be proved under this Act, or to appear as a witness to prove the matters,

transactions and accounts recorded therein, unless by order of the Court made for special cause, to be

recorded in writing.

(2) For the purposes of sub-section (1), the expression “special cause” means the following,

namely:––

(a) where accuracy or genuineness of the entry or information in the bankers’ book is doubtful;

or

(b) where any event has occurred, which suggest that the regularity or ordinary nature of record

keeping in the bank is interrupted; or

(c) where the bank does not comply with any order made under section 9.

8

9. Inspection of books by order of Court.—(1) On an application by any party to a legal

proceeding, the Court may order that such party be at liberty to inspect and take copies of any entries

in a banker’s book for any of the purposes of such proceeding, or may order the bank to prepare and

produce, within such period as may be specified in such order, the certified copies of all such entries,

accompanied by a further certificate that no other entries are to be found in the books of the bank

relevant to the matters in issue in such proceeding, and such further certificate shall be dated and signed

or authenticated in the manner specified in sub-section (3) of section 3.

(2) An order under this section or section 8 may be made either with or without summoning the bank

and shall be served on the bank three clear days (exclusive of bank holidays) before the same is to be

complied with, unless the Court otherwise directs.

(3) The bank may, at any time before the expiry of the period provided for compliance of any order

in sub-section (2), either offer to produce their books at the trial or give notice of their intention to show

cause against such order and thereupon the same shall not be enforced without being heard before

making any further order.

10. Costs.—(1) The costs of any application to the Court under or for the purposes of this Act and

the costs of anything done or to be done under an order of the Court made under or for the purposes of

this Act shall be in the discretion of the Court, which may further order that such costs or any part

thereof be paid by the party to the bank, or by the bank to any party where such party had incurred

expenditure in consequence of any fault or improper delay on the part of the bank.

(2) Any order made under this section for the payment of costs to or by a bank, may be enforced as

if the bank were a party to the proceeding.

(3) Any order under this section awarding costs may, on an application to any Civil Court designated

in the order, shall be executed by such Court as if the order were a decree for money passed by itself.

(4) Nothing contained in sub-section (3) shall be construed to derogate from any power, which the

Court making the order may possess for the enforcement of its directions with respect to the payment

of costs.

11. Order of Court to be construed as order made by specified officer.—(1) Where the

provisions of section 8, 9 or 10 are applied for conduct of any investigation or inquiry referred to in

sub-clause (iii) of clause (f) of sub-section (1) of section 2, the order of Court referred to in the said

sections shall be construed as referring to an order made by an officer not below the rank of a

Superintendent of Police or such other officer as may be specified in this behalf by the appropriate

Government.

(2) In sub-section (1), the expression “appropriate Government” means the Government by which

the police officer or any other person conducting the investigation or inquiry is employed.

12. Power of Central Government to amend Schedules.—The Central Government may, by

notification, modify the certificates specified in the Schedules from time to time, as may be necessary,

to give effect to the provisions of this Act.

13. Protection of action taken in good faith.—No suit, prosecution or other legal proceeding shall

lie against any person for anything which is in good faith done or intended to be done under this Act.

14. Power to remove difficulties.—(1) If any difficulty arises in giving effect to the provisions of

this Act, the Central Government may, by order, published in the Official Gazette, make such provisions

not inconsistent with the provisions of this Act as may be necessary or expedient for removing the

difficulty:

9

Provided that no such order shall be made under this section after the expiry of two years from the

date of commencement of this Act.

(2) Every order made under this section shall be laid, as soon as may be after it is made, before each

House of Parliament.

15. Laying before Parliament.—Every notification issued under this Act shall be laid, as soon as

may be after it is issued, before each House of Parliament.

16. Repeal and savings.—(1) The Bankers’ Books Evidence Act, 1891 (18 of 1891) is hereby

repealed.

(2) Notwithstanding the repeal of the enactment referred to in sub-section (1), such repeal shall not

affect—

(a) the previous operation of the enactment so repealed and orders or anything duly done or

suffered thereunder; or

(b) any right, privilege, obligation or liability, acquired, accrued or incurred under the enactment

so repealed; or

(c) any investigation, inquiry, legal proceeding or remedy in respect of any such right, privilege,

obligation, liability, penalty, forfeiture or punishment; or

(d) the previous operation of any certificate in respect of any entry or information in a banker’s

book, or notification or order so issued, amended, repealed, superseded or rescinded or anything

duly done or suffered under the enactment so repealed; or

(e) any proceeding including that relating to an appeal, review or reference, instituted before, on,

or after the date of commencement of this Act under the repealed enactment and such proceeding

shall be continued under the said enactment as if this Act had not come into force and the said

enactment had not been repealed; or

(f) any reference to the repealed enactment in any other legislation, rule, order, or any other legal

instrument shall, in so far as it is not inconsistent with the provisions of this Act, be construed as a

reference to this Act or its corresponding provisions; or

(g) revive anything not in force or existing at the time of such repeal.

(3) Without prejudice to the provisions of sub-section (2), the provisions of section 6 of the General

Clauses Act, 1897 (10 of 1897) shall apply with regard to the effect of repeal.

10

THE FIRST SCHEDULE

[See section 3(1)]

CERTIFICATE

(To be filled by the Branch Head or Office Head or such other officer of the bank duly authorised

by the bank in this behalf)

I,_________________(Name), Son/daughter/spouse of____________residing/employed

at____________________________ (Branch/Office Address) do hereby solemnly affirm and sincerely

state and submit to the best of the knowledge and belief as follows:—

(a) that the copy of the entry or information is a true and correct copy of such entry or

information;

(b) that such entry or information is contained in one of the ordinary books of the bank and

was made in the usual and ordinary course of business of the bank;

(c) that such books are still in the custody of the bank, but where the book from which such

copy was prepared was destroyed, it was destroyed in the usual course of business of the bank after

the date on which the copy had been so prepared; and

(d) that such copy itself ensures its accuracy, if that copy was obtained by mechanical or other

process.

Date (DD/MM/YYYY): _____ (Full name and signature)

Place: ____________ Official Designation

11

THE SECOND SCHEDULE

[See section 3(2)]

CERTIFICATE

(To be filled by the Branch Head or Office Head or such other officer of the bank duly authorised

by the bank in this behalf)

I,_______________(Name), Son/daughter/spouse of_______________residing/employed at

__________________________(Branch/Office Address) do hereby solemnly affirm and sincerely state

and submit to the best of the knowledge and belief as follows:—

(a) the copy of the entry or information is produced from the computer system or communication

device (hereinafter referred to as “the system”) being described as

____________________________________[brief particulars of the system be provided (see

section 3(2)(a)];

(b) the said copy of the record was produced by the system during the period over which the said

system was regularly used to create, store, or process information for the purpose of any activities

regularly carried on over that period by the person having lawful control over its use;

(c) during the said period, information of the kind contained in such copy of the record or of the

kind from which the information so contained is derived was regularly fed into the system in the

ordinary course of the said activities;

(d) throughout the material part of the said period, the system was operating properly or, if not,

then in respect of any period in which it was not operating properly or was out of operation during

that part of the period, was not such as to affect the record or the accuracy of its contents;

(e) the information contained in such copy of the record reproduces or is derived from such

information fed into the system in the ordinary course of the said activities;

(f) the said copy is a true copy of such entry or information and is prepared from all the relevant

records, and correctly represents or appropriately derived from such record;

(g) data entry or any other operations had been performed only by authorised persons and no

unauthorised alteration or change of the data is observed or detected during the relevant time;

(h) adequate safeguards were taken to transfer the data relating to such entry or the information

accurately from the computer system or communication device to an identifiable removable media,

including but not limited to optical or magnetic media, semiconductor memory, discs or otherwise,

in any electronic or digital form, and all steps for safe storage and custody of such removable device

were taken;

(i) no tampering with the system or other event which may vouch for the integrity and accuracy

of the system, were observed or detected; and

(j) the network, devices, and the data contained therein are secure and equipped to meet the

challenge of cyber risks or threats.

Date (DD/MM/YYYY): _____ (Full name and signature)

Place: ____________ Official Designation

12

STATEMENT OF OBJECTS AND REASONS

The Bankers’ Books Evidence Act, 1891 was enacted to facilitate the use of certified copies of bank

records as evidence in legal proceedings without requiring production of the original records. The Act

was enacted at a time when banking records were predominantly maintained in physical form. With the

advancement of technology and growth of digital banking, bank records are increasingly created, stored

and maintained using contemporary technology. It has, therefore, become necessary to modernise and

strengthen the existing legal framework to meet the requirements of the present banking system.

2. Accordingly, it is proposed to repeal the Bankers’ Books Evidence Act, 1891 and introduce the

Bankers’ Books Evidence Bill, 2026, which, inter alia, provides for the following:––

(a) to expand the scope of the definition of “bankers’ books” to include all forms of records

maintained by banks, whether in physical, electronic, digital, virtual, cloud-based or in any other

form, thereby providing a comprehensive, technology-neutral and future-ready legal framework;

(b) to provide for standardised certificate formats and authentication by manual or digital or

electronic signature;

(c) to expressly recognise admissibility of electronic bank records and permit their production

in either physical or electronic form;

(d) to empower the Central Government to extend applicability of the proposed legislation to

any entity or class of entities operating in the financial sector subject to certain conditions; and

(e) to define the expression “special cause”, for which a Court may, by order in writing, compel

an officer of the bank to produce any bankers’ books or to appear as witness to prove matters,

transactions or accounts, in any legal proceeding where the bank is not a party.

3. The Bill seeks to achieve the above objectives.

NIRMALA SITHARAMAN.

NEW DELHI;

The 28th July, 2026.

title: The All-India Institutes of Medical Science Act, 1956

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of the All-India Institute of Medical Sciences Act, 1956
Key Provisions:
1.	Establishment of AIIMS 
o	The Act provides for the establishment of the All-India Institute of Medical Sciences (AIIMS), New Delhi as an institution of national importance. 
o	AIIMS is empowered to provide teaching, training, and research facilities in medical and related fields. 
2.	Incorporation of the Institute 
o	AIIMS is established as a body corporate having: 
	Perpetual succession. 
	A common seal. 
	Power to acquire, hold, and dispose of property. 
	Power to enter into contracts and undertake legal proceedings. 
3.	Objectives and Functions of AIIMS
The Institute is responsible for: 
o	Providing undergraduate and postgraduate medical education. 
o	Conducting research in respect of community health problems. 
o	Developing advanced healthcare facilities. 
o	Training of medical professionals. 
4.	Governing Bodies 
o	The Act provides for the constitution Governing body responsible for the administration of AIIMS, and standing committee. 
5.	Powers of the Institute
AIIMS has the power to: 
o	Prescribe courses and award degrees, diplomas, and other academic qualifications. 
o	Conduct examinations. 
o	Establish departments and research centres. 
o	Make regulations for its functioning. 
6.	Recognition as an Institution of National Importance 
o	AIIMS is declared an Institution of National Importance, giving it special status and autonomy for achieving excellence in medical education and research. 
 
7.	Financial Provisions 
o	The Act provides for grants and financial support from the Central Government. 
o	The Institute maintains accounts and prepares annual reports for submission to the Government.

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of the The Auroville Foundation Act, 1988
Purpose: Establish the Auroville Foundation to manage and develop Auroville in accordance with its founding ideals. *Scope: Covers the establishment, governance, financial provisions, and operational aspects of the Auroville Foundation.
Key Components
1. Establishment and Governance
•	Auroville Foundation: A body corporate with perpetual succession.
•	Governing Board:
•	Composition: Up to 7 members (nominated for their service, dedication, or contributions to Auroville) + 2 Central Government representatives.
•	Responsibilities: Promote Auroville's ideals, review policies, approve programmes, manage properties.
•	Residents' Assembly:
•	Composition: All registered Auroville residents (18+ years).
•	Functions: Advise the Governing Board, manage resident activities, formulate the master plan.
•	Auroville International Advisory Council:
•	Composition: Up to 5 members (nominated for devotion to human unity, peace, and progress).
•	Role: Advise the Governing Board.
2. Acquisition and Management of Undertakings
•	Vesting of Undertakings: Initially in the Central Government, potentially vested in the Auroville Foundation via notification.
•	Liabilities and Assets: Assumed by the Central Government (or the Foundation if vested).
3. Financial Provisions
•	Grants, Loans, and Assistance: The Central Government may provide financial support.
•	Fund Management: Deposits in approved banks or investments as decided by the Governing Board with Central Government approval.
4. Oversight and Reporting
•	Annual Budget and Accounts: To be prepared and audited by the Comptroller and Auditor General of India.
•	Reports to Central Government: Annual activities report and financial statements to be laid before Parliament.
