1. Gramin Rozgar Guarantee Card—(1) Household Registration—The adult member of every

household residing in any rural area and willing to undertake unskilled manual work, may submit the

names, ages and address of the household to the Gram Panchayat within whose jurisdiction they reside,

for the purpose of registration of the household and issuance of a Gramin Rozgar Guarantee Card.

(2) Special Gramin Rozgar Guarantee Card, where the job seeker is—

(a) a single woman; or

(b) a person with disability; or

(c) persons above sixty years of age; or

(d) a released bonded labourer; or

(e) a person belonging to a Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Group; or

(f) a transgender person.

(3) The Special Gramin Rozgar Guarantee Card of a distinct colour, shall ensure special protection

in the providing work, work evaluation, and worksite facilities, as applicable.

(4) It shall be the duty of the Gram Panchayat, after making such enquiry, as it deems fit, to issue

a Gramin Rozgar Guarantee Card within fifteen days from the date of receipt of such application,

containing therein a unique Gramin Rozgar Guarantee Card number with details of the registered adult

members of the household, their photos, Bank or Post office account number, insurance policy number

and the Aadhaar numbers, if any.

(5) The Gramin Rozgar Guarantee Card issued, shall be valid for three years, after which it may

be renewed after due verification.

(6) No Gramin Rozgar Guarantee Card shall be cancelled except on any of the following

grounds—

(a) where it is found to be a duplicate;

(b) where the entire household has permanently migrated to a place outside the jurisdiction of

the Gram Panchayat and no longer resides in the village; or

(c) where all adult members of the registered household are deceased.

(7) The State Government shall make arrangements for updating the following details in the

Gramin Rozgar Guarantee Card regularly while mentioning the key guarantees under the Act are clearly

listed as follows:—

(a) number of days for which work was demanded;

(b) number of days of work allocated;

(c) description of the work allocated along with the muster roll number;

(d) measurement details;

(e) unemployment allowance, if any, paid;

(f) date-wise amount of wages paid;

(g) delay compensation paid if any;

(h) asset provided, if any.

2. Demand for work—(1) Every adult member of a registered household whose name appears in

the Gramin Rozgar Guarantee Card, shall be entitled to apply for unskilled manual work under the

Scheme; and every such application shall be compulsorily registered, and a receipt issued with the date,

which shall be entered in the given digital platform.

(2) The State shall proactively verify the requirements of the Vulnerable Groups and provide them

with work.

(3) Application for work may be oral or written and made to the Ward member or to the Gram

Panchayat or to the Programme Officer or any person authorised by the State Government or through

digital platforms, or through any other means authorised by the State Government.

(4) Applications for work may be filed individually or for a group together.

(5) There shall be no limit on the number of days of employment for which a person may apply, or

on the number of days of employment actually provided to him subject to the aggregate guarantee of

the household.

(6) Normally, applications for work must be for at least six days of continuous work.

(7) Provision shall be made in the Scheme for advance application, that is, application which may

be submitted earlier than the date from which employment is sought.

(8) Provision shall be made in the Scheme for submission of multiple applications by the same

person provided that the corresponding periods for which employment is sought do not overlap.

3. Allocation of work—(1) The Gram Panchayat and Programme Officer shall ensure that every

applicant shall be provided unskilled manual work in accordance with the provisions of the Scheme

within fifteen days of receipt of an application or the date from which he seeks work in case of advance

application, whichever is later.

(2) Priority shall be given to women in such a way that at least one-third of the beneficiaries shall

be women who have registered and requested for work. Efforts to increase participation of single

women and the person with disabilities shall be made.

(3) Applicants who are provided with work shall be so intimated in writing, by means of a letter

sent to him at the address given in the Gramin Rozgar Guarantee Card or through any other effective

mode of communication or by a public notice displayed at the office of the Panchayats at district,

intermediate or village level.

(4) A list of persons who are provided with the work shall be displayed on the notice board of the

Gram Panchayat and at the office of the Programme Officer and at such other place as the Programme

Officer may deem necessary and the list shall be open for inspection by the State Government and any

interested person.

(5) As far as possible, the employment shall be provided within a radius of five kilometers of the

village where the applicant resides at the time of applying.

(6) A new work under the Scheme can be commenced if at least ten labourers become available for

work, provided that this condition shall not be applicable for new works, as determined by the State

Government, in hilly areas and in respect of afforestation works.

(7) In case the employment is provided outside the radius specified in sub-paragraph (5) of

paragraph 3, it shall be provided within the Block, and the labourers shall be paid ten per cent. of the

(8) A period of employment shall be for at least six days continuously, with not more than six days

4. Worksite management—(1) For the purpose of transparency at the worksite, the following shall

(d) a Citizens' Information Board shall be put up at every worksite and updated regularly in the

(e) the vigilance and Monitoring Committee set up according to the instructions of the Central

in the format specified by the Central Government and submitted to the Gram Sabha during the

Social Audit.

(2) The facilities of safe drinking water, shade for children and periods of rest, first aid box with

adequate material for emergency treatment for minor injuries and other health hazards connected with

the work being performed shall be provided at the worksite.

(3) In case the number of children below the age of five years accompanying the women working

at any site is five or more, provisions shall be made to depute one of such women workers to look after

such children. The person so deputed shall be paid wage rate.

5. Welfare—(1) If any personal injury is caused to any person employed under the Scheme by any

accident arising out of and in the course of his employment, he shall be entitled to such medical

treatment as required, free of cost.

(2) Where hospitalisation of the injured worker is necessary, the State Government shall arrange

for such hospitalisation including accommodation, treatment, medicines and payment of daily

allowance which is not less than half of the wage rate.

(3) If a person employed under the Scheme meets with death or becomes permanently disabled by

accident arising out of and in the course of employment, he or his legal heirs, as the case may be, shall

be paid by the implementing agency an ex gratia as per entitlement under the Pradhan Mantri Suraksha

Bima Yojana or as may be notified by the Central Government.

(4) If any personal injury is caused by accident to a child accompanying a person who is employed

under the Scheme, such person shall be entitled to medical treatment free of cost; and in case of death

or disablement of the child due to the said accident, ex gratia shall be paid to the legal guardians as

determined by the State Government.

6. Wage payment—(1) In case the payment of wages is not made within fifteen days from the date

of closure of the muster roll, the wage seekers shall be entitled to receive payment of compensation for

IndiaCode

33

the delay, at the rate of 0.05% of the unpaid wages per day of delay beyond the sixteenth day of closure

of muster roll.

(2) Any delay in payment of compensation beyond a period of fifteen days from the date it becomes

payable, shall be considered in the same manner as the delay in payment of wages.

(3) For the purpose of ensuring accountability in payment of wages and to calculate culpability of

various functionaries or agencies, the States shall divide the processes leading to determination and

payment of wages into various stages such as,—

(a) measurement of work;

(b) computerising the muster rolls;

(c) computerising the measurements;

(d) generation of wage lists; and

(e) uploading Fund Transfer Orders (FTOs), and specify stage-wise maximum time limits along

with the functionary or agency which is responsible for discharging the specific function.

(4) The computer system shall have a provision to automatically calculate the compensation

payable based on the date of closure of the muster roll and the date of deposit of wages in the

accounts of the wage seekers.

(5) The State Government shall pay the compensation upfront after due verification within the time

limits as specified above and recover the compensation amount from the functionaries or agencies

who are responsible for the delay in payment.

(6) It shall be the duty of the District Programme Coordinator or Programme Officer to ensure that

the system is operationalise.

(7) The number of days of delay, the compensation payable and actually paid shall be reflected in

the Management Information System.

(8) Effective implementation of sub-paragraph (1) shall be considered necessary for the purposes

of section 29 of the Act.

7. The payment of wages shall, unless so exempted by the Central Government, be made through

the individual savings accounts of the workers in the relevant Banks or Post Offices.

8. In case of employment provided under the Scheme, there shall be no discrimination solely on

the ground of gender and the provisions of the Equal Remuneration Act, 1976 (25 of 1976), shall be

complied with.

9. Record maintenance and grievance redressal system—The Gram Panchayat shall prepare and

maintain or cause to be prepared and maintained such registers, vouchers and other documents in such

form and in such manner as may be specified in the Scheme containing particulars of Gramin Rozgar

Guarantee Cards and pass books issued, name, age and address of the head of the household and the

adult members of the households registered with the Gram Panchayat.

10. (1) Notwithstanding anything contained in this Schedule, in the event of any national calamity

such as flood, cyclone, tsunami and earthquake resulting in mass dislocation of rural population, the

adult members of rural households of areas so affected may—

(a) seek for registration and get Gramin Rozgar Guarantee Card issued by the Gram Panchayat

or Programme Officer of the area of temporary relocation;

IndiaCode

34

(b) submit written or oral applications for work to the Programme Officer or the Gram

Panchayat of the area of temporary relocation; and

(c) apply for re-registration and re-issuance of Gramin Rozgar Guarantee Card in the event of

any loss or destruction.

(2) The details of such Gramin Rozgar Guarantee Cards shall be intimated to the District

Programme Coordinator.

(3) In the event of restoration of normalcy, the Gramin Rozgar Guarantee Card so issued shall be

re-endorsed at original place of habitation and clubbed with the original Gramin Rozgar Guarantee Card

on being retrieved.

(4) The number of days of employment provided shall be counted while computing 125 days of

guaranteed employment per household.

11. Every worker shall have an opportunity of being heard and register any grievance either orally

or in writing, at all implementation levels for disposal as per the provisions of the Grievance Redressal

Mechanism under the Scheme.

IndiaCode

35

STATEMENT OF OBJECTS AND REASONS

Viksit Bharat—Guarantee for Rozgar and Ajeevika Mission (Gramin): VB—G RAM G (विकवित

भारत—जी राम जी) Bill, 2025 is proposed to be introduced with the following background, object and

reasons.

2. Post-independence rural development policies in India focused on addressing poverty, improving

agricultural productivity, absorbing surplus and under-employed rural labour through various wage

employment schemes, strengthening rural infrastructure, etc. Over the decades, the approaches have

evolved, ranging from community development programs to employment generation schemes to uplift

rural communities. The nature of rural employment generation schemes has undergone continuous

change based on the evolving socio-economic scenario.

3. India’s rural employment schemes have evolved through several phases, starting with early

programs, like, the Rural Manpower Programme (1960s) and Crash Scheme for Rural Employment

(1971). In the 1980s, the National Rural Employment Programme and Rural Landless Employment

Guarantee Programme were launched, later merged into Jawahar Rozgar Yojana in 1993 which

consolidated into the Sampoorna Grameen Rozgar Yojana in 1999, to streamline structured rural

employment efforts. The Employment Assurance Scheme was introduced in 1993 to provide work

during agricultural lean seasons. The Food for Work Programme, initiated in 1977-78 and later

expanded as the National Food for Work Programme in 2004, provided food grains as wages for manual

labour on public works, targeting most backward districts to improve both food security and

employment. Notably, the Maharashtra Employment Guarantee Act, 1977 provided right to work to

adult members of every rural household who volunteered to do unskilled manual work, thus bringing

in the concept of a statutory right.

4. While the earlier initiatives offered some relief to rural households, their scale and resources

remained limited in relation to the broader challenges of unemployment and poverty in rural India. It

was in this background that, in 2005, the Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act,

2005, (Mahatma Gandhi NREGA) was enacted to provide a statutory framework for employment

generation in rural areas.

5. Over the past twenty years, Mahatma Gandhi NREGA has provided a guaranteed wageemployment to rural households ensuring wage income; however, further strengthening has become

necessary in view of the significant socio-economic transformation witnessed in the rural landscape

driven by widespread coverage of the social security interventions and saturation-oriented

implementation of major Government schemes. Similarly, rural connectivity, rural housing,

electrification, financial inclusion and digital access have deepened, the workforce has diversified, and

aspirations have shifted towards better incomes, growth-oriented infrastructure, sustainable livelihoods

and greater climate resilience.

6. To cater to the changing aspirations, stronger convergence is required to establish an integrated,

Whole-of-Government rural development framework covering several complementary Government

schemes. It is essential that rural infrastructure creation must transition from fragmented provisioning

to a coherent and future-oriented approach and it is also essential that resources are distributed in a fair

manner to reduce disparities and promote inclusive growth across all rural areas of the country based

on objective parameters.

7. As national development advances, rural development programs require periodical revision to

remain aligned with emerging needs and further aspirations. In the vastly changed circumstances of

today, a transformational approach to rural development is essential to achieve the objectives of Viksit

IndiaCode

36

Bharat @2047. The expanding scale of development interventions is expected to create additional

employment opportunities for rural households. It is imperative to engage the rural workforce more

effectively to support the vision of Viksit Bharat, while empowering them through enhanced livelihood

gurarantee. Therefore, the Government has resolved to enhance the wage-employment guarantee for

rural households from one hundred days to one hundred and twenty-five days per financial year for

anchoring rural asset creation through the enactment of an appropriate Act.

8. The proposed Bill is titled the “Viksit Bharat—Guarantee for Rozgar and Ajeevika Mission

(Gramin): VB—G RAM G (विकवित भारत—जी राम जी) Bill, 2025” to establish a rural development

framework aligned with the national vision of Viksit Bharat @2047, by providing a statutory guarantee

of one hundred and twenty-five days of wage employment in every financial year to every rural

household whose adult members volunteer to undertake unskilled manual work; to promote

empowerment, growth, convergence and saturation for a prosperous and resilient rural Bharat.

9. The salient features of the proposed Bill are as follows:—

(a) The primary objective of the Bill is to align the rural development framework with the

national vision of Viksit Bharat @2047 by providing an enhanced statutory wage-employment

guarantee of one hundred and twenty-five days in each financial year to such rural households whose

adult members volunteer to undertake unskilled manual work, thereby enabling them to participate

more effectively in the expanded livelihood security framework.

(b) In view of the enhanced wage-employment guarantee for the rural workforce, it is also crucial

to facilitate the availability of farm labour, especially during the peak agricultural season. In this

context, the Bill shall have a provision to empower the States to notify in advance, certain duration,

covering peak sowing and harvesting seasons, during which execution of works under this Bill will

not be undertaken.

(c) The focus shall be on empowerment, growth, convergence and saturation with Gram

Panchayats as the primary institutions for participatory planning and execution, backed by

appropriate professional and technical capacity.

(d) The convergence, saturation-driven planning and whole of Government delivery shall be

institutionalised through integration of Viksit Gram Panchayat Plans with the PM Gati Shakti to

address the varying needs of Gram Panchayats, and powered by geospatial systems, digital public

infrastructure, District and State planning mechanisms, with such plans aggregated at the Block,

District, State and consolidated into Viksit Bharat National Rural Infrastructure Stack.

(e) Every State Government shall prepare a Scheme for giving effect to the guarantee proposed

under this Bill, within a period of six months from the date of the commencement of the Act and that

shall be implemented as a Centrally Sponsored Scheme.

(f) The Central Government shall make normative allocation to each State, to be estimated based

on objective parameters, as prescribed in the rules. Further, expenditure in excess of the approved

normative allocation shall be the responsibility of the State Governments.

(g) Special relaxations shall be permissible during natural calamities or extraordinary

circumstances as decided by the Central Government, enabling temporary modifications to the

provisions for timely response and relief.

(h) The wage rates for unskilled manual work shall be notified by the Central Government for

the purpose of this legislation. Until such time as separate rates are notified, the wage rates notified

under the Mahatma Gandhi NREGA shall be deemed to be the applicable rates.

IndiaCode

37

(i) If an eligible applicant is not provided work as per the provisions of this Bill within the

prescribed time limit, it will be obligatory on the part of the State Government to pay unemployment

allowance at the prescribed rate.

(j) The Central Gramin Rozgar Guarantee Council and the State Gramin Rozgar Guarantee

Councils shall be constituted for review, monitoring and effective implementation of the provisions

of the legislation in their respective areas. Steering committees at Central and State Level shall be

constituted to recommend on matters concerning normative allocations, convergence and other such

matters.

(k) Provision for transparency and accountability shall be ensured through Biometric

authentication, spatial technology-enabled planning, mobile and dashboard-based monitoring, and

weekly public disclosure systems. The social audit mechanism shall be strengthened.

(l) Provisions for Minimum features of the Scheme to be made under the Bill, have been laid

down in the Bill.

10. The Bill seeks to achieve the above objectives.

SHIVRAJ SINGH CHOUHAN.

NEW DELHI;

The 13th December, 2025. IndiaCode

 Presidential Assent date - December 20, 2025

Precedent & Historical Rationale

●	Overhaul and Repeal of MGNREGA: Repeals and replaces the two-decade-old Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act (MGNREGA), 2005, reforming the statutory employment guarantee framework to align with the national vision of Viksit Bharat @2047.
●	Enhanced Employment & Normative Asset Creation: Raises the annual statutory wage employment guarantee from 100 days to 125 days per rural household. It introduces a 60-day agricultural pause during peak farming seasons, establishes state-wise normative financial allocations (60:40 Centre-State ratio; 90:10 for Himalayan/NE states), and aggregates works under the Viksit Bharat National Rural Infrastructure Stack.
 
Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

●	Formulation: Introduced by the Ministry of Rural Development to transform rural wage employment from a standalone social welfare program into an outcome-oriented, asset-building framework integrated with technology (AI planning, biometric verification, and geospatial tracking).
●	Parliamentary Passage: Introduced, debated, and passed by both the Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha during the Winter Session of Parliament in December 2025.
●	Presidential Assent: Received the assent of the President of India on December 20, 2025.
●	Enforcement: Enforced on December 20, 2025.

title: The India International Arbitration Centre Act, 2019

meta.dc.description.abstract:
The India International Arbitration Centre Act, 2019
Overview
•	Act Name: India International Arbitration Centre Act, 2019
•	Enactment & Commencement: Enacted on 26th July 2019, deemed effective from 2nd March 2019
•	Purpose: Establish the India International Arbitration Centre (IAIC), transfer undertakings from the International Centre for Alternative Dispute Resolution (ICADR), and declare IAIC an institution of national importance.
Key Provisions
1.	Establishment & Structure
•	IAIC: Established as a body corporate with its head office in New Delhi.
•	Branches: Potential for branches in India and abroad.
2.	Governance
•	Chairperson: Appointed by the Central Government in consultation with the Chief Justice of India.
•	Members:
•	2 Eminent persons in institutional arbitration.
•	1 Representative from a recognized commerce and industry body.
•	Ex Officio:
•	Secretary, Department of Legal Affairs.
•	Financial Adviser, Ministry of Finance.
•	Chief Executive Officer (IAIC).
3.	Tenure and Eligibility
•	Term: 3 years for both Chairperson and Members, with potential for re-appointment.
•	Age Limit: 70 years for the Chairperson, 67 years for Members.
4.	Remuneration and Benefits
•	Salaries, Allowances, and Traveling Allowances: As prescribed by the Central Government for respective positions.
5.	Functions and Powers
•	Primary Objectives: Promote arbitration, manage transferred undertakings, and ensure operational standards.
•	Detailed Functions: (Not fully elaborated in the provided context, refers to promoting arbitration, managing undertakings, and other objectives as per the Act’s unreferenced sections).
6.	Acquisition and Transfer
•	Transfer of Undertakings: From ICADR to the Central Government, then to IAIC.
•	Management of Transfer: Oversight and duties regarding the transfer process.
7.	Regulatory and Protective Measures
•	Rule Making Power: Granted to IAIC.
•	Protection for Actions Taken in Good Faith.
8.	Dissolution and Savings
•	Repeal of Previous Ordinance: New Delhi International Arbitration Centre Ordinance, 2019.
•	Savings Clause: For actions taken under the repealed ordinance.
Limitations and Recommendations
•	Incomplete Context: Detailed functions (e.g., Section 15) and some administrative aspects are not covered.
•	Recommendation: Consult the full Act for comprehensive understanding, especially for Sections not provided in the context.

THE NEW DELHI INTERNATIONAL ARBITRATION CENTRE ACT, 2019
ACT NO. 17 OF 2019

[26th July, 2019.]

An Act to provide for the establishment and incorporation of the 1[India International Arbitration Centre] for the purpose of creating an independent and autonomous regime for institutionalised arbitration and for acquisition and transfer of the undertakings of the International Centre for Alternative Dispute Resolution and to vest such undertakings in the 1[India International Arbitration Centre] for the better management of arbitration so as to make it a hub for institutional arbitration and to declare the 1[India International Arbitration Centre] to be an institution of national importance and for matters connected therewith or incidental thereto.
WHEREAS dispute resolution process has a huge impact on the Indian economy and global perception on doing business in our country and it has become necessary to inspire confidence and credibility among the litigants of commercial disputes;
AND WHEREAS rapidly changing economic activity demands expeditious settlement of disputes and creation and establishment of institutional arbitration;
AND WHEREAS the International Centre for Alternative Dispute Resolution was set up in the year 1995, under the aegis of the Central Government and registered under the Societies Registration Act, 1860 (21 of 1860), with the objective of promoting alternative dispute resolution mechanism and providing facilities for the same;
AND WHEREAS the International Centre for Alternative Dispute Resolution has received land and substantial funding by way of grants and other benefits from the Central Government for constructing infrastructure and making other facilities;
AND WHEREAS the International Centre for Alternative Dispute Resolution has not been able to actively engage and embrace developments in the arbitration ecosystem and to create a reputation par excellence keeping pace with the dynamic nature of arbitration over more than two decades;
AND WHEREAS studies conducted by the High Level Committee appointed by the Central Government indicate that the International Centre for Alternative Dispute Resolution has failed to address the growing needs of the institutional arbitration and also to bear optimum caseload and to become better choice to the parties for arbitration;
AND WHEREAS it has become expedient to take over the undertakings of the International Centre for Alternative Dispute Resolution including its regional offices without interfering with its activities and without adversely affecting its character as a Society but to utilise its existing infrastructure and other facilities which have been set up by using the public funds provided by the Government and to incorporate a robust institution for domestic and international arbitration to be known as the 2[India International Arbitration Centre];
AND WHEREAS it is considered necessary to declare the 2[India International Arbitration Centred] as an institution of national importance for its overall development as a major arbitration hub by promoting quick and efficient dispute resolution mechanism.
BE it enacted by Parliament in the Seventieth Year of the Republic of India as follows:--

Precedent & Statutory Rationale

1. Promoting Institutionalized Arbitration and Global Hub Status:

o To establish an independent and autonomous regime for institutionalized arbitration, positioning India as a premier global hub for commercial dispute resolution and minimizing judicial intervention.

o Grounded in the necessity to provide transparent, cost-effective, and timely arbitration, conciliation, and mediation services at both domestic and international levels.

2. Acquisition of Undertakings and National Importance:

o Provides for the acquisition and better management of the undertakings of the International Centre for Alternative Dispute Resolution (ICADR).

o Statutorily declares the Centre as an institution of national importance to bolster confidence in Indian legal and arbitration mechanisms.

title: The National Institutes of Design Act, 2014

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of the National Institute of Design Act, 2014 
Objectives of the Act
•	To declare specified National Institutes of Design as Institutions of National Importance. 
•	To provide for their incorporation, administration, and governance. 
•	To promote high-quality education, research, and innovation in design and allied disciplines. 
•	To strengthen India's design capabilities in support of industry, commerce, public services, and society. 
Key Provisions
•	Institutions of National Importance: The Act declares the National Institute of Design, Ahmedabad, and the National Institutes of Design at Andhra Pradesh, Haryana, and Madhya Pradesh as Institutions of National Importance. 
•	Incorporation of Institutes: Each Institute is constituted as a body corporate with perpetual succession and a common seal, with the power to acquire, hold, and dispose of property, enter into contracts, and sue or be sued. 
•	Governance Structure: The Act provides for a Board of Governors, a Senate, and other authorities responsible for the academic, administrative, and financial management of the Institutes. 
•	Academic Functions: The Institutes are empowered to provide instruction, conduct research, offer consultancy, collaborate with national and international institutions, and award degrees, diplomas, certificates, and other academic distinctions. 
•	Faculty and Administration: The Act contains provisions relating to the appointment, service conditions, and responsibilities of the Director, faculty members, officers, and other employees. 
•	Finance and Accountability: It provides for grants from the Central Government, maintenance of funds, preparation of budgets, audit of accounts, and submission of annual reports to ensure transparency and accountability. 
•	Statutes, Ordinances, and Regulations: The Institutes are empowered to frame statutes, ordinances, and regulations, subject to the provisions of the Act, for carrying out their academic and administrative functions.

The National Institutes of Design Act, 2014

Short Title The National Institutes of Design Act, 2014

Precedent & Statutory Rationale

1. Limitations of Society and Non-Degree Status:

o Prior to 2014, the National Institute of Design operated as a registered society. While recognized globally for excellence, it faced severe structural limitations regarding statutory autonomy and the legal authority to award formal university degrees (historically granting professional diplomas instead), restricting its integration into standard higher education frameworks.

2. Institutionalizing Design Excellence for Industrial Competitiveness:

o Grounded in national manufacturing and innovation strategies, the legislation was enacted to elevate NID into an institution of national importance, providing a robust legal framework to promote advanced education, multi-disciplinary research, and training in industrial, communication, textile, and IT-integrated design disciplines.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

• Formulation: Developed and piloted by the Ministry of Commerce and Industry to provide statutory backing and formal academic powers to premier design institutions.

• Parliamentary Passage: Tabled, scrutinized, and passed by both Houses of Parliament during the mid-2014 parliamentary session.

• Presidential Assent: Received formal Presidential Assent from President Pranab Mukherjee on July 17, 2014, entering the statute book as Act No. 18 of 2014.

• Enforcement: Enforced on September 16, 2014.

The Competition Act, 2002

Short Title The Competition Act, 2002

Act Number / Year 12 of 2003

Presidential Assent Date January 13, 2003

Precedent & Historical Context

1. Inadequacy of the MRTP Act, 1969:

o Post-1991 economic reforms (LPG policy), the command-and-control framework under the MRTP Act, 1969 proved inadequate to foster fair market competition and regulate cross-border corporate combinations.

2. The Raghavan Committee Report (2000):

o The High-Level Committee on Competition Policy and Law (headed by S.V.S. Raghavan) submitted its landmark report in May 2000 recommending the complete repeal of the MRTP Act and the establishment of a modern, proactive competition regulatory framework.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Phased Implementation

• August 6, 2001: Introduced in the Lok Sabha as The Competition Bill, 2001.

title: The Life Insurance Corporation (Modification of Settlements) Act, 1976

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of the Life Insurance Corporation (Modification of Settlements) Act, 1976
Objective
The Life Insurance Corporation (Modification of Settlements) Act, 1976 was enacted to modify certain settlements reached between the Life Insurance Corporation of India (LIC) and its workmen, particularly regarding the payment of annual cash bonus. The Act was intended to alter the terms of the settlements in the public interest and to ensure uniform implementation of the Government's policy relating to employee benefits. 
Key Provisions
•	Modification of Settlements: Overrides specified provisions of the settlements entered into between LIC and its workmen under the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947. 
•	Withdrawal of Annual Cash Bonus: Declares that the provisions in the settlements providing for payment of an annual cash bonus at the rate of 15% of annual salary to Class III and Class IV employees shall have no force or effect from 1 April 1975. 
•	Overriding Effect: Gives the Act overriding effect over anything inconsistent contained in the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 or the relevant settlements. 
•	Definitions: Defines key terms such as "Corporation", "salary", and "settlements" for the purposes of implementing the Act. 
•	Retrospective Operation: Gives retrospective effect to the modification by deeming the bonus provisions ineffective from 1 April 1975, even though the Act came into force on 29 May 1976.

title: The Human Immunodeficiency Virus and Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndrome (Prevention and Control) Act, 2017

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of the Human Immunodeficiency Virus and Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndrome (Prevention and Control) Act, 2017
Passed by the Parliament of India, The Human Immunodeficiency Virus and Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndrome (Prevention and Control) Act, 2017 came into force to safeguard the legal and human rights of persons infected and affected by HIV and AIDS. The legislation provides a statutory framework to prevent social stigma, discrimination, and breaches of confidentiality. 
1. Objectives of the Act
The primary objectives of the legislation include:
•	Prevention and Control: To curb and manage the spread of HIV and AIDS across the country. 
•	Combating Stigma: To address and eliminate widespread social stigma and discrimination directed against Persons Living with HIV (PLHIV) and those closely affected by them. 
•	Protecting Rights: To legally secure and reinforce fundamental human rights, such as the right to healthcare, employment, education, and property. 
•	Ensuring Accountability: To establish structured mechanisms for grievance redressal and penalize acts of discrimination or privacy breaches. 
2. Key Provisions
A. Prohibition of Discrimination
The Act strictly prohibits unfair treatment or discrimination against "protected persons" (defined as any HIV-positive person or anyone who resides/has resided with an HIV-positive person) across multiple domains: 
•	Employment: Forbids denial or termination of employment, or unfair bias in occupation. 
•	Healthcare & Education: Prohibits denying entry, treatment, or educational services, or segregating students/patients. 
•	Housing and Property: Protects the right to rent, purchase, or reside in property without obstruction. 
•	Public/Private Office: Ensures they can stand for public or private offices. 
•	Insurance: Prevents unfair denial or differential pricing of life/health insurance policies without actuarial justification.
B. Informed Consent and Testing
•	No Forced Testing: Compulsory HIV testing cannot be mandated as a pre-requisite for employment, securing healthcare, or accessing other services, except in specific scenarios mandated by court orders. 
•	Informed Consent: Prior, voluntary, and informed consent is mandatory before conducting an HIV test, initiating medical treatment, or entering a person into medical research. 
C. Right to Confidentiality
•	Privacy Maintenance: The HIV status of an individual is strictly confidential. 
•	Exceptions: Disclosure is permissible only with the explicit written consent of the individual, or when mandated by a competent court order in the interest of justice. Healthcare providers are bound to maintain privacy regarding a patient's status. 
D. Healthcare and Treatment Rights
•	Access to Treatment: The Central and State Governments are mandated to take measures to provide, as far as possible, diagnostic facilities, Anti-Retroviral Therapy (ART), and Opportunistic Infection Management to PLHIV. 
•	Guardianship of Minors: Special provisions protect the property and welfare rights of children affected by HIV/AIDS, allowing them or their representatives to approach Child Welfare Committees for safeguard support. 
E. Prevention of Hate Speech
•	The Act prohibits any individual from publishing, broadcasting, or propagating feelings of hatred, discrimination, or physical violence against protected persons through spoken words, written material, signs, or visible representations. 
F. Grievance Redressal and Compliance Mechanisms
•	Complaints Officer: Every establishment (corporate body, cooperative society, or institution meeting statutory criteria) must designate a Complaints Officer to handle internal grievances regarding violations of the Act. 
•	Ombudsman: State Governments are required to appoint an Ombudsman to hear and decide legal appeals and complaints against establishments that fail to comply with the legislation.
3. Penalties for Non-Compliance
To enforce strict compliance, the Act prescribes penalties for violations:
•	Breach of Confidentiality or Discrimination: Disclosing an individual's HIV status without authorization or violating provisions of the Act can attract imprisonment ranging from 3 months up to 2 years, and/or a fine of up to 1 Lakh Rupees. 
•	Spreading Hatred: Engaging in acts promoting hatred or physical violence against protected persons is similarly punishable under the legal penalties framework.

title: The Lushai Hills District (Change of Name) Act, 1954

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of the Lushai Hills District (Change of Name) Act, 1954

The Lushai Hills District (Change of Name) Act, 1954 (Act No. 18 of 1954) was enacted to change the name of the Lushai Hills District in the State of Assam to the Mizo District. The Act reflected the evolving identity of the inhabitants of the region and aligned the district's official name with the commonly accepted designation of its people.

Objectives
•	To change the official name of the Lushai Hills District to the Mizo District. 
•	To provide legal recognition to the new name in all laws, official records, and administrative documents. 
•	To ensure continuity in the administration and legal status of the district despite the change in name. 

Key Provisions
•	Officially renamed the Lushai Hills District as the Mizo District. 
•	Provided that references to the "Lushai Hills District" in any existing law, notification, order, rule, regulation, agreement, or official document would be construed as references to the Mizo District. 
•	Ensured that the change of name did not affect the validity of existing rights, liabilities, legal proceedings, or administrative actions. 
•	Included consequential provisions to facilitate the implementation of the new name in government records and legal instruments.

meta.dc.legislation.history:
Legislative History:

The Lushai Hills District (Change of Name) Act, 1954

Act Title The Lushai Hills District (Change of Name) Act, 1954

Act Number Act No. 18 of 1954

Act ID (India Code) 195418

Presidential Assent date April 29, 1954

Enforcement Date September 1, 1954

Nodal Ministry Ministry of Home Affairs

Precedent & Historical Rationale

1. Recognition of Tribal Identity & Demand for Rename: Under colonial rule, the hill district was officially named the "Lushai Hills District" after the Lusei tribe. However, the region was inhabited by multiple sub-tribes who collectively identified as Mizos. Following Indian independence, political representatives and local tribal leadership strongly demanded that the exonym "Lushai" be replaced with the endonym "Mizo" to reflect their unified identity.

2. Constitutional Amendment of the Sixth Schedule: The district was an autonomous district in the tribal areas of Assam under Part A of the table in paragraph 20 of the Sixth Schedule to the Constitution of India. To formally change the name in legal and constitutional usage, an Act of Parliament was required to amend the Sixth Schedule.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

● Formulation: Introduced by the Central Government (Ministry of Home Affairs, under Minister Dr. Kailas Nath Katju) in January 1954 to rename the autonomous district from Lushai Hills District to Mizo District.

● Parliamentary passage: Debated and passed by both Houses of Parliament (First Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha) in early 1954.

● Presidential Assent: Received Presidential Assent on April 29, 1954.

● Enforcement: Brought into force on September 1, 1954, via Gazette Notification S.R.O. 2832(E). (Note: The Mizo District remained an autonomous district within undivided Assam until it was constituted into the Union Territory of Mizoram in 1972, and eventually became the full-fledged State of Mizoram in 1987).

● Source: Official Record of Parliament, India Code, and Ministry of Home Affairs

title: The Industrial Reconstruction Bank (Transfer of Undertakings and Repeal) Act, 1997

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of the Industrial Reconstruction Bank (Transfer of Undertakings and Repeal) Act, 1997

Key Provisions

1.	Commencement & Definitions

•	Effective Date: Deemed effective from 24th January, 1997
•	Key Entities:
•	Appointed Day: Date of transfer notified by the Central Government.
•	Company: Industrial Investment Bank of India Limited (under the Companies Act, 1956).
•	Reconstruction Bank: Industrial Reconstruction Bank of India (established under the Industrial Reconstruction Bank of India Act, 1984).

2.	Transfer & Vesting of Undertakings

•	Vesting: All undertakings of the Reconstruction Bank transfer to the Company on the Appointed Day.
•	Scope of Transfer:
•	Assets & Rights: All properties, assets, rights, and privileges.
•	Liabilities & Obligations: All debts, liabilities, and contractual obligations.
•	Contracts & Proceedings: Automatically transferred to the Company with full force and effect.
3.	Operational & Financial Implications

•	Employees: Transfer with the same terms for up to 6 months (excluding top management).
•	Tax Benefit: 5-year income-tax exemption for the Company on income from transferred undertakings.
•	Guarantees & Concessions: Remain operative in favour of the Company.

4.	Legislative & Regulatory Adjustments

•	Repeal: Industrial Reconstruction Bank of India Act, 1984, repealed with specific savings.
•	Substitution in Laws: References to the Reconstruction Bank are substituted with the Company’s name across all applicable laws and regulations.
•	Approved Securities: Shares, bonds, and debentures of the Company are deemed approved securities under relevant Acts.
•	Bankers' Books Evidence Act, 1891: Applies to the Company’s books, facilitating the admissibility of its records as evidence.

• Structural Economic Reforms and Corporate Flexibility:

o Prior to 1997, the Industrial Reconstruction Bank of India (IRBI) functioned as a statutory corporation established under the 1984 Act to aid in the reconstruction and rehabilitation of industrial concerns.

title: The Departmentalisation of Union Accounts (Transfer of Personnel) Act, 1976

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of the Departmentalisation of Union Accounts (Transfer of Personnel) Act, 1976
Objective
The Departmentalisation of Union Accounts (Transfer of Personnel) Act, 1976 was enacted to provide for the transfer of officers and employees of the Indian Audit and Accounts Department to Ministries, Departments, and offices of the Central Government. Its objective was to facilitate the departmentalisation of Union Government accounts, enabling Ministries and Departments to independently compile and maintain their accounts, thereby improving financial administration and efficiency. 
Key Provisions
•	Transfer of Personnel: Authorises the Central Government to transfer officers and employees of the Indian Audit and Accounts Department to Ministries, Departments, or offices of the Central Government when accounting functions are departmentalised. 
•	Protection of Service Conditions: Ensures that transferred personnel retain their pay, seniority, pension, leave, and other service benefits after transfer. 
•	Departmentalisation of Union Accounts: Facilitates the transfer of the responsibility for compiling Union Government accounts from the Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG) to the concerned Ministries and Departments. 
•	Transfer Committee: Provides for the constitution of a Committee to advise the Central Government on matters relating to the transfer of personnel. 
•	Retrospective Commencement: Deems the Act to have come into force on 1 March 1976, ensuring continuity in the departmentalisation process. 
•	Repeal and Saving: Repeals the Departmentalisation of Union Accounts (Transfer of Personnel) Ordinance, 1976, while preserving actions already taken under the Ordinance.

Key Provisions
Establishment & Structure
1.	Family Courts Establishment: - Mandatory in areas with over 1 million population.
•	Established by State Governments in other areas as needed, with High Court consultation.
•	Judges appointed by State Governments with High Court concurrence, prioritizing women and those with at least 7 years of judicial or legal experience.
Jurisdiction
2.	Civil & Criminal Jurisdiction:
•	Civil: Suits under various family laws.
•	Criminal: Maintenance cases under the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973.
•	Exclusive: No other court can hear specified family matters in areas with a Family Court.
Procedure
3.	Conciliation First: - Mandatory attempt at settlement before proceeding.
•	Adjournments for conciliation efforts.
4.	Procedure Highlights: - Generally follows civil and criminal procedure codes with modifications.
•	In camera proceedings.
•	Expert assistance for welfare and medical issues.
•	Limited legal representation; court can appoint amicus curiae.
•	Flexible rules for evidence, judgment, and execution.
Miscellaneous
5.	Overriding Clause: - This Act takes precedence over conflicting laws.
6.	Rule Making: - High Court: Procedural rules within its jurisdiction.
•	Central & State Governments: Various aspects including judge qualifications and service conditions.

THE FAMILY COURTS ACT, 1984
ACT NO. 66 OF 1984

[14th September, 1984.]

An Act to provide for the establishment of Family Courts with a view to promote conciliation in, and secure speedy settlement of, disputes relating to marriage and family affairs and for matters connected therewith.
BE it enacted by Parliament in the Thirty-fifth Year of the Republic of India as follows:--
meta.dc.identifier.reference_sites: Ministry Of Law and Justice  https://www.lawmin.gov.in/
meta.dc.legislation.history:
Legislative History:

The Family Courts Act, 1984

Act Title - The Family Courts Act, 1984

Act Number/Year - Act No. 66 of 1984

Act ID (India Code) - 198466

Presidential Assent Date - September 14, 1984

Enforcement Date- It shall come into force on such date as the Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, appoint, and different dates may be appointed for different States.

Nodal Ministry - Ministry of Law and Justice

Precedent & Historical Rationale

1. Protracted Litigation and Breakdown of Family Systems:

o Prior to 1984, disputes relating to marriage, divorce, child custody, maintenance, and family property were adjudicated through regular civil courts. These traditional judicial forums were characterized by adversarial procedures, long delays, heavy backlogs, and rigid technical rules of evidence.

o Prominent women's organizations, social reformers, and the Law Commission of India (in its 59th Report) strongly recommended the creation of specialized forums that would prioritize conciliation, settlement, and a humanistic approach over formal litigation for family matters.

2. Establishment of Specialized Conciliation-Oriented Tribunals:

o The legislative intent centered on establishing specialized Family Courts to promote conciliation and secure swift, amicable settlements of disputes relating to marriage and family affairs.

o Key structural reforms introduced by the Act included mandatory pre-litigation/pretrial conciliation efforts, simplified procedural rules, exclusion of legal practitioners as a matter of right (unless permitted by the court), and the association of social welfare experts and counselors to preserve family harmony and protect the welfare of children.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

• Formulation: Drafted by the Ministry of Law and Justice to fulfill constitutional obligations regarding gender justice and reform the administration of justice in family law matters.

• Parliamentary Passage: Introduced, deliberated, and passed by both Houses of Parliament (Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha) during the monsoon session of 1984.

• Presidential Assent: Received Presidential Assent on September 14, 1984.

• Enforcement: Enforced on September 14, 1984.

• Source: Official Records of Parliament, India Code, and Ministry of Law and Justice (Department of Legal Affairs).

title: The Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006, 
Key Provisions
1. Procedural Rights and Penalties
•	Goods of Greater Value: Cannot be made under a specific section without the appellant having a chance to make a representation and, if desired, be heard in defense.
•	Penalties for contravening various sections, including imprisonment up to 3 years and/or a fine up to ₹5,000 for some offences, and stricter penalties for others (imprisonment not less than 6 months but may extend to 3 years and a fine not less than ₹2,000).
•	Section 58 (implied, not fully provided): Suggests penalties for unspecified contraventions, implying a broad enforcement net.
•	Only specific authorities (Designated Officer, Food Safety Officer, or authorised voluntary organisation representatives) can initiate legal proceedings.
•	Companies and their responsible officers can be held liable, with defenses for proving lack of knowledge or due diligence.
2. Regulatory and Protective Provisions
•	Protection of Action Taken in Good Faith: Immunity for the Government and specified officers/organisations for actions taken in good faith.
•	This Act works in addition to, not in derogation of, other food safety standards acts.
•	Power to Make Rules : Central Government's power to make rules, with parliamentary oversight.
3. Enforcement and General Principles
•	Authorities Responsible for Enforcement (Section 29): Outlines the roles of the Food Authority, State Food Safety Authorities, and Food Safety Officers.
•	Licensing and Registration (Section 31): Mandatory licensing for food businesses, with exemptions for petty operators who must register.
•	General Principles (Section 18): Emphasizes risk management, consumer protection, and transparency in food safety administration.

THE FOOD SAFETY AND STANDARDS ACT, 2006
ACT NO. 34 OF 2006

[23rd August, 2006.]

An Act to consolidate the laws relating to food and to establish the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India for laying down science based standards for articles of food and to regulate their manufacture, storage, distribution, sale and import, to ensure availability of safe and wholesome food for human consumption and for matters connected therewith or incidental thereto.
BE it enacted by Parliament in the Fifty-seventh Year of the Republic of India as follows:--

meta.dc.legislation.history:
Legislative History:

The Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006

Short Title The Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006

Act Number / Year Act No. 34 of 2006

Act ID (India Code) 200634

Presidential Assent Date August 23, 2006

Enforcement Date Initial provisions commenced on 15th October 2007 with full operational implementation effective 2nd November 2021.

Nodal Ministry Ministry of Health and Family Welfare

Precedent & Statutory Rationale

1. Consolidation of Fragmented Legal Frameworks:

o Prior to 2006, food safety management in India was governed by a multiplicity of independent, overlapping central statutes and control orders such as the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954, the Fruit Products Order, 1955, the Meat Food Products Order, 1973, and the Edible Oils Packaging (Regulation) Order, 1998. These laws were administered by various ministries, resulting in jurisdictional friction, compliance inconsistencies, and obsolete standards.

2. Transition to Science-Based Regulation:

o The legislation was enacted to create a single, unified, science-based regulatory framework aligned with international standards (such as Codex Alimentarius) to ensure public health safety, streamline food business operations, and regulate manufacturing, storage, distribution, sale, and import.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

• Formulation: Prepared by the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare to overhaul the country's food safety architecture and eliminate multi-agency overlaps.

• Parliamentary Passage: Tabled, debated, and passed by both Houses of Parliament during the mid-2006 session.

• Presidential Assent: Received formal Presidential Assent on August 23, 2006, entering the statute book as Act No. 34 of 2006.

• Enforcement: Initial provisions commenced on 15th October 2007 with full operational implementation effective 2nd November 2021.

• Source: Official Records of Parliament, India Code, and Ministry of Health and Family Welfare

Summary of the Disaster Management Act, 2005
Key Provisions
1.	National Disaster Management Authority (NDA):
•	National oversight, policy formulation, National Plan approval.
•	Enhancement: Regular review and update of National Plan to incorporate new disaster management techniques.
2.	State Disaster Management Authorities (SDMAs):
•	State-level coordination, State Plan preparation.
•	Enhancement: Mandatory annual drills with local authorities to test response readiness.
3.	District Disaster Management Authorities (DDMAs):
•	District-level implementation, District Plan preparation.
•	Enhancement: Community-level awareness and training programs at least twice a year.
4.	National Executive Committee (NEC):
•	Assists NDA, coordinates national response, implements policies.
•	Enhancement: Quarterly review meetings to assess preparedness across states.
5.	National Crisis Management Committee (NCMC): Handles major, nationally impactful disasters.
•	Enhancement: Advanced simulation training for crisis scenarios.
6.	High Level Committee: - Provides financial assistance for disasters and mitigation needs.
•	Enhancement: Allocation of a dedicated fund for innovative disaster mitigation technologies.
7. Core Responsibilities and Powers with Preparedness Focus
•	National policy formulation with emphasis on proactive measures.
•	Resource allocation (funds, personnel, military) for enhanced readiness.
•	Coordinates disaster management nationally with a focus on inter-state drills.
•	Monitors and evaluates preparedness and response through regular audits.
•	Issues directives for capacity building in Ministries/Departments and States. 
•	Implementation of District Plans with community engagement strategies.

meta.dc.legislation.history:
Legislative History:

The Disaster Management Act, 2005

Short Title The Disaster Management Act, 2005

Act Number / Year Act No. 53 of 2005

Act ID (India Code) 200553

Presidential Assent Date December 23, 2005

Enforcement Phased enforcement: Initial provisions commenced on July 28, 2006, with subsequent chapters and sections brought into force across multiple phases up to 2011.

Nodal Ministry Ministry of Home Affairs

Precedent & Statutory Rationale

1. Shift from Reactive Relief to Proactive Mitigation:

o Prior to 2005, disaster management in India was largely reactive, ad-hoc, and relief-centric, coordinated primarily through administrative manuals and the erstwhile National Contingency Action Plan without a dedicated statutory framework.

o The devastating impact of recurring catastrophic events—such as the 1999 Odisha Super Cyclone, the 2001 Bhuj Earthquake, and the 2004 Indian Ocean Tsunami—exposed severe systemic gaps in coordination, early warning distribution, and institutional preparedness.

2. Establishment of a Multi-Tiered Institutional Architecture:

o The legislation was enacted to create a holistic, institutionalized mechanism spanning national, state, and district levels, emphasizing prevention, mitigation, capacity building, and rapid response.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

• Formulation: Drafted by the Ministry of Home Affairs following extensive reviews of national disaster vulnerability profiles and international frameworks.

• Parliamentary Passage:

o Introduced in the Rajya Sabha by Home Minister Shivraj Patil on May 11, 2005.

o Reviewed by the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee (submitting its report on August 25, 2005).

o Passed by the Rajya Sabha on November 28, 2005, and by the Lok Sabha on December 12, 2005.

• Presidential Assent: Presidential Assent on December 23, 2005.

• Enforcement: Initial provisions commenced on July 28, 2006, with subsequent chapters and sections brought into force across multiple phases up to 2011.

• Source: Official Records of Parliament, India Code, and Ministry of Home Affairs

•	Powers: Includes conducting research, awarding degrees (including honorary), establishing infrastructure, and autonomous management of staff and finances.
4.	Admissions, Employment & Discipline
•	Admissions: Merit-based, inclusive policy.
•	Employment: Transparent recruitment processes with provisions for staff discipline and appeal mechanisms.
•	Student Discipline: Ordinances govern student conduct and disciplinary actions.
5.	Financial & Administrative Provisions
•	Status & Management: Not-for-profit, aiming for self-sufficiency.
•	Sponsored Schemes: Separate funding management for sponsored projects.

The Punjab Disturbed Areas Act, 1983

Act Title - The Punjab Disturbed Areas Act, 1983

Act Number/Year - 35 of 1983

Act ID (India Code) - 198335

Presidential Assent Date - December 8, 1983

Enforcement Date - October 7, 1983

Nodal Ministry - Ministry of Home Affairs

Precedent & Historical Rationale

1. Severe Internal Security Crisis in Punjab:

o During the early 1980s, the State of Punjab witnessed an unprecedented surge in violent extremist activities, separatist insurgencies, and terrorist violence, leading to a complete breakdown of civil administration and law and order.

o Standard legal provisions under the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, were inadequate for security forces to effectively contain, deter, and combat the heavily armed militant networks operating across the state.

2. Special Statutory Powers for Security Forces:

o The legislative intent centered on empowering the Governor of Punjab or the Central Government to officially declare the whole or any part of the State of Punjab as a "disturbed area."

o This designation vested police officers (and later extended to armed forces deployed in aid of civil power) with extraordinary legal authority, including the power to fire upon or use force against persons acting in contravention of law, and to conduct searches and arrests without warrants to restore public safety and sovereignty.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

• Formulation: Drafted by the Ministry of Home Affairs as an urgent counter-terrorism legislative instrument alongside parallel ordinances and acts for Chandigarh to provide uniform legal backing to security operations in the region.

• Parliamentary Passage: Initially promulgated as an ordinance, it was introduced, debated, and passed by both Houses of Parliament (Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha) during the autumn session of 1983.

• Presidential Assent: Received Presidential Assent on October 6, 1983.

• Enforcement: Enforced on October 7, 1983.

• Source: Official Records of Parliament, India Code, and Ministry of Home Affairs

meta.dc.legislation.history:
Legislative History:

The Central Educational Institutions (Reservation in Teachers Cadre) Act, 2019

● Act Title - The Central Educational Institutions (Reservation in Teachers' Cadre) Act, 2019

● Act Number / Year - 10 of 2019

● Act ID (India Code) - 201910

● Assent Date - July 9, 2019

● Enforcement Date - March 7, 2019

● Nodal Ministry - Ministry of Education

Precedent & Historical Rationale

● The Department-Wise 13-Point Roster Controversy (Vivekanand Tiwari Case) - In April 2017, the High Court of Judicature at Allahabad in Vivekanand Tiwari v. Union of India quashed the University Grants Commission's (UGC) policy of treating a university/institution as a single "unit" (University-wise 200-point roster) for applying reservations in teaching faculty, directing instead that reservations be applied "department-wise/subject-wise" (13-point roster). Following the Supreme Court's dismissal of the Union Government's Special Leave Petition and Review Petitions upholding the High Court's ruling in early 2019, the implementation of the 13-point roster caused a near-total collapse in the representation of Scheduled Castes (SC), Scheduled Tribes (ST), and Other Backward Classes (OBC) because smaller academic departments lacked the requisite threshold number of posts to trigger reserved recruitment slots.

● Statutory Restoration of the Institution-Wise 200-Point Roster and EWS Inclusion - Formulated to provide for the reservation of posts in appointments by direct recruitment of persons belonging to SCs, STs, and Socially and Educationally Backward Classes (SEBCs/OBCs), as well as Economically Weaker Sections (EWS), to teachers' cadre in Central Educational Institutions. The Act statutorily defined an entire "Central Educational Institution" as a single unit rather than treating individual departments or subjects as separate units, mandating the restoration of the 200-point roster system to ensure adequate, constitutional representation across professorial, associate professorial, and assistant professorial cadres while simultaneously incorporating the newly enacted 10% EWS quota (103rd Constitutional Amendment).

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

● Formulation & Promulgation of Ordinance - Drafted by the Ministry of Human Resource Development (now Ministry of Education); following nationwide academic unrest and the dismissal of review petitions, the Union Cabinet approved the measure and the President promulgated The Central Educational Institutions (Reservation in Teachers' Cadre) Ordinance, 2019 (Ordinance No. 13 of 2019) on March 7, 2019, to immediately halt non-compliant recruitments.

● Parliamentary Passage - Introduced as a replacement statutory bill, The Central Educational Institutions (Reservation in Teachers' Cadre) Bill, 2019 (Bill No. 126 of 2019), by Human Resource Development Minister Ramesh Pokhriyal 'Nishank' in the 17th Lok Sabha on June 27, 2019; debated and passed by the Lok Sabha on July 1, 2019, and passed by the Rajya Sabha on July 3, 2019.

● President's Assent - Received the assent of the President of India (Ram Nath Kovind) on July 9, 2019, and was published in the Gazette of India on July 10, 2019.

● Enforcement - Enforced on March 7, 2019.

Sources - Parliamentary Debates (Lok Sabha & Rajya Sabha), The Gazette of India, India Code, and Ministry of Education.

Establishes the university by upgrading the Institute of Rural Management Anand, aiming to provide technical and management education in the co-operative sector, promote co-operative research, and strengthen India's co-operative movement.
Key Provisions
1.	Establishment: 
- Upgrades Institute of Rural Management Anand to Tribhuvan Sahkari University.
•	Headquarters in Anand, Gujarat, with potential national and international campuses (subject to Central Government approval).
2.	Objects of the University: - 
Train manpower for the co-operative sector.
•	Offer education/training for co-operative society personnel.
•	Standardize co-operative education and research.
•	Establish centers of excellence in co-operative education, research, and consultancy.
•	Foster innovation, entrepreneurship, and global partnerships in the sector.
3.	Powers and Functions:
 - Design and conduct co-operation-focused academic/training programs.
•	Award degrees, diplomas, and certificates.
•	Establish outlying campuses, incubation centers, and skill development hubs.
•	Collaborate globally with universities and institutions.
•	Provide advisory services to the Government on co-operative sector matters.

4.	Governance: - 
Chancellor: Appointed by the Central Government for a 5-year term or until 70 years of age.
•	Vice-Chancellor, Registrar, Finance Officer, and other officers appointed per Statutes.
•	Governing Board, Executive Council, Academic and Research Council, etc., for management.
5.	Employee & Student Provisions:
•	Seamless transfer of Institute of Rural Management Anand employees.
•	Protection of post-retirement benefits.

6.	Central Government Oversight:
 - Review, inspection, and directive powers.
•	Authority to annul non-compliant proceedings.
7.	Financial & Asset Provisions:
•	Inheritance of Institute of Rural Management Anand’s assets.
•	Power to acquire, manage property, and borrow (with Central Government approval).

Summary of The Manipur (Hill Areas) District Councils Act, 1971
Purpose: To provide for the establishment of District Councils in the Hill Areas of Manipur, ensuring autonomous governance and development.
Key Components
1.	Constitution of District Councils
•	Autonomous Districts: Hill Areas divided into autonomous districts by the State Government.
•	Composition:
•	Elected members (maximum 18 seats).
•	Nominated members (up to 2) by the State Government.
•	Elections & Tenure:
•	Elections conducted under state election rules.

2.	Functions of District Councils
•	Infrastructure development (roads, bridges, schools, health facilities).
•	Market and fair management.
•	Water supply and public health oversight.
•	Environmental conservation and regulation of land use practices.
•	Additional responsibilities as delegated by the State Government.
3.	Financial Provisions
•	Taxation Powers: Authority to levy taxes on professions, trades, and certain activities.
•	Fee Collection: For services provided by the Council.
•	Procedure for Imposing Taxes: Includes public consultation and State Government approval.
•	Recovery and Appeals: Taxes recoverable as public dues, with a defined appeal process to a Magistrate or higher authority, whose order is final.
4.	Governance and Administration
•	State Government's Role: Oversight, including division of Hill Areas, nomination of members, and approval of taxes.

Key Legislative Metadata

Precedent & Statutory Rationale

1. Safeguarding Tribal Autonomy and Local Governance:

o Prior to its elevation as a full-fledged state under the North-Eastern Areas (Reorganisation) Act, 1971, Manipur was administered as a Union territory. While the valley region of Manipur possessed a unified administrative structure, the distinct tribal communities inhabiting the surrounding hill areas required specific institutional mechanisms to protect their cultural identity, land rights, customs, and socio-economic development.

o To fulfill these aspirations and fulfill constitutional commitments toward decentralized local self-governance for Scheduled Tribes, Parliament enacted the Manipur (Hill Areas) District Councils Act in December 1971.

2. Establishment of Autonomous District Councils (ADCs):

o The 1971 Act provided for the establishment of Autonomous District Councils across the hill districts of Manipur (such as Ukhrul, Sadar Hills, Churachandpur, Tamenglong, Senapati, and Chandel).

o It instituted a democratic framework comprising elected representatives from the tribal populations, vested the councils with statutory powers over local administration, agriculture, public health, sanitation, minor public works, and traditional customs, and established mechanisms to advise the state government on matters affecting tribal life and development.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

• Formulation: Drafted and piloted by the Ministry of Home Affairs as part of a comprehensive legislative package to reorganize the northeastern region and protect tribal autonomy.

• Parliamentary Passage: Tabled, debated, and passed by both Houses of Parliament, receiving Presidential Assent on December 26, 1971.

• Enforcement: Enforced on December 26, 1971.

Legislative History:

The Prohibition of Electronic Cigarettes (Production, Manufacture, Import, Export, Transport, Sale, Distribution, Storage and Advertisement) Act, 2019

Short Title - The Prohibition of Electronic Cigarettes (Production, Manufacture, Import, Export, Transport, Sale, Distribution, Storage and Advertisement) Act, 2019

Act Number / Year - Act No. 42 of 2019

Act ID (India Code) - 201942

Presidential Assent / Enactment Date - December 5, 2019

Enforcement Date - January 10, 2020

Nodal Ministry - Ministry of Health and Family Welfare

Precedent & Statutory Rationale

1. Safeguarding Public Health and Preventing Youth Addiction:

o Prior to 2019, the emergence and aggressive marketing of electronic cigarettes, vape pens, e-shisha, and other Electronic Nicotine Delivery Systems (ENDS) posed a severe, rapid public health threat, particularly targeting youth and adolescents by masking nicotine addiction as a safe alternative to traditional tobacco.

o Recognizing that these devices act as a gateway for nicotine addiction among non-smokers and youth, urgent preventive legislative intervention was deemed necessary to protect public health.

2. Absolute Ban Across the Supply and Distribution Chain:

o The Act was formulated to prohibit the production, manufacture, import, export, transport, sale, distribution, storage, and advertisement of electronic cigarettes in the interest of public health.

o It establishes strict penal provisions, including imprisonment and hefty financial penalties for violations relating to storage, manufacture, and commercial distribution of e-cigarettes.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

• Formulation: Initially promulgated via the Prohibition of Electronic Cigarettes Ordinance in September 2019 before being introduced and passed as a permanent statutory enactment by Parliament.

title: The Comptroller Auditor-General's (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act, 1971

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of the Comptroller Auditor-General s (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act, 1971
Purpose
•	Defines the conditions of service for the Comptroller and Auditor-General (C&AG) of India.
•	Outlines the duties and powers of the C&AG, with a note on the State Government's role in rule-making.
Key Provisions
Conditions of Service
1.	Tenure and Retirement: - Serves for 6 years or until 65 years of age, whichever is earlier.
2.	Remuneration and Benefits: - Salary equivalent to a Supreme Court Judge.
•	Pension:
•	For previous government servants: Pension based on previous service with C&AG tenure counted.
•	For others: ₹15,000 per annum pension.
•	Eligibility for the General Provident Fund.
•	Benefits (travel, residence, etc.) akin to a Supreme Court Judge.
Duties
1.	Account Compilation and Submission: - Compiles Union and State accounts, unless exempted by the President/Governor.
•	Submits accounts to the President, Governors, and Administrators of Union Territories.
2.	Audit Responsibilities: - Audits expenditure from Consolidated Funds.
•	Verifies legal expenditure and compliance.
•	Audits transactions, trading accounts, and substantially financed bodies.
3.	Support and Oversight: - Provides financial information and assistance to the government.
•	Audits Government companies, corporations, and specified authorities.
Powers
1.	Operational Authority: - Inspects accounts offices.
•	Requests and examines documents.
•	Interrogates personnel for audit purposes.
2.	Regulatory Powers: - Delegates audit duties.
•	Contributes to rule-making for audit processes, in conjunction with State Governments where applicable.
Miscellaneous
1.	Legislative Impact: - Repeals the 1953 Act.
•	Addresses doubts on the cessation of the 1936 Government of India Order.
2.	Amendments: - Subject to amendments (e.g., 1976, 1984, 1987, 1994) that refine duties, powers, and service conditions.
Amending Acts (Implicit in Context)
•	1976, 1984, 1987, 1994 Acts: Modify the C&AG's duties, powers, and service terms to enhance audit efficacy and align with governance needs.

Key Legislative Metadata

Legislative Stage / Attribute Official Details

Short Title The Comptroller and Auditor-General's (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act, 1971

Act Number / Year Act No. 56 of 1971

Act ID (India Code) 197156

Presidential Assent / Enactment Date December 15, 1971

Official Gazette Publication December 1971

Enforcement Date January 1, 1972

Administrative Nodal Ministry Ministry of Finance

Precedent & Statutory Rationale

1. Fulfillment of Constitutional Mandate under Article 149:

o While Articles 148 to 151 of the Constitution of India established the high-office of the Comptroller and Auditor-General (CAG) as an independent guardian of the public purse, Article 149 expressly mandated that the CAG shall perform such duties and exercise such powers in relation to the accounts of the Union, States, and other bodies as may be prescribed by or under law made by Parliament.

o Prior to 1971, the office operated largely under transitional adaptations of colonial administrative orders. Parliament enacted this comprehensive legislation to formally, definitively, and statutorily crystallize the tenure, salary, rights, duties, and broad auditing powers of India's supreme audit institution.

2. Core Statutory Powers and Scope of Authority:

o Tenure and Service Conditions: Fixed the CAG's term at 6 years or until attaining the age of 65 years (whichever is earlier), guaranteeing security of tenure equivalent to a Supreme Court Judge.

o Compiling and Auditing Accounts: Outlined clear statutory parameters for auditing expenditure, transactions, and receipts payable to the Consolidated Fund of India and States, alongside overseeing government companies, corporations, and bodies substantially financed by public revenues.

o Access to Information: Empowered the CAG to inspect any office, demand records, books, papers, and documents, and frame independent auditing standards to enforce financial accountability across executive machineries.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

• Formulation: Drafted and piloted by the Ministry of Finance to operationalize full parliamentary oversight over public finances pursuant to constitutional requirements.

• Parliamentary Passage: Tabled, debated, and passed by both Houses of Parliament, receiving Presidential Assent on December 15, 1971.

• Enforcement: Enforced on January 1, 1972.

•	Protection for actions taken in good faith.

Precedent & Historical Rationale

●	Overcoming Branch-Specific Disciplinary Barriers: Overcomes jurisdictional limitations under individual service statutes (The Army Act, 1950; The Navy Act, 1957; The Air Force Act, 1950) by empowering Commander-in-Chiefs or Officers-in-Command of Inter-Services Organisations to exercise administrative and disciplinary authority over personnel regardless of their parent service.
●	Enabler for Jointness and Integrated Theatre Commands: Serves as a foundational legislative stepping stone for military integration, establishing unified command-and-control structures without altering the distinct service conditions, rank structures, or appeal mechanisms of the respective Armed Forces branches.
 
Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

●	Formulation: Introduced by the Union Minister of Defence, Shri Rajnath Singh, to streamline inter-services administrative efficiency, prevent procedural delays in tri-services establishments, and support the operationalization of integrated theatre commands.
●	Parliamentary Passage: Introduced in the Lok Sabha on March 15, 2023; passed by the Lok Sabha on August 4, 2023; and passed by the Rajya Sabha on August 8, 2023.
●	Presidential Assent: Received the assent of the President of India on August 15, 2023.
●	Enforcement: Enforced on May 10, 2024  .
