meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971
The Contempt of Courts Act, 1971 was enacted to define and limit the powers of courts in punishing for contempt, regulate the procedure for contempt proceedings, and protect the authority and dignity of the judiciary. The Act classifies contempt into civil contempt and criminal contempt, prescribes the circumstances in which punishment may be imposed, and recognizes certain defenses and exceptions, including truth as a valid defense in specified cases. The Act applies throughout India and seeks to balance the need to maintain the authority of courts with the fundamental right to freedom of speech and expression.
Objective
The main objectives of the Act are to:
•	Maintain the authority, dignity, and independence of the judiciary. 
•	Ensure the proper and uninterrupted administration of justice. 
•	Define the law relating to civil and criminal contempt. 
•	Lay down a uniform procedure for contempt proceedings. 
•	Prevent acts that obstruct, interfere with, or undermine the judicial process while safeguarding fair criticism and free expression. 
Key Provisions
•	Definition of Contempt: Defines civil contempt as wilful disobedience of any judgment, decree, direction, order, writ, or other process of a court, or wilful breach of an undertaking given to a court. Defines criminal contempt as publication or acts that scandalize or lower the authority of the court, prejudice or interfere with judicial proceedings, or obstruct the administration of justice. 
•	Punishment for Contempt: Provides for punishment with simple imprisonment for up to six months, or a fine up to ₹2,000, or both. The court may discharge the contemnor or remit the punishment upon a satisfactory apology. 
•	Innocent Publication: Protects innocent publication and distribution of material relating to judicial proceedings where the publisher had no reasonable grounds to believe that proceedings were pending. 
•	Fair and Accurate Reporting: Permits fair and accurate reporting of judicial proceedings and fair criticism of judicial acts made in good faith. 
•	Truth as a Defence: Allows truth as a valid defence if the court is satisfied that it is in the public interest and the request for invoking the defence is made bona fide. 
•	Limitation Period: Prescribes that no court shall initiate contempt proceedings after the expiry of one year from the date on which the alleged contempt is committed. 
•	Jurisdiction of Higher Courts: Recognizes the powers of the Supreme Court and High Courts to punish for contempt of themselves and, in the case of High Courts, contempt of subordinate courts. 
•	Procedure for Cognizance: Provides that criminal contempt may be initiated by the court on its own motion or on a motion made by the Advocate General or with the Advocate General's consent in specified cases

Legislative History: The Contempt of Courts Act, 1971

Source: India Code (indiacode.gov.in) and Ministry of Law and Justice Official Records

Key Legislative Metadata

Legislative Stage / Attribute Official Details

Short Title The Contempt of Courts Act, 1971

Act Number / Year Act No. 70 of 1971

Act ID (India Code) 197170

Presidential Assent / Enactment Date December 24, 1971

Official Gazette Publication December 1971

Enforcement Date December 24, 1971

Administrative Nodal Ministry Ministry of Law and Justice

Precedent & Statutory Rationale

1. Codifying and Balancing Contempt Jurisprudence:

o Prior to 1971, the law relating to contempt of courts was governed by the Contempt of Courts Act, 1952, supplemented by the inherent powers of the Supreme Court (under Article 129) and High Courts (under Article 215) as courts of record. However, ambiguities remained regarding the exact boundaries of what constituted contempt, especially concerning freedom of speech and expression under Article 19(1)(a).

o To address these ambiguities, the Government of India appointed a committee chaired by H.N. Sanyal (Additional Solicitor General) in 1963. The Sanyal Committee's exhaustive report recommended clearly defining and categorizing contempt, setting procedural limitations, and protecting fair criticism of judicial acts, which formed the basis of the 1971 enactment.

2. Core Structural Innovations of the 1971 Act:

o Categorization of Contempt: Formally distinguished between Civil Contempt (willful disobedience of a court order, judgment, or decree) and Criminal Contempt (publications or acts that scandalize, lower the authority of, prejudice, or interfere with the due course of any judicial proceeding).

o Statutory Defenses and Safe Harbors: Introduced crucial safeguards for the press and public, establishing that innocent publication, fair and accurate reporting of judicial proceedings, and fair criticism of a judicial act do not amount to contempt.

o Limitations and Penalties: Imposed a strict limitation period of one year from the date on which the contempt is alleged to have been committed for courts to initiate proceedings, and standardized penalties (imprisonment up to six months, a fine up to two thousand rupees, or both), while providing provisions for the apology of the contemnor to be accepted.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

• Formulation: Drafted and piloted by the Ministry of Law based on the Sanyal Committee recommendations and extensive parliamentary consultations to balance judicial independence with democratic freedoms.

• Parliamentary Passage: Tabled, debated, and passed by both Houses of Parliament, receiving Presidential Assent on December 24, 1971.

• Enforcement: Enforced on December 24, 1971.

title: The Aadhaar (Targeted Delivery of Financial and Other Subsidies, Benefits and Services) Act, 2016.

meta.dc.description.abstract:
Summary of the Aadhaar Act, 2016
Purpose
•	To provide for targeted delivery of subsidies, benefits, and services by assigning unique identity numbers to residents in India, with recent updates focusing on enhanced security, privacy, and verification processes.
Key Definitions & Updates
•	Aadhaar Number: Unique ID issued to an individual.
•	Authentication: Process of verifying an individual's Aadhaar number, with offline verification now emphasized for privacy.
•	Central Identities Data Repository (CIDR): Central database, with strengthened security measures implied through recent amendments.
•	"Specified Transaction": Introduced for enhanced due diligence, including high-value cash transactions, foreign exchange, and high-risk money laundering scenarios.
Structure and Key Provisions
1.	Authentication and Verification Methods
•	Clause (a): Aadhaar authentication with privacy safeguards.
•	Alternatives: Offline verification, passport, and other officially valid documents.
•	Voluntary Choice: Emphasized, with no service denial for lacking Aadhaar.
2.	Enhanced Due Diligence 
•	Pre-Transaction Verification: For specified high-risk or high-value transactions.
•	Additional Steps: Examining ownership, financial position, and transaction purpose.
•	Non-Compliance: Transaction prohibition if conditions not met.
3.	Record Maintenance and Confidentiality 
•	Transaction Records: Maintained for 5 years.
•	Client Information: Stored for 5 years after the relationship ends.
•	Confidentiality: Mandated, with exceptions for legal requirements.
4.	Access to Information and Enhanced Safeguards
•	Director's Access Rights: To records for the Act's purposes.
•	Additional Safeguards: At the Central Government's discretion for verification.
Notable Updates and Provisions
•	Strengthened Privacy Measures: No storage of core biometric information or Aadhaar number post-authentication/offline verification.
•	Specified Transactions: Enhanced scrutiny for high-value or suspicious transactions.
•	Voluntary Aadhaar Use: Reiterated, ensuring privacy and choice.

Legislative History:

The Aadhaar (Targeted Delivery of Financial and Other Subsidies, Benefits and Services) Act, 2016

Short Title - The Aadhaar (Targeted Delivery of Financial and Other Subsidies, Benefits and Services) Act, 2016

Act Number / Year - Act No. 18 of 2016

India Code Act ID - 201618

Introduced In - Parliament (Lok Sabha)

Official Gazette Publication - March 26, 2016

Enforcement Date - September 12, 2016

Nodal Ministry - Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY)

Precedent & Statutory Rationale

1. Transition from Executive Order to Statutory Backing:

o Prior to 2016, the UIDAI functioned purely as an attached office under the administrative control of the Planning Commission (later NITI Aayog) via an executive notification. The absence of a governing parliamentary statute created legal ambiguities regarding data collection, privacy safeguards, and the mandatory linkage of identity credentials for public welfare schemes.

2. Efficiency, Transparency, and Leakage Prevention in Welfare Delivery:

o Grounded in national governance goals to plug structural leakages in state-sponsored welfare, the legislation was enacted to legally mandate the use of unique identity credentials for the targeted delivery of subsidies, benefits, and services funded directly from the Consolidated Fund of India.

Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment

• Formulation: Developed and piloted by the Union Government to provide a comprehensive legal framework for digital identification, authentication architecture, and data protection.

• Parliamentary Passage: Introduced in the Lok Sabha by Finance Minister Arun Jaitley on March 3, 2016. Because it was designated as a Money Bill under Article 110 of the Constitution—focusing on expenditures drawn from the Consolidated Fund of India—it bypassed the requirement of formal concurrence from the Rajya Sabha, ultimately securing parliamentary passage in March 2016.

• Presidential Assent: Received formal Presidential Assent on March 25, 2016, entering the statute book as Act No. 18 of 2016.
